0.title: The King Has Come
0.overview:
Matthew begins where the Old Testament ends — with promises. His opening genealogy is not a genealogy at all; it is a theology compressed into names. Abraham to David to the exile to Jesus: the whole arc of Israel’s story, told in three movements, arriving at the one name toward which every other name was pointing. Matthew’s first words are biblos geneseos — the book of origins, the book of genesis. A new creation has begun.

Matthew wrote for Jewish Christians, probably in Antioch, in the decades after the destruction of Jerusalem. His readers knew the Old Testament. They had grown up with the promises of a coming King from David’s line, a new Moses who would deliver God’s people, a suffering servant who would bear the sins of many, a son of man who would receive an everlasting dominion. Matthew’s argument, sustained across twenty-eight chapters, is that all of these promises find their yes in Jesus of Nazareth (2 Cor. 1:20). The fulfillment formula — to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet — appears again and again like a refrain, stitching the Old Testament to the New until you cannot see the seam.

The great theme of Matthew is the kingdom of heaven. Where Mark asks who this man is, and Luke traces the universal reach of grace, Matthew announces the arrival of a reign. Heaven’s rule has broken into earth’s disorder in the person of the King. He teaches with authority (not as the scribes). He heals with a word. He calms the sea. He feeds the multitude. He raises the dead. And then he goes to the cross not as a victim of circumstances but as the King who lays down his life to ransom many (20:28) — the supreme act of royal authority disguised as utter weakness.

Matthew’s Jesus is the new Moses, but greater. Moses gave the law from Sinai; Jesus gives the new law from the mountain (chapters 5–7). Moses delivered Israel through the Red Sea; Jesus passes through death and comes out the other side. Moses saw the promised land from a distance and died; Jesus enters it, conquers it, and invites all nations to follow him in. “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them” (5:17). In Jesus, the Old Testament does not end — it arrives.

The name given to him in chapter 1 is the key that unlocks the whole: Emmanuel — God with us. And the Gospel ends with the same promise, spoken now in resurrection glory: I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20). Matthew is bracketed by the presence of God. What began in a manger in Bethlehem does not end at a tomb in Jerusalem. It ends with a commission that will reach every tongue and tribe and nation — because the one who sends is the one to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given.

Read Matthew as someone meeting the King for the first time. Let the authority of his teaching arrest you. Let the tenderness of his healing move you. Let the cross unmake your comfortable religion. And let the resurrection send you — into all the world, making disciples, baptising, teaching. The Gospel of Matthew is not a story that ends; it is a commission that begins.

1.title: Emmanuel — God With Us
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. <sup>2</sup>Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, <sup>3</sup>and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, <sup>4</sup>and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, <sup>5</sup>and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, <sup>6</sup>and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, <sup>7</sup>and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, <sup>8</sup>and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, <sup>9</sup>and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, <sup>10</sup>and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, <sup>11</sup>and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. <sup>12</sup>And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, <sup>13</sup>and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, <sup>14</sup>and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, <sup>15</sup>and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, <sup>16</sup>and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. <sup>17</sup>So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations. <sup>18</sup>Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. <sup>19</sup>And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. <sup>20</sup>But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. <sup>21</sup>She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” <sup>22</sup>All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: <sup>23</sup>“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). <sup>24</sup>When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, <sup>25</sup>but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
1.overview:
Matthew opens not with a manger scene but with a list of names, and the list is the point. Every name is a promise kept: from Abraham, through whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), to David, whose throne would endure for ever (2 Samuel 7:16), through the exile and back, to the name Jesus. God kept his word through every generation, including the dark ones.

Four women appear, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and “the wife of Uriah”, each linked with scandal or with foreign birth. From the first page Matthew signals that this King comes for sinners and for the nations.

Then the birth, and its two names. Jesus: he will save his people from their sins (v. 21). Immanuel: God with us (v. 23). Isaiah’s sign to Ahaz (Isaiah 7:14) reaches its goal in the Son of God taking our flesh, becoming man without ceasing to be God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew opens with a list of names, and in doing so roots the gospel in real history. The genealogy traces Jesus' legal descent through Joseph from Abraham, to whom God promised blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:3), and from David, to whom he promised an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Three groups of fourteen generations are a teaching structure rather than a complete record, and Matthew shortens the list to fit it. Four women appear, and dark names too, Ahaz, Manasseh and the cursed Jechoniah, and then centuries of silence. Verse 16 breaks the pattern, announcing the virgin birth in the grammar before it is told in the story.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy presents Jesus as the Christ (the Anointed One), the Son of David (the royal heir) and the Son of Abraham (the heir of the promise). Its pattern of fourteens shows God ordering history toward this moment through faithfulness, failure, exile and return. Providence is not the absence of scandal; it is God steering all things to the end he has appointed.
verseByVerse.examples: Salvation is not a timeless idea but something God did in history, through a long chain of real people. His promises survived murder, adultery, exile and foreign rule to arrive at their fulfilment. The God who kept his word to Abraham keeps his word to you.

verseByVerse.quote: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew opens the New Testament with a family tree, and it is not a preface to the gospel but its first proclamation. In seventeen verses he shows that Jesus is the Christ, the King promised to David and the blessing promised to Abraham, carried through two thousand years of saints, scoundrels, foreigners, exiles and forgotten men without once being dropped. Then he tells how the Son of God entered that family: conceived by the Holy Spirit in the virgin Mary, named Jesus because he will save his people from their sins, and called Immanuel, God with us. The chapter begins with a list of the dead and ends with the living God in a cradle.

The setting. Matthew was one of the Twelve, a former tax collector (9:9). He writes chiefly for Jewish believers, probably in the AD 60s, to show that Jesus is the Messiah the Old Testament promised. He quotes the Old Testament more than any other Gospel writer, and his Gospel stands first in the New Testament because it is the bridge from the Old.

The book of the genealogy. Matthew’s first two words in Greek are biblos geneseōs, the book of the genesis, and a Jewish reader with the Greek Old Testament in his ear would have caught the echo at once. The same phrase stands over the generations of the heavens and the earth (Genesis 2:4) and over the generations of Adam (Genesis 5:1). Before a single event is narrated, Matthew has claimed that the story is starting again: something as great as creation is beginning, and it begins with a man.

Jesus Christ. “Jesus” is his personal name (its meaning comes in v. 21). “Christ” is not a surname but a title: the Greek form of Messiah, meaning anointed one. Kings, priests and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil for their office (1 Samuel 16:13), and the prophets promised a final Anointed One. Matthew’s first claim is that Jesus is that King. Every time you say “Jesus Christ” you confess that the carpenter from Nazareth is the one on whom the hopes of Israel rested.

The son of David. God promised David that one of his descendants would reign on his throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1). By the time of Jesus, Son of David was a title for the Messiah. Matthew uses it more than any other Gospel: blind men cry it out (9:27), crowds wonder whether this could be he (12:23), and Jerusalem shouts it as he rides in (21:9).

The son of Abraham. God promised Abraham that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). Jesus is the offspring through whom that blessing comes (Galatians 3:16). David comes first because Matthew’s main theme is Jesus as King; Abraham is there to show that the King is for the nations too, and the Gospel that opens with the son of Abraham ends with the command to make disciples of all nations (28:19).

Abraham … Isaac … Jacob … Judah. The genealogy begins with Abraham, the father of Israel, not Adam as Luke’s does (Luke 3:38). Matthew is tracing Jesus’ place in Israel. Judah is named because God promised that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10): the royal tribe.

Why a genealogy? Modern readers often skip it, and skipping it costs something. For Matthew’s first readers it was essential, for three reasons. First, it anchors Jesus in real history. Matthew counts forty-two generations, most of them checkable against the Old Testament records his readers knew, which is the literary equivalent of putting your address at the top of the page. He is not offering a timeless tale about the human condition; he is tying a man to named ancestors his readers could look up. Second, in Israel a genealogy was a legal document: it established a person’s right to land, to the priesthood, or to a throne. Matthew is not being sentimental about family history. He enters Jesus’ legal claim to David’s crown into the record in the first breath, because everything afterwards depends on it. Third, it shows that the story of Jesus did not begin in Bethlehem. It began two thousand years earlier, with God’s promise to Abraham, and every generation in between was carrying that promise forward.

Receipts, not a register. Read the names as receipts. Each one is a generation in which God did not abandon what he had said, including the long stretches of slavery, exile and faithlessness when the promise was carried by people who never saw it land. When a promise you lean on seems slow, perhaps that he will never leave you (Hebrews 13:5), set it beside this list: every name is a stretch in which it looked as though nothing was happening, and every name is proof that something was.

What does it actually mean for me that Jesus is the Christ? It means he is not only a teacher to admire but a King to whom you belong. If he is the Anointed One, then his word is law in your life, his promises are the ground of your hope, and his enemies, sin and death, are already on the losing side. In practice it means you bring your decisions to him rather than only your troubles, you read his words in this Gospel as commands and not suggestions, and you rest on the fact that the King has come to save, not to crush. Confessing “Jesus is the Christ” is the beginning of the Christian life (16:16), not an advanced doctrine for later.

For worship. Our God remembers. He spoke to a childless man under the stars and to a shepherd king, let whole centuries go by, and never forgot a word. The promise passed through faithful hands and filthy ones, through slavery and exile and silence, and when it arrived, it arrived as a Person: the Son of David who is David’s Lord, the Son of Abraham in whom every nation is blessed.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” marks Jesus as the promised king; “son of Abraham” as the one through whom the nations would be blessed.

parallels.desc: Luke’s genealogy, traced back to Adam
the promise of a son of David on the throne forever
all the families of the earth blessed in Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women in a genealogy. Jewish genealogies normally listed fathers only, and a woman’s name has appeared, and it is this woman. Matthew names five women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, the wife of Uriah, and Mary. The first four were foreigners or connected with foreigners, and each had a story involving scandal or irregularity. He had no obligation to mention any of them, and he puts the first in the third verse of the New Testament.

The story of Tamar (Genesis 38). Matthew expects the story to be known. Tamar married Judah’s eldest son Er, who was wicked, and the Lord put him to death. By the custom later written into the law (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), the next brother, Onan, was to give her a child to carry on his dead brother’s name; he refused, and he too died. Judah, afraid of the woman, sent Tamar back to her father’s house, promising her his youngest son Shelah when he grew up, and never kept the promise. She was left a childless widow with no standing and no future, waiting for a wedding her father-in-law had privately decided would never happen.

What she did. Years later, Tamar covered her face and sat by the road as a prostitute. Judah, now a widower, hired her, leaving his seal, cord and staff as a pledge. When word came that his daughter-in-law was pregnant by immorality, Judah ordered her burned, and she sent him his own seal, asking whose it was. His answer is the sentence on which the whole episode turns: she is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah (Genesis 38:26). She bore twins, Perez and Zerah.

Why Matthew names her. Judah, the royal tribe’s father, behaved disgracefully; Tamar, probably a Canaanite, took a desperate and sinful way to what was hers by right. If you were forging a pedigree for a king, you would strike her out. Matthew writes her in. That is hard news for the respectable, who quietly hope God chooses people like them because they are decent, and wonderful news for anyone who knows he is not. The line of the Messiah was never a reward for good behaviour; it was grace from the first generation.

Perez and Zerah. Perez means breach or breaking through, because he burst out ahead of his twin at birth (Genesis 38:29). The royal line runs through a boy named for pushing in where he was not expected. The line runs through him to David (Ruth 4:18–22).

The Lion from a broken house. Judah’s confession, she is more righteous than I, is the turning point of his life. A few chapters later the man who once sold his brother Joseph offers himself as a slave in place of his brother Benjamin, so that the boy may go home to his father (Genesis 44:33). From Judah came the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), who did what his ancestor only offered: he took the place of the guilty and bore what they had earned, so that they could go home to the Father.

Hezron … Nahshon … Salmon. The generations in Egypt and the wilderness. Nahshon was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7; 7:12). Through the centuries of slavery, the line of the King of kings was among the brickmakers.

Was Tamar right to do what she did? No, and yes, and the Bible lets both stand. Her method was sinful: she deceived and committed sexual sin, and Scripture never holds it up as a pattern. But her cause was just. She had been wronged and abandoned, and she was seeking the child and the name that the law and Judah’s own promise owed her. Judah’s verdict, that she was more righteous than he, does not call her sinless; it says his sin was greater. The lesson is not that the end justifies the means. It is that God can bring his good purpose through a tangle of wrongs on every side, without approving any of them, and that he sees the wronged widow nobody else is watching.
verseByVerse.note: Tamar is the first of four women Matthew includes before Mary, each with an irregular story.

parallels.desc: the line from Perez to Nahshon

verseByVerse.quote: and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab. Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho (Joshua 2:1), a Canaanite city under sentence of destruction. She hid two Israelite spies under the flax on her roof because she believed that the LORD was God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath, and she and her family were spared when the city fell (Joshua 2; 6:22–25). She is honoured for her faith (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). The Old Testament does not record her marriage to Salmon; Matthew does. Only four generations are listed from her to David, centuries later, but genealogies often skip generations (see v. 8), and Matthew clearly means the famous Rahab. The woman of the scarlet cord became a great-great-grandmother of King David.

Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth. Ruth was a Moabitess. The Moabites descended from Lot’s incest with his daughter (Genesis 19:36–37), and the law barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Yet Ruth, a widow, chose Israel’s God: your people shall be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16). Boaz, a kinsman-redeemer (a near relative with the right and duty to buy back a poor relative’s land, Leviticus 25:25), married her and redeemed her family’s land at his own cost, for a foreign widow who could never pay him back. Their son Obed was David’s grandfather. The woman the law kept at the door was carried over the threshold by a redeemer, and her great-grandson was the king.

Jesse the father of David the king. David is the only one in the genealogy called “king”. He is the turning point of the list (v. 17).

David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah. Matthew does not write Bathsheba’s name. He names her husband instead: Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner and one of David’s most loyal soldiers. David committed adultery with Bathsheba while Uriah was at war, then arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle to hide the pregnancy (2 Samuel 11). By naming Uriah, Matthew makes it impossible to read the line without saying the name of the man David had killed. Israel’s greatest king stands here as king, adulterer and murderer in one breath. Yet God gave David and Bathsheba Solomon, the heir, after David’s deep repentance (2 Samuel 12; Psalm 51).

David took, his Son gave. David saw, took and killed, and then he prayed, create in me a clean heart, O God (Psalm 51:10). He could ask for that clean heart but not give it, and every king after him proved it. So the genealogy is waiting for a Son of David who is unlike David at exactly this point. Where David took a poor man’s lamb, Jesus gives himself as the Lamb. Where David sent a loyal soldier to die in his place to cover his own sin, Jesus goes to die in the place of disloyal men to cover theirs. The line runs through David’s sin, and it ends at the one who bore it.

The four women together. Not the honoured mothers of Israel, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, but Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba: all foreigners or married to one, all with stories of scandal, real or suspected. His likely reasons: first, to show that the Messiah came for Gentiles as well as Jews; second, to show that God works through sinners and outsiders by grace; and third, to prepare for Mary, whose pregnancy also looked scandalous, though she was innocent (vv. 18–19).

Your own line. Most families have a name that is not mentioned, or a stretch nobody talks about: the affair, the child born outside a marriage, the drinking, the prison sentence, the parent who left. People carry that quietly and assume it has disqualified them. The Messiah’s own family tree reads like that, and God did not tidy it before he used it. He wrote it down.

What it does not mean. Not that sin does not matter. Matthew’s choice to name Uriah rather than Bathsheba seems meant to make us remember a murdered man. Grace that pretends nothing happened is not grace. Nor is it a criticism of the women: Rahab and Ruth are models of faith, and Bathsheba was more sinned against than sinning.

Did God approve of Rahab’s lie? Rahab told the king’s men the spies had gone, when they were on her roof (Joshua 2:4–5). Scripture praises her faith and her welcome of the spies (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25), not her lie. She was a new believer in a pagan city, acting in faith with the moral understanding she had, and God honoured the faith. Christians have long debated whether deception is ever right to protect innocent life from murderers, and sincere believers come down on different sides of that hard case; this commentary holds that deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids. What is clear is that Rahab is not a licence for ordinary lying; she is a picture of a sinner who turned to the true God when everything around her said not to.

Was Bathsheba to blame? The text puts the guilt on David. He saw, sent, took and then killed (2 Samuel 11:2–4, 15). He was the king, she was the wife of a soldier at the front, and it is very hard to refuse a king. The prophet Nathan’s parable makes her the poor man’s lamb, taken by the rich man (2 Samuel 12:1–4), and God’s rebuke falls on David alone. That is why the commentary calls her more sinned against than sinning. Abuse of power is never tolerated by God, even in his greatest king, and Bathsheba is honoured in the end as the mother of the heir.

On a Tuesday. Look round your church this Sunday for the Ruths: the foreigners, the newcomers, the people with a history. Learn a name and ask them home. Their kind are in his genealogy.
verseByVerse.note: Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and Ruth a Moabite — Gentiles in the royal line. “The wife of Uriah” is Bathsheba.

verseByVerse.quote: and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good and bad together. Some were faithful: Asa removed idols (1 Kings 15:11–14); Jehoshaphat sought the LORD (2 Chronicles 17:3–6). Some were wicked: Rehoboam’s foolishness split the kingdom; Joram murdered all his brothers to make the throne safe (2 Chronicles 21:4) and married into the idolatrous house of Ahab. Uzziah grew proud and was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Matthew writes them all in the same rhythm, with no verdict and not one adjective. What is being traced is not the quality of the men but the durability of the promise that passed through their hands, and the chain does not thicken at the good names or wear thin at the bad ones.

Three kings missing. Matthew writes that Joram was the father of Uzziah, but 1 Chronicles 3:11–12 lists Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah between them. Three generations have simply gone. This is not a slip. “Father of” in Hebrew and Greek can mean ancestor of, just as Jesus is called son of David a thousand years after David died. Genealogies were legal documents, often shortened to make a pattern easier to remember, and Matthew omits names to arrive at his three groups of fourteen (v. 17).

Why these three? Perhaps because they were descendants of Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, who married into David’s line, brought Baal worship with her and murdered the royal family (2 Kings 11:1). God had pronounced judgment on Ahab’s house (1 Kings 21:21–22). Matthew may be quietly letting that judgment show. We cannot be sure, and he does not say. Omitting names from a list does not remove the men from history; the line itself was unbroken. And see how close it came to being broken: when Athaliah killed the royal heirs, one baby, Joash, was hidden in the temple for six years (2 Kings 11:2–3). The whole promise to David lay all that time in one small boy, and God kept him.

Another child hidden from a killer. Athaliah slaughtered the royal children to keep her throne, and one son of David was hidden. Herod would slaughter the boys of Bethlehem to keep his, and the Son of David was carried away by night into Egypt (2:13–16). But the child hidden in Egypt was not hidden for ever. When his hour came he walked openly into Jerusalem and let wicked rulers take him, because he had come not to escape the sword of kings but to lay down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). Joash was saved from death. Jesus was saved for it.

Textual note: Asaph. The ESV reads “Asaph”, following the oldest manuscripts; the king was Asa. Later manuscripts and many translations read “Asa”. This commentary’s view: “Asaph” is probably original, either an alternative spelling of the king’s name current in the Greek-speaking world or a deliberate echo of Asaph the psalmist. Either way, the king meant is Asa, and nothing is amiss.

If the promise did not depend on them, does it matter how leaders live? Very much. God told David in advance that if his sons sinned he would discipline them with the rod of men (2 Samuel 7:14), and he did: Judah’s wicked kings brought ruin, war and finally exile on the people they ruled. What God promised was that the line would not be cut off, not that sin would be painless. The same holds for pastors, parents and elders today. Christ will build his church whatever we do (16:18), but a faithless leader still wounds real people and will answer for it. God’s faithfulness is a reason to serve humbly, never a reason to serve carelessly.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Asa for Asaph. Matthew’s list skips several kings between Joram and Uzziah; “father of” can mean ancestor.

verseByVerse.quote: and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz. One of the worst kings in Judah’s history. He burned his own son as an offering, following the despicable practices of the nations (2 Kings 16:3): child sacrifice, by a son of David, in Jerusalem. He stripped the temple to buy Assyrian protection and finally shut its doors (2 Chronicles 28:24). Yet Ahaz is the king to whom Isaiah spoke the promise Matthew will quote at the end of this chapter: the virgin shall conceive and bear a son (Isaiah 7:14). Ahaz trusted Assyria and would not look at the sign (see v. 23); the promise spoken over the worst of David’s sons is fulfilled in the best of them, and it came, as grace always comes, to people who had not asked for it.

Hezekiah. A great reforming king who trusted the LORD, destroyed idols, and saw Jerusalem miraculously delivered from the Assyrian army (2 Kings 18–19).

Manasseh. Hezekiah’s son, and the worst of all. He reigned fifty-five years, the longest reign in Judah, and filled them with idolatry, sorcery, the burning of his own sons and so much innocent blood that God declared he would wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish (2 Kings 21:1–16). His sins were the reason God gave for the exile (2 Kings 24:3–4).

Manasseh’s repentance. But 2 Chronicles 33:10–17 adds what Kings does not record. The Assyrians took Manasseh captive with hooks and bronze chains to Babylon. There, in distress, he humbled himself greatly before God and prayed, and God heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem. Manasseh spent his last years tearing out what he had spent decades building. The darkest name in the genealogy is one of Scripture’s strongest proofs that no one is beyond God’s mercy.

Amos … Josiah. Manasseh’s son Amon (the ESV reads “Amos”, following the oldest manuscripts, probably a variant spelling of the king’s name) was wicked and was murdered after two years. His son Josiah became king at eight and led the greatest reformation in Judah’s history, after the Book of the Law was rediscovered in the temple (2 Kings 22–23).

The lesson of the four. Ahaz the faithless, Hezekiah the faithful, Manasseh the monstrous and repentant, Josiah the reformer: the chain holds as well in the hand of Manasseh as in the hand of Josiah.

What it does not mean. Not that Manasseh’s sins had no consequences: the damage he did led to the exile, even after his repentance (2 Kings 23:26). God forgives, but sin often leaves wounds in history. Nor does it mean that repentance can be safely put off until the end of a wicked life.

Is it my fault that my child has turned from God, though I tried to raise him well? Hezekiah was one of the best kings Judah ever had, and his son was the worst. Scripture does not blame Hezekiah for Manasseh. Parents are responsible for faithfulness, teaching, example and love, and every parent fails in some of these and can confess it. But parents cannot give a new heart; only God can (Ezekiel 36:26). A child’s rebellion is not proof that you were a bad parent, any more than a child’s faith would prove you were a good one. Keep loving, keep the door open, keep praying, and remember that the son of Hezekiah came home from Babylon.

Could God really forgive someone who has done what I have done? If he forgave Manasseh, the answer is yes. Manasseh was guilty of idolatry, the occult, murder and the deaths of children, and God heard him. Forgiveness is not measured by the size of the sin but by the worth of the sacrifice, and the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). The only sin that cannot be forgiven is the one never brought to him. Come as Manasseh came: humbly, without excuses, asking for mercy.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have privately given up on, whose case seems closed? Manasseh stands in the line that leads to the Christ, and he repented in a foreign prison at the end of a wasted life. Pray again.

For worship. Our God gave his greatest promise to a king who did not want it and heard the prayer of a king who had done everything to deserve never being heard. And the Son born of this line is the reason: Manasseh was led to Babylon in hooks and bronze chains for his own crimes, and Jesus was led away bound for crimes not his own (27:2), so that Manasseh could go home.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Amon for Amos. Hezekiah and Josiah were reforming kings; Manasseh was the worst.

verseByVerse.quote: and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah the father of Jechoniah. Josiah was in fact Jechoniah’s grandfather; Jehoiakim, Josiah’s son, stands between them (1 Chronicles 3:15–16). As elsewhere in the list, “father of” means ancestor of, and Matthew probably omits Jehoiakim to keep his pattern of fourteen. Jechoniah (also called Jehoiachin or Coniah) reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8–15).

And his brothers. Perhaps Jechoniah’s uncles and relatives, including Zedekiah, the last king, who saw Jerusalem destroyed in 586 BC.

The deportation to Babylon. Here the list breaks. The temple burned, Jerusalem destroyed, the king blinded and taken captive, and the people carried away (2 Kings 25). To those who lived through it, it seemed that God’s promises to David had failed: no throne, no temple, no land, and the king of Judah in a Babylonian prison. Matthew makes it one of the two hinges of his genealogy: a turning point, not the end.

The curse on Jechoniah. A reader with an open Bible will find a shadow over this name. God had said through Jeremiah that this man was to be written down as childless, and that none of his offspring would succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:24–30). Yet Matthew runs the royal line straight through him. How can the Messiah sit on David’s throne if he descends from the one man God cursed off it?

The answer. Jesus is Joseph’s son legally, not biologically (v. 16). The legal right to David’s throne passed to him through Joseph, the heir of Solomon and Jechoniah. But Jesus was not physically descended from Jechoniah, because he was born of Mary by the Holy Spirit, not fathered by Joseph. (Luke’s genealogy, whichever line it traces, runs from David through Nathan, not Solomon, Luke 3:31.) So the curse stands, and the promise stands: two divine words that look as though they cannot both be true, and the virgin birth is the needle that threads them. God did not go back on his word; he found a way through it that nobody saw coming.

After the deportation … Shealtiel … Zerubbabel. In exile, the line continued. Jechoniah was released from prison in Babylon and treated kindly, eating at the king’s table for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27–30). His grandson Zerubbabel led exiles home after 538 BC and governed Judah while the temple was rebuilt (Ezra 3:8; Haggai 1:1). God called Zerubbabel his signet ring (Haggai 2:23), the very image he had used when he rejected Jechoniah (Jeremiah 22:24): the ring pulled off God’s hand was put back on it.

Is an adopted child a real son? In Israel, and in the eyes of God, yes. Jesus’ whole claim to David’s throne rests on his legal sonship through Joseph, which shows how seriously Scripture takes adoption: it was enough to make the Son of God the heir of a king. If you were adopted, or have adopted, you are not in a second-class family. Every Christian is adopted. We were not born God’s children by nature, but in Christ God has made us his sons and heirs (Romans 8:15–17; Galatians 4:4–7), with the full rights of the family. The pattern runs both ways: Joseph adopted the Son of God, so that the Son of God could bring us into his Father’s house.
verseByVerse.note: The deportation to Babylon came in 597 and 586 BC. Zerubbabel later led the return and the rebuilding of the temple.

parallels.desc: Zerubbabel as the LORD’s signet ring

verseByVerse.quote: and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unknown names. After Zerubbabel the light goes out. Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud: the rest of the Bible never mentions them. No king, no prophet, not one recorded sentence. They lived under Persian, Greek and Roman rule in a small, occupied country, and they worked, married and had children. Every one of them was load-bearing.

The silent centuries. Between Zerubbabel (about 520 BC) and Jesus, about five centuries passed. Persia gave way to Alexander, the temple was desecrated in 167 BC, the Maccabees briefly won independence, and Rome took control in 63 BC. During all this time, after Malachi, there was no prophet in Israel.

Remembered because of him. There is only one reason anyone knows the names Azor and Achim: they lead to Jesus. Written into his genealogy, they will be read as long as the Gospel is read: a small picture of what Christ does for all his people. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), and their names are written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 21:27), not for anything they did but because they belong to him. Belonging to Christ is enough to be remembered for ever.

What it does not mean. Not that God was absent or inactive during these centuries. He was preparing the world for Christ: the spread of the Greek language, the Roman roads and peace, the scattering of Jews and synagogues through the empire, and the translation of the Scriptures into Greek. Paul calls the moment of Christ’s coming the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4).

What do I do when God seems silent in my life? Do what these men did: keep going in ordinary faithfulness. Go on reading the Scripture God has already given, because his silence in your feelings is not silence in his Word, which speaks every time you open it. Go on praying, even when it feels like talking to a ceiling; the Psalms are full of believers who did exactly that (Psalm 13; 88). Stay among God’s people. And judge God’s activity not by what you can see this month but by what he has promised. Five hundred years of apparent silence were the final preparation for the loudest word God has ever spoken, his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).

On a Tuesday. Almost none of your life will be visible to anybody in three hundred years, and these men prove that is not insignificance. Change the nappy, finish the shift, pray with the child at bedtime. The line runs through days like that.
verseByVerse.note: These men after Zerubbabel are mentioned nowhere else in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleazar … Matthan … Jacob … Joseph. Joseph’s father is Jacob. Luke calls Joseph the son of Heli (Luke 3:23), probably because Matthew traces the legal royal line and Luke another line, perhaps Joseph’s physical descent or Mary’s.

The broken pattern. Verse 16 does something invisible in English and plainly deliberate. Thirty-nine times in a row Matthew has used the same construction: A was the father of B. The Greek verb is egennēsen, an active verb, a man begetting a son. It runs like a drumbeat down the page from Abraham to Jacob. Then, at the last link, the beat breaks. Matthew writes not Joseph the father of Jesus but Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. In Greek, “of whom” is feminine singular: it can refer to one person only, and that person is not Joseph. And the verb goes passive: Jesus was born, not was fathered. The chain reaches Joseph and goes sideways into a woman. Matthew has not yet said the word virgin, but he has already said it in his grammar.

The husband of Mary. Joseph and Mary were betrothed, which counted legally as married (v. 18), and Joseph took her as his wife (v. 24). As Mary’s husband who named and received Jesus, Joseph became his legal father, and passed on to him the legal rights of David’s line. In Israel a son by adoption was a true heir, so Jesus is truly the son of David through Joseph, though not by blood.

Who is called Christ. The whole genealogy has been travelling toward this title. Forty-two generations of waiting, and the last word of the list is not a name but an office: the Christ.

So should I call Joseph Jesus’ father? Yes, in the sense Scripture does. Luke calls Joseph and Mary his parents and has Mary say “your father and I” to the twelve-year-old Jesus (Luke 2:41, 48), and the people of Nazareth called him the carpenter’s son (13:55). Joseph was his father in law, in the home and in daily care: he fed him, taught him a trade and took him to the feasts. But he was not his father by nature. Jesus himself gently corrected Mary that day: he must be in his Father’s house (Luke 2:49). Joseph is honoured precisely because he was willing to raise a Son who was not his, for a Father greater than he.

For worship. For thirty-nine generations men begot sons, and every one was born into Adam’s ruin and needed saving. Then God broke the pattern. The Son who stands at the end of the list was not begotten by any man, because he was the eternally begotten Son of the Father before there was an Abraham to begin the list (John 8:58). He did not come out of the line as its product. He came into it as its Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew breaks the pattern at the end: Jesus was born of Mary, not fathered by Joseph. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

parallels.desc: “being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph”

verseByVerse.quote: So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three groups of fourteen. Matthew stops and shows his working, which no other evangelist does. The first group rises from Abraham to David: the promise given and the kingdom established. The second falls from David to the exile: the kingdom’s decline and destruction. The third waits from the exile to Christ: the long, silent preparation. A promise given, a promise apparently destroyed, a promise kept: history, in this Gospel, is an argument going somewhere.

From the deportation to the Christ. The exile was the great wound of Israel: no king, no temple, the people scattered for their sins. Some came home, but the prophets kept promising a deeper return, when God would forgive iniquity and gather his people to himself (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:24–28). Matthew’s count says that return has come, and its name is Jesus, who will save his people from their sins (1:21).

Why fourteen? Perhaps because of David. In Hebrew, letters also served as numbers, and the consonants of David’s name (D-V-D) add up to fourteen (4 + 6 + 4). Three times fourteen says David, David, David: this is the Son of David. Others point out that three fourteens make six sevens, so Jesus begins the seventh seven, the number of completion. Either way, Matthew is showing design.

Counting the names. If you count the third group you find thirteen names, not fourteen. The likely explanation is that Jechoniah is counted twice, at the end of the second group and at the start of the third: the exile split his life in two, so he stands on both sides of it. Or Matthew is counting generations rather than names. His numbers are a teaching structure, not a census.

Matthew and Luke. Luke’s genealogy (Luke 3:23–38) differs from Matthew’s. From David the two lines part company: Matthew traces the line through Solomon, Luke through Nathan; Matthew names Joseph’s father as Jacob, Luke as Heli. Christians have offered three main explanations.

Mary’s line. Luke gives Mary’s genealogy, with Joseph as Heli’s son-in-law; Matthew gives Joseph’s.

Levirate marriage. One of Joseph’s fathers was legal and the other natural, through a levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), as the early church historian Julius Africanus suggested: when a man died childless, his brother married the widow, and their first son was counted as the dead man’s heir.

Royal and physical lines. Matthew traces the legal royal succession, the line of throne-heirs through Solomon; Luke traces Joseph’s physical descent through Nathan.

Which explanation is right? This commentary’s view: we cannot be certain, but the third best fits Matthew’s purpose: he traces the legal, royal line by which David’s throne passed to Joseph’s son, through Solomon and Jechoniah, while Luke follows physical descent through Nathan. Each explanation is held by careful readers, and none requires an error in Scripture. Both genealogies agree on what matters: Jesus is the son of David and the son of Abraham, and every promise God ever made to either of them lands on him.

What should I do when I meet a difficulty in the Bible I cannot solve? First, remember that the church has known about this one for eighteen hundred years, and many careful believers have looked at it honestly and kept their faith; Julius Africanus was writing about it around AD 220. Second, remember that there are several reasonable answers, and you do not need to know which one is right to know that the problem need not be a contradiction. Third, hold the difficulty with patience rather than suspicion. A Bible that has proved true in a thousand places has earned the benefit of the doubt in the one place where you cannot yet see how the pieces fit. Ask a pastor, read a good commentary, and keep reading.
verseByVerse.note: Three sets of fourteen give the story its shape: rise to David, fall to exile, and the wait for the Christ. The counts are arranged, not exhaustive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Birth of Jesus Christ: God with Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew tells the birth from Joseph's side. Joseph finds Mary pregnant, resolves to divorce her quietly, and is told by an angel in a dream where the child came from; he obeys at once. Two names define the child: Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins, and Immanuel, God with us, fulfilling Isaiah 7:14.
verseByVerse.theology: The virgin birth is not decoration. A Saviour who was himself under Adam's guilt would need saving. Conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of a woman (Galatians 4:4), Jesus is truly human and free from sin. The two names hold the gospel together: God has come to be with us (Immanuel), and being with us, he saves us from our sins (Jesus).
verseByVerse.examples: Joseph received no applause and no public vindication, only the angel's word. He obeyed at real cost: accepting suspicion, raising a child not his own, and giving up his right to defend his name. God still calls his people to act on his word before the full picture is visible, and he is no less faithful to them than he was to Joseph.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. “Birth” is genesis, the word that opened the Gospel’s first line: the new beginning. Matthew tells the story from Joseph’s side; Luke tells it from Mary’s (Luke 1:26–38).

In the flow. Verse 16 left a question: if Joseph did not father Jesus, how was he born? Verses 18–25 answer it. The genealogy showed Jesus as David’s legal heir through Joseph; this story shows him as the Son of God, conceived by the Spirit, and how Joseph came to take him as his own.

Betrothed. Betrothal was a legally binding marriage contract, often made when the girl was in her early teens. The couple were called husband and wife but did not yet live together; that often came about a year later. Only a formal divorce could end a betrothal, and unfaithfulness during it was treated as adultery, punishable under the law by death (Deuteronomy 22:23–24), though in Jesus’ time this was probably rarely carried out.

She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Matthew tells the reader at once where the child came from. Joseph did not yet know. He saw a pregnant bride and knew the child was not his: a husband with a legal case, a public remedy available to him, and the sympathy of everyone he knows.

Her husband Joseph, being a just man. “Just” (dikaios) means righteous: a man who kept God’s law. That righteousness pulled him two ways. The law required him not to treat an apparently adulterous marriage as if nothing had happened. But he also did not want to humiliate her.

Unwilling to put her to shame. He could have made a public accusation before the village court. The law was on his side, the evidence appeared conclusive, and he could have destroyed her and been congratulated for his piety.

Resolved to divorce her quietly. Instead, he decided on a private divorce, probably before two or three witnesses, with as little shame for her as possible. He would take the ambiguity onto himself, let the village think whatever it liked about him too, and cost her as little as the situation allowed.

What Joseph shows. True righteousness is not harsh legalism. Joseph did not pretend that nothing had happened: he still intended to divorce her. What he refused was the destructive version of a legitimate act. He chose the least harmful honest course, which is nearly always available, and nearly always more expensive. His righteousness made him gentle (Micah 6:8). And God met him on the road he had already begun to walk: the angel came while Joseph was considering the merciful course (v. 20).

Holy, and whispered about. The child at the centre of this scandal is the Holy One himself, and the first thing the world did with the sinless Son of God was suspect him. The whisper may have followed him; years later his enemies would retort, we were not born of sexual immorality (John 8:41), perhaps hinting that he was. He would be numbered with the transgressors, condemned as a blasphemer and crucified between thieves, the innocent counted guilty from the womb to the cross, so that the guilty could be counted innocent. His humiliation began in a village rumour before he was born.

Mary’s position. Mary said nothing in these verses. She had obeyed God, and now her reputation was at risk, and anything she said would sound like what a guilty girl says. The vindication, when it came, came privately to Joseph in a dream; Scripture records none for the neighbours. If you are doing the right thing and paying for it in the eyes of people whose opinion matters to you, you are standing where Mary stood. God knows the truth, and that is enough.

If my spouse has been unfaithful, does Joseph’s example mean I must stay, or must I leave? Neither is commanded here. Jesus himself teaches that sexual unfaithfulness is a ground on which divorce is permitted (19:9), and Scripture also allows it for wilful desertion (1 Corinthians 7:15; the Westminster Confession 24.6), so Joseph was not wrong to plan one. But permitted is not required. Many wronged husbands and wives, with God’s help, have forgiven and rebuilt, and that is a beautiful thing when there is true repentance. What Joseph shows is the spirit in which either path should be walked: honestly, without revenge, without humiliating the other person publicly, and seeking counsel and God’s guidance. If there is violence or danger, safety comes first: seek it at once, and the church must stand with the one being harmed. Persistent, serious abuse can itself amount to desertion, and the elders can help judge each case.

On a Tuesday. When someone has, as far as you can tell, wronged you badly, and you hold the power to expose them, remember that Christ has covered your shame rather than exposing it. Before you speak, post or reply, ask Joseph’s question: which remedy heals, and which humiliates?
verseByVerse.note: Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; ending it required a divorce. The couple did not yet live together.

parallels.desc: the law on a betrothed woman

verseByVerse.quote: But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. Joseph had made his decision, but he had not yet acted; God intervened while he was thinking it over. This is the first of several dreams in which God guides Joseph (2:13, 19, 22). Like Joseph son of Jacob, this Joseph is a man of dreams who will protect his family by going to Egypt.

Joseph, son of David. The angel calls him by his royal ancestry, a title this Gospel otherwise keeps for Jesus himself. The man asked to take this child is the man through whom the child will inherit a throne.

Do not fear to take Mary as your wife. Joseph’s fear was reasonable: of disgrace, of marrying an apparently unfaithful woman, of breaking God’s law. The angel does not argue with the fear; he answers it with the truth.

That which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. No human father was involved. This is the virgin conception: the Holy Spirit created the child’s human life in Mary’s womb. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) is beginning a new creation. Mary is the willing soil (Luke 1:35), but the life within her is the Spirit’s gift, not man’s achievement: grace from the very first breath.

Why the virgin conception matters. Every child of Adam inherits a sinful nature (Psalm 51:5; Romans 5:12). Jesus was truly human, Mary’s real son, real flesh and blood, but his conception was a fresh act of God, so that he was without sin. Only a sinless Saviour could save sinners: a Redeemer who was himself under Adam’s guilt would need redeeming. And it shows that salvation comes from God’s side, not from human achievement.

She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. The name is not chosen by either parent but issued from heaven. “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua (Yehoshua), meaning the LORD saves. Joshua led Israel into the promised land; this Jesus will lead his people into a greater inheritance. By naming the child, Joseph would adopt him legally as his son.

For he will save his people from their sins. The explanation of the name. Not may save, but will save: he will certainly accomplish it. To a first-century Jew, salvation meant rescue from Rome; the angel says the real enemy is sin. Psalm 130:8 had said that the LORD would redeem Israel from all his iniquities; now that work of the LORD is given to Jesus, which is itself a claim about who he is. At the Last Supper Jesus explains how: his blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (26:28). The manger aims straight at the cross.

What saved from their sins includes. From sin’s penalty: the guilt and condemnation we had earned were laid on him at the cross, so that there is no condemnation for those in Christ (Romans 8:1). From sin’s power: sin will not rule over them (Romans 6:14); the chains are struck off and the daily war of grace begins. And finally from sin’s presence: in the new creation, nothing unclean will enter (Revelation 21:27), and we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

His people. Those who belong to him. At first this sounds like Israel, but by the end of Matthew it includes believers from all nations (28:19), the true Israel of Jew and Gentile together, everyone the Father has given him. Reformed Christians see here the definite purpose of Christ’s work: he came not merely to make salvation possible for everyone but actually to save his people (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). This does not limit the offer of the gospel, which goes to all (28:19). Many faithful Christians hold instead that Christ died to make salvation possible for all, with each person’s response deciding the outcome; the Reformed reading rests on the angel’s wording: he will save, not merely offer to.

What it does not mean. Not that Mary was sinless or had no need of a Saviour. She called God her Saviour (Luke 1:47), as only a sinner can. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary was conceived without original sin, but Scripture never says so, and it would only move the problem back a generation. Jesus’ sinlessness comes from the Spirit’s work in his conception, which set that human life apart and kept it free from sin from its first moment (Luke 1:35).

Where Christians differ: the virgin birth. Since the nineteenth century some scholars have treated the virgin birth as a legend added to make Jesus seem divine. But it is plainly taught by both Matthew and Luke, who tell it from different sides (Joseph’s and Mary’s) and so seem to draw on separate sources rather than one legend, and confessed in the earliest creeds (the Apostles’ Creed: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary). This commentary’s view: the virgin birth is historical fact and essential Christian doctrine.

Is a virgin birth not simply impossible? In the ordinary course of nature, yes, and Matthew knows it as well as we do: Joseph’s first thought was not a miracle but unfaithfulness. That is the point. The virgin birth is not offered as something nature does but as something God did. So the real question is not about biology but about God. If there is a God who made the world out of nothing, giving a child life in a virgin’s womb is not hard for him; nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). And if there is no such God, the virgin birth is the least of our problems, because then there is also no one to save us. The miracle at the start of the story belongs with the empty tomb at its end.

If Jesus came to save his people, how do I know I am one of them? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by coming to Jesus. His people are known by this: they come to him, trusting him to save them from their sins. Jesus promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you are turning from your sin and resting on Christ, however weakly, that is the mark of his people, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The doctrine is not a wall to keep you out. It is a guarantee that once you are in, he will not lose you.

Does God still guide people by dreams and angels? Not ordinarily. Many Reformed Christians, this commentary among them, hold that such direct revelations belonged to the founding era of God’s saving work, when Scripture was being given, and that God now guides his people chiefly through the completed Scriptures, prayer, wise counsel and his providence (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Brothers who see this differently are to be held in charity, God is free to do as he pleases, and many believers have testified to dreams that drew them to Christ; the test of any such experience is whether it agrees with the Bible, which it can never add to. Joseph had the dream because this was a unique moment. You have the whole of Matthew, which tells you everything the angel told him and far more.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

parallels.desc: the name given to Mary too
he will redeem Israel from all its iniquities

verseByVerse.quote: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel" (which means, God with us).
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this took place to fulfil. The first of Matthew’s ten or so fulfilment formulas (2:15, 23). God is the speaker, Isaiah his mouthpiece. And “fulfil” means more than a prediction coming true: the events of Jesus’ life bring Israel’s whole story and Scriptures to their intended goal.

Isaiah’s original setting. Around 734 BC, Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel marched on Jerusalem. King Ahaz was terrified, his heart shaking as the trees of the forest shake before the wind (Isaiah 7:2). Ahaz refused the sign Isaiah offered, preferring Assyria’s help, so God gave one anyway: a young woman would conceive and bear a son, called Immanuel, and before the child knew right from wrong, the two kings Ahaz feared would be gone (Isaiah 7:14–16). In its own day the sign said: God has not abandoned his people.

The virgin. Isaiah’s Hebrew word, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age, and in the Old Testament it is never clearly used of a married woman, so an unmarried girl, and so a virgin, is the natural sense. Critics charge that Matthew over-read it. But two centuries or so before Christ, Jewish scholars translating Isaiah into Greek (the Septuagint) rendered it parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for virgin. The reading virgin was not a Christian invention; it was already in the Jews’ own Greek Bible.

Immanuel. Hebrew for God with us. No one in the Gospels calls Jesus “Immanuel” as a name, because Immanuel was never a label but a confession: the prophecy is fulfilled in who he is, God present with his people in a human life. Matthew frames his whole Gospel with this truth: it begins with God with us (1:23) and ends with Jesus’ promise, I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20).

Truly God and truly man. The virgin conception means that Jesus is fully human, born of a woman, and fully God, the eternal Son come in the flesh (John 1:14). The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) confessed this: one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation. In plain words: there is one Jesus, not two, everything God is and everything a man is, without the two being blended. Remaining what he was, he became what he was not: not God in a costume, nor a good man promoted upward, but the eternal Son who took a true and complete human nature. Both are necessary: a Christ who is less than God cannot save us, and a Christ who is less than man has not stood in our place.

What it does not mean. Not that the virgin birth is borrowed from pagan myths. Pagan stories told of gods having sexual relations with women, as Zeus did; some of the stories most often cited, like those of Mithras or Horus, either describe nothing of the kind or come from sources later than the Gospels. None clearly describes a conception with no sexual union at all. And Matthew’s first readers were Jews, among the people least likely to borrow a pagan myth, and he grounds the virgin birth in Isaiah.

How could a sign for Ahaz be fulfilled seven hundred years later? Prophecy often has a near horizon and a far one. There was most likely a child in Ahaz’s day, and before he was old enough to choose good, Syria and Israel were crushed, just as Isaiah said. That near sign was real. But Isaiah himself kept speaking about the child, until the language grew too large for any ordinary boy: Mighty God, a throne without end (Isaiah 9:6–7). The first child was a signpost; Jesus is the destination. Matthew is not twisting Isaiah. He is reading Isaiah to the end.

What does God with us mean when I feel alone? It means his presence does not depend on your feelings. Jesus is with his people by his Spirit, really and constantly, whether you sense him or not (28:20; John 14:16–18). Feelings come and go with sleep, health and circumstance; his promise does not. So when you feel abandoned, speak to him as one who is present, because he is. Read a psalm aloud to him. Go to church even when you would rather not, because he meets his people there. And remember that Immanuel himself cried out on the cross, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (27:46). He knows that darkness from the inside, and he went into it so that you would never be truly forsaken.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him. Woke, and did: no interval, no attempt to negotiate the terms. Each of the four times God speaks to Joseph, he responds the same way, at once. Take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt, and he rose and took them by night (2:14). Go back, and he went (2:21). Turn aside to Galilee, and he did (2:22).

He took his wife. What he was agreeing to was not small: marrying a visibly pregnant woman, living for the rest of his life among neighbours who could count the months, and raising as his own a child he had been told was not his. It may well have cost him his reputation.

But knew her not. “Knew” is the Bible’s modest word for sexual union (Genesis 4:1), and there is beauty in it: the joining of husband and wife is two people truly knowing each other. Joseph and Mary had no sexual relations before Jesus’ birth, so the sign of the virgin birth was guarded.

“Until she had given birth to a son” states only what did not happen before the birth, but the natural meaning is that afterwards they lived as a normal married couple. (The KJV and NKJV read her firstborn son here, following later manuscripts; the earliest read simply a son, though Luke 2:7 does call him her firstborn.)

And he called his name Jesus. By naming the child, Joseph formally acknowledged him as his son. This gave Jesus his legal standing as a son of Joseph, and so of David.

The silent man. Not one word of Joseph’s is recorded anywhere in the New Testament. He is spoken to and spoken about, and he acts decisively at every turn. Then he disappears. He is present when Jesus is twelve, and after that nothing; by the ministry Mary appears without a husband, and Jesus himself is called the carpenter (Mark 6:3). The likeliest reading is that Joseph had died, leaving his trade to the boy he had adopted into David’s line. He was given the hardest assignment of any man in the Christmas story, carried it out without complaint, received no vindication that we know of, and left no words behind.

The obedient man and the obedient Son. The child Joseph named would grow up in his house and be submissive to him and to Mary (Luke 2:51): the Lord of the law obeying a village carpenter. And that boyhood obedience was the beginning of a life of perfect obedience to his Father, from the manger to the moment he said, not as I will, but as you will (26:39). Joseph obeyed as a sinner who had been told what to do. Jesus obeyed as the Son who always did what pleased the Father, at once and in everything, and that obedience, counted to his people, is the righteousness in which they stand before God. Counted means credited: God puts Christ’s perfect obedience to the account of everyone who trusts him, as though they had lived it themselves (Romans 5:19).

Where Christians differ: did Mary have other children? Rome and the Orthodox teach that Mary remained a virgin all her life, but the natural reading of Matthew’s until, with his naming of Jesus’ brothers and sisters (13:55–56), is that she bore other children after Jesus. This commentary’s view: Mary was a faithful wife who bore other children after her firstborn, and this takes nothing from her honour. (See Luke 2:7 for the fuller answer.)

How then should we think of Mary? With deep honour, and without worship. She was chosen by God’s grace, she believed when belief was costly, and she bore and raised the Son of God; all generations rightly call her blessed (Luke 1:48). Her example of humble faith, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38), is one every believer should follow. But she is a fellow sinner saved by her Son, not a mediator between us and him. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5): the only go-between that sinners have with God is her Son, who is himself both God and man. We do not pray to her; we thank God for her, and we share her faith.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word is clear, how long do you take to obey it? You obey as one already clothed in the Son’s obedience, not to earn a standing. So name one thing God has plainly told you in Scripture that you are still negotiating over: a reconciliation, a habit, a gift, a confession. Joseph woke and did. Do it today, before the reasons to delay gather.
verseByVerse.note: “Knew her not” means they had no sexual relations until the birth.

1.theology:
God and man in one Person. Immanuel, God with us (1:23) is the truth the Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) put into careful words: Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, two natures in one Person. He is not God in a human costume, nor a man raised to divine status, but the eternal Son who took a true and complete human nature, remaining what he was while becoming what he was not.

Both halves matter. Against the claim that Christ only seemed to be human, the church confesses that he was born of a woman, grew, wept, hungered and died. Against those who make him less than God, it confesses that he is the Lord who forgives sins, raises the dead and will judge the world. Only one who is both could save us.
1.examples:
Then: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba show God’s grace running through broken and foreign lives to accomplish his purpose. Matthew writes them into a royal pedigree, because the gospel humbles the self-righteous and welcomes the unlikely.

Now: We are often weighed by background, achievement and social position. The line of the King runs through exiles, foreigners, adulterers and the forgotten. If your story has chapters you would rather not name in public, you are in good company here: the God who wrote Rahab into his Son’s family writes sinners into his own.

2.title: The King and the Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.” <sup>3</sup>When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; <sup>4</sup>and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. <sup>5</sup>They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: <sup>6</sup>‘And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’” <sup>7</sup>Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. <sup>8</sup>And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him.” <sup>9</sup>After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. <sup>10</sup>When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. <sup>11</sup>And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. <sup>12</sup>And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way. <sup>13</sup>Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him.” <sup>14</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt <sup>15</sup>and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” <sup>16</sup>Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. <sup>17</sup>Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: <sup>18</sup>“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.” <sup>19</sup>But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, <sup>20</sup>saying, “Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead.” <sup>21</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. <sup>22</sup>But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee. <sup>23</sup>And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is a chapter of contrasts. Gentile magi travel hundreds of miles to worship a Jewish king they have never met. In Jerusalem the chief priests and scribes can quote the prophecy of his birthplace from memory, and do not take a step toward Bethlehem. The magi needed the star and then the Scriptures, and they found the King.

The flight to Egypt brings Matthew’s second fulfilment: Out of Egypt I called my son (Hosea 11:1). What Hosea said of Israel, Matthew sees completed in Jesus, the true and faithful Son who lives Israel’s story over again and keeps it where Israel did not.

The killing of Bethlehem’s boys is the chapter’s darkest moment, and Matthew does not soften it. Rachel weeps for her children (Jeremiah 31:15). The coming of the King provoked a ruler who killed to protect himself, and the child who escaped that night would later die for others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Visit of the Magi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wise men from the East arrive in Jerusalem following a star, seeking the one born King of the Jews. Gentiles travel far to worship the Jewish Messiah, while the Jewish king plots his murder and the scholars who know the Scriptures stay at home. Herod's pretended wish to worship covers a plan to kill. Sent on by the Scriptures to Bethlehem, the magi see the light stop over one house. They worship the child, give their gifts and, warned in a dream, go home another way.
verseByVerse.theology: The magi's journey begins the fulfilment of Isaiah's vision of the nations coming to Zion's light (Isaiah 60:1–6). Herod knows who the child is and opposes him anyway; knowing changes nothing if the heart does not bow. The scribes recite Micah 5:2 and do not go, a standing rebuke to knowledge without submission.
verseByVerse.examples: The magi travelled perhaps a thousand miles, following a light they only partly understood, to bring costly gifts to a child. Many people today know far more theology than they did and show far less devotion. Their story asks what we would gladly spend to come to Christ, who spent everything to come to us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 1 showed who Jesus is; Matthew 2 shows how the world responds to him, and the whole Gospel is foreshadowed. Gentile scholars travel from the East to worship him; Herod tries to kill him; the Bible experts in Jerusalem know where he is to be born and do not go. Jesus relives the story of Israel: the true Son called out of Egypt, the new Moses rescued from a murderous king. Over all the danger and grief, God is quietly, completely in control.

Bethlehem of Judea. A small town about six miles (ten kilometres) south of Jerusalem, the hometown of David (1 Samuel 16:1). It is named for prophecy: the city of David, the place where the Messiah must be born (Micah 5:2).

In the days of Herod the king. Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome from 37 to 4 BC. He was not a Jew by birth but an Idumean, a descendant of Esau, handed the title King of the Jews by the Roman Senate. He was a brilliant builder, who rebuilt the temple on a magnificent scale, and a paranoid killer of anyone he suspected, his own family included; the emperor Augustus is said to have joked that it was safer to be Herod’s pig than his son. Since Herod most likely died in 4 BC, Jesus was born a little before that, probably around 6–5 BC. (On why our calendar is a few years out, see v. 19.) Two kings of the Jews now stand face to face in the story: one crowned by Rome and drenched in blood, one born of God and worshipped by strangers.

Wise men from the east. Greek magoi, magi. Originally a Persian priestly caste, they were experts in astrology, dreams and ancient wisdom. They probably came from Persia or Babylon, where many Jews had lived since the exile and where Daniel had been head of the wise men (Daniel 2:48). They may have known Jewish hopes of a coming king. Matthew does not say how many there were; the tradition of three comes from the three gifts. Nor were they kings; that idea came later, from Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60:3. They were Gentiles, outsiders to the covenant, and yet they are the first in this whole Gospel to seek the King and bow down.

Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? Not who will become king, but who has been born king. He is King by birth. It is the right question asked in the wrong place: they come to the palace looking for a newborn King and find only Herod. The title will appear again only at the end of the Gospel, on the lips of Pilate and the soldiers, and on the sign over the cross (27:11, 29, 37). The Gentiles call him King at his birth and at his death.

For we saw his star when it rose. Many explanations have been offered: a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn (which happened three times in 7 BC), a comet, or a nova. But the star in verse 9 moves ahead of them and stops over a particular house, which no natural star does. This commentary’s view: most likely a supernatural light, a sign God gave, perhaps in a form these star-watchers would understand. Some connect it with Balaam’s prophecy: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17).
