And have come to worship him. The Greek word (proskyneō) means to bow down, to fall prostrate in homage. It can be used of honouring a king, but in Matthew it regularly describes worship of Jesus (14:33; 28:9, 17). At the least they meant to do a king honour, but at the house they fall on their faces and pour out their treasures (v. 11), rendering to this child what belongs to God alone. Gentiles travel perhaps a thousand miles to worship the King, while Jerusalem will not walk six miles to see him.

Is it right to worship a baby? Worship belongs to God alone, and Scripture is fierce about it: when John fell down before an angel, he was told at once to worship God (Revelation 22:8–9). So if the magi were wrong to worship this child, Matthew would have to correct them, and he does the opposite. He records their worship with approval because of who the child is: Immanuel, God with us (1:23). The baby in Mary’s arms was the eternal Son, as fully God at a few months old as on the mountain of transfiguration. Jesus received worship throughout his life (14:33; 28:9, 17) and never refused it. To bow before him is not idolatry; it is the only right response.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “wise men” renders the Greek magi — scholars of the stars, probably from Persia or Babylon. Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC.

parallels.desc: a star shall come out of Jacob
nations bring gold and frankincense to the light

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled. Foreigners were asking for someone born to the title Rome had given Herod. To a paranoid old king, this meant a rival.

And all Jerusalem with him. The city knew that when Herod was disturbed, people died. And perhaps many were comfortable with things as they were and did not want disruption, even from God.

Assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people. The chief priests were the high priest and the leading priestly families who ran the temple, mostly Sadducees. The scribes were experts in the law of Moses who taught and interpreted it, mostly Pharisees. Together they formed much of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council. They are summoned not for worship but for information, treated as a reference library by a man who has no intention of bowing.

He inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. Herod connects King of the Jews with the Christ. He knows enough theology to be afraid of Jesus, and not enough humility to worship him.

Afraid of the wrong thing. Herod feared that the child would take his palace, and he was wrong about that and right about everything else. When crowds later tried to make him king by force, he slipped away from them (John 6:15), and he told Pilate that his kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). Herod held his crown by killing others; Jesus would take his by being killed. Yet Herod was right to tremble, because this child is the King to whom every crown on earth will answer. The threat was to Herod’s soul, and it was also an offer: the King whom Herod tried to murder was the only one who could have saved him.

The scholars exposed. The men in this scene are not sceptics or pagans but Bible scholars. They can produce the right chapter and verse from memory, under pressure from a king, and they will not walk the short road south that they themselves have just identified. That is not a failure of information but of appetite, and the person most at risk of it is the person reading a commentary. Study can become a substitute for the thing it is meant to serve, and a comfortable one, because it feels like devotion and costs nothing. Ask what knowing about Christ has moved you to do this month; if the answer is only to know more, Bethlehem is still six miles away.

What it does not mean. Not that every person in Jerusalem was hostile. Luke tells of Simeon and Anna in the temple, longing for the Messiah (Luke 2:25–38). But as a whole, the capital was troubled rather than glad.

How does Jesus disturb the throne in my own heart? Every heart has a Herod in it: the part of us that wants to rule our own life and resents anyone who claims the right to. Jesus disturbs it whenever his word touches something we have kept for ourselves: our money, our time, our sexuality, our grudges, our plans. You can tell the throne is being disturbed when you feel that reluctance to read a particular passage, or the urge to change the subject when a sermon comes close. Herod’s answer was to get rid of the rival. The Christian’s answer is to step down and let the true King reign, and to discover that he rules for our good and not to crush us.

For worship. The King who troubled Herod’s palace was too small to lift his head, and the most powerful man in the land shook at the rumour of him. The kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2). Herod is dust. The child he feared reigns.
verseByVerse.note: Herod was notoriously jealous of rivals; he had members of his own family killed. The chief priests and scribes were the experts in the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: 'And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Bethlehem of Judea. It was common knowledge that the Messiah would come from David’s town (John 7:42). Micah 5:2, here combined with 2 Samuel 5:2, comes to their lips at once and is obeyed not at all.

And you, O Bethlehem … are by no means least. Micah’s Hebrew says that Bethlehem is too little to be among the clans of Judah. Matthew’s quotation says it is by no means least. The two are not in conflict: Bethlehem was small in size, but because the Messiah would come from it, it is by no means least in importance. Micah’s point was that God delights to choose what the world overlooks; Matthew’s is what that small place has now become. The apparent misquotation is the gospel in miniature: grace does not leave little things little. God chooses small places, as he chooses small people (1 Corinthians 1:27–28).

For from you shall come a ruler. Micah goes on to say that this ruler’s coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2): a hint that the ruler’s origin is older than Bethlehem. He was born in a town, but he did not begin there.

Who will shepherd my people Israel. These words come from 2 Samuel 5:2, where God told David that he would shepherd Israel. The prophets condemned the false shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock and promised that God himself would shepherd his people through a new David (Ezekiel 34:11–24). Herod was a wolf-king; Jesus is the Shepherd-King (John 10:11). The shepherds of his people refused to go and find the Shepherd.

In the flow. Bethlehem is the first of four places in chapter 2, each tied to a word of Scripture: Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), Egypt (Hosea 11:1), Ramah (Jeremiah 31:15) and Nazareth (v. 23). Every stop on his strange road was marked out beforehand.

What should I do when I know a lot about the Bible but my heart feels cold? Do not stop reading; that would only make it worse. But change how you read. Read less at a time and more slowly, asking at each passage what it shows you of Christ and what it asks of you today. Turn what you read straight into prayer, speaking it back to God. Then do one concrete thing it says, the same day, however small. Coldness is often the result of knowledge that has never been allowed to become obedience. And ask God plainly to warm you; it is a prayer he loves to answer (Psalm 119:36–37). The magi did not have more information than the scribes. They had more desire, and desire is something God gives.
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem, David’s hometown, lies about six miles south of Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, "Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly … ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. He asked carefully, because he wanted to calculate the child’s age. This explains why he later killed boys up to two years old (v. 16): the star had probably appeared some time before, perhaps a year or more. The magi’s honest answer becomes the data for a massacre.

The star and the stargazers. In the ancient East it was taken for granted that the births and deaths of kings were written in the sky, and the magi were its scholars. Yet the Bible forbids God’s people to steer their lives by the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 47:13). How then does God use one? In sheer grace he stooped to meet these outsiders in the one language they knew, not to bless astrology, but to draw them up out of it and onto the road to Bethlehem. God often calls a man through the dim light he already has, but leads him on to his Word. We are not to scan the heavens for messages. We have the prophetic word more fully confirmed (2 Peter 1:19), and the true Morning Star has already risen.

That I too may come and worship him. Herod uses the magi as unknowing spies and wraps the murder of a child in the language of worship. To weld lying and murder together in one breath is the devil’s own signature: Jesus said he was a murderer from the beginning and the father of lies (John 8:44). Revelation shows the picture behind the picture: a great dragon crouching before the woman, so that when she bore her child he might devour it (Revelation 12:4).

Dressed as devotion. The deadliest hatred of Christ rarely comes snarling; it comes dressed in the clothes of devotion. True worship dethrones the worshipper; Herod wanted information to eliminate a rival. It is a warning to religious people, not only to tyrants. Whenever we use God to protect our own position, our standing in a church, our reputation for goodness, our control of a family, we are doing in small what Herod did in large: keeping the throne and borrowing the language of worship to do it.

Mock worship at both ends. Matthew’s Gospel opens and closes with a false bow to the King of the Jews. Here a king promises to come and worship, meaning to kill. At the end, soldiers kneel before Jesus in a scarlet robe and hail him King of the Jews, then spit on him and lead him out to be crucified (27:29–31). The Son of God was met with counterfeit worship in his cradle and at his cross, and he went to the cross for people whose worship is never perfectly pure, so that the Father might receive them in him and teach them to bow in truth.

How can I tell whether my own worship is real or for show? Herod is an extreme case, but the question is fair for everyone. Real worship bows; false worship uses. Ask what you want from God when you worship: is it God himself, or something he can get you, such as standing, comfort or a good name? Ask whether your worship changes anything you do on Monday. Ask whether you would still praise him if no one saw. No one’s motives are perfectly pure, and that is no reason to stop worshipping; it is a reason to come as a sinner, asking him to make your heart true. Herod never asked. The tax collector who beat his breast did (Luke 18:13), and he went home justified. To be justified is to be declared right with God, forgiven and accepted, not because his worship was pure but because God had mercy on a sinner who asked.

parallels.desc: rulers take counsel against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The star … went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. The magi went on alone; no one from Jerusalem came with them. No ordinary star or planet moves before travellers at walking pace down the Bethlehem road and stops over a single house. Whatever may have stood in the sky at its rising (v. 2), by verse 9 this light is behaving less like an object in the heavens than like the pillar of cloud and fire that went before Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21): a light God set in front of his people to bring them precisely where he wanted them. He does not lose the people he is calling.

They rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. Matthew piles up words: literally they rejoiced a great joy exceedingly, a verb, its own noun, an adverb and an adjective. It is a man reaching for four words because one will not do. The same news brings fear to some and joy to others, depending on whether they want the King.

The joy of the right road. They have not yet reached the house. They rejoiced because the light they had been following stopped moving: confirmation, after months on the road and a wrong turn into a hostile palace, that the journey had not been foolish.

The light stops over a child. Not the palace, not the temple, but a house where a small boy lived with his mother. The God who once went before Israel in a pillar of fire and dwelt above the tabernacle has brought these travellers to the place where he now dwells in flesh. All true guidance ends here. The star was a borrowed light for a season; the child under it is the light of the world (John 8:12), and the one who follows him will not walk in darkness. God’s leading ends not at a doctrine or a place but at a Person.

What if I have never felt that kind of joy about Christ? Feelings vary greatly from person to person and from season to season, and joy is not always a flood; often it is a quiet gladness that he is there, or a settled peace under trouble. Do not measure your faith by the strength of your emotions. But do not settle for coldness either. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), and it grows as we look at Christ: read the Gospels, sing his praises with his people, remember what he has saved you from. Ask God for joy; David did (Psalm 51:12). And remember that the magi’s joy came after a long and uncertain road. Some joys are given at the end of the journey.

On a Tuesday. Think back to a time when it became clear that God had been leading you all along, the job that fell through, the church you nearly did not visit, the friend who spoke at the right moment. Thank him for it today, out loud. And if you are still on the road, keep walking. The light has not gone out.

verseByVerse.quote: And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going into the house. Not a stable. By now, perhaps months later, the family was living in a house in Bethlehem. Luke’s shepherds came on the night of the birth and found the baby lying in a manger (Luke 2:16); the magi come to a child (paidion) in a house. Herod’s calculation of two years or under (v. 16) suggests the visit came some time after the birth. The truth is better than the tidy nativity scene: not a crowd round a cradle on one magical evening, but the slow, sovereign gathering of the nations to Christ, begun here with a handful of foreign astrologers, and still going on.

They saw the child with Mary his mother. Matthew always mentions the child first (vv. 13, 14, 20, 21). Mary is honoured, but the child is the centre.

And they fell down and worshipped him. They worshipped the child, not Mary. Wealthy, learned foreigners lay face down before a child of an ordinary family.

Opening their treasures. One did not approach a king empty-handed. Gold was the gift for a king. Frankincense, a fragrant resin from trees in Arabia and Somalia, was burned as incense in worship, including in the temple (Exodus 30:34–38). Myrrh, another resin, was used in perfume, medicine and for preparing bodies for burial (John 19:39); it was offered to Jesus again on the cross, mixed with wine (Mark 15:23).

The meaning of the gifts. From early times, Christians have seen the gifts as pointing to who Jesus is: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for one who would die. Matthew does not say this, and the magi probably intended simply to give the most precious gifts they had. But the gifts fit, and Isaiah had spoken of the nations bringing gold and frankincense to the Lord (Isaiah 60:6; Psalm 72:10–11). The old reading may well be right.

Provision before the need. Take the gifts also as what they plainly were: portable wealth. A fortune arrives in a working family’s house immediately before Joseph is told to flee by night to a foreign country with no means of support, carried by strangers who had no idea what it was for. Matthew does not draw the connection, but the timing is hard to miss: God may well have funded the exile before he announced it. Sometimes a provision that seems out of proportion to anything currently going on is not for now.

They departed to their own country by another way. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they avoided Jerusalem, and God protected both the child and the magi. Matthew says no more about them. Everyone who truly meets Christ goes home by another way.

What can I give Jesus, since he needs nothing? Nothing he needs, and everything he asks. God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25). But he delights to receive from his children what love offers, as a father treasures a child’s drawing. Give him first yourself (Romans 12:1; 2 Corinthians 8:5). Then give him your worship, your obedience, your time in prayer and his Word, and your money given gladly to his church and to the poor; Jesus counts what is done for the least of his brothers as done for him (25:40). And give your gifts and skills in serving his people. The magi brought what they had. So can you.

For worship. The child on his mother’s knee is worth every treasure the East could carry, and yet the true exchange runs the other way. The magi opened their treasures to him, but he opened heaven’s treasures to us, and became poor so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He is the gift the whole world was waiting for.
verseByVerse.note: By now the family is in a house, not a stable. Frankincense was a resin burned in worship; myrrh a fragrant resin also used in burial.

parallels.desc: kings bring gifts to the king

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Flight to Egypt and the Return to Nazareth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The family flees to Egypt to escape Herod's killing of Bethlehem's boys, returns after Herod's death, and settles in Nazareth, and each move fulfils a word of Scripture. Matthew sees in them the story of Israel lived again: called out of Egypt, Rachel's weeping at the exile, and a humble home in despised Galilee.
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew's quotations here (Hosea 11:1; Jeremiah 31:15; and the prophets' picture of the Branch for Nazarene) show how he reads Israel's history: its great events were patterns waiting for their fulfilment in Christ. Jesus does not merely happen to visit Egypt; he is the Son whom God calls out of Egypt. This is not proof-texting but fulfilment.
verseByVerse.examples: Matthew does not explain the killing of Bethlehem's boys; he quotes Jeremiah's lament and lets it stand. There are moments when the honest response to evil is grief, not explanation. The Messiah's death would be God's answer to such suffering, not by explaining it away but by entering it and overcoming it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him." And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rise, take the child and his mother. The second of Joseph’s dreams in this chapter, and again he obeys at once: quiet, steady obedience to a voice only he has heard, which is harder than heroism.

And flee to Egypt. Egypt was outside Herod’s territory, under direct Roman rule, perhaps a week or more of travel from Bethlehem. Large Jewish communities lived there, especially in Alexandria. Egypt had long been a refuge for God’s people: Abraham went there in famine (Genesis 12:10), and Jacob’s family went there under Joseph (Genesis 46). The land of Israel’s ancient bondage now becomes the Messiah’s refuge.

For Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him. The first attempt on Jesus’ life: from the beginning, the world’s powers set themselves against God’s King (Psalm 2:1–2; Revelation 12:4). And Joseph rose and took the child and his mother by night, without waiting for morning’s reassurance.

Refugees. A family wakes in the dark, takes what it can carry, and crosses a border to escape a ruler who wants their child dead. They arrive in a foreign country with no standing, no relatives named in the text, and no idea how long they will be there. The Son of God spent part of his childhood as a refugee. God could have protected the child in Bethlehem; he had already turned the magi aside with a dream. Instead he sent him down the road every displaced family has walked.

The pattern. Jesus relives Israel’s story. Like Israel, he goes down into Egypt; like Israel, he will be called out of Egypt (v. 15); like Israel, he will pass through water (3:16) and be tested in the wilderness (4:1–11). But where Israel failed, he will be faithful: the true Israel. The one who will lead the new exodus first goes down into Egypt himself.

What it does not mean. Not that fleeing danger shows a lack of faith. God himself commanded it, and Jesus later told his disciples to flee persecution when they could (10:23).

So how should a Christian think about refugees and migrants? With compassion first, because our Lord was one. Scripture commands God’s people again and again to love the sojourner, remembering that they were strangers in Egypt themselves (Leviticus 19:33–34; Deuteronomy 10:19), and that command now has a face. Christians in good conscience differ on questions of borders and government policy, and Scripture gives governments a real duty to keep order (Romans 13:1–4). But no follower of this King is at liberty to speak of people fleeing violence with contempt. In practice that might mean befriending a refugee family in your town, supporting churches that serve them, and praying for persecuted believers who have had to run.
verseByVerse.note: Egypt had long been a refuge; large Jewish communities lived there.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s family goes down to Egypt

verseByVerse.quote: and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, "Out of Egypt I called my son." Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of Egypt I called my son. The family remained in Egypt until Herod died in 4 BC, perhaps a few months, perhaps a year or two. The quotation is from Hosea 11:1. In Hosea, the verse looks back on the exodus: God called his son Israel out of Egypt. How can Matthew say this is fulfilled in Jesus, when Hosea was looking back, not forward?

How Matthew reads Hosea. Matthew is not saying that Hosea predicted this event directly. He is saying that Israel’s history was a pattern that Jesus completes. Israel was God’s son (Exodus 4:22) but was unfaithful; Hosea goes on to say that the more God called them, the more they went away and sacrificed to the Baals (Hosea 11:2). Jesus is the true and faithful Son, who lives out Israel’s story perfectly. What happened to Israel as a nation happens to Jesus as its representative. (Reading Old Testament people and events as patterns pointing to Christ is called typology.)

Two rules for reading this way. Matthew is not playing loose with Hosea; he is reading the Old Testament as the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it, as one story, by one Author, about one Saviour (Luke 24:27). Two rules keep this honest. First, we never erase what a text meant in its own day: Hosea truly did mean the exodus. Second, we read every text in the light of the whole Bible, whose centre is Christ. That is no licence to make a verse say whatever we please.

Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men. Herod knew he was pursuing a child, not an army, and he killed infants anyway.

And he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under. Bethlehem was a small town of perhaps one thousand people, so the number of boys killed may have been around ten to twenty. The slaughter of the innocents is the first shadow of Golgotha: the powers of this world respond to the presence of Christ with violence against the most vulnerable.

But did it really happen? The silence of the Jewish historian Josephus is regularly produced as proof that Matthew made the story up, and it sounds stronger than it is. Begin with the scale, which Christmas art has thoroughly distorted: there is no host of martyred innocents, but a handful of families in a small town, and one terrible morning. Then set that against the reign it belongs to. This is the man who murdered his wife Mariamne, executed three of his own sons, and had his teenage brother-in-law drowned in a swimming pool for being too popular. An argument from silence is weak at the best of times, and weakest for small events far from the capital. Josephus wrote the better part of a century later, selecting from a reign crowded with atrocities. On most datings Matthew wrote within living memory, probably for readers not far from the region, who could have challenged a freshly invented atrocity. We cannot prove the event from outside sources, but nothing in it is out of character, and silence is not evidence against it.

The parallel with Moses. Matthew’s readers would think of Pharaoh, who ordered the Hebrew baby boys to be killed, and of Moses, who was saved (Exodus 1:22–2:10). Jesus is the new Moses, saved from a murderous king to become his people’s deliverer.

On a Tuesday. Jesus did not come to a safe world; he came to save a broken one. Stand against violence toward the vulnerable: the unborn, the abused, the trafficked, the child in your street whose home is not safe. In the ledgers of power, poor children in an unimportant village do not count. God keeps a different ledger, and so should his people.

For worship. Where Israel stumbled and Adam fell, this Son would stand. God called his son out of Egypt once, and the son went off after idols; he called his Son again, and the Son came, and never once turned aside. That is our salvation: not that we kept Israel’s story, but that Jesus kept it for us, and his faithful obedience is counted as ours, so that all who belong to him are sons in him.
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem was a small town; the number of boys killed was probably small, but the act fits Herod’s known cruelty.

parallels.desc: “Out of Egypt I called my son”
Pharaoh orders the Hebrew boys killed

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then was fulfilled. Elsewhere Matthew says that something happened to fulfil Scripture; here, quoting Jeremiah 31:15, he says then was fulfilled, and avoids saying that God intended the massacre. Herod’s evil was his own, though it fitted the pattern Scripture described. Herod is fully guilty, and God is wholly holy; it is the same mystery Peter will preach at the cross, where Jesus was delivered up by God’s definite plan and killed by lawless men (Acts 2:23).

A voice was heard in Ramah. Ramah was a town about five miles north of Jerusalem. In 586 BC the Babylonians gathered the captives of Judah there before marching them into exile (Jeremiah 40:1).

Rachel weeping for her children. Rachel was Jacob’s beloved wife, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and so a mother of Israel. She died giving birth to Benjamin and was buried on the way to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:16–20). Jeremiah pictures her weeping from her tomb as her descendants are led away into exile. Matthew hears the same weeping in Bethlehem, near her tomb, and does not soften it.

She refused to be comforted, because they are no more. Scripture does not hurry grief. Grief is not a lack of faith; Christians grieve, though not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The Bible puts an inconsolable woman in the Christmas story and does not rebuke her. There are losses that are not to be tidied up, and God is not embarrassed by tears he has recorded on purpose.

The context in Jeremiah. Jeremiah 31 is a chapter of hope. Immediately after this verse, God tells Rachel to keep her voice from weeping, because there is hope for her future and her children will come back (Jeremiah 31:16–17). And a little later comes the promise of the new covenant, in which God will forgive his people’s sin (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The weeping of Bethlehem marks the moment just before God’s greatest comfort: the child who escaped will establish the new covenant in his blood (26:28). Rachel weeps, but not for ever, and not without hope.

Why did God warn Joseph and not the house next door? It is the sharpest form of the oldest question there is, and it is put here at the very beginning of the Gospel, where nobody can pretend the New Testament has not noticed. First, Scripture itself refuses to explain. Matthew offers no reason and no consoling remark about a better plan. Second, we must admit the limit: the secret things belong to the LORD our God (Deuteronomy 29:29), and anyone who offers a grieving parent the reason is guessing. But third, and this is not a guess: the child who was rescued that night was rescued for Golgotha. Thirty years later the sword that missed him in Bethlehem found him on a hill outside Jerusalem, and this time the Father sent no angel. God is not a God who keeps his own family clear of the grief he permits in yours. He entered it, at the deepest point, deliberately.

Are the little ones of Bethlehem with God? Scripture does not tell us about these particular children, so we speak carefully. But the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). David, when his infant son died, said I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Samuel 12:23), and many believers have found great comfort in that hope. We may entrust such children to a God who is both just and very merciful, whose Son took little children in his arms and blessed them (19:14). The Judge of all the earth will do what is right. If you have lost a little one yourself, this is not a cold doctrine to you. The Lord who took children in his arms is the same Lord in whose arms you may leave yours.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving, you do not have to pretend. Bring your tears to God; the Psalms give you words for it. And sit with those who grieve, without rushing them toward comfort. You do not need an explanation to offer. You need to be there, to listen, and to remember them in a month when everyone else has moved on.
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay north of Jerusalem, on the road into exile. Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was buried near Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: Rachel buried on the way to Bethlehem

verseByVerse.quote: But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying, "Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Herod died. The tyrant who tried to kill God’s King died, and the King lived. Josephus describes an agonising illness, borne with rage, at Jericho in the spring of what we call 4 BC.

Why our calendar is a few years out. If Herod died in 4 BC and Jesus was born before that, then Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1. The error is not in Scripture but in a sixth-century monk who began numbering the years from the incarnation and miscalculated. The date on the wall is wrong; the events are not.

An angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt. The third dream. Joseph had been told to remain until I tell you (v. 13): no duration. He waited in a foreign country with a small child and no idea whether it would be months or a decade. He was not given a date. He was given a person who promised to speak again, and the promise was kept.

Go to the land of Israel. The phrase, found only here in the New Testament (vv. 20–21), recalls God’s promise of the land to Abraham, and the exodus journey back to it. Like Israel, Jesus is called out of Egypt into the land.

For those who sought the child’s life are dead. Those who sought: plural, though only one man had died. The sentence is a quotation. In Midian, God told Moses to go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking his life were dead (Exodus 4:19). Matthew has reproduced it almost word for word, plural and all, and has simply reversed the direction of travel: Moses is told to go back to Egypt, Joseph to come back from it. Matthew has left the grammar showing. Jesus is the new Moses, returning to deliver his people, and more than Moses: Moses led Israel out of Egypt, and Jesus will lead a new humanity out of bondage to sin and death.

Is it wrong to feel relief when a wicked ruler dies? No. Scripture itself records the relief of God’s people when oppressors fall, and Israel sang when Pharaoh’s army was overthrown (Exodus 15:1). It is right to thank God when he ends a reign of cruelty and protects the vulnerable. But it is wrong to delight in any person’s death for its own sake, because God himself takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). We rejoice in God’s justice and his rescue, we leave vengeance to him (Romans 12:19), and we remember that we too deserved judgment and were shown mercy.

On a Tuesday. If you are in the middle of a wait without a date, a diagnosis, a job search, a prodigal, do the next faithful thing in the place where you are, as Joseph did in Egypt, and trust the one who has promised not to forget you.

parallels.desc: “all the men who were seeking your life are dead”

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod. When Herod died, Rome divided his kingdom among three of his sons. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea. He began his reign by massacring about three thousand people at the temple during Passover, and Rome removed him in AD 6, putting Judea under Roman governors such as Pontius Pilate.

He was afraid to go there. Joseph’s fear was reasonable: Bethlehem, in Judea, was under Archelaus. God does not scold him for it. In the fourth and last dream he confirms and directs Joseph’s caution; divine guidance does not override prudence.

He withdrew to the district of Galilee. Galilee, the northern region, was ruled by another of Herod’s sons, Herod Antipas, who was less violent (he later executed John the Baptist, 14:1–12). Galilee, with its mixed population, was looked down on in Judea. Isaiah had spoken of Galilee of the nations, where those in darkness would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16).

The King who withdrew. Matthew’s word for Joseph’s move, withdrew (anachōreō), is one he will use again and again of Jesus himself. He withdraws when John is arrested (4:12), when the Pharisees plot against him (12:15) and when he hears of John’s death (14:13). The pattern begins here: the King steps back from the reach of murderous rulers, not from fear of death, but because his hour has not yet come. And then, when it has, he stops withdrawing. He sets his face toward Jerusalem and tells his disciples that he must go there and suffer and be killed (16:21).

How does this fit Luke’s account? Luke has the family return to Nazareth after the presentation in the temple (Luke 2:39). A likely order, though neither Gospel spells it out, is: birth in Bethlehem, where they had come for the census (Luke 2:1–5); the presentation in Jerusalem forty days later; a stay in Bethlehem, now in a house (2:11), where the magi found them; the flight to Egypt; and then Nazareth. Luke compresses the story and Matthew supplies the episode Luke leaves out. Matthew writes as if Nazareth is a new decision because from his angle it was: Joseph’s first thought was to settle in Judea.

Does God still guide by dreams? This is the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and readers genuinely carry the question. First, see how rare this cluster is. Scripture covers thousands of years, and guidance by dream is concentrated at a handful of hinge points in redemptive history: Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in Babylon, and here at the arrival of the Messiah. Second, these dreams tell Joseph something he could not have worked out and needed urgently. None of them tells him what to believe or how to live; for that, God had already spoken. Some faithful Christians believe God still guides through dreams and visions today, pointing to Joel’s promise in Acts 2:17, and they deserve to be heard with respect. The reading this commentary holds more likely is that those revelations belonged to the founding of the church, and that God now guides his people by his finished word. That does not stop God from using a dream in his providence, for example to send someone to read the Bible. But a dream is never a word that binds the conscience, and it must always be tested by Scripture. If a dream moves you to obey Scripture, obey Scripture. If it moves you against it, or merely flatters you, put it down.

Then how do I make a big decision without a dream? Use the means God has actually given. First, ask what Scripture commands or forbids, because many choices are settled there. Then pray, asking for wisdom, which God promises to give generously (James 1:5). Gather the facts, weigh them honestly, and notice your circumstances, as Joseph did when he heard who was ruling Judea. Seek the counsel of mature Christians who know you (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God to close doors if you are wrong. Between two good options, God does not leave you guessing at a hidden answer; you are free to choose, and he goes with you.
verseByVerse.note: Archelaus, Herod’s son, ruled Judea so brutally that Rome removed him in AD 6. Galilee was ruled by his brother Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went and lived in a city called Nazareth. Nazareth was a tiny village in the hills of lower Galilee, probably with a few hundred inhabitants. It is never mentioned in the Old Testament or in Josephus. When Nathanael heard that Jesus came from Nazareth, he asked whether anything good could come from there (John 1:46): a near neighbour’s verdict in seven words.

So that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled. The word is prophets, plural. Elsewhere Matthew names a specific prophet. Here he refers to a theme found in several prophets, not to one verse. No Old Testament verse says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene, and Matthew knows it; he names nobody and quotes no text.

That he would be called a Nazarene. What did Matthew mean? The plain point is that Jesus’ humble hometown fits what the prophets said of the Messiah. There are three main suggestions for how, and they may work together.

The despised one. To be called a Nazarene was to be called a nobody from nowhere. Many prophets said the Messiah would be despised and rejected (Isaiah 53:3; Psalm 22:6–8). Being from Nazareth fitted that pattern.

The Branch. The Hebrew word for branch is netser, which sounds like Nazareth. Isaiah 11:1 promises that a branch (netser) will grow from the stump of Jesse, David’s father: a new shoot from a fallen royal line. Other prophets also call the Messiah the Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12, using a related word), which may be why Matthew says prophets in the plural. If, as many think, the village name comes from the same root, the Branch grew up in Branch-town. Isaiah pictures David’s royal house cut down to a dead-looking stump, and a green shoot coming out of it; by Joseph’s day that was the literal situation: the heir to David’s throne was a carpenter in an occupied province.

A Nazirite. Some connect it with the Nazirite, a person set apart by a vow (Numbers 6), like Samson (Judges 13:5). But Jesus was not a Nazirite (he drank wine, 11:19), and the spelling is different, so this is less likely.

Which is right? This commentary’s view: the first two together. Matthew uses a wordplay on the Branch (netser) to show that the despised village of Nazareth fits what the prophets said of the Messiah: a humble shoot from David’s line, despised by men.

The name that stuck. He is Jesus of Nazareth to the crowds, to the demons, to the blind man on the road. John tells us it was written over his head at Pilate’s order (John 19:19). It is how the angel names him at the empty tomb (Mark 16:6), and it is the name the risen and glorified Christ uses of himself, from heaven, to a man on the Damascus road: I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting (Acts 22:8). He was given a village that was a byword for insignificance, and in glory, with the wounds still on him, he keeps its name.

In the flow. With this verse Matthew’s account of Jesus’ beginnings is complete, and the story leaps some thirty years to John preaching in the wilderness (3:1).

What was Jesus doing in Nazareth all those years? Growing up, working and waiting. Luke tells us he grew in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52), and the townspeople later called him the carpenter (Mark 6:3). For about thirty years the Son of God lived an ordinary life in a small village: learning a trade, keeping the Sabbath, obeying his parents, likely supporting his widowed mother. Those years were not wasted. He was fulfilling all righteousness as a true man, for us, in the ordinary duties where most of our lives are spent. Your hidden, ordinary days can be lived to God as well, because your Lord sanctified them first.

On a Tuesday. If you come from somewhere others look down on, so did your Lord. God’s greatest work often begins in places people dismiss. And if you have ever dismissed someone because of where they come from, their accent, their estate, their country, remember the question Nathanael asked, and the answer he got: come and see.
verseByVerse.note: No single prophecy says “he shall be called a Nazarene”; Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in general. Nazareth was a despised backwater, and the prophets foretold a despised Messiah.

parallels.desc: a branch from the stump of Jesse
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

2.theology:
One story in both Testaments. When Matthew reads “Out of Egypt I called my son” as fulfilled in Jesus, he is not tearing Hosea from its context. Israel was God’s son (Exodus 4:22), and its history was a pattern pointing forward to the Son of God. The Old Testament is not a pile of proof texts but one story moving toward one goal.

Reformed scholars such as Geerhardus Vos call this a redemptive-historical reading: each text read in the light of its place in the one story of God’s saving purpose. Each of Matthew’s quotations in this chapter fits that story: the child in Bethlehem, the flight to Egypt, the return to the land, the settling in Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9:1–2).
2.examples:
Then: The magi are the first fruits of the mission to the nations that Jesus will command in Matthew 28. They come from outside the covenant, are led by a sign in the sky to the Scriptures, and by the Scriptures to the King.

Now: The contrast of this chapter still repeats: people with no church background come a long way to find Jesus, while others with every Bible to hand never move toward him. Matthew’s question is not how much you know but whether you are coming to the King, who came all the way to us first.

3.title: The Voice and the Voice
3.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, <sup>2</sup>“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>3</sup>For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” <sup>4</sup>Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey. <sup>5</sup>Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, <sup>6</sup>and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>7</sup>But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup>Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. <sup>9</sup>And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>10</sup>Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>11</sup>I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>12</sup>His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>13</sup>Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. <sup>14</sup>John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” <sup>15</sup>But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented. <sup>16</sup>And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; <sup>17</sup>and behold, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a chapter of two voices. The first is John’s: rough, urgent, prophetic. He wears Elijah’s clothes (2 Kings 1:8) and preaches with Elijah’s directness. Repent. Your ancestry will not protect you. Bear fruit, because the axe is already laid to the root. His preaching is the law doing its proper work: exposing the emptiness of religious privilege and the need for real turning.

The second voice is the Father’s: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. He speaks it before the first sermon or miracle. The Father’s delight rests on who his Son is, not on a record still to be made.

Between the two voices stands the baptism, and its question: why would the sinless one receive a baptism of repentance? Jesus answers: to fulfil all righteousness. He is not confessing sin; he is standing with sinners, taking their place in the water as he will take it on the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness preaching repentance, the voice Isaiah promised, dressed like Elijah. He saves his sharpest words for the Pharisees and Sadducees, who trusted in their descent from Abraham, and announces one mightier than himself. Then Jesus comes to be baptised, to fulfil all righteousness, and the Father declares him his beloved Son.
verseByVerse.theology: John's baptism is a baptism of repentance, looking ahead to the one who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the first herald of the new. His demand for fruit in keeping with repentance cuts against every confidence in ancestry, tradition or membership: no one inherits faith.
verseByVerse.examples: John confronted the leaders' false security in being Abraham's children. The same temptation runs through every tradition: membership in place of repentance, heritage in place of faith, attendance in place of a changed life. John's question still stands: is there fruit? And the fruit itself is the gift of the one he announced, who gives the Spirit to all who come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew leaps nearly thirty silent years to the start of Jesus’ ministry, about AD 27–29 (Luke 3:1–2, 23). John the Baptist appears in the wilderness as the voice Isaiah promised, dressed like Elijah, calling the nation to repent, warning the religious leaders that descent from Abraham will not save them, and announcing one far mightier. Then that one arrives. Jesus, who has no sin, steps into the water to fulfil all righteousness for his people, and a chapter that begins with a call to turn ends with the whole Trinity revealed.

John the Baptist. John was the son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, a relative of Mary, born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1). No prophet had called the whole nation for about four hundred years, since Malachi; John’s preaching meant that God was speaking to his people again.

Came preaching. Proclaiming like a herald, a royal messenger announcing the king’s decree in the town square: not ideas for discussion, but news from God.

In the wilderness of Judea. The dry, rocky land between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. In Israel’s history the wilderness was the place of new beginnings: Israel was formed there, God met Moses and Elijah there, and the prophets promised that God would lead his people through the wilderness in a new exodus (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). John’s location says: God is starting again.

Repent. Metanoeite. Often explained as change your mind, it means far more: a complete turning of direction. It carries the Hebrew idea of turning (shuv): turning around, coming home to the LORD one has wandered from. The prophets had thundered it for centuries: return, O Israel, to the LORD your God (Hosea 14:1). It includes a change of thinking (seeing sin as God sees it), a change of heart (sorrow for sin and hatred of it), and a change of direction (forsaking sin and turning to God in obedience).

For the kingdom of heaven is at hand. “The kingdom of heaven” means the kingdom of God. Matthew, writing for Jews, usually says heaven in place of God, following the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding God’s name. It does not mean a place where people go when they die. A kingdom is a reign before it is a realm: “kingdom” here means rule, kingship, God exercising his royal power to save his people and to judge evil, as the prophets promised (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14; Isaiah 52:7). “At hand” means it has come near, arriving now, in the person of the King who is about to appear.

Why repent? Because when the King comes, he comes to save and to judge. To be ready for his reign, people must turn from their rebellion and submit to him. The appropriate response to the arrival of the holy King is not first celebration but self-examination. When Isaiah saw the King in the temple, his first words were woe is me, for I am lost (Isaiah 6:5): the nearer the holy God comes, the less any sinner can stand at ease. Jesus will begin his ministry with exactly the same words (4:17).

What it does not mean. Not that repentance earns entry into the kingdom. Repentance is the turning of empty hands to God; the kingdom is his gift. It is the homeward turn of a heart that grace has already begun to thaw (2 Corinthians 7:10). Nor is repentance a single moment only: the Christian life is a life of continual repentance. The first of Luther’s ninety-five theses says that when Jesus said Repent, he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom. Some Bible-loving readers (classic dispensationalists) distinguish the kingdom of heaven, an earthly kingdom offered to Israel and postponed when Israel rejected it, from the kingdom of God. Most interpreters hold that the two phrases mean the same thing. Matthew proves it himself: watching the rich young man walk away, Jesus says it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, and in the very next sentence, easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (19:23–24). The kingdom has come in Christ, grows now through the gospel, and will be consummated at his return. This commentary’s view: one kingdom, already inaugurated and not yet consummated.

How do I know whether I have really repented? Not by the strength of your tears, but by the direction of your life. Ask: Do I now see this sin as God sees it, as an offence against him and not only a problem for me? Have I stopped excusing it and started fighting it? Have I brought it to Christ for forgiveness, trusting him rather than my own resolve? Has anything actually changed, even a little, in how I live? Real repentance often begins small and is imperfect; you will fall again. But it keeps turning back to God. If you are grieved by your sin and still running to Christ with it, that grief and that running are the Spirit’s work in you.

On a Tuesday. Repentance is not only for the day you became a Christian. It is the daily shape of a Christian life, and it is quieter than we expect: a sharp word taken back at breakfast, a habit confessed before it hardens, a heart that keeps coming home to a Father who is always glad to see it.
verseByVerse.note: The wilderness of Judea is the dry, barren land between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. Matthew usually says “kingdom of heaven” where the others say “kingdom of God” — the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah. The quotation is Isaiah 40:3. Isaiah 40 begins the great section of comfort to the exiles, promising a new exodus: God coming in person to lead his people home across the desert, like a shepherd-king at the head of the march (Isaiah 40:10–11).

In the flow. Who is John? Matthew’s answer is a Bible verse: if John is only the voice, the one whose road it is must still come, and in verse 13 he does.

The voice of one crying in the wilderness. In Isaiah, a voice calls for a road to be prepared through the wilderness for God’s coming. John is that voice. He is not the main event but the announcer (John 1:23). By John’s day the verse was a watchword of hope; the community at Qumran, beside the Dead Sea, had withdrawn into the desert on the strength of it. Every devout ear caught its weight: the King is coming, ready the road.

Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. Before a king visited a region, workers levelled and straightened the road (Isaiah 40:4). John’s preaching prepares the way by preparing hearts: repentance removes the obstacles. The proud hills of self-righteousness are brought low, the sunken valleys of despair filled with hope, the crooked dealings made straight.

Whom the road is for. In Isaiah, “the Lord” is the LORD, Yahweh, God himself. Matthew applies it to Jesus. John prepares the way for Jesus, and in doing so prepares the way for God. Jesus is the LORD come to his people.

Now John wore a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. This is almost exactly how the Old Testament describes Elijah: a hairy man, with a belt of leather about his waist (2 Kings 1:8). John dressed as the Elijah promised in Malachi 4:5–6, who would come before the great day of the Lord. Jesus confirms it (11:14; 17:12–13).

And his food was locusts and wild honey. Locusts were permitted food under the law (Leviticus 11:22) and are still eaten by poor people in the region. It was the diet of a man living off the land. He lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anybody, which is precisely why no one can buy him.

What it does not mean. Not that rough clothing or a strict diet makes someone more spiritual. Jesus later contrasted John’s austerity with his own eating and drinking, and said that both were rejected (11:18–19). Nor does it mean that John was literally Elijah returned from heaven: he denied that (John 1:21). He came in Elijah’s spirit and power (Luke 1:17).

How can I point people to Christ rather than to myself? Start by remembering what you are: a voice, not the Word. In conversation about faith, talk more about what Jesus has done than about your own experience or opinions, and open the Bible with people rather than only telling them what you think. Resist the pull to be seen as the wise one or the indispensable helper; John’s joy was to decrease so that Christ would increase (John 3:30). Invite people to come and hear Christ’s word preached, not only to come and hear you. And when you are thanked, pass the thanks upward. A signpost has done its job when people stop looking at it and walk on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him. “All” is a natural exaggeration for very many; Josephus also records John’s popularity. And the people are not going to the temple. They are going out: out of Jerusalem, out of the towns, out to the wilderness and down to the river.

And they were baptized by him. To baptise (baptizō) means to dip, immerse or wash. Gentile converts to Judaism were washed as part of their conversion (a custom clearly recorded a little later, and perhaps older), so John’s baptism was startling: he called Jews to start again like outsiders, saying, you are no cleaner before God by birth than any Gentile.

In the river Jordan. The river where Israel had crossed into the promised land under Joshua (Joshua 3). It is where Elijah struck the water with his cloak, crossed over and was taken up (2 Kings 2:8–11), and where Naaman the Syrian went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kings 5:14). John was asking Israel to go back outside, admit they had no more claim on the land than a Gentile convert, and come in again by grace.

Joshua at the Jordan again. The first time Israel came through this river, they were led by Joshua; the one who will come walking down to the bank bears the same name. Hebrews draws the line itself: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day (Hebrews 4:8). The first Joshua brought Israel into a land, and they lost it through sin. The second Joshua will bring his people into an inheritance that cannot perish, because he deals with the sin itself.

Confessing their sins. Confession means agreeing with God about one’s sin. John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance (Mark 1:4; Acts 19:4). It did not take away sin by itself; it expressed repentance and pointed forward to the forgiveness the coming one would bring.

What did they confess? Matthew does not say, but Luke gives a strong hint: John named some sins when the crowds asked him what they should do. To ordinary people: you keep two coats while your neighbour shivers (Luke 3:11). To the tax collectors: your greed and extortion (Luke 3:13). To the soldiers: your bullying, your false accusations, your discontent with your pay (Luke 3:14). Behind it all lay the sins the prophets had forever exposed: dishonest scales and withheld wages (Malachi 3:5), worship that was all lips and no heart (Isaiah 29:13), the quiet idolatry of loving money and reputation more than God. Their sins were not strange ancient relics. They were ours.

What it does not mean. Not that John’s baptism is the same as Christian baptism. Christian baptism is into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (28:19), and signifies union with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4). Nor does confession mean that we must list every sin to a priest to be forgiven. Confession is made to God (1 John 1:9), and sometimes to those we have wronged or to fellow believers (James 5:16).

Should I confess my sins to another Christian? Not to obtain forgiveness, which comes from God alone through Christ (1 John 1:9). But often it is wise and healing. Confess to anyone you have wronged, and put it right where you can (5:23–24). And when a sin has a grip on you, telling a trusted, mature believer brings it into the light, breaks its secrecy and gives you someone to pray with and keep you accountable (James 5:16). Choose someone discreet and of the same sex for sexual matters. You do not need a priest; you need a brother or sister who will point you to Christ.

Should I be baptised now, if I was baptised as a baby? This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for those who have repented and believed, because in the New Testament it follows repentance and faith, and is rightly given by immersion; so we believe a person baptised in infancy who has come to faith should be baptised as a believer. Many godly Christians, our paedobaptist brothers in Presbyterian and Anglican churches, hold sincerely that infant baptism is true baptism and should not be repeated, and we honour them. Talk it through with the elders of your church, study the passages (28:19; Acts 2:38–41; 8:36–38), and act with a clear conscience. The faith of the one baptised is what John’s riverside crowd teaches us to look for.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and Sadducees. The two leading religious parties, who normally opposed each other. The Pharisees were a respected lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law and the tradition of the elders; their religion often curdled into the self-righteous show Jesus would lay bare (Matthew 23). The Sadducees were the wealthy priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple, cooperated with Rome and denied the resurrection (22:23). Here both groups come together, as they will again against Jesus (16:1).

Coming to his baptism. Possibly to inspect it, possibly to be seen taking part; Luke 7:30 says the Pharisees rejected John’s baptism. Either way, John saw no sign of true repentance.

You brood of vipers! In the desert, when a fire swept through the brush, snakes would flee in front of it. John pictures these leaders as snakes slithering away from the fire of judgment, not because they hate their sin, but because they fear the flames. It may also echo the serpent in Eden (Genesis 3): they are children of the deceiver (John 8:44), carrying poison under religious clothing. Jesus uses the same words of the Pharisees (12:34; 23:33).

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? “The wrath to come” is God’s coming judgment on sin at the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). It was not a new idea but one straight from their own Scriptures: a day of wrath, of distress and anguish (Zephaniah 1:15), the day that comes burning like an oven (Malachi 4:1), the day for which Malachi asked who could endure it (Malachi 3:2). Amos had warned that for the complacent it would be darkness and not light (Amos 5:18–20). But here lay the deadly assumption John meant to shatter: they took it for granted that this wrath was for Gentiles and sinners, and that they, as sons of Abraham, would stand safe among the spectators. John asks sarcastically: what has suddenly made you, so confident in your righteousness, think you need to escape it? The fire is for every unrepentant heart, the religious ones first of all.

Where to flee. John’s question assumes there is somewhere to run. Paul calls the believer’s hope Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10). There is one place the fire cannot reach: the ground it has already burned. At the cross the wrath John announced fell, in full, on the Coming One himself, and everyone who stands where he stood is safe. The Pharisees were fleeing the right fire in the wrong direction, into their own religion. The only way to escape the wrath to come is to run to the Son who bore it.

Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. Fruit is what a tree produces, the visible result of its life. Repentance is invisible, in the heart, but real repentance shows itself in a changed life (Luke 3:10–14, and see v. 6).

What it does not mean. Not that the fruit earns forgiveness: fruit does not make a tree good; it shows that the tree is good (7:17–18), and the change John demands is one only the Coming One can work in a heart (see v. 10). Nor does John’s harshness license Christians to insult people. His anger was aimed at religious leaders who were misleading others, not at seekers or ordinary sinners, whom he received.

If I still struggle with the same sin, is my repentance fake? Not necessarily. Fruit grows slowly and unevenly, and every believer fights remaining sin to the end (Romans 7:15–25; 1 John 1:8). The question John presses is not whether you are perfect but whether you are a fruit-bearing tree at all: is there a real fight, a real grief, a direction of change? The man who has made peace with his sin and hides it behind religion is the viper John exposes. The man who hates his sin, confesses it again and again, and slowly sees a little ground taken back, is a tree with fruit on it, however small. Keep fighting, and keep coming to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law; Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, who denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not presume to say to yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father," for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have Abraham as our father. Do not even think it, says John. Many Jews believed that being physically descended from Abraham guaranteed a place in God’s kingdom. Later rabbinic writings even record the belief that Abraham sits at the gate of Gehenna (hell) to turn back any circumcised Israelite. John says: your ancestry will not save you. Our versions are quieter but just the same: I was raised in church, I have always been a decent person, I am not like them. Anything we lean on instead of Christ, however good, becomes a rival saviour. A Christian home is a great privilege, but privilege does not save; Paul explains that the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham’s faith (Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 3:7).

God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Probably a wordplay in Hebrew or Aramaic: children (banim) and stones (abanim). A pun, and deadly serious: God does not need you; he can make Abraham’s children out of rocks. And think where he is standing. When Israel first came into this land, Joshua had twelve men carry twelve stones up out of the bed of this same river as a memorial for the twelve tribes (Joshua 4:1–7). John stands at that river, gestures at the stones, and tells the sons of Abraham that God could begin the twelve tribes again from the rocks. This anticipates the Gentiles, dead stones, being brought into Abraham’s family by faith (8:11).

Abraham’s one true Son. Who, then, are Abraham’s children? The answer stands a few yards away. Paul says the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, singular, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16), and that if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). Belonging to Abraham does not run through the bloodline into him; it runs through him into everyone who trusts him, Jew or Gentile.

The axe at the root. A woodcutter lays his axe against the base of a tree to measure the stroke. Israel was often pictured as God’s tree or vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), and this is not a gentle warning but an imminent verdict.

The fruitless tree and the fire. A tree that produces no fruit is cut down for firewood (Luke 13:6–9), and fire is a common biblical image of God’s judgment. Grace is real, but so is the axe.

Does verse 10 teach salvation by works? No. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone; our works add nothing to the verdict (Ephesians 2:8–9). Yet the faith that justifies is never a faith that stays alone. A living faith bears fruit as surely as a living tree does; faith apart from works is dead (James 2:26). So John is not saying that fruit earns life; he is saying that fruitlessness exposes death. When Scripture speaks of judgment according to works (Romans 2:6), it means our works are the evidence brought into the court, not the price paid. We are saved by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. And even the fruit is grace, for God must first make the tree good. An axe never turned a dead tree into a living one; that making alive is the Coming One’s work.

Can I assume my children are Christians because they are growing up in a Christian home? Treat them as precious children under the sound of the gospel, with every privilege, and pray and hope for their salvation with great confidence in God’s faithfulness. But do not assume it on the basis of the family alone. Each child must come to Christ personally in repentance and faith. So teach them the gospel plainly, call them to trust Christ for themselves, rejoice at every sign of real faith, and never let them think that being your child, or attending church, makes them right with God. Many children of believers come to faith so early that they cannot remember a time without it. That is a great mercy, and it is still their own faith.

For worship. Our God can make sons out of stones, and we were stones: dead, hard, without a claim on heaven. He who raised Isaac from a barren womb and Adam from the dust has raised us by his Spirit. The axe lay at the root of every tree, and it fell on the one Tree that had borne nothing but good fruit, when Jesus was cut off from the land of the living for us. Now no child of God need fear the axe. He is the root, and we are grafted into him.

parallels.desc: every tree that does not bear good fruit

verseByVerse.quote: I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I baptize you with water for repentance. John’s water was a sign, no more: an outward washing that pictured the inward cleansing the people sought. Water can wash the body; it cannot change the heart.

He who is coming after me is mightier than I. “The coming one” was a title for the Messiah (11:3). John, the greatest prophet (11:11), says that the Messiah is far greater than he. John can lower you into the river; only Jesus can baptise you in the Spirit.

Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. Carrying or untying a master’s sandals was a task given to the lowest slave. John says he is not worthy even of that.

He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. The prophets promised that in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on his people, giving them new hearts and new life (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28–29). The Messiah would do this. It happened at Pentecost, when the risen Jesus poured out the Spirit (Acts 1:5; 2:1–4, 33). To baptise with the Spirit is to immerse a person in the Spirit’s life, and every believer receives it (1 Corinthians 12:13): the Spirit of God comes to live in you, gives you a new heart that wants God instead of running from him, and joins you to Christ and to his people. Water touches the skin; the Spirit reaches the place no water can.

And fire. Fire in Scripture can mean purifying (Malachi 3:2–3; Isaiah 4:4) or judgment (vv. 10, 12). The context, with fire in verses 10 and 12, points to judgment: one does not refine wheat with unquenchable fire. The Coming One brings a double baptism: the Spirit for those who repent, fire for those who do not. Some also see a purifying sense, fulfilled in the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3). This commentary’s view: chiefly judgment, though the Spirit’s work also purifies; the Messiah comes both to save and to judge.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. On a breezy threshing floor, after the grain was trodden, a farmer used a winnowing fork, a large wooden pitchfork, to toss it into the wind. The heavy grain fell back to the floor; the light husks and straw, called chaff, blew to one side. Until he comes, wheat and chaff lie mingled on one floor, the truly repentant and the merely religious side by side; his coming is the wind that sorts them.

He will clear his threshing floor. The wheat, his true people, will be gathered into the barn and kept safe. The chaff was swept up and burned. “Unquenchable” means it cannot be put out: final, eternal judgment (Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:43–48). There is no third heap between wheat and chaff: only the barn or the fire.

In the flow. These verses are the climax of John’s preaching, and we expect the Judge to come with the winnowing fork. What comes next is the surprise of the Gospel: the Coming One asks to be baptised among sinners (vv. 13–15). The Judge first stands with the guilty, and that is how any of them will be found wheat.

What it does not mean. Not that the baptism with the Spirit is a second experience after conversion that only some Christians receive. Some Pentecostal traditions teach this, pointing to the Samaritans (Acts 8:14–17) and the Ephesian disciples (Acts 19:1–7), and they often shame the rest of us by their hunger for God. But those episodes in Acts mark unrepeatable turning points as the gospel crossed from Jews to Samaritans to Gentiles, and Paul says all believers have been baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). This commentary’s view: Spirit baptism happens at conversion for every believer, though believers may be filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18).

How does John’s baptism relate to Christian baptism? John’s looked forward to the One who was coming; Christian baptism looks back to his death and resurrection and is given in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (28:19). That is why the disciples at Ephesus, who knew only John’s baptism, were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:3–5). Christian baptism rests on Jesus’ command, not on his own baptism, which was unique.

Where Christians differ: hell. Some evangelicals, reading Scripture with real reverence, hold that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist (annihilationism). The traditional view holds that hell is conscious, eternal punishment (25:46; Revelation 14:11). This commentary’s view: the traditional view. Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (25:46): if the one is unending, it is hard to read the other as brief.

How can a loving God send people to unquenchable fire? Because his love is holy, and holy love is not indifferent to evil. A judge who shrugged at cruelty and murder would not be loving but corrupt. Sin is not a small slip against a small law; it is rebellion against an infinitely good God, and its punishment is just. But see who is speaking these words: the herald of the Saviour. God warns before he judges, he gives his own Son to bear the fire for all who will come, and he pleads with sinners to turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). No one in hell will be there because God refused to receive them when they came. The fire is real so that the refuge would be precious.

How do I know whether I am wheat or chaff? Not by inspecting your own feelings, and not by comparing yourself with others, but by asking where you are resting. Chaff is not bad wheat; it is empty husk. The way to be found wheat is not to be impressive in oneself but to come to the Coming One in repentance and faith. If you have fled to Christ, trusting him and not yourself, and if your life is turning, however slowly, then you are his, and he gathers his wheat; he does not lose it (John 10:28). If you are not sure, come to him now. He has never yet sent away anyone who came.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back, the chaff blew away and was burned.

parallels.desc: tongues as of fire at Pentecost

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. John would have prevented him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus came from Galilee. From Nazareth, about seventy miles north. This is Jesus’ first appearance as an adult in Matthew, at about thirty years old (Luke 3:23). He walked for days to stand in a queue of sinners.

The hidden years. The eighteen years in a village workshop about which Scripture says nothing were not wasted time but obedience, part of the righteousness he is about to say he came to fulfil.

To the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. He came on purpose, and it is a surprise: John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance, with confession of sins. Why would the sinless Son of God (1:20–21) be baptised?

John would have prevented him. The verb means he tried to stop him, and John meant it: this was not polite modesty but a real protest at the water’s edge. John recognised who Jesus was. (In John 1:31–33 the Baptist says he did not know him until the Spirit descended; perhaps he knew his relative and sensed his holiness, while the sign confirmed that he was the Messiah.)
