I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? John confesses his own sin and need. He has just said that the Coming One will baptise with the Spirit (v. 11); he himself needs that. Even the greatest prophet needs the Saviour. This is the man who has just called the religious leadership a brood of vipers. Of all the men on that riverbank he had least reason to think himself dirty, and he is the one who says out loud that he needs washing. The people most conscious of their own need are almost never the people you would nominate.

Right premises, wrong conclusion. John’s theology is excellent and his conclusion wrong: on the strength of three correct premises he tries to stop the Son of God doing what he came to do. God is always working with more of the picture than we have.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus came to confess his own sins. Scripture is clear that he had none (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). Verse 15 explains why he was baptised.

Do mature Christians still need Jesus as much as new believers do? More, if anything, and they know it better. John was the greatest man born of women, on Jesus’ own testimony (11:11), and his first instinct on meeting Jesus was to say: I need you. Growth in grace does not make us less dependent on Christ; it makes us more aware of how dependent we are. The longer a believer walks with him, the more clearly he sees his own sin and Christ’s sufficiency. If you find yourself feeling that you have outgrown the simple gospel, that is not maturity but drift. The mature saint’s prayer sounds very like the new convert’s: Lord, I need you.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered him, "Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Then he consented. And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let it be so now. For the present, at this stage of God’s plan: Jesus does not deny that he is greater than John; he asks John to accept this for now.

For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. The key sentence, found only in Matthew. “Righteousness” in Matthew means doing what God requires, living in line with his will (5:6, 20; 6:33). Jesus came to fulfil the law (5:17), not to bypass the law’s requirements but to meet them all on behalf of his people. Three truths fit together.

Identification. Jesus stands with sinners in the water of repentance, though he has no sin of his own: the beginning of what the cross completes, when he is numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12).

Obedience. John’s baptism was God’s command for Israel at that time (21:25). Jesus, as the true Israelite, obeys every command of God, so that his righteousness would be complete. Reformed theology calls this Christ’s active obedience: he kept the whole law perfectly on our behalf, so that his righteousness could be credited to us (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Credited means counted to our account: God does not merely wipe the believer’s slate clean and leave it empty; he writes Christ’s obedience on it and treats the believer as one who has kept his law, because Christ kept it for him (Romans 4:5–6; Philippians 3:9).

Commissioning. His baptism marks the start of his public work as Messiah. As priests were washed and anointed for their office (Exodus 29:4–7), and kings were anointed for theirs (1 Samuel 16:13), Jesus is washed and anointed with the Spirit, the true Priest and the true King.

And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water. Jesus came up, probably out of the river after being immersed; the phrase fits immersion, as does the word baptise itself, though Christians who baptise by pouring argue that it describes where Jesus stood. Jesus’ baptism was unique, the anointing of the sinless Son, so it does not by itself settle who should be baptised; that rests on the command to baptise disciples (28:19).

And behold, the heavens were opened to him. Heaven opening was a sign that God was about to reveal something (Ezekiel 1:1; Acts 7:56). Isaiah had prayed that God would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Now he does.

He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him. The Spirit came visibly, in a form like a dove. The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), or Noah’s dove after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12): a new beginning. Isaiah had promised that the Spirit of the LORD would rest on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). Here is the Messiah’s anointing, not with oil, but with the Spirit. And the Spirit comes to rest on him; John’s Gospel adds that he remained (John 1:32), not coming and going as he often had on the judges and kings of old (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 16:14).

In the flow. Verse 15 is the first time Jesus speaks in Matthew, and his first word is about fulfilling all righteousness (5:17); the Spirit who rests on him here leads him straight into the wilderness (4:1), where that righteousness is tested.

Was the Spirit not already with Jesus? Indeed he was, fully, from the very first. This child was conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:20); as the eternal Son he was never for one instant without the Spirit, never less than fully God, never touched by sin. Nothing changes in his person at the Jordan. What happens is two things at once. First, it is his anointing: the Spirit who always dwelt in him now equips the incarnate Son, in his true humanity, for the work that begins this day (Acts 10:38). Second, it is a sign for others: John tells us that the Spirit descending and remaining on him was the appointed sign by which he would know the Messiah (John 1:32–34). The dove was God’s own testimony, pointing out his Son.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism. Some early teachers said Jesus was an ordinary man adopted as God’s Son at his baptism. But Matthew has already shown that he was conceived by the Spirit and is Immanuel, God with us (1:20–23). The baptism publicly declares and equips who he already was. Nor was the Spirit a literal dove: Matthew says like a dove.

Do I need to be baptised to follow Jesus? Yes, because he commands it, not simply because he set an example. His own baptism was unique: he was the sinless Son standing in for sinners. Ours is a sign of something he has done for us: our union with him in his death and resurrection, and our cleansing from sin (Romans 6:3–4; Acts 22:16). Baptism does not save; the thief on the cross was saved without it (Luke 23:43). But a believer who refuses it is disobeying his Lord’s clear command (28:19). If you have come to faith and have not been baptised, speak to your church’s elders this week.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records John’s protest and Jesus’ reply.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a voice from heaven said. God the Father speaks. Not an echo, as later Jewish writings described the voice heard since prophecy ceased, but God’s own voice.

This is my beloved Son. Echoes Psalm 2:7, where God says to his anointed King, you are my Son. It declares Jesus the royal Messiah. But beloved Son also recalls Genesis 22:2, where God told Abraham to take his son, his only son, whom he loved, Isaac, and offer him as a sacrifice. The beloved Son will be offered. And it goes deeper still: Jesus is the Son of God not merely as a title of kingship, but by nature, the eternal Son (11:27).

With whom I am well pleased. Echoes Isaiah 42:1, about the Servant of the LORD: my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. The Servant in Isaiah suffers and dies for the sins of the people (Isaiah 53). In one sentence the Father declares Jesus both the royal Son of Psalm 2 and the suffering Servant: a King who will reign by suffering. The Father’s delight is the fountain from which all of Jesus’ ministry flows: he acts out of a secure identity, not toward an uncertain approval.

The Trinity. Here the three persons of the Trinity appear together, each distinct: the Father speaking from heaven, the Son standing in the water, the Spirit descending. One God in three persons. The same three names appear at the end of the Gospel in the baptismal command (28:19).

The voice everyone wants to hear. Many people spend their lives auditioning: for a parent whose approval never quite arrived, for an employer, for strangers on a screen, aching to hear a voice they trust say: you are mine, and I am pleased with you. Matthew has recorded that sentence said over a man in a river. Has it anything to do with us?

For believers. It has everything to do with us, and the link is not imitation but union. Paul says we are blessed in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6), not accepted alongside him, or for trying to be like him, but in him, our life hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3). The Spirit of God’s Son is sent into our hearts so that we cry Abba, Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:16–17). By faith a believer is joined to Christ so closely that what is true of him is counted true of the believer, as a branch shares the life of the vine (John 15:5). In Christ, God says to every believer: you are my beloved child (1 John 3:1). This is the ground of our assurance, not our performance.

The great exchange. It began here. At the Jordan the sinless one stepped into the place of sinners, taking a washing he did not need. At Golgotha he stepped into the place of sinners again, taking a judgment he did not deserve. He took what was ours: the guilt, the verdict, the abandonment, and on the cross the silence where a voice from heaven should have been. And what he gives in exchange is what was always his: the standing, the sonship, and the Father’s welcome. Paul gathers it into a single verse: the one who never sinned was made sin for us, so that in him we might be made God’s righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21).

What it does not mean. Not that there are three gods, or that one God appears in three different modes at different times. Here all three persons are present at the same moment, distinct from one another, yet one God. And not that God approves of everyone exactly as they are and nothing more need be said. The same chapter has an axe and a fire. The word is spoken over those who are in the Beloved, and there is a door to be walked through to get there: turn, and come.

Textual note. Matthew has This is my beloved Son, spoken about Jesus; Mark and Luke have You are my beloved Son, spoken to him (Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22). The Gospel writers often report speech by its sense rather than word for word, and both forms say the same thing. Matthew’s form stresses the public declaration to the witnesses.

How can one God be three persons? We cannot fully explain it, and should not expect to; God is greater than our minds. But we can say what Scripture says. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God (John 1:1), and the Holy Spirit is God (Acts 5:3–4). They are not three parts of God, nor three masks one God wears, but three persons who each fully possess the one divine nature, eternally loving one another. That is why God is love in himself, before there was a world to love (John 17:24). The Trinity is not a puzzle for clever people; it is the God the gospel reveals: the Father who sends, the Son who saves, the Spirit who gives life.

How can I believe God is pleased with me when I keep failing? Look at when the Father spoke: before a single sermon, before one miracle, before the cross. If the Father’s delight in his Son was not produced by performance, then the delight he has in those who are in his Son is not produced by yours either. You will not settle this by inspecting your feelings, but by looking away from yourself to the one you have come to. God is not pleased with your sin, and he will discipline you as a father does (Hebrews 12:6). But his verdict on you was announced in his Son, it was not earned, and it cannot be forfeited by a bad week. A father can be grieved by his child’s disobedience without ceasing to delight in his child.

For worship. The heavens opened, and for one moment the eternal life of God was shown on earth: the Father delighting, the Son obeying, the Spirit resting on him like a dove come home. The Father who needed nothing opened that circle to let sinners in. The beloved Son went down into the water and down into death, so that the voice which spoke over him at the Jordan might speak over all who are in him. Glory to the Father, who loved us in his Beloved; to the Son, who took our place in the water and on the cross; and to the Spirit, who seals us as children of God.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights
the same voice at the transfiguration

3.theology:
The Trinity at the Jordan. At the baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends on him, and the Father speaks from heaven: three distinct persons, one God, acting together. The Trinity is not a later addition to Christian thought but the shape of the gospel itself.

The Father approves, the Spirit equips, the Son obeys, and that pattern runs through the New Testament: the Father sends, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies. Christians are baptised in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), and pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.
3.examples:
Then: John stands at the end of a line of prophets who prepared the way for God’s action, each a voice and not the Word. His greatness lay in pointing away from himself: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Every faithful preacher and teacher stands where he stood: making the way straight, then getting out of the way.

Now: Many of us spend our lives seeking approval. The Father’s word at the Jordan reaches everyone who is in Christ. We are accepted in the Beloved, not for what we have done but because of who he is and what he has done, and our life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3).

4.title: The Tested King
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. <sup>2</sup>And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup>And the tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” <sup>4</sup>But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” <sup>5</sup>Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple <sup>6</sup>and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>7</sup>Jesus said to him, “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>8</sup>Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. <sup>9</sup>And he said to him, “All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.” <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>11</sup>Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him. <sup>12</sup>Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. <sup>13</sup>And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, <sup>14</sup>so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: <sup>15</sup>“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles — <sup>16</sup>the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.” <sup>17</sup>From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>18</sup>While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>19</sup>And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” <sup>20</sup>Immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. <sup>22</sup>Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. <sup>23</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. <sup>24</sup>So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them. <sup>25</sup>And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
4.overview:
The Spirit who came down at the baptism leads Jesus straight into the wilderness, not to abandon him but to prove him. The forty days echo Israel’s forty years, when God’s people failed every test. Jesus passes each one with the weapon Israel had and we have: the written word of God. Three times the devil attacks, and three times Jesus answers from Deuteronomy.

Each temptation offers a shortcut. Turn stones to bread: use your power for your own comfort. Throw yourself down: make God prove his love in public. Bow to me: take the kingdoms without the cross. Jesus refuses every one. The crown comes by the cross.

Then the ministry begins in Galilee of the Gentiles (Isaiah 9:1), a region of mixed people and poor reputation. The people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light. The first disciples are fishermen with nets and boats, and the light goes first to those who sit in the dark.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Temptation of Jesus in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. The forty days echo Israel's forty years, and the three temptations echo Israel's failures over bread, testing God and idolatry. Where Israel fell, Jesus stands, answering each time from Deuteronomy. He overcomes as our champion, the last Adam and true Israel, and then the devil leaves him, for a time, and angels come and serve him.
verseByVerse.theology: The temptation is not a test of willpower but a conflict at a turning point of God's saving work. The devil who won in Eden now faces the last Adam in a wilderness, and loses. Jesus' weapon is the word of God, believed and obeyed, and that word is the Christian's resource in temptation too, used in the strength of the Spirit who now lives in us.
verseByVerse.examples: Each of the devil's offers has a good thing inside it: food is not evil, God's protection is real, and the nations are Jesus' promised inheritance. The temptation lies in the shortcut: the good thing the wrong way, on the wrong timetable, from the wrong hand. Jesus refuses not because the ends are bad but because the path bypasses his Father's will and the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 4 shows the beloved Son proved in battle and then beginning his work. Where Adam fell in a garden and Israel in the desert, Jesus stands, answering each temptation from Deuteronomy: he will not feed himself outside his Father’s will, force God to prove his love, or buy the kingdoms of the world with one act of false worship. Then he moves to Capernaum in despised Galilee, where Isaiah said the great light would dawn, preaches the kingdom, calls four fishermen and heals every disease.

Then. Immediately after the Father declared him his beloved Son (3:17). First the Father’s word of love, then the testing: Jesus faced the devil secure in the Father’s delight, and the devil’s first attack goes straight at that word: “If you are the Son of God” (v. 3).

Jesus was led up by the Spirit. The temptation was not an accident. The Spirit who had just come upon him (3:16) led him into it deliberately, to prove the Son faithful and to begin his victory over the devil.

Into the wilderness. The Judean desert. Israel spent forty years in the wilderness after passing through the Red Sea (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). Jesus, having passed through the water of baptism, now goes into the wilderness, reliving the story of Israel.

To be tempted by the devil. “Tempt” (peirazō) means both to test and to tempt. From God’s side, this was a test, to prove his Son’s faithfulness, as God tested Israel in the wilderness to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). From the devil’s side, it was a temptation, an attempt to make him sin. “Devil” (diabolos) means slanderer, accuser. He is a real, personal, fallen angel, the enemy of God and his people (John 8:44; Revelation 12:9). He tempted the first Adam and succeeded (Genesis 3); now he tempts the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). Adam stood for the whole human race, and all who belong to him fell with him; Jesus stands for a new humanity, and what he does here he does for all who belong to him (Romans 5:18–19).

After fasting forty days and forty nights. Moses fasted forty days and nights on the mountain when he received the law (Exodus 34:28); Elijah travelled forty days and nights to Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:8); Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33–34). Forty days for Israel’s forty years.

He was hungry. Jesus was truly human, with real hunger and real weakness. The devil attacked him at his weakest point.

The three temptations. They correspond to three tests of Israel in the wilderness, and Jesus answers each with a verse from Deuteronomy 6–8, where Moses reminds Israel of those tests. Israel grumbled for bread, put God to the test and worshipped idols; where Israel failed, the true Son succeeds.

What it does not mean. Not that God tempts anyone to sin. James says that God tempts no one (James 1:13). God tested Jesus; the devil tempted him. The same event can be both: God’s purpose for good, the devil’s for evil (Genesis 50:20). Nor does it mean that being tempted is itself sinful. Our High Priest was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Temptation is the offer of sin; sin is accepting it. A believer who is fiercely tempted has not sinned by being tempted.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some faithful Christians say Jesus was able not to sin, but could have sinned, otherwise the temptations were not real. Most of the Reformed tradition holds that Jesus was not able to sin, because he was one person, the eternal Son of God, who cannot sin. This commentary’s view: he could not sin, yet the temptations were entirely real. A strong army cannot be defeated, but the attack against it is still real; indeed, only one who does not give in feels the full weight of temptation to the end. Jesus knows the pressure of temptation more fully than anyone, which is why he can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

Does a hard season mean God is punishing me? Not necessarily. Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit, sinless, and straight after the Father’s word of love. If you are in a long dry stretch, prayers that seem to go nowhere, a season of loss or waiting with no visible end, take three things from these verses. It is not necessarily discipline; the Spirit sometimes leads his own into hard country on purpose. It has a limit: forty days, and Matthew tells you at the outset that it ended. And you are not alone in it, because the one who has been through this country walked out of it, and is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). The wilderness is where the enemy expects to finish you. In the hands of God it is very often where you are being made.

Is the devil not just a myth from a less scientific age? Jesus did not think so, and he is the one who met him. Science studies the physical world; it cannot rule out a spiritual creature, any more than it can rule out God. And the evil of our own century, its cruelty, its lies and its strange power to ruin what is good, is hard to explain as only chemistry. Scripture gives a sober account: the devil is real, but a creature, already defeated, and no excuse for our own sin (James 1:14). The greater danger is not believing in him too much, but forgetting that he is there.

Should Christians fast today? Yes, as a voluntary help to prayer, not as a rule or a merit. Jesus assumes his disciples will fast (6:16–18; 9:15), and the early church fasted when seeking God’s guidance (Acts 13:2–3). Fasting is not a way to earn God’s favour or twist his arm; it is a way of saying with the body that we need God more than food. Start simply: skip one meal and use the time to pray. Anyone with a medical condition, an eating disorder, or who is pregnant should take advice and may fast from something other than food. Do it quietly, before your Father who sees in secret.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls Moses on the mountain and Israel’s forty years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: tempted as we are, yet without sin

verseByVerse.quote: And the tempter came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread." But he answered, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are the Son of God. The Greek form of the if assumes the statement for the sake of argument: the devil is not openly doubting it but twisting it. The Father had just said, This is my beloved Son (3:17). The devil says, in effect: if you are his Son, act like one. Use your rights. Why should God’s beloved Son go hungry?

Command these stones to become loaves of bread. The Judean desert is strewn with stones that can look like small round loaves. Was making bread wrong? Jesus later fed five thousand people (14:13–21). The poison is in the if: prove your sonship by serving yourself, snatch relief at my suggestion, step out from under your Father’s hand. It was a temptation to distrust: to doubt that the Father would provide, and to take matters into his own hands. Israel did the same in the wilderness, complaining that God had brought them out to starve (Exodus 16:3).

But he answered, It is written. Jesus answers with Scripture. The Greek means it stands written, and remains authoritative. The Son of God submits to the written word, and uses it as his weapon (Ephesians 6:17).

Man shall not live by bread alone. From Deuteronomy 8:3. Moses, looking back over forty years, explains why God led Israel the long, hard way: he humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with manna, so that they would learn that people do not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from God’s mouth. Bread keeps the body alive for a while; God’s word gives life now and for ever.

How we know it was a God-ordained hunger. No verse says the Father commanded him to stay hungry, but the Spirit had led him here on purpose, and Jesus shows how he reads the moment by the text he reaches for: a verse about God deliberately letting his people hunger to teach them dependence.

But by every word that comes from the mouth of God. Jesus would rather be hungry and obedient than full and disobedient. He trusts that the Father who led him into the wilderness will sustain him. And he did: angels came and served him (v. 11). Where Israel said, in effect, give us bread or we perish, Jesus says: my life rests not on bread I can conjure but on every word from my Father’s mouth, including his word that I be here, and wait, and trust.

What it does not mean. Not that physical needs do not matter. Jesus teaches us to pray for daily bread (6:11), and he fed the hungry. The point is the order: God’s word and will come first, and we trust him for the rest (6:33).

How do I actually use Scripture against temptation? Know your particular temptations, and prepare in advance a few verses that speak directly to them: for anxiety about money, 6:31–33; for lust, 5:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:18–20; for anger, James 1:19–20; for fear, Isaiah 41:10. Learn them by heart, because in the moment of temptation you will not have time to look them up. When the temptation comes, say the verse, aloud if you can, and turn it into a prayer. Then do what it says: walk away, close the screen, hold your tongue. Scripture is not a charm; it is the truth that exposes the lie, and the Spirit uses it to strengthen your will.

For worship. He is the obedient Son who keeps the covenant we all broke, and he keeps it as our representative. His victory is counted to us, the spotless obedience that becomes our standing before God. We do not climb up to God’s acceptance by fighting temptation like Jesus. We fight temptation because in Jesus we are already accepted, and never once alone in the fight. He is the Bread of Life, who went hungry so that we might be fed for ever.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, 'He will command his angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.'" Jesus said to him, "Again it is written, 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the devil took him to the holy city. Jerusalem, called the holy city because the temple was there (Nehemiah 11:1; Isaiah 52:1).

How did it happen? Christians who take Scripture with equal seriousness have answered in three ways. Some hold it was bodily throughout: Scripture elsewhere records people carried from place to place (Acts 8:39; Ezekiel 8:3). Others hold that it was visionary, as prophets were shown what their eyes could not otherwise have seen. Others take it as a mixture: a real ascent to the temple, and a showing of the kingdoms no eye could take in from any mountain. Matthew does not tell us, and nothing hangs on it. A temptation presented to the imagination is not a lesser temptation; most of ours arrive that way, and they are quite strong enough to ruin a man. What Matthew wants us to know is that the devil came with real bait, and that the Son of God said no.

And set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The pinnacle (literally little wing) was probably the southeast corner of the temple courts, where the wall towered high above the Kidron Valley. Josephus said that looking down from there made a person dizzy.

If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. Again the challenge to the Father’s word (3:17). The devil suggests: prove that God loves you. Force him to show his care. Perhaps also: give the crowds in the temple a spectacular sign, so that they will accept you without the cross.

He will command his angels concerning you. Now the devil quotes Scripture too (Psalm 91:11–12): knowing the text is not the same as submitting to it. He leaves out a phrase, to guard you in all your ways, meaning the paths of ordinary obedience. The psalm promises protection for those who trust God in danger, not for those who throw themselves into it to force God’s hand: a promise to the humble, not a licence for the presumptuous.

Jesus said to him, Again it is written. Jesus does not argue about the psalm. He answers Scripture with Scripture, showing that the Bible must be interpreted by the Bible. One verse must not be set against the rest.

The sin of Massah. Jesus’ answer is from Deuteronomy 6:16, which in full adds: as you tested him at Massah. At Massah, Israel, thirsty, instead of trusting the God who had just split the sea, turned on Moses and asked whether the LORD was among them or not (Exodus 17:1–7). Massah means testing (Psalm 95:8–9). To put God to the test is to demand that he prove himself on our terms, to create a crisis and dare him to act.

The costume of faith. Israel tested God out of open unbelief: is he even here? The devil dresses the same sin as its opposite, as daring faith: you trust your Father? Then prove it; leap, and let him catch you. Jesus sees through the costume. A faith that must have a spectacle to lean on is not faith but presumption; a trust that demands proof has already stopped trusting. The weak and starving Son trusts the promise without forcing the promise, the very thing Israel, fed with manna every morning, would not do.

But does God not invite us to test him, as in Malachi 3:10? He does, and that is the difference. Testing God is sin when we set the terms and demand proof of our own choosing; it is faith when we take God at his word where he himself has invited it. In Malachi he invites his people to bring their tithes and see whether he will not pour out blessing. That is trusting a promise, not manufacturing a crisis. Gideon’s fleece (Judges 6:36–40) was a concession to a fearful man, not a pattern for guidance.

Is it trusting God to stop taking my medicine? No. Picture a man who stops the treatment his doctor prescribed and announces he is trusting God to heal him, or who makes some rash, ruinous leap with his money and assumes God is bound to catch him. That is not the faith that rests in God; it is the presumption that dictates to him. God ordinarily works through means: food, sleep, doctors, medicine, wise planning. Using them is not a lack of faith but a way of receiving his care. Pray for healing and take the medicine. Trust God for provision and keep a budget. Real faith uses the means God provides and waits on him without demanding he prove his love on cue.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall. The devil quotes Scripture but cuts it short.

parallels.desc: Israel tests the LORD at Massah

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." Then Jesus said to him, "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A very high mountain. Mountains in Matthew are places of revelation: the Sermon on the Mount (5:1), the transfiguration (17:1), and the Great Commission (28:16). This mountain is a counterfeit.

Showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Probably a vision, in a moment of time (Luke 4:5). The temptations escalate, from bread to the temple to all the kingdoms, toward what Jesus actually came to possess.

All these I will give you. The devil claims authority over the world’s kingdoms (Luke 4:6). Jesus calls him the ruler of this world (John 12:31), but his authority is borrowed and limited; it is not truly his to give. Jesus does not dispute the offer’s reality; he refuses its terms.

If you will fall down and worship me. The real offer: the crown without the cross. Jesus had come to receive all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18), but by way of suffering and death (Philippians 2:8–11). The devil offers a shortcut: authority without Gethsemane, good ends by evil means. The Father had already promised him the nations as his heritage (Psalm 2:8). The devil offers to sell him at a discount what was already his by promise.

Be gone, Satan! “Satan” is Hebrew for adversary. It is the only point at which Jesus directly commands the tempter, and a single word sends him away (v. 11). Later Jesus uses almost the same words to Peter when Peter tells him he must not go to the cross (16:23).

For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve. From Deuteronomy 6:13, the command that follows the great confession, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). Israel made a golden calf (Exodus 32); Jesus worships God alone, not for any conceivable reward. He will receive the kingdoms, but from his Father, not from the devil, and by obedience, not compromise: through the cross, not around it.

The three temptations together. The first appealed to physical need, the second to spiritual pride, the third to power and ambition. John later describes the world’s temptations as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16). Eve saw that the fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable to make one wise (Genesis 3:6).

What it does not mean. Not that power, wealth or influence are evil in themselves. Christ will reign over all kingdoms (Revelation 11:15). The question is how they are gained and whom they serve. Nor does Jesus’ victory mean we can conquer temptation in our own strength. We overcome in him: he was victorious for us, and the same Spirit who led him into the wilderness now lives in us, so we share his victory as we trust him and use the same weapon, God’s word.

The shortcut in ordinary clothes. This same temptation comes to us in a hundred ordinary disguises, and underneath it is always a question of worship: the prize you long for, offered at the price of a small bow to something other than God. The promotion is yours if you will fudge the figures; the relationship, if you will set aside what God says about it. Satan’s oldest trick is unchanged: he shows you the kingdoms and hides the bill. Name the shortcut you are being offered and say your own be gone, not in raw willpower but as one joined to the Victor, who refused the bargain for you.

Should I be afraid of the devil? Take him seriously, but do not fear him. He is real, cunning and hostile (1 Peter 5:8), and Christians should not be naive about him. But he is a creature, not God’s equal; he is limited, defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and on a short chain. Here he must leave at one word from Jesus. Peter tells us to resist him, firm in our faith (1 Peter 5:9), and James promises that when we do, he will flee from us (James 4:7). Do not go looking for him in every misfortune, and do not dabble in anything occult. Keep close to Christ, use the armour God gives (Ephesians 6:10–18), and remember that he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).
verseByVerse.note: “Satan” means adversary.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the devil left him. He had to (v. 10). Luke adds that he left until an opportune time (Luke 4:13): a withdrawal, not a surrender.

The opportune times. Matthew shows moments that fit Luke’s phrase. At Caesarea Philippi the offer of the crown without the cross comes from his closest friend, and Jesus says, get behind me, Satan (16:23). The second is at the cross itself. Twice in this wilderness the devil began: if you are the Son of God. And on the hill outside Jerusalem the passers-by say: if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross (27:40). The temptation that opened his ministry closes it. He refused it in the desert on an empty stomach, and he refused it on the cross in agony.

And behold, angels came and were ministering to him. “Ministering” means serving, especially serving food (8:15). Jesus had refused to make bread for himself; now God provided for him. He had refused to call on angels to rescue him from a fall (v. 6); now angels came to serve him on God’s terms: quietly, in an empty wilderness, with no one watching, to a man weak with hunger. What he would not seize, he was given: not on the terms offered or the timetable suggested, but given.

In the flow. Verse 11 closes the scene that 3:17 opened: the Son has proved what the Father said. Now the King is ready to begin.

Why does the same temptation keep coming back after I have resisted it? Because the devil does not give up after one defeat, as this verse shows; he waits for an opportune time. That is not a sign that your resistance failed, but that you are in a real war. Every time you resist, you grow stronger and the habit of obedience deepens. Learn when your opportune times come: when you are tired, alone, hurt, or bored. Plan for them. And when you fall, do not conclude that you have lost the war. Confess, receive forgiveness, and stand again. God promises that no temptation will be beyond what you can bear, and that he will always provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Do angels help Christians today? Scripture says they are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), so God does use them in caring for his people, usually unseen. But we are never told to pray to angels, seek contact with them or worship them (Colossians 2:18; Revelation 22:8–9). Our attention is to be on God, who commands them, and on Christ, who is far above them (Hebrews 1:4). You may take comfort that God has more help for you than you can see, and leave the details to him.

For worship. The angels who had been offered as a stunt came instead as servants, laying a table in the wilderness for the King who would not make his own bread. He who refused to feed himself would give his own body as bread for the world. The one they served that day is the one who will return with all his angels in glory (25:31), the conqueror of the tempter, the faithful Son, the Lord of hosts. The devil left him. The Father never did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — The Beginning of Ministry in Galilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After John is handed over, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and settles in Capernaum, fulfilling Isaiah's promise that light would dawn in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. He preaches that the kingdom of heaven is at hand, calls four fishermen, and teaches and heals throughout Galilee while crowds gather from the whole land.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus' move to Galilee of the Gentiles fulfils Isaiah 9:1–2: the region that went first into the Assyrian darkness receives the first light of the kingdom. The call of the disciples is not recruitment but a summons from the King. Follow me is a command, and the one who gives it also promises, I will make you.
verseByVerse.examples: The fishermen left their nets at once, and James and John left their father in the boat. The passage asks what our nets are, the things we rely on, and reminds us that the one who calls us has already left far more for our sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he heard that John had been arrested. Literally handed over (paradidōmi), not the ordinary word for a legal arrest. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, had imprisoned John because John condemned him for marrying his brother’s wife (14:3–4). The same word is later used again and again of Jesus (17:22; 26:2), of what Judas, the council and Pilate do. The forerunner goes before him in this too.

He withdrew into Galilee. Not fleeing in fear, since Galilee was Herod’s territory too. Matthew uses the same word of Joseph (2:14, 22) and of Jesus moving away from opposition (12:15; 14:13). It is never cowardice: his hour has not yet come, and his timetable is not set by his enemies.

He went and lived in Capernaum by the sea. Jesus left Nazareth, the village where he had grown up, which, Luke tells us, rejected him and even tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:16–30). Capernaum was a prosperous fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, on a major trade route, with a customs office (9:9) and a centurion (8:5–9). It became his own city (9:1), and Peter’s house was there (8:14). Not Jerusalem, but a working town full of the people the respectable would not have chosen: tax collectors, soldiers, fishermen and foreigners passing through. He made his home among the sort of people he intended to save.

In the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali. Two of the twelve tribes had been given these lands in Galilee (Joshua 19). After the Assyrian conquest (v. 15) many Gentiles settled there, and the region was considered spiritually dark and mixed.

Why did God let John be arrested? Scripture does not give a full reason, and John himself later struggled with it in prison (11:2–3). But some things are clear. John’s work was done: he had prepared the way, and the one he announced had come. He decreased so that Christ might increase (John 3:30). His suffering for righteousness was not a sign of God’s absence; Jesus called him more than a prophet (11:9–11), and his faithfulness to death bore witness to the truth. And his being handed over pointed ahead to the greater handing over of Jesus, through which our salvation came. God does not always spare his best servants. He never wastes their suffering.
verseByVerse.note: Zebulun and Naphtali were tribal territories in Galilee, among the first to fall to Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled. The quotation is Isaiah 9:1–2, and its context matters. After the darkness of the Assyrian invasion, Isaiah 9 begins with hope, and then comes the great promise: for to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Matthew is saying: the child of Isaiah 9 has come, and he has come first to the very region Isaiah named.

The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali. These tribes lay furthest north, on the exposed frontier, and when Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria came down around 732 BC they were the first to be carried off (2 Kings 15:29).

First into the dark, first into the light. That is the point of Isaiah’s sentence: in the former time God brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea (Isaiah 9:1). The ground that was first into the darkness is the ground on which the light dawns first. God’s habit is to begin the repair at the place that broke first.

The way of the sea. The great trade route from Egypt to the East. When God chose the spot to plant the light, he did not choose a hidden valley; he chose the roadside of the world, where the caravans of every people would see it.

Galilee of the Gentiles. Galilee of the nations, with its mixed population since the Assyrian conquest. People in Jerusalem looked down on Galileans as half-pagan and unsophisticated, with a strong accent (26:73; John 7:52). The kingdom begins at the edges of respectability and moves outward.

What does Isaiah 9 tell us about who Jesus is? A great deal, because Matthew quotes the opening of a passage everyone knew continued. The light that dawns on Galilee is a child born and a son given, who will sit on David’s throne for ever, and whose names include Mighty God and Everlasting Father (Isaiah 9:6–7). The title Mighty God is used of the LORD himself in the very next chapter (Isaiah 10:21). So by pointing to this passage, Matthew is quietly saying again what he said with Immanuel (1:23): the one who walks along the shore of Galilee is God come to his people, and the Prince of Peace whose kingdom will have no end.

On a Tuesday. Where is the Galilee near you that your church overlooks? And in your own life, the part that went wrong earliest and has been dark longest is the kind of place where God likes to start. Bring that part to him first.
verseByVerse.note: “Galilee of the Gentiles”: the region had a mixed population, looked down on by Judeans.

verseByVerse.quote: "the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people dwelling in darkness. Darkness in Scripture pictures ignorance of God, sin, misery and death (Ephesians 4:18; 5:8). Galilee lived in political and spiritual darkness, and in the darkness of sin that covers every human life.

Have seen a great light. Light pictures God’s presence, truth, salvation and life (Psalm 27:1; John 8:12). The light is not a doctrine but a person: Jesus himself.

The region and shadow of death. The phrase echoes the valley of the shadow of death (Psalm 23:4): deep darkness where death looms over life.

On them a light has dawned. The image is of sunrise after a long night. Zechariah had sung of the sunrise from on high visiting those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace (Luke 1:78–79).

A light that saves. A lamp only shows you the room; this Light does what no lamp can. It does not merely expose the shadow of death; it breaks it. The God who said let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). When this Sun rises on a soul, the night does not merely become visible; it is over.

What it does not mean. Not that everyone who saw Jesus received the light. Many in Galilee, including Capernaum, rejected him (11:23). Light shining is not the same as eyes opened (John 3:19).

I still feel in the dark at times. Has the light really dawned on me? If you have trusted Christ, yes. The light is not your feeling but a Person, and he does not leave the souls he has entered (John 8:12; 10:28). Believers still pass through dark valleys: grief, depression, doubt, the hiding of God’s face for a season (Psalm 88; Isaiah 50:10). Isaiah’s counsel to the one who walks in darkness and has no light is to trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God. Feelings of darkness are real and should be brought honestly to God and to wise friends, and sometimes to a doctor. But the sunrise does not reverse. Christ’s light in you is held by his faithfulness, not by your sense of it.

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that time Jesus began. A turning point. Matthew uses this exact phrase only twice, perhaps marking the two great sections of his Gospel: here, and at 16:21, as Jesus begins to tell his disciples that he must suffer and die.

Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. The message is word for word John’s (3:2), with a difference: John announced the coming King; Jesus is the King. His preaching, his healings and his casting out of demons are signs that God’s reign is breaking in: if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (12:28). The message has two parts: an announcement (the kingdom is here) and a command (repent). Mark adds, and believe in the gospel (Mark 1:15): repentance and faith are two sides of one turning. It is a command, and also a gift (Acts 11:18): God gives the heart that turns. Anyone who has truly turned to Christ can thank God for it, and boast of nothing.

What the crowds hoped for. When an ordinary Jew heard the word kingdom, his heart leapt to the prophets’ hope (Isaiah 52:7; Daniel 7:13–14): that God would throw off Rome, restore David’s throne, regather his people and reign from Zion. Jesus both fulfils and transforms that hope. The kingdom he brings comes first not against Rome but against sin, Satan and death; not by the sword but by a cross; not in one blaze of glory but quietly, like a buried seed, before it fills the earth. It asks not for revolution but for repentance.

Already and not yet. “At hand” means has drawn near, and the best reading holds soon and already together. In Christ’s first coming the kingdom has truly arrived, present now and advancing through the gospel, the Spirit and the church; it will be consummated in fullness only when the King returns.

Where Reformed and dispensational readers part company. Many dear brothers and sisters hold that the kingdom Jesus offered Israel was postponed, to be set up in a future thousand-year kingdom centred on Jerusalem (see 3:2). The Reformed reading, held in this commentary, is that the kingdom was not postponed but inaugurated, that the one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, is the true Israel, and that the Old Testament promises of throne and land are fulfilled in Christ and at last in the new heavens and new earth. Christians also differ, with good arguments on several sides, about whether Scripture promises a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–27). We hold our reading humbly, remembering how much we share.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ message was only moral reform: it is first good news about what God is doing. Nor does at hand mean that Jesus expected the end of the world within a few years and was mistaken. The kingdom came near in his person, and it continues to grow until its full arrival at his return (13:31–33).

If the kingdom has come, why is the world still so broken? Because the kingdom has come the way Jesus said it would: like a seed, like yeast, growing quietly before it fills everything (13:31–33). The King has won the decisive battle at the cross and resurrection, and he now reigns at the Father’s right hand (28:18). His rule is real in every heart he renews and every church that obeys him. But he has not yet returned to remove all evil, because he is patiently gathering his people from every nation (2 Peter 3:9). We live between D-Day and the final victory: the outcome is settled, and the fighting goes on. So we pray, your kingdom come (6:10), and we live now as citizens of the coming world.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is first news to believe, then a call to turn. Share both parts when you speak of Christ. If you only tell people to be better, you have left out the news; if you only tell them the news, you have left out the call. Jesus never separated them.

verseByVerse.quote: While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sea of Galilee. A freshwater lake about thirteen miles long, seven hundred feet below sea level, and full of fish.

Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother. Simon was his name; Jesus later gave him the name Peter, meaning rock (16:18; John 1:42), and he would become the leader of the Twelve. Andrew, a disciple of John the Baptist, had first met Jesus at the Jordan and brought Peter to him (John 1:35–42), so they already knew him; now he calls them to leave everything and follow him permanently.

Casting a net into the sea. A circular net, weighted round the edge, thrown over shallow water.

Follow me. Literally come behind me. In Jesus’ time, students chose their rabbi and applied to study with him. Jesus reverses this: he chooses and calls his disciples (John 15:16). And he does not call them to follow a set of teachings or a law, but to follow him personally. Discipleship is attachment to a person.

And I will make you fishers of men. Jesus uses their trade as a picture of their new calling, and the promise is I will make you: he will make them what he calls them to be. In the prophets, to fish for men was to gather them for judgment (Jeremiah 16:16; Amos 4:2). Jesus turns that solemn image inside out. His fishermen will gather people not to drag them to judgment but to draw them out of it.

Immediately they left their nets and followed him. Their nets were their livelihood and security. Immediately is the word Matthew loves for true discipleship: not after I settle my affairs, but now.

In the flow. The King has announced his kingdom (v. 17); now he gathers its first citizens, the same men he will send to make disciples of all nations (28:19).

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must leave their job to follow Christ. Peter and Andrew were called to be apostles, a special calling. Most believers follow Christ in their ordinary work (1 Corinthians 7:17–24). But every Christian must be willing to leave anything that stands in the way of following him (10:37–39), and every Christian is called to bring others to him.

What does following Jesus look like for me day to day? Following is less about which job you quit than about who now owns your life: Jesus as Lord of the very boat you are in, your work, your family, your ordinary week. In practice it means hearing his voice in his Word and obeying it; turning from sin and trusting him afresh each morning; loving him above all; taking up your cross daily (Luke 9:23), which is not bearing life’s random troubles but dying each day to self-rule for his sake; and abiding in him as a branch in the vine (John 15:5), for apart from him you can do nothing. The fruit grows from the union, not from your striving.

Am I following him well enough? Following is a direction, not a flawless performance. These first followers argued over greatness, slept when he needed them and scattered at his arrest; Peter denied him three times. Yet they were following still, and Jesus did not cast them off but restored Peter and made him a rock. If your heart is turned toward him, grieving sin, longing to obey and rising again after every fall, you are following, however stumbling it feels. Your standing rests not on the quality of your following but on the strength of the One you follow, who began a good work in you and will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Keep near him; he will keep you.

How can I be a fisher of people if I am shy or feel unqualified? Remember who does the making: I will make you. Jesus did not choose these men for their eloquence. Begin where you are, with the people already around you. Pray regularly by name for two or three who do not know Christ. Be a real friend to them. Be honest, when the moment comes, that you belong to Jesus and why. Invite them to read a Gospel with you or come to church. Andrew’s first act of fishing was simply to bring his brother to Jesus (John 1:41–42). Many of the best fishers of people are quiet. Faithfulness matters more than flair.
verseByVerse.note: A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James the son of Zebedee and John his brother. Together with Peter, they became the inner circle of the Twelve, present at the transfiguration (17:1) and in Gethsemane (26:37). Jesus nicknamed them Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17).

In the boat with Zebedee their father. Zebedee ran a fishing business with hired servants (Mark 1:20), so the family was reasonably prosperous. Their mother may have been the sister of Jesus’ mother (27:56; John 19:25).

Mending their nets. The word (katartizō) means to restore, make fit for use; Paul uses it for restoring a brother caught in sin (Galatians 6:1) and its noun for equipping the saints (Ephesians 4:12). They were making torn things fit for use when he called them to do it to people for the rest of their lives.

Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. They left not only their livelihood but their family ties, a serious break in a culture where a son carried on his father’s business. Jesus later says that loyalty to him must come before family (10:37), and that those who leave houses or family for his sake will receive a hundredfold and eternal life (19:29). The kingdom does not abolish family; it reorders it (15:4–6). When family and Christ pull in different directions, Christ comes first.

Christ first, for the family’s good. Though Christ must come before family, in the end he comes for the family’s good as well. The son who loves Jesus first becomes a truer son; love rooted in God loves rightly, not clutching the other as an idol but receiving them as a gift. Often the Lord uses the one who follows him to draw the rest home. We are not told how it came about, but Zebedee’s own wife would later follow Jesus all the way to the cross (27:56), and the gospel would sweep through whole households (Acts 16:31).

The Son who left his Father’s house. The one who asks James and John to leave their father in the boat is the one who had left far more. The eternal Son did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). He left the glory he had with the Father, and later his mother’s table in Nazareth, to have nowhere to lay his head (8:20). And at the cross he would cry out to his Father as one forsaken (27:46). No disciple is ever asked to leave as much as their Lord left for them. When he says follow me, he has already walked the road of loss, so that they could be brought home to his Father for ever.

One call, two roads. Same boat, same father, same morning, same voice. James was the first of the Twelve to be killed, in one sentence of Acts (Acts 12:2); John, by the early church’s testimony, was the last to die, an old man in Ephesus more than fifty years later. And on the shore after the resurrection, when Peter looked at John and asked what about this man, the answer he got was: what is that to you? You follow me (John 21:22). The call is identical; the road never is.

What if my family opposes my following Christ? It is painful, and Jesus warned it would happen to some (10:34–36). Keep honouring your parents and loving your family in every way that does not require disobeying Christ: be kind, respectful, helpful and patient, so that any offence they take is at Christ and not at you (1 Peter 2:12; 3:1–2). Do not argue them into the kingdom; pray for them faithfully and live the gospel in front of them. Where you must say no, say it gently and firmly. Find a church family who will stand with you (Mark 10:29–30). And keep the door open. Many who opposed a believing son or daughter have later followed the same Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went throughout all Galilee. Josephus counted over two hundred towns and villages in Galilee, and Jesus travelled them on foot.

Teaching in their synagogues. The synagogue was the local meeting house for prayer and the reading of Scripture; on the Sabbath, any qualified man could be invited to read and teach (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 13:15).

And proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom. “Gospel” means good news, an announcement of victory or of a new king.

And healing every disease and every affliction among the people. Teaching, preaching and healing: the three parts of Jesus’ ministry (repeated in 9:35). The healings were signs of the kingdom. They were, first, the King’s credentials. Isaiah had promised that in the days of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened and the lame would leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:5–6), and when John later asked whether Jesus was the one, Jesus pointed to exactly these works (11:4–5). Second, they were a window into a deeper healing. Sickness is one of the bitter fruits of the fall, and in mending bodies Jesus showed what he had come to do for the whole person: with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). And third, they were a preview of the new creation, where there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4).

So his fame spread throughout all Syria. The Roman province to the north: the news spread among Gentiles too.

All the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains. Matthew lists them: the sick; those oppressed by demons; those having seizures (literally moonstruck, as people believed the moon caused epilepsy); and paralytics. Listed side by side, not every illness is demonic, and demon-possession is not simply an ancient name for illness. Open demonic activity seems to cluster around Christ’s coming, as the powers of darkness resisted the arrival of the kingdom. And he healed them, all of them: Jesus had authority over every kind of disease and every kind of evil power.

In the flow. Verse 23 is a summary that Matthew repeats almost word for word at 9:35, framing the King’s words (chapters 5–7) and works (chapters 8–9).

What it does not mean. Not that God always heals today when Christians pray, or that sickness shows a lack of faith. Jesus’ healings were signs of the arrival of the kingdom and confirmed his identity (11:2–5). Christians should pray for healing, and God sometimes heals (James 5:14–15). But full healing awaits the resurrection. Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20), and Paul’s own thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

Where Christians differ: healing today. Some, especially Pentecostals, hold that the gift of healing continues as in the apostolic church. Others hold that the miraculous sign-gifts given to confirm the apostles’ message ceased with the apostles (the cessationist view), though God still heals in answer to prayer, because the New Testament links these signs closely with the apostles themselves, calling them the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians read the evidence differently, and we gladly own them as brothers and sisters. This commentary’s view: cessationist, held charitably. God still heals when and as he wills, but no one today has the authority to heal at will, and healing is not promised to every believer in this life. We should be wary of any who guarantee it.

Healing delayed, not denied. These healings were the firstfruits of a coming world. The believer’s healing is therefore never finally denied, only for a while delayed, and the empty tomb has made it certain. The King who healed the sick of Syria will one day heal the whole creation, and close the last grave for ever.

Did these miracles really happen? Matthew reports them as public events, done before crowds and hostile critics. Strikingly, Jesus’ enemies never denied them; they said he did them by the prince of demons (12:24). Someone may say the church wrote all this later, but even outside the New Testament the Jewish historian Josephus seems to call Jesus a doer of surprising deeds, and later Jewish tradition accused him of sorcery, not of fakery. And if God made the world, he is not trapped inside it: healing a body is a small thing for the one who made it. The deeper question is not whether God can, but who this Jesus must be, since he did.

Should I go to the doctor, or just pray? Both. Medicine is one of God’s good gifts, and using it is not a lack of faith; Luke was a physician (Colossians 4:14), and Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). Pray for healing, ask the elders of your church to pray for you (James 5:14), and follow sound medical advice. Then leave the outcome with God, trusting that he is good whether he heals now or later. Be cautious of anyone who tells you to stop treatment or who blames your illness on weak faith.

Should Christians be afraid of demons? No. Demons are real, and Christians face real spiritual opposition (Ephesians 6:12). But they are defeated foes, and believers belong to the one who drove them out with a word. A Christian indwelt by the Holy Spirit cannot be owned by the devil (1 John 5:18). Stay away from occult practices, resist temptation, keep close to Christ in his Word, prayer and his church, and do not be preoccupied with the devil. Most of our spiritual battle is with ordinary temptation and the lies that come with it, and Christ is enough for all of it.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cared for bodies as well as souls. Visit someone who is sick this week, and pray for them. If they are a believer, remind them that their healing is certain, even if it is delayed.
verseByVerse.note: Syria was the Roman province to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great crowds followed him. “Followed” here means physically going after him, not necessarily becoming disciples. Crowds come and go in Matthew; they welcome Jesus at his entry to Jerusalem (21:9) and call for his death a few days later (27:20–23).

The whole land. Galilee, the Decapolis (ten mainly Gentile Greek cities east of the lake), Jerusalem and Judea, and beyond the Jordan: almost the whole territory of ancient Israel, Jewish and Gentile areas alike. It sets the scene for the Sermon on the Mount, which he preaches to his disciples with the crowds listening (5:1; 7:28).

The Shepherd gathering the flock. Through Ezekiel God had promised that he himself would search for his scattered sheep, gather them from the countries and bring them into their own land, and set over them one shepherd, his servant David (Ezekiel 34:11–13, 23). Now the scattered people of the whole land are streaming toward one man. The Shepherd-King of 2:6 is doing what only God promised to do, and he gathers them not by a decree from far away but by walking their roads and laying his hands on their sick.

Which crowd am I in? It is worth asking plainly, because the two look identical from the outside. Both are near Jesus. Both are enthusiastic. Both would have said, that afternoon in Galilee, that they were following him, and Matthew uses the same word for both. The difference is not intensity of feeling; it is what happens when following costs something. The crowd came for what Jesus gave and went home with it. The disciples came for Jesus and left the boats behind. So ask whether he has ever cost you anything you did not want to give: an ambition set down, money given, a relationship ended, a habit surrendered, a reputation risked. If you cannot name a single thing, sit with that rather than explaining it away. It is possible to enjoy Jesus enormously and never once have obeyed him; and if that is you, the way out is not despair but coming to him again, as the next question shows.

And if that question makes me anxious? Do not read it as a demand to prove yourself. It was he who said I will make you; the making is his work and the coming is ours. If you find yourself uneasy at the question, that unease is itself a good sign: the crowds were not troubled by it at all. The remedy is not to whip up more commitment but to go back to the shoreline where the call was issued and answer it again today, in whatever the next costly thing turns out to be.

For worship. From every corner of the land they came, Jew and Gentile, sick and curious, and he did not send them away; he sat down on the mountain and opened his mouth to teach them (5:1–2). He calls out of the crowd a people of his own, and one day the crowd around him will be a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne, and all of them will be disciples (Revelation 7:9).
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

4.theology:
Christ’s obedience counted as ours. Jesus does not only die for our sins, removing the guilt of our disobedience; he also lives in perfect obedience, providing the righteousness we lack. Reformed theology calls this his active obedience: his life of faithfulness to the Father from the baptism to the cross.

In the wilderness Jesus does what Adam failed to do in the garden and Israel in the desert: he trusts God’s word over his own need, refuses to demand signs, and worships God alone. That obedience is credited to everyone who trusts him. We never obey perfectly, but we are justified both by the forgiveness of our sins through his death and by the gift of his righteousness through his life.
4.examples:
Then: Each test matches a failure of Israel in the wilderness: the manna (Exodus 16), Massah (Exodus 17) and the golden calf (Exodus 32). Jesus passes where Israel failed.

Now: Our temptations often take the same three shapes: grab what you need now, make God prove himself, or bend your worship for a quick reward. Jesus’ answer is ours too: It is written. We fight not alone or to earn his favour, but as people already accepted in him, with his Spirit in us and his word in our mouths.

5.title: The New Law from the Mountain
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. <sup>2</sup>And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: <sup>3</sup>“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>4</sup>“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. <sup>5</sup>“Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. <sup>6</sup>“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. <sup>7</sup>“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. <sup>8</sup>“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. <sup>9</sup>“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. <sup>10</sup>“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>11</sup>“Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. <sup>12</sup>Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. <sup>13</sup>“You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people’s feet. <sup>14</sup>“You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup>Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. <sup>16</sup>In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven. <sup>17</sup>“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. <sup>18</sup>For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. <sup>19</sup>Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. <sup>20</sup>For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>21</sup>“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ <sup>22</sup>But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be liable to the hell of fire. <sup>23</sup>So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, <sup>24</sup>leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. <sup>25</sup>Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. <sup>26</sup>Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny. <sup>27</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ <sup>28</sup>But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. <sup>29</sup>If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. <sup>30</sup>And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell. <sup>31</sup>“It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’ <sup>32</sup>But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. <sup>33</sup>“Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn.’ <sup>34</sup>But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, <sup>35</sup>or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. <sup>36</sup>And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. <sup>37</sup>Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’; anything more than this comes from evil. <sup>38</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ <sup>39</sup>But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. <sup>40</sup>And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. <sup>41</sup>And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. <sup>42</sup>Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. <sup>43</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ <sup>44</sup>But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, <sup>45</sup>so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. <sup>46</sup>For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? <sup>47</sup>And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? <sup>48</sup>You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
5.overview:
Jesus goes up on a mountain to teach, and Matthew’s Jewish readers would have heard the echo of Moses on Sinai. But Moses received the law and passed it on; Jesus gives it with his own authority: But I say to you.
