The Beatitudes turn upside down what the world calls blessed: the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek and the persecuted, not the confident and the applauded. They are a portrait of people who receive everything from God, and before that a portrait of Jesus himself.

The six contrasts that follow press the law inward: contempt is murder at the root, and the lingering look is adultery in the heart. No one meets the standard of verse 48 by his own effort. The sermon shows us the fracture and sends us to the only Physician who can heal it, and then, by his Spirit, sets us walking in its way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Beatitudes and the Call to Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus begins with the Beatitudes, eight blessings on people the world would pity, framed by the same promise at both ends (vv. 3 and 10). The first four describe a person’s need before God; the second four describe what grows in a person who has been met in that need. Then Jesus calls his disciples salt and light: a people who preserve and light up the world, not by withdrawing from it but by being visibly different within it.
verseByVerse.theology: The Beatitudes are not a ladder to climb but a portrait of the kingdom’s citizens. The blessings are not rewards for achieving these qualities; they belong to those who have already received the kingdom. Before they describe the Christian, they describe Christ, who alone lived every one of them without a flaw, and whose life is counted to all who are joined to him. That keeps them from crushing the believer. We read them resting in the one who fulfilled them, while his Spirit slowly forms them in us; and the very ache of falling short, the grief over sin and the hunger to be clean, is the first Beatitudes already at work.
verseByVerse.examples: Salt slowed decay; light cannot be hidden without ceasing to be light. Jesus calls his disciples both, and neither picture allows a private, invisible faith. The Christian life is public, not as performance (which chapter 6 will condemn) but as witness. The question is not whether your life will be seen, but what people will see when they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 5 opens the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus sits down on a Galilean hillside and tells his disciples, with the crowds listening, what the people of God’s kingdom are like. The Beatitudes (vv. 3–12) bless eight kinds of people the world would pity. He calls them salt and light (vv. 13–16), says he has come not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them, and asks for a righteousness deeper than the Pharisees’ (vv. 17–20). Six times he presses a commandment to the heart: anger, lust, divorce, oaths, revenge and love for enemies (vv. 21–48), and the chapter ends with the Father himself as the standard. It is grace before it is demand, for it begins by blessing the bankrupt, and every line of it is first a portrait of the one who preached it.

The Sermon on the Mount. Matthew 5–7 is the first of five great blocks of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew (5–7; 10; 13; 18; 24–25), each ending with words like “when Jesus finished these sayings” (7:28); some see an echo of the five books of Moses. The sermon describes the character (5:3–12), influence (5:13–16), righteousness (5:17–48), devotion (6:1–18), trust (6:19–34), relationships (7:1–12), and the call to decide (7:13–27) of those who belong to the kingdom.

Seeing the crowds. These are the crowds of 4:25, from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan. Jesus teaches his disciples, and the crowds listen at the edge and are still there at the end (7:28–29).

He went up on the mountain. Probably a hillside near Capernaum, above the northern shore of the lake. Where Moses received the law, Jesus speaks with his own authority: “But I say to you” (vv. 22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44).

A new mountain. Matthew’s readers would think at once of Sinai (Exodus 19–20). Moses went up a mountain wrapped in fire and smoke, and the people were told to keep back on pain of death. Now a Galilean carpenter goes up a grassy slope, sits down, and his disciples come close. At Sinai the voice of God made the people beg that it stop. On this hill the same God speaks with a human voice, to fishermen, and they are invited near. The law that thundered from a distance is now opened from the inside by the one who gave it.

And when he sat down. Jewish teachers sat to teach; listeners stood or sat at their feet (Luke 4:20). Jesus takes the position of an authoritative rabbi. Matthew adds that he opened his mouth, a solemn Hebrew way of introducing weighty speech (Job 3:1; Acts 8:35).

His disciples came to him. “Disciple” (mathētēs) means learner or apprentice. The sermon is addressed first to men who have already left their nets (4:18–22): it describes the life of those who already follow Jesus, not a way to become his follower.

Not entrance exams but a portrait. The Beatitudes are not eight entrance exams. Every one of the “qualifications” is a disqualification in the world’s eyes: poor, mourning, hungry, persecuted. They do not describe how to reach up to God; they are a portrait of the people God has already stooped down to bless.

The face of the Saviour. And they are, before they are anything else, a portrait of Jesus himself. He was the truly poor in spirit, who said he could do nothing of himself (John 5:19). He wept over Jerusalem. He was meek and lowly in heart. It was his food to do his Father’s will (John 4:34). He was merciful to lepers and tax collectors, pure in heart without a single mixed motive, the peacemaker who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and the persecuted one whom the world hated first (John 15:18). He lived every line that you and I cannot keep. So read the Beatitudes first as the face of your Saviour, and then as what his Spirit is slowly making you.

What it does not mean. Not a ladder for earning God’s favour, nor an impossible ideal meant only to show us our sin, nor a code only for a future kingdom. It does drive us to Christ, but it is also the real pattern for Christian living now, lived by the Spirit’s power.

Where Christians differ: who is the sermon for? Some traditional Lutherans stress that it is chiefly law, showing our inability. Some Anabaptists (ancestors of today’s Mennonites) and pacifists take it as a literal code for Christians, ruling out oaths, military service and courts. Classic dispensationalists, who expect a future thousand-year kingdom on earth, applied it chiefly to that kingdom. Each view sees something real. This commentary’s view: it is Christ’s teaching for his disciples now: it humbles us, drives us to grace, and then shapes the life of those who have received grace. Its sayings must be read as Jesus meant them, sometimes as vivid pictures, in the light of the rest of Scripture.

Is this the same sermon as Luke’s Sermon on the Plain? Very probably the same occasion, or at least the same body of teaching. Luke 6:17–49 has Jesus come down and stand on a level place, and gives a shorter version with four blessings and four woes. A level place on a hillside is no contradiction. Matthew, who loves to gather Jesus’ teaching into large blocks, may also have included sayings Jesus gave at other times, and a travelling preacher certainly repeated his teaching in many villages. Either way, the words are the Lord’s, and each evangelist has recorded them faithfully for his own readers.

What if I do not recognise myself in the Beatitudes? If “pure in heart” stings because you are still battling your thoughts, do not despair. That sting is poverty of spirit. That grief is the mourning. That ache to be clean is the hunger for righteousness. The first Beatitudes are already at work in you. The struggler who keeps running to Christ is not shut out of these blessings; he is the very person they describe. “Blessed are” is God’s word spoken over you now, in Christ, even while he is conforming you to the picture across a lifetime, a work finished only on the day you see him face to face (1 John 3:2).

Where it applies: You sit down on Sunday afternoon and read the three chapters straight through, which takes about fifteen minutes, noticing first who Jesus calls blessed, and then praying over the one line that most exposed you. That is how the King meant his sermon to be heard: as the shape of the life he is giving you.

Where it would be wrong: You read the sermon as a scorecard and use it to grade yourself into despair, or to grade a struggling new believer at church and decide he cannot really be a Christian. The sermon begins by blessing the bankrupt. It drives us to Christ before it shapes us like him, and it is never a stick for beating the weak (12:20).
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach. The mountain setting recalls Moses receiving the law on Sinai.

parallels.desc: Moses goes up to God on the mountain

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Beatitudes. Verses 3–12 are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus, “blessed”: eight (vv. 3–10), plus an expansion of the last (vv. 11–12). They describe not eight types of Christian but eight sides of one character.

The shape of the set. These are one argument, sealed at both ends. Verse 3 is present: theirs is. Verses 4 to 9 are all future: shall be comforted, shall inherit, shall be satisfied, shall receive mercy, shall see God, shall be called. Then verse 10 returns to the present: theirs is. The kingdom is already yours at the front door and still yours at the back, and everything in between is on its way. The order matters too. The first four describe a person’s need: bankrupt, grieving, unassertive, starving. The second four describe what comes out of a person who has been met in that need: merciful, single-hearted, peacemaking, and consequently hated. Nobody arrives at the second four by trying. They are what the first four turn into.

A verdict, not a wish. Makarios is not “may you be happy”. Our word happiness comes from hap, chance, and rises and falls with what has happened lately. Half the people in these eight sentences are mourning, starving, slandered and driven out. To call them happy would be an insult. To call them blessed, on the receiving end of God’s favour whatever the week looks like, is the truth, and it is the only reason these sentences are not cruel. The Psalms open with the word, Blessed is the man (Psalm 1:1), and every Jew listening knew the form. What they had never heard was this list of people attached to it.

The poor in spirit. Not the poor in material terms only, nor those who lack courage. In the Old Testament, “the poor” often meant the humble faithful who depended on God because they had nothing else (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1). To be poor in spirit is to know that before God I am bankrupt, with no righteousness, no merit, nothing to bring. The tax collector who prayed “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” was poor in spirit; the Pharisee who thanked God he was not like others was not (Luke 18:9–14).

The beggar’s word. Greek has two words for poor. Penēs is the working man with nothing spare. The word here is the other one, ptōchos: a beggar, destitute, dependent entirely on what somebody puts into his hand. That is the word Jesus chose for the first sentence of his first sermon. And God had already said through Isaiah: “this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:2).

Good news to the beggars. When Jesus opened his first sermon with the poor, he was announcing himself. At Nazareth he read that the Anointed would bring good news to the poor, and said the Scripture was fulfilled in their hearing (Luke 4:18–21). That is why the promise is in the present tense: the kingdom is theirs now, given to empty hands, because the King is standing in front of them handing it over. The beggar does not have to go and find the kingdom. It has come looking for him, in a Galilean who would himself have nowhere to lay his head (8:20).

How poverty of spirit shows itself. It is not low self-esteem but theological honesty. In prayer, the poor in spirit have nothing to produce before God, only need. In success, they cannot take the credit. In conflict, they do not need to win. In moral failure, they have no deflections left. It is the patient who admits he is ill who finally calls the doctor.

Why “kingdom of heaven”? Matthew usually says kingdom of heaven where Mark and Luke say kingdom of God. They mean the same thing. Devout Jews often spoke of heaven out of reverence for God’s name, much as we might say “Heaven help us”. The phrase does not mean a place we go after death, though it includes that. It means God’s reign, his rule as King, breaking into the world in Jesus, gathering a people now and one day filling the whole earth. To have the kingdom is to belong to the King and to share in everything he is putting right.

What it does not mean. The poor in spirit know their poverty before God, but they also know they are richly loved. Nor is material poverty a virtue that earns heaven. Luke’s “Blessed are you who are poor” (Luke 6:20) speaks of the literally poor, because they often know their need of God; but the rich can be poor in spirit, and the poor can be proud.

Where it would be wrong: Your elders ask you to lead a home group, and you have the gifts for it, but you say, “I’m nobody, I couldn’t.” That is not poverty of spirit. Humility does not deny the gifts God gave; it uses them for others and gives him the credit (Romans 12:3–8; 1 Peter 4:10–11).
verseByVerse.note: “Blessed” means truly well off in God’s sight, not merely happy.

parallels.desc: with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who mourn. It follows naturally from the first Beatitude: those who see their spiritual poverty grieve over it. The mourning includes sorrow for our own sin (Psalm 51:3–4; James 4:9), grief over the sin and suffering of the world (Psalm 119:136), and the sorrows of life in a fallen world, including bereavement. Jesus himself wept (John 11:35).

The heaviest word for grief. Pentheō is the word for mourning the dead: the grief that cannot be hidden, the kind that stops a household, as Jacob mourned for Joseph (Genesis 37:34). So the sorrow called blessed is not a mild regret about one’s failings. It is graveside grief, and the thing grieved is what sin has done. Poverty of spirit is the sight; mourning is what a man does when he has seen it and cannot look away again.

Not a temperature. This is easily twisted into a demand for a certain intensity of feeling, and then people who cannot produce tears conclude they are not really Christians. Jesus is not prescribing a temperature. He is describing what happens when a person genuinely sees his own condition: he does not shrug. Whether it comes as tears or as a long quiet ache is a matter of temperament, and God does not appear to mind which.

For they shall be comforted. “Comforted” (paraklēthēsontai) is related to the word for the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16), and the passive means God is the one who comforts. Isaiah 61:1–3 promised that the Messiah would comfort all who mourn, giving them a garland instead of ashes. The comfort comes partly now, in forgiveness and the Spirit’s presence, and fully when God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

Ashes exchanged. Picture the man who for years shrugged off his sharp tongue or his wandering eye as just how he is, and who at last truly grieves it before God. He finds to his surprise that the tears are not a pit but a doorway, for the LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18), never to the self-satisfied.

The consolation of Israel. Simeon was waiting for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), the same word family as comforted here, and when he took the baby in his arms he knew the waiting was over. The comfort promised to mourners is first a person. Jesus would promise another Helper (John 14:16), which means he was the first: the Comforter in flesh, who gave a widow her son back at the gate of Nain and stood weeping at Lazarus’ tomb. The mourner is blessed because the one who will wipe away the tears has already come close enough to weep beside him.

Is depression the mourning Jesus blesses? No, and the two must not be confused. Godly sorrow moves toward God and produces life (2 Corinthians 7:10). Depression is an illness that often makes a person feel further from God and produces exhaustion rather than repentance. A Christian can have either, or both, or one mistaken for the other by well-meaning friends. Telling a depressed believer that his flatness is a spiritual failing is a cruelty this verse does not authorise. He may need a doctor as well as a pastor, and there is no shame in that. And he is not outside this blessing: Christ is near to him in the dark too, and the comfort promised here is for him as well.

Where it applies: You spoke harshly to your child this morning. Do not shrug it off. Let it grieve you, confess it to God, and apologise to your child.

Where it would be wrong: You confessed a sin years ago, turned from it, and still punish yourself for it every day, as if Christ’s blood were not enough. Mourning over sin leads to comfort; it is not meant to go on for ever. Receive the forgiveness God promises (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The meek. Praeis: gentle, humble, not self-assertive; strength under control (Ephesians 4:2). It is the strength not to insist on one’s own rights, not to take revenge, and to accept God’s dealings without bitterness.

Scripture’s definition is a man. The man called very meek, more than all people on the earth, is Moses (Numbers 12:3): the man who stood before Pharaoh and would not be moved, who smashed the tablets in fury and ground the golden calf to powder. So the word cannot mean timidity or an inability to act. And see when the verse appears: his own brother and sister are attacking him behind his back, and Moses is not recorded as saying a word. God answers for him. That is the picture: a man with every power he needs and no interest in using it on his own behalf.

The connection. Someone who knows how much they have been forgiven does not demand their rights harshly.

For they shall inherit the earth. Jesus quotes Psalm 37:11, which tells God’s people not to fret over the wicked who prosper but to trust the LORD and refrain from anger. The inheritance was once Canaan; Jesus widens it to the whole earth. The proud seize the earth for a while; the meek will inherit the new earth for ever (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1–7): this creation set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:21), with the meek living in it as heirs, not tenants.

Your king is coming, humble. Matthew uses this word three times, and the other two are about Jesus: gentle and lowly in heart (11:29), and your king is coming to you, humble, mounted on a donkey (21:5). The heir of all things entered his capital on a borrowed animal and went on to a cross without lifting a hand in his own defence. That is why the meek inherit the earth: they are joined to the one meek man to whom it has already been given, and he shares the inheritance with his brothers (Romans 8:17).

What if keeping quiet means I am misjudged for years? Then you are in Moses’ company, and in your Lord’s. Meekness does not agree with a false verdict; it simply refuses to make vindication its life’s project. You may state the truth plainly once, where it matters, and correct a falsehood that harms others. What you hand over to God is the campaign: the rehearsed speeches, the need to be seen to be right. He keeps perfect records, and the day is coming when he will bring forth your righteousness as the light (Psalm 37:6).

Is this not the weak making a virtue of their weakness? That has been said, but it does not fit the text. The meek of Scripture are Moses, who faced down Pharaoh, and Jesus, who cleared the temple. Their meekness was not a lack of strength but freedom from the need to use it for themselves. And the objection has the human heart the wrong way round. The person who must always grab, assert and win is usually the insecure one, afraid that if he lets go he will be left with nothing. The meek can let go because their inheritance is safe in God’s hands. Grabbing is what people do when they trust no one to give.

Better to let it go: In a meeting a colleague presents your idea as his own. Unless the work or someone else suffers by it, you do not need to correct the record or win the point. God sees it, your reputation is in his hands, and you are free of the need to be noticed.

Wrong to let it go: The care home is neglecting your elderly mother, or a manager is bullying a junior colleague who is too afraid to speak. Here keeping quiet is not meekness. Speak up calmly and firmly, through the proper channels, and keep at it. Meekness gives up its own rights for love; it does not give up the rights of the weak (Proverbs 31:8–9). Even for himself, Paul used his rights as a Roman citizen when it served the gospel and protected others (Acts 16:37; 22:25).
verseByVerse.note: “Meek” means gentle and humble before God, not weak.

parallels.desc: the meek shall inherit the land
“I am gentle and lowly in heart”

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who hunger and thirst. Not a mild wish, but desperate desire: as a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Psalm 42:1). He could have said those who value righteousness. He chose instead the two appetites a body cannot argue with. Picture the gap between idly wishing you were a little fitter and the gasping thirst of a man lost in a desert.

For righteousness. In Matthew, righteousness usually means doing God’s will, a life that is right before God (5:10, 20; 6:1, 33). So the hunger includes longing to be made right with God (God declaring the guilty righteous for Christ’s sake); longing to be holy (the Spirit’s slow and sure remaking of us in Christ’s likeness); and longing for justice in the world. Because dikaiosynē so often means justice, a person who aches at the trafficked child and the cheated widow is inside this verse as much as the one who aches at the state of his own heart.

For they shall be satisfied. Chortazō began as a word for feeding animals on grass, and by Jesus’ day meant eating your fill; the five thousand all ate and were satisfied, with twelve baskets over (14:20). In part now: those who come to Christ are given his righteousness (Philippians 3:9) and changed by his Spirit. In full at the end, when righteousness dwells in the new heavens and new earth (2 Peter 3:13). Nearly every hunger a person has can be starved, spoiled or fed with the wrong thing. This is the one appetite God guarantees to fill.

The bread this hunger is for. Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30). He came to fulfil all righteousness (3:15), and he did. The one handing out the bread to the five thousand was himself the bread of life, and whoever comes to him shall not hunger (John 6:35). So the beatitude does not send the hungry away to manufacture righteousness for themselves. It sends them to a table where he is the food: his obedience counted to them, his life growing in them.

What if I do not feel this hunger? Start by telling God so, honestly; that admission is itself the beginning of hunger. Then notice what is filling you. Appetite is dulled by snacking, and a soul that grazes all day on screens, news and noise rarely feels hungry for God. Make room: an unhurried time in Scripture, a psalm read slowly, the Lord’s Supper taken with attention. Spend time with Christians who are hungry; it is catching. And remember the strange test in this verse. It does not ask whether you are righteous but whether you want to be. A man who has lost his appetite is more ill than a man who is starving, and the surest sign that God is at work is not that you have arrived but that you cannot stop wanting.

Where it would be wrong: You are so hungry for justice in the world that you rage at every injustice online, despise everyone on the other side, and have stopped praying for your own heart. Hunger for righteousness begins at home and is fed by God, not by outrage. Seek justice with clean hands, and remember that only God can finally put the world right (Romans 12:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The merciful. Mercy is compassion in action toward those in distress, and forgiveness toward those who have wronged us: both pity for the suffering (Luke 10:33–37) and pardon for the guilty (18:21–35). God himself is merciful (Exodus 34:6), and his people reflect him.

The turn. The first four Beatitudes describe our relationship to God; the next four, how that shows itself toward others. Those who have received mercy become merciful.

For they shall receive mercy. From God, at the final judgment and now. James says that judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy (James 2:13).

Have mercy on us, Son of David. In this Gospel the cry for mercy is addressed to one person. Two blind men shout it after him (9:27), a Canaanite mother will not stop crying it (15:22), two more by the Jericho road refuse to be silenced (20:30–31), and he answers every one of them. He became a merciful and faithful high priest, to make propitiation for the sins of the people (Hebrews 2:17): an offering that takes God’s righteous anger upon itself, so that it no longer rests on us. The merciful of this verse are not producing a virtue of their own. They are people whose own cry was answered, and they have caught the family likeness of the one who answered it.

The logic. This is not a deal: “be merciful, and God will pay you back”. Those who know God’s mercy cannot help showing it.

Jesus does not treat this one gently. Of all the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, forgiveness is the only one he stops to explain: if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive you (6:14–15). The parable of the unforgiving servant (18:21–35) ends with a man released from ten thousand talents, a debt no man could clear in a hundred lifetimes, handed over to the jailers because he would not release a hundred denarii. Mercy shown does not purchase mercy received. But mercy withheld is evidence that mercy was never truly received, and Jesus says so in the strongest terms he has.

What if the hurt keeps coming back after I have forgiven? Then you have not failed. Forgiveness is first a decision and then often a long road. You decide before God not to repay, not to hold the wrong over the person, and to hand the account to him. Then, when the memory returns with its sting, you make the same decision again; that is not failure but faithfulness. Peter asked how many times, and Jesus answered, in effect, without counting (18:21–22). The feelings usually follow slowly. Pray for the person by name each time it hurts. Over months you may find that the prayer has begun to change you more than the memory has.

On a Tuesday. Mercy on a Tuesday is usually small: the late reply forgiven without a lecture, the old grievance not brought up again at supper. Each is a little echo of the mercy you live on yourself.

Where it would be wrong: A volunteer at church has harmed a child, or an employee keeps stealing. Mercy does not mean covering it up or giving another chance that puts others at risk. You can forgive personally and still report it; abuse must always be reported to the authorities (Romans 13:4). Mercy that leaves the vulnerable exposed is not mercy.

parallels.desc: should not you have had mercy?

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pure in heart. The “heart” in the Bible is the centre of the person: mind, will, desires and feelings. Purity of heart means moral cleanness, especially in thought and desire (5:28), and singleness: an undivided heart, wholly devoted to God (James 4:8). The Pharisees were outwardly clean but inwardly full of greed and self-indulgence (23:25–28). Jesus wants purity at the source.

The opposite is a divided heart. Katharos is the ordinary word for washed dishes, clear water, and metal with the dross taken out. Its opposite is not so much dirty as mixed: the person who wants God and also wants three or four other things, and could not tell you which he would give up. The pure in heart is the one whose loves have been simplified, who wants God more than the gifts of God. That is a mercy to hear, because a divided heart is the honest description of most Christians much of the time, and it is exactly what God has promised to work on: unite my heart to fear your name (Psalm 86:11).

More than David dared to write. Psalm 24 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and stand in his holy place. The answer is those who have clean hands and a pure heart (Psalm 24:3–4), the phrase Jesus uses here. To it he attaches something David did not dare to write: not merely shall stand in his holy place, but shall see God.

For they shall see God. The highest blessing, and the hope of God’s people (Job 19:26–27; Psalm 17:15). In part, believers see God now by faith in Christ, the image of the invisible God (John 14:9; 2 Corinthians 4:6). In full at the end: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4).

The one thing refused. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Where anyone in the Old Testament is said to see God, as Jacob at Peniel (Genesis 32:30), it is told as an astonishing exception: they marvel that they lived. The tabernacle and temple, the curtain and the priesthood, existed to say in cloth and stone that this was the one thing not yet available. And a man sitting on a hillside in Galilee tells fishermen and farmers that some of them will. Within about three years the curtain was torn in two, from top to bottom (27:51), at the moment Jesus died. The pure in heart will see God because the one pure heart in history was broken open, and through that torn curtain, his flesh (Hebrews 10:20), the way to the face of God now stands open to the unclean who are washed in him.

How can anyone be pure in heart? No one is by nature (Jeremiah 17:9). Purity is first God’s gift: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25–26), cleanses it by faith (Acts 15:9), and through the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7). Then it is a lifelong pursuit: everyone who hopes to see him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3; Hebrews 12:14).

What it does not mean. Not sinless perfection in this life. The pure in heart still struggle with sin; what marks them is that they hate it and fight it. Nor is purity merely the absence of sexual sin, though it includes that.

What will it mean to see God, since God is spirit? Scripture does not explain it fully, and we should not pretend to know more than it says. But it says enough. We shall see the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, risen in a real body (2 Corinthians 4:6; John 1:14). And we shall know God directly, face to face, as a friend is known, no longer through a mirror dimly (1 Corinthians 13:12). The seeing will change us: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Every other gift of the gospel is something from God. This one is God himself.

Where it would be wrong: You decide that purity of heart means cutting yourself off from every film, book and friend outside church, and look down on believers who do not. Purity is an undivided heart toward God, not a fortress of rules, and Jesus, the pure one, ate with sinners (9:10–13). Guard your heart, but do not mistake withdrawal or a critical spirit for cleanness.

parallels.desc: he who has clean hands and a pure heart
holiness, without which no one will see the Lord
we shall see him as he is

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The peacemakers. Not peace-lovers, who simply like quiet, nor peace-keepers, who avoid conflict at any price, but peace-makers. “Peace” here is the Hebrew shalom: wholeness and right relationship. Making peace includes sharing the gospel, by which people are reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:18–20); reconciling people in conflict; and refusing to stir up division (Romans 12:18).

Makers, not keepers. The word, eirēnopoioi, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: peace plus make. A peacekeeper stops two parties hitting each other. A peacemaker walks into the quarrel and does the far more expensive work of getting them back together. Keeping the peace usually means arranging for a difficulty not to be mentioned, while the thing left unsaid goes on rotting. Making peace means going into the difficulty on purpose, and that may be why this beatitude sits immediately before persecution: peacemakers get hit from both sides.

For they shall be called sons of God. “Called” means recognised by God, who gives the name, not the two parties, who may well be ungrateful. In Hebrew idiom, a “son of” something shares its character. Christ is the great peacemaker (Ephesians 2:14–17), and those who make peace show the family likeness. “Sons” includes daughters (Galatians 3:26–28).

What peace cost God. God did not make peace by overlooking anything or by arranging for the matter not to come up. He made peace by the blood of the cross (Colossians 1:20), absorbing the whole cost himself so that the wrong could be truly dealt with rather than quietly ignored. So a peacemaker is not someone with a talent for smoothing things over. It is someone willing to carry a cost that is not his so that something broken can be properly mended.

How do I actually help two people make peace? Pray first, and check your own motives: you are not there to win or to be the hero. Listen to each separately and let them feel heard before you say anything. Help each see the other’s view and his own part, however small. Encourage each to own his wrong specifically, without “but you”. Do not carry tales between them or take sides in gossip. Suggest a meeting where both can speak with you present, and keep the aim in view: not who was right but restored love. Some quarrels need the elders. Be patient; peace often comes slowly.

Where it would be wrong: A relative is mocked at every family gathering, or a teacher in your church is denying that Jesus is God, and everyone keeps quiet to keep the peace. That is not peacemaking. The false prophets cried peace when there was none (Jeremiah 6:14). Godly wisdom is first pure, then peaceable (James 3:17): true peace deals with the wrong instead of burying it.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are persecuted. Persecution includes violence, imprisonment and death, but also exclusion, mockery, loss of jobs and reputation (v. 11).

For righteousness’ sake. Not suffering for their own foolishness or rudeness (1 Peter 2:20), but because lives of mercy, purity and peacemaking expose and challenge the world (John 15:18–20).

Not always a prison cell. Persecution need not be a prison cell. It may be the colleague quietly sidelined for refusing to fudge the figures, or the teenager frozen out for not joining the cruelty in the group chat. When obedience to Christ costs you something at others’ hands, you stand exactly where the citizens of the kingdom have always stood.

That righteous man. Before this Gospel ends, Pilate’s wife will send a message to the judgement seat: have nothing to do with that righteous man (27:19). He was the one person ever persecuted purely for righteousness’ sake, with no folly of his own mixed in, and the world nailed a title over his head that said, in mockery, exactly what was true: the King of the Jews (27:37). That is why the persecuted are told the kingdom is theirs. They suffer with its King, for the same reason, and the world that may take everything from them cannot take the kingdom he won on that cross.

Two distortions. In comfortable countries this verse is easily shrunk to social awkwardness, while much of the church elsewhere faces prison and death. Avoid both manufacturing a persecution one does not have and deciding the verse belongs to other people; and stand by brothers and sisters for whom it is daily bread (Hebrews 13:3).

Where it would be wrong: Colleagues avoid you because you are preachy, rude or always late, and you tell yourself you are being persecuted. Ask honestly first whether they are offended by Christ or by you (1 Peter 4:15). And being blessed in persecution does not forbid lawful protection: Paul appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11).

parallels.desc: if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you. Eight times he has said blessed are those, describing a category. Now he turns from describing to addressing: Jesus expects his disciples to face this.

And utter all kinds of evil against you falsely. To revile is to insult to your face; this is slander behind your back. The early Christians were accused of cannibalism (because they spoke of eating Christ’s body), atheism (because they refused the gods), and hatred of the human race.

On my account. In verse 10, “for righteousness’ sake”; here, for Jesus’ sake. The prophets suffered for the name of the LORD, and Jesus sets his own name where the LORD’s had stood.

Rejoice and be glad. The least natural command in the sermon. Agalliaō is exultant, overflowing joy. Jesus is not telling his people to pretend the slander does not hurt, but that when it comes there is something to be glad about, and he gives two reasons, one looking forward and one looking back. The apostles, beaten by the council, rejoiced that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

For your reward is great in heaven. Not earned wages but God’s generous gift, kept with God, safe, not yet visible (1 Peter 1:4).

For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. Elijah was hunted (1 Kings 19:2), Jeremiah beaten and imprisoned (Jeremiah 37:15), Zechariah stoned (2 Chronicles 24:21). The natural reading of being attacked for your faith is that something has gone wrong. Jesus gives a different reading. Suffering does not prove you are right, since plenty of people suffer for being wrong; but this kind of suffering, for this reason, has a long and honourable history, and the people in it are the ones God kept sending.

Should I defend myself against false accusations? Sometimes, yes. Jesus did not answer every charge, but he did ask the man who struck him why (John 18:23), and Paul defended his ministry at length when the gospel was at stake (2 Corinthians 10–12). Correct a lie calmly where it harms the gospel, your family, or others who trust you, and use proper channels if your livelihood is threatened. What you lay down is the bitterness, the counter-slander and the need to win. Say what is true once, plainly and gently, and then leave your name with God, who will vindicate his people on the last day.

Where it applies: A relative sneers at your faith over a family meal and everyone laughs. Do not sulk or hit back. Remember that the prophets stood where you are sitting, answer gently if there is an opening, and thank God quietly that you were counted worthy of a small share of the reproach of Christ.

parallels.desc: rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings

verseByVerse.quote: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are. Not “you should become”, but “you are”. The poor, mourning, meek and persecuted of the Beatitudes are the very people who affect the world. Their task is not to manufacture saltiness but, by his Spirit, to keep it.

The salt of the earth. Salt preserved food from decay in a world without refrigeration, gave flavour, and was used in sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13). Christians in the world hold back moral decay and give the world a taste of God’s goodness.

Salt by the lake. The men listening knew salt as a trade. Salted fish from the Sea of Galilee were carried to markets far afield; Magdala is usually identified with the town the Greeks called Taricheae, a name drawn from the salting of fish. Disciples work like that. A household of truthful, kind people on a street does not change it by force or noise, but the way salt works into meat: slowly, from the inside.

But if salt has lost its taste. Pure sodium chloride cannot lose its saltiness, but the salt of Palestine, often gathered from the Dead Sea marshes, was mixed with other minerals. If damp, the salt could be washed out, leaving a white powder that looked like salt but was useless. The word (mōranthē) also means “become foolish”.

How it happens. Nobody decides to become indistinguishable. It happens by a hundred small accommodations: the joke you laugh at because not laughing would be awkward, the figure you round in your favour because everyone does, the opinion you keep to yourself for so long that you stop holding it. Together they make a life exactly like every other in the office, with a religious residue on top.

How shall its saltiness be restored? It cannot: the question is a warning. The rest of the verse says what happens instead. Useless salt was thrown on paths, no longer good for anything except to be trampled under people’s feet. A church that becomes just like the world will be despised by the world.

A light for the nations. Isaiah’s Servant was told, I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6), and Jesus said it of himself: I am the light of the world (John 8:12). So when he says to a handful of fishermen, you are the light of the world, he is sharing his own title. Israel’s calling has been fulfilled by the one true Israelite, and he hands it on to the people joined to him (Acts 13:47). They shine as the moon shines, with light that is all his.

A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Many towns in Galilee were built on hills, their lamps visible for miles at night; perhaps Jesus also thought of Zion, to which the nations would come (Isaiah 2:2–3). The Christian life is unavoidably public, not as performance but as testimony. The question is not whether to be visible but what the visible life will say about the one who lit it.

Does this mean a Christian can lose his salvation? No. The salt that is thrown out describes those who looked like disciples and had none of the substance, the same people Jesus describes in 7:21–23, who called him Lord and were never known by him. Those who truly belong to Christ will be kept: no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). The warning is real, and God uses it to keep his people. It is aimed at the danger of a profession without a life.

How would I know if I had lost my saltiness? Ask the diagnostic question rather than the anxious one. The anxious question, have I lost it, tends to produce either despair or a burst of forced intensity that fades by Thursday. The better question is this: if someone who knows me well were asked what difference Christ has made to how I work, spend, speak and treat people, could they name anything? Not something impressive; something different. If nothing comes to mind, that is not a verdict but information, and it is exactly what the rest of this sermon sets about changing.

Where it applies: The office is tearing a manager to pieces over lunch. You do not join in, and when the chance comes you say something fair and kind about her. Nobody makes a speech; the conversation simply changes, and the salt has done its work.

Where it would be wrong: You decide that being salt means correcting every colleague’s language, refusing every office social, and making sure everyone knows you disapprove. That is not salt but vinegar. Salt works by being rubbed in, not by standing apart and frowning. Be different in your goodness, not in your superiority (Colossians 4:5–6).
verseByVerse.note: Salt preserved and flavoured food. Impure salt, such as that from the Dead Sea, could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”
shine as lights in the world

verseByVerse.quote: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a flax wick. The “basket” (modios) was a grain measure of about eight litres. Lighting a lamp to hide it would be absurd.

But on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. Many ordinary homes were one room; one lamp on a stand lit the whole house.

Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works. The light is the life of the Beatitudes made visible in deeds of love, mercy, honesty and justice that flow from faith (Ephesians 2:10). The world should be able to see Christianity, not just hear it.

And give glory to your Father who is in heaven. The disciple’s good works are like a window, not a mirror: people look through them to God (1 Peter 2:12). “Your Father”: the first time in Matthew that Jesus calls God the disciples’ Father, and the phrase runs through the whole sermon.

The tension with 6:1. Later Jesus says not to practise righteousness before others to be seen by them (6:1). The difference is the motive: here, that people glorify God; there, to be praised oneself. Show your works when you are tempted to be cowardly; hide them when you are tempted to show off. The quiet test is whose praise you are hungry for. If a good work would feel wasted because nobody noticed it, the heart is still performing for an audience, and the cure is to want the Father’s approval more than anyone else’s.

Two opposite failures. Salt works by being different, quietly and from the inside; light works by being seen. So there are two ways to fail. The first is the salt that leached away: you are pleasant, entirely assimilated, and nothing about your life would need explaining if there were no God. The second is the lamp under the basket: you are visibly different, honest and unusually kind, and nobody has ever been told why. The first failure has nothing to say; the second has something to say and never says it.

The one who walks among the lampstands. When John saw the risen Christ, he was standing among seven golden lampstands, and the lampstands were the churches (Revelation 1:12–13, 20). The lamp does not light or tend itself. The Lord who lit it walks among his churches, and he warns that a lampstand which will not shine may be removed (Revelation 2:5). The good works people see are his workmanship in us, and the oil is his Spirit.

What does shining actually look like? Mostly it is unglamorous. It is the expense claim that is accurate when nobody checks; declining to join the character assassination without making a speech about it; how you speak to the person who can do nothing for you, the cleaner, the junior, the difficult customer, when there is no audience; being known as the one who tells the truth when it is expensive. None of it needs a platform, and none of it makes you insufferable; people notice it because it is rare. And then the light is simply being ready to say why when the question comes, and it does come to people who live like that. Not a prepared speech, but a plain answer, briefly given: this is what I believe, and this is the difference it has made. Peter adds the manner: with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

Where it applies: Your neighbour is in hospital. Organise meals for her family, openly, as a Christian, so that people see a church that loves.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

parallels.desc: they may see your good deeds and glorify God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–48 — The Law Fulfilled: A Righteousness That Exceeds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus says he has come not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. Then come six contrasts, each setting what was said to those of old beside his own But I say to you. He opens the law’s inner meaning: murder begins in anger and adultery in the look, and love must reach the enemy. The section ends with the Father himself as the standard (v. 48), which no one reaches by effort, and which sends us to the Christ who fulfilled the law in our place and to the Spirit who reshapes us from within.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrasts show that the law was always concerned with the heart. The Pharisees’ righteousness was wide but shallow; the righteousness Jesus requires goes deeper into the same ground, to motive and desire, and no one produces it by effort. To fulfil the law (v. 17) is to bring it to its goal: Jesus meets its every demand, is the substance its shadows pointed to, and bears its curse at the cross. So the greater righteousness comes in two layers: first Christ’s perfect righteousness, credited to us through faith, which alone opens the kingdom; then the real but imperfect righteousness the Spirit grows in a new heart. The law that exposes the unbeliever’s sin becomes, for the believer, the shape of a life of love.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 48 has been read in two ways: as an impossible ideal that drives us to grace, or as a call to wholeness and maturity (the word can mean complete or mature). Both see something true: the standard is God’s own character, which we cannot reach by effort, but to which the Spirit is steadily conforming us (2 Corinthians 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not think that I have come to abolish. Jesus answers a charge before it is made. A teacher who would set his own word beside Moses’ (vv. 21–48), eat with sinners and heal on the Sabbath could easily be taken for one who was setting the law aside.

The Law or the Prophets. The Old Testament Scriptures as a whole (7:12; 22:40).

I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. “Fulfil” (plēroō) means to fill up, to bring to its intended goal. He fulfils the Old Testament’s prophecies by bringing them to pass (1:22), its commands by obeying them perfectly (3:15), its ceremonies (sacrifices, priesthood, temple) by being what they foreshadowed (Hebrews 10:1–14), and its meaning by revealing what the law truly required all along, as he does in verses 21–48.

He fulfils its penalty too. The law does not only command; it curses those who break it. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The law prescribed a righteousness no sinner could produce. Jesus is the one who at last produced it, and he is himself its goal: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4).

In the flow. The phrase the Law and the Prophets appears here and again at 7:12, and everything between is Jesus showing what Scripture looks like when it is fulfilled in his people. If the kingdom is given to beggars (vv. 3–16), does God’s law no longer matter? It matters more than ever.

For truly, I say to you. Others said “amen” at the end of a statement, to agree with it. Jesus says it at the start, to affirm his own authority.

Not an iota, not a dot. The iota is the smallest Greek letter (like the Hebrew yod, little more than an apostrophe). The “dot” (literally “horn”) is a tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. Not even the smallest detail of God’s word will be lost, as long as the present world lasts.

Will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Christ accomplished much of it in his life, death and resurrection; the rest will be complete at his return.

Died to the law, and free for it. This is why Paul can say that the believer has died to the law (Romans 7:4–6): because Christ has accomplished it and borne it for us, we are released from it as a way of earning life by doing, and from its condemnation. Yet for the one not yet in Christ, it still exposes sin and drives the sinner to the only Saviour (Galatians 3:24). For the one in Christ, its moral heart, love for God and neighbour (Romans 13:10), remains the shape of the redeemed life, and the Spirit now writes it on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), so that the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in us who walk by the Spirit (Romans 8:3–4). Freed from the law as a way to be saved, we are freed for it as the way of love.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must keep every Old Testament law as Israel did. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); the sacrifices ended with his once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:18). The Reformed tradition distinguishes the moral law (summed up in the Ten Commandments, still binding), the ceremonial law (fulfilled in Christ, no longer practised), and the civil law of Israel as a nation (expired with that nation, though its principles of justice remain useful) (Westminster Confession 19.3–5). Every part is still God’s word, read through Christ.

Where Christians differ: the law and the Christian. Antinomians hold that the Old Testament law has no role for Christians. Theonomists hold that Israel’s civil laws, including their penalties, should still be applied by nations today. Some in “New Covenant Theology” hold that the Mosaic law as a whole has been replaced by “the law of Christ”. This commentary’s view: the threefold distinction of the Reformed confessions. The moral law remains the rule of life for believers, not to earn salvation, but as the shape of love (Romans 13:8–10).

How dispensationalists read it. Many faithful believers draw a sharper line between Israel and the church. On their reading, the Law of Moses came to an end for the believer at the cross, and the Christian now lives under the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2; 1 Corinthians 9:21), so many are wary of the threefold division. The difference is narrower than it looks. Both sides confess that we are saved by grace through faith, that Christ fulfilled the law, and that the law still convicts and drives us to him; both walk the same road of Spirit-empowered love.

If Christ has fulfilled the law, why should I read Leviticus? Because it is still God’s word, and it is about him. Leviticus shows you how holy God is, how seriously he takes sin, and how costly it is for sinners to come near him. Every sacrifice, every priest, every washing, and the great Day of Atonement are pictures drawn in advance of what Christ would do, and the letter to the Hebrews cannot be understood without them. Its moral laws, like love your neighbour as yourself (Leviticus 19:18), still bind us. Read it asking what it shows of God’s holiness, and how Christ is the sacrifice, the priest and the way in. You will find the cross on every page.
verseByVerse.note: The iota is the smallest Greek letter; the “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter. Nothing in the law is too small to matter.

parallels.desc: Christ is the end of the law

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments. “Relaxes” means loosens, treats as not binding. The rabbis distinguished “light” and “heavy” commandments. Jesus agrees that some matter more than others (23:23), but says no command is to be treated lightly.

The great relaxers. The men who looked strictest were in truth the great relaxers. By the rule of Corban a man could dedicate his money to God and so leave his aged parents without support, and so they made void the word of God by their tradition (15:3–6). To keep the letter while killing the heart is the worst relaxing of all.

Will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Teachers carry a special responsibility (James 3:1). Such a person is still in the kingdom, but least: Jesus speaks of degrees of honour within it.

But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great. Doing comes before teaching. But hear it through the gospel: it is about the direction of a life, not the perfection of it. The great in the kingdom are not the flawless but those whose hearts mean to obey, who keep turning back after every stumble, and whose doing springs from grace received, not merit earned.

Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. A shock to the first hearers. The scribes and Pharisees tithed even their garden herbs (23:23), fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12), and kept the Sabbath in minute detail. The ordinary listener thinks: what hope is there for me? The Pharisee bristles. Jesus means to unsettle them both, closing every road of self-confidence before he opens the only door that works.

Exceeds how? Not in quantity, more rules, but in kind. The Pharisees’ righteousness was largely external: actions, not the heart; the letter, not the spirit; and often done to be seen (6:1–18; 23:25–28). It also tended to lower the law to what could be managed, while adding human traditions (15:1–9). Jesus demands a righteousness of the heart: no anger, no lust, no deceit, no revenge, love for enemies. Verses 21–48 show what he means. Without it, he says, you will never enter the kingdom: not least, but excluded, for a merely external religion does not belong to the kingdom.

All that Jesus began to do and teach. Luke sums up his Gospel as all that Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1:1), the very order of verse 19. Jesus relaxed no commandment, not the least. So when he demands a righteousness greater than the Pharisees’, he is describing himself. The greater righteousness has a name: the LORD is our righteousness (Jeremiah 23:6).

How can anyone have this righteousness? Start with what Jesus means here. In the sermon itself, the greater righteousness is the righteousness of the heart that he goes on to describe in verses 21–48: no contempt, no lust, no deceit, no revenge, love for enemies. That is what his first hearers would have understood, and we should hear it too. But the standard is so high that Jesus ends the section with, be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (v. 48), and no one meets it. The sermon itself points to the answer: the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit (5:3), and disciples ask daily for forgiveness (6:12). The rest of Scripture then explains how God gives this righteousness, in two ways, held together by the Reformers. First, Christ’s righteousness is credited to those who trust him: he fulfilled the law perfectly in their place (Romans 3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). That is the only righteousness that counts before God’s judgement, and it is the answer to verse 48. Second, God gives his people a new heart and writes his law on it (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that the very righteousness of verses 21–48 really grows in them by the Spirit. This does not earn entry, but it marks those who have entered. Both are gifts. Jesus’ hearers heard the demand; after the cross, we also know the gift that meets it.

Must I still keep the Sabbath, the food laws and the feasts? Read verse 19 with verses 17–18 in hand. Jesus upholds the law’s full authority, but he fulfils it, and its ceremonial parts, the sacrifices, clean and unclean foods and holy days, reach their goal in him. They were a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). We honour those laws not by repeating the shadows but by trusting the one they always pointed to; to rest in Christ is not to relax the law but to keep it at its deepest. On the Sabbath itself, Christians hold different views: some keep the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment, others see the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ’s rest while gladly keeping Sunday for worship. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day is his gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5). The view of the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree that a rhythm of rest and worship is God’s good gift.

Where it applies: You have never missed a Sunday and you give faithfully, but you have not spoken to your sister in two years. Outward religion is not enough. Ask God to search the heart, rest your standing on Christ, and let the righteousness he grows in you reach your sister this week.

Where it would be wrong: You hear this verse and set out to beat the Pharisees at their own game, adding rules, keeping a tally, and hoping to earn your place. That is the very righteousness Jesus said falls short. The only righteousness that surpasses theirs is Christ’s, received by faith; the heart-obedience that follows is its fruit, not its price (Philippians 3:8–9), and even that fruit, never perfect in us, is accepted because his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19).

parallels.desc: the righteousness from God that depends on faith

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment." But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, "You fool!" will be liable to the hell of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The six contrasts. Verses 21–48 contain six examples, often called the antitheses, each beginning “You have heard that it was said … But I say to you”. They show what the deeper righteousness of verse 20 looks like. Jesus is not contradicting the law of Moses but correcting the way it had been taught and limited, and revealing its full meaning.

You have heard that it was said to those of old. Most people heard the law read and explained in the synagogue. What they heard included the law itself plus later interpretations.

You shall not murder. The sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13), with the law’s penalty in a human court (Exodus 21:12). The popular teaching stopped there: as long as you have not killed anyone, you have kept the commandment.

But I say to you. Jesus speaks on his own authority, as the lawgiver himself. The prophets said, “Thus says the LORD.” Jesus says, “I say to you.”

Everyone who is angry with his brother. Anger is the root of murder: Cain was angry before he killed Abel (Genesis 4:5–8). The sinful anger Jesus means is the anger of resentment, hatred and contempt. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add without a cause; the earliest do not, though the sense is the same. It is liable to judgment, the same phrase as for murder.

The image of God. Murder was forbidden because man is made in the image of God (Genesis 9:6), and the same reason reaches behind the act to the heart and the tongue. With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God (James 3:9). Jesus treats contempt not as a social failing but as a moral catastrophe.

Whoever insults his brother. Literally “says Raca”, an Aramaic insult meaning “empty-head”, liable to the council, the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court.

Whoever says You fool! Greek mōre, from which we get “moron”. In Scripture, the “fool” is morally and spiritually worthless (Psalm 14:1): to call someone that is to write them off.

Three courts. The first hearers would have felt the climb. Judgment was the local town court. The council was the Great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the supreme court of the nation. And then the hell of fire, Gehenna, the valley of Ge-hinnom south of the city, where kings of Judah had burned their sons as offerings to Molech (2 Kings 23:10), which Jeremiah renamed the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7:32), and to which Isaiah’s picture of the worm that does not die became attached (Isaiah 66:24). So the escalation is from the village court, to the supreme tribunal, to the judgment seat of God himself. Jesus is not setting out a legal code with exact penalties; he is showing that the inner attitudes that lead to murder are themselves deadly before God. Gehenna is his word for the final, conscious punishment of the wicked.

The voice of the last court. The one who says But I say to you is the one who will sit on his glorious throne when all the nations are gathered before him (25:31–32). He is not a rabbi guessing at hearts but the Judge who already reads them. And this Judge, before whom contempt is a capital charge, is not ashamed to call sinners his brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and the people he refuses to write off are the very people who wrote him off.

What it does not mean. Not that every use of the word “fool” is forbidden: Jesus himself called the Pharisees blind fools (23:17). The issue is contempt, not truthful description of folly. Nor is anger as harmful to others as murder, and human courts rightly treat murder more severely. But before God, the heart that hates is guilty (1 John 3:15).

How can I tell holy anger from sinful anger? Holy anger is real. God is a God who feels indignation every day (Psalm 7:11), and Jesus drove the traders from his Father’s house. When you hear that a child has been abused and something in you burns, that fire can be right: it is love for the good recoiling at evil. But holy anger is rarer than we like to think, and it has marks. It is stirred by God’s concerns, not by my wounded pride. It stays under control instead of flaring into contempt. It is slow, for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (James 1:20). And it spends itself in doing good and seeking justice, never in writing a person off. Hold most of our anger up to that test and we find it is really about us: our rights, our comfort, our honour.

If I have spoken in contempt, am I in danger of hell? The warning describes the settled heart of contempt, the kind that never repents and is never broken, and it is meant to frighten us out of it. But it is also exactly the kind of sin the gospel exists to forgive. A believer who has spoken in anger is not condemned (Romans 8:1). He is to see it for what it is, confess it without excuse, and go and put it right, which is where the next verses lead. No one can say, I have never murdered, so I am safe. That is the point: Jesus closes every escape route so that everyone must come to him for mercy, and he has mercy.

What do I do the next time anger rises? First, be slow. Do not speak or type in the heat; a soft answer turns away wrath (Proverbs 15:1). Second, look underneath it. Ask what was really threatened, and you will usually find bruised pride or a cherished comfort rather than the glory of God; name it honestly to him. Third, take the anger to God before you take it to the person. Pour it out to him and leave room for his justice (Romans 12:19). Fourth, remember the gospel: you are the servant forgiven an unpayable debt (18:21–35), and that memory melts contempt into mercy. Then move toward the person: forgive, bless, and where you can, be reconciled. When you fail, do not despair. Confess it, receive fresh forgiveness, and let the Spirit go on retraining your heart.

Where it applies: Your brother mocks your faith at dinner, and the word “idiot” forms in your head. Refuse it, in words and in thought: Christ has not written you off.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “insults” renders the Aramaic term of abuse Raca. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice. “The council” is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom
everyone who hates his brother is a murderer

verseByVerse.quote: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are offering your gift at the altar. So: because anger is so serious. For a Galilean, the journey to the temple took about three days. Jesus imagines someone who has made it and is about to hand his animal to the priest.

And there remember that your brother has something against you. Not that you have something against him: you have wronged him, or he thinks you have, and your responsibility is to take the initiative. Elsewhere, if someone sins against you, you are to go to him (18:15). Neither the wronged nor the wrongdoer is left an excuse to sit still.

Leave your gift there before the altar and go. Startling. The gift waits while the broken relationship is attended to, because God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6). The animal can wait three days. The brother cannot.

First be reconciled to your brother. Whoever does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20). And then come and offer your gift: worship is not cancelled, only postponed until it can be offered with integrity.

The gift on the altar now. For Christians the altar has given way to a cross. Christ offered himself once for all (Hebrews 10:12), and every gift we bring now, a prayer, a song, a place at the Lord’s Table, is accepted only for his sake. That raises the stakes. Our worship rests on the blood of the one who broke down the wall between estranged people (Ephesians 2:14–16). To come into his presence nursing a quarrel with a brother he died to reconcile is to bring the gift and slight the sacrifice that makes it acceptable.

What does being reconciled actually look like? Go, and go humbly. Name the specific wrong plainly: I was wrong to speak to you the way I did. Do not dress it up, excuse it, or smuggle in blame; no “I’m sorry if you were offended”, no “but you started it”. Own it, show real sorrow, and ask the costly little question pride hates: will you forgive me? Where damage can be repaired or repaid, repair it. And the brother, for his part, is called to forgive as God in Christ forgave him (Ephesians 4:32), and then to keep his word: not to rake it up again, hold it over you, or rehearse it to others. Forgiveness is a promise to bury the matter, as God remembers our sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34).

What if I go and he will not be reconciled? Then you are free. So far as it depends on you: you are answerable for your own part, an honest confession and a genuine reaching out, not for the other person’s response, which you cannot control. Having truly sought peace, you may come and worship with a clear conscience, leaving your brother in God’s hands and ready to be reconciled the moment the door opens. Another’s unforgiveness can grieve you, but it cannot hold your worship hostage.

Where it applies: You snapped at a friend last week, and she has gone quiet. Send the message before Sunday: “I was wrong. Will you forgive me?”

Where it would be wrong: The person you wronged has asked you not to contact them, or meeting would put you in danger, for example with a violent former partner. You are not required to force a meeting. Do what depends on you (Romans 12:18): perhaps a letter, or putting right what you can through someone else, and leave the rest with God.
verseByVerse.note: The gift at the altar is a sacrifice brought to the temple.

parallels.desc: forgive, so that your Father may forgive you
so far as it depends on you

verseByVerse.quote: Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come to terms quickly with your accuser. The accuser is someone suing you, perhaps for a debt; there was still time on the way to the judge.

Lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard. Debtors’ prison was common in the Roman world: a debtor was held until the debt was paid, often by family.

You will never get out until you have paid the last penny. The kodrantēs (Latin quadrans) was the smallest Roman coin.

Two levels. First, practical wisdom: settle disputes quickly, even at a cost. Second, a deeper warning: elsewhere in Matthew, jailers and full payment picture God’s final judgment (18:34–35). We are all on our way to God’s court. Be reconciled with God now, while there is time (2 Corinthians 5:20; 6:2).

The Judge on the road. The one urging us to settle before we reach the court is the one to whom the Father has given all judgement (John 5:22). He walks the road beside us, telling us the verdict in advance so that we need never hear it pronounced. And he is not only the Judge; he is the settlement: Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:1–2). The settling he wants is not the first instalment of a payment plan but the surrender of a debtor with empty hands to a Judge who has already paid.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never use courts: Paul appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11). But Christians should not be quick to sue, especially fellow believers (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). Nor does “the last penny” teach purgatory, a place where believers pay off their sins after death, as some Roman Catholic interpreters have argued. Christ has paid the debt of believers in full (Colossians 2:13–14).

But does “until” not imply a release? It is a fair question, and three things answer it. First, the kind of speech: Jesus is urging two men to settle before they reach the court, with the most ordinary scene imaginable. Doctrine cannot be read off the furniture of a parable; by that method another story would teach that God helps people only to stop them pestering him (Luke 18:1–8), the opposite of its meaning. Second, the idiom: a man in a debtors’ prison could not earn. That was the whole horror of it. So “until you have paid” is not a release date but a closed door, the way we say when pigs fly. Third, what the debt of sin cost. It was never a sum to be worked off by degrees in this life or another. It was paid in one payment by someone else, who cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30). A purgatory implies that something was still outstanding when he said it.

Where it applies: Your neighbour claims your fence is a foot over the boundary. Instead of solicitors and years of bitterness, offer to share the cost of a survey and accept the result, even if you lose a little ground.

Where it would be wrong: A company is cheating many customers, or a settlement would require you to keep silent about abuse. Then settling quickly is not the godly course. You may need to see it through, for the sake of others and of justice (Proverbs 31:8–9). Settle your own quarrels quickly; do not sell out someone else’s cause to do it.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” (Latin quadrans) was a small Roman copper coin, worth about 1/64 of a denarius.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have heard that it was said, You shall not commit adultery. The seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14). The popular teaching limited it to the act: as long as you have not slept with another man’s wife, you are innocent.

But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent. Literally “looks at a woman in order to desire her”: not a passing glance or an involuntary thought, but a deliberate look feeding the imagination. The tenth commandment already forbade coveting your neighbour’s wife (Exodus 20:17), and Job made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1).

Has already committed adultery with her in his heart. What is entertained in the imagination is sin before God, even if it never becomes an act (15:19).

Covenant love begins in the eyes. This demolishes every defence that stops at I have not done anything. The look Jesus forbids uses another person, made in God’s image, as an object for one’s own gratification. The modern objection that what happens in my head harms no one misses two things: the imagination is where a person is trained in how to treat others, and the one imagined is a real person, someone’s daughter or son, being used as a thing.

Why the man? In that culture, men had more freedom and power, and women were often blamed for men’s lust. Jesus puts the responsibility squarely on the one who looks. The principle applies equally to women.

What it does not mean. Not that noticing someone is attractive is sin. God made beauty, and the eye that registers it is working as he designed. Our Lord himself in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). It is entertaining the thought, dwelling on it and feeding it that is sin (James 1:14–15). Luther, borrowing an old saying, said that you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them nesting in your hair. Nor does it condemn sexual desire itself, which God created good for marriage (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Nor does it mean that a person who has lusted might as well commit the act, which adds betrayal and harm to others. But before God, both are sin, and both need forgiveness.

Today. Pornography is exactly what Jesus describes: looking at someone in order to desire them sexually. It is adultery of the heart, and it exploits real people.

The faithful Bridegroom. Behind every marriage stands the one it was made to picture: Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). The prophets called Israel’s idolatry adultery (Ezekiel 6:9). Into that long history of a wandering bride came a Bridegroom whose eyes never once wandered from her. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25–27).
