So purity of the eye is not a bleak abstinence. It is faithfulness learned from the only faithful lover.

Why do I still feel guilty when I have looked away? Often the guilt is false. Suppose your eyes keep being drawn where they should not linger, and you look away, and then walk off weighed down with guilt. Hear this clearly: the looking away is not your failure but your obedience, a small daily victory, and heaven is not frowning at it. Much of that burden is false guilt, the accuser heaping condemnation on someone who actually fought and won, and there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Where you did let the gaze linger and feed, do not wallow. Confess it at once, receive the cleansing already promised (1 John 1:9), and walk on forgiven.

How do I fight it? Scripture hands you tools. Make Job’s covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1): decide in advance what you will not look at. Bounce the glance away quickly, and flee rather than negotiate (2 Timothy 2:22). Do not merely suppress the thought but replace it: turn the heart to Christ, give thanks to God, even breathe a prayer for that person as a soul you will meet at the judgment, not an object to be used. Bring it into the light with a trusted Christian friend. And deepest of all, the cure for a wandering eye is a captured heart. As Christ becomes your greater treasure and joy, purity grows less from gritted teeth and more from love.

Where it applies: A suggestive image appears in your feed during the lunch break. Do not scroll back to it. Close the app, thank God for your wife or for the purity he is growing in you, and get on with your sandwich. That is the whole battle, won in three seconds.

Where it would be wrong: A young man is so frightened by this verse that he treats every woman at church as a danger, will not speak to her or look her in the eye, and calls it purity. Jesus forbids the look that feeds lust, not ordinary friendship and courtesy. Treat younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2): sisters are spoken to and cared for, not avoided.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet your neighbour’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your right eye causes you to sin. “Causes you to sin” (skandalizei) means trips you up; the related noun first meant the trigger of a trap. The right eye and right hand were the most valued.

Tear it out and throw it away. Deliberate exaggeration, common in Jewish teaching, not literal self-mutilation: even with one eye, a person can still lust, for the problem is the heart (15:19). Origen is reported to have castrated himself on the basis of a similar verse (19:12), and the church has always judged it a tragic misreading.

The price of the exchange. What the exaggeration does is set a price. Even the favoured eye and the working hand must go if they have become the instrument of your fall. No one enjoys losing a hand, but no one haggles with gangrene. Sin is that serious, and hell is that real.

What “cutting off” means today. Removing the internet from your phone, installing filters and accountability, ending a relationship that leads you into sin, changing your route home to avoid a bar, cancelling a subscription, refusing to be alone with a certain person, changing jobs if necessary. Paul calls it putting to death what is earthly in you (Colossians 3:5) and making no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14).

The whole body given. Jesus speaks of a whole body thrown into hell, and he knew what he would do about it. On the night he was betrayed he took bread and said that it was his body, given for them (Luke 22:19). The hands that never reached for anything forbidden were nailed, and the eyes that never lingered were darkened, so that the bodies of his people would be raised whole. The surgery he asks of us is real and costly, but it is done beside a Saviour who paid the incomparably greater price, and in the power of his Spirit (Romans 8:13).

Is there hope for me if I have cut things off and still fall? Yes. Look where this paragraph sits: twenty-six verses after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to the spiritually bankrupt, in a sermon preached by the one who would shortly be cut off in the place of everyone listening. The severity is real, and it is not the last word. Keep fighting, keep confessing, and keep running to Christ. Ask whether something is still feeding the sin that you have not yet cut off, and bring a mature Christian into the fight. Some battles last years. The Christian who falls and gets up again, hating the sin, is not the person this warning describes.

Where it would be wrong: Someone takes these words literally and thinks of harming their body. Jesus is not asking for that. He speaks in vivid exaggeration, and sin comes from the heart, not the eye (15:19). If you find yourself thinking of hurting yourself, tell someone and seek help today.
verseByVerse.note: The right eye and hand were thought the more valuable. Jesus is using deliberate exaggeration to demand radical action against sin, not self-mutilation.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: It was also said, "Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce." But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was also said, Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce. A summary of Deuteronomy 24:1–4. That law did not approve divorce; it regulated it, requiring a written certificate that protected the wife by freeing her to remarry. Jesus later explains that Moses allowed divorce because of the hardness of people’s hearts, but from the beginning it was not so (19:8).

The debate in Jesus’ day. Deuteronomy 24:1 allows divorce for “some indecency”. The school of Shammai said this meant only serious sexual sin. The school of Hillel said it could mean anything that displeased the husband, even burning his food.

Who was hurt. Divorce had become casual and one-sided. A man could hand his wife a certificate and send her off for the flimsiest reason, and she was left shamed and often destitute, for a woman alone had almost no way to live. When Jesus speaks here he is not being harsh on the weak; he is defending them. He is taking the side of the woman sent away with a piece of paper.

But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife. Jesus returns to God’s original design: one man and one woman, one flesh, for life (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). Marriage is not a contract to be ended when it stops suiting one party; it is a covenant made before God, and its breaking is a moral rupture.

In the flow. The divorce saying follows straight on from lust. A man who sent his wife away so that he could marry a woman he desired was doing, with a certificate in hand, exactly what verse 28 forbids in the heart, and calling it lawful.

Except on the ground of sexual immorality. “Sexual immorality” (porneia) is a broad word for sexual sin, including adultery. Where one partner has broken the marriage covenant by sexual unfaithfulness, divorce is permitted, though not commanded.

Makes her commit adultery. In that culture, a divorced woman would almost always need to remarry to survive. A husband who divorced his wife without just cause effectively pushed her into a marriage that, in God’s eyes, was adulterous, because the first had not been rightly ended, and the husband bears the guilt.

The hinge of the exception. Does this forbid every divorced person from ever remarrying? Not quite. By making an exception, Jesus shows that there is a ground on which a marriage is truly broken, where divorce is permitted and a later remarriage is not adultery. So the sweeping words about remarriage are aimed at remarriage after an unjust, groundless divorce.

The Husband who calls his bride back. Jeremiah says the LORD sent faithless Israel away with a decree of divorce (Jeremiah 3:8), yet in the same chapter he calls her to return (3:12). Into that history Jesus came as the Bridegroom (9:15). When he defends the wife sent off with a scrap of paper, he speaks as the Husband who will not send away his own. He gave himself up for his bride (Ephesians 5:25–26), and no hardness in our hearts will ever end that marriage.

What it does not mean. Not that divorced people are second-class Christians or beyond God’s forgiveness; many were the wronged party. Nor does the innocent party in a marriage broken by adultery sin by divorcing.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Roman Catholic teaching holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, so divorce and remarriage are not permitted (though annulments are granted). Some Protestants hold that divorce is permitted for adultery, but remarriage is not. Others allow divorce and remarriage widely. The Westminster Confession (24.5–6) holds that adultery, and wilful desertion by an unbelieving spouse that cannot be remedied (1 Corinthians 7:15), are the only grounds for divorce, and that the innocent party may remarry. This commentary’s view: the Westminster position. Marriage is lifelong; divorce is permitted only for sexual unfaithfulness or desertion; and the innocent party is free to remarry. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion: the abused should seek safety at once, the elders help judge each case, and abuse is never to be tolerated. Each case needs careful, compassionate pastoral wisdom.

What does sexual immorality cover? The word is broad. It includes adultery and other serious sexual sins that break the marriage covenant in the same way. Some take it more narrowly, of unfaithfulness during betrothal, or of a marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship. The broader reading is the more likely. And permission is not command: where there is repentance, forgiveness and reconciliation remain the better path, as Hosea took back his unfaithful wife (Hosea 3:1).

Why do Mark and Luke leave out the exception? Most likely because they state the general rule, while Matthew, writing for Jewish readers who knew the debates about divorce, records the exception everyone assumed (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18). Those who hold that remarriage is never permitted while a former spouse lives rely on these shorter texts, on Paul’s statement that a wife is bound while her husband lives (Romans 7:2–3; 1 Corinthians 7:39), and on many early church fathers. Their view deserves respect, but it leaves Jesus’ exception without a clear meaning.

What about violence and abuse? Two things must be said plainly. First, without any hedging: an abused spouse must get to safety. God never calls anyone to remain in danger, and the church must protect, never pressure. Call the police and tell the elders. Second, whether brutal, persistent, unrepentant abuse amounts to the wilful desertion the Confession speaks of is a question for the elders to weigh carefully in each case. Many faithful Reformed pastors judge that it can, since such a spouse has abandoned every vow to love and cherish; others counsel separation without divorce. None should ever bind a victim to ongoing harm. The God who hates the treachery of unjust divorce (Malachi 2:16) does not delight in the slow destruction of one of his children.

What about those already remarried on wrong grounds, or the guilty party? The way back is the same as for every sin: repentance and forgiveness. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage, and it should not be broken by a further sin; the call is to live faithfully in it from now on. Whether the guilty party in a divorce may remarry is disputed among Reformed Christians, and such cases need the counsel of the elders. What is not in doubt is that there is full forgiveness at the cross for this sin as for every other, and grace to walk faithfully from today.

Where it applies: Your marriage has grown cold. You feel you would be happier with someone else. That is not a ground for divorce. Stay, get help from your pastor or a counsellor, and work at it, leaning on the Bridegroom who has never given up on his bride. Many marriages that seemed dead have come back to life.

Where it would be wrong: Your spouse has committed adultery and will not repent, or has walked out on the marriage for good. Scripture permits divorce there (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15). And where there is violence, get to safety first.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry. Rabbis disputed the grounds for divorce, some allowing it for trivial reasons.

verseByVerse.quote: Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn." But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. Let what you say be simply "Yes" or "No"; anything more than this comes from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn. A summary of several laws (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23). An oath calls on God as witness that you are telling the truth or will keep a promise.

The problem. People had developed a system of evasion. An oath by God’s name was binding; one by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, or by one’s own head was not. Swearing by the temple was not binding; by the gold of the temple, it was (23:16–22).

A machinery for lying honestly. It produced a form of words that sounded binding to the hearer while leaving a back door open for the speaker, and anyone who has read the small print of a contract knows the instinct has not died. Underneath it lies a wish to stay in control: to be trusted by others while keeping one’s own future in one’s own hands.

But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all. There is no neutral object to swear by. Heaven is the throne of God and earth his footstool (Isaiah 66:1); Jerusalem is the city of the great King (Psalm 48:2); you cannot make one hair of your own head white or black. Every oath drags God in.

Let what you say be simply “Yes” or “No”. Not a better formula but no formula: a word that does not need one (James 5:12).

Anything more than this comes from evil. Or “from the evil one”. The need for oaths exists only because lying is common, and the habit of adding “I swear” or “honestly” suggests that our normal words cannot be trusted.

The Amen. Jesus is the answer to this verse in person. He opened his weightiest sayings with Amen, truly, I say to you, staking everything on his own word (5:18), and Revelation names him the Amen, the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14). When the high priest put him on oath by the living God, he did not evade, and that answer sent him to the cross (26:63–64). His yes was yes at the cost of his life.

What it does not mean. Not that every oath is forbidden. God himself swears oaths (Hebrews 6:13–18), Jesus answered under oath before the high priest, and Paul called God as his witness (Romans 1:9; Galatians 1:20). What Jesus forbids is the casual, manipulative use of oaths to create two levels of truthfulness.

Where Christians differ: oaths in court. Quakers, and Mennonites and other Anabaptist groups, refuse to take any oath, including in court, and take this verse literally. Most Christians, including the Reformed tradition, hold that lawful oaths, such as in court or when taking office, are permitted when required by legitimate authority for a serious purpose (Westminster Confession 22.1–3). This commentary’s view: lawful oaths are permitted; casual and evasive oaths are forbidden. In many countries, those with conscientious objections may make an affirmation instead, which is a reasonable accommodation.

What about wedding vows and membership vows? They are not what Jesus forbids. Scripture honours solemn vows made before God and tells us to keep them (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). A wedding vow is not an attempt to prop up a word that cannot otherwise be trusted; it is a public, covenant promise made in God’s presence, and the same Lord who said let your yes be yes is the witness to it. Those who refuse every oath out of conscience deserve respect; they err, if at all, on the side of taking their Lord at his word.

Must I always tell everyone everything? No. Being truthful is not the same as being transparent about everything at all times. Scripture forbids us to deceive; it nowhere commands us to tell everyone everything. There is room for holy discretion: keeping a confidence, guarding what is not yours to share, the silence Jesus himself kept before his accusers (26:63; 27:14), declining a question that is not rightly asked. The line is clear. You may keep silent, but you may not lie. You need not say everything, but what you say must be true.

Where it applies: Instead of “I swear I’ll pay you back on Friday”, just say “I’ll pay you on Friday”, and pay.
verseByVerse.note: People swore by heaven or Jerusalem instead of by God, treating such oaths as less binding.

parallels.desc: do not swear by my name falsely
do all that proceeds out of his mouth
heaven my throne, the earth my footstool
the city of the great King

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth." But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. From Exodus 21:24 and parallels. This law (the lex talionis) was a principle for judges, not for individuals, and its purpose was to limit punishment to what was proportionate, preventing escalating blood feuds; in practice it was probably often applied through compensation (compare Exodus 21:26–27). But people had turned a principle of justice in court into a licence for private revenge.

But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. Jesus does not abolish justice; he takes personal revenge out of the hands of his people: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:17–19).

But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. A blow to the right cheek was probably a backhanded slap, a deliberate insult in Jewish culture. Jesus is talking about insult, not a life-threatening attack.

The slap today. It is the colleague who belittles you in the meeting, the driver who leans on the horn, the cutting reply waiting to be typed under someone’s post. The flesh wants the last word and the even score. To turn the other cheek is to let the insult fall without firing back, and in the home, to answer the snapping spouse or the barbed teenager with calm instead of returning fire.

And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. The cloak was the outer garment, used as a blanket at night, and by law a poor man’s cloak could not be kept overnight as a pledge (Exodus 22:26–27). Give even what you have a legal right to keep.

Holding rights loosely. Today it is the neighbour who wrecks your hedge or the relative who never repays the loan. Hold personal rights loosely, suffer loss without bitterness, and refuse the arithmetic of revenge.

The cheek he turned. Isaiah’s Servant gave his back to the strikers and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6), and in the high priest’s house they spat in his face and struck him (26:67). The one who taught this verse did it, not from weakness, for he had all authority to strike back. He absorbed the insult because he had come to absorb the wrath the sins of his people deserved. Measured justice was not abolished at the cross; it was satisfied there. That is why his people can let personal revenge go.

What it does not mean. Jesus is speaking about personal insults, not the duties of governments. The state is God’s servant to punish wrongdoers (Romans 13:1–4). Protecting your wife, children or neighbour from an attacker is an act of love, not revenge. Victims of abuse need not stay and accept it: Jesus himself withdrew from danger (Luke 4:30). We leave vengeance to God and to lawful authority, not to ourselves.

Where Christians differ: pacifism. Some Christian traditions (Mennonites, Quakers and others) take this passage to forbid all use of force, including military service and police work. Most of the church, following Augustine and the Reformers, has held that the state may use force justly (the “just war” tradition), and that Christians may serve as soldiers and police (Luke 3:14; Acts 10). This commentary’s view: Jesus forbids personal revenge and retaliation, not the lawful use of force by governments, nor the defence of the vulnerable. Christians who hold pacifist convictions should be respected.

May a Christian ever go to court? Yes. Paul appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11) and used his rights as a Roman citizen, so lawful redress is not forbidden. What Jesus forbids is the grasping spirit that will fight for every right. And Paul tells believers not to take one another to court before unbelievers, but to settle disputes within the church (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). A Christian may defend himself in court and may seek justice for others, but he should first seek peace, and be ready to lose.

Wrong to let it go: Your spouse hits you, someone assaults your child, or a man is harassing a colleague. Jesus is speaking of personal insult and revenge, not of protecting the vulnerable or of crime. Report it. The state bears the sword for exactly this (Romans 13:4). When Paul was beaten without trial, he made the magistrates own their wrong (Acts 16:37).
verseByVerse.note: “Eye for eye” was a rule for judges, to keep punishment in proportion, not a licence for private revenge. A slap on the right cheek — probably with the back of the hand — was an insult. The cloak was the outer garment, used as a blanket at night.

parallels.desc: a cloak taken in pledge returned by sunset

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone forces you to go one mile. Roman soldiers could compel a civilian to carry their equipment for one Roman mile, a hated symbol of occupation.

Go with him two miles. The first mile was forced; the second is a free gift. At the milestone the conscript becomes a volunteer. Jesus is not commending the occupation; he is showing how to answer it without bitterness.

Simon’s mile. Matthew uses this verb for compelling, angareuō, only once more, when the soldiers compelled Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus’ cross (27:32). The Lord who taught his people to carry a soldier’s pack a second mile was himself so broken that a passer-by was pressed into carrying his load. Yet nobody compelled him onto that road. He walked the whole of it freely, obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).

Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. Lending to the poor without interest was a duty in Israel (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11).

Does the second mile mean endless overtime? No. The extra mile is a free gift of love, not bondage to another’s every demand. It is the worker who serves heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23), the person asked for one favour who cheerfully gives a little more. But caring for your household is itself a command of God (1 Timothy 5:8). A man who neglects his wife and children to chase his employer’s approval, or his own ambition, has not gone the extra mile; he has only changed which duty he is failing. Jesus himself withdrew to rest and pray, and said no when love required it.

Must I lend to everyone who asks? Jesus calls for a willing heart, ready to lend without interest and even without hope of return (Deuteronomy 15:7–8; Luke 6:35). But Scripture also warns against rash guarantees for other people’s debts (Proverbs 6:1–5; 22:26). Love seeks the real good of the person asking. Sometimes that means lending; sometimes it means giving outright and not expecting it back; sometimes it means helping in another way rather than feeding a pattern that harms him. Two ditches line the road. One is the hard heart that hides its stinginess behind “they’d only waste it”. The other is thoughtless giving that funds the very thing destroying a man. When in doubt, lean toward open-handed mercy; it is better now and then to be taken advantage of than to nurse a miserly heart.

Better to let it go: A neighbour asks you to help carry a sofa in. Stay and help set up the room too. A colleague is short of money for lunch: buy it, without making him feel small.

Wrong to let it go: A relative asks for cash again, and you know it will go on drink or gambling; a stranger online wants your bank details. Giving that feeds an addiction or a scam is not love. Buy food, pay a bill directly, or help them find help, and refuse the scam (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Jesus forbids a tight fist, not wisdom.
verseByVerse.note: Roman soldiers could compel a civilian to carry their gear for a mile, as Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry the cross.

parallels.desc: Simon compelled to carry the cross
open your hand to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy." But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall love your neighbor. From Leviticus 19:18, where “neighbour” meant a fellow Israelite, though 19:34 extends it to foreigners living among them.

And hate your enemy. These words are not in the Old Testament; they were a popular inference. The Qumran community taught its members to hate the sons of darkness. Some psalms ask God to judge the wicked (Psalm 139:21–22), but those are prayers about God’s enemies, not permission for personal hatred. Jesus tears down the fence the gloss had built around the word neighbour.

But I say to you, Love your enemies. Not warm feelings, but active goodwill, seeking another’s good whatever they deserve. Some later manuscripts of Matthew, followed by the KJV, add do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles leave them to Luke (Luke 6:27–28). Even the Old Testament commanded helping an enemy’s donkey (Exodus 23:4–5) and feeding a hungry enemy (Proverbs 25:21).

And pray for those who persecute you. To pray for a persecutor is to stand before God on his behalf and begin to want for him what God wants, and you cannot do that for long and go on nursing his ruin. Stephen prayed for those who stoned him (Acts 7:60), as his Lord had done.

So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. Not to become God’s children by loving enemies, but to show that you are, by sharing his character, as the peacemakers are called sons of God (v. 9).

For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. Every sunrise and every rainfall is a gift to the wicked as well as the righteous: what theologians call common grace (Acts 14:17).

For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? Anyone can do that. It is not distinctive. Tax collectors were Jews who collected taxes for the Romans or for Herod, often cheating and overcharging, and were despised as traitors and thieves. Even they love their friends. Do not even the Gentiles do the same? Pagans do it too: they greet their own, and greeting in that culture meant wishing someone peace and wellbeing, a sign of acceptance. To love only those who love you back costs nothing and proves nothing. It is the ordinary arithmetic of every tribe and club on earth. The kingdom calls for a love that reaches past tribe, family and liking to the very people outside the circle, and that is what makes it visible as something from heaven.

You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. “Perfect” (teleios) means complete, whole, undivided: in context, complete in love, loving enemies as God does. Luke’s parallel says, be merciful, even as your Father is merciful (Luke 6:36). It echoes Leviticus 19:2: you shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy. The standard is God himself, not a standard lowered to what we can manage.

In the flow. Verse 48 is the summit of everything since verse 17: its perfect answers the exceeds of verse 20. It also opens chapter 6, where the same Father becomes the audience of every gift, prayer and fast (6:4).

The only perfect Son. Only one Son has borne the Father’s likeness without a flaw. The beloved Son of 3:17 went to the cross for those who hated him, and there he prayed for their forgiveness (Luke 23:34). Some early manuscripts of Luke lack that prayer, but many scholars judge it original, and Stephen’s echo of it (Acts 7:60) shows how early it was known. In him the Father’s complete love walked the roads of Galilee, and the command that would crush his people becomes the shape of the life he is growing in them.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must achieve sinless perfection in this life, or that they are lost if they fall short. No one keeps this command perfectly except Christ, who kept it in our place, so that his perfect obedience is counted as ours and our faltering love is welcomed for his sake. It is the goal of the Christian life, the direction we grow, and it drives us to Christ for forgiveness and to the Spirit, now living in us, for strength.

Where Christians differ: perfectionism. Some Wesleyan and holiness traditions teach that Christians can reach “entire sanctification” in this life, a state of perfect love in which they no longer sin deliberately. The Reformed tradition holds that believers remain sinners until death, though truly and increasingly made holy (1 John 1:8; Romans 7:14–25; Westminster Confession 13.2). This commentary’s view: perfection is the goal, never fully reached in this life; complete only when we see Christ (1 John 3:2). Those who hope for entire sanctification are usually earnest about holiness, and in that longing they are right.

What does loving an enemy actually look like? It is praying, by name and for their good, for the colleague who undermined you or the relative who has turned cold. It is the neighbour everyone gossips about finding his path cleared of snow and no note left. It is choosing words that bless rather than bite when you speak of the one who wronged you, and quietly doing him a kindness when the chance comes. It is refusing to gloat when an enemy stumbles (Proverbs 24:17). None of it waits for the other person to deserve it; that is exactly the point.

How does this fit the psalms that call down curses on enemies? Psalms such as 35, 69 and 109 hand vengeance to God rather than taking it; they are cries for his justice, not plans for private revenge. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and yet the martyrs in heaven still cry out for justice (Revelation 6:10). Both belong. The believer prays first for his enemy’s repentance, and if the enemy will not repent, he leaves the judgment to God, who will do right.

Does loving enemies rule out national defence? Pacifist Christians say it does, and they should be respected. The more likely reading is that Jesus is speaking to his disciples about their personal conduct. The state has a different calling, to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), and Scripture honours the soldier (8:5–13; Luke 3:14). The bridge between the two is Romans 12:19–21: do not take revenge yourself, but leave room for God’s justice, and overcome evil with good.

Where it would be wrong: Someone has abused or defrauded you. Loving them does not mean trusting them again, or letting them near your home, your children or your money. You can pray for them and wish them good while keeping firm boundaries. Love seeks their good; it does not require you to be naive (10:16).

For worship. While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). He sent rain on our fields while we ignored him, and then he gave his Son into the hands of his enemies, and the Son’s prayer from the cross reached as far as us. Every sunrise is a sermon of his patience; the cross is the whole of it.
verseByVerse.note: “Hate your enemy” is not in the law; it was a popular inference from it. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators.

parallels.desc: you shall be holy, for I am holy

5.theology:
The law and the gospel: the three uses of the law. Reformed theology speaks of three uses of the law: it restrains evil in society, it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ, and it guides the life of the believer. Matthew 5 presses the second use hard: Jesus takes the law so far inward that no one can claim to have kept it, and so sends every hearer to the one who kept it for us.

But the chapter also does the third. The Beatitudes, salt and light, and love for enemies describe the life the Spirit produces in those who already belong to the kingdom. Held together, the two make a life that depends on God, is changed by him, and is lived for the Father’s glory.
5.examples:
Then: The Beatitudes describe faithful Israel all along: Abraham, a sojourner in a land not his own; Hannah, who mourned and was comforted; David, poor in spirit, who wrote that God will not despise a broken and contrite heart (Psalm 51:17). They are the values of God’s faithful people, now fully embodied in the King.

Now: The world has its own beatitudes: blessed are the confident, the successful, the popular and the comfortable. A Christian who takes Jesus’ beatitudes seriously will often find himself out of step with them, and Jesus promises opposition (vv. 10–12), but the kingdom belongs to the persecuted.

6.title: The Hidden Life of the Kingdom
6.text: <sup>1</sup>“Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. <sup>2</sup>“Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>3</sup>But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, <sup>4</sup>so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>5</sup>“And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>6</sup>But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>7</sup>“And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. <sup>8</sup>Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. <sup>9</sup>Pray then like this: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. <sup>10</sup>Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. <sup>11</sup>Give us this day our daily bread, <sup>12</sup>and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. <sup>13</sup>And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. <sup>14</sup>For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, <sup>15</sup>but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. <sup>16</sup>“And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>17</sup>But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, <sup>18</sup>that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>19</sup>“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, <sup>20</sup>but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup>For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. <sup>22</sup>“The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, <sup>23</sup>but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! <sup>24</sup>“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money. <sup>25</sup>“Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? <sup>26</sup>Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? <sup>27</sup>And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>28</sup>And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, <sup>29</sup>yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>30</sup>But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? <sup>31</sup>Therefore do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ <sup>32</sup>For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. <sup>33</sup>But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. <sup>34</sup>“Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is about the hidden life. Give in secret, pray in secret, fast without showing it, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you. Religion performed for human approval trades a lasting reward for a passing one.

At the centre stands the Lord’s Prayer. It begins with God’s name, kingdom and will, and only then turns to our needs: bread for today, forgiveness received and given, and protection from temptation and evil.

The chapter ends with worry, and traces it to its root: a heart divided between God and money (v. 24). Seek first the kingdom, and the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies will add what you need. That is a promise about priorities, not about prosperity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Piety Before the Father: Giving, Prayer, and Fasting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus takes three practices at the heart of Jewish devotion, giving, prayer and fasting, and in each case sets doing them for human notice against doing them before the Father. The hypocrites have their reward, human applause, paid in full; those who live before the Father receive what only he can give. At the centre is the Lord’s Prayer.
verseByVerse.theology: Giving, prayer and fasting are not optional extras but the basic disciplines of covenant life, touching our neighbour, our God and ourselves. Jesus assumes his disciples will practise them; the question is motive and audience. The Father’s reward, his presence, approval and delight, is far greater than human applause.
verseByVerse.examples: The Lord’s Prayer teaches the order of the Christian life: God first, then us. A disciple who prays it daily is being trained to see God’s kingdom as the first reality, his own needs as real but second, and forgiveness received as forgiveness to be passed on.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 5 showed a righteousness deeper than the Pharisees’ in what we do (5:20); Matthew 6 shows it in why we do it, and then in what we trust. Giving, prayer and fasting are each ruined by the wish to be seen and made real before the Father who sees in secret, with the Lord’s Prayer at the centre. Then come money and worry (vv. 19–34). The whole chapter is lived before the face of a Father: he sees, rewards, hears, forgives, feeds the birds, and knows.

The banner over all three. This verse governs everything that follows. It is not the deeds Jesus forbids but the audience you perform them for: the same act can spring from opposite hearts. In a culture built on honour and shame, religion was a recognised road to status, and his first word, beware, warns that the danger is subtle and belongs to religious people especially.

Practicing your righteousness. Doing religious duties: acts that are right in themselves. Jesus assumes his disciples will give, pray and fast (“when you give”, “when you pray”, “when you fast”, vv. 2, 5, 16). The issue is not whether but how. (The KJV reads alms here, following later manuscripts; the earliest have righteousness, the heading over all three duties.)

Before other people in order to be seen by them. The Greek word for “seen” (theathēnai) gives us “theatre”. Religion becomes a performance, and other people the audience.

For then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. You chose your paymaster. If you do your righteousness to win human applause, then human applause is the whole of your pay: not because the Father is stingy, but because the deed was never really done for him.

The reward. Jesus speaks freely about reward (5:12; 6:4, 6, 18; 10:42). It is not wages earned, as if God were in our debt, but God’s fatherly recognition of what his children do for him, and above all God himself. C. S. Lewis observed that the proper rewards are not simply tacked on to the activity, but are the activity itself in its completion, as marriage is the proper reward of real love.

The one who did not seek his own glory. Jesus said that the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true (John 7:18), and he was describing himself. He healed a leper and told him to say nothing to anyone (8:4). When the crowds wanted to make him king, he withdrew (John 6:15). At the Jordan, before he had preached a sermon, the Father opened heaven to say he was well pleased with him (3:17). Those who are in the beloved Son are given that pleasure as their own, and so they are free to stop performing. When the Father looks at someone who trusts in Jesus, he sees a child accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6), and the applause the heart was straining for has already been given.

How can I tell whether I am doing it to be seen? The test is not whether anybody knows. In that culture almsgiving, prayer and fasting were public and could not have been otherwise. The test is what you would feel if nobody ever knew, and, harder still, what you feel when somebody else gets the credit for something you did. If the thought of your service going unnoticed for ever leaves you quietly content because the Father saw it, you are working for him. If it stings, it does not mean you are a hypocrite; it means a little of the heart is still turned toward the audience, and you can turn it back today. Nobody’s motives are perfectly pure. Do the good thing anyway, and ask his Spirit to purify the motive as you go.

Where it applies: You have spent a Saturday helping clear a widow’s garden, and you are itching to mention it at home group. Leave it unmentioned. Let the Father who saw it be the only one who knows, and see how the pleasure deepens.

Where it would be wrong: You are asked to share at church how God has helped you through a hard year of serving, and you refuse in case it looks like boasting. Telling what God has done, so that others are encouraged and he is praised, is not performing for applause (Psalm 66:16). The aim decides it.

parallels.desc: they do all their deeds to be seen

verseByVerse.quote: Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you give to the needy. Literally “when you do mercy”. Giving to the poor was a central duty in Judaism (Deuteronomy 15:7–11), one of the three pillars of devotion with prayer and fasting.

Mercy, not reward, is the motive. We give because we have seen a brother in need and love will not look away (1 John 3:17), and because we are imitating a God who is rich in mercy and gave to us when we could never repay (Ephesians 2:4). So the secrecy Jesus commands is not coldness. It is love so taken up with the person in need that it forgets itself. Giving to be seen keeps one eye on the mirror; giving for mercy’s sake has both eyes on the neighbour and on God.

Sound no trumpet before you. Probably a figure of speech, like “blowing your own trumpet”, though some suggest the trumpet-shaped collection boxes in the temple. Either way: do not advertise your giving.

As the hypocrites do. “Hypocrite” (hypokritēs) was the Greek word for a stage actor, who wore a mask and played a part for an audience, and Jesus uses it more in Matthew than anywhere else (chapter 23).

Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. “Received” (apechousin) was a commercial term written on receipts: “paid in full”. They wanted praise; they got it; nothing further is outstanding.

But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing. A vivid exaggeration: give so quietly that it is almost hidden from yourself, without keeping a mental record of your generosity. The religious person is tempted here most of all, because giving can quietly become a way of proving to God and to himself that he is a good person. Grace sets him free to give without keeping score, because his standing with God was never bought and cannot be topped up.

And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. The giving is in secret, but not unseen. And it is “your Father”: a child does not perform for a father; he loves him. No one claps; but the Father saw, and the quiet gift is laid up with him for ever.

The one who sat opposite the treasury. Jesus sat down opposite the temple treasury and watched; many rich people put in large sums, and then a poor widow put in two small copper coins (Mark 12:41–44). Nobody else noticed her. He told his disciples she had given more than all the rest. That is the eye this verse promises: the eye of the Son, who sees the gift nobody records and weighs it by love and cost, not by size.

What it does not mean. Not that every gift must be anonymous: Barnabas’ gift was known (Acts 4:36–37). Nor is giving an investment that God will repay with money, as the prosperity gospel (the teaching that faith and giving bring health and wealth) claims. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add that he will reward you openly; the earliest do not.

How much should I give? Jesus sets no figure here; the New Testament asks for giving that is regular, proportionate, willing and cheerful, and many find the tithe a helpful starting point. (See Matthew 19:22 for the fuller answer.)

Where it applies: A family in your church is struggling to pay the rent. Give through the deacons, without your name, so they never feel they owe you anything.

Where it would be wrong: You refuse to let anyone see your church’s accounts, or you avoid a giving receipt because it feels like boasting. Secrecy about motive is not hiding from accountability: churches and charities should be open about money (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). The test is whose praise you want, not whether anyone could ever know.
verseByVerse.note: “Sound no trumpet” is probably a figure of speech for making a show of giving.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you pray. Jesus assumes his disciples pray. Devout Jews often prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:10; Acts 3:1).

For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners. Standing was the normal posture, and if the hour of prayer came while one was out, one stopped and prayed where one was. The hypocrites made sure they were at the street corner or a prominent place in the synagogue when the hour arrived. Jesus is not condemning the posture but the spot chosen for its sightlines.

But when you pray, go into your room. The word (tameion) means an inner storeroom, often the only place in a Galilean house with a door that could be shut: not a study or a prayer corner, but the pantry, the least impressive space available. That removes the last excuse. Nobody needs a suitable place.

And shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. God is not seen, but he is present. Prayer is a meeting with a person, not a performance.

Somebody is watching. The phrase your Father who sees in secret comes three times in this section, once for each discipline. It is not first a warning that God is watching. It is the promise that somebody is: that the giving nobody thanked you for, the praying nobody counted and the fasting nobody noticed were all, in fact, observed. The hypocrite’s real problem is not that he wants an audience. It is that he has settled for a small one.

The Son in the dark. Jesus did what he commanded. Rising very early, while it was still dark, he went out to a desolate place and prayed there (Mark 1:35); after feeding the five thousand he went up on the mountain by himself to pray (14:23). The Son still sought the Father in private, because the relationship was real. And it is because of him that a sinner can shut a storeroom door and speak to the Father at all: we come in his name, and he always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25).

The shut door makes public prayer honest. Taken flatly, this would close every prayer meeting in the world. But the prayer Jesus is about to teach assumes company all the way through: give us, forgive us, lead us not. What he regulates is the audience, not the address. The shut door is the one place where the audience has been removed, so that the habit formed there comes out honest everywhere else.

What if my mind wanders as soon as I shut the door? Everyone’s does. Do not give up because of it. Pray aloud quietly, or write your prayers down; both help a wandering mind. Use a pattern, such as the Lord’s Prayer, or a psalm, and pray through it phrase by phrase. When your mind drifts, turn the distraction into a prayer and come back. Keep it short at first: ten honest minutes are better than an hour of guilt. And remember who is in the room. You are not performing even for yourself. Your Father is glad to have you there, wandering mind and all.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing, at set hours; the “room” was an inner storeroom, the one private space in a small house.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee and the tax collector

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not heap up empty phrases. The word (battalogēsēte) may imitate the sound of babbling: repeating words mechanically, without thought or heart.

As the Gentiles do. Pagan religions often used long lists of divine names, magic formulas and endless repetitions to get the gods’ attention. The prophets of Baal cried “O Baal, answer us!” from morning to noon (1 Kings 18:26).

Magic, not length. The Gentile error is not length but magic: the assumption that the right words, enough times, compel attention. It is the difference between a child speaking to his father and a man operating a machine. Emptiness is a quality of the heart and not of the vocabulary. The Psalms have been the prayer book of God’s people for nearly three thousand years, and neither they nor the Lord’s Prayer is empty when it is meant.

For your Father knows what you need before you ask him. The first wrong motive in prayer was to impress people (v. 5); the second is to manipulate God. We do not pray to inform him or persuade him to be kind; we pray because he is our Father, who wants his children to depend on him and receive from his hand.

Heard before he spoke. At Lazarus’ tomb Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me (John 11:41–42). There was no heap of phrases, only a Son speaking to a Father who had already heard. That is the relationship this verse describes, and Jesus does not keep it to himself. Those joined to him come with his name on their lips, and the Father who always heard him hears them for his sake.

If God knows, why pray? Because prayer is not about giving God information. It is about relationship: children talking with their Father. It expresses our dependence and trust. And God has chosen to work through the prayers of his people; he gives some things because we ask (James 4:2). Calvin said that we pray not to inform God, but to stir ourselves to seek him, to learn to bring every desire to him, and to receive his gifts with thanks. And God’s sovereignty does not make prayer pointless. The God who has planned what he will do has also planned the prayers through which he will do it, so that asking is one of the ways his purposes come about.

The cure is a written prayer. In the very next sentence Jesus gives a set form of words. So pray at length when your heart is full, and briefly when it is not. Use the words others have written when your own will not come; that is what they are for. Only do not imagine that God is worn down by volume or won over by technique.

Does praying in tongues or repeating a phrase count as empty words? Words a person does not understand cannot be prayed with the mind, and Paul insists that prayer in church be understood, so that others can say Amen (1 Corinthians 14:15–17). This commentary holds that the miraculous gift of tongues has ceased with the apostles, chiefly because the New Testament ties such sign gifts to the apostles’ founding work (Hebrews 2:3–4; Ephesians 2:20). Many brothers and sisters disagree, and it holds that view charitably: if your church prays in tongues, nothing here questions your sincerity or your love for Christ. The principle of this verse applies to everyone: the danger is any prayer, in any form, used as a technique rather than spoken to a Father. Repeating a short prayer such as Lord, have mercy is not wrong if it is meant; it becomes empty when it is a mantra to produce a feeling.

On a Tuesday. A Tuesday prayer can be very plain: a few honest words at the sink or the bus stop, said to a Father who already knows the rest. You are not filling a quota; you are talking to someone who is listening.

parallels.desc: the prophets of Baal cry from morning to noon

verseByVerse.quote: Pray then like this: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray then like this. Not “pray only these words”, but in this way. Luke’s shorter version (Luke 11:2–4) shows that Jesus gave it as a model, though it can also rightly be prayed word for word, as the church has always done.

Your, then us. The first three requests concern God: his name, his kingdom, his will, and each says your. The second three concern our needs, bread, forgiveness and protection, and each says us. Half the prayer is about bread, guilt and danger, which is a fair summary of what a human life contains. But the order teaches something. A prayer that begins with me will very often never get past me.

Our Father. “Father” in Aramaic is Abba, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and the Spirit teaches believers to say it (Romans 8:15). Jews sometimes called God “Father” in prayer, but the intimacy with which Jesus addressed God, and taught his disciples to do so, was striking and new. We may say it only because we are adopted through Christ (John 1:12): God brings outsiders, by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3), into his family as truly his sons and daughters, with the Son’s own access to him (Romans 8:15–17). “Our”: even when prayed alone, it is prayed as one of a family.

The wonder of the address. The eternal God, who dwells in unapproachable light, invites us to call him Father. Jesus hands his ragged disciples the family word he used himself. This is no distant force and no stern tyrant, but the father of the prodigal, who runs down the road to meet his returning son.

Is God the Father of everyone? He is the Creator of all, and he cares for all (5:45; Acts 17:28). But the Father Jesus teaches us to address is the Father who adopts his people in Christ (John 1:12; Galatians 4:4–6). Anyone may come to him through Jesus, and that is how he becomes our Father.

In heaven. Our Father is near, but he is also above us, sovereign, holy and all-powerful. “Our Father” gives intimacy; “in heaven” gives reverence. He is a Father who is able to do what we ask.

Hallowed be your name. “Hallow” means to treat and honour as holy. God’s “name” means himself as he has revealed himself: his character, reputation and glory (Exodus 34:5–7). We cannot make God holier than he is. We ask that he would be recognised and worshipped as holy, in our lives, in the church and throughout the world: that God would be treated as God, the opposite of taking his name in vain (Exodus 20:7).

It begins with me. This petition asks that God be revered in a world that uses his name as a curse or forgets it, and first of all in my own heart and on my own lips.

Your kingdom come. God’s kingdom came with Jesus, grows as the gospel spreads, and will come in full when Christ returns. We pray for both. The early church prayed Maranatha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22).

Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. In heaven, God’s will is done perfectly and gladly (Psalm 103:20–21). To pray this sincerely means surrendering our own wills, as Jesus did in Gethsemane (26:39, 42). “On earth as it is in heaven” probably belongs to all three requests.

Submission, mission and hope. This petition is at once submission (let your will, not mine, rule me), mission (let your will sweep over this rebellious world) and hope (let the day come when heaven and earth are one). The first three petitions do not ask God to acquire anything. They ask that what is already true in heaven become true here, on the ground where the person praying is standing.

What it does not mean. Not that “your will be done” is passive resignation, a shrug that whatever happens is God’s will. Nor do we bring the kingdom by our own efforts, social or political. We pray for it, proclaim it, and live under it, but he brings it.

Can I pray your will be done and still ask for what I want? Yes, and Jesus shows how. In Gethsemane he asked plainly, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me, and then, not as I will, but as you will (26:39). Asking honestly and surrendering wholly belong together. God does not want you to hide your desires behind pious words; he wants them brought to him and placed under his wisdom. Pray for the job, the healing, the husband, the child, and then add from the heart, your will be done, trusting that his will is better than your wish.

Where it applies: Your daughter is ill and you come to pray in a panic. Begin anyway with Father, hallowed be your name. It does not push your daughter aside; it reminds you whom you are speaking to, and you will pray for her more trustingly for it.

Where it would be wrong: You think praying for God’s glory first means you should never pray about your own small needs, and you feel selfish asking for a parking space or help with an exam. The same prayer that begins with God’s name goes on to daily bread. He wants the small things too (Philippians 4:6). The order is about priority, not about shutting out your needs.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us this day our daily bread,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give us. We ask as dependants. Even those who earn their own food receive it from God, who gives the health to work, the rain and the harvest (Deuteronomy 8:17–18).

This day. One day at a time, like the manna in the wilderness. Except before the Sabbath, Israel could not gather manna for two days without it breeding worms (Exodus 16:4, 19–21): the arrangement was designed to make a nation ask again every morning. After God’s name, kingdom and will, the first thing we ask for is the humblest: bread, and only for today.

Our daily bread. “Bread” stands for all the necessities of life. Luther’s Small Catechism explains daily bread as everything that belongs to the support and needs of the body: food, drink, clothing, home, family, work, good government, peace, health and friends.

A famous puzzle. Before the Lord’s Prayer, “daily” (epiousios) does not appear in surviving Greek literature at all. It may mean bread necessary for existence, or bread for the coming day; either way it is one day’s supply, asked for one day at a time. The old reading “supersubstantial bread”, taken of the Lord’s Supper, is almost certainly not what Jesus meant: the context is ordinary, and the prayer was given to men who had not yet been to the Supper.

Every pronoun is plural. Give us. Our daily bread. Forgive us. Lead us not. Deliver us. There is not one I, me or my in the Lord’s Prayer. A man can pray it alone at three in the morning and still cannot say me. He is asking for bread for people he has never met, which quietly makes it impossible to pray this prayer and remain unconcerned whether anybody else has any.

The bread from heaven. Yet the manna pointed past itself. When the crowd reminded Jesus that their fathers ate manna in the wilderness, he answered: I am the bread of life (John 6:32–35). That does not spiritualise the petition; he cared enough about ordinary food to feed five thousand on a hillside. But every loaf the Father gives is a sign of the greater gift, and the one who gives us bread gave his own body for us (Luke 22:19).

Why should I pray this when my cupboard is full? Because the man with a full bank account needs it as much as anyone, perhaps more, since wealth tempts us to forget that every loaf comes from the Father’s open hand. Money in the bank cannot make your heart beat, hold off illness or secure tomorrow; rich and poor alike live each day on mercy. That is why Proverbs prays to be kept from riches as well as poverty, lest I be full and deny the LORD (Proverbs 30:9). To ask for daily bread when the cupboard is stocked is to confess gladly that it is all a gift. And under this one word you may bring everything today requires: health and work, wisdom for the meeting, patience with the children, courage for the hard conversation.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your next meal before you eat it. Then, because the Father feeds you, do one thing this week for those who will pray this prayer with empty cupboards: give to a food bank, or take a meal to a neighbour.

Where it would be wrong: Someone stops looking for work and says God will provide. God gives daily bread, ordinarily through work (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). Praying for bread is not a reason to stop earning it.

parallels.desc: feed me with the food that is needful for me

verseByVerse.quote: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And forgive us. We need forgiveness as much as we need bread. Even forgiven Christians still sin and need to come back to their Father for cleansing (1 John 1:8–9).

Our debts. Sin pictured as a debt we can never pay (18:24); Luke’s version says “sins” (Luke 11:4).

Debts or trespasses? Matthew’s word is opheilēmata, the ordinary commercial term for what is owed. Behind it probably stands the Aramaic Jesus spoke, in which the word for a debt had long been used for a sin. The familiar trespasses reached most English speakers through Tyndale and the Book of Common Prayer, and it is a fair rendering, though something is lost. A trespass is a line crossed. A debt is a sum outstanding, and it goes on being outstanding whether or not anyone mentions it. That is the more uncomfortable picture, and the truer one. Sin is not only a series of boundary violations, each over when it is over. It is an account that accumulates.

As we also have forgiven our debtors. Not that our forgiving earns God’s forgiveness. But we cannot honestly ask God to forgive our vast debt while we hold others to their small debts (18:21–35). This is the only request in the prayer that Jesus explains further (vv. 14–15).

Settle it downstairs first. The tense is striking: not as we promise to forgive, nor as we are willing to if pressed, but as we have forgiven. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read as we forgive; the earliest have the past tense. The petition assumes a person comes to God having already dealt with what he holds against others. It is the same order as 5:23–24: leave the gift, go and be reconciled, and then come and offer it.

The debt paid at the cross. To forgive a debt is to cancel it, and someone always bears the loss. God can cancel our debts because Christ paid them: he cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, setting it aside and nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:13–14). Every time a believer prays forgive us our debts, he is asking the Father to apply what the cross has already paid.

If I am already forgiven, why ask for forgiveness every day? Because two things must be held apart. Our standing before God as forgiven children, our justification, is settled once for all by faith in Christ and cannot be lost (Romans 8:1). Justification is a courtroom word: the Judge pronounces a sinner righteous in his sight, not for anything found in the sinner, but because Christ’s death is counted as paying for his sins and Christ’s obedience is counted as his (2 Corinthians 5:21). But our daily fellowship with the Father is like a child’s warmth with a parent: it is chilled by sin left unconfessed, and by bitterness held on to. So the child does not ask to be adopted again every morning; he comes to his Father and says sorry, and is cleansed and restored (1 John 1:9). Daily confession is not insecurity. It is how forgiven children live at home.

Where it applies: You pray the Lord’s Prayer at church on Sunday, and at the words as we forgive our debtors your brother-in-law’s face comes to mind. Stop there. Tell God you release him from what he owes you, and ask for grace to mean it when you see him at the next family lunch.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of praying this petition dishonestly that you leave it out, or stop praying the Lord’s Prayer altogether until you feel you have forgiven everyone perfectly. Do not. Pray it, and let it do its work on you; tell God honestly where you are struggling, and ask him to make you willing. The prayer is a gift for weak forgivers, not a test only the strong can pass.
verseByVerse.note: Sin is pictured as a debt owed to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And lead us not into temptation. The word (peirasmos) means both testing and temptation. God does not tempt anyone to sin (James 1:13), but he does lead his people into testing, as he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1). The request means: keep us from trials that would overwhelm us. Jesus told the disciples in Gethsemane to watch and pray that they might not enter into temptation (26:41). Peter, who boasted he would never fall, fell that same night.

No bravado. The Lord does not tell his disciples to pray for courage under trial, or for strength to prevail. He tells them to ask not to be tried at all, and then, when it comes anyway, to ask to be got out. There is no bravado anywhere in it. The prayer owns our fragility and casts the whole burden of protection on the Father.

But deliver us from evil. Deliver is a rescuer’s word: to pull somebody clear of something that has hold of them. “Evil” can be translated “the evil one”, the devil (the ESV footnote), the tempter of 4:3. Either way, only God can rescue us.

The one who was led in first. This petition is prayed to a Father who once did lead his Son into testing. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil (4:1), and he went in hungry and stood, so that his people could pray to be kept from it. He is a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and he told Peter that he had prayed for him, that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32). So we pray this under the protection of one who has already won, and who is praying the same thing for us.

The doxology. Many later manuscripts add “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.” This ending is not in the earliest manuscripts; it was probably added in early church worship, following David’s prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11.

Why does my Bible put the ending in a footnote? Because the oldest and best manuscripts of Matthew do not have it; it appears in later copies. The early church, praying this prayer aloud in worship, very probably added a fitting note of praise at the close, in words that echo David’s, yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory (1 Chronicles 29:11), and over time that response was copied into the text. So it was probably not part of what Matthew wrote, but there is nothing wrong with praying it. It is thoroughly biblical, and it ends the prayer where the prayer means to end: not on our need or the evil one’s threat, but on the Father. Pray it freely, and know why your Bible sets it in a footnote. No teaching of the faith depends on it.

What it does not mean. Not that God might lure us into sin if we do not ask him not to. Nor does the prayer promise that believers will never face trials (James 1:2). God promises that with every temptation he will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Where it applies: You know that business trips are where you are most tempted to drink too much and flirt. Pray this petition before you leave, then ask for a room away from the bar, and ring home every evening. Praying and avoiding go together.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of trials that you refuse a hard but right calling, a difficult job or a move abroad for the gospel, and tell yourself you are praying lead us not into temptation. The prayer asks God to keep you from falling, not to excuse you from obedience. He led his own Son into the wilderness, and he will be with you in the hard place he sends you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the evil one,” and that some manuscripts add “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.”

parallels.desc: God will not let you be tempted beyond your ability
keep them from the evil one

verseByVerse.quote: For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. “Trespasses” (paraptōmata) pictures a fall or false step. Jesus returns to the one request in his prayer that needs comment.

But if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. A solemn warning. Someone who refuses to forgive cannot have truly received God’s forgiveness, because grace received makes a person gracious, as the unforgiving servant shows (18:23–35).

As God in Christ forgave you. Paul writes, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32), and the words in Christ carry the whole weight. The forgiveness we pass on was bought at the cross by one who never needed forgiving. He restored Peter, who had denied him three times, beside a charcoal fire over breakfast (John 21:9–17). Our forgiving is not the cause of God’s forgiveness, but its fruit: the Son’s own way of loving showing up in his brothers.

Forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same. Confusion here has done real damage. Forgiveness is one-sided: you can do it whatever the other person does, and you are told to. Reconciliation takes two, and it depends on the other person’s repentance: if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3). And Paul writes, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). He knew it would not always be possible, and he did not lay the failure at the door of the one who tried.

What am I actually being asked to do? To forgive is to give up your right to collect: to cancel the debt, to stop rehearsing the offence, to refuse to make the person pay in the small currencies we actually use for it, the cold silence, the story retold to a friend, the reminder produced at the useful moment. That is a decision rather than a feeling, and it usually has to be made again tomorrow. You are not being asked to say it did not matter; the cross is the measure of how much it mattered. You are not asked to feel warmly, or to stop the memory hurting. You are not required to hand trust back as though nothing had happened; trust is rebuilt slowly, where there is real change. You are not obliged to stay within reach of someone who is still harming you or your children. And you are not obliged to shield an offender from lawful consequences; reporting a crime is not revenge.

What if they are not sorry and never will be? You can still release your own claim. The Lord did it in front of you from the cross, praying for men who had not repented that afternoon (Luke 23:34; some early manuscripts of Luke lack the prayer, but many scholars judge it original). What waits on their repentance is not your forgiveness but the restored relationship, and that may never come. That is a grief, and it is not your sin.

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian who struggles to forgive, or who has to forgive the same hurt many times, is unforgiven. Jesus’ words are aimed at a settled refusal, not at the struggle. Nor does forgiving others earn salvation. Only Christ ever forgave as fully as this asks; his perfect obedience is counted as ours, and our halting forgiveness is welcomed for his sake.

How do I know whether I have really forgiven? The test is not that the wound has stopped aching, nor that you never think of it. It is whether you have stopped wanting the person’s ruin and stopped trying to collect. If you cannot get there yet, do not pretend otherwise to God. Tell him plainly that you are unable, and ask him to make you willing to be made willing; that prayer is honest, and he has never despised it. This command was never a demand to feel differently by Friday. It is the slow work of a heart being melted by a mercy it never deserved, and the melting is the work of his Spirit.

Where it would be wrong: You forgive a business partner who embezzled, and think this means you must drop the police report and give him back the account. Forgiveness gives up your personal revenge (Romans 12:19); it does not cancel justice, which belongs to the authorities (Romans 13:4), nor does it restore trust that must be earned again. Forgiving an abuser never means letting him near children.

parallels.desc: forgive your brother from your heart

verseByVerse.quote: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you fast. Jesus assumes his disciples will fast (9:15). The only fast the law required was on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31), but people fasted in times of mourning, repentance, danger, or seeking God (2 Samuel 12:16; Esther 4:16; Daniel 9:3). Some Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12).

Do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces. Some made a show of their fasting, unwashed and unkempt. There is a wordplay in Greek: they make their faces disappear so that they may appear to be fasting.

But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face. Anointing the head with olive oil was normal grooming, like combing your hair. Jesus reverses the signal, so that the fast stays between you and your Father. The pattern of the section is now complete: the secret act, the seeing Father, the certain reward.

Why fast? Fasting expresses humility and dependence on God; it sharpens prayer; it expresses sorrow for sin; and it trains us to say no to the body’s appetites, which helps us say no to sin. It is not a way of forcing God to act or earning his favour, but a way of seeking him with our whole self. Isaiah 58 condemns fasting that is combined with injustice, and calls for a fast that shares bread with the hungry.

Better than bread. Above all, fasting turns the body’s hunger into a cry of the heart: Lord, I want you more than I want food (4:4). It adds nothing to a standing already complete in Christ; we fast not to be loved but because we are loved. And Jesus said his disciples would fast when the bridegroom was taken away (9:15). We fast because he is away for now, and we long for the day the fast gives way to the wedding feast.

Should I fast if I never have? Start with what Jesus says: when you fast, not if. He assumes it, as he assumes giving and praying.
