He fasted himself (4:2), and the early church fasted and prayed before sending out missionaries and appointing elders (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Yet nowhere is it laid down as a law with required days. So fasting is a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: no one should bind your conscience or make you feel condemned for neglecting it, and neither should you simply shrug off what your Lord assumed his people would do.

How do I actually fast? Start small and simple. Skip one meal, drink water, and let each pang of hunger send you to prayer; fasting without seeking God is merely dieting. Use the time you would have spent eating to read Scripture and pray, perhaps for one specific matter: a decision, a sin you are fighting, a person you long to see saved. Keep it hidden, as these verses urge. If you are ill, pregnant, elderly or have a history of eating difficulties, set aside some other comfort instead, for God looks at the heart, not the empty stomach. Do it as worship, free of legalism and free of guilt.

Where it applies: Skip lunch on Thursday, and spend the hour praying for your church, without mentioning it to anyone.
verseByVerse.note: Anointing the head with oil was part of ordinary grooming. Some Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). A wordplay: they disfigure (aphanizousin, literally “make invisible”) their faces so that they may appear (phanōsin) to others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — Treasure, Vision, and Trust: Seeking the Kingdom First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of the chapter turns to money and worry. Jesus sets treasure on earth, which moth, rust and thieves destroy, against treasure in heaven, which lasts. A good eye is generosity, and no one can serve both God and money. Then comes the great passage on anxiety: the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the wildflowers knows what his children need, so seek first his kingdom. A guard belongs here, and the verse notes give it in full: this passage must never be used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus is not commanding a carefree life but a rightly ordered one. Anxiety often comes from seeking lesser things first and then hoping God will manage them, instead of seeking God first and trusting him with the rest. Underneath, much worry is a practical doubt about the Father’s care, and Jesus answers it not with a rebuke but with reasons.
verseByVerse.examples: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness gathers up the whole sermon. A person who is truly seeking God’s kingdom first often finds that anxiety about lesser things loosens, not because circumstances change but because the heart’s centre has moved.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth. “Lay up” means to store, accumulate, hoard. “For yourselves”: for selfish security and enjoyment.

In the flow. Verses 1–18 spoke of the reward the Father keeps for what is done in secret; now Jesus calls it treasure, and asks where we are storing ours. The subject moves from religion to money, but the question is the same: whose approval is the heart living for?

Where moth and rust destroy. Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths ate, or as metal and grain. “Rust” (brōsis) literally means “eating”: anything that consumes.

And where thieves break in and steal. Thieves could literally “dig through” mud-brick walls. Today it may be inflation, fraud, or simply death, which takes us away from everything we own (Luke 12:20).

But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. Treasure in heaven is everything done for God and his kingdom: generosity to the poor (19:21; Luke 12:33), faithful service, people won to Christ, a life spent for God. It cannot be destroyed.

Come, follow me. Later a rich young man is told to sell what he has and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me (19:21). The treasure and the following come in the same breath. Treasure in heaven is finally a person: Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). The young man went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions, and could not see that the one standing in front of him was worth more than all of them.

Treasure in heaven is mostly ordinary. When Jesus describes the judgement, the deeds he names are everyday ones: food for the hungry, a drink, a welcome, a visit to someone sick or in prison, and the righteous do not even remember doing them (25:35–40). Even a cup of cold water will not lose its reward (10:42). Paul tells slaves doing ordinary daily work to do it heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23–24), and the rich to be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:18–19).

What it looks like this week. Patience with a toddler at six in the morning. Honest work done well when no one is checking. Sitting with an elderly neighbour who has no visitors. Listening properly to a colleague who is struggling. Paying a bill quietly for someone who cannot. Being faithful and kind in your marriage. Caring for an ageing parent. Treating the waiter, the cleaner and the call-centre worker as people made in God’s image. Giving generously and cheerfully. None of this is out of the ordinary. Done in faith and love, for Christ’s sake, all of it is treasure in heaven.

Why this matters. The Reformers recovered this truth: a maid sweeping a floor in faith pleases God as truly as a monk at prayer. What makes something treasure is not its size or how religious it looks, but that it is done in faith, out of love, to please him (Hebrews 11:6). It is never a way of earning heaven, which is a gift; but our Father delights to honour the small faithful things his children do for him (25:21).

For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. We assume the heart leads and the money follows. Jesus says it also runs the other way: put your money somewhere, and your heart moves in after it. Do you want to love God’s kingdom more? Invest in it. Giving is not only the fruit of a generous heart; it is one of the ways God makes a heart generous.

The eye is the lamp of the body. The eye was thought to be like a lamp, letting light into the body. “Healthy” (haplous) means single, sound, and also generous: looking at money and people with one aim, to please God, so that a neighbour’s need looks like an opportunity to give rather than a threat to your savings.

But if your eye is bad. “Bad” (ponēros) also means evil, and in Jewish idiom an “evil eye” meant a stingy, grasping attitude (20:15; Deuteronomy 15:9), while whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor (Proverbs 22:9). So these verses, set between the treasure and the money, are not a change of subject. Generosity is the light; grasping is the dark.

If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! If the very thing that should give you light is corrupted, you are in deep darkness without knowing it. The miser who calls his grip mere prudence cannot even see his own night. Greed is rarely confessed, because it so easily wears the clothes of wisdom.

No one can serve two masters. “Serve” means to be a slave, and a slave could not belong to two owners with full loyalty. Hate the one and love the other is Hebrew idiom for preferring one over the other (Genesis 29:31; Luke 14:26).

You cannot serve God and money. “Money” translates mamōnas, an Aramaic word, “mammon”, wealth. Jesus personifies it as a rival master, almost a god: it demands loyalty, promises security, and competes with God for our trust. You can have money; the question is whether it has you.

The thing you rely on. Some scholars think the word’s root is the one that lies behind our amen: that in which one puts one’s trust. If so, the rival god is simply the thing you rely on instead of God. And the two masters issue opposite commands. One says hold loosely and give; the other says grip tight and keep. Both say trust me. Money is a good servant and a deadly master.

What it does not mean. Not that owning property, saving, or planning is wrong. Scripture commends the ant that stores up food (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the man who leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren (Proverbs 13:22), and a man who does not provide for his family is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). Stewardship holds money as God’s, saves wisely, gives generously, and trusts God, not the bank balance. Covetousness hoards for self and trusts wealth instead of God (Luke 12:15–21).

How can I tell whether money has become my master? Run three simple tests. Where do my daydreams drift when my mind is free? What would rob my peace if I lost it tomorrow? What could I not bear to part with if God asked? A poor man can worship money as surely as a rich man, and a rich man can hold his wealth open-handed for God. Then act on what you find. Give first, before you spend, and give enough that you notice it. Enjoy God’s good gifts with thanksgiving, for he richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and hold all of it as a steward, not an owner.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing (eaten by moths). A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess. The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mammon in another dress. The passage opens with therefore: because you serve God, not money (v. 24). The person who trusts money is anxious when money is short. Anxiety is often Mammon-service in another form: the heart gripped by what it dreads losing. Underneath, worry is often a bid for control: by rehearsing tomorrow over and over we try to master it, when it was never ours to hold. So Jesus floods the fear with reasons.

Do not be anxious about your life. “Anxious” (merimnaō) means to be pulled apart, troubled by care; the word appears six times here. Many in Galilee lived one bad harvest from hunger. Yet Paul uses the same word approvingly of his concern for the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). So Scripture is not against caring. It is against being torn.

Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? God gave you life and a body, the greater gifts. Will he not give the lesser things needed to sustain them?

Look at the birds of the air. Jesus does not say birds do not work: any bird works from first light to dusk. What it does not do is hoard against a future it cannot see, or lie awake doing sums. If God cares for birds, he cares far more for his children, worth a great many sparrows (10:31).

And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? Or “a single cubit to his height” (ESV footnote). The word is pēchys, a cubit, about eighteen inches, and the noun with it can mean either height or length of life. Either way worry has never once altered a measurement. It drains today without mending tomorrow. Someone has said it is like a rocking chair: plenty of motion, and it gets you nowhere.

Consider the lilies of the field. Wildflowers, perhaps the red anemones that covered Galilean hillsides in spring. They neither toil nor spin, the women’s daily work of making cloth, yet even Solomon, famous for his splendour (1 Kings 10), was not arrayed like one of these.

The grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. In a country with almost no timber, dried grass and wildflowers were the fuel, swept up and burned to heat an oven for a single batch of bread. So God dressed a weed more finely than Israel’s richest king, for a life of a few weeks, ending as kindling. Will your Father forget to clothe his own child?

O you of little faith. Oligopistos is almost unique to Matthew (8:26; 14:31; 16:8), and every time it is said to disciples, never to unbelievers. It is a word for people who have some faith, and are frightened anyway: one of the gentlest rebukes in the Gospels.

Asleep in the boat. Matthew’s next use of little faith comes in a boat. A great storm is swamping it, and Jesus is asleep (8:24–26), the one untroubled man on board, because he knew whose world it was. He had nowhere to lay his head (8:20), owned no barn, and never fretted about tomorrow, though he knew exactly what tomorrow held for him; even in Gethsemane he carried the whole weight to his Father. The one who tells us to consider the lilies is the one through whom the lilies were made. Trust in the Father is not a technique; it is being in the boat with the Son.

For the Gentiles seek after all these things. Pagans, who do not know God as Father, make food and clothing the focus of life. They have nothing else to trust.

And your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. The heart of the passage. You are not an orphan in a hostile universe; you have a Father who knows exactly what you need. And the Father who knows also rules. Not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from him (10:29), so nothing reaches his children by chance; it comes through the hand of a Father who is both almighty and kind.

But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Make God’s reign and his righteous will your first priority: before food, before clothing, before career, before comfort. “His righteousness” means living as he wills (5:6, 20). “First” does not mean only, but foremost.

What seeking the kingdom looks like in real life. It is not first a call to leave your job for “full-time ministry” or to fill every evening with church. It is what you pray for in the Lord’s Prayer: your kingdom come, your will be done (v. 10), and his righteousness is to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8). Seeking it first does not usually add new activities to your week so much as change the first question you ask in the ordinary ones: not what will I get, or what am I afraid of, but what does God want here?

Some everyday examples. Choosing a job: you weigh not only the salary, but whether you can be honest in it and care for your family. Your budget: you set aside your giving first. Your Sunday: worship with God’s people is the fixed point. In a tight month: you pray and keep your integrity, instead of panicking or bending the rules. Looking for a husband or wife: you ask first whether the person loves Christ.

Not a way of earning. The kingdom is a gift before it is a task: it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32). We seek it because he has already given it, and because the King is good. And it is a kingdom of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17): seeking it first is the way to freedom from worry, not a new burden on top of it.

And all these things will be added to you. God will provide what you truly need. Not necessarily luxury, but provision. This is a promise to those who seek the kingdom first. David said that he had never seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread (Psalm 37:25).

Does this promise that faithful Christians will never go hungry or poor? No. Believers have starved, been imprisoned and died for Christ (Hebrews 11:35–38), and Paul knew hunger (Philippians 4:12). The promise is that the Father will not abandon his children, that he will give what he knows they need to do his will, and above all that he gives himself. It is not a guarantee of comfort or income, and it gives no support to the teaching that faith brings wealth. When God’s people do go without, the church is often the means by which he adds these things, which is why the previous verses told us to store treasure by giving.

Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. The line is nearly humorous: tomorrow is pictured as perfectly capable of doing its own worrying without help from today. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble: the closing proverb comes with no promise that the trouble will be light. Jesus does not say tomorrow will be fine. He says today has enough in it already, and that the Father who gives grace for today will give it again tomorrow, like the manna.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should not work, plan or save: Proverbs commends planning (Proverbs 21:5). Planning thinks ahead and takes reasonable steps, then trusts God; worry runs the same fears round and round. Nor does it mean that nothing hard will come: nothing can separate us from his love (Romans 8:35–39), but the hard things come.

If I have an anxiety disorder, is Jesus telling me I am sinning? No. This passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin, and the damage has been real. Jesus is addressing a settled orientation of the heart, a life organised around what one is afraid of losing. Clinical anxiety is different: a body and mind doing what they were not designed to do, a racing heart and a mind that will not stop, arriving uninvited in people who love God. The command is not a lever to be pulled harder; a Christian who could stop by deciding to would have stopped years ago. Medical help is not a failure of faith, any more than a splint is. Read the passage for its reasons rather than as a rebuke: Jesus does not stand over frightened people. He reasons with them, gently, and so does his Spirit.

Where it applies: You are waiting for a hospital test result. Pray, tell your Father your fear, then go to bed and sleep. Tomorrow will have its own trouble.

For worship. The heavenly Father knows. He feeds the sparrows and dresses the anemones on the hills of Galilee. He did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all; how will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.” Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

parallels.desc: do not be anxious about anything
cast all your anxieties on him

6.theology:
Prayer and the fatherhood of God. Christian prayer is shaped by the Trinity. We pray to the Father, through the Son who taught us this prayer and intercedes for us (Romans 8:34), and in the power of the Spirit, who helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26).

The address Our Father rests on adoption: those who trust in Christ are received into God’s family as his sons and daughters (Galatians 4:5–6). We pray as children to a Father who has already given us his Son, and the confidence of prayer rests on what God has done in adopting us, not on how fervently or often we pray.
6.examples:
Then: The Old Testament knows this hidden devotion. Hannah prayed so quietly that Eli thought she was drunk (1 Samuel 1:13), and God heard her. Daniel prayed three times a day at his window toward Jerusalem without announcing it, though it put his life at risk (Daniel 6:10). They prayed to an audience of One.

Now: Worry is a familiar companion for many people today, fed by constant news of what might go wrong. Jesus’ answer is not better information but a different centre: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who holds all things will hold yours. That is not naive: you are not in control of tomorrow, and your Father is.

7.title: The Narrow Gate
7.text: <sup>1</sup>“Judge not, that you be not judged. <sup>2</sup>For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. <sup>3</sup>Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>4</sup>Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? <sup>5</sup>You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. <sup>6</sup>“Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. <sup>7</sup>“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>8</sup>For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>9</sup>Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? <sup>10</sup>Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? <sup>11</sup>If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! <sup>12</sup>“So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. <sup>13</sup>“Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. <sup>14</sup>For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. <sup>15</sup>“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. <sup>16</sup>You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? <sup>17</sup>So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. <sup>18</sup>A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. <sup>19</sup>Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>20</sup>Thus you will recognize them by their fruits. <sup>21</sup>“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. <sup>22</sup>On that day many will say to me, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?’ <sup>23</sup>And then will I declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.’ <sup>24</sup>“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. <sup>25</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. <sup>26</sup>And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. <sup>27</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.” <sup>28</sup>And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, <sup>29</sup>for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 brings the Sermon on the Mount to a close with a series of choices: the wide gate or the narrow, the false prophet or the true, the one who hears and does or the one who hears and does not. The sermon that began with blessings ends with warnings.

“Judge not” (v. 1) is often quoted to forbid any moral judgement at all. Jesus means something narrower. He requires discernment in the same chapter (vv. 6, 15–16); what he forbids is hypocritical judgement, condemning in others what you excuse in yourself.

The parable of the two builders is the sermon’s climax. Building on the rock is not mere agreement with his teaching but doing it, the obedience that grows from real faith. The crowds are astonished at his authority, and he is the rock on which the house stands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Judgment, Prayer, and the Two Ways: Concluding the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sermon closes with a warning against hypocritical judging (vv. 1–6), an invitation to persistent prayer to a generous Father (vv. 7–11), the Golden Rule (v. 12), and then four pairs that call for a decision: two gates, two trees, two confessions and two foundations (vv. 13–27). The crowds are left astonished, not by the gentleness of what they heard but by the authority of the one who said it.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus forbids the hypocritical judgement that ignores one’s own sin while scrutinising another’s, and he makes self-examination the first step of all correction. The sermon then ends with the question of foundation. Hearing Jesus’ words and not doing them is building on sand.
verseByVerse.examples: The closing verse, he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes, is Matthew’s first portrait of Jesus as teacher. That is either astonishing arrogance or the voice of the one to whom all authority belongs, and Matthew does not leave the reader in the middle. The crowd was astonished. The question is what they, and we, do with the astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, "Let me take the speck out of your eye," when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 7 brings the Sermon on the Mount to its close. Jesus warns against harsh judging while ignoring one’s own sin, yet against naivety too (vv. 1–6); calls disciples to keep asking, because their Father is generous (vv. 7–11); and gathers the law about our neighbours into the Golden Rule (v. 12). Then comes a call to decide, in four pairs: two gates, two trees, two confessions and two builders (vv. 13–27). The chapter ends where everything in Matthew is heading: with Jesus himself as the way, the Judge and the rock.

Judge not. “Judge” (krinō) can mean to evaluate or to condemn. Here it means the critical, condemning spirit that sets itself up as judge over others, hunting for their faults and passing sentence (Luke 18:9–11). Jesus is not banning moral evaluation; he names wrong all through the sermon. He is banning the hypocritical tribunal of the self-righteous, who build careful cases against others while suppressing the evidence against themselves. That you be not judged means by God.

Measure for measure. If you condemn without mercy, you will be judged without mercy (James 2:13); in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself (Romans 2:1). The picture is a merchant measuring grain. The standard a person applies to others is the standard he is choosing to be tried by, and he sets it every time he opens his mouth about somebody else, before a God who sees every page of the file.

But do not notice the log that is in your own eye? A tradesman’s joke. A speck (karphos) is a splinter, a bit of straw or sawdust; a log (dokos) is a beam, a roof timber. Both come from the same building yard, and the picture was told by a carpenter’s son to people who had watched carpenters work: a man with a joist sticking out of his eye, leaning in to remove a wood chip from someone else’s. It is meant to be laughed at, and the laugh is the argument. Nobody would think this reasonable if he could see it from outside, and that is the whole difficulty: the man with the beam is the one person in the room who cannot see it. We see others’ faults sharply and our own hardly at all. Often the faults that irritate us most in others are our own. You hypocrite: an actor (6:2), playing the righteous judge while hiding his own sin.

Qualified, not excused. Jesus does not say leave the speck. He says take the log out of your own eye first, and then you will see clearly to help your brother. Removing a speck from an eye is delicate work: if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself (Galatians 6:1). Self-examination is not an excuse never to correct. It is the qualification for correcting rightly, as one patient helping another.

The only eye without a beam. One man has stood in this scene with no log in his eye at all. When a woman caught in adultery was dragged before him, Jesus said, let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her (John 8:7). Most modern Bibles set this story in brackets, because it is missing from the earliest manuscripts of John, though many believe it records a true event. The one person present who was without sin did not throw it, but said, neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more (John 8:11): clear sight, a true word about the sin, and a gentle hand. The only one qualified to be our critic chose to be our physician.

Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs. Dogs here are wild scavengers; pigs were unclean animals to Jews. Both picture people who treat holy things with contempt. The holy things and the pearls are the gospel and the truths of God’s kingdom. Some people answer God’s truth with mockery and violence, and Jesus says, do not keep pressing it on them (10:14; Acts 13:46).

What it does not mean. “Judge not” does not mean that no one may ever say anything is wrong. Paul commands the church to judge those inside it who persist in sin (1 Corinthians 5:12–13), and courts, parents and elders must make judgments. What Jesus forbids is a fault-finding spirit that assumes the worst and pronounces verdicts that belong only to God. Nor does verse 6 permit us to write off people as “pigs” easily: the same Jesus ate with sinners.

The proof is in the same chapter. Verse 1 says judge not, yet verse 6 requires the hearer to work out who is behaving like dogs and pigs, and verses 15–20 to identify false prophets by their fruit. Whatever judge not forbids, it cannot forbid what Jesus requires in the next breath. The problem was never judging. It was judging badly: on appearances, by a standard the judge exempts himself from.

When I hear someone say it is not my place to judge, how should I answer? Gently, and with the whole passage. Agree with what is true in it: none of us may condemn another’s soul, assume the worst, or set ourselves above anyone, and we must always start with our own sin. Then point out that Jesus himself tells us in the same chapter to tell good fruit from bad, and that he says elsewhere, judge with right judgment (John 7:24). Calling something wrong because God calls it wrong is not condemning a person; it is agreeing with God, and it can be done with tears and humility. The difference is between a judge with a gavel and a friend who has had the same disease and knows the cure.

Where it would be wrong: A friend is drifting into an affair, and you say nothing because you must not judge. Jesus does not forbid all judgement. Warn your friend gently (Galatians 6:1). A church must exercise discipline (18:15–17), and parents must judge who is safe with their children. Take out the log first; then you will see clearly to help (v. 5).

For worship. The carpenter who told this joke knew timber, and in the end he was fastened to it. The beam we could never see in our own eye was laid on him, and the measure we had measured out to everyone else was measured to him in full. The righteous Judge was judged for us, and he has become our Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Dogs and pigs were unclean animals, images of those who scorn what is holy.

parallels.desc: in passing judgment you condemn yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The door that opens. The sermon has described a life impossible by human effort. The demands drive us to our knees, and on our knees we find that the door opens.

Ask … seek … knock. Three pictures, each stronger than the last: a child asking a parent, a search for something lost, a caller at a closed door. All three are present imperatives, which suggests keep on asking, seeking, knocking (Luke 11:5–10; 18:1–8). The passives, it will be given and it will be opened, point to God as the giver, and the promise is for everyone who asks.

Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? Never a counterfeit. The round, flat loaves of Galilee looked like the smooth stones of the region (4:3), and some fish of the lake, such as the catfish, could look like snakes. What father would trick his hungry child? No father would give a dangerous snake instead of food. So bread and stone, fish and serpent, are not random opposites. They are things that look alike. The picture is not a father handing over something obviously cruel; it is a father palming off a convincing fake, something that looks right in the hand and turns out to be inedible or dangerous. That is the fear underneath much unanswered prayer. Nobody seriously suspects God of malice. What people quietly suspect is a substitution: that they asked for bread and got a stone that resembles it. Jesus says the one thing that is never in the parcel is a counterfeit.

If you then, who are evil. Jesus calls his own audience evil in a passing clause, as an agreed fact needing no defence, on the way to a point about generosity (Ephesians 2:3). An assessment of human nature bleak enough to stop us in our tracks becomes an argument for how kind God is.

How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! God is not a reluctant giver. Luke’s version says, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13): the Spirit is the greatest of the good things.

How much more, at the cross. Paul carries the same argument to its summit: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Romans 8:32). And the Son himself once knelt and asked. In Gethsemane he prayed that the cup might pass from him, and for our sake the answer was no. Because the one Son who asked received the cup, the many sons who ask receive bread, though even then the Son was heard (Hebrews 5:7), which is why the Father’s goodness to us can never be in doubt.

What it does not mean. Not that God will give us anything we ask for, if only we persist. A good father does not give a knife to a toddler. God gives “good things”, and he decides what is good; sometimes the answer is “no” or “wait” (1 John 5:14–15). Nor is persistence a way of wearing God down (6:7–8). It is the persistence of trust.

The Father fathering. A prayer answered differently is not the Father failing but the Father fathering. Bring anything that befits a child of this Father: daily provision, wisdom for a hard decision, the salvation of a wayward son, courage to obey this very sermon.

If I already have the Holy Spirit, why ask for him? Every believer receives the Spirit when he trusts Christ, and has him for good (Ephesians 1:13; Romans 8:9). In its first setting, Luke’s promise looked ahead to Pentecost, when the disciples waited and prayed for the promised Spirit (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:14). For us now, we do not ask for a Guest we lack. We ask the Guest who lives within to fill the whole house: to be filled afresh (Ephesians 5:18), as already Spirit-filled believers were filled again for boldness (Acts 4:31); for his comfort, his power to put sin to death and bear fruit, his help to understand Scripture. And Luke can call him the supreme good thing the Father gives, because in giving us the Spirit, God gives us himself.

Where it applies: Your son has walked away from the faith. Keep asking God for him, for years if need be. Your Father hears.
verseByVerse.note: Flat loaves could look like stones, and some fish like snakes.

parallels.desc: every good gift is from above
if we ask according to his will

verseByVerse.quote: So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Golden Rule. Think how you would like to be treated, with kindness, honesty, patience and forgiveness, then do it to them first, without waiting for them to do it.

A fence and a road. It is often said that Jesus taught nothing new here. Hillel, a generation before, according to a story told in the Talmud, said: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole law. Confucius and the book of Tobit said much the same. Two things are distinctive all the same. The first is the direction. A person may keep the negative rule perfectly while sitting still. Jesus’ positive form makes it impossible to obey by inaction: you must work out what you would long for in his place, and go and be that for him. The one rule is a fence; the other is a road.

Family likeness, not prudence. The second is the ground. The verse opens with So, reaching back to the Father who gives good gifts (vv. 7–11). The reason to treat others this way is not that society runs more smoothly, nor that we may hope for the same in return, but that children come to resemble their father. Reciprocity is prudence. This is family likeness.

For this is the Law and the Prophets. The whole Law and the Prophets hang on love for God and love for neighbour (22:37–40), and the Golden Rule is a practical way of applying the second. Jesus has spent two chapters pressing the law beyond the reach of every hearer, and he ends by handing them one sentence they can carry down the mountain: not a lowering of the standard but the whole of it, in a form a person can begin on tomorrow morning.

He did it first. The bracket from 5:17 to 7:12 has a person at its centre. Jesus came to fulfil the Law and the Prophets, and here he sums them up in a sentence that he alone has ever kept. He did not wait for us to treat him well. Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3); he saw us harassed and helpless and did for us what we would have begged for, had we known how lost we were. Paul calls it the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2): to bear one another’s burdens is to treat others as he has treated us.

What it does not mean. The Golden Rule is not the whole of Christianity, or the way of salvation, as if we could earn heaven by being nice. No one keeps it perfectly. It shows us our sin, drives us to Christ, and then becomes the shape of the new life his Spirit gives.

Since people want different things, will I not just impose my tastes on others? It is a fair objection to the rule taken bare, and the second half of the verse answers it. This is the Law and the Prophets: what you may wish for another is bounded by everything God has revealed about what is good. The rule is a summary of the law, not a licence to substitute your appetites for it. And it asks you to imagine yourself in his place, with his needs and his situation, not to assume that he is you. The person who loves his introverted friend will not throw him the surprise party he himself would enjoy.

Where it would be wrong: A drunk friend wants his car keys back. He wants them, but treating him as you would want to be treated means taking them away: sober, you would want to be stopped. The rule is to do what you would rightly want done, not to give people whatever they ask.
verseByVerse.note: Other ancient teachers put this rule negatively (“do not do what you would hate”); Jesus puts it positively.

parallels.desc: the whole law in one word

verseByVerse.quote: Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conclusion of the sermon. Verses 13–27 call for a decision through a series of contrasts: two gates, two trees, two builders. There is no neutral ground. It is not enough to admire the sermon; one must enter.

For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction. “Easy” literally means broad, spacious. The broad road has room for everything: no self-denial, no repentance. It is the way of the crowd, and it leads to destruction.

Broad-minded and narrow. Our culture prizes being broad-minded and suspects anything narrow, and Jesus reverses the valuation. Popularity is no proof of truth. And the broad road is not crowded only with the obviously wicked. It is thronged with respectable, religious people too, even some who will cry Lord, Lord (vv. 21–23), which is exactly what makes the warning so searching.

For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life. “Hard” (tethlimmenē) means pressed, constricted, and is related to the word for affliction. The gate is narrow because it admits only those who come on Jesus’ terms, by repentance and faith; the way is hard because following him involves self-denial, opposition and suffering (16:24; Acts 14:22).

You enter low and empty-handed. The word pictures a passage one must squeeze through. You cannot carry your self-righteousness, your sins or your idols through it. It is narrow, but it is not exclusive in the sense of keeping out the wrong kind of person: the beggar, the prostitute and the tax collector go through it, and the proud do not.

And those who find it are few. Jesus does not give numbers; he gives a warning. When asked whether those being saved are few, he answered: strive to enter through the narrow door (Luke 13:23–24). Nor are the few presented with satisfaction: he lamented over Jerusalem, longing to gather her children as a hen gathers her brood (23:37). But he refuses to soften the reality, because a guide who will not mention where the broad road ends is no friend to those walking it.

Is the narrow gate Christ himself? In short, yes, though Matthew says it by implication rather than in so many words. It is a fair question. Matthew 7 does not have Jesus calling himself the gate or door: that is John’s picture (John 10:9). Read on its own, the sermon could sound as if the gate were simply a better way of behaving. How can we be sure what Jesus meant? Read in widening circles, starting with the closest.

1. The immediate context. The picture of two ways is old: Moses set before Israel life and death (Deuteronomy 30:15–19), and Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked. And a few verses later Jesus explains his own picture: the wise builder is the one who hears these words of mine and does them (v. 24). The narrow way is the life of a disciple of Jesus, lived by his words.

2. The sermon itself points to Jesus, not to self-improvement. It begins with the poor in spirit, to whom the kingdom is given (5:3). It demands a righteousness no one can produce (5:20, 48), and teaches us to ask daily for forgiveness (6:12). Jesus also puts himself at the centre: his people are persecuted on his account (5:11), he sets his own word beside Moses’, and the judgement that follows the two gates turns on whether he knew them (7:21–23). The narrow road ends at Jesus.

3. The rest of Matthew. Jesus calls the weary to come to him (11:28), and gives his life as a ransom for many (20:28).

4. The whole Bible. Only then do we bring in John: I am the door; if anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9). This does not give Matthew 7 a new meaning; it says openly what the sermon already implies.

This commentary’s view: in Matthew 7 the narrow gate is entering the kingdom as Jesus’ disciple, and the narrow road is the life he has just described. But that life begins with poverty of spirit, lives on God’s mercy, and ends before Jesus as judge, so the gate cannot be anything other than coming to Jesus himself in faith. It is not good behaviour instead of Christ, nor Christ without changed behaviour. It is coming to Christ and following him: the gate is entered by faith, and the road is walked in obedience.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by a hard life. The gate is entered by grace through faith; the hardness is the cost of following Christ in a hostile world, and his yoke is easy (11:30). Nor does “few” mean that heaven will be thinly populated: Revelation sees a great multitude that no one can number from every nation (Revelation 7:9).

Where Christians differ: exclusivism. Pluralists hold that all religions are equally valid paths to God. Inclusivists hold that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him explicitly, and many hold this out of real compassion for those who have never heard. This commentary’s view: exclusivism. There is one way in, through Christ, and salvation is found in no one else (Acts 4:12). This is why the gospel must be preached to all nations.

Is it not arrogant to speak of only one narrow gate? That charge would hold if Christians had invented the way or earned their place on it. But the narrow gate is not a club for the better sort; the passage itself says it is entered low and empty-handed. Every religion is exclusive somewhere: even the claim that all paths are equal rules out every faith that says otherwise. The real question is whether Jesus is who he said he is. If God has truly come in his Son and died for sinners, then to point to him is not pride but the kindness of someone who squeezed through the gate empty-handed calling back to show others where it is (Acts 4:12).

What about those who have never heard? Scripture gives no second way in. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Romans 10:13–15), which is exactly why Paul asks how they will hear without a preacher, and why the church sends missionaries. Those who have never heard are not condemned for rejecting a Christ they never knew, but for sin against the light they had, the witness of creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and God will judge with perfect justice. Infants who die before they can believe are in a different case, and Reformed Christians have long held that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest in the kindness of the Lord who welcomed little children and laid his hands on them (19:13–15). The right response is not speculation but going and telling.

Where it would be wrong: Someone thinks being odd, harsh or rule-bound proves he is on the narrow road. The narrow way is coming to Christ in faith and following him in love, not a pose of being different.

parallels.desc: life and death set before you
the way of the wicked will perish

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus you will recognize them by their fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware of false prophets. A false prophet claims to speak for God, but does not. The Old Testament warned of them repeatedly (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Jeremiah 23:16–22), and Jesus warns that they will multiply (24:11, 24).

Dressed for the job. They come in sheep’s clothing: they look like believers, use Christian words, and may even be leaders. Zechariah describes false prophets who put on a hairy cloak, the prophet’s uniform, in order to deceive (Zechariah 13:4). The danger is precisely that they do not look like wolves. This is a threat from inside the flock.

But inwardly are ravenous wolves. Their real aim is to devour: to exploit the flock for money, power, sex or fame (Acts 20:29–30). Ravenous is harpax, from the verb to seize or snatch, used of the wolf in John 10:12. The false teacher is not only mistaken; he is taking something, and the flock is what he takes it from.

A Lamb, not a wolf in fleece. The false prophet is a wolf who puts on a sheep’s coat in order to take. Jesus is the Shepherd who became a Lamb in order to give (John 1:29), and the wolf’s snatching verb is the very one he uses when he promises that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). He is the true Prophet whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15), and the surest way to recognise a forgery is to know the original well.

You will recognize them by their fruits. Fruit is what a tree produces: for a false prophet, his character and conduct (2 Peter 2:1–3, 14), his teaching (1 John 4:1–3; Galatians 1:8–9), and its effect on those who follow him.

What good and bad fruit look like. Look in three places. The teaching: good fruit exalts Christ and his cross and calls people to repentance and grace; bad fruit makes light of sin, sells a gospel of self, money or works, and draws disciples after the teacher (Acts 20:30). The character: the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), or pride, greed, immorality, manipulation and a trail of wounded people. The effect: people loving Christ more, or people puffed up, crushed or fleeced, with the leader exalted.

The root decides the fruit. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? Character produces conduct, and the heart shows itself in time. Good works do not make a person good, but a person made good by God’s grace does good works, as a good tree bears good fruit. And every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire, the words John the Baptist used (3:10).

Judged in autumn. An orchard is judged in autumn, and a bad tree can look identical to a good one for most of the year. A great deal of the damage done in churches has been done by men whose fruit would have been obvious in five years and who were given authority in five weeks (1 Timothy 3:6; 5:22). The instruction is not be suspicious. It is wait, and watch what actually grows.

Are there prophets today, true or false? The prophets and apostles laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and with the completion of Scripture the canon is closed; this commentary holds, charitably, that the revelatory gift of prophecy has ceased. Many faithful Christians believe God still gives prophecy, usually meaning a lesser word that must be tested and never rivals Scripture; they are brothers and sisters, and they too insist that every word be weighed. So anyone today who claims a new word from God that adds to Scripture or binds the church is to be tested with great care. But the warning reaches wider than titles. Any preacher, author, podcaster or teacher who claims to tell you what God says is to be weighed by Scripture and by his fruit (1 John 4:1; Acts 17:11).

Where it applies: A popular online preacher says God wants you rich, and his own life is marked by luxury and pride. Test him by Scripture and by his fruit, and stop listening.

Where it would be wrong: You treat your own pastor as a false prophet because he differs from you on a secondary matter, such as baptism or the end times, or because his style annoys you. False prophets deny the gospel, or live in persistent sin. A brother you disagree with is not a wolf.

For worship. On the way to the cross Jesus said, if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry? (Luke 23:31). The green tree went into the fire that the dry and fruitless trees deserved, and rose again to make them live. Every grape of love and fig of patience in his people is his own life rising in them.

parallels.desc: the axe laid to the root

verseByVerse.quote: Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. On that day many will say to me, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" And then will I declare to them, "I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord. The double “Lord, Lord” expresses fervour or familiarity. These people use the right words, the right confession. But words are not enough to enter the kingdom of heaven on the last day.

But the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Doing God’s will is the mark of a true disciple (12:50). Not perfect obedience, but a life of genuine submission to God, shown in repentance and in obedience to Christ’s words (v. 24).

Many will say to me. On that day is a standard phrase for the day of judgment (Isaiah 2:11; Malachi 3:17). Only God judges the world (Genesis 18:25), yet Jesus quietly claims to be the one before whom everyone will stand (25:31–46; John 5:22).

Did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? Impressive religious activity, done in Jesus’ name, with apparent power. Yet it is not enough. Judas was among the Twelve who were sent to heal and cast out demons (10:1–8). Spiritual gifts and results are not proof of saving faith.

A résumé at the bar of God. Every word of their defence is about them: we prophesied, we cast out, we did. What is entirely absent is any mention of mercy, of the cross, of needing to be forgiven; the poor in spirit come with empty hands (5:3). And Jesus does not answer that they did too little. The issue is not the volume of the service but the absence of the relationship. So the anxious question, have I done enough, is the very question these men were asking. They are not failed disciples. They are strangers who were extremely busy.

I never knew you. In the Bible, “to know” often means a personal, covenant relationship (Amos 3:2; John 10:14). Jesus does not say “I used to know you”, but “I never knew you”. They were never his. He knows every deed of every person; he never took them as his own, as a shepherd knows his sheep by name (John 10:3).

Depart from me. From Psalm 6:8, and among the most terrible words in the Bible: banishment from Christ’s presence (25:41; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). In Psalm 6 David says these words to his enemies, trusting the LORD who alone judges. Jesus takes them on his own lips as the Judge who pronounces them.

You workers of lawlessness. “Lawlessness” (anomia) means living without regard to God’s law. Their impressive works covered lives that did not submit to God’s will.

How do I know I am not one of them? Start with the fact that these men are surprised. Nobody in this scene was worried on the way in. The person lying awake frightened by this verse is showing the opposite of what it describes; fear of self-deception is not the mark of the self-deceived, who are perfectly comfortable. Then examine yourself honestly with the tests John gives (1 John 5:13): do you believe that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh; do you love other Christians in practice; is there real obedience, a turning from sin, however slow? Does your sin grieve you? Do you want Christ, or only his benefits? Then look away from yourself. Your grip on Christ will be unsteady all your life; his grip on you is not (John 10:28–29). And if you still cannot be sure, come again today with nothing, for whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). The one thing you must not do with this passage is assume.

Where it applies: You attend church, but have never personally trusted Christ or turned from sin. These verses are a mercy to you: come to him today.

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them. Jesus claims that our eternal destiny depends on how we respond to his words, a weight only God’s word carries (Isaiah 40:8). Both builders hear; the difference is doing.

The landscape behind it. Much of that country is cut by wadis, watercourses bone dry most of the year. In summer a wadi bed is an inviting building site: flat, the sand easy to dig, and in July the man who built there would look like the sensible one. Luke says the wise man dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock (Luke 6:48): perhaps the same ground, gone down through until he hit something that would not move.

And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house. Sudden storms turned the dry wadis into torrents in minutes. The storm pictures all the trials of life, and above all the final judgment of God (Isaiah 28:16–17; Ezekiel 13:10–14).

Underground work. The foundation is the one part of a house that is never admired, and in fair weather it makes no visible difference at all. That is exactly the point about obedience. Most of what this sermon has asked for, dealing with anger, cutting off what feeds lust, loving an enemy, giving in secret, forgiving a debt, is invisible. Nobody applauds it. It is also the only thing that makes any difference on the day the water comes down.

And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. The foolish builder’s problem was not ignorance; he heard. It was not hostility; he was building a house too, perhaps a religious one. He heard and did not do.

The houses look identical. Both men built, both finished, both slept under a roof, and you could not tell them apart by walking past. To build on sand is to sit under good preaching and nod along, to know your Bible and enjoy discussing it, to be baptised and decent, while the words never change how you live on Monday morning.

The sound of a house going down. And it fell, and great was the fall of it. The sermon simply stops with the noise of a collapse, with no summary and no softening. In every pair the wrong option is the comfortable one, and the two are hard to tell apart from outside: a broad road looks like freedom, a wolf looks like a sheep, Lord, Lord sounds like faith, and a house on sand looks like a house.

Is the rock Christ, or obedience? In short, the rock is hearing and doing Jesus’ words, and that means building on Jesus himself. Read plainly, the parable says the wise man is the one who hears Jesus’ words and does them. Jesus does not say here, I am the rock. And the crowd on the hillside did not yet know that he would die for sins and rise again; even his disciples did not grasp that until much later (16:21–23). So we must not hurry past what the text says. How do we know what it means? As with the narrow gate (vv. 13–14), read in widening circles.

1. What the first hearers would have heard. In the Old Testament, God himself is the Rock of his people (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 18:2), and Isaiah spoke of a sure foundation laid by God and a storm of judgement that sweeps away every refuge of lies (Isaiah 28:16–17). Now Jesus says that the one secure foundation for the day of judgement is these words of mine. Even before the cross, the parable confronts them with Jesus himself.

2. What “these words” actually ask. Doing Jesus’ words cannot mean keeping the sermon perfectly, because the sermon demands perfection (5:48) and teaches disciples to ask daily for forgiveness (6:12). So the wise builder is not the person who never fails. He is the one who comes as a beggar for mercy and then lives as Jesus teaches. The foolish builder hears, perhaps admires, and carries on as before.

3. The verses just before. The judgement in verses 21–23 turns on whether Jesus knew them. Hearing and doing Jesus’ words is not a substitute for knowing him. It is what knowing him looks like.

4. What the rest of Scripture makes explicit. Peter applies Isaiah’s foundation stone directly to Christ (1 Peter 2:4–7), and Paul says no one can lay a foundation other than Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). These passages show what was in the parable all along.

This commentary’s view: in the parable, the rock is hearing and doing Jesus’ words, and we should let it say that, as a sharp warning against hearing without obeying. But because those words begin with mercy for the poor in spirit, and because the one who speaks them is the Lord who will judge, building on them means building on Jesus himself: trusting him and following him. Obedience does not earn the foundation. It is what building on it looks like.

What it does not mean. Not that we build our own salvation by obeying Jesus’ teaching perfectly; only Jesus did that, and his obedience is counted as ours, so our faltering doing is accepted for his sake. Obedience is the evidence that we have dug down to the rock (James 1:22–25). Nor do wise builders escape storms. Faith in Christ does not exempt us from trouble; it keeps us standing through it.

What if I have heard sermons for years and done little? Then this parable is God’s kindness to you today, because the storm has not yet come and the digging can begin now. Do not try to rebuild everything at once. Take one thing from this sermon you have heard many times and not done, perhaps forgiving someone, giving in secret, or praying in your room, and do it this week, trusting Christ for mercy and his Spirit for strength. Tell a Christian friend so that he can ask you about it. Build on the rock one shovelful at a time. The Lord who calls you to dig is the rock you are digging toward, and he does not despise small beginnings.

Where it would be wrong: A believer whose life has fallen apart, through illness, redundancy or bereavement, concludes that his house must have been built on sand. Both houses faced the same storm. The wise man’s house was battered too; it simply did not fall. Trouble is not proof of a bad foundation. Standing through it, still clinging to Christ, is proof of a good one (Romans 8:35–39).
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season; a house on sand could be swept away overnight.

parallels.desc: a wall smeared with whitewash falls

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Jesus finished these sayings. Matthew’s formula closes each of five great discourses (5–7; 10; 13; 18; 24–25), until at 26:1, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, the passion begins. Five books of teaching, beginning on a mountain, given by one who has already come out of Egypt (2:15) and been tested forty days in the wilderness: a greater than Moses is giving the law its full meaning.

The crowds were astonished at his teaching. Ekplēssō is a strong word for being overwhelmed, and the tense suggests that it went on. What struck them, Matthew says, was his authority.

For he was teaching them as one who had authority. He spoke as the one who fulfils the law (5:17), who will judge the world (7:22–23), and whose words are the rock on which life stands (7:24).

There is no modest reading. The scribes taught by quoting earlier authorities: Rabbi so-and-so said, and Rabbi so-and-so replied. They were careful men doing careful work, but their authority was borrowed. What the crowd had never heard was a man who cited nobody, who opened Moses on his own word and then told them that their eternal safety depended on doing what he had just said. Some say the church put such claims on his lips later, yet the pattern of But I say to you is so characteristic that even many sceptical scholars trace it to Jesus himself. It is either breathtaking arrogance or the voice of the one to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given (28:18), and the rest of Matthew’s Gospel is the working out of which.

How should I respond, having read the whole sermon? Not by feeling impressed and moving on, which is what most of that crowd did. Come to him first as the poor in spirit, admitting that you have not kept these words and cannot in your own strength, and receive the mercy and righteousness he gives. Then take him at his word as your King: his words are now the final authority over your money, your eyes, your tongue, your enemies and your worries. Read the sermon again, slowly, over the coming weeks. Ask your Father daily for the Spirit to make it true in you. And expect him to do it, because the one who taught it is also the one who lives it in his people.

Where it would be wrong: You decide that because Jesus’ words carry final authority, the rest of Scripture, Moses, the prophets and Paul, matters less, and you read only the red letters. Jesus came to fulfil the Law and the Prophets, not to set them aside (5:17), and he sent his apostles to speak with his authority. All Scripture is his word (2 Timothy 3:16).

For worship. He quoted no one, because there was no one above him to quote. The voice that once said let there be light now said blessed are the poor in spirit. All authority in heaven and on earth is his, and he spends it on blessing beggars and building them on himself. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not.
verseByVerse.note: Scribes taught by citing earlier authorities; Jesus spoke on his own authority (“But I say to you”).

7.theology:
Hearing and doing: faith and works. Matthew 7:24–27 has sometimes been read as teaching salvation by works: do Jesus’ words and be saved. But the doing is not the foundation; the rock is, and the rock is Christ himself, received by faith. The doing is the evidence and expression of real faith, what James calls faith shown by its works (James 2:17–18).

Calvin wrote that we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. Obedience to the sermon is not the cause of salvation but its fruit, and the foundation, as Paul says (1 Corinthians 3:11), is Jesus Christ himself, the one whose words these are.
7.examples:
Then: Proverbs sets wisdom, who has built her house (Proverbs 9:1), against folly (9:13–18). Israel’s history shows both kinds of building: kings such as Hezekiah and Josiah who built on God’s word, and long years in which the nation heard it and ignored it, until the storm of Babylon came and the temple fell, as Jeremiah had warned (Jeremiah 7:1–15).

Now: The sermon ends with a personal question: what are you building on? Storms of suffering, loss and death will come. The person who is impressed by the sermon and does nothing with it is building on sand. The person whose failures under its demands drive him to the Christ who fulfils them, and who by the Spirit begins to do what it says, is building on rock.

8.title: The King’s Authority Over All
8.text: <sup>1</sup>When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. <sup>2</sup>And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>3</sup>And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>5</sup>When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, <sup>6</sup>“Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly.” <sup>7</sup>And he said to him, “I will come and heal him.” <sup>8</sup>But the centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. <sup>9</sup>For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>10</sup>When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, “Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. <sup>11</sup>I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, <sup>12</sup>while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” <sup>13</sup>And to the centurion Jesus said, “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed at that very moment. <sup>14</sup>And when Jesus entered Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. <sup>15</sup>He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him. <sup>16</sup>That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.” <sup>18</sup>Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. <sup>19</sup>And a scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>21</sup>Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” <sup>23</sup>And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. <sup>24</sup>And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. <sup>25</sup>And they went and woke him, saying, “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” <sup>26</sup>And he said to them, “Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?” Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. <sup>27</sup>And the men marveled, saying, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” <sup>28</sup>And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. <sup>29</sup>And behold, they cried out, “What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” <sup>30</sup>Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. <sup>31</sup>And the demons begged him, saying, “If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs.” <sup>32</sup>And he said to them, “Go.” So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. <sup>33</sup>The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men. <sup>34</sup>And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
8.overview:
In Matthew 8 the King who has just finished speaking begins to act. He heals a leper with a touch, a Gentile’s servant with a word and a feverish woman with his hand, and stills a raging sea with a rebuke. The disciples ask the right question: “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” Matthew means the reader to answer: the Son of God, who holds all authority in heaven and on earth.

The chapter also shows grace to outsiders. A leper is touched rather than avoided. A Roman centurion shows a faith that puts Israel to shame, and Jesus says many will come from east and west to the feast of the kingdom while those who rely on their birth are shut out. The centurion’s faith is the model: he rests wholly on the word of the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Messiah Heals: Authority over Leprosy, Paralysis, and Fever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew gathers ten miracles in chapters 8 and 9, presenting Jesus as the Servant Isaiah promised, who took our illnesses and bore our diseases (v. 17; Isaiah 53:4). The first three are a leper, a centurion’s servant and Peter’s mother-in-law: the unclean, the Gentile and the woman, people kept at the edge of Israel’s religious life.
verseByVerse.theology: Each healing is an acted picture of salvation: Jesus touches the untouchable, heals at a distance by his word alone, and raises up those laid low. Isaiah 53:4 ties these healings to the cross, where Jesus would carry not only our diseases but their root, our sin.
verseByVerse.examples: The centurion’s faith astonishes Jesus and points ahead to the Gentiles coming in: with no one in Israel had he found such faith. Faith is not a matter of background or upbringing; it is the trust that recognises Christ’s authority and rests on it.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 8 is the chapter in which the King who has just finished speaking begins to act. The sermon ended with the crowds astonished at his authority (7:29); now that authority meets the world as it actually is. Disease, the sea and the demonic each obey at a word, while a Gentile believes, the disciples have little faith, and a town asks him to leave. The chapter’s own question, what sort of man is this, is answered: the Lord himself, come near enough to touch.

The connection. Chapters 5–7 showed Jesus’ authority in word; chapters 8–9 show it in deed: ten miracles, in three groups, over disease, nature, demons and death (4:23; 9:35). Here the one who said blessed are the poor in spirit goes down the hill and shows what he meant.

When he came down from the mountain. Like Moses coming down from Sinai (Exodus 34:29). Moses came down with the law on tablets of stone and a face so bright that the people were afraid to come near him. The greater Moses comes down from his mountain, great crowds follow him, and the first person to come near him is a man whom the law of Moses forbade to come near anyone. The law could diagnose a leper and exclude him. It could not cleanse him. What the law could not do, the Lord of the law is about to do with his hand.

A leper. “Leprosy” in the Bible (Hebrew tsara’at, Greek lepra) covers a range of skin diseases, not only what is now called Hansen’s disease. It was a category of ritual defilement, and that does not soften the picture; it widens it. A person with such a disease had to live outside the camp or town, wear torn clothes, leave his hair loose, cover his upper lip, and cry out that he was unclean to warn others away (Leviticus 13:45–46). Anyone who touched him became unclean too. He was cut off from the temple, from family, from work and from all human touch. Josephus, writing in the first century, says lepers were treated as no different from dead men. In the Bible, leprosy also became a vivid picture of sin: a defilement that separates us from God and others, which we cannot cleanse ourselves.

A man at his own funeral. Torn clothes and loose hair were the dress of a mourner, so he attended his own funeral every morning. Later Jewish tradition fixed the distance he must keep at four cubits, about six feet, and at a hundred cubits if the wind was blowing from him towards you. He lived as a walking warning.

He had not been touched. Not by his wife, if he had one; not by his children; not by a friend’s hand on his shoulder. However long the disease had been on him, that is how long it had been since another human hand had rested on him. Loneliness of that kind does something to a person’s sense of whether anybody could want him near, and it explains the exact shape of the prayer he is about to make.

Came to him. He should not have. Every step towards that crowd broke the rule he had lived under for years. Desperation drove him past it, and so did something more: he had heard enough about this man to think the rules might not be the last word.

And knelt before him. The word (prosekynei) is the same as “worship” (2:11), the word used of the wise men before the child in Bethlehem. He knelt before he had received anything. The worship came first and the healing second, which is the right order, and it is the order of every true approach to Christ.

Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. “Lord” may simply mean “sir”, but in Matthew it carries more. He does not doubt the power: you can. He doubts the welcome: does Jesus want to touch someone like me? That is exactly what years of being untouchable will do to a person, and many of us are the same: we find it easy to believe that Christ can do anything, and hard to believe that he wants to do it for someone like us. And he asks to be made “clean”, not just “healed”: he is asking not only to be well but to be allowed back in, to God’s people and to worship.

What it does not mean. Not that “if you will” shows weak faith. It is humble faith, which leaves the outcome to Christ. Jesus does not rebuke him for it. Nor is it a model for doubting God’s willingness to forgive. When we come to him for cleansing from sin, he is always willing (John 6:37; 1 John 1:9). We may pray “if you will” about healing or circumstances, because God has not promised them; we need not pray it about forgiveness, because he has.
