Is leprosy in the Bible a punishment for sin? Not as a rule. Occasionally God struck a person with it as a direct judgement: Miriam for opposing Moses (Numbers 12:10), Gehazi for his greed (2 Kings 5:27), King Uzziah for forcing his way into the priest’s work (2 Chronicles 26:19–21). But the law of Leviticus treats it as a condition, not a crime, and nobody in the Gospels suggests this man had brought it on himself. Its uncleanness was a picture of what sin does to all of us, not a verdict on the particular person who had it. So if you are ill, do not conclude that God is punishing you. Sickness belongs to a fallen world, and Jesus treats the sick with compassion, never with accusation.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you feel makes you untouchable to God: a sin, a shame, an illness, a history you would rather nobody knew? Then do what the leper did. Do not wait at a distance until you are presentable. Come to Jesus as you are, kneel, and say the honest sentence: Lord, you can.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, "I will; be clean." And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him. Jesus could have healed with a word, as he does a few verses later for the centurion’s servant (v. 13). Nothing was gained by the contact except the contact itself, and that was the point. This man may not have been touched by anyone for years. And the order matters: he touched him first, and only then said be clean. For the length of one sentence the Lord of glory was in physical contact with an unclean man who had not yet been healed. By the law, touching him should have made Jesus unclean too (Leviticus 5:3). It did not. The flow ran the other way: Jesus did not become unclean; the leper became clean. That is the whole gospel acted out in a single gesture, a holiness that is not defiled by contact with the defiled, but destroys the defilement. Our sin was laid on him at the cross, and his righteousness is counted as ours (2 Corinthians 5:21).

The outstretched hand. The phrase is the language of the exodus: God would strike Egypt and redeem his people with an outstretched arm (Exodus 3:20; 6:6). The hand that once stretched out over Egypt now stretches across the six feet the law had put between this man and everyone else, and rests on skin that nobody had willingly touched in years. It is the same God, coming down to deliver.

Saying, I will; be clean. The direct answer to the man’s question. Jesus is willing. And his word has power: he speaks, and it happens, as God spoke at creation (Psalm 33:9). No formula, no process, no prayer to someone higher: simply the will of the Creator restoring what disease had destroyed. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed, skin that had been rotting for years made whole without a period of recovery.

See that you say nothing to anyone. Jesus often told people not to spread news of his miracles (9:30; 12:16). This is sometimes called the “messianic secret”. Reasons: to avoid crowds who wanted only miracles, which hindered his teaching; to avoid the political misunderstanding that he was a military Messiah who would overthrow Rome; and so that his identity would be revealed in God’s time, through the cross. Mark tells us how this particular command went: the man went out and talked about it freely, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (Mark 1:45). A reputation as a healer had buried the preaching under a queue of patients.

But go, show yourself to the priest. The law required a cleansed leper to be examined by a priest, who would declare him clean (Leviticus 14:1–32). Only then could he return to society and worship. Jesus respects the law of Moses (5:17), and he wants the man fully restored, not just healed: back in his home, back at the table, back in the house of God.

And offer the gift that Moses commanded. The ritual of Leviticus 14 is elaborate: two birds, one killed and the other dipped in its blood and released; cedarwood, scarlet yarn and hyssop; seven days of waiting; and on the eighth day lambs, flour and oil. It may rarely, if ever, have been performed: in the whole Old Testament only Miriam and Naaman are recorded as cleansed of this disease, and neither went through the rite in Jerusalem.

For a proof to them. A testimony to the priests: evidence that something extraordinary had happened, and that the one who cleanses lepers had come. When a man walked into the temple courts and asked for the rite for a cleansed leper, he was handing the priesthood a page they had seldom had cause to open, and somebody had to ask why. When John the Baptist later asks whether Jesus is the Messiah, Jesus points to this: lepers are cleansed (11:5).

How does Jesus touch people now that he is not here in the body? Through his word and his Spirit first of all: the same voice that said I will, be clean, speaks in the gospel and makes guilty people clean before God (John 15:3). He also touches people through his body, the church. When a believer sits with the dying, visits the prisoner, holds the hand of someone everyone else avoids, Christ is at work through his members (25:40). And in the Lord’s Supper he gives visible, tangible signs that his body was given for us. So if you have felt untouched for years, go where his word is preached and his people gather. That is where his hand is most often felt.

On a Tuesday. Who are the untouchables around you: the lonely, the stigmatised, the person with the prison record, the one with the smell? The one who touched you while you were still unclean sends you to them. Choose one person whose company you avoid because it costs you something, and make one concrete approach this week: a visit, a meal, a hand on the shoulder.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, "Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A centurion. When Jesus entered Capernaum, his home base (4:13), a Roman-style army officer came to him. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers: a career officer promoted from the ranks, disciplined and responsible. This one was probably serving Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, whose troops were organised on the Roman pattern. Either way he was a Gentile soldier in an army the locals resented, the visible face of foreign power. Luke adds that he loved the Jewish nation and had built their synagogue, and that Jewish elders came to Jesus on his behalf (Luke 7:3–5). In the New Testament, centurions are almost always presented favourably (27:54; Acts 10; 27:43), a striking fact in an occupied country.

His synagogue. The white limestone synagogue visitors see in Capernaum today is later, but it stands on a first-century basalt foundation that may well be the floor of this man’s synagogue: a Gentile soldier very likely paid for the room in which the Son of God first preached there (Mark 1:21).

Did the centurion come himself, or send others? Matthew has the centurion come to Jesus and speak with him directly. Luke says he sent Jewish elders first, and then friends with the message about not being worthy, and does not have the two men meet at all (Luke 7:3–8). This is a difference of reporting, not a contradiction. In the ancient world, as in ours, a man is said to do what he does through his agents: we say a king built a palace or a company wrote a letter without supposing that either held the trowel or the pen. Matthew shortens the story and presents the request as the centurion’s own, as a message sent through others is the sender’s message, because his point is the centurion’s faith. Luke, who is interested throughout his Gospel in how Jews and Gentiles actually dealt with each other, keeps the messengers in. This is the explanation most careful readers have given, and it fits the way ancient writers told stories; either way, both Gospels agree on everything that matters: the request, the humility, the word spoken at a distance and the healing.

Came forward to him, appealing to him. A Roman officer, a man of power, coming to a Jewish teacher with a request. The word (parakalōn) is the language of urgent entreaty. He does not command; he pleads. The man used to giving orders has met someone he cannot order.

Lord, my servant. The word (pais) can mean “boy”, “child” or “servant”; Luke uses the word for slave, and adds that the man was highly valued by him (Luke 7:2). The centurion cared deeply for a slave, someone his society regarded as property. Roman law allowed a master to do as he liked with a slave, and the agricultural writers advised selling off old and sick ones like worn-out tools. This man, who had every right to replace his servant, goes out to plead for him. (The recent suggestion that the relationship was sexual has no support: pais was a common word for a servant, and Luke’s plain word for a slave removes the ambiguity.)

Is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly. Perhaps near death (Luke 7:2). He does not tell Jesus what to do; he lays the need before him, which is what prayer often is.

Another servant, suffering terribly. The word the centurion uses for his servant, pais, is the word Matthew later uses for Jesus himself, when he quotes Isaiah: behold, my servant whom I have chosen (12:18). So a master pleads for a servant lying in agony, and the one he pleads with is the Father’s own Servant, who would lie in agony himself, not for his own fault but for ours. The centurion had every right to replace a broken slave and would not. The Father, who could have abandoned a broken race, sent his Servant to suffer terribly in its place.

Can I come to Christ on behalf of someone else? Yes, and this man shows how. He came for his servant, and Jesus healed the servant without ever meeting him. Praying for others is not a lesser kind of prayer; it is one of the most Christlike things a believer does, because it is what Christ himself does for us at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34). Bring the names of your unbelieving family, your sick friend, your colleague in trouble. But notice the limit too. Your faith can bring someone to Christ in prayer; it cannot believe for them. Every person must in the end trust him for himself. So pray for them, and pray that they will come.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I will come and heal him." But the centurion replied, "Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will come and heal him. Jesus is willing to go, even to a Gentile’s house. Some translate it as a question: Shall I come and heal him? The Greek can bear it. On that reading Jesus is probing, raising the very issue of a Jew entering a Gentile house so that the centurion can answer it, which is exactly what he does. Either way the sense is much the same.

Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. A devout Jew who entered a Gentile’s house became ritually unclean (Acts 10:28; 11:12). It is why Peter needed a vision before he would go to Cornelius,. The centurion knows this, and does not want to put Jesus in that position. He is protecting Jesus, not only humbling himself. It is the courtesy of a man who has taken the trouble to learn what his neighbours believe, offered at the very moment when his servant is dying and he has every excuse to think of nobody else. “Not worthy” expresses real humility. The Jewish elders said he was worthy (Luke 7:4); he says he is not. True greatness knows its unworthiness before Christ.

But only say the word, and my servant will be healed. He believes that Jesus’ word alone has power, even at a distance. Jesus does not need to be present, see the patient, touch, or perform a ritual. His word is enough. What makes this faith rather than respect is what it assumes about the way things work. The word alone is what acts, and that is precisely what Genesis says about how the world came to be: God said, and it was so. The centurion is, in effect, ascribing to Jesus the creative word of God, and he sees it more clearly than anyone in Israel yet had.

The prayer the church kept. His sentence has never been forgotten: millions of Christians who have never thought about a Roman officer have prayed his words before communion. It is fitting, because this is how every believer approaches the ascended Christ: we cannot see him or touch him, and we do not need to.

If I feel unworthy, should I stay away from the Lord’s Supper? No. The Supper is for people who know they are unworthy and trust Christ, and the centurion’s words are exactly the right frame of mind for it. Paul warns against eating in an unworthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27–29), which means coming carelessly, with unconfessed sin you mean to keep, or with contempt for the body of believers. It does not mean coming while feeling unworthy. If you waited until you felt worthy you would never come, and if you ever did feel worthy you would be coming wrongly. Examine yourself, confess your sin, put things right with anyone you have wronged, and then come, resting on his word and not on your worthiness.
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house; the centurion spares Jesus the problem.

parallels.desc: unlawful for a Jew to visit a foreigner
he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, "Go," and he goes, and to another, "Come," and he comes, and to my servant, "Do this," and he does it." When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, "Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I too am a man under authority. He is part of a chain of command: his authority comes from those above him, and when he speaks the weight of the army stands behind his word. Go, come, do this: three short commands, and three men move.

The logic. The centurion reasons: just as I give orders and they are obeyed, because I carry the authority of those above me, so Jesus carries the authority of God, and sickness obeys him. This is the heart of faith: not confidence in the one praying, but confidence in the authority of the one addressed.

Further than he could see. Press his analogy one step further than he could. He pictures Jesus as he pictures himself, a man set under authority whose word carries weight because a greater power stands behind it. That is true so far as the Son is sent by the Father and does nothing of his own accord (John 5:19). But it is not the whole truth. Jesus is more than an agent. When Elisha raised the dead, he prayed and stretched himself on the child (2 Kings 4:33–35); when Jesus heals, he simply speaks, and the thing is done. The centurion had hold of the right end of the truth and did not yet know how far down it went.

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. “Marvelled” means amazed, astonished. Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to marvel: here, at faith, and in Nazareth, at unbelief (Mark 6:6): faith’s presence where it had no business being, and its absence where it should have been guaranteed. Faith is the one thing that could still astonish the Son of God.

And said to those who followed him, Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. Israel had the Scriptures, the covenants and the promises (Romans 9:4–5). Yet a Gentile soldier, with none of these advantages, showed greater faith than anyone in Israel. And Jesus says it to those who followed him, which means he says it to his own disciples. They needed to hear that the outsider had seen further than they had.

How can Jesus be amazed if he is God and knows everything? Because he is truly man as well as truly God, one person with two natures. As God the Son he knows all things. But in taking our nature he took a real human mind, which learned and grew: Luke says he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), and he said that he did not know the day of his return (24:36). His human mind received knowledge, perceived, and responded, as ours do, and the marvel is a real human response to something wonderful. It does not mean God was caught off guard. It means the Son of God became human enough to be moved by a soldier’s trust, and that is part of the wonder of the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And to the centurion Jesus said, "Go; let it be done for you as you have believed." And the servant was healed at that very moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many will come from east and west. From the ends of the earth: the Gentile nations (Isaiah 49:12; 59:19; Malachi 1:11). The centurion is the first of a great multitude. The picture is drawn from the prophets’ promises of gathering (Isaiah 43:5; Psalm 107:3). The imagery is entirely Jewish and entirely familiar. What is unfamiliar is who is being gathered.

And recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. At formal banquets, guests reclined on couches around a low table, and to recline at a man’s table was to share his life. The prophets pictured the age to come as a great feast that God would prepare for all peoples, with rich food and fine wine (Isaiah 25:6–9). Many devout Jews of that day would not eat with Gentiles at all, and here the Gentiles lie down beside Abraham himself, the father of the nation, at the most honoured meal there will ever be, as members of the family, not as servants, while some of Abraham’s own descendants stand outside. That was always where the promise to Abraham was heading: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3). A Roman soldier in Capernaum is its first instalment.

When and where is this feast? Jesus does not give a date, but the passage itself gives strong clues, and the rest of Scripture fills them in.

1. In the verse itself. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had been dead for many centuries. For them to sit at a table, they must be raised from the dead. So the feast lies on the far side of the resurrection (22:31–32). And the other side of the picture is final judgement: the outer darkness, with weeping and gnashing of teeth, is the language Matthew uses for the end of the age (13:40–43, 49–50; 25:30, 46). The feast and the exclusion happen at the same moment, at the end.

2. In the rest of Scripture. Jesus is drawing on Isaiah’s feast for all peoples, at which God swallows up death for ever and wipes away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:6–9), and Paul says that this happens at the resurrection, when Christ returns (1 Corinthians 15:51–54). At the Last Supper Jesus says he will drink the cup new in his Father’s kingdom (26:29), and Revelation calls it the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), in a new creation where there is no more death (Revelation 21:1–4).

3. Already, and not yet. The kingdom is already present in Jesus (12:28), and the centurion is the first of the many from east and west. Gentiles are coming in now, through the preaching of the gospel to all nations (28:19), and every Lord’s Supper is a foretaste of the feast (1 Corinthians 11:26). But the feast itself, in full, comes when Christ returns, the dead are raised, and the new creation begins.

Where Christians differ: the feast and the thousand years. Revelation 20:1–6 speaks of a thousand-year reign, and Christians read it in different ways, which affects how they read this verse. Premillennialists believe that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth, and many see this verse as describing that kingdom: the patriarchs raised and sharing in Christ’s reign, with believing Gentiles, before the final state. Postmillennialists see the coming of many from east and west being fulfilled as the gospel gradually wins the nations before Christ returns. Amillennialists take the thousand years as a symbolic picture of the present age, in which Christ already reigns; at his one return come the resurrection, the judgement and the new creation, and that is where the feast belongs.

This commentary’s view: the amillennial reading fits this verse best. (1) The verse places the feast at the resurrection and the final judgement, which Jesus elsewhere teaches happen together, at one return (25:31–46; John 5:28–29); it leaves no room for a thousand-year stage in between. (2) Isaiah’s feast comes when death is swallowed up for ever, but in premillennial views death still continues during the thousand years. (3) Nothing in the verse mentions a thousand years. That idea comes from Revelation 20, a book full of symbols, and it is not wise to read it into a plain saying of Jesus. To be fair to premillennialists, they are right that this is an earthly hope: the patriarchs will be raised bodily, and the meek will inherit the earth (5:5). Amillennialists agree. The feast is not in a ghostly heaven, but in the renewed creation, the new world (19:28; 2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–3). This is a difference among faithful Christians, to be held charitably. What all agree on is the heart of the verse: people from every nation will sit with Abraham at God’s table, by faith in Christ.

While the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. “Sons of the kingdom” means those who seemed to be its natural heirs: Jews who relied on their descent from Abraham (3:9). The bitterness of the title is the point. To be a son of the kingdom was to be an insider by birth, and Jesus takes the phrase people would have used of themselves with satisfaction and attaches it to the ones being put out. The banquet hall is pictured as brightly lit at night, and “outer darkness” is the darkness outside, away from the light, warmth and joy.

Weeping and gnashing of teeth. A phrase Matthew uses six times for final judgment (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30). Weeping is grief and regret; gnashing of teeth is anguish, and perhaps anger. It is a picture of hell: exclusion from God’s presence and joy. The first time Matthew uses it, the people in view are the sons of the kingdom.

And to the centurion Jesus said, Go; let it be done for you as you have believed. He received what he trusted Jesus for. Faith is the hand through which the healing came, but it is not the source of it. The centurion’s faith did not heal his servant; Jesus’ word did. And the servant was healed at that very moment: Luke tells us the messengers went back and found him well (Luke 7:10).

What it does not mean. “As you have believed” does not mean that we get whatever we believe hard enough for. The centurion trusted Christ’s authority, and Christ honoured it. Faith receives; it does not command.

A warning transferred, not retired. This verse has sometimes been used to say that God has finished with Israel and replaced her with the church. The apostle who wrestled hardest with that question asked it outright, whether God had rejected his people, answered it with an emphatic no, and pointed to himself as evidence (Romans 11:1). Then he warned Gentile believers in the strongest terms against arrogance towards the branches that were broken off (Romans 11:18–21). The apostles and the earliest church were Jews, and Paul expects many Jews to come to faith (Romans 11:25–26). What Jesus is dismantling is not Israel but presumption: the assumption that descent secures anything. And it is exactly as false when a Gentile assumes that a Christian upbringing or church membership secures it.

Is the outer darkness the same as hell, and is it for ever? Yes. Jesus uses several pictures for the final judgement of the unrepentant: darkness outside the feast, fire that is not quenched (Mark 9:48), a furnace (13:42). The pictures differ, because no single image can hold it, but they agree on what matters. It is real, it is conscious (people weep), it is exclusion from the presence and joy of God, and Jesus says it is eternal, just as eternal life is (25:46). He speaks of it more than anyone in the Bible, and he does so not to frighten us for its own sake but to warn us while the door is still open. The same verse that speaks of the darkness speaks first of the feast and of many who come in.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly what you would say if asked why God should let you in. If the answer begins with anything you have done or anywhere you were born, it is the answer of a son of the kingdom. If it begins and ends with Christ, you are with the man from east and west. If the question frightens you because you know you have nothing to offer, take heart: that is exactly the guest this feast is for, and the one who knows he has no claim is the one Christ welcomes in.

For worship. The table is set, and the guest list is longer than anyone in Capernaum imagined. The Son of God ate with sinners and was thrown out of the city for it, cast into the darkness at noon on the cross, so that strangers from east and west might be brought into the light of his Father’s house. The host paid for the feast with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew’s recurring picture of final judgment.

parallels.desc: from the north and from the west

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus entered Peter's house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus entered Peter’s house. In Capernaum. Archaeologists have found a house there that Christians honoured very early, perhaps from the first century, as Peter’s, and that was later built over by a church. From a leper on the road and a soldier in the street, Jesus walks into a fisherman’s kitchen.

A married apostle. His mother-in-law: Peter was married, and Matthew records it in passing, without comment. Years later Paul, arguing for his rights as an apostle, asks whether he too may take a believing wife with him, as the other apostles do, and Cephas, which is Peter (1 Corinthians 9:5). None of this is an argument against celibacy freely chosen (1 Corinthians 7:7; 19:12). The point is narrower: whatever office Peter held, it was one a married man could hold, and a rule requiring priests to be celibate, which Rome itself treats as a church discipline rather than a doctrine, cannot appeal to him.

He touched her hand. She was lying sick with a fever; Luke, the physician, calls it a high fever (Luke 4:38). Jesus touched her hand, another touch (v. 3). A rabbi would probably not have touched a woman who was not his relative, but Jesus is not bound by such customs when compassion calls. And the fever left her, completely and at once; Luke says he rebuked it (Luke 4:39), as something that had no right to be there. There is something very homely in it: the first thing we learn about the leading apostle’s household is that Jesus was in it, sitting with a sick woman and taking her by the hand.

And she rose and began to serve him. After a fever a person normally needs days to recover strength; she got up at once. “Serve” (diakoneō) means to wait on, to provide a meal. Her response to being healed was service. This is the pattern of the Christian life: those whom Christ restores serve him (20:28). She makes no speech of thanks; she puts food in front of him.

She rose. Matthew’s verb for her getting up, egeirō, is the word he will use on Easter morning: he is not here, for he has risen (28:6). It is the ordinary word for getting out of bed, and it is also the word for resurrection, and Matthew lets it be both. The Lord who lifted this woman from her fever will himself be laid in a grave and raised from it, and the raising of the Lord is the guarantee of the raising of all who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20). So a small domestic healing becomes a picture of the gospel in miniature: Christ takes the hand of one who cannot rise, lifts her up, and she spends her new strength on him.

The three healings. The first group of miracles (vv. 1–15) reaches a leper, a Gentile’s servant and a woman, all at the edge of Israel’s religious life: Jesus’ kingdom welcomes those whom others keep at a distance. And there is no threshold of seriousness below which he loses interest: leprosy on the road, a fever in the back room.

Does Jesus care about ordinary illnesses and small troubles? Yes. This is a fever, the kind of thing every household in Capernaum had seen many times, and Matthew sets it beside a leper and a dying servant as though it were just as much his concern. Peter, who was in that house, later wrote that we should cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). All of them, not only the large ones. Do not save your prayers for emergencies. The child’s temperature, the sleepless night, the worry that seems too small to mention: bring them. The Lord who walked into Peter’s kitchen is not too grand for yours.

On a Tuesday. Gratitude need not be dramatic: she served a meal. Find the ordinary, unseen service in front of you, a meal cooked, a lift given, a sick neighbour looked in on, and do it for him.

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick, This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening. Mark tells us it was the Sabbath (Mark 1:21, 32). When the Sabbath ended at sunset, people could carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules. Mark adds that the whole town gathered at the door (Mark 1:33). It is one of the most moving scenes in the Gospels: the sun going down over the lake, and up every street the stretchers and the supporting arms, until the doorway of Peter’s house is surrounded.

They brought to him many who were oppressed by demons. Demon-possession is a condition in which an evil spirit controls or severely afflicts a person. The Gospels distinguish it from illness, though they sometimes overlap. Jesus cast out the spirits with a word: no rituals, incantations or long prayers, as exorcists of the time used, just a command. His casting out of demons shows that he has come to defeat Satan’s kingdom (12:28–29).

And healed all who were sick. All, not the most deserving or the most faithful. The breadth of his healing anticipates the breadth of the gospel: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

He took our illnesses and bore our diseases. Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4, the fourth song of the Servant of the LORD who suffers for his people. The Hebrew words, often translated griefs and sorrows, literally mean sicknesses and pains, and Matthew renders them exactly, where the Greek translation most people used, the Septuagint, had turned them into sins. The next verse says he was pierced for our transgressions. Matthew applies the first part to Jesus’ healing ministry. Jesus does not catch our diseases; he takes them away. But Matthew’s choice of Isaiah 53 points ahead: the healings are possible because of the cross, where the Servant bore the root of all disease, which is sin (1 Peter 2:24).

A shadow of Calvary. Matthew takes Isaiah’s great sin-bearing chapter and applies it, not yet to the cross, but to an evening of healings in Galilee. The healings are not separate from the atonement, the work by which Christ, dying in our place, takes away sin; they are its advance expression. Every healing was a down payment on the full healing his death and resurrection would secure: a new body, in a new creation, without sickness or death (Revelation 21:4).

Does God still heal like this today? Two things must be held together. First, yes: God is sovereign and good, he still hears prayer, and we are plainly told to pray for the sick (James 5:14–15). He has never stopped healing in answer to the cries of his people. But second, these Gospel healings must be read in their place. They came in a cluster, and the clusters of miracles in Scripture gather around the great moments of fresh revelation, Moses and the exodus, Elijah and Elisha, and now Christ and his apostles, not evenly across every age. Their purpose was largely to authenticate: to mark Jesus out as the Messiah and his apostles as his accredited messengers (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). They were signs of a unique hour, not a promise of constant healing on demand. Even in the apostolic age healing was never automatic: Paul’s thorn was left in place (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), he left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20), he prescribed wine for Timothy’s stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Epaphroditus nearly died (Philippians 2:27).

Where Christians differ: does the gift of healing continue, and is healing promised now? Some Christians (continuationists) hold that all the Spirit’s gifts continue today. They point out that no text says the gifts will end, that Paul lists gifts of healing among the gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9), and that James tells the sick to call for the elders to pray (James 5:14–16); some also read Isaiah 53:4 as promising healing in this life to all who have faith. Others (cessationists) hold that the miraculous gifts, healing among them, belonged to the apostolic age and confirmed the apostolic message, while God continues to heal in answer to the prayers of his people. This commentary’s view: the cessationist reading is the more likely, for the reasons given just above. God still heals in answer to prayer, but Isaiah 53:4 does not guarantee healing in this life. Its final fulfilment is the resurrection, and Peter applies the same chapter to sin-bearing (1 Peter 2:24). This is a difference among godly Christians, to be held charitably, and all agree that God hears and answers prayer for the sick.

So what should I do when I or someone I love is ill? Pray boldly, and trust God to answer as he wills. Ask the elders of your church to pray, as James directs (James 5:14). Use doctors and medicine thankfully: Luke was a physician, and Paul recommended a remedy to Timothy. And beware the cruel teaching that healing is guaranteed if only your faith is strong enough. It was not promised even to apostles, and it heaps guilt on the suffering for their own pain. Sometimes grace is given to carry us through the sickness rather than to remove it (2 Corinthians 12:9). And every believer will be perfectly and finally healed at the resurrection, if not before.

Why are demons everywhere in the Gospels and so rare elsewhere? The dark powers are real throughout Scripture, but the spotlight moves. In the Old Testament they stay mostly in the background: behind idolatry, which Scripture calls sacrificing to demons (Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 106:37), in the occasional evil spirit (1 Samuel 16:14), in Satan the accuser (Job 1; Zechariah 3). Open possession and exorcism are almost absent. Then in the Gospels it erupts, because the King has come. The arrival of God’s kingdom in Jesus forces the kingdom of darkness into the open; the demons show themselves, scream, and are routed with a word. If it is by the Spirit of God that Jesus casts out demons, the kingdom of God has come (12:28); the strong man is being bound and his house plundered (12:29). The eruption is less a new activity than the enemy’s panic before the invading King.

And why does it fade in the rest of the New Testament? Not because the demonic vanished, but because the decisive battle was won. At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The letters still take the unseen war with deadly seriousness, but they reframe it: less the spectacular seizing of individuals, more the believer’s daily, sober resistance to the spiritual forces of evil, clothed in the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:11–12), resisting the devil so that he flees (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9), and giving him no foothold (Ephesians 4:27). The defeated enemy still prowls, but he now meets a people covered by Christ’s victory.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. A believer can be tempted, deceived and harassed by the devil, but one indwelt by the Holy Spirit belongs to Christ and is not owned by any other power (1 John 4:4); if dark thoughts or fears trouble you, do not conclude you are possessed, but bring them to Christ and to a wise pastor. (See Acts 5:16 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. The sun went down over the lake, and the Servant of the LORD stood at Peter’s door until the last stretcher had gone home empty. Then he walked on to Jerusalem and took the town’s sins on himself, and a darker evening fell over him. What he did for a few streets in Capernaum he will do in the end for the whole creation: no more death, no more mourning, no more pain, and no one left lying at the door. Blessed be the Physician who became the patient, and the Servant who carried what we could not.

parallels.desc: by his wounds you have been healed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–34 — The Cost of Following and the Lord of Storm and Demons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 8 moves from healing to the cost of following Jesus and his authority over creation and the demonic. Two would-be followers learn that he offers no earthly security. Then he stills a storm and sends demons out of two men into a herd of pigs, and the section ends with three responses to his authority: little faith, the demons’ terror, and a town’s refusal.
verseByVerse.theology: The stilling of the storm is the centre of the chapter: what sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? Only the Creator commands his creation. The sea and the demonic, the two great terrors of the ancient world, both submit at once. The right response is not only comfort but worship, and the disciples are beginning to learn it.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadarenes counted the loss of their pigs and not the freedom of their neighbours, and asked Jesus to go. Every age has its pigs. The question for every community, and every heart, is what it values more than the freedom Christ brings.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. And a scribe came up and said to him, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gave orders to go over to the other side. To the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, Gentile territory. Jesus withdraws from the crowds, who were drawn by miracles. He is not building a following by numbers.

Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go. A scribe, an expert in the law (2:4), makes the offer. Most scribes opposed Jesus, but not all (13:52), and this is the only scribe in the Gospels recorded as offering to follow him, with no limit at all: the boldest promise anyone makes in the chapter. But he calls Jesus “Teacher”; the next man says “Lord” (v. 21).

Teacher or Lord. That distinction runs through the whole Gospel. In Matthew, disciples call Jesus Lord; outsiders, opponents and enquirers call him Teacher. The Pharisees, the Sadducees and the rich young man all say Teacher (12:38; 22:24; 19:16). At the Last Supper the eleven ask, is it I, Lord, while Judas alone says Rabbi (26:22, 25). So the scribe’s first word gives him away. He has come to attach himself to a famous rabbi, a step he understands and a career he can picture, not to bow before a Lord.

Volunteers and the called. A pattern recurs in the Gospels: those who volunteer are tested, and those who are called simply go. Peter and Andrew were casting a net and offered nothing; they were told to follow and they did (4:18–20). Jesus does not accept the scribe’s offer and does not refuse it. He tells him one fact about the life he is proposing to join, and Matthew never tells us what the man did with it. That is very probably the point. The story is left open because the reader is meant to finish it.

Where he was going. The scribe said wherever you go without knowing where that was. Jesus was going to Jerusalem, to be handed over, to suffer and to be killed (16:21). Only one person has ever made this scribe’s promise and kept it to the letter, and he made it to his Father: I have come to do your will (Hebrews 10:7). The Son followed that will wherever it went, into a desert, into Gethsemane (26:38), and up a hill outside the city. And because he went there alone, he can now say follow me to people who will fail him, and bring them through. The only safe wherever is the one he has already walked.

Is it wrong to make big promises to Christ? Not wrong, but dangerous if they rest on yourself. Peter promised that he would die rather than deny Jesus, and denied him that night (26:33–35, 69–75). The problem was not that he loved Jesus too much but that he trusted his own strength too much. So by all means commit yourself to Christ wholeheartedly, in baptism, in church membership, in the vows of marriage. But make the promise leaning on him, and ask him to keep you in it. Christian faithfulness is not a man keeping his word to God so much as God keeping his word to a man, and the man holding on because he is held (John 10:28).

parallels.desc: “Let us go across to the other side”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." Another of the disciples said to him, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." And Jesus said to him, "Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nowhere to lay his head. Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests: even wild animals have a place to rest and shelter. Jesus had no permanent home during his ministry; he depended on others’ hospitality (Luke 8:3). Following him means sharing his homelessness, his insecurity and his rejection. The scribe was offering to follow a famous rabbi to a lecture hall, and Jesus answers that he is going nowhere comfortable. The one through whom the world was made had no pillow of his own. The first bed he had was a manger, and the last bed he had was a borrowed tomb.

The Son of Man. The first time in Matthew that Jesus uses this title, his favourite way of referring to himself (about thirty times in Matthew). It can simply mean a human being, as in Psalm 8:4 and Ezekiel 2:1. But it comes especially from Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given everlasting dominion over all peoples. Jesus uses the title both for his humility and suffering (here, and 17:22; 20:28) and for his glory and coming as judge (24:30; 26:64). It hid and revealed his identity at once: people could not easily turn it into a political slogan.

Why use that title here? Because the contrast is the message. The one to whom Daniel saw all dominion given has, today, not even a hole in the ground. Glory and poverty in a single phrase: the King of everything chose the life of a man without a roof. That is not a failure of his kingship. It is the way his kingship comes, through humiliation to the throne.

Another of the disciples said to him, Lord, let me first go and bury my father. Burying one’s father was one of the most sacred duties in Jewish life, taking priority over almost everything, including some religious duties. Burial happened on the day of death. If the father had just died, the son would not be standing with Jesus but at home among the mourners. So the man probably meant: let me wait until my father has died (perhaps years later), fulfil my family duties, and receive my inheritance; then I will follow. “First” is the key word: he wanted something else first. It was a request for indefinite postponement, dressed as duty.

And Jesus said to him, Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead. A shocking statement. “The dead” who bury are probably the spiritually dead, those who do not follow Christ (see Ephesians 2:1). Spiritually dead means alive in body but unresponsive to God, which was the condition of every one of us until God made us alive together with Christ (Ephesians 2:4–5). Jesus’ call is urgent and comes before every other loyalty, even sacred family duty (10:37; Luke 9:59–62). Only one person in history could rightly say this, because only God can claim a loyalty above father and mother.

Two kinds of would-be disciple. The first was too quick: enthusiastic but unaware of the cost. The second was too slow: willing, but not yet. Both needed to understand that following Jesus is total and immediate. None of us follows without hesitating; only Jesus never turned back from the road to the cross, and his steadfastness is reckoned to us, so our faltering steps are accepted because of him.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should neglect their parents, or not attend family funerals. Jesus condemned those who used religion as an excuse to neglect parents (15:3–6), on the cross he provided for his mother (John 19:26–27), and Paul says that anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Looking after your family is one of the ways you follow Christ. The point is priority: when following Christ and family duty conflict, Christ comes first.

What if following Christ costs me my family? For some readers the collision is real and sharp: a family that will cut you off, a parent who forbids church, a household where becoming a Christian costs you your place in it. Jesus is telling such a person the truth in advance, and it is a hard truth kindly told. He comes first, and he knows what that will cost you. Keep honouring your parents in every way that does not mean denying him: stay courteous, stay in touch where they allow it, keep praying for them, help them when they are in need. And hold on to his promise that no one who has left house or family for his sake will fail to receive far more, now in the family of the church and in the age to come eternal life (19:29).

The quieter form. For most of us the application is closer to the bone and much less dramatic. The man in this story is not refusing Jesus. He is saying later, and he has an excellent reason that nobody could criticise. That is the shape it usually takes with us. I will get serious about this when the children are older, when work settles down, when this hard season passes, when I retire. The reasons are good, which is what makes them effective. The kingdom cannot wait for the next convenient moment, because there is never going to be one. The one who went without a pillow for your sake says follow me now, and he gives his Spirit for the step he asks.

So is it wrong to own a home and want security? No. Jesus stayed in Peter’s house, ate at many tables, and was glad of the home in Bethany. Scripture never despises a house, a savings account or a settled life. The question is ownership. A home held as God’s gift, opened to others and ready to be given up if he asks, is a blessing. A home that has become the thing you could not lose, the reason you will not move, give or risk anything for him, has become a rival. Ask yourself what you would refuse him if he asked, and you will know where your security is.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died. Jesus’ call outranks even that.

parallels.desc: no one who looks back is fit for the kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. And they went and woke him, saying, "Save us, Lord; we are perishing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. Matthew uses the word “followed” deliberately after verses 18–22. This is what following Jesus looks like: getting into the boat with him, and into the storm. They were out on the water because he had told them to go; obedience put them there.

And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea. The word for storm (seismos) usually means earthquake, a great shaking, the word behind our “seismic”; Mark uses the ordinary word for a squall (Mark 4:37). Apart from the earthquakes of the last days (24:7), Matthew uses the word again at the cross, when the earth shook and the centurion said truly this was the Son of God (27:51–54), and at the tomb on Easter morning, a great earthquake, the same two words as here (28:2). Three convulsions of the created order in this Gospel, and each is the setting for a revelation of who Jesus is.

The lake itself. The Sea of Galilee lies about seven hundred feet (210 metres) below sea level, in a basin ringed by hills. Cold air rushing down the ravines onto the warm water can turn the surface from flat to dangerous in a quarter of an hour. The boat was being swamped, literally covered by the waves, and at least four of the men aboard had fished that water all their lives and thought they would drown.

But he was asleep. Jesus was truly human, and truly exhausted after a long day of ministry. It is the only time the Gospels record him sleeping, and it is in a boat filling with water. His sleep also shows complete trust in his Father. The psalmist says: in peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8).

A greater than Jonah. Any Jew in that boat should have felt the echo (12:39–41). There is one other man in the Scriptures who slept through a storm at sea. Jonah went down into the ship and fell fast asleep while it threatened to break up, and the terrified captain came and woke him with almost the disciples’ words: get up, call on your god, perhaps he will spare us so that we do not perish (Jonah 1:5–6). Every element is reversed. Jonah slept because he was fleeing from God; Jesus sleeps because he is resting in him. Jonah’s presence was the cause of the storm; Jesus’ presence is the end of it. The sailors had to throw Jonah into the sea to save themselves; the disciples wake a man who stands up and speaks to the water, and it stops. Jonah was swallowed by the deep for three days and came back. So, said Jesus, would the Son of Man.

And they went and woke him, saying, Save us, Lord; we are perishing. A cry of panic, but also of faith: they turned to Jesus. “Lord” and “save” are words with deep meaning in Matthew: Jesus’ very name means “the LORD saves” (1:21). In Greek it is three words, and the church has prayed them in every kind of crisis since.

What it does not mean. Not that following Jesus means calm seas. The disciples were in the storm precisely because they followed him. Christians are not promised freedom from trouble; they are promised his presence in it (Isaiah 43:2). Nor does Jesus’ sleep mean he does not care. Mark records that the disciples asked whether he cared that they were perishing (Mark 4:38). He did; he was with them.

If Jesus is God, how could he sleep? Because he is truly man. The eternal Son took a real human body, which grew tired, hungry and thirsty, and needed sleep like ours. His human nature slept in the stern of the boat. But his divine nature did not cease to be what it is: the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4). While the man lay asleep on the cushion, the Son was still upholding all things by the word of his power, including the wind and the water (Hebrews 1:3). That is the mystery of the incarnation, and it is full of comfort. The Lord who sustains the stars knows what it is to be exhausted.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a storm because you followed Christ, you are not out of his will. The prayer that was enough was three panicked words. You do not need to compose something fine when the water is coming in. And if he seems asleep, he is still in the boat, and the boat is not going down with him in it.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?" Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. And the men marveled, saying, "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you afraid, O you of little faith? In Matthew, Jesus speaks to the disciples first, before the storm (Mark puts the rebuke after the calm). Matthew’s order makes a point. Their fear was the more dangerous of the two, and it was the thing he addressed before he said a word to the wind. “Little faith” (oligopistoi) is not no faith: they did call on him. In Matthew, Jesus uses this word only of his disciples (6:30; 14:31; 16:8; 17:20). He is patient with weak faith, but he wants it to grow.

Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea. He spoke to the storm as one rebukes a disobedient servant, or as he rebuked demons (17:18). In the Old Testament, the raging sea often pictured chaos and evil powers opposed to God, and only God could rule it (Psalm 89:9; Job 38:8–11). God rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up (Psalm 106:9). The sea that swallowed armies and frightened Israel for centuries goes quiet at the voice of a carpenter from Nazareth.

And there was a great calm. A great storm (v. 24), and a great calm. Normally the waves run on long after a storm; here the sea became calm at once, as sudden as the great shaking had been.

And the men marveled. They had been afraid of the storm. Now they are afraid of something greater, and Mark says they feared with a great fear (Mark 4:41). It is the right fear, the fear that falls on people who realise they are in the presence of God.

What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? The key question of the passage. Psalm 107:23–30 describes sailors in a storm who cried to the LORD, and he made the storm still and hushed the waves, and brought them to their desired haven. The disciples have just seen Jesus do what only God does. The answer to their question is that he is not merely a man. He is Immanuel, God with us (1:23). They will confess it fully later: truly you are the Son of God (14:33). It is the question Matthew’s whole Gospel is written to answer, and the psalm had answered it already: the one who stills the sea is the LORD.

The honest word. These verses can be preached as though every storm ends in flat calm before breakfast. Sometimes he calms the storm; sometimes he calms the disciple. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be taken away, kept it, and was given grace to carry what was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). What is promised is not always a change in the weather. It is that he is in the boat, that he is not indifferent though he may seem so, and that there is a far shore. He gave orders to go over to the other side, and he has never yet failed to land anyone he set out with.

Is this a real event, or a story about finding inner calm? Matthew tells it as an event: a real lake, a boat filling with water, and seasoned fishermen who thought they would drown. Nobody in the boat came away soothed; they came away more afraid than before, because a man had spoken to the weather and it obeyed. What settles it is not whether such things usually happen but who Jesus is. If he is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3), a word to the wind is no harder for him than the word that made the wind. The story does bring peace to anxious hearts, but only because it first happened on the water. So the question cannot be settled by this story alone; it belongs with the larger evidence for who Jesus is, above all his resurrection.

Is it a sin to be afraid? The feeling of fear is not itself sin. Jesus himself was in anguish in Gethsemane, and the psalmist says, when I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). Fear is what a frail creature feels in danger. What Jesus rebukes is fear that has pushed trust aside, so that we act and speak as though he were not there, or did not care, or could not help. The cure is not to pretend we are not frightened, but to take the fear to him and set beside it what we know of him. The disciples’ mistake was not that they woke him. It was that they thought, even with him in the boat, that they were going to drown.

For worship. A great storm, and then a great calm, and the calm was in his voice before it was on the water. The peace he spoke over the lake he made over us with his blood: he is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), and having been justified by faith we have peace with God (Romans 5:1), a calm between heaven and sinners that no wind will ever break again. And the sea itself is on notice. In the new creation John saw that the sea was no more (Revelation 21:1). The one who hushed a squall in Galilee will hush every terror for ever, and his people will stand on the far shore and marvel.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. And behold, they cried out, "What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The country of the Gadarenes. The eastern shore of the lake, Gentile country. The manuscripts of Matthew divide between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes, and those of Mark and Luke divide in the same way (Mark 5:1; Luke 8:26), which is why most Bibles have a footnote here. Gerasa is a large city some thirty miles from the lake, too far for any herd to run from; Gadara, a city of the Decapolis, is about six miles off, close enough that its lands may well have run down to the shore; Gergesa, modern Kursi, is on the eastern bank, with a steep slope running straight into the lake. The likeliest account is that the district was known by the name of its nearest major town, and different writers reached for different landmarks. What is not in doubt is that the terrain the story requires exists.

Two demon-possessed men. Mark and Luke mention only one, probably because he was the more prominent and later became a witness (Mark 5:18–20). Mentioning one does not deny that there were two. Matthew often mentions two where others mention one (9:27; at Jericho two blind men, where Mark names only Bartimaeus, 20:30; Mark 10:46), perhaps because two witnesses were needed for testimony under the law (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Coming out of the tombs. Tombs were caves cut into the hillside. They were unclean places, associated with death and, people believed, with evil spirits. The men lived there, cut off from society. Uncleanness on every side: Gentile land, the tombs of the dead, unclean spirits, and in a moment a herd of unclean animals. Jesus has crossed the lake into the most defiled place Matthew could describe.

So fierce that no one could pass that way. Mark describes the man breaking chains and cutting himself with stones (Mark 5:3–5). Demonic possession destroys the person: their mind, their body, their relationships. Nobody could help them; nobody could even get near them. They were beyond every human remedy, and that is exactly where Jesus walks up the beach.

What have you to do with us, O Son of God? A Hebrew idiom meaning: what is there between us? Why are you interfering with us? The demons recognise Jesus immediately as the Son of God, before the disciples do. James says even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). Recognising who Jesus is does not save; demons have the knowledge without the trust or love.

Have you come here to torment us before the time? The demons know that a time of judgment is coming, when they will be punished (25:41; Revelation 20:10). They are afraid that Jesus has come to bring it early. In a sense he has: his coming means the beginning of their defeat (12:28–29). They are not disputing the outcome. They know there is a fixed date and that it goes against them; the only thing in doubt is the calendar: a settled certainty about the future, and no intention whatever of changing course.

Was this really demon possession, or mental illness misunderstood? The Gospels distinguish the two (4:24), and these men’s demons speak, recognise Jesus as the Son of God and know the time of their judgement, which no illness does. But that gives no reason to treat mental illness today as demonic. Those who suffer should be given medical care and pastoral love, and every believer can know that he belongs to Christ, not to any other power.

What should I do about horoscopes, tarot cards, spiritualism or the occult? Leave them completely. Scripture forbids every attempt to consult spirits, read omens or contact the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they are silly but because the powers behind them are real and hostile, and they destroy, as they were destroying these men. If you have dabbled, confess it to God, renounce it plainly, get rid of anything connected with it (as the believers in Ephesus burned their books, Acts 19:18–19), and tell a pastor you trust. You do not need special rituals. You need Christ, whom the demons themselves call the Son of God, and you need to stay close to his word and his people.
verseByVerse.note: Gadara was a Gentile city of the Decapolis, south-east of the lake; Mark and Luke say “Gerasenes” and mention only one man. Tombs were unclean places.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. And the demons begged him, saying, "If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A herd of many pigs. Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13). Pigs were unclean animals for Jews (Leviticus 11:7). A large herd shows that this was Gentile territory. Two thousand pigs was somebody’s living.

And the demons begged him. They have no power to resist Jesus; they can only plead. They do not dispute his authority to cast them out; they bargain only about the destination, and even that must be submitted to him. They cannot so much as enter a pig without his permission.

If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs. Why? Perhaps because demons seek to inhabit and destroy something. Luke adds that they begged not to be sent into the abyss (Luke 8:31), the place of their final confinement. There is a dark irony in it: they would rather have the bodies of unclean animals than face what is coming.

Every knee, even under the earth. Mark says the man ran and fell on his knees before Jesus (Mark 5:6), and here the demons can only beg. It is a small, early picture of the end Paul describes: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11). The powers of darkness will bow, not in love but in defeat, and they are bowing already on this beach. They kneel because they must, and dread him; the redeemed kneel because he has won them, and adore him.

What about the man who owned the pigs? A thoughtful reader will ask, and deserves better than silence. In a single afternoon a herd of about two thousand animals was destroyed. Four things can be said honestly. First, the destruction is the demons’ work, not Jesus’. He does not send them into the pigs; they ask, and he permits. What follows is exactly what one would expect: the thing that had been driving two men to live among graves and cut themselves does the same to a herd of animals within a minute of getting hold of them. The pigs are a demonstration of what the demons do, not of what Jesus does. Second, this was Gentile territory, which is why there were pigs at all; the owners were almost certainly Gentiles breaking no law of their own, so this is not a judgement on Jews for keeping unclean animals. Third, Jesus states the valuation elsewhere in this Gospel: of how much more value is a man than a sheep (12:12)! Two men beyond anyone’s reach were given their minds back. Set against that, a herd of livestock is a real cost and a small one, and the town that made the opposite calculation is the villain of the story, not its victim. Fourth, Matthew records the loss and the reaction and moves on, neither apologising nor treating the objection as trivial. What cannot honestly be said is that the loss did not matter. It mattered to somebody, and the text lets that stand.

Why did Jesus grant the demons’ request at all? Scripture does not explain fully, and we should not pretend to know more than it says. But some things are clear. The time of their final judgement had not yet come (v. 29), and Jesus was keeping to his Father’s timetable, not theirs. The rush of the herd gave everyone visible proof that the men were truly free, so that no one could say the change was imaginary. And it showed, for anyone with eyes, what these powers had been doing to two human beings: the same thing they did to the pigs in a minute. Jesus is never at the demons’ service. Even when he grants what they ask, he is using it for his own purposes.

On a Tuesday. Whatever has a grip on you must obey him. Notice that the demons tried to negotiate: not the abyss, somewhere nearby, somewhere comfortable. Sin does the same with us. It rarely asks to stay in full; it asks to be allowed to remain in a corner. Do not negotiate with what Christ has told to go.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a large herd shows this was Gentile country.

parallels.desc: the pig is unclean to you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go." So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them, Go. One word, and the demons must obey. It is the latest in a chapter of single words. To the leper: be clean. To the centurion: go, let it be done. To the wind and sea, a rebuke. And now to the demons who had terrorised a district for a long time and whom no chain could hold (Mark’s account gives their name, Legion): go. Jewish exorcists of the period used incantations, roots, rings and the names of angels; Jesus uses one word and does not raise his voice.

So they came out and went into the pigs. The men were freed. Mark says the man was found sitting, clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). Three phrases that tell a whole story. He had been restless; now he sits. He had been naked, Luke tells us (Luke 8:27); now he is clothed. He had been out of his mind; now he is in his right mind, at the feet of Jesus.

And behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. Everyone could see that the demons had left, and what they would have done to the men if they had stayed: wherever they go, they destroy (John 10:10).

The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything. They might have shaded the account; instead they reported the whole thing, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men. So the first report of Jesus in that Gentile town came from a group of frightened pig-keepers, telling a story that was mostly about their own disaster, and telling it truthfully.

Is being set free from evil the same as being saved? Not quite, and the difference matters. Jesus warned that when an unclean spirit leaves a person, it may return with others worse than itself and find the house swept and empty (12:43–45). Freedom from a bondage, whether an addiction, a dark habit or something worse, is a great mercy. But the house must not be left empty. It must be filled by Christ himself, through faith in him, his word and his Spirit. That is why the freed man in Mark’s account begged to go with Jesus (Mark 5:18). Do not be content to be rid of something. Be joined to someone.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region. All the city came out to meet Jesus, in words often used of a town going out to welcome a visiting dignitary, and it begged him to go. The demons begged Jesus not to send them away (v. 31); the townspeople begged Jesus to go away. It is the same word (parekaloun): the city begs as the demons begged. They had seen two of their neighbours restored to sanity, but they were frightened by Jesus’ power, and perhaps angry at the loss of the pigs. They preferred their pigs and their comfort to the presence of the Son of God. Luke says they were seized with great fear (Luke 8:37).

And Jesus left. Jesus does not force himself on those who do not want him. But even here there is mercy. Mark tells us he left the freed man behind, clothed and in his right mind, to tell what the Lord had done for him (Mark 5:19–20), and later, when Jesus returned to the Decapolis, crowds came to him (Mark 7:31–37). He is slow to give up even on those who send him away.

The most sobering answer to prayer. We are rightly fond of the Jesus who seeks the lost, and the seeking Shepherd of Luke 15 is gloriously real. But here is the other side of the truth: when people settle their hearts against him and say depart, he can take them at their word. This is the judgement Paul names in Romans 1, where three times God gave them up to what they preferred (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). Over Jerusalem Jesus wept that he had longed to gather her children and she would not, and that her house would be left desolate (23:37–38). He grieves to leave, but he leaves. The Gadarenes asked him to go, and he went.

Could Jesus give up on me? If you are worried about it, that worry is itself a sign that he has not. The people Jesus leaves are those who want him gone and are glad to see him go, not those who fear losing him. The Gadarenes did not lie awake grieving his departure. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and those the Father has given him he will lose none of (John 6:39). If you belong to Christ, he will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5). And if you are not yet sure that you belong to him, the door is still open today, and he still knocks (Revelation 3:20). The Gadarenes heard him at the shore and sent him back to the boat; do not send him away from yours, but open while he is standing there. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your heart (Hebrews 3:15).

For worship. The Lord who commands storms and demons will not force his way into a town that begs him to leave. He is so great that nothing can resist him, and so gentle that he lets us refuse him; and that should make us tremble at the thought of refusing. He is the patient Saviour, who let a town send him back to his boat, and later let the world send him to a cross, so that those who once refused him might be welcomed in.

8.theology: The authority of Christ. Chapter 8 shows the authority of the Son of God over disease (the leper, the fever), over distance (the servant healed by a word), over demons and over creation (the storm). It is not borrowed: Jesus is not a prophet holding God’s power on loan but the eternal Son, in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). His healing word and his saving word are the same word, and both do what they say. Faith rests on that word.
8.examples:
Then: A Roman officer, used to chains of command, recognised the authority of Jesus, while many who had grown up with the Scriptures had shrunk their expectations of the Messiah.

Now: Our culture often treats faith as a way of coping, valued because it makes us feel better. The centurion’s faith is the opposite: it rests on who Jesus is. We trust Christ because he is the Lord of heaven and earth, whose word does what he sends it to do. When we pray, we speak to the one who stilled the Sea of Galilee.

9.title: The King’s Authority to Forgive
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. <sup>2</sup>And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” <sup>3</sup>And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.” <sup>4</sup>But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? <sup>5</sup>For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>6</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he then said to the paralytic—“Rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>7</sup>And he rose and went home. <sup>8</sup>When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men. <sup>9</sup>As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>10</sup>And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. <sup>11</sup>And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>12</sup>But when he heard it, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>13</sup>Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>14</sup>Then the disciples of John came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>15</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. <sup>16</sup>No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made. <sup>17</sup>Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.” <sup>18</sup>While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. <sup>20</sup>And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, <sup>21</sup>for she said to herself, “If I only touch his garment, I will be made well.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” And instantly the woman was made well. <sup>23</sup>And when Jesus came to the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, <sup>24</sup>he said, “Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they laughed at him. <sup>25</sup>But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. <sup>26</sup>And the report of this went through all that district. <sup>27</sup>And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” <sup>28</sup>When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” <sup>29</sup>Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith let it be done to you.” <sup>30</sup>And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows about it.” <sup>31</sup>But they went away and spread his fame through all that district. <sup>32</sup>As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. <sup>33</sup>And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, “Never was anything like this seen in Israel.” <sup>34</sup>But the Pharisees said, “He casts out demons by the prince of demons.” <sup>35</sup>And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. <sup>36</sup>When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. <sup>37</sup>Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; <sup>38</sup>therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 opens with Jesus’ boldest claim yet: your sins are forgiven. The scribes see at once what it implies, that only God can forgive sins, and they charge him with blasphemy. Jesus answers by healing the paralysed man as proof that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The miracle is the sign; forgiveness is the substance.

He calls Matthew, a tax collector and outcast, with two words, and Matthew rises and follows. At the meal Jesus eats with sinners and quotes Hosea 6:6 to the scandalised Pharisees. Through the chapter faith stands beside unbelief: friends carry the paralytic while the scribes accuse; the ruler kneels and the woman reaches while the mourners laugh; the blind men say yes, Lord, while the Pharisees say he casts out demons by the prince of demons (v. 34). The same works divide every heart that meets them. The chapter closes with Jesus’ compassion for the harassed crowds and his call to pray for workers for the harvest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Forgiveness, Fellowship, and Fasting: Who Has Authority?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to Capernaum and heals a paralysed man, first forgiving his sins, which brings the first open conflict with the scribes. He then calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with sinners, and the Pharisees are outraged. When John’s disciples ask why Jesus’ disciples do not fast, he answers with three pictures: the bridegroom, the unshrunk cloth and the new wine.
verseByVerse.theology: The healing of the paralytic is the turning point: Jesus claims an authority to forgive sins that belongs to God alone. The scribes are right that only God forgives sins, and badly wrong to conclude that Jesus is blaspheming. Matthew’s call and the meal with sinners then show what forgiveness looks like in practice: the Physician comes for the sick.
verseByVerse.examples: The three pictures of newness, the bridegroom, the cloth and the wineskins, announce that Jesus does not patch up Israel’s religion but fulfils it. The question about fasting shows that John’s disciples and the Pharisees are still waiting; Jesus announces that the bridegroom has come.
