verseByVerse.quote: And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 9 carries on from chapter 8 and raises the stakes. Jesus has shown his authority over disease, storm and demons; now he claims an authority that belongs to God alone, to forgive sins on earth by his own word, and proves it by making a paralysed man walk. The opposition grows, and the same evidence produces worship and hatred. The chapter ends with his compassion for the harassed crowds and a call to pray for workers. Its question is the Gospel’s: who is this, who forgives sins, raises the dead and pities the lost?

And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. Rejected by the Gadarenes (8:34), Jesus returns to Capernaum (4:13). The town that begged him to leave got what it asked for; the town that welcomed him is about to hear him claim more than he has claimed yet.

Some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. A man who could not walk, carried on a mat or stretcher by his friends. Mark and Luke tell how they dug through the roof to lower him down (Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26). Matthew tells the story briefly, but the effort is worth picturing. When the crowd blocked the door, the friends went up the outside stairs, broke open a roof of beams and packed earth, and lowered him into the room.

When Jesus saw their faith. Faith can be seen: in this case, by the effort the friends made to bring the man to Jesus. “Their” faith is chiefly that of the people who brought him, though probably the man’s too, and Jesus notices it.

He said to the paralytic, Take heart, my son. “Take heart” means be encouraged, have courage. “My son” (literally “child”) is warm and affectionate. Before anything has been done for him, he is spoken to like a member of the family.

Your sins are forgiven. Unexpected. The man’s obvious need was physical, but Jesus addresses his deepest need first. Paralysis would end at death; unforgiven sin would last for eternity. The present tense means the forgiveness is happening now, on Jesus’ word. A sceptic may think that unkind, as though Jesus were lecturing a disabled man about his morals. It is the opposite. He speaks to him as a son, not a case, and gives him first the gift no doctor could give, before the one that everyone could see.

A verdict, not a process. Jesus does not say: God will forgive you if you do this, or, seek God and perhaps you will find pardon. He says: your sins are forgiven. It is a verdict handed down, a thing accomplished, spoken over a man who has done nothing yet but be carried through a roof. This is what the Reformers meant by justification: not a process by which a sinner is slowly made good enough, but a declaration in which the Judge himself pronounces the guilty righteous. It is a courtroom word before it is a hospital word. And the declaration is not cheap. The Judge who pronounces the pardon here will pay for it himself, outside a city wall, so that the verdict is not only merciful but just (Romans 3:26).

Sin and sickness. Was the man’s paralysis caused by a specific sin? Sickness can sometimes be connected with sin (John 5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30), but Jesus denied that it is always the sufferer’s own fault (John 9:1–3), and here he simply shows that forgiveness is the deeper need of every person. No one who is ill should be told that it proves some hidden sin.

For those doing the carrying. You may have a husband who will not come, a son who has walked away, a friend sunk in a depression too heavy to pray out of. You cannot believe on their behalf, but you can carry them to where Jesus is, and that is a real work. It looks like praying for them by name for years without visible result, keeping the relationship intact so that there is still a stretcher when they need one, and being willing to look foolish and go through the roof. Keep carrying: the Lord who saw their faith sees yours.

For the one who is being carried. Perhaps you suspect you are the paralytic. Your faith feels too thin to count, and you are not sure it would qualify as faith at all. Then look hard at what this man contributes to the scene, because it is nothing whatever. He does not argue his case, express his confidence or say a word. He is carried in, flat and helpless, and the first thing he hears is: take heart, my son, your sins are forgiven. That is what the church is for on the days you cannot hold yourself up: others sing when you cannot, and pray when your own praying has dried up. You are not required to arrive under your own power.

Do I need to feel forgiven to be forgiven? No. This man had no feeling to go on but the word of Jesus, and the word was enough. Forgiveness is God’s verdict, not your emotion. If you have turned from your sin and trusted Christ, your sins are forgiven because he says so, and because he died for them, whether you feel light-hearted today or heavy. Feelings follow slowly and come and go. When guilt keeps returning over a sin you have already confessed, do not confess it again as though the first time failed. Answer it with his word: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).
verseByVerse.note: “His own city” is Capernaum, his base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, "This man is blaspheming." But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, "Why do you think evil in your hearts?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man is blaspheming. Some of the scribes said it to themselves, silently; the charge was formed in the room and never left anybody’s mouth, and Jesus answers it out loud. Blasphemy means speaking against God, insulting him, or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone. A person can forgive wrongs done to himself, but sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4). Under the law, blasphemy was punishable by death (Leviticus 24:16). This is the first mention of the charge for which Jesus will finally be condemned (26:65).

Their theology is right. These men are often treated as fools, but they reasoned correctly that only God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7). In Isaiah God says that he, he alone, is the one who blots out transgressions for his own sake (Isaiah 43:25). No priest in Israel ever forgave anybody; the priest declared a forgiveness God had granted through the sacrifice he prescribed. So if this man is claiming to forgive in his own right, and he is not God, he is committing blasphemy.

An honest note on the grammar. Your sins are forgiven is a passive, and a passive of this kind was a common Jewish way of avoiding the divine name, so in principle Jesus might be announcing that God has forgiven, as the prophet Nathan once announced to David (2 Samuel 12:13), rather than claiming to do it himself. The scribes plainly did not hear it that way: Mark records their reasoning in full, that no one can forgive sins but God alone (Mark 2:7). Jesus does not correct them. He goes on to prove the claim they think he has made.

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts. Jesus knew what they were thinking without being told. Prophets were sometimes shown a hidden fact (2 Kings 5:26), but Scripture reserves the searching of hearts to God (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). So before the paralytic moves a muscle, Jesus answers their unspoken accusation in a way that already points to what he claims.

Why do you think evil in your hearts? Their evil was not in their logic, which was right, but in their refusal to consider that Jesus might be who his words implied. They assumed the worst. The word is ponēros, the word used of wicked men and of the evil one. He does not say, why do you think this, but, why do you think evil. That would be outrageous if their reasoning were merely mistaken. It is not the conclusion he indicts but the closed heart underneath it. They had settled the question before they weighed it, and settled it against a man who had done them no harm.

Is it wrong to have doubts or questions about Jesus? No, not if you bring them honestly. The scribes’ problem was not that they had questions but that they had already decided the answer and would not look at the evidence in front of them. Honest doubt that wants the truth is a different thing. John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus really was the one, and Jesus answered him gently with the evidence (11:2–6). Thomas said he would not believe without seeing, and Jesus showed him his hands (John 20:27). Bring your questions to him: read the Gospels, ask a mature Christian, pray as you read. Ask yourself only whether you would be willing to follow the answer if it came.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows your thoughts, which is a warning against secret sin and a comfort in secret sorrow. The resentment you have never said aloud is as plain to him as words spoken in the room, and so are the griefs you have never told anyone. And he is the one who forgives. Today, tell him something you have only ever said to yourself.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "For which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" — he then said to the paralytic — "Rise, pick up your bed and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For which is easier. To say “your sins are forgiven” is easier, because no one can see whether it has happened. To say “rise and walk” is harder, because everyone will immediately see whether it works. But actually to do either is equally impossible for a mere man; both require the power of God. So Jesus takes the harder, testable claim and stakes the untestable one on it, in public, with a paralysed man as the test: that you may know. The miracle is not a distraction from the theology; it is the proof of it.

Authority on earth to forgive sins. “Authority” (exousia) means the right and the power to act, and here God’s authority to forgive is exercised on earth, by a man, in person. Son of Man is the modest title with Daniel’s glory folded into it (see 8:20), and when he used it plainly, under oath before the high priest, they tore their robes and condemned him (26:64–65).

On earth. Two small words carry the weight. Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven; the disputed point is the place. This man is saying that the transaction can be completed here, in a crowded house in Capernaum, by a voice: without a temple, without a priest, without a sacrifice, and without waiting for the Day of Atonement or the final judgement. Heaven’s verdict has come down to earth in a person.

He then said to the paralytic, Rise, pick up your bed and go home. Three commands, each impossible for a paralysed man. Carrying his own bed would show the healing was complete. The stretcher that had carried him would now be carried by him.

What it does not mean. Not that priests or ministers today have the authority to forgive sins in themselves. Jesus has authority as God. The church announces his forgiveness to those who repent and believe (John 20:23; 2 Corinthians 5:18–20), but it does not create it. The Roman Catholic practice of priestly absolution in the confessional claims more than this. Reformed churches declare the gospel’s assurance of pardon to the penitent, as messengers of Christ, not as judges in his place.

How can I know my sins are forgiven when I cannot see it? In the same way as the crowd in Capernaum: by looking at what Jesus has done that can be seen. He healed the visible to prove the invisible. For us the great visible proof is greater still: he died in public, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, seen by hundreds of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The resurrection is God’s public declaration that the sacrifice for sin was accepted (Romans 4:25). So rest your assurance on his word and his finished work, not on your feelings, and look for the fruit his Spirit produces in you: a new hatred of sin, a new love for him and his people. Those are the legs moving.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he rose and went home. Immediately, in full view of everyone. The man walked out through the crowd that had blocked the door on the way in, carrying the mat he had been lowered on.

When the crowds saw it, they were afraid. “Afraid” here means filled with awe, reverent fear at seeing God at work. It is the usual biblical response to God acting close at hand, and here the fear turned into worship.

Who had given such authority to men. Unlike the scribes (v. 3), the crowds glorified God, the right response. They see that God’s authority has been given to a man, though they do not yet grasp that this man is God himself. Only Matthew records this line, and its plural is strange: not to this man, as anyone would expect, but to human beings (anthrōpois). Matthew has perhaps kept the plural because he can see where it goes: this is the Gospel that records Jesus giving the keys of the kingdom to Peter (16:19) and telling the church that what it binds on earth is bound in heaven (18:18). The authority to forgive is Christ’s alone; the announcing of it would be handed to ordinary men, and Matthew lets a crowd say more than it knew.

Should I be afraid of God? In one sense yes, and in another no. Believers are not to be terrified of God as an enemy, because Christ has taken away the punishment, and perfect love casts out that kind of fear (1 John 4:18). But they are to hold him in reverent awe for ever, because he is holy and great, and his love has not made him small. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10), as Proverbs never tires of saying, and the forgiven man has more reason for that awe than anyone. The crowd’s response is the right pattern: fear that leads to glorifying God. If your Christianity has no awe in it, you may be thinking of a smaller God than the one who forgives sins and makes the paralysed walk.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him. And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth. By the church’s earliest testimony, the author of this Gospel. Mark and Luke call him Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27); many Jews had two names. The booth was not a poll-tax office but a customs post. Capernaum sat on the great trade road, at the frontier between the lands of Herod Antipas and those of his brother Philip, and Matthew’s job was to assess duty on goods crossing the border. Collectors bought the right to collect and made their living on the margin, so the system paid them to overcharge.

A name and a label. Matthew means gift of God, and it may be the name he took, or was given, when the gift of God laid hold of him at that booth. The other Gospels, listing the apostles, simply name him. He alone writes Matthew the tax collector (10:3), pinning the old, shameful label to his own name for good. A man truly forgiven does not hide what he was saved from. He makes it a monument to grace.

Tax collectors. They were hated by fellow Jews for three reasons. They collaborated with the occupying powers (Rome, or Herod who served Rome). They were often dishonest, collecting more than required and keeping the profit (Luke 3:12–13; 19:8). And their frequent contact with Gentiles made them ritually unclean. They were classed with prostitutes and sinners (21:31), and later Jewish law barred them from serving as witnesses. For a rabbi to call one as his disciple was scandalous.

And he said to him, Follow me. The same call as to the fishermen (4:19). Two words, and no conditions: no probation, no demand that he first pay everything back. The call creates what it commands: the word that tells Matthew to follow is also the power that makes him willing to follow: as God said let there be light, and there was light, Christ says follow me, and a man gets up from his money (Genesis 1:3; 2 Corinthians 4:6).

And he rose and followed him. Immediately. Matthew gave up a lucrative career, and the one who had grown rich by taking now followed the one who gave. When the fishermen left their nets, the trade was still waiting for them after the crucifixion (John 21:3). Matthew’s booth, probably a purchased concession, was not: he burned the bridge in the act of crossing it. Luke records the detail Matthew leaves out: he left everything (Luke 5:28).

As Jesus reclined at table in the house. Matthew’s house (Luke 5:29). He held a great feast for Jesus and invited his friends, other tax collectors and “sinners”. His first instinct as a disciple was to introduce his friends to Jesus.

Many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus. Eating together in that culture expressed friendship and acceptance. Jesus ate with them.

The man who counted the price. A customs officer spends his days putting a price on things, and it is this Gospel, written by the man from the booth, that alone tells us what the Lord was sold for: thirty pieces of silver (26:15), the price Zechariah had called a lordly sum when the shepherd of Israel was valued by his people (27:9–10; Zechariah 11:12–13). Matthew had once taken money from his neighbours; he lived to record how cheaply his neighbours valued the Son of God. And he records the other side of the transaction too, in Jesus’ own words: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). The call at the booth cost Matthew his trade. The price of Matthew cost Christ his life.

Are there limits to this? Jesus went to tax collectors’ tables as a physician, not as one of the party, and his call was always: follow me. Christians are free to eat with unbelievers, to love them and reach them (1 Corinthians 5:9–10; 10:27). What Paul forbids is treating an unrepentant professing brother as if nothing were wrong (1 Corinthians 5:11). And wisdom adds a personal rule: go with a purpose, and do not walk into the places where you are weakest.

Can God use someone with a really bad past? Look at who wrote this book. The first of the four Gospels, read in more languages than almost any other book for two thousand years, was by the church’s ancient testimony written by a man whose neighbours regarded him as a traitor and a thief. God does not merely tolerate converted sinners; he delights to use them, so that the glory goes to his grace and not to their record. Paul called himself the foremost of sinners and said that was exactly why he received mercy, as an example to others (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Your past does not disqualify you. What matters is that you rise and follow now, and make restitution where you can, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8).

On a Tuesday. When grace called Matthew from his booth, he invited his friends to meet Jesus too. Plan a meal at your home this month with a Christian friend or two and someone who does not yet know Christ. You do not need to stage a sermon. Matthew simply put Jesus and his friends at the same table and let the evening happen.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke call this tax collector Levi. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" But when he heard it, he said, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." Go and learn what this means: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners? To the Pharisees, eating with such people made one unclean and showed approval of their way of life. Many teachers kept away from them. The Pharisees saw holiness as separation from sinners. The question is put to the disciples, not to Jesus: a familiar way of undermining a teacher, by unsettling his followers.

Who the sinners were. In these arguments the word was close to a technical term. It did not simply mean bad people. It certainly covered the openly wicked, and in the Pharisees’ mouths it probably also took in those whose trade or ignorance of the law kept them outside the observant circle. The Pharisees had divided the population into the clean and the unclean, and Jesus accepts the division and reverses the conclusion: yes, there are two groups, and I have come for the other one.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. A proverb. A doctor goes to the sick; that is his job. Jesus came as a doctor for sin-sick souls. He does not become sick by being among the sick; he heals them. The sick who know they are sick can receive the physician; those who think themselves healthy cannot. Self-righteousness is the one condition that keeps the cure out.

I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. Go and learn what this means was a rabbinic phrase used to send students back to a text, and Jesus uses it on the professional interpreters of the very verse he quotes. The verse is Hosea 6:6, where God rebuked Israel for offering sacrifices while lacking steadfast love and faithfulness. God does not reject sacrifice altogether (he commanded it); the Hebrew idiom means mercy more than sacrifice.

Matthew’s verse. No other writer in the New Testament quotes Hosea 6:6. Matthew does it twice, here and at 12:7, and both times it is aimed at religious men who are technically correct and pastorally cruel. Israel was producing a great volume of religion, and God said their love was like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes away early (Hosea 6:4): it evaporated by breakfast. Then he said what he actually wanted, and the word rendered mercy is hesed, the great covenant word for steadfast, loyal love. The charge is not that the Pharisees are too religious. It is that their religion has come loose from the thing it was for.

For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. “The righteous” are those who think they are righteous, like the Pharisees, who see no need of a doctor. In reality, no one is righteous (Romans 3:10). Jesus calls those who know they are sinners. The only qualification for being called by Jesus is to need him.

If Jesus came for sinners, does it matter how I live? Very much. A doctor who comes to the sick does not come to leave them sick. He comes to heal them, and the treatment changes the patient. Paul faced this exact question: shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? and answered, by no means (Romans 6:1–2). Those Christ calls, he also cleanses and changes (1 Corinthians 6:11). The call is for sinners just as they are; it does not leave them as they are. If you find that you want his forgiveness but not his healing, ask whether you have understood what kind of physician he is.

On a Tuesday. As one he sought out first, seek out the person at work or in your street whom church people tend to avoid, and treat them this week with the kindness of a friend.

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice
to seek and to save the lost

verseByVerse.quote: And then the disciples of John came to him, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made." Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples of John came to him. John was in prison (4:12). His disciples continued to follow his austere way of life. They ask sincerely, not with hostility, and Jesus answers them gently.

In the flow. This is the third of three questions in a row, and each is answered by who Jesus is: the Son of Man with authority on earth (v. 6), the physician (v. 12), the bridegroom (v. 15). The newness of the kingdom is not a new set of rules but a new person in the room, and what he brings will not fit inside the old forms.

Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? Pious Jews fasted regularly, and Pharisees twice a week (Luke 18:12). Jesus’ disciples were feasting with sinners (vv. 10–11). It looked unspiritual.

Custom, not command. The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to afflict itself (Leviticus 16:29–31). Every other fast was added later. By Jesus’ day the devout fasted on Mondays and Thursdays: custom, not command. Behind it lay real longing: fasting expressed grief over sin, repentance, and yearning for God to send his deliverance and his Messiah. At its best it was the posture of a people still waiting. And that is just why Jesus’ disciples were not fasting. The waiting was over.

Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? Fasting was associated with mourning and sorrow. A Jewish wedding often lasted a week. The wedding guests (literally “sons of the bridal chamber”, the bridegroom’s close friends) were excused from religious duties such as fasting during the festivities. Jesus is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5–6; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus takes that role. His coming is a wedding feast, the time of joy that the prophets promised. John himself had called Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29). It is a staggering claim made in passing: the husband of Israel, the LORD himself, has come, and the wedding has begun.

The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. “Taken away” suggests violent removal: Jesus’ first hint in Matthew of his death. After his death and ascension, his disciples would fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). The bridegroom knows already that he will be torn from his friends, and he speaks of it at a feast.

No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. A new patch, not yet shrunk, sewn onto an old garment would shrink when washed and tear the old cloth, making the hole worse. Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. Wineskins were made from goatskins, and new wine continues to ferment and expand. A new skin is soft and stretches; an old skin has become hard and brittle, and would burst under the pressure.

But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved. The new life of the kingdom that Jesus brings cannot simply be added to the old system of Pharisaic tradition. The kingdom needs new forms: a new covenant, a new people. Jesus is the new wine; the old is the whole framework of mourning, waiting and man-made ritual that belonged to the age before the King appeared.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless: Jesus came to fulfil the law and prophets (5:17). The old wineskins are the human traditions of the Pharisees’ religion, not the Scriptures themselves. Luke adds that people who have drunk old wine say the old is good (Luke 5:39): people often prefer the familiar.

So should Christians fast? Jesus plainly assumes we will: then they will fast, and, when you fast (6:16). The early church fasted at prayer and at weighty decisions (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Yet the letters lay down no command, no required days, no rule. Fasting is therefore a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: a way to humble ourselves, sharpen prayer and hunger for God, never a badge to earn his favour, and Jesus’ own instruction is to do it in secret, for the Father who sees (6:16–18).

How would I actually begin? Simply. Choose a meal or a day, perhaps before a decision or when you are burdened for someone, and use the time you would have spent eating to pray and read Scripture. Tell no one who does not need to know (6:17–18). Drink water. If you have a medical condition, are pregnant, or have struggled with eating disorders, do not fast from food; give up something else for a time instead, and talk to your doctor and pastor. The point is not the empty stomach but the turning of the whole self towards God. A fast that leaves you proud has failed, and a fast that leaves you hungrier for Christ has done its work.

Does new wineskins mean churches should always be changing their worship? No. This is not a charter for novelty. The new wine is Christ and his gospel, and the old skins are the Pharisees’ system of human tradition that could not contain him. The gospel itself does not change, and the Scriptures are the fixed rule for what the church believes and how it worships. What the saying warns against is binding Christ’s people with man-made rules, old or new, and trying to fit his grace into a religion of earning. A church can be old-fashioned or modern in its style and fail this test either way.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine still ferments and expands; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–38 — The Harvest Is Plentiful: Four More Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew gathers four more miracles into a quick sequence: a ruler’s dead daughter raised, a woman with a long illness healed on the way, two blind men given sight, and a mute man freed from a demon. These complete the ten mighty works of chapters 8 and 9. The crowds marvel and the Pharisees accuse, and the chapter ends with Jesus’ compassion for the crowds and the call to pray for labourers.
verseByVerse.theology: The two stories of verses 18–26 are woven together: the girl dies while Jesus stops for the woman, who is healed by touching his garment. Both are linked by twelve years (the woman’s illness and, in Mark, the girl’s age), and both cases are uncleanness at its worst, which should have defiled him and instead was cleansed. Jesus does not hurry past one need to reach another, and each receives what she needs.
verseByVerse.examples: The harvest saying (vv. 37–38) concludes the two miracle chapters: the need is vast, the labourers few, and the first response is prayer, asking the Lord of the harvest to send workers. The church has often answered the harvest with more activity; Jesus begins with prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, "My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, for she said to herself, "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, "Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well." And instantly the woman was made well. And when Jesus came to the ruler's house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, he said, "Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. And the report of this went through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ruler came in and knelt before him. Mark and Luke tell us he was Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41), responsible for organising services. He is a man of religious rank, from the very circles that are growing suspicious of Jesus, and he kneels in public. Desperation for a child does that to a man’s dignity.

Why the accounts differ. In Mark and Luke the father comes saying his daughter is at the point of death, and only later, while Jesus is delayed with the woman, do messengers arrive to say she has died (Mark 5:22–23, 35). Matthew has him say at the outset that she has just died. The best explanation is a habit of Matthew’s. He tells in nine verses what Mark takes twenty-three to tell, giving the father’s request in its final form rather than walking us through the stages, as any of us does in summarising. Throughout his Gospel Matthew compresses the miracle stories, and ancient readers expected a shortened account to give words in summary.

But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live. Remarkable faith: he believed Jesus could raise the dead. And Jesus rose at once and followed him, with his disciples (v. 19), without a question or a condition. That is how he answers a sincere cry: he goes where he is needed.

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years. Probably a chronic menstrual or uterine bleeding. Under the law, such a woman was ritually unclean, and anyone she touched became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). For twelve years she had been excluded from worship and from normal contact, probably unable to marry or remain married. Mark adds that she had spent all she had on doctors and had only grown worse (Mark 5:26). To press through the crowd at all was to defile everyone she brushed against: an act of sheer desperation.

Came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. She came from behind, secretly, because she was ashamed and knew she should not touch anyone. The “fringe” (kraspedon) was one of the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment, as God commanded, to remind them of his commandments (Numbers 15:37–41). What she touched was the sign of the very law that had shut her out. She reached past the law that condemned her to the one who keeps it perfectly, and found him kinder than any rule.

For she said to herself, If I only touch his garment, I will be made well. Her faith was real, perhaps mixed with superstition. She believed Jesus’ power was so great that even his clothes could heal. She does not announce herself; she reaches. And instantly she was made well: twelve years of suffering ended in a moment.

Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well. Jesus would not let her slip away unseen. He called her “daughter”, the only time in the Gospels he is recorded addressing a single person by that word, welcoming her into God’s family. “Your faith has made you well” (literally “has saved you”): not the touch or the cloth, but her trust in Jesus. The word “saved” (sesōken) includes both physical healing and the wider salvation of the whole person. Take heart is the same word he spoke to the paralytic (v. 2). Faith did not heal her by itself; it joined her to the one who did.

And when Jesus came to the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion. Mourning in that culture was loud and public. A rule recorded in the Mishnah, written down a little later, says that even the poorest man must hire at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife’s funeral. Wailing and lament filled the house.

Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping. Jesus does not deny that she has died physically; the mourners know she has. But for him, death is like sleep, because he is about to wake her. In the New Testament, “sleep” becomes a Christian way of speaking of the death of believers (John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), because they will be raised. To the Lord of life, death is a sleep he can break whenever he chooses.

And they laughed at him. The mourners’ grief turned instantly to mockery. It is the laugh of people who know a corpse when they see one, and death did not have the last laugh in that house.

He went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. Again Jesus touches the unclean: a dead body made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11). Again, life flows from him. Mark records his words in Aramaic: Talitha cumi, “Little girl, I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41). The verb for arose is the resurrection word again (see 8:15; 28:6).

Why the two stories are woven together. Mark notes that the girl was twelve (Mark 5:42): the woman had been suffering for as long as the girl had been alive. They are bound by more than timing. Both are stories of uncleanness and death: the woman ceremonially unclean, the girl a corpse, which was uncleanness at its height. By every rule of the law the woman’s touch and the dead girl’s hand should have defiled him; yet instead of their uncleanness reaching him, his power reaches them. And the interruption itself preaches. While Jesus stops for the woman, the girl dies, which stretches the father’s faith from heal her to raise her, and shows that Jesus is Lord not only over long disease but over death itself. A ruler of the synagogue and a nameless, penniless, unclean woman: he calls her daughter, and he gives the man back his.

Why does Jesus delay when I am praying for something urgent? Stand where the father is standing. His daughter is dying, he has found Jesus, Jesus has agreed to come, and then Jesus stops, for somebody else, for a woman who had lived with her illness for twelve years and could, on any reasonable calculation, have waited another hour. And in the delay the child dies. Anyone who has watched a clock while heaven said nothing knows what that pause feels like. Two things must be said. First, the delay was not neglect. It changed what the father was going to receive. He set out asking for a recovery and went home with a resurrection. God’s delays are very often the distance between what we asked for and what he intended to give. Second, not everyone gets the child back. Jairus did. Many have prayed this exact prayer and buried their child, and the passage must never be preached as though the outcome were the promise. What is promised is what Jesus said in the room: that to him the dead are sleeping, and he can break that sleep. This raising was a sign, not the destination; the girl would one day die again. I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25) is the promise. Jairus’s daughter is the preview.

For the one whose suffering has gone on for years. She is the person in the passage who waited longest and was helped last, and she is the one woman in Matthew whom Jesus is recorded calling daughter. If your affliction has outlasted your patience and everyone else’s interest, take that detail with you. He was not too busy with the emergency to stop for the long, unglamorous, chronic thing. And when he stopped, he did not only heal her. He gave her a name in his family.

Was her faith superstitious, and does Jesus accept faith that is mixed and muddled? Her idea about the clothes was imperfect, and Jesus gently corrected it by turning and speaking to her, so that she would know it was not the cloth but the person. But he did not reject her for it. He honoured the faith and fixed the theology. That is a great comfort, because all of us come to him with mixed motives and half-formed ideas. Faith does not save by being well informed or pure; it saves by reaching for the right person. Then he teaches us, as he taught her, to know him better.

Does sleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes the body, which lies still and will be woken; the believer’s soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; Luke 23:43). (See Mark 5:39 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. He calls death sleep because he will wake his people. He took a dead child by the hand and spoke to her as a father wakes his daughter in the morning, and she got up. He went down into death himself and was not held by it. The last enemy will be destroyed, and the one who said Talitha cumi in a little room in Capernaum will say it over every grave of his people on the last day. Then the hired mourners will be put out for ever, and the laughter in the house will be ours.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke name the ruler Jairus, a synagogue leader. A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch. Hired flute players and mourners were customary at a death. The “fringe” was the tassel the law required on garments.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, "Have mercy on us, Son of David." When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" They said to him, "Yes, Lord." Then he touched their eyes, saying, "According to your faith let it be done to you." And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, "See that no one knows about it." But they went away and spread his fame through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two blind men followed him. Blindness was common in the ancient world, caused by disease, injury and poor hygiene. Blind people usually lived by begging. Isaiah promised that in the age of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened (Isaiah 35:5; 42:7).

Crying aloud, Have mercy on us, Son of David. “Have mercy” (eleēson) is the cry of those who have no claim and can only appeal to kindness. The church has prayed it for centuries: Kyrie eleison, “Lord, have mercy”. “Son of David” is a messianic title (see 1:1). They cannot see him, yet they see him more clearly than the Pharisees do.

In the flow. These two men are the first people in Matthew’s story to call Jesus Son of David, the title with which the Gospel opens (1:1). The cry will come again from a Canaanite mother (15:22), from two more blind men at Jericho (20:30), and from the crowds and children as he rides into Jerusalem, while the chief priests take offence (21:9, 15). Blind beggars see first what the city will shout and then reject.

When he entered the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus did not respond on the road. He waited until they had followed him into the house, perhaps testing their persistence, and avoiding a public messianic demonstration.

Do you believe that I am able to do this? Jesus asks about their faith in him personally: not whether they believe in healing, but whether they trust him. The question is searching, not rhetorical. Faith is meant to come to the surface and say what it believes, and theirs does: yes, Lord. Two words, unhesitating and complete, and they use the disciples’ word for him.

Then he touched their eyes, saying, According to your faith be it done to you. Their faith in him received what he gave. “According to” does not mean “in proportion to”, as though a little faith gets a little sight. It means “in response to”: faith is the hand that receives. Their eyes were opened.

And Jesus sternly warned them, See that no one knows about it. “Sternly” means strongly, with deep feeling.

Why the command to silence? It is often called the messianic secret, and several threads run through it. First, timing: Jesus moved on his Father’s schedule towards the cross, and a wildfire of publicity could force a premature collision with the authorities. Second, the danger of a faith built on signs: the crowds chased miracles, not the Messiah, and he told them so when they followed him for the loaves (John 6:26). Third, and deepest, the title itself could not be rightly understood until the cross defined it. To proclaim Son of David or Christ without Calvary was to broadcast a false messiah, the political deliverer the crowds once tried to make king by force (John 6:15). That is why, even after Peter’s confession, Jesus told the disciples to tell no one, and at once began to speak of his death (16:20–21). Matthew also sees in this reticence the portrait of Isaiah’s gentle Servant, who would not quarrel or cry aloud in the streets (12:18–21). And the silence was never absolute. In Gentile country, where no messianic frenzy threatened, Jesus told the freed demoniac to go and tell what the Lord had done (Mark 5:19). The secret was provisional, fitted to a work not yet finished. After the cross and the empty tomb, the command is gloriously reversed: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19). What had to be hushed before Calvary is to be shouted from the rooftops after it.

But they went away and spread his fame through all that district. They disobeyed. Who could keep silent after seeing for the first time? But Jesus had a reason, and the cost of their enthusiasm fell on his ministry. Loving him means doing what he says, even when we think we know a better way to serve him (John 14:15).

Why did Jesus ask whether they believed, when he already knew? Not to find out, but to draw it out. Faith that is spoken becomes clearer to the one who has it, and Jesus wanted them to know that their healing came through trusting him personally, not through a lucky meeting on the road. He still asks the same question, through his word, of everyone who comes: do you believe that I am able? Your answer does not need to be eloquent. Yes, Lord, is enough. It is also why Christians confess their faith openly, in baptism and before the church (Romans 10:9–10). What is believed in the heart is meant to be said with the mouth.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah, the king of David’s line.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, "Never was anything like this seen in Israel." But the Pharisees said, "He casts out demons by the prince of demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A demon-oppressed man who was mute. Here the inability to speak was caused by a demon. Not every disability is demonic (see 4:24), but in this case it was. He was brought to Jesus; he could not ask for himself. Others did his speaking for him, as others had done the carrying for the paralytic.

And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. Isaiah promised that the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:6). Matthew does not linger: the accumulation of miracles is the point.

And the crowds marveled, saying, Never was anything like this seen in Israel. The crowds sum up chapters 8–9. Moses, Elijah and Elisha did great works, but nothing like this.

The tenth. Count them: the leper, the centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, the storm, the Gadarene demoniacs, the paralytic, the ruler’s daughter, the woman with the flow of blood, the two blind men, and this mute man. Ten mighty works, arranged by Matthew rather than by strict order of time (Mark and Luke place several of them elsewhere), and the number may well not be accidental. Matthew has already shown Jesus as the new Moses, from the slaughter of the infants to the mountain and the law (chapters 2–7). Ten mighty works following a mountain of teaching recalls the exodus, with one great difference. Moses’ ten were plagues that fell on Egypt. These ten fall on disease, death, the storm and the demonic. The signs of the first deliverance destroyed; the signs of this one heal.

But the Pharisees said, He casts out demons by the prince of demons. The Pharisees cannot deny the miracles, so they explain them away: Jesus is in league with Satan. This is the beginning of their charge that Jesus is demonic. Jesus will answer it fully in 12:22–32.

A textual note. A few early manuscripts leave out verse 34, and some scholars think it was brought in from 12:24. The evidence for keeping it is good and most editions do, but a reader who finds a footnote in his Bible has met a real question rather than an invented one. Nothing in the teaching of Scripture depends on it, since the same charge is recorded beyond dispute in chapter 12.

Two responses. His opponents in the Gospels argue about the source of his power, not about whether it was real, and later the council says the same of an apostle’s healing: we cannot deny it (Acts 4:16). The mute man was standing there talking. So there were only two possible explanations for a power that was plainly real and plainly not theirs, and having ruled out God they had one left. Immediately before verse 34, the crowd says nothing like this was ever seen in Israel. Same day, same man, same evidence: one group concludes that God has visited his people, and the other that the devil is loose in Galilee. Evidence alone does not produce faith. The difference was never the data.

Is this the unforgivable sin, and could I have committed it? Jesus later warns that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven (12:31–32), and he says it in answer to exactly this charge. That sin is not a careless word or a passing doubt. It is the settled, deliberate refusal to accept the Spirit’s plain witness to Christ, calling the light darkness and holding to it, so that the heart can no longer repent. Those who commit it do not care that they have. If you are troubled that you might have committed it, your very trouble shows that the Spirit is still at work in you, and the promise stands: whoever comes to Christ he will never cast out (John 6:37).

Why don’t miracles convince everyone? Because unbelief is not finally a problem of information. Jesus said that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31), and when he raised Lazarus some went to plot his death (John 11:45–53). The heart decides how the evidence is read. That is why faith is a gift of God and not merely a conclusion (Ephesians 2:8): the Spirit must open blind eyes. It is also why we should pray for unbelieving friends and not only argue with them. Arguments matter, but only God can change a heart. None of this means that every honest question is stubbornness: when John the Baptist doubted, Jesus answered him patiently with the evidence (11:2–6).

On a Tuesday. Use your tongue as the healed man did: say one thing today that you could not have said before Christ opened your mouth, a word of thanks, of witness, or of praise.

parallels.desc: the tongue of the mute sing for joy

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few;" therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages. Almost word for word the summary of 4:23: teaching, preaching and healing, the three inseparable expressions of the kingdom’s arrival. And nothing the Pharisees say stops what God is doing. The accusation of verse 34 is followed not by a retreat but by a wider mission.

When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them. “Compassion” (splanchnizomai) comes from the word for the inward parts, and it is one of the strongest words for pity the language had. It is not a decision to be sympathetic; it is what happens in the body when something goes right through you, and it moves a person to act. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus (14:14; 15:32; 20:34) and of characters in his parables who picture God: the father who sees his son on the road (Luke 15:20), the Samaritan who sees the man in the ditch (Luke 10:33).

Because they were harassed and helpless. The first word (eskylmenoi) had once meant flayed, but by this time it meant harassed or worn down; the second (errimmenoi) means thrown down, lying where they fell. So the sentence is stronger than, they looked tired: they were knocked about and left lying. The people were oppressed by Rome and burdened by the religious leaders’ demands (23:4), with no one to care for them.

Like sheep without a shepherd. An Old Testament image (Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17). In Ezekiel 34 God condemns Israel’s shepherds, who fed themselves instead of the flock and had not strengthened the weak, healed the sick or bound up the injured, so that the sheep were scattered (Ezekiel 34:2–5). And he promises that he himself will shepherd his people, through his servant David. Jesus is that Shepherd (2:6; John 10:11). The flock was not shepherdless because nobody held the office. It had shepherds; that was the problem. And Jesus had spent two chapters in conflict with them.

Then he said to his disciples, The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Jesus changes the picture from sheep to a harvest field. In the prophets, harvest often pictured the final judgment (Joel 3:13), but here it pictures the gathering of people by the gospel (John 4:35–38). Jesus takes the sickle of judgement and turns it into a tool of rescue. Both pictures are true at once: the crowds are lost sheep, which is need, and ripe grain, which is opportunity.

Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest. God is the Lord of the harvest: he owns it and directs it. The first response to the need is not to organise but to pray. “Pray earnestly” (deēthēte) is the asking of someone in need. Labourers are God’s provision, not human production.

To send out laborers into his harvest. “Send out” (ekbalē) is the verb used for casting out demons; it can simply mean send out, but it often carries force: thrust out, drive out. Workers are needed, and God must send them. The prayer often turns back on the one who prays: in the next verses, Jesus sends out the very disciples he told to pray (10:1–5).

Does Jesus still feel this compassion now that he is in heaven? Yes. He did not leave his human heart behind when he ascended. He is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, because he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). The same gut-wrenching pity he felt on a Galilean hillside he feels now for the harassed and helpless, including you on the day when you feel mauled and thrown aside. Come to him with confidence; you will find mercy and grace to help in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).

How can an ordinary Christian be a labourer? By living and speaking for Christ where God has put you. Most of the harvest is gathered not by professionals but by ordinary believers among their own families, neighbours and colleagues: praying for them by name, loving them practically, and being ready to explain the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15). Support those sent further afield with your giving and your prayers. Serve in your church so that its shepherds are free to shepherd. And keep praying the prayer Jesus taught here, holding yourself ready to be part of the answer.

On a Tuesday. His compassion reached you first. Next time you are in a crowd, a station, a shopping centre, a hospital waiting room, look at the faces and ask the Lord to let you see them as he does: not as an inconvenience but as sheep without a shepherd. Then pray for three of them silently before you leave.

For worship. He looked at a crowd harassed and thrown down by the men who should have fed them, and what he felt turned him inside out. Ezekiel had heard God say, I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and here he is, God in the flesh, walking the villages of Galilee and binding up the wounded. The Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep is the Lord of the harvest who sends workers into his own field, and the flock that was harassed and scattered he gathers in his arms.

parallels.desc: not as sheep that have no shepherd
scattered, because there was no shepherd

9.theology: Justification and the forgiveness of sins. The healing of the paralytic is Matthew’s clearest window onto justification. Jesus does not say God will forgive you if you do something; he says your sins are forgiven, a verdict already given. That is the heart of the gospel: the guilty are declared righteous by the Judge himself, on the ground of the Son’s merit, through faith. The one who pronounces the pardon here will bear the penalty on the cross that makes the pardon just.
9.examples:
Then: Matthew the tax collector was the last person anyone expected in the kingdom. His conversion was a public scandal and a public testimony, and the meal he gave brought people who needed the physician to the physician.

Now: A church that welcomes the broken, the addicted and the outcast is continuing Matthew’s meal. The temptation of respectable Christianity is the Pharisees’ error, protecting the community by keeping the sick out. Jesus reverses it: the church is a hospital for sinners, where the Great Physician is at work.

10.title: Sent as Sheep Among Wolves
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. <sup>2</sup>The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; <sup>3</sup>Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; <sup>4</sup>Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>5</sup>These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, <sup>6</sup>but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. <sup>7</sup>And proclaim as you go, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’ <sup>8</sup>Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay. <sup>9</sup>Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, <sup>10</sup>no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food. <sup>11</sup>And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. <sup>12</sup>As you enter the house, greet it. <sup>13</sup>And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. <sup>14</sup>And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. <sup>16</sup>“Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. <sup>17</sup>Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues, <sup>18</sup>and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. <sup>20</sup>For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. <sup>21</sup>Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death, <sup>22</sup>and you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>23</sup>When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. <sup>24</sup>“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. <sup>25</sup>It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household. <sup>26</sup>“So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>27</sup>What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. <sup>28</sup>And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. <sup>29</sup>Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. <sup>30</sup>But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. <sup>31</sup>Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>32</sup>So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, <sup>33</sup>but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. <sup>34</sup>“Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. <sup>35</sup>For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. <sup>36</sup>And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. <sup>37</sup>Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. <sup>38</sup>And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. <sup>39</sup>Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>40</sup>“Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. <sup>41</sup>The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. <sup>42</sup>And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.”
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the mission discourse, the second of Matthew’s five great sections of teaching. Jesus gives the Twelve his authority and sends them first to Israel. The instructions then reach beyond that first journey to the whole mission of the church. Persecution is not an accident but the normal condition of mission: “I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves.”

The answer to the fear of persecution is the fear of God. Three times Jesus says do not fear (vv. 26, 28, 31), and he grounds each in the Father’s knowledge and care: not a sparrow falls without him, and the hairs of the head are numbered. The cross appears for the first time in verse 38: only those who lose their lives for Christ’s sake will find them. The chapter ends with a cup of cold water that God will not forget.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Twelve Sent Out: Authority, Message, and Provision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls the Twelve, names them, and sends them out with authority over unclean spirits and disease. For this first mission they go only to the lost sheep of Israel, not to Gentiles or Samaritans. They are to preach the kingdom and do the works Jesus has been doing, travelling with nothing, and towns that refuse them are solemnly left to God’s judgement.
verseByVerse.theology: The mission of the Twelve extends Jesus’ own: he gives them his authority (v. 1) and his message (v. 7). The restriction to Israel (vv. 5–6) is not a permanent exclusion of Gentiles but the order of God’s plan, to the Jew first (Romans 1:16), and after the resurrection the Great Commission sends them to all nations (28:18–20).
verseByVerse.examples: Travelling with no money, no bag and no spare sandals is not poverty for its own sake but trust in the Lord of the harvest to provide through those who receive his messengers. The worker is not self-sufficient, and that dependence is itself a witness to the King who sent him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Having told his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest (9:38), Jesus now sends the very men who prayed. He calls twelve, gives them his own authority over demons and disease, and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel with the news that the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Then the horizon widens to the whole future mission of his people, and to what it will cost.

The connection. This is the second of the five great teaching sections in Matthew, the mission discourse. It covers the first mission (vv. 5–15) and then looks beyond it to the mission of the church in a hostile world (vv. 16–42).

And he called to him his twelve disciples. Jesus had many disciples, but chose twelve to be with him and to be sent out (Mark 3:14). Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is forming a new Israel, the restored people of God, around himself. What does that mean? Not that God has thrown Israel away: all twelve are Jews, and they are sent first to Israel (v. 6). It means that the people of God is now gathered around Jesus, so that whoever belongs to him, Jew or Gentile, belongs to that people (Ephesians 2:19). The Twelve will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (19:28).

A claim before it is an arrangement. The number is not a headcount. Ten of the twelve tribes had been carried off by Assyria over seven hundred years before and never came back as tribes, so the appointing of exactly twelve men is a declaration. In the Old Testament only the LORD founds Israel, and he promised to gather it again himself (Ezekiel 34:11–13). When Jesus names a new twelve and sets them around himself, he is quietly doing what only Israel’s God does. Its centre is not a tribe or a temple but a person.

And gave them authority. His own authority (see 7:29; 9:6). They do not have power of their own; it is delegated, as an ambassador carries the authority of his king. The word is exousia, the flashpoint of the last two chapters (9:6, 8), and here, one chapter after having to defend it, he gives it away.

And to heal every disease and every affliction. Unclean spirits are demons, morally impure and defiling those they possess. The words for healing are the very ones used of Jesus’ own ministry (4:23; 9:35): the disciples extend his work. And the limits are exact. Authority over unclean spirits, and to heal disease. Not to forgive sins: that is nowhere delegated in this passage. They are given the works. The word that only God can speak stays where it belongs.

The names of the twelve apostles are these. The only time Matthew uses the word “apostles”, at the precise moment they stop only learning and start being sent. An apostle (apostolos) is one sent, an envoy with the authority of the sender.

First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother. Peter is the leader and spokesman of the Twelve throughout the Gospels (16:16–19). He always appears first in the lists of apostles (Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13), and in the Gospels Judas always comes last. The list is in pairs, perhaps because Jesus sent them out two by two (Mark 6:7). Andrew had brought Peter to Jesus in the first place (John 1:41). James the son of Zebedee and John his brother complete, with Peter, the inner circle (17:1; 26:37).

What it does not mean. Not that Peter was given authority over the other apostles as a pope over the church. He was first among equals, a leader and spokesman.

Are there apostles today? Not in this sense. An apostle of Christ had to have seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (Acts 1:21–22), and the apostles’ foundational teaching is now in the New Testament; nobody today carries an apostle’s authority, whatever title he gives himself. (See 1 Corinthians 9:1 for the fuller answer.)
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

parallels.desc: the twelve apostles on the city’s foundations

verseByVerse.quote: James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip and Bartholomew. Philip came from Bethsaida, the same town as Peter and Andrew (John 1:44). Bartholomew means “son of Tolmai”; he is often identified with Nathanael, whom Philip brought to Jesus (John 1:45–49), because in John’s Gospel Philip and Nathanael are paired, and Bartholomew appears next to Philip in the lists.

Thomas. His name means twin. He is known for doubting the resurrection until he saw Jesus, and then for one of the greatest confessions in the Gospels: my Lord and my God (John 20:24–29). Matthew the tax collector is, by early tradition, the author of this Gospel, and only this Gospel adds the tax collector to his name.

James the son of Alphaeus. Probably the one called James the younger (Mark 15:40). Thaddaeus is probably the man Luke calls Judas the son of James (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13); some manuscripts call him Lebbaeus. Many people had more than one name.

Simon the Zealot. Literally the Cananaean, from an Aramaic word meaning zealous; Luke calls him the Zealot (Luke 6:15). He may have belonged to the nationalists willing to use violence to overthrow Rome, or the name may describe his zeal for the law.

Six pairs. The list runs in six pairs, and it sharpens the point about the Zealot and the tax collector. Nationalists of Simon’s kind hated no one more than Jews who worked for the occupation, and tax collectors were at the top of that list. Yet they walked the same roads for some three years and ate at the same fires. Nothing suggests that Jesus arranged a reconciliation or that either man changed his politics. He simply called them both, and the calling turned out to be larger than the thing that should have made them enemies.

And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. “Iscariot” probably means “man of Kerioth”, a town in southern Judea; he may have been the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee. He always comes last, labelled by his betrayal (26:14–16, 47–50). Jesus chose him knowingly (John 6:70–71). His presence among the Twelve is a solemn warning: it is possible to be close to Jesus, to share in his ministry, even to do miracles in his name (7:22), and yet not belong to him.

Who betrayed him. Every name on the list is defined by the one who is not on it. Simon is called Peter because Jesus named him; Matthew is the tax collector because Jesus called him from the booth; and the list ends with the word him, handed over. The Lord who chose these men was not choosing a team to protect him. He chose the man who would deliver him up, knowing it, and walked on towards Jerusalem with Judas at his side. That is how the list becomes good news: the betrayal written at its end was the road by which the Shepherd went to lay down his life for the other eleven, and for every name that would ever be added after them.

Why did Jesus choose Judas? He knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64, 70–71), and he chose him so that Scripture would be fulfilled: he who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18; Psalm 41:9), within God’s plan (Acts 2:23). Yet Judas was fully responsible (26:24). He was sent out with the others and did the same works, which shows that ministry and outward power are no proof of saving grace (7:21–23).

Could I be a Judas, close to Jesus but not his? The question is a healthy one to ask once, and a dangerous one to ask endlessly. Judas’s problem was not weak faith but no faith: he loved money (John 12:6), he kept up appearances, and when he was sorry he went to the priests and not to Christ (27:3–5). The test is not whether you have struggles, but where you take them. If you hate your sin, trust Christ alone for forgiveness, and keep coming back to him when you fail, you are not a Judas. You are a Peter, who also failed badly, and wept, and was restored. Judas never stops being a warning; he must never become a torment to a believer who is running to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Somewhere in your church is the person whose politics, background or temperament you find hardest. Christ called you both with his eyes open. This week, bring them before God and do one kind thing for them: the calling that made the Twelve one is larger than what divides you.
verseByVerse.note: Bartholomew is often identified with Nathanael of John’s Gospel. Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, "Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans. A surprising restriction. The Samaritans, in the region between Judea and Galilee, are usually said to have descended from northern Israelites who intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest of 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim instead of in Jerusalem (John 4:20), and Jews and Samaritans despised each other. The tension with Acts 1:8, where the same Lord sends these men to Samaria by name, is real, but it is not a contradiction. It is a sequence.

But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. “Lost sheep” echoes 9:36: the people of Israel were like sheep without a shepherd. God had made his covenant promises to Israel, and the Messiah came first to them. Jesus said the same of his own mission (15:24). And there is tenderness in it: the Twelve are sent to exactly the people over whom their Master had just been moved with compassion.

Why the restriction? Not because Jesus did not care about Gentiles. He has already healed a Gentile’s servant and praised his faith (8:5–13), and he will command his disciples to go to all nations (28:19). The order reflects God’s plan in history: first Israel, then the nations. The prophets pictured Israel restored first, and then the nations streaming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3; 49:6). After the resurrection, the mission goes to Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).

Three reasons for the order. First, faithfulness. The promises were made to Israel, and from Israel came the Christ (Romans 9:4–5). The Son of David comes to David’s house first and knocks on his own door. Second, the message. The kingdom of heaven is at hand presumes a throne, a covenant and centuries of prophets; in a Galilean village everyone knew what was claimed, while in a pagan market town it would have meant nothing yet. Third, and deepest, the cross. At this hour the Gentiles are still strangers to the covenants of promise (Ephesians 2:12), and what tears down the dividing wall is not a change of policy but a cross. That is why the Great Commission begins: all authority has been given to me; go therefore (28:18–19). Matthew 10 stands on this side of Calvary; Matthew 28 stands on the other.

The door shut so that it could be opened. For every reader who is not a son of Abraham by birth, here is the wonder. Had the Twelve gone to the nations then, they would have carried a kingdom announcement with no cross in it and no atonement behind it. Instead the Lord kept them home, walked to Jerusalem, and did the work that alone could bring a Gentile near: in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). He always meant to come for you. He simply had to go to the cross first.

Should Christians share the gospel with Jewish people today? Yes, with love, humility and respect. The gospel is still the power of God for salvation to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16), and the apostles, all of them Jews, preached Jesus as Israel’s Messiah in synagogue after synagogue. Christians must never be arrogant towards Jewish people, and must reckon honestly with the long, shameful history of Christian hostility towards them (Romans 11:18–20). But it would be no kindness to keep from Abraham’s children the news that their Messiah has come. Christians hold different views about God’s plans for the Jewish people in the future; all agree that today, Jew and Gentile alike, salvation is found in Jesus alone (Acts 4:12).
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans lived between Judea and Galilee, a people of mixed descent who worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. The mission to the nations would come after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: And proclaim as you go, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is at hand." Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And proclaim as you go. The disciples were heralds. A herald does not invent his message or improve it. He carries it, loudly and accurately, from the king to the people. The message is the one John (3:2) and Jesus (4:17) preached: God’s reign has arrived in Jesus. The King himself had come, with the power the prophets had promised for the last days (Isaiah 35:5–6).

Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. Exactly what Jesus did in chapters 8–9: a leper in 8:3, demons at Gadara, a ruler’s daughter raised in chapter 9. The works were signs confirming the message that the kingdom’s power is driving back sickness, death and evil. The mission of the church is not an idea about Jesus but a continuation of him.

Borrowed life. No prophet ever told his servants to go and raise the dead. Elijah and Elisha stretched themselves on a single body and cried to the LORD (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34). Jesus hands the power out as a commission, because it is his to hand out: he is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). The Twelve carried life the way the moon carries light, from a source outside themselves. And before long the one who sent them would go down into death himself and come up out of it, not as a sign of the kingdom but as its firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20).

You received without paying; give without pay. They had received authority and the message freely from Jesus, and must not charge for it. Wandering philosophers and miracle-workers often made money from their teaching and healing; Jesus’ messengers must not. The Greek word behind both halves is dōrean: as a gift, for nothing. What the messenger carries was obtained by nobody, and cost its owner everything.

What it does not mean. Not that those who preach the gospel may not be supported by others. Jesus immediately says the labourer deserves his food (v. 10), and Paul defends the right of ministers to be paid (1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18). What is forbidden is charging admission: putting a price on the thing itself, so that the sick are healed and the good news is preached in proportion to what somebody can pay. The moment the kingdom has a tariff, it has stopped being the kingdom.

Where Christians differ: is this commission to heal and raise the dead for the church today?
