Continuationists (who hold that all the Spirit’s gifts continue today) believe it is, at least in part; cessationists hold that these powers were signs given to the Twelve, and to those closely linked with them, to confirm their message at the founding of the church (both views are set out at 8:16–17). This commentary’s view: the cessationist reading is the more likely. The signs are called the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), and Hebrews speaks of God bearing witness by signs and wonders through those who first heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4). The church still prays for the sick, and God still heals in answer; but no one today holds the apostles’ authority to raise the dead or cleanse lepers at a word. This is a difference among godly Christians, to be held charitably, and many continuationist believers put the rest of us to shame by the earnestness of their prayer for the sick.

So may churches charge for anything? They may cover costs honestly: a book costs money to print and a conference hall costs money to hire, and the worker deserves his wages. But some things must never carry a price: the preaching of the gospel, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, prayer, pastoral care, a welcome to the poor. Beware anyone who links God’s blessing to your giving, who promises healing or prosperity in return for a gift, or who treats the needy as less welcome than the wealthy. And in your own service, ask whether you would still do it if nobody paid you or thanked you. That is what freely given means.

parallels.desc: what I have I give you

verseByVerse.quote: Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts. Coins were often carried in the folds of a cloth belt: no money at all. And no bag for the journey, whether a traveller’s bag for supplies or a beggar’s bag for collecting gifts.

Or two tunics or sandals or a staff. No spare clothes, no extra sandals, no walking stick.

Matthew and Mark together. Mark says they could take a staff and sandals (Mark 6:8–9), while Matthew and Luke forbid a staff (Luke 9:3). A common explanation compares the verbs. Matthew’s word is not take but acquire: do not go out and equip yourselves for this journey; go as you stand, with the stick already in your hand. Luke also says take, so this does not settle every detail, and some think the Gospels give the gist of the order in different words. All three agree on the point, which is that provisioning is forbidden: twelve men leave town with nothing but what they already had.

For the laborer deserves his food. Those who receive the gospel should support those who bring it. The disciples were to trust God to provide through hospitality. Paul quotes the same principle (1 Timothy 5:18). The support of gospel workers is not charity; it is what is owed.

The point. The worker who arrives with nothing shows that the kingdom has sent him; his survival is his master’s responsibility. Jesus sends these men out so that they must trust him for the next meal (6:11, 34), which is exactly what a love of control resists.

Like their Master. The men who walked out of that town with empty belts looked exactly like the one who sent them. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (8:20). He who was rich, for our sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9): he preached from a borrowed boat and rode into his city on a borrowed colt. The Twelve were not being asked to do something their Lord had not done first. Their empty hands were his own poverty extended into the villages of Galilee, and that poverty was the very way his riches came to us.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. At the Last Supper, Jesus told the disciples that from then on they should take a moneybag and a knapsack (Luke 22:35–36). Conditions changed. But the principles remain: simplicity, urgency, dependence on God, and the duty of God’s people to support those who serve them with the gospel.

Should missionaries today raise support or earn their own living? Either can be right. Paul defended the right of gospel workers to be supported (1 Corinthians 9:14), and gladly received gifts from the Philippians (Philippians 4:15–18); yet he often worked with his hands as a tentmaker so as to be no burden and to set an example (Acts 18:3; 2 Thessalonians 3:8–9). What matters is that the worker depends on God whichever way the bread arrives, that the gospel is never sold, and that churches take seriously their duty to provide for those they send. If you support a missionary, you are not doing him a favour. You are a partner in his work.

For worship. The Lord who sent his apostles with empty hands fed every one of them. When he asked them later whether they had lacked anything, they said, nothing (Luke 22:35). He owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10), and he has never sent a servant out and failed to provide for him. He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)?
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt. The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.

parallels.desc: those who proclaim the gospel get their living by it

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. As you enter the house, greet it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Find out who is worthy in it. Worthy here means open to the message, ready to welcome God’s messengers, like the son of peace in Luke 10:6: not morally perfect, but receptive. The word (axios) runs through the paragraph four times: the labourer is worthy of his food; find who is worthy; if the house is worthy; if it is not. And the definition is entirely practical. A worthy house is one that opens its door. There is no test of character.

And stay there until you depart. Do not move from house to house looking for better hospitality. A Christian handbook from around the end of the first century, the Didache, warns that a travelling apostle who stays three days, or who asks for money, is a false prophet. The first door that opens is the one you use.

As you enter the house, greet it. The normal greeting was Shalom, peace (Luke 10:5). From Jesus’ messengers it was more than a polite word: it was a blessing offering the peace of the kingdom, and in that culture a blessing was often understood to convey something, not merely to wish it.

The Lord who came in at the door. These instructions are a portrait of Jesus himself. He never asked whether a house was respectable before he entered it. He looked up into a sycamore tree and said to a tax collector, Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today, and salvation came to that house the same day (Luke 19:5, 9). The open door is all he asks, because the gift he brings is himself, and the poorest house in Galilee could be worthy of it simply by letting him in.

How can I show hospitality if my home is small or I live alone? Hospitality is not about the size of the house or the quality of the food. It is about an open door and an open heart. A bowl of soup at a kitchen table, a spare sofa for a visiting student, a cup of tea with a new family after church: these are hospitality in the New Testament sense (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9). If your home really cannot be opened, open your time instead: take someone out for coffee, give a lift, invite yourself to help in someone else’s home. The point is to receive Christ’s people as you would receive him.

verseByVerse.quote: And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it. The blessing of peace comes on those who receive it. Peace here is the shalom of the kingdom: God’s blessing and salvation, the wholeness that comes with the arrival of God’s rule.

But if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. If they reject it, the blessing does not take effect on them. Jesus speaks of peace almost as a substance: it can come to rest on a house, or come back, undamaged, into the messenger’s hands, to be given somewhere else.

And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words. The condition is stated precisely: refusal to hear, not slowness to agree.

Shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. Gentile soil was counted unclean, and strict Jews are said to have shaken its dust from their feet on returning to the holy land, so as not to carry it in. For the disciples to do this to a Jewish town was a startling act: it declared that the town, by rejecting the Messiah, had made itself like a pagan land, and that the messengers were no longer responsible for it. Paul and Barnabas did exactly this at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

Why the peace cannot be lost. The peace these men carried could come back undamaged because it was never theirs. It was Christ’s. He himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), and he would make that peace in the costliest way possible, by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). A greeting from a fisherman on a doorstep is a small thing; but behind it stood the one who would be rejected by his own town, his own nation and his own friends, and still say, peace I leave with you (John 14:27). What men refuse does not lessen it. What Christ paid for cannot be wasted.

What it does not mean. Not an act of personal anger or contempt. It was a solemn warning, done with sorrow, leaving the town to God.

The freedom in it. The gesture is also a release. The messenger is not responsible for the result. If the door shuts, he shakes his feet at the gate and walks to the next town without dragging the failure along the road behind him. The loss, the gesture says, is entirely on the other side of the door.

When should I stop sharing the gospel with someone? Rarely, and never stop loving or praying. The apostles were on a short, urgent tour, and Jesus told them not to linger where the door was shut. In ordinary life, most of us live alongside the same people for years, and many come to faith slowly. But there is wisdom in knowing when to stop pressing. If someone has heard the gospel clearly and asks you not to raise it again, respect that, keep living it in front of them, keep praying, and be ready when they ask (1 Peter 3:15). Do not throw what is holy before those who only mock it (7:6). And remember that God can open a door you have no strength left to knock on.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: Paul and Barnabas shake off the dust

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It will be more bearable on the day of judgment. Truly, I say to you: a solemn statement of Jesus’ own authority. There are degrees of judgement. All who reject God face judgement, but not all equally (11:22–24; Luke 12:47–48), and the degrees follow the light each person received. Every case is weighed on exactly what that person had.

For the land of Sodom and Gomorrah. Cities destroyed by fire from heaven for their great wickedness (Genesis 18–19; Jude 7), and a byword for God’s judgement. Ezekiel’s summary is often a surprise: Sodom had pride, excess of food and prosperous ease, and did not help the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49). The assault on the visitors in Genesis was real and wicked; but Ezekiel puts the arrogant, well-fed indifference first, which describes something rather close to a prosperous modern town. That is worth knowing before the name is used as a weapon against others.

Than for that town. Sodom was the worst example of a wicked city, yet a town in Israel that rejects the Messiah’s messengers will face worse judgement.

The light that walked their streets. What made the difference was not that Galilee had better sermons. It was that the light was a person. Sodom had Lot, a compromised resident who sat in its gate. Capernaum had the Son of God living in its houses, healing its sick at sunset and teaching in its synagogue. The judgement is this, Jesus said, that the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light (John 3:19). To refuse a prophet is grave. To look into the face of God’s own Son, and hear his messengers knock in his name, and close the door, is the one sin Sodom never had the opportunity to commit.

In the flow. From verse 16 Jesus looks further ahead, to the persecution of his messengers; and in 11:20–24 he pronounces this warning himself on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, the towns that saw most of his works.

What it does not mean. Not that Sodom will escape judgment. Nor that sexual sin does not matter. The point is that rejecting Christ, with knowledge, is the most serious sin of all (John 3:18–19; Hebrews 10:26–29).

Who is most in danger from this verse? Not the people who never heard. The ones who have heard often, and well, and can predict the sermon, and have arranged their lives so that nothing in it ever has to be acted on. The principle cuts towards the religious reader, not away from him. If reading this makes you afraid that you are that person, the fear itself shows the word is still reaching you: act on it today, and you are not.

What about those who never heard the gospel? They are judged by the light they had, not by light they never received, and the judgement will be perfectly fair. But Scripture is clear that all have sinned against the light of creation and conscience and are without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:12–15), and that salvation is found only through faith in Christ (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). That is why Paul asks how they can believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14), and why the church sends missionaries. The right response to the question is not speculation but prayer, giving and going: a question like this is best answered on our knees and with our wallets and, for some, with a one-way ticket. (Infants who die in infancy, who cannot hear or understand, are in a different case: the elect among them, those God has chosen, are saved by Christ through the Spirit, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession (10.3) and the Westminster Confession (10.3) both say. Grieving parents may rest their little ones in the hands of a God who is more tender than they are, and whose Son took children in his arms, Mark 10:16.)

For worship. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25). He weighs every soul with perfect justice, and no one will be punished for more than he knew or less than he deserved. And this same Judge sent his messengers to warn the towns before the day came, and then went himself to bear the judgement of all who would believe. Fire fell on Sodom; on Calvary the fire of God’s wrath fell on his Son, so that those who flee to him will never feel it. Justice and mercy have met in him.

parallels.desc: the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–42 — Persecution, Confession, and the Cross: The Cost of the Mission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of the discourse turns from method to cost. Jesus warns of persecution before councils, governors and kings, and promises that the Spirit of their Father will give them words. Three times he says do not fear. His coming divides even families, he must be loved above father and mother, and every disciple must take up a cross. The section ends with the promise that whoever receives his messengers receives him, and that even a cup of cold water will be rewarded.
verseByVerse.theology: The persecution discourse is not pessimism but realism: a disciple is not above his teacher. Jesus will be persecuted, and his followers will share his lot. The fearlessness Jesus commands rests not on natural courage but on what is true of God: he knows, he values, he reigns.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus speaks of the cross (v. 38) before he has spoken of his own death, and the Twelve heard it as a condemned man’s walk to execution. Every disciple takes up his own cross: the end of the self-directed life, at the cost of reputation and safety. And the paradox of verse 39 is the deepest saying in the chapter: whoever clutches his life loses it, and whoever gives it up for Jesus finds it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. Sheep are defenceless; wolves are predators. The image is not of eventual triumph but of immediate vulnerability, and Jesus does not promise that his messengers will be safe. He promises that they are sent: I am sending you.

The Shepherd who meets the wolf. Any other shepherd who drove his flock into a pack of wolves would be a hireling or a madman. Jesus can say it because of what he will do. The hireling sees the wolf coming and flees, he says, but the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11–12). He sends his sheep among wolves only because he is going in ahead of them, to be surrounded himself by bulls of Bashan and dogs (Psalm 22:12, 16), and to be torn so that they need never be lost. The men in this verse go out defenceless, but not unguarded. The wolves will get to the Shepherd first.

So be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Snakes were proverbially shrewd and cautious (Genesis 3:1): disciples must be prudent and alert, not naive, not taking needless risks. Innocent (akeraioi) means pure, unmixed, without guile, as doves were proverbially harmless.

What the wisdom looks like. Shrewdness is not a failure of faith. Jesus declined to answer Herod at all (Luke 23:9), and told these very men to flee from one town to the next (v. 23). Paul was lowered over a wall in a basket (Acts 9:25) and used his Roman citizenship as a legal shield (Acts 22:25; 25:11). So: do not be provocative about things that do not matter; do not hand opponents ammunition; know when to speak and when to be silent; answer the question actually asked; and where the law protects you, use it without embarrassment.

What the innocence guards. Shrewdness easily curdles into cunning: the half-truth, the quiet manipulation, the small deceit that seems justified because the other side is fighting dirty. The dove forbids it absolutely. You may be as careful as you like about how you speak; you may not lie, spin, flatter or scheme. Doves without serpents get needlessly destroyed and call it faithfulness. Serpents without doves win most arguments and lose the thing they were sent to carry. Jesus asks for both at once, in the same person, on the same afternoon.

Beware of men. Opposition will come from people, including religious people. This is not a call to suspect everyone, but Jesus knew what was in man (John 2:25), and he does not send his friends out with illusions.

For they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues. The courts (synedria) are local Jewish councils; the word is related to Sanhedrin. Synagogues had authority to discipline Jews by flogging. The law allowed forty lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and the practice was thirty-nine, to avoid exceeding the limit. Paul received this five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).
verseByVerse.note: Synagogues had the authority to flog; the law allowed up to forty lashes, kept to thirty-nine in practice.

parallels.desc: five times the forty lashes less one

verseByVerse.quote: and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake. Governors were Roman officials, like Pilate, Felix and Festus; kings were client rulers, like Herod Agrippa. Paul stood before Felix, Festus and Agrippa (Acts 23–26). James was executed by Herod (Acts 12:2). Every category in this sentence was filled within thirty years.

To bear witness before them and the Gentiles. Persecution becomes an opportunity for witness; the trial room becomes a pulpit (Acts 26:1–29). Forbidden to go to the Gentiles in verse 5, they are told in verse 18 that they will be dragged to them. The gospel did not reach the empire because a committee planned it, but because Christians were arrested, and the man who wanted to go to Spain arrived in Rome in chains at the government’s expense.

When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say. Anxious is the same word as in 6:25–34. Jesus forbids worry about a trial, as he forbade worry about food.

For what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. God will provide the words when they are needed, as he promised Moses (Exodus 4:12), and Stephen spoke with such wisdom that his opponents could not resist it (Acts 6:10). The promise is shaped exactly to the fear. He does not promise they will be spared the trial, or acquitted. He promises that when the moment comes there will be something to say.

Before governors and kings. Every word of this verse was first true of Jesus. He was delivered over by the council, struck in the face, and brought before a governor, Pilate, and a king, Herod (Luke 23:1–12). Before the king he said nothing at all; before the governor he testified to the truth and to a kingdom not of this world (John 18:36–37). He is describing a road he will walk before any of them. They will stand in the dock where he stood, and the Spirit who fills their mouths is the Spirit who rested on him.

What it does not mean. Not that preachers need not prepare sermons. This is a promise for those suddenly put on trial for their faith, not an excuse for laziness in teaching (2 Timothy 2:15).

What if I go blank when someone challenges my faith? It happens to most of us, and it is not a sign that God has left you. The promise here is first for the hour of real persecution, but the Father who gives words in a courtroom does not forget his children in a staffroom. Do what you can beforehand: know your Bible, be able to say simply what Christ has done for you, and think through the questions you are most often asked (1 Peter 3:15). Then in the moment pray silently, say what you know, and do not be afraid to say, I don’t know, but I will find out. Faithfulness is not eloquence.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. The exact phrase, the Spirit of your Father, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. The wording is doing pastoral work. Jesus does not simply say the Spirit will speak, which would be true and cold. The one who supplies the words in the courtroom is named by his relation to them, and the relation is family. A man on trial for his life is being told that his Father will do the talking.

Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child. The gospel will divide families. In the early church converts were sometimes disowned, reported or killed by their own families, and it still happens in many parts of the world.

And it happened. Not as a figure of speech. Roman justice ran on informers, and there were rewards for it. One of the earliest outside accounts of Christian persecution, Pliny’s letter to the emperor Trajan about AD 112, describes a stream of anonymous accusations naming Christians, and in a household the people who knew were relatives.

He was handed over by his own. Jesus speaks of divided families as one who knew them from the inside. He was delivered to death by a man who had eaten at his table. Yet the one betrayed by his household makes a household of his own. Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven, he says, is my brother and sister and mother (12:50). And as he hung dying, deserted by nearly all, he gave his mother a son and his friend a mother (John 19:26–27). The Christ who costs some people their families is the Christ who gives them a family that cannot be broken.

How should I pray for persecuted Christians? Specifically and regularly, as for members of your own body, because they are (Hebrews 13:3). Pray that they will stand firm and not deny Christ; that the Spirit will give them words when they are questioned; that their families will be won rather than lost; that their persecutors will be converted, as Saul was; and that governments will allow them to live peaceful and quiet lives (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Find out about one country where Christians suffer and learn the names of a few believers there. Give to help them if you can. And let their courage shame our comfortable silence.

For worship. When father and mother forsake me, the LORD will take me in (Psalm 27:10), and he takes them in by name. The Spirit who speaks in the dock is the Spirit of adoption, crying Abba, Father, in the hearts of children whose earthly fathers have disowned them (Romans 8:15). No informer’s list can strike a name from the Father’s house, and no family that turns away can unmake a child of God.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: and you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. All means people of every kind, not literally every individual. For my name’s sake: because you belong to Jesus. The world hated him first (John 15:18–20). It is the name of Jesus that provokes the hatred, not the disciples’ personalities or methods.

The name they hate. The name that draws the world’s hatred is the name the angel gave before he was born: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (1:21). Men rage against the one name under heaven by which they could be saved (Acts 4:12). And the disciple who is hated for that name holds on, not by his own grit, but because the name is written on him. The Lord who endured the hatred of all, and the cross at the end of it, is the one who carries his people to the end.

Endurance to the end. To endure means to remain, to hold on under pressure. To the end may mean to the end of one’s life, or to the end of the age. True faith perseveres; those who fall away under persecution show that their faith was not genuine (13:20–21; 1 John 2:19).

When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. Fleeing persecution is not cowardice. Martyrdom is not to be sought, and the next town still needs the gospel. Persecution in Jerusalem scattered the church and spread the gospel (Acts 8:1–4).

For truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. A difficult verse. Albert Schweitzer built a whole portrait of Jesus on it: here, he claimed, Jesus predicted the end of the world within his disciples’ lifetime and was simply wrong. But the key is the phrase the Son of Man comes. It is drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where the Son of Man comes not down to earth but up to the Ancient of Days, to be enthroned and given a kingdom. It speaks of his vindication and reign, and need not mean his final return at all.

Where Christians differ: which coming of the Son of Man is meant? There are three main views. 1. The resurrection and ascension. The Son of Man “comes” in vindication when he is raised and receives all authority (28:18; Daniel 7:13–14). 2. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A coming in judgment on the nation that rejected him (24:30, 34). 3. The second coming. The mission to Israel will continue until Christ returns at the end of the age; it will never be finished. This commentary’s view: most likely the coming in judgment in AD 70 (view 2), within the generation of the disciples, as Jesus says in 24:34, though this event itself foreshadows the final coming. On any view, the point is: the mission to Israel is urgent, and it will not be complete before the Son of Man acts.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by endurance. Endurance is the fruit of true faith, and God himself gives it: this is what is meant by the perseverance of the saints.

If I must endure to the end, can I lose my salvation? No one whom God has truly saved will finally be lost. Jesus says of his sheep that no one will snatch them out of his hand or his Father’s (John 10:28–29), and Paul is sure that he who began a good work will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). But the way God keeps us is not by letting us coast; it is by working in us to keep believing, keep repenting and keep following. So the warning is real, and it is one of the means by which he keeps us. A believer may fall badly and for a time, as Peter did, but he will be brought back. If you are afraid of falling away, run to Christ with that fear. The fear itself is not the mark of the lost, who are untroubled; it is the Spirit stirring you to hold on.

On a Tuesday. Endurance is built day by day, and God builds it through ordinary means of grace. Read a chapter of Scripture when you do not feel like it; go to church when you are tired; confess the same sin again rather than hiding it; keep the promise you made. Perseverance is mostly made of ordinary days in which he keeps you faithful.

parallels.desc: the one who endures to the end

verseByVerse.quote: A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A disciple is not above his teacher. A proverb: students do not expect better treatment than their teacher. If Jesus was rejected and persecuted, his disciples should expect the same. Being like him is honour enough (John 15:20).

If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul. The Pharisees had accused Jesus of casting out demons by the prince of demons (9:34; 12:24). Beelzebul was a name for Satan. They called Jesus the devil, and if they insulted the head of the house, they will insult his household.

A grim pun. The element zebul means an exalted dwelling, so Baal-zebul is something like lord of the house. The word for master of the house is oikodespotēs, and for his household oikiakoi, so there is a bitter play on words. They have taken the true master of the house and given him the devil’s title, lord of the house; if they do that to him, what will they call his servants?

A ceiling and a floor. The proverb is usually quoted as a warning against arrogance. Here it does another job. When we are slandered for our faith, it is natural to think that a better Christian would have been better received, but the measure of a good disciple is not a better reception than the master got; it is the same reception. Nobody should expect the world to think better of him than it thought of Christ, and nobody who is thought badly of for Christ’s sake should conclude that he has failed.

On a Tuesday. When you are misrepresented for your faith, remember what they said about your Master. Before you take it to heart, ask honestly whether it is for Christ or for your own folly (1 Peter 4:15). If it is for Christ, do not retaliate and do not despair. Rejoice, as the apostles did, that you were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

parallels.desc: a servant is not greater than his master

verseByVerse.quote: So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three fears, three answers. So have no fear of them: the first of three do not fear commands, and fear of people is the great enemy of witness (Proverbs 29:25). Have no fear of them (v. 26), because everything hidden will come out. Do not fear those who kill the body (v. 28), because there is a worse thing than dying, and only one person controls it. Fear not, therefore (v. 31), because you are valued. Three fears: being misrepresented, being killed, being insignificant. He does not treat any of them as unreasonable, and he does not tell anyone to stop feeling them by an act of will. He answers each with a fact.

For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. God will vindicate his people and expose their persecutors at the judgment, and the gospel, which now seems hidden and small, will be known by all. The faithfulness of disciples, hidden in obscurity, and the wickedness of persecutors, disguised as respectability, will both be brought into the light.

What I tell you in the dark, say in the light. Jesus taught his disciples privately, often explaining what he did not explain to the crowds (13:10–11). After his resurrection they must proclaim it all openly.

And what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. Houses had flat roofs, used as public spaces, and announcements made there could be heard across the village. The gospel is not secret wisdom for a few, but public news for all: nothing he said to them in a room was meant to stay there.

Not done in a corner. The greatest hidden thing that has been brought into the light is Christ himself: the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints, Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:26–27). And he made the pattern of this verse his own. He was arrested at night and condemned behind closed doors. Then the most hidden plot in Jerusalem became a death as public as any in the world, beside a road where every passer-by could see, with the charge written in three languages (John 19:20). Paul could tell a king that this thing was not done in a corner (Acts 26:26). What his enemies did in the dark, God proclaimed from a hill.

I am shy, and I find it very hard to speak about my faith. What should I do? Start where you are, not where the bold are. The housetop is wherever you can be heard: your kitchen table, a message to a friend, a quiet word at work. Shy believers are often the best listeners, and listening earns the right to speak. Pray for one opportunity a week, and when it comes, say one true sentence about Christ: that you go to church, that you pray, what he means to you. Ask a bolder friend to help you, and invite people to hear someone else preach. God does not need you to become someone else; he needs you not to be silent from fear. And he loves to use the weak (2 Corinthians 12:9).
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do not fear those who kill the body. The worst persecutors can do is kill the body. Jesus does not make light of it; being killed is a real and terrible thing. But it is less than what God can do.

But cannot kill the soul. The soul, the inner self, survives the death of the body. Persecutors cannot touch the believer’s relationship with God or eternal life. Here the Bible distinguishes body and soul, and teaches that the soul continues after death (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23).

Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. That is God. Hell here is Gehenna. Fear of God is not cringing terror, but reverent awe of the one who holds final judgement, and fear of God drives out fear of people (Isaiah 8:12–13). It is Isaiah’s woe is me before the holy God, which finds rest only when God takes the guilt away (Isaiah 6:5–7).

No authority except from above. Jesus lived this verse before he asked it of anyone. In Gethsemane he poured out his soul to the Father and was heard because of his reverence (Hebrews 5:7). An hour later, standing before the man who could kill his body, he was unafraid: you would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above (John 19:11). The governor was afraid of the crowd and of Caesar; the prisoner feared only God. And because he feared God perfectly, he could do what no one else could: walk into the destruction of soul and body that we deserved, bear it in our place, and leave his people nothing to fear from it.

Who is the one to be feared? Most readers assume God, and a minority through the centuries have argued for Satan, because it seems strange to be told to fear the Father in one breath and to trust him about sparrows in the next. The answer is God, and the reasons are decisive. The devil has no authority to destroy soul and body in hell; he is a creature under judgement himself, and nowhere in Scripture does he send anybody there. The whole passage contrasts two fears, of which the lesser is fear of men, and a warning to fear the devil would break the argument. And Jesus says it elsewhere in the plainest terms: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell; yes, I tell you, fear him (Luke 12:5). But the strangeness is real, and it is the point. The same God is named as the one to be feared above all and, in the next verse, as your Father who attends to the death of a bird. A God who were only terrible could not be loved, and a God who were only kind could not be trusted with anything that matters.

Gehenna. It is not a general word for the afterlife but a place name. The Valley of Hinnom ran along the southwest of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under Ahaz and Manasseh, until Josiah defiled the site so it could never be used for that again (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). So the word carries a real ravine with a real history, the one piece of ground in Israel most associated with the destruction of the innocent, and Jesus uses it for the thing truly worth being afraid of.

Where Christians differ: does destroy mean that the lost cease to exist? Some (annihilationists, or conditionalists) take “destroy” to mean that the wicked cease to exist. But the same word is used of the lost sheep (v. 6), who are not annihilated but ruined, and Matthew uses it of wineskins that burst (9:17). Elsewhere Jesus speaks of eternal punishment (25:46), eternal fire (25:41) and unquenchable fire (3:12). Some evangelical Christians, John Stott among them, have leaned towards the annihilationist view, and it deserves a careful answer, not contempt. This commentary’s view: “destroy” means ruin, the loss of all that makes life life, not cessation of existence. The traditional view of hell as conscious, eternal punishment is the biblical one, which is why God is to be feared above those who can only kill the body.

Is it not unworthy to make people obey out of fear of hell? Only if fear were the whole of it. But Jesus is not frightening people into a religion of their own effort. He is telling the truth about God to men who are about to face enemies who can kill them, because only the truth about who holds the final verdict sets a person free from the fear of everyone else. To warn someone truthfully of a real and final danger is not manipulation; it is kindness. And in the very next breath Jesus speaks of the Father who counts sparrows. The God we rightly fear is the God who gave his Son so that those who trust him will never meet his judgement unprotected (Romans 8:1). The fear of God and the love of God are not rivals: the same believer trembles before him and runs to him.

Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food. A “penny” (assarion) was a small copper coin, about a sixteenth of a day’s wage. Luke says five sparrows for two pennies (Luke 12:6): if you bought four, it seems, a fifth was thrown in free. The fifth bird was the makeweight, worth nothing, not even counted in the price. And Luke’s form of the promise is that not one of them is forgotten before God. Not the four that were paid for. Not one, including the one nobody charged for.

And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. God is in control of the smallest events: the death of a sparrow. “Apart from your Father” means without his knowledge and will. This is the doctrine of providence: God governs all things, great and small. If he governs the death of a sparrow, he governs the death of his children: persecution and death come, but never by accident.

If God governs everything, is he the cause of evil? No. Scripture holds two truths together. God governs all things, so that not a sparrow falls without him; and God is perfectly holy, never the author of sin, and never forces anyone to do evil (James 1:13). Those who persecute Christians are fully responsible for what they do. Yet God rules over their wickedness and turns it to his purposes, as Joseph said to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The supreme example is the cross, where wicked men did what God’s hand had planned (Acts 4:27–28). The Westminster Confession puts it carefully: God orders all things, yet the sinfulness proceeds only from the creature (Westminster 5.4; 1689 5.4). That is why a believer can suffer injustice and still say, my times are in your hand (Psalm 31:15).

On a Tuesday. Whose opinion do you fear most: a boss, a parent, a group of friends, the online crowd? Set beside it what this passage says: they can at worst kill the body, and the one who holds your soul is your Father. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life (Proverbs 14:27).

For worship. The God who holds body and soul in his hand is the God who watches the cheapest bird in the market fall: so great that hell is in his power, so tender that the bird nobody paid for is not forgotten. And this Father let his own Son be sold, for thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave. We were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). The sparrow is counted; the child bought with such blood is held. We fear him, and because we fear him we fear nothing else.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna. Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; the “penny” was a small copper coin.

verseByVerse.quote: But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Most people have over 100,000 hairs. Nobody knows the number about himself, yet the Father has counted. And the tense is a perfect passive: they have been numbered and stand numbered. Not a running tally kept out of curiosity, but a completed reckoning.

Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. The third do not fear (vv. 26, 28, 31), and a gentle, almost humorous comparison: if God cares for sparrows, how much more for you, his children, made in his image and redeemed by his Son.

The sparrow falls. A good deal of shallow comfort has been built on these verses: God watches the sparrows, so nothing bad will happen to you. The context makes that impossible. The sentence before says, do not fear those who kill the body; the sentences after speak of losing your life for his sake; and James was beheaded little more than a decade later. The sparrow saying itself says the bird falls. The promise is not that it is caught before it hits the ground, but that it does not fall outside the Father’s knowledge and government. A guarantee of safety would be worthless within a lifetime; this one holds at the graveside, for nothing can separate us from God’s love, not even death (Romans 8:35–39).

The fear underneath. The logic is not: you are safe, therefore fear not. It is: you are known and you are valued, therefore fear not. The fear being answered is the fear of dying for nothing, unremarked, with nobody keeping count. Somebody is keeping count, down to the hairs.

Not one lost. The Son who spoke these words kept them on the night he was arrested. When the soldiers came into the garden with torches and weapons, he stepped forward and said, if you seek me, let these men go, so that his word would be fulfilled: of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (John 18:8–9). He let the band take him so that not one of the eleven was taken with him. That is what numbered hairs look like in the hands of Jesus: a Shepherd who counts his sheep and then puts himself between them and the swords. The Father’s care for the smallest thing about us is not a sentiment; it has a body, and it was bound and led away in our place.

Then why did God let this happen to me? When suffering comes, this passage does not give us the reason, but it closes off the worst answers. It was not an accident; he was not looking the other way; you did not slip through his fingers; you are not worth less to him than you thought. Often we will not know why in this life, as Job never learned why. But we can know who: the Father who numbers your hairs, who did not spare his own Son, and who works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Bring the question to him honestly, as the psalmists did. He can bear your why, and he will hold you while you wait for the answer.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So everyone who acknowledges me before men. “Acknowledge” (homologeō) means to confess, to declare publicly, to say the same thing. To acknowledge Jesus is to say openly that you belong to him and that he is Lord (Romans 10:9–10).

I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. At the final judgement Jesus will say: this one is mine. To deny him is to disown him, to say I do not know him, and he will say the same of such people: I never knew you (7:23).

Two courtrooms. The two halves of the sentence are built identically: same verb, setting and authority. What is said in a village square in Galilee is reproduced, exactly, in the presence of God, and Jesus casts himself as the witness in both courts. That is the answer to the fear the passage has been addressing. He tells them what the scene looks like from the other side: whatever is said down here is being said up there, by him, about them.

What the church learned. In the persecutions under Decius and Diocletian, large numbers of Christians denied Christ. When many wanted to come back, rigorists said this verse shut the door, and the church did not follow them. The man who denied Christ three times, the last time with oaths, to servants and bystanders, had been restored by name and given the flock to feed (John 21:15–19). Whatever verse 33 means, it cannot mean less mercy than Jesus showed to Peter.

I have kept quiet about my faith out of fear. Have I denied Christ? You have failed him, and that is worth grieving over, but you have not done what this verse warns against if you are grieved. Peter’s failure was worse than yours, and Jesus came looking for him. Confess it to God, plainly and without excuses, and receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9). Then ask his Spirit for courage, and take the next opportunity, however small, to say that you belong to him. The difference between Peter and Judas was not the size of their failure but what they did next. Peter went back to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to hide that you are a Christian? He is not ashamed to call you his; acknowledge him gently and clearly. It might be as simple as saying you were at church on Sunday, praying before a meal in public, or declining something and saying why. And if you have never confessed him publicly in baptism and church membership, ask whether it is time.

For worship. The Son of God will stand before his Father and the holy angels and name his people as his own, one by one, and not one who is his will be left unnamed. He was not ashamed of us when we were his enemies; he made the good confession before Pilate and was crucified for it, and he is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He is the faithful witness, and he never denies his own.

parallels.desc: if we deny him, he also will deny us

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. Surprising words from the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Jesus does bring peace: peace with God (Romans 5:1), and peace among those reconciled to God (Ephesians 2:14). But the immediate effect of his coming is division, because people respond to him in opposite ways.

I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. The sword is a picture of division, not of violence by his followers. It cuts between those who follow him and those who reject him. Simeon said that Jesus was appointed for the fall and rising of many and as a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34–35).

Two misuses. Critics quote this verse to show that Jesus was not the peaceable figure Christians claim, and a certain kind of believer quotes it as permission for a combative Christianity. Both misread it. The sentence is about the effect of his coming, and Luke’s version supplies the interpretation: not peace, but rather division (Luke 12:51), diamerismos, a splitting into parts. The sword is not a weapon in anybody’s hand; it is what a blade does to a thing laid across it. The man who said it told Peter to put his sword away, and healed the man Peter had struck (26:52; Luke 22:51). In the whole New Testament there is not one instruction to a Christian to use force for the faith.

For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Jesus quotes Micah 7:6, which describes a time of social and family breakdown in Israel’s sinfulness. When one member of a family follows Christ and others do not, their deepest loyalties now differ.

The birth pains of the Messiah. Jewish tradition came to read Micah 7:6 as a description of what would happen just before the Messiah came; a list of such signs in the Mishnah, written down about AD 200, includes exactly these words, and the reading may well be older. So when Jesus says, I have come to set a man against his father, he is taking a text read as a picture of the birth pains of the messianic age and saying: this is now, and I am the reason.

Micah’s next verse. The passage he quotes does not end in the ruins. Micah’s next sentence is the turn: as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me (Micah 7:7). The chapter ends with God delighting in steadfast love and casting all our sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:18–19).

parallels.desc: son against father, daughter against mother

verseByVerse.quote: and a person's enemies will be those of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. The end of the quotation from Micah 7:6. The people most likely to oppose a new disciple are often not strangers but relatives whose own commitments feel threatened by his conversion.

Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. In Jewish law, honouring father and mother was one of the highest duties (Exodus 20:12). Jesus claims a loyalty above even that, and above the love of son or daughter. Only God could claim such loyalty: the first commandment says, you shall have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3). Jesus is implicitly claiming to be God. Luke’s version uses stronger language: if anyone does not hate his father and mother he cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:26), a Hebrew idiom meaning love less. Not worthy means not fit to be his disciple: not that anyone earns worthiness, but that a person who puts anything above Christ has not truly received him as Lord.

Am I wrong to love my family so much? No. The verse does not set your love for them against your love for God, as though the affection itself were the problem. God commanded you to honour your parents, and he does not withdraw the command here. This is not a measurement of how warmly you may feel about people. It is about who wins when the two pull in opposite directions: when keeping your place in the family would require you to disobey Christ. Most days there is no conflict at all, and on those days loving your family with everything you have is obeying him.

Am I sure the division is over Jesus? This is the guard the passage most needs, because the sword he speaks of is one he brings; it is not one we are licensed to swing. Much family friction that gets filed under persecution is nothing of the kind. It is the Christian who has become insufferable: who corrects at the dinner table, cannot let a remark pass, and wears his disapproval where everyone can see it. Peter draws the line plainly: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler (1 Peter 4:15). So run the test honestly. Are they rejecting Christ, or rejecting you, your tone, your superiority, your need to win? If it is the second, that is not a cross. It is something to repent of.

Is this not what cults say? The words sound alike, but the difference is total. A cult leader demands first place so that he can take from you: your money, your judgement, your family. Jesus demands first place as the one who gave himself for you (Galatians 2:20). A cult cuts you off from your parents; Jesus rebuked those who used religion as an excuse to neglect them (15:4–6). And the claim stands or falls on who he is. From a mere man it would be monstrous; from the Son of God, the Lord of the first commandment, it is simply the truth about where love belongs, and the love that results makes better sons, daughters and parents, not worse ones.

So what do I actually do? Keep honouring them, which costs more than arguing with them and persuades far more. Honour a mocking parent with courtesy, presence, practical help, and a refusal to retaliate. You may not obey anyone into sin, but you are nowhere permitted to be rude. Do not make your love conditional on their agreement, or you will prove their suspicion that faith has made you colder. Answer questions when they are asked, and resist preaching when they are not. And play a long game: how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband (1 Corinthians 7:16)? Households have been won slowly, by years of ordinary faithfulness, far more often than by argument.

And if the division never closes? Some do not, this side of eternity. Jesus does not promise reconciliation in this life. He promises that no one who has left house or family for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold, and eternal life (19:29), and he says the loss is real enough to be worth mentioning. If you carry that grief, remember who is speaking to you. His own family once came to seize him because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). One of those brothers later opened a letter by calling himself a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1). He is not asking you to bear anything he declined to bear himself, and he has been known to finish these stories long after everyone else had given up on them.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whoever does not take his cross and follow me. The first mention of the cross in Matthew. Crucifixion was the cruellest and most shameful Roman execution, used for slaves, rebels and criminals. Such a man is not worthy of me: not fit to be his disciple.

Before he had spoken of his own. Jesus first plainly predicts his death at 16:21, six chapters later, and Peter’s horrified reaction shows it was news. So when the Twelve heard these words, they probably had no idea that their Master would die on a cross. The image landed on them as pure horror, with none of the softening that two thousand years of jewellery have supplied.

The walk, not only the death. A condemned man carried his own crossbeam through the streets to the place of execution (27:32; John 19:17), publicly, in front of his neighbours, with no possibility of appeal. That is the image: walk out of your front door carrying the thing you are going to be killed on, past everyone you know. And it is his cross, each man’s own. Christ’s cross was not shareable in what it achieved: Simon of Cyrene could carry the wood for him (27:32), but only he could bear the sin, and he bore it alone, for us.

What taking up the cross means. Not putting up with ordinary hardships (“my bad back is my cross to bear”). It means dying to self: renouncing the right to run your own life, accepting rejection and shame for Christ, and being willing to die if necessary. It is a decisive, total surrender. Jesus will repeat it after he first predicts his own death (16:24), and Luke adds “daily” (Luke 9:23).

Whoever finds his life will lose it. Life (psychē) means the self, the whole of what a person is. Whoever tries to save his life by avoiding the cost of following Christ, protecting comfort, reputation and safety, will in the end lose everything, including his soul (16:26).

And whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Whoever gives up his life for Christ, in martyrdom or in daily self-giving, will find true life: life with God now and for ever. The paradox of the gospel: the way to life is through death, and Jesus himself walked it first (John 12:24–25). For my sake: not any self-sacrifice, since losing your life for a cause, a career or an ideology is not the same.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by suffering. Christ carried his cross to save us; we carry ours because we have been saved and now follow him. We carry it unsteadily, but he walked the whole road for us, and the Father receives our stumbling steps for his sake. Nor does it mean that Christians should seek suffering for its own sake, or despise ordinary joys. The cross is the willingness to give up anything for Christ, not the rejection of God’s good gifts (1 Timothy 4:4).

What does carrying my cross look like on an ordinary day? Mostly it looks small and unseen. It is saying no to yourself so that you can say yes to Christ: telling the truth when a lie would be easier; giving up the evening you planned to help someone in need; refusing to join the gossip and accepting that you will be thought odd; obeying his word about money, sex or forgiveness when it costs you. It is accepting being misunderstood for him without retaliating. For some believers, it will one day mean prison or death. For most, it means a thousand daily deaths to self, each of them a step behind Jesus. And each one, he promises, is a finding and not a losing; his Spirit, living in you, is the one who makes each of them possible.

For worship. He told his disciples to take up a cross before they knew he would take up his. And then he did: he went out carrying his own cross to the place called the Skull (John 19:17), and there he lost his life so that we might find ours. Because he died, we die with him; because he rose, we find our life hidden with him in God. Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Galatians 6:14).
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet's reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person's reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever receives you receives me. The apostles are Jesus’ representatives. To welcome them is to welcome Jesus; to reject them is to reject him (Luke 10:16).

The law of agency. Jewish law expressed the principle in a saying recorded in the Mishnah: a man’s agent is as the man himself. A legally appointed representative, a shaliach, carried the full standing of the one who sent him, and his acts within his commission bound his sender. Many scholars think the Greek word apostle answers to this same idea, though the link is debated.

And whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Jesus is the Father’s agent. To welcome him is to welcome God (John 13:20). A chain of three: the apostle stands for Christ, and Christ stands for the Father.

The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. “Because he is a prophet” means for the sake of his message, recognising him as God’s messenger. Someone who supports God’s messenger shares in the messenger’s work and reward. The widow of Zarephath, who fed Elijah, shared in God’s provision (1 Kings 17:8–16); the Shunammite woman who welcomed Elisha received a son (2 Kings 4:8–17).

And the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. “Righteous person” probably means an ordinary faithful disciple. Those who support and welcome believers because they belong to Christ share in their reward.

The motive is weighed. The phrase is repeated: because he is a prophet, because he is a righteous person, and in verse 42, because he is a disciple. Hospitality offered because the guest is impressive or useful is an ordinary transaction. Hospitality offered because of what the man carries, when there is nothing to be got out of him and some risk in being seen with him, is counted as a share in his work. And the reward is the same wage. In the kingdom’s accounting the man who preached and the woman who fed him are on the same line.

Do pastors today carry this authority? In part, and with a limit. A faithful minister of the gospel is Christ’s messenger, and when he speaks what Scripture says, he is to be received as one sent by Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20; 1 Thessalonians 2:13; Hebrews 13:17). But he is not an apostle, and his authority extends only as far as his message agrees with the word of God. An agent who exceeds his commission binds nobody. So receive faithful preaching as the voice of your Lord, support and honour those who bring it, and test everything by Scripture (Acts 17:11). No preacher’s personality, title or popularity adds anything to that authority, and none can replace it.

parallels.desc: the widow of Zarephath receives Elijah

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whoever gives one of these little ones. Little ones means humble, ordinary disciples, those who seem least important (18:6, 10, 14). In this chapter the little ones are the Twelve themselves: sent out with no money, no bag, no spare clothes, dependent on strangers for supper. Not a child, but an apostle, reduced by his instructions to someone who needs a drink of water and cannot pay for it.

Even a cup of cold water. The simplest, cheapest act of kindness. In a hot climate cold water from a deep well was a real refreshment, but it cost almost nothing, only the trouble of fetching it. That is the size of the act being promised a reward: somebody walked to the well. And it is given because he is a disciple, literally in the name of a disciple: because the person belongs to Jesus.

Truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward. God notices the smallest act of kindness done for his people. Nothing is wasted (Hebrews 6:10). The double negative in Greek (ou mē) is the strongest form of denial the language has: there is no possibility whatever that it will be lost.

The end of the chapter. The mission discourse began with authority to cast out demons and raise the dead (v. 8), and ends with a cup of cold water. Between those two ends the chapter has passed through floggings, courtrooms, family betrayal, hatred by all, and a cross. And the last word is not about heroism. It is about a person in a doorway who did one small kind thing for somebody with nothing, because of whom that somebody belonged to.

I thirst. The Lord who promises a reward for a cup of water knew what it was to need one. He sat tired by a well in Samaria and asked a woman for a drink (John 4:7). And at the end, on the cross, the one through whom the rivers were made said, I thirst (John 19:28), and was given sour wine on a sponge. Every cup handed to a thirsty disciple is handed to him, because he has so joined himself to his people that their thirst is his: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (25:40). He was given sour wine for his thirst so that he could become, for all who come to him, a spring welling up to eternal life (John 4:14).

What it does not mean. Not that kindness to non-Christians does not matter. Jesus commands love to all, even enemies (5:44). Here he speaks specifically of supporting his messengers.

Will some Christians have greater rewards in heaven than others? Scripture speaks of rewards that differ (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Luke 19:16–19), and this verse is one of the promises. But they are rewards of grace, not wages earned. Every believer is accepted wholly because of Christ, and the works rewarded are works God himself prepared and enabled (Ephesians 2:10). Augustine said that when God crowns our merits he crowns his own gifts. And there will be no envy in heaven: every cup will be full, and every one of us will gladly cast our crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). The point of the promise is not to make us calculate, but to assure us that nothing done for Christ, however small, is wasted.

On a Tuesday. Look for the least noticed person in your church, the one who never leads anything and whom nobody thanks. Do one small kind thing for them this week, a meal, a lift, a word of encouragement, because they belong to Christ.

parallels.desc: as you did it to one of the least of these

10.theology: Providence and mission. Matthew 10 grounds mission in God’s providence. The disciples go out into hostility and likely suffering, not because God has abandoned them but because he governs every detail of their way. That does not make the messenger passive; it gives him courage. The one who governs the sparrow governs the prison cell, the court and the place of execution.
10.examples:
Then: The Twelve went out with no bag, no spare tunic and no staff, depending on the hospitality of those who received the gospel. Their empty hands showed that the kingdom advances by God’s power through human weakness, not by human resources.

Now: The church in every generation is sent as sheep among wolves. Where Christians are comfortable and free, the temptation is to make the church a refuge from the world rather than a mission into it. Where they are persecuted, as many are, Matthew 10 is a survival manual: do not fear those who can kill the body; fear him who holds the soul.

11.title: Are You the One Who Is to Come?
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. <sup>2</sup>Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples <sup>3</sup>and said to him, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>4</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: <sup>5</sup>the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>6</sup>And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>7</sup>As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>8</sup>What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. <sup>9</sup>What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>10</sup>This is he of whom it is written, “‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>11</sup>Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. <sup>12</sup>From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. <sup>13</sup>For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, <sup>14</sup>and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. <sup>15</sup>He who has ears to hear, let him hear. <sup>16</sup>“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates, <sup>17</sup>“‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’ <sup>18</sup>For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>19</sup>The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” <sup>20</sup>Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. <sup>21</sup>“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>22</sup>But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>23</sup>And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. <sup>24</sup>But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.” <sup>25</sup>At that time Jesus declared, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; <sup>26</sup>yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>27</sup>All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. <sup>28</sup>Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. <sup>29</sup>Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. <sup>30</sup>For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
11.overview:
Chapter 11 turns on a question from a prison: “Are you the one who is to come?” John the Baptist, the greatest of the prophets, sits in Herod’s fortress and sends to ask. His doubt is faith under strain, and he takes it to Jesus. Jesus answers from Isaiah: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1). Then he honours John as the Elijah who prepared the way.

The responses darken: a generation that will accept neither John nor Jesus, and towns that saw his mightiest works and did not repent. Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum will fare worse than Tyre, Sidon and Sodom, because greater light brings greater accountability. The chapter ends with Jesus thanking his Father and then calling every weary person to come to him for rest, from a heart that is gentle and lowly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — John's Question, Jesus's Invitation: The Kingdom in Paradox
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist, imprisoned, sends to ask whether Jesus is the one who is to come. Jesus points to his deeds in the words of Isaiah, praises John, rebukes the generation that rejected both, pronounces woes on the unrepentant towns, and closes with the great invitation to the weary: from doubt to judgment to grace. Jesus leaves out of his answer the one clause of Isaiah 61:1 that promises liberty to the captives; and he changes a pronoun in Malachi 3:1 (v. 10), so that the way prepared for the coming of God becomes the way prepared for him.
verseByVerse.theology: John is the greatest of the prophets, yet the least in the kingdom is greater, not because he is better but because he lives after the cross and resurrection and sees what John only announced. Since John came, the kingdom has broken in with power and met violent opposition: its herald is in chains. The towns that saw the most and did not repent face the heaviest judgment, because their privilege was the greatest.
verseByVerse.examples: The invitation of verses 28–30 is the gospel in miniature, addressed to those worn out by trying to earn God’s favour, weighed down by guilt, or exhausted by life. It calls them not to a programme but to a person. His yoke is easy because it is borne with him, and the rest he gives is the rest of a soul that has found what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 11 is the chapter in which the kingdom meets every kind of response. John the Baptist, in prison, asks whether Jesus really is the one; Jesus answers from Isaiah and praises John. He compares his generation to sulky children, pronounces woe on the towns that saw his mightiest works, and thanks his Father for revealing these things to infants. Then he calls every weary person to come to him for rest, and tells us, as nowhere else in the Gospels, what his own heart is like.

When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples. This is the second of five times Matthew rounds off a block of teaching with almost the same sentence: after the Sermon on the Mount (7:28), the mission charge (11:1), the parables (13:53), the teaching on life in the church (19:1) and the teaching on the end (26:1), after which the passion begins. Many readers have seen a deliberate echo in this, in a Gospel written largely for Jewish readers: the Law came in five books, and here is the word of the Lord in five discourses, delivered by a greater Moses who went up a mountain to give the first of them.

He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. Having sent the Twelve out to the towns, he goes to the towns himself. He does not delegate and withdraw; he works the same ground at the same time, and sends them nowhere he is unwilling to go himself.

The new section. Chapters 11 and 12 set out the responses to Jesus, darkening as they go: honest doubt (11:2–6), indifference (11:16–19), unrepentance (11:20–24) and open hostility (chapter 12). In the middle stands his invitation to the weary (11:28–30). He offers rest in the very chapter in which he is being rejected.

Does this mean that those who serve Christ should never stop working? No. The point is that Jesus never asks of his servants what he will not do himself, not that rest is unspiritual. The same Lord took his disciples away to a desolate place to rest a while (Mark 6:31), slept in a boat in a storm, and withdrew to pray. What the verse rules out is the leader who hands every task to others and keeps the platform for himself. Those who lead in a church, a home or a ministry should still be found doing the ordinary work they ask others to do, and they should also keep the rest their Master kept.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples and said to him, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" And Jesus answered them, "Go and tell John what you hear and see:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when John heard in prison. Herod Antipas had imprisoned John for telling him that he could not have his brother’s wife, Herodias (14:3–4). Josephus says John was held at Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea. He had been there for months, and he would not come out alive. This is a man in darkness, whose certainty is being tested by circumstances that do not fit what he expected. Prison does not destroy faith, but it strips it of comfort and forces it down to its foundations.

About the deeds of the Christ. The works of chapters 8 and 9. Matthew calls them the deeds of the Christ on purpose: the reader is to know these are the Messiah’s works, even while John is unsure.

Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? The one who is to come was a title for the Messiah (3:11; Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1). Why would John, who had baptised Jesus and seen the Spirit descend and heard the Father’s voice (3:13–17), ask this? Most likely because Jesus was not doing what John had expected. John had announced a Messiah with a winnowing fork and unquenchable fire, who would cut down every fruitless tree (3:10–12). Instead Jesus was healing, eating with sinners and showing mercy, while John sat in a dungeon and Herod went unpunished. Where was the fire? Where was the liberty to the captives that Isaiah had promised (Isaiah 61:1)? It is one of the most honest questions in the Gospels. John is not pretending; he is genuinely uncertain.

Who is doing the doubting. This is the passage for anyone whose faith has gone quiet, and there are more such people in any congregation than ever say so. This is the prophet who saw the heavens opened, the man Jesus is about to call the greatest born of women (v. 11). If John can arrive here, doubt is not proof that your faith was never real. Such questions are usually asked from a prison of one kind or another: illness, grief, a marriage that failed, a prayer unanswered for years.

What John did with it. John did not bury the question, and he did not walk away with it. He sent it to Jesus. Doubt carried toward Christ becomes faith with its foundations exposed; doubt carried away from him hardens into something else. A church where nobody may admit a hard question will lose the people who have one.
