What Jesus does not do. He does not rebuke John or shame him. He sends back evidence and treats an honest doubt as worth answering carefully. He is not fragile, and neither is the truth. You may bring him the question you are most afraid of.

What Jesus does not send back. He does not explain why John is in prison, and he does not promise release. What he sent was not an explanation but a declaration of who he is. Very often that is the only answer given, and it is the one that holds.

Is it a sin to doubt? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. Unbelief refuses God’s word and turns away; doubt is faith struggling to hold on while something does not make sense. John doubted and Jesus called him great. Thomas doubted and Jesus showed him his hands. Scripture even says to have mercy on those who doubt (Jude 22). What matters is direction. Doubt nursed in private, used as a reason to stop praying or to stay away from God’s people, can harden. Doubt brought to Christ, in prayer, in the Scriptures and in honest conversation with a mature believer, is often how he deepens a faith that was resting on feelings rather than on him.

What if I bring my doubts to Jesus and nothing seems to change? Then you are where John was, and you are in good company. Jesus did not change John’s circumstances; he gave John himself to look at, and the Scriptures to hold. Keep doing the ordinary things: read the Gospels, where the deeds of the Christ are recorded; keep gathering with the church; keep praying, even if the prayer is only the question. Faith is not a feeling you must manufacture but a person you keep turning toward. Feelings of assurance often return slowly, and sometimes only later can you see that he was holding you all along.
verseByVerse.note: John was imprisoned by Herod Antipas, according to Josephus in the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go and tell John what you hear and see. Jesus does not answer yes directly. He points to the deeds Isaiah had said would mark the coming of God to save, and lets John draw the conclusion.

The blind receive their sight and the lame walk. Isaiah 35:5–6: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, and the lame man shall leap like a deer. Isaiah 35 pictures God himself coming to save his people. The signs Jesus lists are the signs of the new creation, the reversal of the curse that came with sin (Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 5:12): previews of the day when death shall be no more (Revelation 21:4). John would recognise the passage at once.

Lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up. Isaiah 26:19 promises that the dead shall live. Cleansing lepers is not in Isaiah’s lists, but Elisha did it (2 Kings 5), and Jesus has done it (8:2–3), touching the man nobody touched.

And the poor have good news preached to them. Isaiah 61:1: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor, the passage Jesus read at Nazareth (Luke 4:18–21). The climax of the list is not a miracle at all. It is preaching: the gospel to the poor.

The clause that is missing. Isaiah 61:1 goes on: he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. The one clause that speaks directly to a man in a cell, and Jesus leaves it out, in a reply to a man in prison. In a quotation assembled with such care, that is very likely deliberate, and the answer is honest to the point of severity: the signs are real, the age has begun, and the prison door is not going to open. The day of vengeance in the next verse of Isaiah is not mentioned either. Jesus is gently telling John: I am fulfilling the promises, but in God’s order, mercy now and judgment later.

Not offended. Offended translates skandalisthē: to be tripped up and fall away, the language not of intellectual objection but of a man brought down by something he did not see. Many stumbled over a humble, merciful, suffering Messiah (1 Corinthians 1:23); many still do. As the ending of this message it is almost unbearable, and exactly right: the kingdom has come, I am the one, and I am not getting you out, and blessed is the man who can hold those three together without stumbling.

Who the beatitude was first spoken to. Not to sceptics, but to the greatest man born of women at his lowest hour. And it is a kindness, not a threat: Jesus names, tenderly, the one real danger, that the Christ who is not doing what you expected might become the reason you turn from him, so that it will not happen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that miracles alone prove Jesus is the Messiah. False messiahs could appear to do signs (24:24). It is the combination of the works with Scripture’s promises, and above all the preaching of good news to the poor, that identifies him.

Why does Jesus not do miracles like these everywhere today? He still heals, and Christians are right to pray for the sick and to give thanks when he answers (James 5:14–16). But the signs in this list had a particular purpose: they were the credentials of the Messiah, the evidence Isaiah said would mark his coming, and they were continued through the apostles to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4). This commentary holds, charitably towards brothers who differ, that those sign-gifts ceased with the apostolic age. The reason is that the New Testament ties them to the apostles’ founding work (2 Corinthians 12:12; Ephesians 2:20), and once that foundation was laid they had done what they were for. Many faithful Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers among them, read these passages differently and expect such gifts today; they are our brothers and sisters, and both sides pray for the sick and trust the same Lord to answer. The sign that has not ceased is the last one in the list: the poor still have good news preached to them. Every faithful sermon to needy people is the same work of the Messiah going on.

What if God does not rescue me from my prison? Then this verse was written for you. John was not rescued, and Jesus called him blessed if he did not stumble. God does sometimes open prison doors (Acts 12), and you may ask him to. But his love is not measured by whether he changes your circumstances. It is measured at the cross. A Christian can be in hospital, in debt, in grief, or in an actual cell, and still be in the kingdom and loved without limit. The question is not whether he will do what you want, but whether you will trust him if he does not.

For worship. The blind see, the lame leap, the lepers are clean, the dead rise, and the poor hear good news: this is God himself come to save. He left one clause unspoken for John so that he could fulfil it for ever. He went down into the deepest prison of all, death itself, and broke it open from the inside, and on the day every grave is opened, liberty will be proclaimed to every one of Christ’s prisoners, John first among them.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

parallels.desc: the blind see, the lame leap

verseByVerse.quote: As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings' houses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John. Jesus turns from answering John to defending him, so that no one would think less of John because of his question. He waits until John’s disciples are leaving, so the praise is not flattery to be carried back. He does not mention the wavering at all. He defends the doubter in public, at the very hour of his doubting, and so far as we know John never heard a word of it.

What did you go out into the wilderness to see? Crowds had gone out in great numbers to hear John (3:5), walking for days into the desert. Jesus asks what they were looking for, and the question reaches the reader too. What do you go to church to find: comfort, or truth? A performer, or a word from God?

A reed shaken by the wind? Reeds grew thickly in the marshes along the Jordan and at the north end of the lake, bending with every breeze. So a shaken reed is first a picture of the ordinary: nobody walks into a desert to look at grass. And it is a picture of a weak man who bends with public opinion. John was not that. He stood firm against a king. But there may be a sharper edge. Herod Antipas founded a new capital on the lake shore, Tiberias, and the early coins he struck there seem to have carried a reed. If so, the question carries a second meaning: you did not walk into the wilderness to look at the man on the coinage. You went to see someone who was his opposite.

A man dressed in soft clothing? Fine, luxurious clothes, the dress of the wealthy and the courtier. John wore camel hair and a leather belt and ate locusts (3:4). And those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. That is not a general remark about luxury. There is a king’s house in this story, and a man in soft clothing in it, and another man underneath it in the dark wearing camel hair. His imprisonment is the mark of his faithfulness, not his failure. A prophet who ends in prison for speaking the truth has not mismanaged his calling; he has fulfilled it.

The temptation to become a reed. The temptation is not usually felt as cowardice but as reasonableness, as keeping the peace. By any sensible measure, telling a king he could not have his brother’s wife was unnecessary. It cost John his head, and Jesus calls him the greatest man ever born.

A bruised reed he will not break. John was no reed shaken by the wind; yet he had just sent from prison a question that trembled. And the Lord who praises the unbending prophet is the Servant of whom Isaiah wrote, a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3; Matthew 12:20). On the same afternoon he answered John’s wavering gently and praised his firmness publicly: the King who stands unshaken before Herod and the Shepherd who will not snap the faith of a man whose courage is near its end.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that fine clothing or wealth is sinful in itself; Joseph of Arimathea was rich. The point is the contrast between John’s fearless integrity and the comfortable compromise of those who serve the powerful.

How do I know whether I am standing firm or simply being stubborn? Ask three questions. First, is the thing I am holding to clearly taught in Scripture, or is it my preference? John stood on God’s law about marriage, not on a personal opinion. Second, what does standing cost me, and what does bending gain me? If bending would bring comfort, approval or advantage, be suspicious of your reasons for bending. Third, am I saying it with love and for the other person’s good? John’s words to Herod were a call to repentance, not a performance. Firmness on what God has said, with gentleness in how it is said, is the mark of a prophet. Firmness on everything, with harshness, is just pride.

On a Tuesday. Name the place this week where you are most tempted to bend: the conversation at work where the faith is mocked, the family gathering where a sin is celebrated. You need not make a speech, but you must not pretend. Settle with him in prayer now what you will not say, and what you will gently say if asked; he who held up John’s trembling faith will hold up yours.

verseByVerse.quote: What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is he of whom it is written, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet? The people regarded John as a prophet (21:26). Zechariah, Simeon and Anna spoke by the Spirit around his birth, but John was the first prophet to call the whole nation since the Old Testament closed, about four hundred years before.

Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. The great prophets spoke about a day they would not see. John is the only one who could point with his finger and say: that man there. He was himself the subject of prophecy (Malachi 3:1), the last of the line. Which is what makes his question from prison so moving: the one prophet who saw what he had prophesied was, near the end, no longer sure he had seen it.

Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. Malachi 3:1, combined with words from Exodus 23:20, and here the boldest claim in the chapter is hidden in a pronoun. In Malachi, God is speaking: I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. Jesus gives it as before your face, your way. The Father is now addressing the Son, and the way prepared for the arrival of God is the way prepared for Jesus. Nothing is argued; a pronoun is changed, and a sentence about God coming to his temple becomes a sentence about the man standing in front of them.

If Jesus is the LORD, is he the same person as the Father? No. In this very verse the Father speaks to the Son: I send my messenger before your face. There are two persons in the sentence, the one who sends and the one before whom the messenger goes. Yet the words of Malachi that belonged to the coming of God now belong to Jesus. That is the doctrine of the Trinity in seed form: one God, existing as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, distinct persons sharing one divine nature. Jesus is not a second god, nor merely the Father wearing a different mask. He is God the Son, come to his own temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Of all the great people of the old covenant, Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, none was greater than John, because of his place: he stood at the hinge of history and pointed directly to the Messiah. And Jesus says it on the day John sent to ask whether he was the one.

Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. This is not an insult to John, and not a claim that the least Christian is holier than John. It is a matter of where a man stands in the story. John died before the cross. Believers after the resurrection see it fulfilled, receive the Spirit poured out at Pentecost, and know the whole gospel; prophets and kings longed to see what they see (13:16–17; 1 Peter 1:10–12). The least believer knows what John did not, not because he is better but because he is later. John saw the dawn from a distance; the disciples live in the sunrise.

The kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. From the days of John until now is a short span, but the turning point of history. The Greek verb (biazetai) can mean either suffers violence or forcefully advances. On the first reading, which the ESV text follows, the kingdom has been attacked by violent men: John is in prison, Jesus will be killed, the disciples will be persecuted (10:16–25), and the verse is a lament. On the second (the ESV footnote), the kingdom has been forcefully advancing, and forceful people, tax collectors and sinners, are shouldering their way in. Luke has a similar saying: everyone forces his way into it (Luke 16:16).

Where Christians differ over the violence. Both readings are held by careful scholars, and neither can be settled from the grammar alone. This commentary’s view: the first fits best in Matthew’s context, between John’s imprisonment and the mounting opposition of chapters 11 and 12. Since John came, the kingdom has broken in with power, and it has met violent opposition. Both truths are taught in the Gospels, and the same period saw the kingdom advancing hardest and its herald in chains.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we must seize the kingdom by force; it is God’s gift to the poor in spirit (5:3). Nor does least in the kingdom mean that John is outside it. Like all the faithful of the old covenant, he will sit at the feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (8:11), saved by the same Lamb he announced.

But I feel very ordinary. How can I be greater than John? Because the measure is not you but what you have been shown. The most privileged man of the old order would have given everything for what an ordinary Christian takes for granted on a wet Tuesday: that it is finished, that the grave is open, that God is not angry with those who are in Christ. You may never preach to crowds or stand before kings. But you know the name of the Saviour, the meaning of his death and the fact of his resurrection, and the Spirit lives in you. That is not a compliment to your character. It is a measure of the gift.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 12 is a notoriously difficult saying; it may describe the kingdom’s forceful advance or the violent opposition to it.

verseByVerse.quote: For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. The whole Old Testament looked forward to the Messiah and his kingdom, and John was the last voice of that age of anticipation. Unusually, Jesus says that the Law prophesied too: in its sacrifices, priesthood, festivals and very demands, it pointed ahead to the One who would fulfil it (5:17).

And if you are willing to accept it. There is a condition in the sentence, and it attaches not to the fact but to the hearer’s willingness. Accepting John as the promised Elijah commits a person to something much larger. Elijah comes immediately before the day of the LORD; if the messenger has arrived, the one he announced is standing in front of you. To receive John is to receive Jesus; to reject one is to reject both.

He is Elijah who is to come. Malachi 4:5–6, the last words of the Old Testament in our order, promised that God would send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD. Many Jews expected Elijah himself to return, since he had not died (2 Kings 2:11). Jesus says John fulfilled the promise. John came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), dressed like him (3:4; 2 Kings 1:8), preached repentance as he did, and confronted a wicked king and his wife, as Elijah did Ahab and Jezebel.

But John denied being Elijah. In John’s Gospel he answers the priests: I am not (John 1:21). Popular expectation held that the historical Elijah would physically come back, and John’s answer to that was correct. What Jesus affirms is what the angel had said: he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Not the person, but the office.

What it does not mean. It is not reincarnation: John was a new person, born to Zechariah and Elizabeth, who fulfilled Elijah’s prophetic role. Nor do we wait for another Elijah before Christ returns (17:10–13).

How do I read the Old Testament as pointing to Christ without forcing it? Follow the lines the New Testament draws. Start with what a passage meant to its first readers, then ask how it fits the whole story that ends in Christ: a promise he keeps (Genesis 3:15), a pattern he fills (the Passover lamb, the priest, the king), a need he meets (the law’s demand that no one could keep), or a longing he answers (the psalmist’s cry). Jesus said all the Scriptures speak of him (Luke 24:27), but that does not mean every detail is a hidden code. Not every tent peg is the cross. Read whole passages, let the apostles guide you, and Christ will come into view naturally.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah the prophet
in the spirit and power of Elijah

verseByVerse.quote: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has ears to hear, let him hear. A phrase Jesus uses after important or puzzling teaching (13:9, 43). Everybody in the crowd had ears. The point is that hearing in the sense that matters is not automatic, which is what he thanks the Father for at the end of this chapter: these things are hidden from the wise and revealed to infants. The call to hear and the teaching that hearing is given stand ten verses apart in the same speech.

The ear that was opened. Only one man ever heard God perfectly. Isaiah’s Servant says, the Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward. I gave my back to those who strike (Isaiah 50:5–6). Jesus heard his Father all the way to the cross, and when he calls a generation to listen, it is the Son whose own listening became our salvation.

But to what shall I compare this generation? This generation means the people of Jesus’ time, especially those who rejected both John and Jesus. In Matthew it is often a dark phrase: an evil and adulterous generation (12:39, 45; 16:4; 23:36).

It is like children sitting in the marketplaces. The marketplace (agora) was the town square, where children played while adults did their business. The two great public events in a village were weddings and funerals, pipes and dancing at the one, hired mourners wailing at the other, and children imitated both.

Does this generation include me? Jesus meant first the people who saw and heard him and rejected him. But the phrase describes a kind of heart as well as a period of time, and every generation has it: people who have heard God’s message and keep finding reasons not to respond. You are not part of this generation in Jesus’ sense if you have come to him in repentance and faith. But the warning is for everyone who still has ears and is still deciding what to do with what they have heard.

On a Tuesday. Before you next hear a sermon or read the Bible, pray a one-line prayer: Lord, give me ears to hear. Then, afterwards, ask one question: what did God say, and what will I do? The Lord who opens the ear also gives the strength to do what it hears.

verseByVerse.quote: "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn." For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, "He has a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We played the flute for you, and you did not dance. Children played at weddings, with pipes and dancing. One group strikes up the wedding tune, and nobody dances.

We sang a dirge, and you did not mourn. So they switch to funerals, and nobody mourns. The complaint is not that the game was played badly. It is that no game was acceptable.

The symmetry. The dirge that got no mourning corresponds to John, all fasting and warning. The pipe that got no dancing corresponds to Jesus, at the tables of sinners. Two men, opposite in every visible respect, and one generation with an answer ready for each. It is not preferring one; it is refusing both, and the refusals contradict each other.

The Bridegroom and the man of sorrows. Both songs are found in Jesus himself. He is the Bridegroom, whose presence makes fasting impossible (9:15), who turned water into wine at a wedding. And he is the man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3), who would weep over a city that would not come. To refuse the pipe and the dirge is finally to refuse him whole, his feast and his cross. This generation would not dance at his wedding, and in the end it gave him a funeral instead.

For John came neither eating nor drinking. John lived an austere life: fasting, eating locusts and wild honey, drinking no wine (3:4; Luke 1:15). His message was the funeral song: mourn for your sins, for the axe is at the root.

And they say, He has a demon. His strictness was dismissed as possession, the same accusation they made against Jesus (9:34; 12:24). It is the standard explanation for a man whose authority is undeniable and whose message is unacceptable: something is at work in him, so it must not be God. Such verdicts are easiest to reach from a distance.

How do I tell a fair criticism of a preacher from this kind of excuse? Fair criticism asks whether what was said is true to Scripture, and it is willing to be answered. The excuse in these verses changes its complaint whenever the messenger changes, and is never satisfied. Ask yourself honestly: if this preacher did exactly what I say I want, would I then obey what he says from the Bible? If you would not, the problem is not the preacher. Christians may and should test teaching (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). But testing is aimed at the message, and it ends in obedience when the message proves true.
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, "Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man came eating and drinking. Jesus’ ministry was the wedding song: joy, feasting, the bridegroom present (9:15), at Levi’s table, with Pharisees and with crowds on a hillside (9:10).

Look at him, a glutton and a drunkard. The insult echoes a legal formula. Parents of a son who will not be governed are to bring him to the elders and say that he is stubborn and rebellious, a glutton and a drunkard; and the men of the city are to stone him (Deuteronomy 21:20–21). So the crowd is laying against Jesus the formal charge for a son who has broken with his father’s authority, a charge carrying death. Said of the one man who always did what pleased his Father, it is more terrible than they understood, and it ended, in a sense, as the law said: outside the city, condemned.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners! Meant with contempt, and gloriously true (9:10–13). Intended as evidence for the prosecution, it is the best short description of him anyone produced during his lifetime, and his enemies produced it. And the charge says more about the accusers. Men who thought they had no need of a physician (9:12) could only resent a grace spent on people worse than themselves. That is the danger for the religious heart in every age: to be less troubled that sinners are lost than that they are welcomed.

Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. Wisdom here is God’s wisdom, at work in both John and Jesus. Justified is a courtroom word: vindicated. The generation’s verdict will itself be overturned, not by argument but by results: changed lives, and the works of the Christ (v. 2, the same word, deeds). Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). Some manuscripts read by her children, as in Luke 7:35; nothing turns on it.

A comfort for the misunderstood. The vindication of wisdom is usually not an explanation but a harvest, arriving later. If you have obeyed God and been misread for it, you are standing where Jesus stood. Let the fruit speak, and let God choose the day.

Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. Jesus has defended John; now he turns to judge. The mighty works (dynameis) were meant to lead to repentance, and had not. The towns that saw the most fall under the sharpest condemnation: to see the greatest miracles in history and stay unchanged is not neutrality.

Did Jesus drink wine? Yes. He came eating and drinking, and the charge of drunkenness was slander. Scripture condemns drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), not the cup itself, and calls wine a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15). Christians are free to drink in moderation, and free not to, and the strong should take care not to wound a weaker brother’s conscience or tempt someone who struggles with alcohol (Romans 14:21). Anyone for whom drink has become a master should abstain completely; freedom in Christ is never freedom to be enslaved again.

What does it mean for me that Jesus is the friend of sinners? First, it means he is your friend, if you have come to him: not a reluctant master who tolerates you, but one who chose to eat with people like you. Second, it shapes how you treat those outside the church. Jesus went to their tables, listened to them and welcomed them, without approving their sin and without hiding his call to repent. That means real friendships with unbelieving neighbours and colleagues, meals and time, not only invitations to events. You will be misunderstood for it, as he was. Keep your own life clean while you keep your door open.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you. Woe is a cry of grief and warning, the opposite of blessed (5:3–12). Jesus does not pronounce it as a man glad to be proved right, but as one who will weep over Jerusalem (23:37).

Chorazin and Bethsaida. Chorazin lay two or three miles north of Capernaum, in the hills. The Gospels record no miracle there, yet Jesus says many were done, which shows how little of his work is recorded (John 21:25). Bethsaida was a fishing village on the northern shore, the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44), where he healed a blind man (Mark 8:22–26).

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon. Wealthy Gentile ports north of Galilee, condemned by the prophets for their pride (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28). The comparison would have shocked: the pagan cities will fare better on judgment day than the privileged Jewish towns.

They would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Sackcloth was rough goat’s hair, worn in mourning, and ashes were sprinkled on the head or sat in (Jonah 3:5–8; Daniel 9:3). Pagan Nineveh did it at one sermon from a reluctant prophet. The Jewish towns that saw the Son of God did not.

Crumbs in the region of Tyre. A few chapters later Jesus walks into that very district, and a Canaanite woman cries, have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David (15:21–22). She asks only for the crumbs, and Jesus says, O woman, great is your faith (15:28). The towns that had the whole table refused it; a pagan mother from the coast of Tyre took a crumb and was filled. The Lord who denounces privileged unbelief goes looking for faith where no one expected it.

But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. Greater light means greater accountability. The miracles of Jesus were not entertainment but the final call to repentance.

A question about knowledge. Jesus does not say that Tyre and Sidon might have repented, but that they would have. God knows not only what happens but what would have happened in other circumstances. Some theologians, following the Jesuit Luis de Molina, use this knowledge to explain election: God chooses those he foresees would believe in the circumstances he places them in. The Reformed tradition affirms that God knows all possibilities, but holds that his own free and eternal purpose, not his foreknowledge of what people would do, is the basis of election (Ephesians 1:4–5).

Then why did God not send the miracles to Tyre? Thoughtful readers stop dead here. If he knew they would have turned, why were the works done in towns that would not? Be honest about what we are not told. Scripture nowhere explains why the light falls where it falls. It says that God determines the times and places in which people live (Acts 17:26), and it draws a line we are not invited to cross: the secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children (Deuteronomy 29:29). When Paul reached this wall he did not climb it; he asked instead who we are to answer back to God (Romans 9:20). And look where Jesus aims the sentence. He is not lecturing on the distribution of grace across the nations. He is indicting two towns that saw everything and did nothing. The comparison measures their guilt, not Tyre’s. So the verse is a mirror, not a riddle. The question it presses is not why others were given less light, but what you have done with the light you were given, and the man asking the first question is very often avoiding the second.

Will some people be punished more than others in hell? Yes. Jesus says it will be more bearable for some than for others on the day of judgment (see also Luke 12:47–48). Hell is real, conscious and eternal, and no one there is innocent; but God is perfectly just, and the judgment of each person is measured by what they did with what they knew. The sobering application is not for the pagan who never heard but for the person who has heard the most. Every sermon, every Bible on the shelf, every praying parent adds to the light, and therefore to the accountability, of someone who will not come.

What about people who have never heard of Jesus? They will be judged for their sins against the light they had, in creation and conscience, not for rejecting a gospel they never heard (Romans 1:20; 2:12–16), and no one is saved by that light, which is why the church sends. (See Acts 3:23 for the fuller answer.)
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities. Sackcloth was coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, Capernaum. Jesus’ own town (4:13; 9:1), the base of his ministry, the city most saturated with his presence and his works: the centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, the paralysed man let down through the roof, Jairus’ daughter, and many more.

Will you be exalted to heaven? The words are a quotation, and the original is the most famous taunt in the Old Testament. Isaiah 14 addresses the king of Babylon, who said in his heart that he would ascend to heaven and set his throne above the stars of God, and was brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit (Isaiah 14:13–15). That is addressed to the proudest power on earth at the height of its arrogance. Jesus takes it and applies it to a fishing town on the north shore of a lake: perhaps a thousand or so people, a customs post, a synagogue and a beach. The disproportion is the point. Capernaum had no imperial ambitions. What it had was the Son of God living in it, and it received him as a local celebrity and went on with the fishing. And the sentence written for Babylon fits it exactly, because the pride that does not need God is the same in a palace and a fishing village.

He who descended. The taunt has a mirror image in the Gospel. The king of Babylon said, I will ascend, and was brought down. The Son of God came down to a fishing town, to the death of a criminal and a borrowed grave, and he who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens (Ephesians 4:9–10; Philippians 2:8–9). The town that would not bow to him was living next door to the one who would come back from death holding the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).

You will be brought down to Hades. Hades is the Greek name for the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol); here it means deep humiliation and judgment. Some manuscripts make the first line a statement rather than a question; the sense is the same. The ground gives a sober picture, though not a proof: all three towns are gone. Chorazin is a field of black basalt ruins, Capernaum an archaeological site, and the site of Bethsaida is still argued over. They simply declined and emptied, and the lake went on without them.

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Sodom, the Bible’s byword for judgement (Genesis 19), would have repented if it had seen what Capernaum saw, and the town that hosted the Son of God will be brought lower.

A guard for the tender conscience. This passage frightens the wrong people. It falls on towns that watched the works and were unmoved, not on the person who worries he has not responded well enough. That worry is itself a response; Chorazin was not troubled by anything. If you are troubled, go to Christ with it: it is a sign that he is still speaking to you.

I grew up in church and know it all. Am I Capernaum? Only if you have heard it all and never actually turned to Christ. Capernaum’s sin was not that it saw much but that it did not repent. Familiarity is the danger: the gospel can become so ordinary that it no longer surprises you, and what no longer surprises you no longer moves you. The way out is simple and humbling. Stop treating your knowledge as if it were faith. Come to Jesus today as a sinner who needs him, as if you were hearing for the first time, and ask him to make the old words new.
verseByVerse.note: Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus declared, "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time Jesus declared, I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth. Jesus responds to the unbelief of the cities by turning to his Father, and the prayer is thanksgiving. Rejection does not shake him; he rests in the Father’s plan. He calls God Father with the intimacy of the only Son, and Lord of heaven and earth: what he does, he has the right to do. These things are the truths of the kingdom: who Jesus is, and what his works mean.

From the wise and understanding. The pairing comes from a prophecy of judgement against the religious establishment: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden (Isaiah 29:14). Paul quotes it to explain why the cross looks foolish (1 Corinthians 1:19). Jesus is reaching for the text in which God confounds the professionally religious, and applying it to the men who have just said John had a demon and he was a drunkard: wise in their own eyes. God hides the truth from the proud, in judgment on their pride.

And revealed them to little children. Nēpioi means infants, entirely dependent, with no accomplishments and no capacity to acquire any: the disciples, fishermen, tax collectors and sinners. The contrast is not between the educated and the simple but between people who can do something and people who can do nothing at all. Revelation is God’s gift: no one can work it out for himself (16:17).

Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. The word (eudokia) is the Father’s sovereign good pleasure (Ephesians 1:5, 9). Jesus does not lament the hiding or apologise for it. He thanks the Father for it and rejoices in it (Luke 10:21). That is the harder half, and it should not be softened. There is a mercy in it too, since a kingdom reached by cleverness would be closed to almost everybody. But the passage does not offer that as an excuse. It offers thanks.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that education or intelligence are bad. The man praying this knew the Scriptures better than anyone alive, and he chose Paul, one of the most trained scholars of his generation (Acts 22:3). What is condemned is self-sufficiency, including the form peculiar to the well-taught: having enough answers not to need anything. God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6).

Where Christians differ over God’s choice. Arminian Christians hold that God reveals the truth to those he foresees will be humble and believe, so that the little children are those who humble themselves and respond, and God reveals himself in answer to their openness. Reformed theology holds that God’s revealing is his sovereign, gracious choice, which creates the humility and faith (v. 27; Ephesians 1:4–5; 2:8). Both sides want to honour God’s fairness and his grace, and many earnest believers hold the first view. This commentary’s view: God’s revealing is according to his good pleasure (v. 26), not caused by anything in us. The openness is itself God’s gift. That is why it is grace, and why there is no room for boasting. Yet Jesus sets this beside two other truths: the cities that did not repent are guilty, and the invitation that follows is to everyone who labours. God’s choosing never cancels human responsibility, and it never closes the door on anyone who comes.

Is it unfair of God to hide the truth from some? No. Those from whom it is hidden are not eager seekers turned away at the door. They are proud people who have already rejected the light they had, and God gives them over to what they chose (Romans 1:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:10–11). No one is owed revelation. That anyone sees is pure mercy. And no one who wants Christ is ever refused him; the wanting itself is the sign that the Father is revealing him.

How do I know whether I am one of the little children? Not by finding something impressive in yourself, but by the opposite. Do you know you cannot save yourself? Do you look to Christ and find him beautiful, and want him? Do the Scriptures speak to you, however imperfectly you understand them? Those are the marks of a heart to which the Father has revealed the Son. You did not produce them; they were given. And if you are unsure, do what the next verse says: come to him. No one who comes is turned away (John 6:37).

On a Tuesday. If you understand the gospel, it is because God revealed it to you, not because you were cleverer than your neighbour. Thank him for it today, and come to his word this week as a child and not as a critic: obey what you understand before you argue about what you do not.

parallels.desc: God chose what is foolish in the world

verseByVerse.quote: All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things have been handed over to me by my Father. All authority, all knowledge, all revelation. Before the resurrection Jesus already claims what he will declare after it (28:18). Handed over is the language of passing on an inheritance: the Father has entrusted everything to the Son.

And no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son. That the Son knows the Father with the same completeness as the Father knows him, and that no one else does, places him on the far side of the line between creatures and God, because a creature does not comprehend his Maker. This is a claim to equality with God, as a son shares his father’s nature.

The thunderbolt. This verse has been nicknamed the Johannine thunderbolt: a sentence that reads exactly like the Gospel of John, dropped into Matthew (compare John 1:18; 10:15; 14:6–9), and again in Luke (Luke 10:22). That tells against the long-made argument that the high view of Christ is a late development found only in John. Because Matthew and Luke share the saying, many scholars think it belongs to one of the earliest layers of the tradition.

And anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Chooses (boulētai) means wills. Knowledge of God comes only through Christ, as he chooses to reveal it. And this last clause turns the whole thing outward: the wall around the knowledge of God is sheer, but here is a door in it, and the Son holds it open.

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden. Then one of the most abrupt turns in the Gospel. The sentence before is the language of a locked door: no one knows the Father, the knowledge is given at the Son’s discretion. And the very next word is: come. No preparation, no conditions, no narrowing. An invitation from someone with lesser credentials would not be worth accepting, and credentials without an invitation would leave everyone outside. The one who holds the only key opens the door himself and asks people in.

Who are the weary? Labour means to toil to the point of exhaustion. Heavy laden means carrying a heavy load, like a pack animal. Especially they are those burdened by the religious leaders’ demands: the scribes and Pharisees tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders (23:4). They are also everyone weary of sin and guilt, of trying to earn God’s favour, of anxiety and grief and the troubles of life: moral failure, religious performance, all of it. All are invited. All.

And I will give you rest. Not more rules, but rest. The word (anapausis) means refreshment, ceasing from labour. Jesus offers what only God can give, rest for the soul (Exodus 33:14), and he gives it himself: I will give.

Does it not sound proud to say that only the Son can reveal the Father? From anyone else it would. If a teacher claimed to know God better than everyone else, we would rightly distrust him. But Jesus is not claiming to have climbed higher than the rest of us by effort or insight. He is claiming to be the Son, who has always known the Father (John 1:18), telling us what only the Son could tell. If that is true, saying so is not arrogance but honesty, and the humblest thing we can do is listen. And see what he does with his unique knowledge. He does not use it to keep people out. In the very next breath he invites all who are weary.

What does coming to Jesus actually look like? It is not a physical journey or a special ceremony. To come to him is to trust him: to stop relying on your own efforts to put yourself right with God, and to rely on him instead, on his death for sinners and his risen life. In practice it begins with prayer, in your own words: telling him that you are weary and guilty, that you believe he can give you rest, and that you give yourself to him. It continues every day, because Christians keep coming. Every time you are burdened, the invitation is still open.

I have come to Jesus, and I am still tired. What is wrong? Perhaps nothing. The rest he promises is first rest of soul: peace with God, freedom from condemnation, the end of trying to earn his love. It does not remove every burden of life at once, and it does not cure physical exhaustion; for that he also gave sleep and sabbath and the care of others. But ask honestly whether you have picked up again a yoke he lifted off: trying to prove yourself, carrying guilt he has forgiven, worrying over what you have handed to him. Bring that to him specifically. And if the tiredness is the heaviness of grief or depression, that is not a failure of faith; it is a burden he carries with you, and seeking medical help is part of caring for the body he made. Coming is not once for all; it is the daily habit of laying things down.

parallels.desc: the Father has given all things into his hand
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.quote: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take my yoke upon you. A yoke was a wooden frame over the necks of two oxen so that they could pull together. Rabbis spoke of the yoke of the law and the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, meaning the acceptance of God’s commandments as interpreted by the teacher. The Pharisees’ yoke was heavy (23:4). Jesus invites people to take his instead: not the abolition of demand, but a different kind of demand, borne with him. Rest does not come by throwing off every yoke, but by taking the right one.

And learn from me. Learn his teaching, and learn him (Ephesians 4:20), the way an apprentice learns a master by working beside him every day. The yoke is the classroom, and the teacher is pulling alongside.

For I am gentle and lowly in heart. In all four Gospels this is the only place where Jesus tells us what his own heart is like. He says many things about himself, the door, the vine, the bread, but only here does he open the very centre of his being: not harsh and exacting, but gentle and lowly. Gentle (praus) is the same word as meek in the beatitude (5:5). Lowly (tapeinos) means humble, unassuming, the very opposite of the proud religion that had been crushing these people. He does not break a bruised reed (12:20), and this is the settled disposition of his heart, not a mood he is in on his better days. When you come to him weary, ashamed, having failed again, you are not coming to a reluctant judge who tolerates you. You are coming to a heart more ready to receive you than you are to come.

And you will find rest for your souls. From Jeremiah 6:16, where God tells Israel to ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and find rest for their souls. But they refused. Jesus offers the same rest, and he is himself the ancient path that Jeremiah’s generation would not take.

For my yoke is easy. Easy (chrēstos) means kind, well-fitting. As a carpenter (Mark 6:3), Jesus would have known how a yoke was shaped so that it did not chafe. It is easy not because it asks little but because he bears it with us, and because it is the yoke of love, not of law-keeping to earn acceptance.

And my burden is light. Not that following Jesus involves no demands (16:24), but that his commands are not burdensome (1 John 5:3): he carries the weight with us, and by his Spirit in us he gives the strength to keep them (Philippians 2:13). We still keep them imperfectly, but the burden of earning salvation he carried himself, obeying perfectly in our place (Romans 5:19), and what is left is the light burden of serving a gracious Master who has already saved us. An old saying, often credited to Augustine, compares the burden of Christ to wings on a bird: they seem to add weight, but they lift it up.

In the flow. Matthew sets the very next scene on a Sabbath (12:1), where the Pharisees accuse his disciples of breaking the law by plucking grain. The contrast is deliberate: the men with the heavy yoke argue about rest, while the Lord of the Sabbath (12:8) stands among them giving it.

What is Christ’s yoke, concretely? It is his rule over your life, received as his disciple: his teaching to believe and his commands to obey, learned in his company. Concretely that means listening to his word, praying, belonging to his church, being baptised as he commanded, forgiving as you have been forgiven, and loving God and neighbour. It is not a new list of rules to earn his favour. It is the shape of life lived next to him, by people he has already accepted. The difference is not in how many commands there are but in who you are pulling with, and why.

If his burden is light, why does the Christian life feel so hard? Because it is hard, and Jesus never said otherwise: there is a cross in it, and a fight with sin, and suffering. But the hardness is the strain of growth and battle, not the crushing weight of having to save yourself. Often the heaviness we feel is not his yoke at all, but a yoke we made: perfectionism, people-pleasing, the need to be admired, worry about what we cannot control. Those chafe because they were never made for us. His yoke rubs only where our pride resists it, and the closer we walk with him, the lighter it becomes.

For worship. Blessed be the Lord who told us what his heart is like. He might have said that he is holy, mighty and just, and he is. But when he opened his heart to the weary, he said that it was gentle and lowly. The Lord of heaven and earth puts his neck into the yoke beside ours and takes the weight. There is rest for our souls, because there is such a heart in him.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals to pull together; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

parallels.desc: you will find rest for your souls
a yoke our fathers could not bear

11.theology: The gentleness of Christ. “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (v. 29) is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes his own heart. The word for gentle (praus) is the word used of Moses in Numbers 12:3. His gentleness is not weakness but strength held in restraint: the one to whom all things have been handed over bends down to receive the weary. Thomas Goodwin wrote that Christ’s heart is more moved by our miseries than by all his own glory. The invitation is to come as we are, not worthy first.
11.examples:
Then: John in prison stands for every believer whose faith has been tested by circumstances that did not match what he expected. Jesus points him to what the Scriptures said the Christ would do: faith is anchored in the word.

Now: The invitation of 11:28–30 still addresses every tired, guilt-laden, performance-exhausted person. The yoke of Christ is easy not because it makes no demands but because the one who makes them has already borne their weight, and bears it with us.

12.title: Lord of the Sabbath
12.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. <sup>2</sup>But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” <sup>3</sup>He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup>how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? <sup>5</sup>Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? <sup>6</sup>I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. <sup>7</sup>And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. <sup>8</sup>For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>9</sup>He went on from there and entered their synagogue. <sup>10</sup>And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”— so that they might accuse him. <sup>11</sup>He said to them, “Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? <sup>12</sup>Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” <sup>13</sup>Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. <sup>14</sup>But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. <sup>15</sup>Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all <sup>16</sup>and ordered them not to make him known. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: <sup>18</sup>“Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; <sup>20</sup>a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory; <sup>21</sup>and in his name the Gentiles will hope.” <sup>22</sup>Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. <sup>23</sup>And all the people were amazed, and said, “Can this be the Son of David?” <sup>24</sup>But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons.” <sup>25</sup>Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? <sup>27</sup>And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>28</sup>But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>29</sup>Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>30</sup>Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>31</sup>Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>32</sup>And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. <sup>33</sup>“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit. <sup>34</sup>You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. <sup>35</sup>The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. <sup>36</sup>I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, <sup>37</sup>for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” <sup>38</sup>Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” <sup>39</sup>But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. <sup>40</sup>For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. <sup>41</sup>The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>42</sup>The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>43</sup>“When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none. <sup>44</sup>Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. <sup>45</sup>Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.” <sup>46</sup>While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. <sup>48</sup>But he replied to the man who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” <sup>49</sup>And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>50</sup>For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”
12.overview:
In chapter 12 opposition to Jesus hardens into a plot to destroy him (v. 14). He makes two great claims: “something greater than the temple is here” (v. 6) and “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (v. 8). To claim authority over the place where God dwelt and the sign of the covenant is to claim to be God.

The chapter also names the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The Pharisees have watched the blind see, the mute speak and the possessed set free, and they call it the work of Satan. That settled, informed, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s plain work is the sin that will not be forgiven: not because the blood of Christ is insufficient, but because the one who commits it refuses the only Spirit who brings sinners to repentance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Lord of the Sabbath and Servant of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two Sabbath disputes open the chapter: the disciples plucking grain, and the healing of a man with a withered hand. Following straight on from the offer of rest (11:28), Jesus answers from Scripture (David, the priests, Hosea) and declares himself greater than the temple and lord of the Sabbath. The Pharisees then plot his death, and Matthew explains Jesus’ quiet withdrawal with his longest Old Testament quotation, Isaiah’s first Servant Song: the gentle Servant who will not break a bruised reed.
verseByVerse.theology: The Pharisees had turned the Sabbath into a burden and a means of judging others; Jesus is the one in whom the rest it pointed to is found (11:28–29). The Servant Song (Isaiah 42:1–4) shows that his withdrawal from conflict is not weakness but the Servant’s way: he does not quarrel or cry aloud, yet he will bring justice to victory.
verseByVerse.examples: The healing of the withered hand turns on the question whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath. If you would lift a sheep out of a pit on the Sabbath, how much more a man, made in God’s image? The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27), and doing good is fitting on the day of rest.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, "Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 12 is the chapter in which opposition to Jesus hardens into a plot to kill him. Two Sabbath disputes end with Jesus claiming to be greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath. As the Pharisees plan his death, Matthew quotes Isaiah’s portrait of the gentle Servant. Then the Pharisees say Jesus casts out demons by Satan; he answers, warns of the blasphemy against the Spirit, refuses any sign but Jonah’s, and points to his disciples: here is my family. Through it all one claim rises: something greater than the temple, than Jonah, than Solomon is here.

At that time. The phrase links back across the chapter break. Jesus has just offered rest to all who labour (11:28), and the very next thing is a fight about the day of rest, with men who had made it into work.

The Sabbath. The seventh day, from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday, kept in memory of God’s rest after creation (Exodus 20:8–11) and of the rescue from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:12–15): a weekly gift of freedom for people who had once been slaves without a day off. By Jesus’ time teachers had built a detailed system of rules; the Mishnah, a later collection of rabbinic teaching, lists thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, among them reaping, threshing and winnowing.

His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. Only Matthew adds that they were hungry, because the argument turns on it: David was hungry too. The law allowed travellers to pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25). The issue was the day.

Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath. The charge is precise. A man pulling heads of grain, rubbing them between his palms to loosen the husk (Luke 6:1), and blowing the chaff away has, on a sufficiently determined reading, performed three of the thirty-nine forbidden works before breakfast: reaping, threshing and winnowing. Not greed, not trespass. Harvesting, on a technicality, in a quantity that would fit in two hands. And they hold Jesus responsible, as a teacher was for his students. They are not concerned with the disciples’ hunger, only with the breach of their interpretation. And there is a reason rules like these feel safe. A rule you can measure lets you know you are doing well before God and better than your neighbour; mercy cannot be measured, so it gives the rule-keeper nothing to stand on.

Is it wrong for my family to have its own rules for Sunday? No. A family may wisely decide how it will keep the Lord’s Day: no homework, no shopping, a shared meal, a walk, time with church friends. Such arrangements can be a great blessing. The Pharisees’ fault was not having practices but treating their own additions as God’s law and condemning others by them. So keep your household customs, and explain them to your children as gifts, not as the measure of holiness. And never judge another Christian family because they draw the lines in a different place.
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you not read. Jesus says it six times in Matthew, always to the professionally religious (here; 12:5; 19:4; 21:16; 21:42; 22:31). Of course they had read it; they had not understood it. It is a withering thing to say to a scholar, and it is his standard opening.

What David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him. 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David, fleeing from Saul, came to the tabernacle at Nob and asked the priest Ahimelech for food, and there was none except the holy bread. He lied that he was on the king’s business, and the day ended in atrocity: Saul had eighty-five priests of Nob put to the sword (1 Samuel 22:18–19). Jesus reaches not for a tidy precedent but for a desperate, compromised day in the life of the anointed king who had not yet come into his kingdom.

How he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves were set before the LORD each Sabbath, and when replaced were eaten by the priests only (Leviticus 24:5–9). Yet the priest gave them to David, and Scripture does not criticise it.

The argument. Two points. Human need can take priority over ceremonial rules. And David was God’s anointed king. Here is the anointed King who has not yet come into his kingdom, hungry, with his men, pursued by the authorities. If the son of Jesse could eat the holy bread, the Son of David and his men may take a handful of grain.

A note for a reader with a harmony. Mark names Abiathar as high priest (Mark 2:26), while 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech, his father. It is a genuine difficulty with several proposed answers, including that Mark’s phrase means in the passage about Abiathar. Matthew names nobody, so nothing here turns on it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God’s laws can be ignored whenever convenient. Jesus is showing that the ceremonial laws were meant to serve people, not to harm them. Nor does the end justify any means: David’s lie is not approved; the bread is.

How do I tell God’s moral law from the ceremonial law? The ceremonial law covered the sacrifices, priesthood, festivals, food laws and rules of ritual purity. It was given to Israel as a picture of Christ and his cleansing, and it is fulfilled in him, so Christians no longer keep it (Hebrews 9–10; Mark 7:19; Colossians 2:16–17). The moral law expresses God’s unchanging character. It is summed up in the Ten Commandments and in loving God and neighbour, and the New Testament repeats it: do not murder, steal, lie or commit adultery, honour your parents, worship God alone. A useful test is whether the New Testament renews a command or says it is fulfilled. The one commandment Christians debate is the fourth; this commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is a glad gift rather than a law of rules. The reason is that Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow whose substance is Christ (Colossians 2:16–17); many godly Christians, following the Westminster and 1689 London Baptist Confessions, hold instead that it continues as the Christian Sabbath on Sunday, and they deserve respect.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? The priestly argument is stronger than it looks. The Sabbath did not reduce the temple’s workload; it doubled it. The daily offering was one lamb morning and evening, and on the Sabbath two more lambs were added (Numbers 28:9–10). The bread of the Presence was changed on the Sabbath (Leviticus 24:8). And a boy born on a Sabbath was circumcised on the following Sabbath, because the eighth day is the eighth day (John 7:22–23). So on the one day in seven when all Israel rested, the priests worked harder than usual, inside the sanctuary, by God’s command, and no one had ever suggested they were sinning. That establishes the principle Jesus needs: the Sabbath yields to something, and it always has. The question was never whether there are higher obligations, but what they are. Temple service took priority over Sabbath rest.

I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. An astonishing claim. The temple was where God dwelt among his people, behind a curtain only the high priest passed, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16:2, 34). Now the holy presence hidden there is standing in the open, in a field. If temple service could override the Sabbath, how much more the service of the one greater than the temple: God present among his people (1:23; John 2:19–21).

Three times greater. The Greek is neuter: not someone greater, but something. Jesus does it twice more in this chapter: greater than Jonah (v. 41), greater than Solomon (v. 42). The three are the pillars of Israel’s life: the temple, the prophet and the king. All three were God’s arrangements, and they are being quietly fulfilled in the One they were arranged for, standing in a cornfield in the middle of an argument about breakfast.

What does this mean for where I worship? It means no building is a temple now. A church building is a useful room, not a holy house where God lives more than elsewhere. The temple of God today is Christ himself, and in him his people: you, together, are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit dwells in you (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22). So you meet God not by going to a sacred place but by coming to Christ, wherever you are. And you are part of a holy temple whenever the church gathers, which is a reason to gather gladly and not to treat it as optional.
verseByVerse.note: The priests worked hardest on the Sabbath, offering extra sacrifices.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice," you would not have condemned the guiltless. For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. Hosea 6:6, quoted only by Matthew, and twice: at Levi’s table (9:13), and here, both times about food and Pharisees. The disciples had broken the Pharisees’ traditions, not God’s law. Hosea wrote to a nation whose religious machinery was in excellent order and whose life was rotten: the worship had become a substitute for what it was meant to produce. And these men were not lax. They were the most rigorous, scripturally literate people in the land, and their failure came at the point of their strength.

For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. The climax. The Sabbath was the Sabbath to the LORD your God (Exodus 20:10), and Jesus claims authority over it, as only God could. The Pharisees thought they were correcting a careless rabbi; they were lecturing the Lord of the day itself. Mark adds that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

The Sabbath and Christ. There is more in the title than authority. Matthew has set side by side the invitation, I will give you rest (11:28), and this claim: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. The Sabbath was never merely a day off; from the beginning it was a signpost. God rested on the seventh day of creation, and Israel kept the day as a weekly rehearsal of a rest still ahead, a rest Joshua did not finally give them (Hebrews 4:8–9). Hebrews says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, entered by faith in Christ (Hebrews 4:1–11). So when Jesus calls himself lord of the Sabbath, he is claiming to be what the day was about. The rest the seventh day promised is finally not a date on the calendar but a Person, and he is standing in a cornfield being told off for letting hungry men eat. The Pharisees were guarding the signpost so fiercely that they could not see they were arguing with the destination. After his resurrection on the first day of the week, Christians gathered on that day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10).

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Some (Seventh-day Adventists, Seventh Day Baptists) hold that Christians must keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Many Reformed, Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist Christians, godly brothers following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy with rest from ordinary work and devotion to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day is binding as the Sabbath (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5), while Sunday is the Lord’s Day for the church’s gathering. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is his gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). The Westminster and 1689 view, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment, is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

Is it wrong to work on a Sunday? Some work must be done on any day: nurses, doctors, police, carers, farmers with animals. Jesus defended works of necessity and mercy, and no Christian in such a job should feel second-class. But where you have a choice, guard the gathering of the church; it is commanded whatever view of the day you hold (Hebrews 10:25). Do not let Sunday become simply another day for catching up on work or shopping by default. And if your employer requires Sunday work regularly, look for ways still to worship with God’s people, perhaps at another service, and keep some real rest elsewhere in your week.

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: He went on from there and entered their synagogue. And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" — so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went on from there and entered their synagogue. Their synagogue: Matthew uses the possessive repeatedly (4:23; 9:35; 10:17; 13:54), the language of an institution that has begun to close against Jesus.

And a man was there with a withered hand. Shrunken or paralysed. Luke says it was his right hand (Luke 6:6), so he probably could not do much of his work. But his condition was not life-threatening.

Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? The trap is more precisely made than it appears, because the rabbinic position on this exact question was settled and everybody in the synagogue knew it. The rule was that danger to life overrides the Sabbath. If a man’s life is at risk, you act: you dig him out of rubble, you treat the wound, and the Sabbath waits. That principle is generous and right. But the corollary was equally firm: where there is no danger to life, it waits. The rule is written down in the Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, but the Gospels show the same thinking in Jesus’ day: a synagogue ruler once told a crowd to come and be healed on the six working days, not on the Sabbath (Luke 13:14). A chronic condition had been there for years and would still be there tomorrow. Now look at the man. A withered hand: useless, the ruin of his living, but not dangerous. So by the standard of the day the answer was obvious. Wait until sundown, heal him then, and nobody objects. That is exactly what makes it a trap. They are not asking whether healing is good. They are asking whether it is urgent, and the honest answer, on their terms, is no.

So that they might accuse him. They used a suffering man as bait. When a suffering human being becomes a means to score points, something has gone deeply wrong with the religion.

Why did Jesus not simply wait until the evening? Because the man’s hand was not the only thing being decided. Jesus heals him anyway, in the synagogue, in front of them, on that day, when a delay of a few hours would have cost nothing and avoided everything. What was on trial was whether the day God gave for rest and restoration could be used to restore somebody, and answering that on Monday would have answered nothing. Jesus was not being provocative for its own sake. He was refusing to let a man’s suffering be postponed to keep a man-made rule intact.

The healing that cost him. Jesus knew what the question was for, and he healed anyway. This hand would cost him his life: as soon as the Pharisees left the synagogue, the plot to destroy him began (v. 14). Every healing in Matthew moves him a step nearer the place where, as Isaiah said, he took our illnesses and bore our diseases (8:17). The man in the synagogue went home with two good hands; the one who restored him walked out with a price on his head. That is the shape of all his mercy. He does not heal from a safe distance. He walks into the trap set for him, takes on himself the hostility that our healing provokes, and carries it to the cross.
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. In the rabbis’ rulings, healing a condition that was not life-threatening had to wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Jewish teachers debated what could be done for an animal in a pit on the Sabbath: later rabbinic sources allow feeding it or helping it out, while the community of the Dead Sea Scrolls forbade lifting it out at all. Jesus appeals to what his hearers would actually do. The precedent they already accept commits them to the conclusion they want to deny.
