Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! An argument from lesser to greater. Every human being, however damaged, is made in God’s image, made to know God and reflect his character, which is why to harm a person is to wrong God himself (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9). Healing a person on the Sabbath honours its purpose far better than leaving him to suffer.

So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. Mark adds Jesus’ question: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? (Mark 3:4). The irony is plain: Jesus was doing good on the Sabbath, while the Pharisees were about to plot his death (v. 14).

Lifted out of the pit. The sheep in the pit is a picture Jesus would fill with his own body. Psalm 40, which Hebrews puts in the mouth of Christ (Hebrews 10:5–7), says: he drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock (Psalm 40:2). The Shepherd went down into the grave on the eve of a Sabbath and lay there through it, and on the first day of the week the Father lifted him out. The one who would not leave a sheep in a hole was not left in his, and because he was lifted out, every one of his sheep will be.

Does this mean animals do not matter? No. A righteous man cares for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10), and the Father feeds the birds and notices every sparrow (6:26; 10:29). Jesus assumes that rescuing the sheep is right. His point is not that animals are worthless but that people are worth far more, because they alone bear God’s image. A culture that will spend lavishly on pets and little on the poor, or that protects animals while despising unborn or disabled human beings, has reversed the order Jesus taught.

Does any of this bind me? Two Sabbath controversies in fourteen verses leave a reader with an obvious and practical question. Should Christians keep a Sabbath, and is Sunday it? Believers who love the Scriptures land in two places here. Some hold that the fourth commandment stands with the other nine as part of the moral law, and that the day has moved to the first of the week in honour of the resurrection, so the Lord’s Day is to be set apart from ordinary work for worship and rest. That is the historic Reformed and Puritan position, and it has produced some of the most joyful, well-ordered lives the church has seen. Others hold that the Sabbath belonged to the shadows that have found their substance in Christ, and that no particular day now binds the conscience, pointing to Paul, who writes that one person esteems one day as better than another while another esteems all days alike, and tells them both to stop judging each other (Romans 14:5–6). The second fits the New Testament better and is the view taken here: Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), the apostles laid no Sabbath on the Gentile churches (Acts 15:28–29), and the church gathered on the first day without calling it a Sabbath (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). The Lord’s Day remains a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest. Even so, Paul’s chief concern is to forbid the quarrel, and that should shape how firmly any of us holds an opinion here.

Where the danger lies for us. The Pharisees’ error was too much Sabbath, fenced with rules; ours is almost never that. It is a life with no boundary anywhere: work bleeding into every evening, a phone that never stops. So whatever your conviction, put a real boundary in your week and defend it: work put down, worship unhurried, some deed of mercy. Do it not to earn anything, but because you are a creature and not a machine, and because the day always pointed to the Person who is your rest. And if your practice becomes a stick to measure other people with, you have reproduced the Pharisees’ mistake, whichever side of the question you are on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stretch out your hand. A command he could not obey in his own strength, and Jesus’ command carried the power to obey it. A withered hand is a thing you keep in your sleeve. He is told to hold it out in the middle of a synagogue with every eye on him. The healing did not come first. He had to extend the ruined thing before there was anything to see.

And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. Jesus did no work in the Pharisees’ sense: he did not touch the man. He spoke. The verb for restored (apokathistēmi) is the one used of restoring the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6), and its noun is Peter’s word for the time of restoring all things (Acts 3:21). A small sample of the last day happened in a synagogue on a Sabbath morning, in one man’s hand.

But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. The first mention in Matthew of a plot to kill Jesus. Healing was work; the response is to hold a meeting about how to kill him. Matthew lets the reader do the arithmetic. Mark adds the Herodians (Mark 3:6), and that Jesus looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). What angered him was not the plot against his life but the willingness to watch a disabled man stay disabled rather than lose an argument.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that all Pharisees were murderous. Nicodemus, a Pharisee, came to Jesus and later helped to bury him (John 3:1; 19:39), and Paul was a Pharisee.

How could religious men be so angry at a healing? Because the healing threatened what they were standing on. Their careful Sabbath-keeping was their proof that they were right with God and better than others, and a man who healed by God’s authority, outside their rules, made that proof worthless. When religion becomes the way we save ourselves, anyone who gives grace away freely looks like an enemy. The danger is not only theirs. Any of us can come to love our own record more than the mercy of God, and then resent those who receive mercy they did not earn, like the elder brother outside the party (Luke 15:28–30).

What is my withered hand? It may be a sin you have hidden for years, a shame you never speak of, a wound you protect, a weakness you are embarrassed by. Jesus does not usually heal what we refuse to bring out. Stretching it out means telling him the truth about it in prayer, and often telling a trusted brother or sister as well (James 5:16). It feels like exposure. It is the moment healing begins, because you are holding out to him the very thing you could not fix.

parallels.desc: seeking to kill him over the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all and ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. Not out of fear, but because the cross would come on the Father’s timetable (compare 26:18). Matthew uses the verb (anachōreō) again and again (2:14, 22; 4:12; 14:13): always away from danger, and every time followed by more ministry, not less.

And many followed him, and he healed them all. Condemned for healing, with a plot under way, he goes on healing everybody who comes, which is a sufficient answer to the suggestion that he withdrew out of fear.

And ordered them not to make him known. What he stops is not the work but the publicity (see 8:4). And Matthew declines the obvious explanation, that a hunted man must keep quiet. He says it happened to fulfil Isaiah, and quotes four verses about a Servant who does not shout in the street.

Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because before the cross, the news that a miracle-working Messiah had come would have been heard as a call to arms against Rome, and would have drawn crowds who wanted bread and victory but not a crucified Saviour. Jesus would not be made king on those terms (John 6:15). After his death and resurrection, when the meaning of his messiahship was clear, the command changed: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19). So the silence was for a season. Our calling now is to speak, and to speak above all of the cross, which is what the silence was protecting.

On a Tuesday. Do one good thing today that no one will ever know you did. Notice the small tug to mention it to someone. Jesus did good without seeking attention, and the Father who sees in secret is enough of an audience (6:4).

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 42:1–4, the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew, the first of Isaiah’s four Servant Songs. He quotes it to explain not a miracle but the absence of spectacle.

Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. The Father’s voice at Jesus’ baptism said almost exactly this (3:17), together with Psalm 2:7. From the outset the identity announced was the Servant, and the Servant’s story runs on to Isaiah 53, to a man despised and rejected, wounded for transgressions not his own. His greatness is the greatness of a servant (20:28).

I will put my Spirit upon him. Fulfilled at his baptism (3:16). Jesus casts out demons by this Spirit (v. 28), which is why the charge that he works by Beelzebul is so terrible.

And he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. Justice (krisis) is God’s right order set right in the world, brought not only to Israel but to the nations (v. 21; 28:19). The one the Pharisees plot to destroy is the one appointed to reach every nation.

An honest note on the text. Matthew’s Greek here matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament exactly; he seems to translate as he goes, without bending the sense.

If Jesus is God, how can he be God’s servant? In becoming man, the eternal Son took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). He did not stop being equal with the Father; he added a human nature and, as man and as our Mediator, he obeyed the Father perfectly, even to death on a cross. So the Father can call him my servant and my beloved in the same breath. The Servant is not a lesser being; he is the Son stooping to do the work of a servant for us.

parallels.desc: my chosen servant, with my Spirit upon him
the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory;
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. The Servant is no self-promoter or demagogue. That explains why Jesus withdrew and told people not to publicise him (vv. 15–16). The Pharisees quarrel and cry aloud with accusations; the Servant does not.

A bruised reed he will not break. A reed is a hollow stalk used for a pen or a pipe. Once cracked, it will not write or play, and the ordinary thing is to snap it and throw it away. The Servant does not.

And a smoldering wick he will not quench. A wick with no flame left is a thread of smoke, and you pinch it out. The Servant shields it and fans it back to flame. Both are things a reasonable person discards, and the promise is that he will not.

Who are they? The weak, the failing, the crushed, those with almost no faith left, those whom others have given up on: the sick he healed, the sinners he ate with, the weary he called (11:28). The Puritan Richard Sibbes wrote a famous book on this verse, The Bruised Reed (1630), to comfort struggling Christians: Christ is gentle with weak faith. And this was written about somebody, and it should be said to somebody. If your faith is down to a flicker; if your praying has shrunk to a sentence or two, and not good ones; if you turn up to church out of habit rather than hunger and feel a fraud for being there; if you have failed at the same thing so many times that you have stopped making promises about it, this verse has your name on it. He is not standing over you with his fingers ready to pinch. And see where Matthew has placed this quotation: immediately after the Pharisees walk out to plan a murder (v. 14). The world around him was as hard as it gets, and this is the sentence Matthew reaches for to describe how he treats the weak in the middle of it.

Until he brings justice to victory. His gentleness is not weakness, and this keeps the comfort from going soft: the tending has a destination. He is not indifferent to your ruin; he is patient with it, and he intends to finish the repair.

The reed in his hand. When the soldiers dressed Jesus as a mock king, they put a reed in his right hand, and then took the reed and struck him on the head with it (27:29–30). The bruised reed was handled the way bruised reeds always are: snapped, mocked and used to hit somebody. He went through that so that he would never have to do it to you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ is soft on sin or never confronts evil. He rebuked the Pharisees fiercely (chapter 23). His gentleness is for the broken and the repentant; his severity is for the proud and hard-hearted.

Does his gentleness mean he never disciplines me? No. The Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and sometimes that discipline is painful: a sin exposed, a plan frustrated, a hard season. But his discipline is never meant to break you. It is the pressure of a hand straightening a bent reed, not snapping it; the breath that fans a wick, not the fingers that pinch it. If you are under his correction, it is because he has not given up on you. The gentlest heart in the universe is also the most determined to make you whole.

On a Tuesday. If your faith feels like a smouldering wick, bring it to Christ as it is. Then look for one bruised reed around you, a struggling believer, a person who has failed publicly, and be gentle with them this week. Treat them as he treats you.
verseByVerse.note: A bruised reed and a smouldering lamp-wick are pictures of the weak and failing, easily finished off.

parallels.desc: he will not cry aloud, nor break a bruised reed

verseByVerse.quote: and in his name the Gentiles will hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in his name the Gentiles will hope. His name means his person and authority. The nations, without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12), will find hope not in the Pharisees’ religion or Rome’s armies, but in his name.

An honest textual note. Isaiah 42:4 in the Hebrew reads that the coastlands wait for his law; Matthew follows the Greek tradition. The coastlands are the Gentile lands, and waiting for his instruction is close kin to hoping in his name, but the difference is real.

Two reeds. Matthew has put two reeds a chapter apart. In chapter 11 Jesus asked the crowd whether they had gone out to see a reed shaken by the wind (11:7), the emblem of the man who bends whichever way the weather goes. Here the Servant will not break a bruised reed (v. 20). The same plant, and two entirely different things done with it. There is the reed a man can become, blown about and worth nothing. And there is the reed a person can be reduced to, already crushed, no use to anybody. Jesus has no patience with the first and will not lay a finger on the second.

The direction. What is not in doubt is the direction of the song. It ends by reaching past Israel to everybody else, and Matthew puts that sentence at the exact point where Israel’s leaders have begun plotting to kill him. The nations get their hope in the same paragraph in which his own people decide he must die. And the cross they plan will not end his name; it will make it the name above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). Their murder becomes his throne.

What does it mean to hope in his name? Hope in the Bible is not wishful thinking but confident expectation resting on a promise. To hope in Jesus’ name is to rest your future, your forgiveness, your eternity and your daily needs on who he is and what he has promised, rather than on your own record, your health, your money or your country. It shows itself in prayer offered in his name, in steadiness when things fall apart, and in patience as you wait for his return.

For worship. We were the far nations, without hope and without God in the world, and the Servant’s song reached across the sea to us. The name the rulers tried to blot out is now spoken in every language under heaven. The coastlands waited, and not in vain: every knee shall bow to him.

parallels.desc: the coastlands wait for his law
in him will the Gentiles hope

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–50 — The Unforgivable Sin, the Sign of Jonah, and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus heals a blind and mute demoniac, and the crowd begins, hesitantly, to wonder whether he is the Son of David. The Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus shows the charge is absurd and inconsistent, explains that he casts out demons by the Spirit of God because he has bound the strong man, and warns of the blasphemy against the Spirit. Asked for a sign, he offers only the sign of Jonah, his death and resurrection, and he warns of a swept house left empty. The chapter ends with his true family: whoever does the will of his Father in heaven.
verseByVerse.theology: The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, calling the Spirit’s plain work in Christ the work of Satan, is the one sin Jesus says will not be forgiven. It is not beyond God’s mercy; it shuts the door through which mercy comes, by calling the Spirit who convicts and draws sinners a demon. The warning is given in love, as a doctor warns a patient who is choosing death, and the person who fears he has committed it shows by that fear that he has not.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign of Jonah, three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, is the only sign Jesus offers an evil and adulterous generation. Yet no sign will convince a heart already set against him: the story put about after the resurrection admitted the empty tomb and only disputed how it came to be empty (28:13–15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. And all the people were amazed, and said, "Can this be the Son of David?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute. A threefold ruin. He could not see who had come to him or ask for anything. There is no record of his faith; Matthew says only that he was brought. Somebody else carried the whole transaction, which is worth knowing for anyone praying for a person who is past asking for themselves.

And he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. Complete healing, all at once: the man now sees the face of the one who freed him and speaks his first words in his presence.

Can this be the Son of David? The crowd were amazed, and the question is more hesitant in Greek than in English, and the hesitation is the point. Matthew uses a construction that expects the answer no. It is closer to: this cannot be the Son of David, can it? The crowd is not making a confession; it is edging toward one and flinching. They have seen enough to raise the question and not enough to want to own it. That is very often how faith begins. The sentence is usually read as enthusiasm, but it is the sound of people saying something they are not ready to have overheard. They are close to faith (see 1:1; 9:27).

Why Son of David. Son of David means the Messiah, but it also recalled Solomon, famed as a master of spirits. Josephus describes an exorcist drawing out a demon before Vespasian with a ring and a root, by methods said to come from Solomon. A man who casts out demons with a word is doing what the son of David was famous for, without the ring, the root or the incantation.

Is demon possession real today, and what should I think about it? Scripture treats demonic oppression as real, and missionaries in many lands have met it. But two guards are needed. First, many conditions that look strange are medical or psychological, and they should be treated with medical care, prayer and patience, not labelled demonic. Second, there is no need for rituals or special techniques. Jesus cast out demons by a word, and Christians resist the devil by faith in Christ, prayer, the word of God and the fellowship of the church (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). A believer, whose life is the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, cannot be possessed by a demon: a house already occupied by its rightful Lord is not for let (1 Corinthians 6:19).
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, "It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons." Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons. The Pharisees saw the crowds moving toward faith and acted to stop it. And the most important thing is what they do not say: that it did not happen. A blind, mute man is standing there seeing and talking, and the official response is an explanation of the mechanism. His enemies had every motive to deny the works, and in the Gospels they never do (John 11:47; 28:13). Beelzebul was a name for Satan, meaning something like lord of the house: the most serious accusation they could make.

Reckoned with the devil. The one Isaiah called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God (Isaiah 9:6), on whom the Spirit rests (v. 18), is called by the name of the prince of demons. Jesus does not storm out; he answers with patient reasoning. It is the beginning of a road on which he will be numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12), so that the guilty who trust him might be counted among the righteous.

Knowing their thoughts. As in 9:4: he answers what lay underneath the sentence, as only God can (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10).

Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand. The logic descends, kingdom, city, house, and the last word is the one he needs, because in four verses Satan will be a strong man whose house is being robbed (v. 29). The reasoning is simple enough for a child: if the accusation were true, the devil would be dismantling his own operation, one prisoner at a time, in public, on request.

Why did they not simply deny the miracle? Because they could not. Too many people had seen the man before and after. That is why the Gospels’ accounts of Jesus’ works are so hard to dismiss: the people who most wanted them to be false admitted they had happened. A sceptic may reply that the Gospel writers supplied that admission themselves; but a hostile Jewish tradition preserved in the Talmud also says that Jesus practised sorcery, which concedes the deeds and disputes only their source, exactly as here. Faced with undeniable evidence they would not accept, they chose a theory that let them keep their hatred. It is a warning for every age. The problem with unbelief is rarely a lack of evidence; it is what the heart will do with the evidence.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan, probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.

verseByVerse.quote: And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? The first argument: the charge is absurd. Satan has a kingdom (Colossians 1:13; Ephesians 6:12). He is wicked, but not foolish enough to destroy it from within.

And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? The second argument is inconsistency, and it needs one fact to land properly: Jewish exorcism was a real and respected practice. Josephus describes it and treats it as an ancient national skill. The book of Acts records seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva going about Ephesus attempting it, badly in that instance (Acts 19:13–16). Your sons means the Pharisees’ followers or other Jewish exorcists of the time. So Jesus is not scoring a point off a hypothetical. He is pointing at practitioners the Pharisees knew and approved, possibly men in their own circle.

Therefore they will be your judges. If exorcism as such is satanic, their own people stand condemned. If it is not, their explanation was invented for the occasion.

The difference they could not explain. Other exorcists worked with apparatus: names, rings, formulas, the invocation of a higher authority. Jesus says go, and it is over. A man with borrowed authority has to name his source. A man who never names one is either a fraud, in which case the demons would not leave, or he is not borrowing. Their only remaining move is to name the wrong owner.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” probably means Jewish exorcists of their own circle.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can someone enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons. The decisive argument: the true explanation is God’s Spirit (3:16; 12:18). Luke has: by the finger of God (Luke 11:20), almost certainly an echo of Pharaoh’s magicians, who could not match the gnats and said, this is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19). So the exorcisms are a new exodus: prisoners taken out of a house that had held them, and the resident experts unable to reproduce it. The Pharisees stand where Pharaoh’s magicians stood, and choose the other answer.

Then the kingdom of God has come upon you. A rare kingdom of God in place of Matthew’s usual kingdom of heaven. The verb (ephthasen) means it has actually arrived. This is the already of the kingdom, and the sting: it has come upon you, and the men it has overtaken are the ones explaining it away.

Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? A parable, and the picture is a burglary. The strong man is Satan. His house is the world under his power, and his goods are the people he holds captive. Nobody walks into an occupied house and starts carrying out the furniture while the owner is standing there. The goods come out only after the owner is on the floor. So every demon that leaves is not a negotiation; it is evidence that somebody has already been dealt with in the next room. The image is Isaiah’s before it is his. Can the prey be taken from the mighty? the prophet asks, and answers that even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, for the LORD will do it (Isaiah 49:24–25). He raises it as an impossibility and then says God will do it anyway.

Then indeed he may plunder his house. Jesus is the stronger one (3:11; Luke 11:22). He bound Satan, beginning in the wilderness (4:1–11) and completing it at the cross (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15). Every person set free from sin is Jesus plundering Satan’s house.

Where Christians differ over the binding of Satan. Revelation 20:1–3 pictures Satan bound so that he can no longer deceive the nations. Amillennialists, who read the thousand years as a picture of the present age between Christ’s two comings, see this binding as beginning with his first coming; premillennial readers take that passage as a future binding during a thousand-year reign after Christ returns. This commentary’s view: Satan is bound now, in the sense this verse describes (Luke 10:18; Colossians 2:15), and the gospel is plundering his house among the nations. He is still active and dangerous, but restrained, and that fits what Jesus says here. The reason is that Jesus uses the very word bind for what he is doing now (v. 29), and the gospel now reaching the nations shows the restraint Revelation 20 describes. Premillennial brothers and sisters read it differently, and all agree that Christ has already defeated Satan at the cross and will come again to finish the work.

If Satan is bound, why is there still so much evil? Because bound does not mean idle: he still tempts, accuses and deceives, but he cannot stop the gospel going to the nations or keep any person Christ sets free. (See Mark 3:27 for the fuller answer.)

On a Tuesday. Whatever has held you captive, a habit, a fear, a lie you have believed about yourself, name it to Christ today, and tell a mature Christian, so that you are not fighting alone. The strong man is already bound.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty
he disarmed the rulers and authorities

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is not with me is against me. In the war between Jesus and Satan, there is no neutrality. The Pharisees thought they were serving God; by opposing Jesus, they were serving Satan. And whoever does not gather with me scatters the harvest he is gathering (9:36–38).

In the flow. Verse 31 opens with Therefore: the warning about the Spirit grows straight out of the argument. Jesus casts out demons by the Spirit (v. 28); the Pharisees say he does it by Satan (v. 24). That is the sin he now names.

Two sayings that seem to clash. Elsewhere Jesus says, the one who is not against us is for us (Mark 9:40; Luke 9:50). Both are true, because they answer different questions. Here he speaks of a man’s own standing before Christ: there is no neutral ground. There he spoke of an outsider casting out demons in his name whom the disciples wanted to stop. Be strict with your own allegiance and generous about somebody else’s. Most of our trouble comes from getting those two the wrong way round.

The mercy behind the word every. The Son of Man who speaks this sentence has come to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). The breadth of the promise is the breadth of his cross: no sin is heavier than the death of the Son of God.

Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people. Do not let the warning at the end of this verse swallow the promise at the beginning. The sentence contains the widest offer in the Gospel and the single exception to it, and most readers only hear the second half. Weigh the company Jesus kept: a tax collector made an apostle, a woman with a reputation defended, a thief promised paradise (Luke 7:36–50; 23:43). And blasphemy is the strongest word available: Paul called himself formerly a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent who received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13). No sin is too great to be forgiven, if it is repented of.

But the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. Whatever a reader is carrying, the thing said about God in a hospital corridor at the worst hour, the years spent arguing against him, this verse was drafted wide enough on purpose. Exactly one sin is named as beyond forgiveness: looking at the Spirit’s plain work in Christ and calling it the devil’s, with a heart that has no wish to be forgiven.

What if someone I love seems neutral, neither for nor against? Jesus’ words mean they are not safe while they stay there, however kind or respectful they are. That should move you to pray for them and to speak to them, gently and honestly, not to write them off. Neutrality is often a holding position, and people move from it. Many who once shrugged at Christ have come to love him. Keep loving them, keep praying, and look for natural ways to tell them why Jesus matters to you.

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. Those who spoke against him in ignorance could be forgiven, since his identity was partly veiled during his earthly life.

Spoken against, and still forgiving. No one in history was spoken against as the Son of Man was. He was called a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of sinners, a blasphemer, a man with a demon, a deceiver; and at the last, men wagged their heads at him on the cross. And the words against him are forgivable because he was going to die for them. From the cross he prayed, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Peter, who denied him, was forgiven; Saul, who persecuted him, was forgiven; and not long afterwards a great many priests in Jerusalem became obedient to the faith (Acts 6:7). The Son of Man made the words against him forgivable by bearing them.

But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. In context, the Pharisees had seen the Spirit’s work clearly and deliberately called it the work of Satan (vv. 24, 28; Mark 3:30). They were not ignorant; they were calling light darkness, against the evidence, because they hated Jesus. It is a settled, clear-eyed hatred of the light that looks straight at the work of God, calls it the devil’s, and feels no grief at doing so.

Why is it unforgivable? Not because God’s grace is too small, but because this sin rejects the only source of forgiveness. The Holy Spirit is the one who convicts people of sin and draws them to Christ (John 16:8–11). To reject his testimony deliberately and finally, calling it satanic, is to shut the only door to forgiveness. Such a person does not want forgiveness and will not repent. It is a settled, wilful hardening of the heart against God’s clear revelation of Christ. The sin forecloses forgiveness not by a limit on God’s mercy but by a person’s self-exclusion from it.

If you are afraid you have committed it. No verse in Scripture has frightened tender souls more than this one, so the pastoral word must be said plainly. If you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, that very fear is the surest proof you have not. The person who commits it has no desire for Christ and no fear of having offended him. But a trembling conscience, a longing to be right with God, a dread of having sinned against him: these are the Spirit’s own work in a soul, and the Spirit does not grieve over a heart he has abandoned. As the old pastors said, the tears you weep over this question are tears the unpardonable sin never sheds. Come to Christ; he has never yet cast out one who came (John 6:37).

Either the tree is good and its fruit good, or the tree is bad and its fruit bad. A tree is known by its fruit (7:16–20). The fruit of Jesus’ ministry, people freed and healed, is good; the Pharisees’ fruit, slander and plotting murder, reveals what they are.

What it does not mean. It is not a careless word, a doubt, an unwanted blasphemous thought, or a sin committed in weakness, even a serious one. And either in this age or in the age to come does not imply that other sins may be forgiven after death, as in the later doctrine of purgatory. It is a Jewish way of saying never. Forgiveness is found in this life, at the foot of the cross (Hebrews 9:27).

Can this sin still be committed today? Some think it was possible only for those who saw Christ’s own miracles and called them Satan’s. Others think it recurs wherever someone knowingly and finally rejects the Spirit’s witness to Christ (Hebrews 10:26–29). The second is the more likely. Either way, the person who fears he has committed it shows by that fear that he has not; the hardened heart does not grieve. It is the sin of the hardened, never of the grieving.

What about horrible thoughts about God that come into my mind against my will? These torment many sincere believers, especially in times of anxiety or depression. A thought you hate, resist and are distressed by is not blasphemy against the Spirit; it is a burden you are carrying, and often an attack of the enemy or a symptom of an anxious mind. Do not argue with it endlessly or keep checking whether you meant it. Tell God that you reject it and love him, turn your mind to a promise of Scripture, and if it persists, speak to a pastor and, if needed, a doctor. Christ is not angry with you for being tormented.

verseByVerse.quote: You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? John said it first (3:7); Jesus says it here and in the temple in the last week (23:33). The first man to say it was beheaded, and the second was crucified. And in a chapter about what comes out of a mouth, the animal is exact: the viper’s danger is all in its mouth.

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The word (perisseuma) means overflow, what spills when a container is full. So speech is not primarily a decision. It is a leak. A man can control his words while he is thinking about them; nobody controls what he says when he is startled, or tired, or contradicted in front of others. That is when the level shows. The Pharisees’ slander against Jesus was not a slip; it was their own self-portrait.

The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. Treasure means a storehouse: what we store in our hearts eventually comes out in our words (6:21).

A new storehouse. If words leak from the heart, no amount of tongue-control will save a viper. What is needed is what God promised through Ezekiel: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezekiel 36:26). And that promise has a price and a giver. Christ bore the judgement due to every evil word, and from his throne he pours out the Spirit who fills the storehouse with new treasure: the word of Christ dwelling richly (Colossians 3:16). The vipers of this verse had only one hope, and it was the man they were slandering. Some Pharisees, like Saul of Tarsus, later found it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every harsh word reveals a wholly evil heart; Christians still sin with their tongues (James 3:2). Nor that the storehouse cannot be changed. It says the mouth reports the current stock honestly.

May I call people a brood of vipers? No. Jesus forbade calling a brother a fool (5:22). Here he speaks as prophet and judge to hardened teachers who had just blasphemed the Spirit. His disciples are not licensed to copy the words as personal abuse (James 3:9–10; Titus 3:2), though there are times when false teaching must be named sharply (Galatians 1:9; Titus 1:13). The tone of a Christian online or in argument should be marked by gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), even when the content is firm.

How do I change what is in my heart? Not by willpower alone, but by what you let fill it. God changes the heart by his Spirit, and he does it through means: his word read, heard and memorised (Colossians 3:16), prayer, worship with his people, and repentance whenever you hear something ugly come out of yourself. Notice what you feed on: what you watch, read and listen to most. The right response to hearing something ugly come out of your mouth is therefore not merely to resolve to say less. It is to ask what has been going in, and to bring that to God.

For worship. There was once a heart so full of good treasure that every word that overflowed from it was grace and truth (Psalm 45:2). Even on the cross what spilled out was forgiveness for his enemies and comfort for a thief. Out of the abundance of his heart he spoke, and it was love; and one day the mouths he has made new will speak nothing but his praise.

parallels.desc: what comes out of the mouth

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak. Argos means idle, the word for the labourers standing with nothing to do (20:3, 6). So the words in view are the idle ones: the joke at someone’s expense, the gossip, the throwaway forgotten within the hour by everybody except the person it was about. Many of us still carry a sentence someone said to us years ago without a second thought. And if careless words matter to God, how much more the Pharisees’ deliberate slander.

For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned. How does that fit with being saved by faith? A believer is declared righteous the moment he trusts Christ, because Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5; 5:1). On the last day that verdict is made public, and words are brought out as evidence. In a court, evidence does not create a fact; it establishes one. The words are exhibits, not payment, and what they show is the storehouse, which grace changes and nothing else does.

With the mouth one confesses. One word above all justifies a sinner: if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved (Romans 10:9). And the Lord who will hear every word at the judgement stood silent before his accusers, like a sheep before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7), refusing to speak in his own defence so that he could become the defence of those who confess him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we are saved by our words. We are justified by faith in Christ (Romans 3:28), but words, like works, are evidence of genuine faith or its absence (James 2:18). Nor will every careless word condemn a believer: Christ’s blood cleanses them from all sin (1 John 1:7). The verse is terrifying to a man who thinks his words are trivial, and not to a man whose heart has new contents and whose tongue keeps embarrassing him.

What do I do about words I said that I cannot take back? Confess them to God specifically, and believe that in Christ they are forgiven; you will not be condemned for them on the last day. Then, where you can, go to the person you hurt and apologise plainly, without excuses. Where a word has spread, gossip for instance, correct it with the people who heard it. Some damage takes time to heal, and you may need to show changed speech over months. But do not live under a cloud. The same Lord who weighs every word has spoken a better word over you: no condemnation (Romans 8:1).

On a Tuesday. Pray Psalm 141:3 before your first conversation today: set a guard over my mouth. Then say one word today that does a job: an encouragement, a thank you, a truth spoken in love.

parallels.desc: death and life are in the power of the tongue

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, "Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you." But he answered them, "An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you. In this Gospel those who come in faith call Jesus Lord, while those who call him Teacher are almost always outsiders: the scribe who volunteered (8:19), the rich young man (19:16), the Pharisees (22:16, 36), and Judas, alone among the Twelve, saying Rabbi (26:25). The address is the assessment. A sign means a miraculous proof of his authority, on their terms.

The sign that had just happened. They have just watched a man who was blind, mute and possessed walk away seeing, speaking and free (v. 22), and called it Satan’s work. So what they want is not evidence but a demonstration on demand, of their choosing: the very thing the devil had proposed at the temple, and Jesus refused there too (4:5–7).

An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign. Adulterous is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness: the covenant is a marriage, and Hosea was told to marry an unfaithful woman so that the nation could see itself (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3). This generation is not a stranger to God but a wife who has gone elsewhere. A wife does not require her husband to prove his identity.

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. Jesus will not perform on demand. It is a refusal to play the game of the hardened heart, which will always require more evidence as a reason for never believing. The one sign they will get is a man who went down into death and came up again.

Come down from the cross. The demand for a sign on their terms was made once more, at the end. As he hung dying, the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him: let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him (27:42). It was the same request as this one, a demonstration of their choosing, and he refused it for the same reason, and with infinitely more at stake. Had he come down, there would have been a spectacle and no Saviour. He stayed, and by staying he gave them the very sign he had promised: the Son of Man laid in the heart of the earth, and raised on the third day. The sign they refused to accept was purchased by the sign he refused to give.

Would a sign not settle it for a sceptic today? Jesus’ answer is that it would not, because the problem was never missing evidence. These men had just seen a blind, mute man healed and explained it away (v. 24). Elsewhere Jesus says that people who will not listen to Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31). That is no refusal to engage honest doubt. God has given a public sign that can be examined: a man who died and rose again, seen by more than five hundred witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Paul wrote that list within about twenty-five years of the events and noted that most of those witnesses were still alive, as if inviting anyone to go and ask them (1 Corinthians 15:6). The honest sceptic is invited to weigh that sign. What God will not do is perform on demand for a heart that has already decided.

Is it wrong to ask God for a sign when I have a decision to make? It is not wrong to ask God for wisdom, and he promises to give it (James 1:5). But the normal way God guides his people now is through his word, which is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17), through prayer, through wise counsel from mature Christians, and through the ordinary circumstances he arranges. Setting tests for God, if the phone rings in the next five minutes I will take the job, is risky: it treats chance events as messages and can bypass the wisdom he has already given. Pray, search the Scriptures, seek counsel, then decide, trusting that he directs the steps of those who seek him (Proverbs 3:5–6).
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish. Jonah 1:17. Jonah himself describes it as a death: out of the belly of Sheol he cried; he went down to the land whose bars closed upon him for ever; and God brought up his life from the pit (Jonah 2:2–6). It is the language of a man describing his own death, from underneath.

So will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Jesus predicts his death, burial and resurrection: the greatest sign of all, the one that makes all other signs unnecessary. The heart of the earth answers Jonah’s heart of the seas (Jonah 2:3). The sign is the whole of what Jonah’s prayer describes: going down into the place from which nobody negotiates a return, and being brought up out of it so that Gentiles could be preached to.

How is Friday to Sunday three days and three nights? Jesus was buried on Friday afternoon and rose on Sunday morning, which looks like only two nights. The answer is the Jewish way of counting time: any part of a day was reckoned as a whole day and night. So Friday, Saturday and Sunday were counted as three days and three nights, even though only part of Friday and part of Sunday were involved. Scripture counts this way elsewhere. Esther calls a fast for three days, night or day, and then goes to the king on the third day (Esther 4:16; 5:1); the same idiom appears in 1 Samuel 30:12–13 and 2 Chronicles 10:5, 12. A few have proposed a Wednesday crucifixion to fit a literal seventy-two hours, but the Gospels’ own timing, that Jesus rose on the third day and not the fourth (16:21; 27:63–64), fits the ordinary Jewish reckoning best.

The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it. Nineveh was a great city of Assyria, Israel’s most brutal enemy. They repented at the preaching of a reluctant, angry prophet who, so far as we are told, worked no miracles there, and the whole city repented, from the king down (Jonah 3:5–10).

And behold, something greater than Jonah is here. A willing Saviour, not a reluctant prophet; the Son of God, not a mere messenger. And a last irony: Jonah went into the deep because he was running from the commission to preach to pagans. Jesus goes into the earth in order to fulfil it.

Was Jonah a real person? Many critics treat the book as a parable. But Jesus sets Jonah beside his own death and resurrection and says the men of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment (see also Luke 11:30). That makes best sense if the events happened, and the more likely reading is that Jesus believed they did. Jonah is also named as a historical prophet in 2 Kings 14:25. If the Lord of the Scriptures treated the account as history, his people may do the same without embarrassment.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask for a new sign. Read one Gospel’s account of the resurrection slowly this week, and ask whether you have repented at the preaching of one greater than Jonah, or only listened.
verseByVerse.note: “Three days and three nights” was a way of counting any part of a day as a day. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

parallels.desc: three days and three nights in the fish

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South. The queen of Sheba, probably from Saba in south-west Arabia (modern Yemen), some 1,300 miles from Jerusalem. She came to test Solomon with hard questions, was overwhelmed by his wisdom, and praised his God (1 Kings 10:1–13). She was a Gentile.

Will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it. She made a long, costly journey to hear wisdom; this generation would not walk a few steps. Both witnesses for the prosecution are Gentiles: Nineveh, the city of the empire that carried the northern tribes into exile, and a pagan monarch from the far end of the known world. Neither had the Scriptures, the temple or the promises. Nineveh had one reluctant preacher; Sheba had a rumour about a clever king. Both responded, and they will stand on the last day against people who had everything, watched Jesus heal a blind mute, and called it Beelzebul.

And behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The true Son of David, Wisdom itself (11:19; 1 Corinthians 1:24, 30; Colossians 2:3). Jonah ran away and sulked; Solomon ended badly. They are not Israel’s finest; they are simply the two who reached the Gentiles. With this claim the list begun in the grainfield is complete: temple, prophet and king, each surpassed by what has now arrived.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Gentiles are saved by seeking wisdom or by sincerity. The queen praised Israel’s God; Nineveh turned to him at his word. Salvation still comes only through the One greater than Solomon.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, in south-west Arabia.

parallels.desc: the queen of Sheba visits Solomon

verseByVerse.quote: Then it says, "I will return to my house from which I came." And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest. Deserts were thought of as the haunt of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). I will return to my house, it says: the person is still its house, because no one else has moved in.

And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. All three are approving words. On any inspection it would pass. And the first of the three is the fatal one: empty. It is in excellent condition and there is nobody in it, which is exactly the state a life is left in by a reformation that goes no further than removal. The habit was given up, the language cleaned. Nothing has moved in.

Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself. Seven is a complete number: a full occupation.

Worse than the first. Reformation without regeneration produces a clean space and no defender. Reformation is what we can do ourselves, changing behaviour on the outside. Regeneration is the new birth only God can give: the Spirit giving a new heart that loves God and trusts Christ (John 3:3–8).

So also will it be with this evil generation. The application is stated outright, unusually for a parable. They had had a genuine national awakening: crowds at the Jordan confessing sins, and the healings and exorcisms of Jesus. The house had been swept. Then the one who was to fill it arrived, and they said he had a demon. Within forty years the temple was rubble (AD 70), and the last state was worse than the first.

The tenant who binds the strong man. A few sentences earlier Jesus described himself as the stronger one who binds the strong man (v. 29). A house is not safe merely because the old occupant has been evicted; it is safe when the one who evicted him moves in, that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:17). The whole difference between the last state worse than the first and a life secure for ever is whether Jesus himself is living in the rooms he has cleared.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a true believer, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, can be repossessed by demons. There is no indwelling in the story; that is the entire problem. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). The warning is about moral reform without new birth.

I have given up some bad habits. How do I make sure the house is not empty? Ask first whether Christ himself lives there: have you trusted him, not just tidied up for him? Then fill the space deliberately. When you stop one thing, put something better in its place: time with God’s word where the screen used to be, friendship in the church where the old company used to be, serving others where the old habit used to sit. Paul’s pattern is always put off and put on (Ephesians 4:22–32). An emptied life is not a safe life; it is a vacant one, and the previous tenant knows the address.

parallels.desc: the last state worse than the first

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. Someone told him, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers. Mary and Jesus’ brothers, James, Joseph, Simon and Judas, with sisters also (13:55–56). Mark tells us why they came: his family went out to seize him, for people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31). His brothers did not believe in him at this time (John 7:5). They stood outside, physically and perhaps spiritually.

He appeared to James. After the resurrection the brothers believed. James became a leader of the Jerusalem church and traditionally wrote the letter of James; Judas, or Jude, the letter of Jude (Acts 1:14; 15:13; Galatians 1:19). What changed them? Paul’s list of witnesses says: then he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). The risen Lord went looking for the brother who had once come to take him home as a madman, and showed himself alive. The Christ whose family misunderstood him did not wait for them to work it out; he came to them.

Textual note. Some important early manuscripts omit verse 47, perhaps because verses 46 and 47 end with almost the same words and a copyist’s eye jumped. This commentary’s view: probably original; it is needed for verse 48 to make sense. Nothing turns on it either way.

On the brothers. Christians have read this in three ways. The oldest Eastern view takes them as Joseph’s children by a previous marriage; the Western Catholic view, from Jerome onward, as cousins; most Protestants today (though not Luther) as later children of Joseph and Mary, pointing to Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (1:25) and her firstborn (Luke 2:7). That plain reading is followed here. The virgin birth, which is what matters, is affirmed by all three and untouched by the question.

My family thinks my faith has made me strange. What should I do? You are in good company: Jesus’ own family thought he had lost his mind. Stay patient and loving. Keep honouring your parents and serving your family in practical ways, so that the change in you is seen in kindness, not only in words (1 Peter 3:1–2). Do not give up following Christ to keep the peace, but do not be harsh or superior either. And keep praying. His brothers came to believe; the family that stood outside ended up in the upper room.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 47: “Someone told him, ‘Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, asking to speak to you.’”

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to the man who told him, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? A shocking question in a culture where family was everything. Jesus is not rejecting his family, but redefining what family means in God’s kingdom. And it is worth being honest about how hard the saying is. His mother is outside. She had carried him and been told by an angel who he was, and, as Luke tells us, had watched shepherds arrive and kept all these things in her heart. She is standing outside unable to get in, and Matthew does not tell us that he went out. The Gospel does not soften that, and neither should a commentary.

And stretching out his hand toward his disciples. Matthew uses the same verb (ekteinō) as in verse 13. So the chapter has two outstretched hands: a ruined one, held out on command in front of a hostile congregation and restored, and this one, held out over a circle of ordinary men to say: here is my family.

Here are my mother and my brothers! The bond of faith is deeper than the bond of blood. The church is not a religious club but a family, with God as Father (23:8–9), and all the closeness and mutual care that family implies.

Where Mary ended up. Mary is in the upper room after the ascension, devoting herself to prayer with the apostles (Acts 1:14). She did not stay outside. She got in, not as his mother, but by the door he was describing, open to her on the same terms as everybody else. He is not disowning her. He is saying what she would come to know: the relationship she was about to need was not the one she already had.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus despised his mother; on the cross he provided for her (John 19:26–27). But family loyalty is not the highest loyalty (10:37). And the passage gives no support for devotion to Mary as a mediator: Jesus pointed away from his family to his disciples, and Mary herself was saved by faith in her Son (Luke 1:47).

If the church is my family, what do I still owe my natural family? A great deal. Scripture commands children to honour their parents (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:2), husbands and wives to love and be faithful to each other, parents to raise their children in the Lord, and anyone who does not provide for his relatives to be counted worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus himself cared for his mother from the cross. The church does not replace those duties; it sets them in order. Christ comes first, so that when family demands conflict with obeying him, you follow him. But in ordinary life, following him means loving your family better, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven. The mark of Jesus’ family is not birth but doing God’s will, which begins with believing in Jesus and goes on in obeying him (7:21; John 6:29). Anyone may join.

Is my brother and sister and mother. Count the relations he names: brother, sister, mother. He does not say father. The place is taken already: the will of my Father in heaven. He will say it outright: you have one Father, who is in heaven (23:9). And he includes sister explicitly, in a culture that kept women at the edge of religious life.

What this family is. It is not an association of like-minded people, and it is not a replacement for the household. It is a household, with siblings and a mother’s place in it, and one Father, and everybody else at the same level under him. Christians are not asked to be fond of each other, which is beyond arranging. They are told what they are: people with the same Father, which is a fact about the arrangement rather than a description of the feeling. He said it standing in a house with his own mother outside and his brothers convinced he was out of his mind. The church has lived under this definition ever since: held together not by temperament, nation or blood, but by one Father in heaven and a will that everybody in the room was learning to do badly. The men he stretched his hand over would all abandon him on the night of his arrest, and not one of them was struck off the list.

What it does not mean. We do not earn a place in Jesus’ family by our works. Those adopted by grace (Ephesians 1:5) show it by doing his will.

I am single, or my family has rejected me. Does this promise mean anything for me? It means everything. Jesus promised that no one who has left home or family for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life (Mark 10:29–30). The church is meant to be that hundredfold. If you feel alone, tell your pastor or a mature believer; you are not imposing. And if you belong to a church, make it your business that no single person, widow or rejected believer in it lacks a family table to sit at.

For worship. The Son by nature makes sons and daughters by grace, and shares with them his own Father: I am ascending to my Father and your Father (John 20:17). We were outsiders, standing in the street, and he drew us in: one Father in heaven, one elder Brother who died for his family, and a household gathered from every nation.

parallels.desc: you are my friends if you do what I command

12.theology: Christ the fulfilment of the Sabbath. The Sabbath rest of creation (Genesis 2:2–3) and of the covenant (Exodus 20:8–11) pointed forward to a final rest for God’s people. Hebrews 4 draws the line: the rest Joshua could not give, and the weekly Sabbath pictured, is found in Christ. Jesus claims to be both the giver of that rest and what it was about. The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a weekly reminder that the rest has arrived in him and will be completed at his return.
12.examples:
Then: The Pharisees had multiplied rules around the Sabbath until the day of rest became a burden, and they cared more for the rule than for hungry men and a withered hand. Religious observance had turned against the people it was meant to bless.

Now: Every religious tradition is tempted to mistake the form for the substance. The Lord’s Day is a gift from the Lord of the Sabbath, a weekly celebration of the resurrection, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, not a legal test by which to judge one another.

13.title: The Kingdom in Parables
13.text: <sup>1</sup>That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. <sup>2</sup>And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach. <sup>3</sup>And he told them many things in parables, saying: “A sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them. <sup>5</sup>Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, <sup>6</sup>but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. <sup>8</sup>Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. <sup>9</sup>He who has ears, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” <sup>11</sup>And he answered them, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. <sup>12</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>13</sup>This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. <sup>14</sup>Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: ”’“You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.” <sup>15</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>16</sup>But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. <sup>17</sup>For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. <sup>18</sup>“Hear then the parable of the sower: <sup>19</sup>When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. <sup>20</sup>As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, <sup>21</sup>yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. <sup>22</sup>As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>23</sup>As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” <sup>24</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, <sup>25</sup>but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. <sup>26</sup>So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. <sup>27</sup>And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?’ <sup>28</sup>He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ So the servants said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and gather them?’ <sup>29</sup>But he said, ‘No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. <sup>30</sup>Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’” <sup>31</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. <sup>32</sup>It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” <sup>33</sup>He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened.” <sup>34</sup>All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. <sup>35</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” <sup>36</sup>Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” <sup>37</sup>He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>The field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, <sup>39</sup>and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. <sup>40</sup>Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. <sup>41</sup>The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers, <sup>42</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>43</sup>Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear. <sup>44</sup>“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. <sup>45</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, <sup>46</sup>who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. <sup>47</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. <sup>48</sup>When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. <sup>49</sup>So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous <sup>50</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>51</sup>“Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.” <sup>52</sup>And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” <sup>53</sup>And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there, <sup>54</sup>and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? <sup>55</sup>Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? <sup>56</sup>And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?” <sup>57</sup>And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.” <sup>58</sup>And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the third of Matthew’s five great teaching sections: seven parables about the kingdom of heaven. Jesus turns to parables as opposition grows (chapters 11–12): they open the kingdom to those who come and ask, and stay shut to those who have hardened their hearts. That is God’s judgment on people who have refused the light again and again (v. 15; Isaiah 6:9–10).

The parables show a kingdom that is truly present but not yet complete, growing but hidden, and mixed until the harvest. The sower shows the same word meeting different hearts. The weeds and the net show good and evil side by side until the end. The mustard seed and the leaven show small, hidden beginnings that will fill the world. The treasure and the pearl show a kingdom worth more than everything. Together they answer the question why the kingdom is not more obvious: this is the season of sowing, and the harvest is coming.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — The Parable of the Sower and the Mystery of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes to the lakeshore and teaches in parables for the first time in Matthew. The parable of the sower describes four ways the word of the kingdom is received: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns and the good soil. Parables open the kingdom to those with ears to hear and hide it from hardened hearts (Isaiah 6:9–10); then he explains the sower. Three things are easily missed. The sower is not careless: a field sown by hand always has path, rock and thorn in it. The yields are the point: thirty, sixty and a hundredfold are far beyond an ordinary harvest. And Matthew and Mark describe the hardening from two sides: Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables because they do not see, Mark that it is so that they may not see (Mark 4:12). Both halves are in the Isaiah passage: they closed their own eyes, and God confirms the closing.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable of the sower is really a parable of soils: the sower and the seed stay the same; what differs is the heart that receives the word. The soils are not fixed types of people, for by God’s grace hard ground can be broken and shallow ground deepened. The parable searches the hearer (what kind of soil am I?) and looks to the end (the harvest will show what was real). Jesus’ explanation names the enemies of fruitfulness: the devil, persecution, the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches.
verseByVerse.examples: The secrets of the kingdom follow a steady pattern: those who have ears to hear receive more, and those who close their ears lose even what they have. Good soil is God’s gift (Ezekiel 36:26), and the disciple’s part is to keep coming to Christ with an open, honest heart, hearing the word and understanding it (v. 23), so that the seed bears its fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 13 is the third of Jesus’ five great teaching sections: the parables of the kingdom. After the rejection of chapters 11 and 12 it answers the obvious question: if the kingdom has really come, why do some refuse him, and why is evil still everywhere? The kingdom comes quietly, like seed; it meets different soils; it grows hidden from tiny beginnings until it fills the world; it is worth more than all a man owns; and good and evil grow side by side until the harvest. The chapter ends in Nazareth, where those who knew Jesus best stumble over him.

Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. That same day was the day of the Beelzebul controversy, and the house is the one where his mother and brothers stood outside (12:46–50). So a scene about who truly belongs to him comes right before a teaching about who truly receives his word. A rabbi sat to expound (5:1; Luke 4:20).

So that he got into a boat and sat down. The boat became a pulpit. Near Capernaum the ground rises from the water in a natural curve, and a voice from a boat a few yards out carries well up the slope. He had no building, so he used the shape of the ground.

And the whole crowd stood on the beach. Within that crowd were all four soils of the parable he was about to tell.

Wiser than Solomon, sitting in a boat. Hours earlier Jesus had said that something greater than Solomon is here (12:42). Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, the Hebrew mashal, the word behind parable, of trees, beasts and birds (1 Kings 4:32–34). Now the Wisdom of God sits on the water and speaks of seed and birds, yeast and nets. Solomon taught about the world God made; Jesus is the one through whom it was made.

Why does Jesus teach in stories at all? Because stories reach people who would not sit through a lecture, stay in the memory long after an argument is forgotten, and require the hearer to think. A parable also leaves a person free to walk away with only a story, or to ask what it means and receive more. Jesus will explain this himself in verses 10–17. For now, it is enough to see that the Lord of glory sat in a fishing boat and talked about seed and soil, weeds and yeast, nets and pearls. He made the deepest truths of God out of ordinary things, so that ordinary people would meet them every day.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach; the boat let the crowd on the shore hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them many things in parables, saying: "A sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parables. A parable (parabolē) is a picture from everyday life placed alongside a spiritual truth. The Hebrew word behind it also covers proverbs and riddles. They usually make one main point, sometimes a few; they are not detailed allegories, though Jesus does interpret some details (vv. 18–23, 36–43).

A sower went out to sow. The sower seems careless: why scatter grain on a footpath, a rock shelf and a thorn patch? On a reading of ancient practice many scholars hold, the ploughing could come after the sowing: a man broadcast seed across the whole field, path and all, and then turned the soil. Either way, when a field is sown by hand, some seed will always land where it cannot grow. The path is a right of way beaten across the field; the thorns have been cut back, but their roots remain. The story is not about a fool with a bag of seed. It is about ground.
