The Sower who went out. Jesus names the sower in the next parable: the one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man (v. 37). So the first sower is the speaker in the boat. A sower went out, and the Son of God did go out: I came from the Father and have come into the world (John 16:28). He did not wait at the edge of the field for good ground to appear. He walked the whole of it, the hard paths of Pharisees, the shallow enthusiasm of crowds, the thorny cares of tax collectors and fishermen, scattering the word on every kind of heart. Every Christian sower since has only carried his seed.

And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path. Soil packed hard by feet. On every other soil the seed at least goes in. Here it lies on top, in plain sight.

And the birds came and devoured them. The birds do not have to dig. The interpretation names them: the evil one (v. 19). No struggle, no gradual erosion. The word arrives, does not go in, and is gone before the man has walked home.

Is the problem ever the seed? Never. The word of God is the same wherever it falls, and it is always good. When people do not respond to faithful preaching, the fault is not in the gospel, and the remedy is not to change the message into something more acceptable. The sower in the parable is not told to sow different seed on the path. He keeps sowing the same seed everywhere, and the harvest comes from the good soil.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil. Not soil full of stones, but a thin layer of soil over a shelf of limestone a few inches down, very common in Galilee.

And immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil. Thin soil over rock warms faster, because the stone holds the sun’s heat, so this seed sprouts ahead of everything else. The fastest green in the field is growing over the shallowest ground. For a few weeks it looked better than its neighbours.

But when the sun rose they were scorched. The roots hit the shelf and run sideways, leaving much leaf on almost no anchorage. Then comes the heat, often the hot east wind off the desert. The deep-rooted plants survive it; the shallow ones cannot.

And since they had no root, they withered away. The parable describes not a man who was never affected but the most impressive-looking plant in the field, and the thing that made it grow so fast was the same thing that killed it.

Rooted in him. The New Testament says where a believer’s roots must go: rooted and built up in him (Colossians 2:7), rooted and grounded in love, the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:17–19). The shallow plant has its roots in its own enthusiasm, and enthusiasm is a few inches of warm soil over rock. Jeremiah drew the contrast long before: the man who trusts in man is a shrub in the desert, but the man who trusts in the LORD is a tree planted by water, which does not fear when heat comes (Jeremiah 17:5–8). The heat does not fall on Christians less. The difference is that their roots run down past the rock into Christ himself, and he does not dry up.

How can I tell whether my own faith has roots? Roots are invisible, so you cannot tell by how you feel on a good Sunday. You tell by what holds when the heat comes. Has your faith survived a disappointment, an unanswered prayer, mockery, a loss, a season with no feelings at all? Do you keep coming to God when it brings you nothing you can see? Roots grow down in the dark: through steady reading of Scripture, honest prayer, belonging to a church where you are known, and obedience when it costs. If you are not sure, do not panic. Ask God to deepen you, and start putting down roots today.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seeds fell among thorns. The thorns had been cut back, but their roots remained. They grew faster and stronger, taking the light and water, and the plants survived but produced nothing. The last seed fell on good soil.

Some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. The numbers everybody skims are the point. On many scholars’ estimates a normal harvest returned perhaps seven to ten times what was sown (others think more was possible on the best land). Either way, a hundredfold is the kind of harvest people talked about for a generation. Isaac sowed in Gerar and reaped in the same year a hundredfold, and the LORD blessed him (Genesis 26:12).

The arithmetic turned upside down. Read quickly, the story is three failures and one success. Read with the yields in place, it is nothing of the kind. One patch of good ground at a hundredfold repays the whole sowing many times over, path, rock and thorns included. The sower does not come home at a loss; he comes home with more than he can carry. And the good soil is not uniform: among those who truly receive the word the return varies, and no reason is given. Not every believer bears the same quantity of fruit, but every true believer bears fruit. There is no category of good soil that produces nothing.

The harvest of the promised Son. Isaac, the son of the promise, reaped a hundredfold because the LORD blessed him, and the promise to Abraham’s offspring pointed to one offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). So the impossible yield is not luck or technique but the reward of his suffering: out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11). Every hundredfold in the kingdom is a share in what the Father promised his Son.

He who has ears, let him hear. The parable has just described four ways of hearing, and it ends by telling the crowd to do the fourth. The parable is itself a test of the hearer.

Should I compare my fruit with other Christians’? No. The parable expressly allows for thirty, sixty and a hundredfold, and gives no ranking among them. Some believers have great gifts, long lives and wide influence; others are faithful in a small corner for many years, or are ill, or young in the faith. The question is not whether you produce as much as someone else but whether the word is bearing real fruit in you: more love for God and people, more holiness, more trust. Comparison breeds either pride or despair, and the Lord of the harvest is the only one who measures the yield.

On a Tuesday. Think of the Sunday school teacher who wonders whether any of it took, or the parent whose teenager seems all path and rock. The sower does not measure his work by the losses, and neither should you: the good soil will repay it all, often long after you have stopped looking.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the disciples came and said to him, "Why do you speak to them in parables?" And he answered them, "To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you speak to them in parables? Jesus had taught plainly before (chapters 5–7). Now he uses parables to the crowds. Why? And the disciples’ question is itself a mark of good soil: they come to Jesus for explanation rather than assuming they understood or giving up. They are distinguished from the crowd not by superior intelligence but by their posture: they come with their questions, and they are with him when the crowd has gone home.

To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven. The word is mystēria, and the English is misleading. The background is Daniel, where the term describes the king’s dream, which no wise man could reach and God revealed (Daniel 2:28–30). A biblical mystery is not a puzzle but a secret that has been told (Ephesians 3:3), and it is about to be proclaimed from the housetops (10:27). The secret is that the kingdom has come, but like seed: hidden and growing, received by some and rejected by others, until the harvest.

It has been given. The passive points to God as the giver. The disciples were no quicker than anybody else; they had to ask. What separated them from the crowd was not capacity but a gift (11:25–27; 16:17).

The secret has a name. God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:2–3). The secrets of the kingdom are not facts that could be handed over without him. They are the King himself, present in a boat in Galilee (11:27). To be given the secrets of the kingdom is to be given Jesus, and to be told who he is.

But to them it has not been given. To the crowds and leaders who have rejected Jesus (chapters 11–12). And the principle runs both ways: to the one who has, more will be given. Faith grows by use.

Even what he has will be taken away. It describes how attention to God works. A man who uses what he understands finds it opening out; a man who does not finds it closing. Nothing was confiscated. It went unused, and it went.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God hides the truth from people who wanted it. Those who did not receive it had already hardened their hearts (v. 15; 12:24). Nor were the disciples cleverer; their understanding was a gift.

If understanding is a gift, what can I do about it? Ask for it, and use what you have. Those two go together throughout Scripture: God gives wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), and to the one who has, more will be given. So pray before you read the Bible, read it regularly, ask questions of those who know it well, and above all obey what you already understand. Many people want more light while ignoring the light they have. The disciples did not understand everything; they simply kept coming to Jesus and asking.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: to everyone who has will more be given

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: "You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why I speak to them in parables. Parables both reveal and conceal. Those who want to understand will ask, as the disciples do; those who do not will receive a story they can enjoy without being confronted, and that is itself a judgment.

Because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. Physical sight without spiritual sight. The word for understand (syniēmi) runs through this chapter six times (vv. 13, 14, 15, 19, 23, 51): the word taken in and joined to a life.

Matthew and Mark. A reader with Mark open will find a real difference here. Matthew writes that Jesus speaks in parables because seeing they do not see: the parables respond to a condition already there. Mark records so that they may indeed see but not perceive, lest they should turn and be forgiven (Mark 4:12): the parables are given with a purpose. One reads as consequence, the other as intention, and both then quote the same passage of Isaiah, which contains both. Matthew has the human side: they had already stopped their ears. Mark has the divine side: a judicial hardening is truly God’s act. Anyone who tidies the tension away has dropped half the truth, and the New Testament never does.

Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled. Isaiah 6:9–10, from Isaiah’s call: God told him in advance that his preaching would harden a people who would not listen. The passage recurs in John (12:39–41), Acts (28:25–28) and Romans (11:8): the settled apostolic explanation for why Israel’s Messiah was so widely refused, not an accident of history but a text from the day a prophet was commissioned.

Whose glory Isaiah saw. John tells us who was on the throne the day Isaiah received these words: Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41), and he means Jesus. The Lord high and lifted up, whose train filled the temple, before whom the seraphim cried holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:1–3), is the man now sitting in a fishing boat telling stories about seed. The King who sent Isaiah to a dull people has come himself, and meets the same dullness. Refusing the parables is not refusing a teacher. It is refusing the Holy One of Isaiah’s vision.

What it does not mean. Jesus was not trying to prevent people from being saved who wanted to be. The hardening is a judgment on those who have already rejected the truth, and the parables also teach: many who heard them later understood.

Could I be hardened without knowing it? It is possible to grow dull slowly, which is why the warning is given; but a hardened heart does not lie awake worrying that it might be hard, and the remedy is not fear but turning back to him (Ezekiel 36:26). (See Romans 11:7 for the fuller answer.)

verseByVerse.quote: "For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them." But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this people’s heart has grown dull. The verb (epachynthē) comes from the word for thick: the heart has thickened, like skin grown callused until it no longer feels. A callus is not formed by one injury but by the same friction in the same place over a long time. Nobody in this crowd decided one morning to stop understanding. They heard and set it aside, until the setting aside became a habit.

And with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed. They closed their own eyes. The verb is active and theirs. The blindness is their own choice, and God’s judgment confirms it.

Lest they should turn and be healed. This clause has troubled every serious reader, because it sounds as though God withholds sight in case somebody is healed, and it must not be softened. Two things hold it in place. First, the order: before the lest comes their eyes they have closed. The judicial hardening is God’s ratification of a shutting already done. Second, Paul writes of Israel’s hardening and asks whether they stumbled in order to fall, and answers with an emphatic negative: by no means (Romans 11:11). The hardening is real, judicial, and not final. And the tragedy is in the last words: if they turned, God would heal them. He is willing to heal; they are not willing to turn.

And I would heal them. Matthew’s readers have just watched who does the healing. In the chapter before, Jesus healed all the sick who followed him, and then a man blind and mute, so that he saw and spoke (12:15, 22). He called himself the physician who came for the sick (9:12). The healing Isaiah’s God longed to give is standing on the shore in person, looking at a crowd with their eyes shut. And the healing he brings is costly: by his wounds you have been healed (1 Peter 2:24). What the hard heart refuses is not a doctrine but a Healer with wounded hands.

But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. The disciples are the happy ones, not because they are better, but because God has opened their eyes, as the pure in heart shall see God (5:8).

The balance. Pharaoh hardened his heart, and God hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exodus 8:15; 9:12). God is sovereign, and people are responsible. He never pushes into darkness someone who is reaching for the light; as Judge, he gives people what they have insisted on having (Romans 1:24). Hardening never turns away a heart that wants him.

How do I keep my heart from growing dull? A callus grows where the same friction is repeated and ignored, so the guard is to stop ignoring it. When God’s word touches a sore place, respond at once: confess, obey, or at least pray about it honestly, rather than filing it away. Keep company with believers who will speak plainly to you (Hebrews 3:13 says to exhort one another daily, so that none is hardened by sin’s deceit). And keep coming to Christ himself, not only to religious routine. A heart that is regularly brought to him stays soft.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. Hear then the parable of the sower:
verseByVerse.commentary:
For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it. The faithful of Israel died without seeing the Messiah (Hebrews 11:13, 39–40). Peter was there that day, and later wrote: the prophets searched and inquired carefully what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating; it was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but us, in things into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:10–12). The prophets did not fully understand their own writings; they were told it was for others; and the angels are still stooping to peer into it, the verb John uses of the disciple bending to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5).

And to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. The teaching of the Messiah himself. Isaiah wrote about a child born and a government on his shoulder, and died. Micah named the village and never saw the birth. David wrote a psalm about pierced hands nearly a thousand years before anybody in Israel had seen a crucifixion (Psalm 22:16, following the ancient Greek translation; the standard Hebrew text reads like a lion). Every one of them worked in the dark, on material they could not fully read, for an audience not yet born. And a group of fishermen and a tax collector are sitting by the lake listening to the Messiah himself explain a story about seed, casually, in the ordinary daylight of an ordinary day, with the possibility of asking him a further question. Prophets longed for it. Angels bend down to look at it. The Twelve had it as their normal working conditions.

Hear then the parable of the sower. The point is the soils. The sower is first Jesus himself (v. 37), and then those who preach his word after him.

What it does not mean. The Old Testament saints were not lost: Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56), trusting the promise of the same Saviour. The difference is between promise and fulfilment.

Do I really have more than the prophets? In privilege of knowledge, yes. You know the name of the Messiah, the meaning of his death, the fact of his resurrection, and you have the Spirit poured out and the whole Bible in your hands. Isaiah would have given anything for one afternoon with a Gospel. That does not make you holier than Isaiah, but it does make you more accountable, and it should make you far more thankful.

verseByVerse.quote: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When anyone hears the word of the kingdom. The seed is the word: the message of the kingdom, the gospel (Luke 8:11 calls it the word of God).

And does not understand it. Not intellectual failure, but refusal to take it in. The path-hearer’s problem is not that the word was too difficult. Nothing was joined to anything: the seed sat on top of a life it never connected with.

The evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. The verb (harpazō) is violent, used of a wolf snatching the sheep (John 10:12). He takes the word before it can take root, through distraction, doubt, mockery or forgetfulness (2 Corinthians 4:4).

The word he could not snatch. The snatcher has met his match. In the wilderness the evil one came to Jesus and tried to pull the word of God out of his heart, and three times Jesus held it fast: it is written (4:1–11). Earlier that same day he told the Pharisees that no one plunders the strong man’s house without first binding him, and his casting out of demons showed him doing exactly that (12:29). The birds on the path are not the strongest thing in the story. A stronger one has come, who kept the word where we let it lie on the surface, and who takes back from the enemy the people the enemy had taken.

As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy. The detail that ought to unsettle a certain kind of Christian gathering: joy. The visible, immediate, delighted response everybody in Christian work is glad to count. It looks like conversion, and it is the mark of the soil that fails.

What it does not mean. Joy in receiving the gospel is not suspicious; good soil also receives the word with joy (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The problem is lack of root (v. 21). But the passage removes joy from the list of reliable signs, which is a hard word for any ministry that measures by response. The only soil that can be identified with certainty is the one still standing at harvest.

Were the rocky and thorny hearers ever truly saved? Some Christians read them as real believers who later fall away. The more likely reading is that they show a profession that was never new birth: no root, no fruit, and they did not last (1 John 2:19; John 8:31). The response was real as far as it went, but it was not the work of the Spirit that endures. That is why the parable is a warning and not a threat to those who have truly come to Christ: the mark of the good soil is fruit and endurance, and those whom God has truly given new birth he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6).

How do I stop the birds taking the word? By giving the word somewhere to go before anything can carry it off. After a sermon or a time in Scripture, do not rush straight into conversation about something else. Pause, pray over what you heard, write down one sentence, talk about it with someone on the way home, act on it that day. The birds feed on seed that lies on the surface. The more quickly the word is turned into prayer and obedience, the less there is lying about to be taken.

On a Tuesday. If you work with new believers, rejoice in their joy, but care for their roots: teach them, visit them, walk with them through the first heat.

verseByVerse.quote: yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet he has no root in himself. The shallowness is an inner condition. The persecution does not cause it; it reveals what was already lacking. Root depth is revealed by the weather.

And when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word. The scorching sun (v. 6). Trouble comes because of the word: opposition, mockery, loss. Christianity costs something.

Immediately he falls away. Falls away (skandalizetai) means to be tripped up, the verb of Jesus’ message to John: blessed is the one who is not offended by me (11:6). He is tripped, going down suddenly over something he did not see coming, which is what persecution feels like to a person who did not expect the Christian life to cost anything.

The stone that trips. What trips the rocky-ground hearer is, in the end, Jesus himself. Scripture calls him a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8), and the same verb is used: people are scandalised by a Messiah who serves, suffers and calls his followers to take up a cross (16:24). The hearer who received a kingdom without a cross falls the moment the cross appears. But the stone that trips the shallow is the foundation of the rooted. Those who build on him will not be put to shame, and he is able to keep them from stumbling and present them blameless before his glory (Jude 24).

As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word. This person goes further: the word takes root and grows. Nothing in this soil is dramatic.

But the cares of the world. The same word as the anxiety of 6:25–34: money, health, family, work, the future. Not open sin, but ordinary preoccupations that crowd out God.

And the deceitfulness of riches. The word (apatē) means a deliberate deception, a con. Money is a liar: it promises that when there is enough the anxiety will stop, and delivers neither security nor satisfaction (6:19–24; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). And the same soil holds the worry of not having enough and the illusion of having it: one preoccupation seen from either end.

Choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. The plant stays green for years and produces nothing. This person may stay in church for decades. The test is quieter than the others: not have you fallen away, but what is there to show?

I am a Christian and I worry a great deal. Am I thorny ground? Not necessarily. Many true believers struggle with anxiety, and Jesus’ answer in chapter 6 is not condemnation but an invitation to trust the Father who feeds the birds. The thorny ground is the heart where worry and wealth have taken over, so that the word is crowded out and nothing grows. If your worries drive you to pray, to Scripture and to Christ, the word is not being choked; it is being tested. Bring your cares to him by name (1 Peter 5:7), and where anxiety is severe, seek help from your pastor and, if needed, your doctor.

On a Tuesday. Thorns rarely look like enemies. They look like a busy diary, a phone at midnight, a worry rehearsed on the drive to work. Cutting one back, one subscription, one late-night habit, one anxious rehearsal turned into prayer, is not legalism. It is a gardener making room for the word to breathe.

For worship. Christ wore the thorns. The curse that made the ground bring forth thorns and thistles (Genesis 3:18) was pressed into a crown and pushed onto his head. He bore the curse of our choked and fruitless lives, so that the word might grow free in us. And he is the treasure that exposes the lie of riches: in him are riches that do not deceive, the unsearchable riches of Christ, and a peace that worry cannot steal.

verseByVerse.quote: As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. Grasping the word with the heart and joining it to life: holding it fast in an honest and good heart, and bearing fruit with patience (Luke 8:15). A man may know a bridge will hold him and still stand on the bank; the good-soil hearer walks across, like the wise man who hears Jesus’ words and does them (7:24).

He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty. Fruit is the mark of the good soil: a changed life, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), good works (Ephesians 2:10), and other people brought to Christ.

Fruit from the Vine. The fruit of the good soil is not the soil’s own produce. Jesus will say it plainly: as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4). The word received in the good heart is the word of Christ dwelling richly (Colossians 3:16), and what grows from it is his own life showing in ordinary people: his patience, his purity, his love for the Father and for the lost. That is why the fruit glorifies the Father (John 15:8). It is the likeness of his Son appearing in the field.

Where does good soil come from? Not from our own efforts: God makes the soil good, giving a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26) and opening hearts to listen (Acts 16:14), while we receive the word humbly (James 1:21). (See Mark 4:20 for the fuller answer.)

Which soil am I? Now use the parable for the purpose it was given, because it is not a scheme for classifying other people. Jesus told it to a mixed crowd and ended it with he who has ears, let him hear. The only honest question is which soil I am, and it is worth asking with specific tests rather than in a vague fog. The path: is there any real hearing at all, or does it slide off the surface? A usable test is not how much you know but when Scripture last changed a decision you had already made. The rocky ground: is the faith attached mainly to feeling, and does it fold when following costs something? Test it against the last time obedience was truly expensive. What happened? And the thorny ground, which is the one most readers of a commentary should worry about, because it is not rejection but crowding. Nothing is refused; the word is simply squeezed into a smaller and smaller corner by things that are not even sinful. Test it by looking at where your mind goes when it is unoccupied, and at your calendar and your bank statement, which between them are a fairly ruthless account of what you actually care about.

Is the soil fixed? This is the question that decides whether the parable crushes you or helps you, because if it is fixed, the honest reader who finds himself among the thorns has just been handed a life sentence. It is not fixed, and the Bible is emphatic about it. Real soil cannot change itself; people are not real soil. Hosea says to a hard-hearted nation, break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD (Hosea 10:12), and Jeremiah says, break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns (Jeremiah 4:3), which is God commanding the very change the metaphor might seem to rule out. And underneath the command is the promise that makes it possible: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). That is the one thing no field can do for itself, and it is precisely what he undertakes to do.

The remedy for each soil. If you recognise yourself in the first three, the recognition is not a verdict but the beginning of the remedy. If the ground is hard, ask him to break it, and stay where the word is faithfully preached. If the trouble is shallowness, the answer is roots: knowing the Scriptures, and being known by people who will not let you drift. If it is thorns, name them and cut them one at a time, in the strength of the God who promised the new heart.

The lessons of the parable. For preachers and witnesses, the comfort is in what the parable does not say. Three soils out of four came to nothing, and the harvest was still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. The sower is not told to stop scattering, or to blame himself for the path and the rocks. Keep sowing.

For worship. No good heart in the world made itself good. God broke up fallow ground that would never have broken itself, took out hearts of stone and gave hearts of flesh, and the harvest will fill his barns for ever. The fruit is his, the soil is his, the seed is his, and so is all the glory.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–58 — Six More Parables: The Kingdom's Hidden Growth and Coming Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six parables follow the sower: the wheat and the weeds (growing together until the harvest), the mustard seed (a tiny beginning, a great tree), the leaven (hidden work through the whole), the hidden treasure and the pearl (everything sold with joy for the kingdom), and the dragnet (a mixed catch sorted at the end). Then Jesus returns to Nazareth, where his neighbours take offence at him. The weeds are darnel, which looks like wheat until the ear forms, so the master forbids early weeding; Jesus himself says the field is the world, and the reapers are angels, so the final sorting is taken out of human hands. That is not a ban on church discipline (18:15–17): discipline deals with conduct and aims at restoration, while the parable forbids deciding who is finally wheat and who is finally weed before the harvest.
verseByVerse.theology: The mustard seed and the leaven correct the expectation that the kingdom would arrive with obvious power and an immediate separation of righteous from wicked. It begins small, grows slowly, works from within, and will be sorted only at the harvest. It is truly present now (the treasure is in the field, the leaven is in the dough) but not yet fully revealed. These parables call for patience and trust in its hidden growth.
verseByVerse.examples: The treasure and the pearl show the kingdom’s surpassing worth: it is worth selling everything to have it. True conversion is like that: not reluctant sacrifice but glad exchange. Nothing is bought by it, for the kingdom is God’s gift; but the one who has seen Christ’s worth lets everything else go gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He put another parable before them. The second of seven parables in this chapter. It addresses the question every serious believer asks: if the kingdom has come, why is there still so much evil, and why does God not sort the false from the true at once?

The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field. The man is the Son of Man (v. 37). The good seed is his; the field is his.

But while his men were sleeping. That is not an accusation; it is simply night. It locates the sabotage where sabotage always happens: unobserved, leaving no trace until months later.

His enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. The weeds are almost certainly darnel (zizania), a ryegrass that looks almost identical to wheat until the heads form. The enemy sows through the middle of the wheat, so that the two come up interleaved and removing the bad would cost the good. Sowing darnel in another man’s field for revenge was a known crime in Roman law.

The enmity of Eden. The parable is the oldest conflict in the Bible, told on a farm. In Eden God said to the serpent, I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring (Genesis 3:15). Jesus will call the weeds the sons of the evil one (v. 38), the serpent’s offspring, and the sower of good seed is the Son of Man, the woman’s offspring at last. So the darnel in the night is not random malice. It is the serpent striking at the heel of the one promised to crush his head, by planting his own among the Son’s people. And the parable already knows how that war ends: in the harvest of the Son.

Where did evil come from, if God made everything good? The parable gives the answer Scripture gives everywhere: an enemy has done this (v. 28). God is not the author of sin. He made the world very good (Genesis 1:31), and evil entered through the rebellion of the devil and of humanity (Genesis 3; John 8:44). Yet nothing happens outside God’s rule: the enemy works in God’s field, under God’s permission, until God’s harvest. Scripture does not explain fully why God allowed evil, but it shows us where it is going: to the fire, while God brings good out of what the enemy meant for harm (Genesis 50:20; Romans 8:28).
verseByVerse.note: The weeds are probably darnel, a poisonous grass that looks like wheat until the heads form.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, "Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. Darnel is indistinguishable from wheat by eye until the heads form. Only at the ear does the difference show: wheat bears heavy golden grain and bows over; darnel bears small dark seed and stands up straight. And it is harmful: its seed is commonly infected with a fungus that causes dizziness and vomiting (its Latin name, temulentum, means drunken). So false disciples cannot be told from the true at first, and they are not harmless presences.

Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds? The servants know their master sowed only good seed, and they ask the ancient question: if God is good and his work is good, where does evil come from? And with the darnel known, the question is not puzzlement but alarm. The servants have discovered that a field they believed was clean is full of something that looks like food and is not, in quantities they cannot estimate, and it is too late to do anything before harvest. It is the perennial question of the troubled pastor and the puzzled believer.

The church’s experience. False profession can look exactly like real faith in its early stages. That is why it is foolish to declare too quickly that someone is or is not a true Christian, and why the fruit of a life over years matters more than the impression of a season.

Darnel among the Twelve. Jesus lived inside this parable. He chose twelve, and one of them was a devil (John 6:70), and he knew it from the beginning (John 6:64). For some three years Judas looked like wheat to everyone else: when Jesus said at the supper that one of them would betray him, not one looked at Judas; each asked, is it I? (26:22). Jesus did not pull him up. John tells us he washed his feet (John 13:2–11); he shared his bread and let him stand until that night. So when darnel appears in a church, the Lord of the church is neither surprised nor defeated. He has already borne it at his own table, and went on to the cross regardless.

How should I react when someone I trusted in church turns out to be false? With grief, but not with despair or cynicism. Jesus warned us that it would happen: there would be weeds among the wheat until the end. A leader’s fall or a friend’s betrayal does not prove that the gospel is false; it proves that the enemy is active. Where wrongdoing must be dealt with, it should be dealt with properly, and any abuse reported to the proper authorities. Then keep your eyes on Christ, who is never false, and remember that the field is still his.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "An enemy has done this." So the servants said to him, "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" But he said, "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An enemy has done this. Evil is the work of an enemy, the devil (v. 39). The answer is a diagnosis, not an explanation: it says who, and it does not say why.

Then do you want us to go and gather them? The servants want to remove the weeds immediately.

No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. The reasoning is agriculturally exact. Darnel roots interlace with wheat roots; pulling one out lifts the other, and any farmer knew it. And at that stage the servants might mistake wheat for weeds. The refusal is not sentimentality about the weeds but a judgment about what would be destroyed in removing them.

A bruised reed he will not break. A few verses earlier Matthew quoted Isaiah about him: a bruised reed he will not break (12:20). The servants want quick work with the field; the Lord will not risk one weak stalk of his wheat to do it. Of those the Father gave him he says, I have lost not one (John 18:9).

A long history. This parable stood at the centre of the Donatist controversy in North Africa in the fourth and fifth centuries. After the persecutions a rigorist party held that the church must be visibly pure, that clergy who had lapsed were no longer clergy, and that a mixed church was no church. Augustine answered from this passage: the field contains both, the servants are not the reapers, and a perfectly pure church before the harvest is a demand God has refused. The argument has had to be made again and again, because the instinct comes from a sincere love of holiness, and it tends to the same result: the sharper the sieve, the more wheat goes out with the darnel. And the heart has its own reasons. The urge to sort the field early often feeds on the quiet pleasure of being counted among the pure, like the Pharisee who thanked God that he was not like other men (Luke 18:11). Wheat that is sure of itself because it is not like the darnel has forgotten who sowed it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the church should never exercise discipline: Jesus commands it (18:15–20), and Paul tells the Corinthians to remove a man living in open sin (1 Corinthians 5). The field is the world (v. 38), not the church. Discipline addresses conduct; it is corrective, aimed at restoration, and can be reversed. What the master forbids is sorting people by their final identity, which requires seeing the ear before the ear has formed.

Does this mean the church should tolerate sin or abuse? No. The parable is about the world and the final judgment, not about ignoring wrongdoing in the church. Sin among members must be addressed lovingly and firmly (18:15–17; Galatians 6:1). Abuse must never be tolerated or covered up; it must be stopped, the vulnerable protected, and crimes reported to the civil authorities, whom God has appointed to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). What the parable forbids is something else: Christians trying to purge the world of unbelievers by force, or pretending that they can see into hearts as only God can.

parallels.desc: do not pronounce judgment before the time

verseByVerse.quote: Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, "Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn." He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let both grow together until the harvest. Good and evil exist side by side in the world until the end of the age (v. 39). The patience is not laxity toward evil but wisdom about timing. The judgment is not avoided, only delayed.

And at harvest time I will tell the reapers. The reapers are the angels (v. 39). Dried darnel was used as fuel, and the weeds’ end is fire; the wheat is gathered safely into the barn.

Into my barn. The speaker says my barn, and he is the one John announced: he will gather his wheat into the barn (3:12). The harvest has already begun: Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first sheaf as pledge that the rest will follow. The barn is the Father’s house, where he has gone to prepare a place (John 14:2–3).

He put another parable before them. The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. The contrast between beginning and end is the point: an astonishingly small origin, a band of Galilean disciples around a travelling teacher, and a vast destiny.

Why does God wait so long? Because he is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). Every year of delay is another year in which the gospel goes out and people who were living like weeds are brought to new birth. You may be one of them; most Christians can name a time when, if the harvest had come, they would not have been ready. The waiting is hard for those who suffer from evil, and Scripture lets them cry how long? (Revelation 6:10). But the delay is not forgetfulness. The date is fixed, and on that day every wrong will be put right.

parallels.desc: the wheat gathered, the chaff burned

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches." He told them another parable. "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the smallest of all seeds. The black mustard seed, about a millimetre across, was the rabbis’ standard of the very small, as in faith like a grain of mustard seed (17:20). The objection that orchid seed is finer misreads ordinary speech: smallest of all seeds was a proverb, and among seed a man sowed in his field, mustard was the smallest. We say the sun rises without asserting that it goes round the earth.

But when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree. The mustard plant could grow in one season to two or three metres, large enough for birds to perch in. There is something close to a joke in calling it a tree.

So that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches. A great tree with birds in its branches is an imperial image: Nebuchadnezzar’s tree (Daniel 4:10–12), and the cedar God himself will plant, under which birds of every sort will nest (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6). His hearers expected the cedar, a kingdom of obvious magnificence. He gives them mustard: small enough to be overlooked, growing in a vegetable patch, and ending with the nations sheltering in it.

Are the birds a bad sign? Some note that birds stand for the evil one earlier in the chapter (vv. 4, 19), and read these birds as a corrupted church. But the image here comes from Ezekiel and Daniel, where birds nesting in a great tree picture nations sheltering in a kingdom. The same image can mean different things in two different parables, and the good sense is the more likely here.

The meaning. The kingdom began obscurely: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve ordinary disciples. Today the church is found in nearly every nation.

The tender twig. Ezekiel’s great tree began as something tiny: God says he will take a sprig from the top of the cedar, a tender one, and plant it on a high mountain of Israel, and it will become a noble cedar (Ezekiel 17:22–23). That twig is the promised Branch of David’s line, and in Jesus it is planted: a carpenter’s son from a despised village, who will be cut down at Golgotha. And the tree grows because he rose. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me, he will say on another Galilean mountain; go therefore and make disciples of all nations (28:18–19). The birds coming from every direction are the nations coming to him.

He told them another parable. The kingdom of heaven is like leaven. Leaven was a lump of old fermented dough kept from the previous batch to make new flour rise.

That a woman took and hid in three measures of flour. Three measures (sata) was a very large amount, perhaps twenty-five to forty litres, enough to make bread for a hundred people; Sarah used the same for the Lord’s visit (Genesis 18:6). Hid is the word used: the leaven disappears into the dough.

Till it was all leavened. The leaven works invisibly, from within. The kingdom does not change the world chiefly by outward force, the constant temptation of political religion, but by the hidden work of the Spirit in human hearts.

In the flow. Matthew sets these two short parables between the weeds and its explanation. The weeds parable might make the kingdom sound weak; the mustard seed and the leaven answer that fear: small and hidden as it is, the kingdom cannot be stopped.

But leaven usually means evil. Israel swept leaven out before Passover (Exodus 12:15); Paul says a little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6–8); Jesus will warn of the leaven of the Pharisees (16:6). So some read this parable as evil corrupting the church. But Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like leaven, exactly as it is like a mustard seed, and a warning would be a strange thing to introduce that way. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what spreads. Sin does that; so does the kingdom.

Where Christians differ over the leaven and the end of the age. Some (postmillennialists) read these parables as promising that the gospel will gradually Christianise the world, leading to a golden age before Christ’s return. Others (premillennialists) expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth, and many of them read these parables as describing the church age before that reign. Amillennialists, who take the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of the present age, see the parables as describing the kingdom’s sure growth through the whole gospel age, alongside continuing evil (the weeds), until the harvest at Christ’s return. This commentary’s view: amillennial. The kingdom will grow powerfully among all nations, but good and evil grow together until the end. The reason is in this chapter itself: one harvest at the end of the age, with no golden age or second stage set between the growing season and the reaping (vv. 30, 39–40). Christians who love the same Lord and the same Bible hold each of these views, and the hope they share, Christ’s visible return, matters far more than the difference.

Our church is small and seems to be making no difference. Does this parable apply to us? Yes, it was told for exactly that situation. The kingdom always looks small at the start and hidden in the middle. You cannot see leaven working, and nobody admires a mustard seed. God’s measure is faithfulness, not size: a small church that preaches Christ, prays, loves its members and serves its neighbours is the leaven in the dough of its town. Do not despise the day of small things (Zechariah 4:10). Keep sowing, keep praying, and leave the growth to God.

For worship. What a mustard seed our God has sown. A baby in a manger, a carpenter in Nazareth, twelve frightened men, a body in a borrowed tomb, and from that the church of every nation, a tree in whose branches the peoples of the earth have found shelter. The kingdom of our God is growing still, and one day it will fill the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man. Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

parallels.desc: birds nest in the cedar’s branches

verseByVerse.quote: All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. Mark adds the other half: privately to his own disciples he explained everything (Mark 4:33–34).

This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet. Psalm 78:2. Its author Asaph is called a seer (2 Chronicles 29:30). Psalm 78 retells Israel’s history, failures included, so that the next generation might set their hope in God (Psalm 78:7): itself parable-teaching, a long story told to children so they would not repeat what their fathers had done.

I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world. Asaph retold Israel’s history to reveal its meaning; Jesus, the greater teacher, reveals purposes hidden from the beginning. What is disclosed on that beach is older than Israel and older than Abraham. It was settled before anything was made, and God had kept it until now.

What was hidden has a face. Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for your sake, says Peter of the Lamb whose precious blood redeems (1 Peter 1:19–20); Paul calls it the mystery hidden for ages, now revealed: Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:26–27). The one opening his mouth in parables is not only the revealer of the secret. He is the secret.

What does fulfil mean when Matthew uses it like this? Matthew uses fulfil in more than one way. Sometimes a prophet directly predicted an event, such as the birthplace in Bethlehem (2:5–6). Sometimes, as here, an Old Testament person or pattern is filled out and completed in Christ: Asaph taught Israel’s history in parables, and Jesus, the greater teacher, reveals God’s hidden purposes in parables. Both are real fulfilment, because the whole Old Testament is moving toward Christ. When you meet the word, ask whether it is a prediction kept or a pattern completed.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm’s author, Asaph, is called a seer in Chronicles; Matthew calls him “the prophet.”

parallels.desc: I will open my mouth in a parable

verseByVerse.quote: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, "Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field." He answered, "The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he left the crowds and went into the house. The chapter turns on this movement. Verse 1: he went out of the house, and the crowds gathered. Verse 36: he left the crowds and went into the house, and the disciples came. The crowd hears a story; the disciples receive the meaning (v. 11).

Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field. The disciples had not understood it either. What set them apart from the crowd was not that they understood the first time, but what they did when they had not understood: they asked (v. 12).

The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The title is the largest claim in the parable. It comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man is given a kingdom that shall not pass away. The ordinary figure walking a Galilean field is the figure of Daniel’s vision, and he appears again at verse 41, sending the angels to reap. The same person plants and harvests.

What should I do when I do not understand a passage of Scripture? Do what the disciples did: ask. Ask the Lord in prayer, because understanding is his gift. Ask other Christians, your pastor, a good study Bible or commentary. Read the passage again in its context, and compare it with clearer passages on the same subject. Do not pretend you understand when you do not, and do not give up and conclude the Bible is impossible. Some things become clear only over years. Meanwhile, live by what is plain, which is most of it.

verseByVerse.quote: the field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The field is the world. Not the church, but the whole world: the element Jesus defines most explicitly. Read as a picture of the church, the parable becomes an argument for tolerating anything in the congregation, which collides with chapter 18 and with Paul. Read as Jesus defines it, it pictures the whole human community, two kinds of people growing side by side until the end of the age.

The world is his field. It is his by creation (Colossians 1:16), his people in it are his by purchase (20:28), and it is his by appointment: all authority in heaven and on earth is given to him (28:18–19). The sons of the kingdom are not scattered across the world by accident. He has planted them there, in every place where the enemy also sows.

And the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The true heirs; in 8:12 the phrase meant those who seemed to be heirs but were excluded.

The weeds are the sons of the evil one. Those who belong to Satan and share his character (John 8:44; 1 John 3:10). The two kinds are described by parentage, not performance: they have different origins. That is why the sorting cannot be done by inspection. Parentage is invisible, and appearance is not what is being sorted.

And the enemy who sowed them is the devil. Satan works in the world to oppose God’s kingdom, planting his own people among God’s.

The harvest is the end of the age. At Christ’s return (24:3; 28:20); not in any reformation or purge, and no amount of zeal can bring the date forward.

And the reapers are angels. Angels will gather people for judgment (24:31; 25:31). Not us, not the servants who volunteered in verse 28. The parable takes the sorting out of human hands and leaves the church a different job in the meantime: to sow, to pray, to bear fruit and to wait.

What it does not mean. The devil does not create people; he sows them in the sense of influencing and placing them to oppose God’s work.

Can the weeds ever become wheat? The parable describes how things stand at the harvest, not a fixed caste in the growing season. Sons of the evil one are brought out of that condition by new birth, transferred from the domain of darkness to the kingdom of God’s beloved Son (Colossians 1:13; John 1:12–13), and that is why the gospel is preached to all. Some object that the image makes conversion impossible, but the parable is about the end of the age, not the beginning of a life. Every Christian was once a child of wrath like the rest of mankind (Ephesians 2:3).

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe

verseByVerse.quote: Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The kingdom in its present form is mixed; it will not always be.

The Son of Man will send his angels. Jesus is the Judge, and the angels are his (16:27; 24:31). Throughout the Old Testament angels are God’s host. Here they are the Son of Man’s, sent at his order, and few first-century Jews would have missed what that implied.

And they will gather out of his kingdom. Out of his kingdom, not out of the world: Christ’s kingdom already extends over the whole world (28:18), though not all acknowledge it. The harvest is a clearing operation within the King’s own realm.

All causes of sin and all law-breakers. Literally all stumbling blocks (skandala), the noun behind the verb of 11:6 and 13:21: whatever in the field brought others down. Someone will be there partly because of what he did to somebody else’s faith. With them go those who live in lawlessness (7:23).

Will I be judged for causing others to stumble? Jesus takes it very seriously (18:6–7). If you have led others into sin, by example, teaching, pressure or abuse, the first thing to do is repent before God and, where possible, put it right with those you harmed. Christ’s blood covers that sin too, for all who come to him (1 John 1:7). Then guard your life now: think about what your example teaches others, especially the young and weak in faith (Romans 14:13).

parallels.desc: I will sweep away the stumbling blocks
he will send out his angels

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And throw them into the fiery furnace. A picture of hell (Daniel 3:6; Revelation 20:15), and the weeping and gnashing of teeth are anguish with no comfort in it (8:12). Jesus does not soften the end. To those made clean in Christ God’s holy presence is light and joy; to those who cling to their sin to the end, the same holiness is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29).

Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. An echo of Daniel, who is told at the end of his book that the wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars for ever (Daniel 12:3). That comes straight after one of the clearest statements of resurrection in the Old Testament: many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to everlasting contempt (Daniel 12:2). And Jesus sharpens it. Daniel says sky and stars; Jesus says the sun, the thing you cannot look at directly. It is the word used of his own face on the mountain of transfiguration, which shone like the sun (17:2). What happened to him there is promised to them here: freed from all sin, glorified, reflecting God’s glory (Philippians 3:21; 1 John 3:2).

In the kingdom of their Father. The possessive again, and this time it is theirs. The kingdom has been the Son of Man’s throughout the explanation; in the last clause it becomes the Father’s, and the ones shining in it are his children.

He who has ears, let him hear. The same formula closes the explanation as closed the parable: once for the crowd, once for the Twelve. Being on the inside of the door does not exempt anybody from the call to hear.

What it does not mean. The righteous did not earn righteousness by their works; they are made righteous by God’s grace in Christ (Romans 3:22–24). Nor is hell a mere metaphor. Fire, darkness and weeping describe a real, conscious and eternal condition under God’s just judgment (3:12; 25:46).

How can a loving God send people to hell? Because he is also holy and just, and sin is not a small thing to him. Hell is not God losing his temper; it is God giving rebels the just reward of their rebellion, and the weeds of this parable are those who have refused him to the end. The question is not finally whether God is loving enough, but how he can be just and still forgive anyone. The answer is the cross, where the fire of judgment fell on Christ in the place of all who trust him (Romans 3:26). No one goes to hell who wanted Christ. Anyone may still come to him today.

On a Tuesday. Both ends of this verse belong in an ordinary week: the colleague who has no thought of God, for whom you may be the only one praying, and your own dimness on a grey Monday. To the first, the furnace is a reason for urgent love. To the second, the promise stands: you will shine like the sun.

For worship. The righteous will shine like the sun, and every ray of it will be borrowed. The Son of Man is the sun of righteousness who rises with healing in his wings (Malachi 4:2), and the Lamb is the lamp of the city of God (Revelation 21:23). Those who were darnel in the dark will stand in his kingdom as wheat in full light, their faces lit by his.

parallels.desc: the wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky

verseByVerse.quote: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. In a world without banks, and with frequent invasion, people buried valuables for safekeeping. Sometimes the owner died, and the treasure was forgotten.

Which a man found and covered up. Perhaps a labourer ploughing someone else’s field. Nothing suggests he had any interest in treasure that morning. He put a spade into something and stopped.

Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. The key word is joy. He does not sell grudgingly, as a painful sacrifice, but gladly, because the treasure is worth far more than all he owns. The selling of everything is what joy looks like when it has found something worth more than everything. This is conversion at its truest: not the grim duty of giving up good things for God, but the delighted exchange of lesser goods for the supreme good. The kingdom found makes everything else look small: not worthless, but small. It also shows us our hearts. Whatever we could not let go for Christ is the thing we really treasure, the place where our heart already is (6:21), and Jesus does not shame us for it; he shows us something better.

Treasure under a carpenter’s field. The treasure lay for years under ground people walked over every day. Matthew’s chapter ends by showing exactly that. In Nazareth the treasure of the kingdom grew up in a carpenter’s house, and the neighbours walked past him for most of thirty years and saw only a tradesman (vv. 54–57). The kingdom is hidden because the King is hidden: in an ordinary man, a borrowed boat, a village synagogue, and later a crucified body. Those who find the treasure are not those who dig harder, but those to whom it is shown that this ordinary-looking man is worth everything.

In the flow. The treasure, the pearl and the net are told in the house, to the disciples alone (v. 36). The parables told to the crowd showed how the kingdom comes and grows; these ask the listener what it is worth to him.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls. Pearls were among the most valuable things in the ancient world, and a merchant in them would search far and wide, with an eye trained over years.

The two parables. A matched pair with one difference: the treasure is found by accident, the pearl after searching. Some are ambushed by the kingdom in the middle of a working day; some search for years. The parables refuse to make either route the only one. Either way, they give up everything for it with joy.

Is Jesus approving of sharp practice? People stumble over the man’s conduct, and it is worth answering. He finds treasure in a field that is not his, covers it again, says nothing to the owner, and buys the field. Two things. First, a parable makes one point, and its details are scenery rather than moral instruction. Jesus tells stories about a dishonest manager, an unjust judge and a thief in the night, and commends none of them; he takes one feature of each and uses it. Here the feature is joy. Second, the man’s conduct was probably less questionable than it sounds to us. The law of the time seems generally to have attached what was buried in a field to the field itself, so the honest route to the treasure ran through buying the field. He could have pocketed it and walked away; instead he paid for the ground it lay in. Either way, it is not what the story is about.

What it does not mean. We cannot buy the kingdom by giving up our possessions; it is God’s gift (5:3). The parables show its worth and the response it calls for.

Who is the man who sells everything? Most read him as the believer, who gives up all for the kingdom because he has seen its worth. Others read him as Christ, who gave all to buy his people (Ephesians 5:25). The first is the more likely, since the next parable makes the same point about a merchant. But the believer buys nothing that earns grace; the invitation is to come and buy without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1). The price is the glad surrender of everything else to Christ. That surrender is real, though it does not always mean literally selling everything (19:21).

So what do I actually have to give up? Everything, in the sense that nothing may be held back from Christ’s ownership: your money, time, ambitions, relationships, reputation and future all become his. In practice that does not usually mean selling your house. It means holding everything with an open hand, giving generously, dropping whatever he forbids, and being willing to lose anything he asks for. The test is the one in the parable: when you think about what following Christ costs you, does it feel like a loss, or like a bargain? The man in the field was not brave. He was glad.
verseByVerse.note: With no banks, people commonly buried valuables in the ground. Pearls were among the most prized luxuries of the ancient world.

parallels.desc: counting everything as loss for Christ

verseByVerse.quote: who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who, on finding one pearl of great value. The merchant who has handled fine pearls all his life recognises it at once. He does not need to be told what it is worth.

Went and sold all that he had and bought it. The joy is not in the sacrifice. A man who exchanges all he owns for something worth vastly more has traded up. No disciple lets go of everything with an undivided heart, but one man did give up all (2 Corinthians 8:9), and his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so our half-open hands are welcomed for his sake.

Christ the pearl. Many have seen Christ himself as the pearl of great value: Paul counted everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:8). To have the kingdom is to have the King. It is not a package of benefits handed over without him, but life under his loving rule (Colossians 1:13).

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea. A dragnet (sagēnē): a long net with floats and weights, drawn between two boats or pulled to shore, sweeping everything in its path. It is not aimed; it takes what is in the water, and the sorting is done later on the sand.

And gathered fish of every kind. Good and bad. The preaching of the kingdom gathers broadly, and the church should not be surprised that it contains both.

What it does not mean. The church should not water down the gospel to gather more. The net gathers widely because it is offered to all.

How can I value Christ more? Not by trying to work up feelings, but by looking at him. The merchant valued the pearl because he looked at it with a trained eye. Train yours: read the Gospels slowly, notice what Christ is like and what he has done, meditate on the cross, sing about him, spend time with Christians who love him. Ask God to show you his worth (Ephesians 1:17–18). As you see more of him, other things will look smaller, not because they are worthless, but because he is greater.

On a Tuesday. A dragnet does not choose its fish, and neither should we: the neighbour who seems least likely, the relative who has heard it all before. Cast the net wide, and leave the sorting to the Lord.

For worship. Christ is worth more than every pearl in every sea, and he who is worth everything became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). We are not worth a pearl; the Lord whose worth is greater than all the world counted us worth his life.
verseByVerse.note: A dragnet was drawn between boats or to shore, catching everything in its path.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. The law allowed only fish with fins and scales (Leviticus 11:9–12), so a Jewish crew on that beach sorted not merely saleable from unsaleable but permitted from forbidden, the ordinary end of a working day for men in his audience. The bad are sapra, worthless, the word for the bad tree (7:17–18). Sorting was careful and final.

So it will be at the end of the age. The same lesson as the weeds (vv. 40–43), given twice, in the two industries his hearers by the lake knew best, so that nobody could file it as farming imagery and move on.

The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous. In the story the fishermen sort their own catch; in the meaning, the sorting passes to the angels, because only God can judge the heart.

The Fisherman who sends the net. Several listeners had been called from this very work: follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (4:19). They will haul the net of the gospel across the nations, but the net is his, the catch is his, and the angels who sort it are his (13:41). The one who called fishermen on the shore will sort the catch (25:31–32).

How can I be sure I will be among the good on that day? Not by your own goodness, which is never enough, but by belonging to Christ. The righteous in this parable are those made righteous by faith in him (Romans 5:1). The marks that you belong to him are that you trust him, love him, and are being changed by him, however imperfectly; and his promise is that whoever believes in him has eternal life and will not come into judgment (John 5:24). Look to Christ, not into the net. Assurance grows as you look at him and see his work in you.

For worship. Under the law no fisherman could make an unclean fish clean; he could only throw it back. The Lord of the net takes what was worthless and by his own blood makes it clean, so that on the last day it is sorted with the good. Glory to the Judge who first became the cleansing of those he will judge.
verseByVerse.note: Fish without fins and scales were unclean under the law and could not be sold as food.

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Have you understood all these things?" They said to him, "Yes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The warning given twice. The fiery furnace and the weeping and gnashing of teeth are the same words as verse 42.

Have you understood all these things? Understanding is the mark of good soil (v. 23). The verb is the one that has run through the whole chapter, and this is its sixth and last appearance. It is put to them now as a direct question. The chapter has been about the difference between hearing and understanding, and it ends by asking the Twelve which side of that line they are on. He asks not to quiz them but to call them to account for their hearing.

They said to him, Yes. One word, nai, and it should be weighed honestly. Within a few chapters Peter will be called Satan for objecting to the cross; they will argue about which of them is greatest; and by the end of the last night every one of them will be somewhere else. Their yes was not false, and not adequate either (16:9–11): they had grasped the outline and almost nothing of what it would cost.

The mercy in his response. That is a mercy for anybody who has said yes to God and discovered later how little he knew he was agreeing to. Jesus does not correct them. He accepts the answer and adds one more parable, as though to say: good, and there is a great deal more in the store. After his resurrection he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45).

I said yes to Christ but understood so little. Was my faith real? Almost certainly, if you meant it and have kept coming to him. No one understands the gospel fully when they first believe; the disciples did not. Faith is trusting Christ with what you know of him, and the knowing grows. What matters is not how much you understood at the start but that you are still with him and still learning. Jesus accepted the disciples’ small yes and went on teaching them. He does the same with you.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old." And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven. A scribe was a teacher of the law (2:4); one trained (literally discipled) for the kingdom has become Jesus’ disciple. This is very probably Matthew’s self-portrait: he quotes the Old Testament more than any other evangelist, arranges his Gospel around five discourses, stops again and again to say this was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet, alone records this saying, and was a tax collector (10:3), a man who kept records for a living.

Is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old. Treasure here means the storeroom. The old is the law, the prophets and the promises; the new is the teaching of Jesus and the gospel, and a good teacher shows how the new fulfils the old (5:17). He has not replaced his library; he has had something added that makes the rest legible. Augustine summed it up: the New Testament is concealed in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New.

The Master of the house. Jesus has already used the word (oikodespotēs) of himself (10:25). He is the householder who brings out what is new and what is old, supremely on the road to Emmaus, when beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The old treasure was always his, and the new treasure is himself.

And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there. The formula ending the third great discourse (see 7:28).

Is this only for preachers? No. Every Christian is to let the word of Christ dwell in him richly, teaching and admonishing one another (Colossians 3:16), and parents teach their children daily. Your storeroom is filled by reading both Testaments over years, and you bring out of it whenever you encourage a friend, answer a child’s question or comfort someone with a promise. You do not need to be learned; you need to be a disciple who keeps adding to the store.

parallels.desc: not to abolish but to fulfil

verseByVerse.quote: and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, "Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue. Nazareth (2:23), on the Sabbath (Mark 6:2); Luke records a similar visit, perhaps the same (Luke 4:16–30). Their astonishment was genuine: at the start they are not hostile.

In the flow. Matthew goes straight from the parables to Nazareth, and the placing teaches. The parables have said that the same word falls on different hearts, and that the kingdom lies hidden in what looks ordinary. Nazareth shows both at once: the King is standing in their own synagogue, and those who know him best see only a carpenter.

Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? That is the right question, and it has an answer they would not accept: from God.

Is not this the carpenter’s son? Carpenter (tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Mark calls Jesus himself the carpenter (Mark 6:3). They knew him as a manual worker, the kind of man who built houses and mended ploughs, and he may well have worked on theirs. How could an ordinary tradesman have such wisdom? They had no category for the incarnation: God in an ordinary man. Nothing in their picture of the world allowed for the Maker of heaven and earth to have sawdust on his sleeves.

Is not his mother called Mary? They knew his family well. They have the family right, the trade right, the names right, as far as a village could know. Their one great mistake, whose son he really was, is the one Matthew’s first chapter has already corrected (1:18–25).

And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? Jesus’ brothers, most naturally Mary’s later children (see 1:25).
