The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life, have taken them to be either cousins (so Jerome) or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (so the Orthodox). The words themselves most naturally mean what they say: these are the later sons and daughters of Joseph and Mary, the younger half-brothers and half-sisters of Jesus, born, unlike him, in the ordinary way. Matthew has already hinted as much, saying Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (1:25), and Luke calls Jesus her firstborn (Luke 2:7). Some of the Reformers themselves held that Mary remained a virgin, so this is a question on which faithful readers have differed. But Scripture does not require it to protect Mary’s honour; her honour is that she bore and raised the Son of God, and then was a mother to his brothers.

The brothers who came to believe. These brothers did not believe in him during his ministry (John 7:5), yet after the resurrection they are in the upper room praying (Acts 1:14). What turns a sceptical younger brother into a man who calls his own brother the Lord? The risen Christ appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7; see 12:46–50). The conversion of the brothers of Jesus is one of the quiet evidences that he rose.

Does my ordinary work matter to God? Yes. The Lord of glory spent most of his earthly life as a craftsman in a small town, and the Father was well pleased with him before he had preached a sermon (3:17). Work done honestly and for God’s glory is never wasted, whether it is building, cleaning, teaching, caring or keeping accounts (Colossians 3:23–24). You do not need a religious job to serve Christ. Do your ordinary work well, as for him.

For worship. The hands that formed the stars planed wood in Nazareth. The Word through whom all things were made was so ordinary that his neighbours could not see past it, and the brothers who doubted him came at last to worship him as Lord. Glory to the Son who became so lowly that he could be overlooked, and who will be worshipped for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?" And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And are not all his sisters with us? Jesus had sisters too, unnamed. All suggests at least two, perhaps more. Jesus grew up in a large family. And the tense is present: his sisters are with us, still living in the village, perhaps married locally. Their neighbours could point to their houses. Nothing about this family was mysterious, and that was the difficulty.

Where then did this man get all these things? The same question they opened with, asked the second time as an objection rather than an enquiry. That is the whole tragedy of the passage. They began by asking where it came from, assembled a complete and correct account of everything they knew about him, found that it did not explain what they were looking at, and concluded that the problem was with him. The evidence had raised a question their information could not answer. The right response was to widen the information. They narrowed the evidence instead. And there was a heart reason under it. A Jesus who fits what we already know leaves us in control; a Jesus who does not fit calls us to bow. It was easier for Nazareth to keep him small than to let him be Lord, and it still is.

And they took offense at him. The chapter’s stumbling word again: the message to John (11:6), the rocky-ground hearer (13:21), the causes of sin at the harvest (13:41), and now his own village. They did not argue him down. They tripped over the very thing that should have made him easiest to believe: they had known him all his life.

A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household. A proverb: people find it hardest to accept greatness in someone they grew up with. And Nazareth was a rehearsal. His nation would refuse him, and the city would put him out to die. Yet the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (21:42; Psalm 118:22).

How do I live as a Christian among people who knew me before? Expect it to be hard, as it was for Jesus, and do not be bitter about it. Those who remember your past may doubt your change, and some may resent it. Let your life do much of the speaking: patience, honesty, kindness, steadiness over years (1 Peter 2:12). Speak of Christ when there is opportunity, simply and without preaching at people. And remember that many who first took offence later believed. The proof that Jesus was who he said was not argued into Nazareth; it walked out of a tomb.

parallels.desc: his own people did not receive him

verseByVerse.quote: And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he did not do many mighty works there. Mark says he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them (Mark 6:5).

Because of their unbelief. Not because Jesus was helpless. Miracles were signs meant to call people to faith; where people refused to believe, signs had no purpose, and he would not perform for sceptics (12:39). Mark adds that Jesus marvelled at their unbelief (Mark 6:6).

Handle it carefully. The sentence is one step away from a cruelty that has done great damage: miracles run on faith, so if God has not acted, the fault is the thinness of your believing. Some have been told exactly that over a hospital bed. It is not what the verse means. He did not do many mighty works there, and Mark says he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Even there some were healed, so this is no mechanism in which a quantity of faith buys a quantity of power. Elsewhere he heals a paralysed man on the strength of his friends’ faith (9:2), raises the dead, who contribute nothing, and restores people who do not yet know who he is. Faith is the open hand, never the currency.

What unbelief prevented. What Nazareth’s unbelief actually prevented was simpler and sadder. They did not bring their sick to him, because they had already settled who he was: the carpenter’s boy, whose family lived down the road. You cannot receive what you have decided not to come for. The verse describes a town that had made up its mind, not a formula governing answered prayer. If you have prayed and not received, this passage is not an accusation against you. Christ’s healings were signs of a kingdom whose full healing waits for the resurrection, and Scripture nowhere promises that every illness will be cured in this life; Paul, no stranger to faith, asked three times and kept his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

The two times he marvelled. The Gospels record Jesus marvelling twice. Once at a Roman centurion, who believed that a word from Jesus at a distance would heal his servant: truly, with no one in Israel have I found such faith (8:10). And once here, at the unbelief of his own town (Mark 6:6). The outsider trusted him and the insiders stumbled, and Jesus had already said what that pattern means: many will come from east and west to recline with Abraham, while the sons of the kingdom are thrown out (8:11–12). The Lord who knows all things was not unmoved by Nazareth. He wondered at it, as a true man grieved by the hardness of those he loved.

The warning that is here. But take the warning that is truly here, because it is aimed at the sort of person who reads commentaries. The people who got least from Jesus were those who had been nearest to him longest. They were not hostile; they were familiar. They had him filed. A lifetime of church can do the same: the sermon heard before, the passage already known, the quiet assumption that there is nothing new here. Nazareth is what happens when knowing about him has replaced knowing him. The chapter of parables ends with a living picture of the hard path: the people who knew Jesus best did not receive him.

So should I pray for healing at all? Yes. Jesus welcomed the sick, and Scripture tells us to pray for them and ask the elders to pray (James 5:14–15). Pray with honest trust, asking boldly and leaving the answer to his wisdom: your will be done. Sometimes he heals; sometimes he gives grace to bear what remains, as with Paul; always he will heal completely at the resurrection. Use doctors and medicine as gifts of his providence. And never tell a suffering believer that their illness continues because they lack faith.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to make you hungry again for a Christ you may have filed away. Then bring him one real need today, as Nazareth would not.

For worship. In Nazareth his hands were full of healing and almost empty of patients, and still he laid them on the few who came. Familiarity cannot shrink him. To those who have heard of him longest he is as mighty as he was to the crowds of Capernaum, and as willing.

13.theology: The hiddenness and growth of the kingdom. These parables guard against two errors. Against triumphalism: the kingdom grows quietly, like leaven, not by worldly power or force. Against despair: the smallest seed becomes a tree, and a little leaven works through the whole batch. So the church advances through the ordinary means of grace (the word, the ordinances, prayer), not through political power or cultural dominance. The sowing is patient; the harvest will be glorious.
13.examples:
Then: The disciples were living in the mustard-seed stage: a small band of Galileans following a teacher the religious leaders were plotting against. Jesus tells them not to judge the end by the beginning.

Now: Many seasons of church history have felt the same: persecution, secularism, churches full of nominal members. The Sower keeps sowing, the leaven keeps working, the net keeps gathering, and the harvest belongs to the Lord.

14.title: Bread in the Wilderness
14.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, <sup>2</sup>and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>3</sup>For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, <sup>4</sup>because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” <sup>5</sup>And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. <sup>6</sup>But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod, <sup>7</sup>so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. <sup>8</sup>Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” <sup>9</sup>And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. <sup>10</sup>He sent and had John beheaded in the prison, <sup>11</sup>and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. <sup>12</sup>And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. <sup>14</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick. <sup>15</sup>Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves.” <sup>16</sup>But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” <sup>17</sup>They said to him, “We have only five loaves here and two fish.” <sup>18</sup>And he said, “Bring them here to me.” <sup>19</sup>Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>20</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>21</sup>And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>22</sup>Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. <sup>23</sup>And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone, <sup>24</sup>but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. <sup>25</sup>And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. <sup>26</sup>But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, “It is a ghost!” and they cried out in fear. <sup>27</sup>But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>28</sup>And Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” <sup>29</sup>He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. <sup>30</sup>But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” <sup>31</sup>Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” <sup>32</sup>And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. <sup>33</sup>And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.” <sup>34</sup>And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. <sup>35</sup>And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick <sup>36</sup>and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 moves from Herod’s banquet of death, where John’s head is brought in on a platter, to Jesus’ meal of life, where five thousand men are fed in the wilderness. The contrast is deliberate. Herod’s table is supplied by cruelty, vanity and fear. Jesus’ table is supplied by compassion, prayer and the Creator’s power, multiplying what is put into his hands. John dies as the forerunner; Jesus will face his own death; but the meal he gives points beyond death to the feast of the resurrection.

The feeding is the only miracle besides the resurrection that all four Gospels record. Matthew tells it with the exodus in view: a desolate place, bread in the wilderness, the Shepherd feeding his flock. Jesus looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks and gives, the same four actions as at the Last Supper. Then he comes to his disciples walking on the sea, Peter walks and sinks and is caught, and the men in the boat worship him as the Son of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Death of John and the Feeding of the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and fears that John has risen from the dead. Matthew then tells how John died: arrested for condemning Herod’s marriage to his brother’s wife, and beheaded at a birthday banquet to keep a rash oath. Jesus withdraws when he hears the news, but the crowds follow him; he heals them and then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, a meal that looks ahead to the Last Supper and the banquet of the kingdom. The prison was probably Machaerus, a fortress palace east of the Dead Sea, so the banquet and the dungeon may well have been in the same building, and the dancer was a girl, probably in her early teens, used by her mother.
verseByVerse.theology: John’s death is the dark centre of the chapter: the forerunner’s fate anticipates the fate of the one he announced. Herod’s fear is wrong (Jesus is not John) and yet ironically close to the truth, for Jesus will rise from the dead. The feeding shows Jesus as the shepherd-king who gives his people bread in the wilderness, as God gave Israel manna. He takes, blesses, breaks and gives, the four actions of the Last Supper.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples’ protest, that they have only five loaves and two fish, is the protest of faith that has not yet learned whom it is living with. They calculate from what they have; Jesus acts from who he is. His command to bring the loaves to him is the word for every situation where our resources fall far short of the need. The miracle happens not in the disciples’ hands but in his, and twelve baskets are left over. The abundance of the kingdom always exceeds the need.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, and he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Two banquets side by side: Herod’s feast, whose last course is a prophet’s head on a dish, and a meal on the grass where a grieving Jesus feeds a city from a boy’s lunch. Then, in the dark, he comes walking on the sea, speaks the words God spoke from the burning bush, and receives his disciples’ first confession in this Gospel: truly you are the Son of God.

At that time Herod the tetrarch. Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great (2:1). When his father died in 4 BC, Rome divided the kingdom, and this son received Galilee and Perea (east of the Jordan) with the rank of tetrarch, a minor ruler below a king. He ruled Galilee for almost the whole of Jesus’ earthly life, and at the end Pilate sent Jesus to him (Luke 23:12). Jesus once called him that fox (Luke 13:32).

Heard about the fame of Jesus. News of the miracles, and perhaps of the Twelve going out through the villages (10:1–8), had reached the palace. The kingdom of heaven was being proclaimed in Herod’s own territory, and the first thing it did in his heart was not to call him but to haunt him.

In the flow. After Nazareth’s offence (13:53–58), the ruler of Galilee gets Jesus wrong in another way. The question running through these chapters is who Jesus is: the carpenter’s son, John come back, Elijah or one of the prophets (16:14). Matthew lets the wrong answers pile up until men in a boat give the right one (14:33), and Peter states it for them all (16:16).

This is John the Baptist. Herod said it to his servants. His explanation is theologically strange. Resurrection was a doctrine about the last day and the whole people, not about one man coming back in the middle of history, though some were already saying it of John (Luke 9:7) and many expected Elijah to return (Malachi 4:5). Herod seized the rumour because it fitted his fear. It is not reasoning from the evidence; it is a man being visited by what he has done. The man who silenced the prophet cannot silence the memory of the prophet’s voice.

He has been raised from the dead. There is a dark irony in it. Herod’s superstitious terror came close to a truth he never grasped. One greater than John had indeed come, and he would rise from the dead, not as a ghost to frighten a murderer but as the firstfruits of a new creation. Firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, the pledge that the whole crop would follow (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him. John did no miracles in his lifetime (John 10:41). Herod imagined that a John back from the grave would have new powers. Guilt is a busy theologian. It confirms that John was innocent and that the deed was murder, and it supplies explanations faster than reason can check them.

Fear without faith. Herod’s fear was superstition and guilt, not faith. Luke adds that Herod sought to see him (Luke 9:9); when at last he had Jesus in front of him he asked for a conjuring trick, received silence, and treated him with contempt (Luke 23:8–11). Fear of God is the beginning of wisdom only when it brings a man to repentance. Herod’s remained dread.

Is a troubled conscience a good thing or a bad thing? It depends entirely on where it sends you. A conscience that accuses you is God’s mercy, a warning light on the dashboard. Herod’s did its work faithfully: it would not let him forget. The tragedy is that he treated the light as the problem and never went to the one person who could deal with what it was reporting. Two men in the Gospels were tormented by what they had done to an innocent man. Judas carried it alone and was destroyed by it; Peter carried it to Jesus and was restored. If something you did years ago still visits you, the remedy is not distraction or self-punishment but confession to God, and where possible putting it right, and then believing that the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea. A tetrarch was a ruler of part of a divided kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John had been saying to him, "It is not lawful for you to have her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison. Matthew now goes back to explain how John died. John had been in prison since 4:12. Josephus tells us where: Machaerus, a fortress palace Herod the Great had rebuilt on a ridge east of the Dead Sea, a stronghold with luxurious apartments above and cells below. Josephus adds that Herod also feared John’s influence over the people.

For the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great, and so the niece of both her husbands. She had been married to Antipas’s half-brother. On a visit to Rome, Antipas fell for her; both divorced their spouses and married each other. Antipas’s first wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, fled to her father, who later went to war with Antipas and defeated him.

Philip or Herod? The name in this verse has drawn fire, and a reader who has met the objection deserves the answer. Josephus names Herodias’s first husband as Herod, another son of Herod the Great, and says that Philip the tetrarch married Salome, Herodias’s daughter. Some critics have concluded that the Gospels muddled the family. That is not the only explanation, and probably not the best, because the tangle is of Herod’s own making. Herod the Great had at least ten wives and a swarm of sons, and he named a remarkable number of them after himself; there are several men called Herod in this family and more than one called Philip, and Josephus himself gives some of them two names. A son known formally as Herod and familiarly as Philip is entirely possible, and Matthew’s readers, close enough to know the family gossip, would have needed the second name precisely to tell one brother from another. We meet the same convention with the man who wrote this Gospel, called Matthew here (9:9) and Levi in Mark 2:14. It does not touch the point of the passage: whichever brother she left, the marriage was unlawful and John said so. The question cannot be settled beyond doubt from our sources, and honest readers should say so. But where the Gospels can be checked against an independent historian they generally hold up, and an apparent collision, patiently examined, often turns out to be a detail we were missing rather than an error the writer made.

Because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her”. “Had been saying”: repeatedly, not once in a heated moment. The law forbade a man to take his brother’s wife while the brother was alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). And the marriage was built on two divorces that had no ground God recognises; as far as we know, neither abandoned spouse had been unfaithful or had deserted (see 5:32; 19:9). John did not soften it for safety; he said to the ruler’s face what was true. Like Elijah confronting Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21), the man who came in the spirit of Elijah (11:14) stood up to a king and his queen, and like Elijah he found that the queen was the more dangerous of the two.

So also the Son of Man. Jesus himself drew the line from John’s prison to his own cross. Coming down from the mountain of transfiguration he said: Elijah has already come, and they did not recognise him, but did to him whatever they pleased; so also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands (17:12). John was seized and bound for telling the truth, and so would Jesus be, in a garden at night. John’s arrest had been the signal for Jesus to begin preaching (4:12), and John’s chains are a preview of the road he himself would walk, bound and led from Annas to Caiaphas, to Pilate and to this same Herod.

What it does not mean. Not that the pulpit is a place for campaigns on every politician’s private sins. But no class of person is above the seventh commandment, and God’s servants must sometimes speak hard truths to power, at personal cost.

Why did John make a private marriage a public issue? Because it was not private. Herod was the ruler of God’s people in Galilee, and his marriage was a public act that told a whole province that the law of God could be set aside by anyone with enough power. John was a prophet, and a prophet’s office is to say what God says about what is done in the open. He was not gossiping or settling a score; he was calling a man to repentance, and Mark tells us Herod kept going back to listen (Mark 6:20). The aim of rebuke is always the sinner’s rescue. Most of us will never address a ruler, but we will face moments when a friend, a relative or a colleague does something openly wrong, and silence would be the comfortable cowardice. Speak, privately where you can, humbly always, and for his good.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

parallels.desc: the nakedness of your brother’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And though he wanted to put him to death. Mark tells us that Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted him dead, while Herod feared John, knowing he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe; he was greatly perplexed by him, and yet heard him gladly (Mark 6:19–20). Herod’s heart was divided: he wanted the prophet silenced and could not stop going to listen to him. It is one of the most recognisable portraits in Scripture: a man who enjoys sermons and will not obey them.

He feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. Fear of public opinion restrained him, not conscience. Matthew sets the two rulers side by side: in seven chapters the chief priests will want Jesus dead and hesitate for exactly the same reason: they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet (21:46). What holds them back is a headcount, and in both cases it only postpones matters. Both prophets died in the end; and the second time, the death of the prophet was the rescue of the very people who called for it.

But when Herod’s birthday came. A lavish banquet for his nobles, military commanders and the leading men of Galilee (Mark 6:21). If Josephus is right about Machaerus, the feast and the cell were in the same building. The music may well have been audible from the dungeon.

The daughter of Herodias danced before the company. Josephus names her Salome, Herodias’s daughter by her first marriage; she later married her uncle Philip the tetrarch. The scene is often painted as seduction by a grown woman, and the text does not say that. Mark and Matthew call her a korasion, the diminutive, a girl, the same word used of Jairus’s daughter (9:24–25), who Mark tells us was twelve (Mark 5:42). She was probably in her early teens. For a princess to dance before a hall of drinking men was shameful in itself, and the sequel shows what kind of dance it was. And she pleased Herod, who was delighted, very likely drunk, and inflamed. The man who yielded to popular fear now yields to appetite, and between them the two weaknesses will seal John’s fate.

What it does not mean. Not that the girl was innocent, for she asked for it herself. But the heavier weight falls on the adults: the mother who used her child as an instrument, and the stepfather who took pleasure in what he should have stopped. Those who lead the young into sin carry a terrible responsibility (18:6).

Can a person enjoy good preaching and still be lost? Yes, and Herod is the proof. He sent for John, listened to him gladly, was troubled by him, and protected him, and none of it was repentance. Enjoying truth is not the same as submitting to it; being moved is not the same as being changed. The test is not whether you like the sermon but whether you obey the word, especially the part that touches the one thing you are determined to keep. Herod’s one thing was Herodias. If there is one area of your life where you have quietly decided God’s word will not be allowed to reach, that is where Herod’s danger lives. The remedy is to name it to God today and ask him for the grace to let it go.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

verseByVerse.quote: so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. Prompted by her mother, she said, "Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. A rash, extravagant oath, made in drunken excitement before guests. Mark gives the full wording: whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom (Mark 6:23). It echoes King Ahasuerus’s promise to Esther at her banquets (Esther 5:3, 6; 7:2), with everything inverted. Esther used her request to save a people from a murderer; this one is used to murder a prophet. Esther risked her life going in unbidden; this girl is sent in. And Herod had no kingdom to give in any case, only what Rome allowed him. Jesus had warned against careless oaths (5:33–37); here is the kind of mouth he meant.

Prompted by her mother. Mark fills in the gap: the girl went out and asked her mother what she should ask for, and came back in haste with the answer and one addition of her own, at once (Mark 6:24–25). Herodias does not appear at the feast or speak in the hall. She arranged the conditions, waited, and used her daughter as the instrument. Hatred is patient in its own way.

She said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter”. A horrifying request, spoken at a feast. A platter was a serving dish: John’s head would be brought in like a course. And one word in it is pure cruelty: here. Not have him executed, but here, on a dish, now, while the guests are still at the table. It turns a murder into the evening’s entertainment. The one who preached repentance is murdered by the very sins he named.

Should I keep a promise I now regret? Usually, yes. Scripture honours the man who swears to his own hurt and does not change (Psalm 15:4), and a Christian’s word should be reliable even when keeping it is costly or inconvenient. But there is one clear exception, and Herod stands in it: no promise can bind you to sin. An oath to do evil is void from the moment it is spoken, and keeping it doubles the sin rather than redeeming it. If you have promised something wrong, the right course is to confess the rash promise, refuse to fulfil it, and accept whatever embarrassment follows. And if you are not sure whether a promise falls into that category, take counsel from a mature believer before acting.

For worship. There is a King who also made a promise at a table, and it was not rash. On the night he was betrayed he took the cup and promised his blood for the forgiveness of sins (26:28), and he kept it the next day, at the cost of his life, not to save his face but to save ours. He has never said yes to evil, and he has never once broken his word to us. Herod swore and kept his word to destroy a righteous man. Christ swore and kept his word to rescue the unrighteous.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. He sent and had John beheaded in the prison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the king was sorry. The sorrow makes the surrender worse. Herod knew it was wrong, was sorry, and did it anyway: not ignorance or compulsion, but the choice of pride over what is right. And the word king is bitter. In verse 1 Matthew used the accurate title, tetrarch; here he gives the courtesy title Herod ached for. A few years later Herodias pressed him to sail to Rome and ask the emperor for it; instead he was stripped of his tetrarchy and exiled to Gaul in AD 39 (so Josephus). He grasped at a crown and lost the little he had.

But because of his oaths and his guests. This phrase is the anatomy of how a decent impulse gets overruled. His oaths: a rash promise to a dancing girl, which no court would have held him to and any decent man breaks. And his guests, the real reason: the room was full of the people whose opinion made up his standing. So a man who privately admired John, and had taken trouble to keep him alive, had him beheaded before the evening was over. He did not lose an argument with his conscience; he valued the people in the room above the man in the cellar, and it took about a minute.

He sent and had John beheaded in the prison. John, the greatest of those born of women (11:11), the forerunner of the Messiah, was killed at a drunken party to satisfy a vengeful woman and a weak man’s pride. He died alone in a dungeon, without a trial, without a farewell. Another innocent man will be killed by a ruler who knows he is innocent, wants to release him, and gives way to the crowd (27:24). The forerunner went before his Lord in his preaching, and he went before him in his death.

Why did God let John die like that? This is the question every believer asks when the faithful suffer and the wicked feast. Scripture does not pretend it is easy. But it gives us three things to hold. First, God was not absent; John’s life was not taken from God’s hands but placed in them, and precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15). Second, John’s death was not wasted; it is part of the pattern by which the kingdom advances, through the suffering of its servants and supremely through the suffering of its King. Third, the story is not finished. Herod’s banquet was not the last word on John; the resurrection will be. The one who was silenced in a dungeon will stand in glory, and Herod will stand before the Judge. When you see the righteous suffer, do not conclude that God has lost control. Look at the cross, where the worst injustice in history was the very means of our salvation.

On a Tuesday. Fear of losing face leads people to terrible choices, and most of them are small and quick. Where are your guests? Whose opinion is in the room when you decide? In Christ you already have the one verdict that finally matters, so you can afford to lose face: admit a wrong promise or decision publicly rather than compound it, and settle now, before the moment comes, that the opinion of God outweighs the opinion of the table.
verseByVerse.note: Antipas was only a tetrarch, but was popularly called king.

verseByVerse.quote: and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. Matthew narrates it without comment, because no comment is adequate. Evil in power can be grotesque, and Scripture does not look away from it.

And his disciples came and took the body and buried it. Verse 12 is one of the quietest sentences in the Gospel. They came, and that took courage. These are the followers of a man executed for criticising the ruler, walking into a royal fortress to claim the corpse, which is precisely what Joseph of Arimathea will do at another execution, and Mark says he took courage to do it (Mark 15:43). They took the body; the head had gone to Herodias. They buried what there was. When John’s disciples laid their master in the ground, his story on earth was over. When Joseph laid Jesus in the tomb, his was about to begin again on the third day, and in that rising John’s own resurrection was made sure.

And they went and told Jesus. Having done the last thing that could be done for their master, they walked to the one man in the country who had told them who John was. These are the disciples who had complained that Jesus’ followers did not fast (9:14) and carried John’s anxious question from prison (11:2–3). John himself had settled the awkwardness: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30). When their teacher was dead, they knew where to go.

Matthew records no reply. The next verse is: now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew. He said nothing that anybody wrote down. He went away to be alone, which, for the man who had called John the greatest born of women, who was his kinsman (Luke 1:36), and who had stood in the Jordan and been baptised by him, is a more eloquent record than any sentence. And then the crowds followed him round the lake, and he came ashore and had compassion on them and healed their sick, and then fed all of them. On the day he heard.

What do I do with grief that has no explanation? Do what John’s disciples did. They did not first work out why God had allowed it, and they did not pretend it was not terrible. They did the practical things love required, and then they went and told Jesus. Prayer in grief does not need to be tidy. It can be nothing more than telling him what happened. And remember that the one they told was himself grieving. You do not bring your sorrow to a Saviour who is above it, but to one who was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3), and who knows what it is to lose a friend to cruelty.

On a Tuesday. When someone else is grieving, be one of the people who come and carry the body: turn up, help with the practical things, and say little.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. He went to grieve, to pray, and perhaps to step out of Herod’s reach for a while. Mark adds that the Twelve had just come back from their mission and needed rest (Mark 6:30–31). Luke places the scene near Bethsaida (Luke 9:10), on the north-east shore of the lake. Jesus was truly human: he needed solitude, and he grieved. The eternal Son had taken a real human nature, with a body that tired and a heart that ached, so that he might be made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:17).

But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. They walked round the shore and arrived before him (Mark 6:33), and his time alone was gone before it began.

And he had compassion on them and healed their sick. Deep, gut-level compassion: the word splanchnizomai, built on the word for the inner organs, where feeling was thought to live, is the same word as 9:36. In his own grief, Jesus did not turn the crowds away in irritation. He saw their need, and his heart went out to them. His mercy is not contingent on his personal comfort.

Three things for the tired and grieving. First, he grieved. Told that his relative had been beheaded to amuse a dinner party, the Son of God went away by himself. Sorrow is not a failure of faith; it is what love does when it loses something, done here by the only person who never sinned. Second, he withdrew deliberately: solitude was a necessity he arranged, and you are not more robust than he was. Third, and hard: he did not get it. He found several thousand people wanting things from him, and he did not send them away.

What it does not mean. Not a theology of burnout, as though the Christian ideal never rests. After the feeding he dismisses the crowds himself and goes up the mountain alone to pray (v. 23). He got his solitude later that night, and he took it: rest postponed once under pressure, not abolished.

What does this mean for me when the demands never stop? For the parent of small children, the one nursing a dying relative, the pastor, the carer who cannot see the end of it, take all four things together. Grief needs room and is allowed. Withdrawal has to be planned, because it will never happen by accident. Interruptions will come, and compassion rather than resentment is only possible for someone who is not treating exhaustion as a permanent policy. And what is taken from you now must be taken back later, as he took it. And see where the day’s resources came from: he fed a city from a boy’s lunch, and the one place he went for supply was up a mountain by himself with his Father. That is still where it comes from. Ask for help from your church too; the body of Christ exists so that no one carries everything alone (Galatians 6:2).
verseByVerse.note: Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida, at the north end of the lake.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves." But Jesus said, "They need not go away; you give them something to eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is a desolate place. It was evening, late afternoon as the light faded, on the day John’s disciples brought the news. Desolate (erēmos) means wilderness, the same word used of the wilderness where John preached (3:1) and where Jesus was tempted (4:1), and in the Greek Old Testament of the wilderness where Israel wandered. The setting is chosen for us: Israel in the desert, hungry, and God feeding them with bread from heaven (Exodus 16).

A table in the wilderness. In the desert Israel once taunted God with a question: can God spread a table in the wilderness? (Psalm 78:19). They had seen water from the rock, and still doubted he could give bread. On this evening the question is answered in person. The one standing in the wilderness with a hungry crowd is the Lord who fed their fathers with manna, and he is about to spread a table on the grass. The disciples are asking, in effect, Israel’s old question. Jesus is about to give God’s answer, and he will give it with his own hands.

And the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves. This was a sensible plan, though the disciples are usually treated as faithless here. It is the responsible answer, and it has exactly one defect: it gets the crowd off their hands.

But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat”. The pronoun is emphatic: you yourselves. He is putting the crowd’s dinner on the account of twelve men whose whole supply is a boy’s lunch, and John, telling the same day, records that Jesus asked Philip where they could buy bread, to test him, for he himself knew what he would do (John 6:5–6). The impossibility was deliberate. And hold the first clause: they need not go away. The disciples’ solution was dispersal; his was provision.

Does this mean the church must meet every need it sees? No church can do everything, and Jesus himself did not heal every sick person in Israel. But this verse forbids one particular reflex: treating needy people as someone else’s problem by default. Before you say send them away, ask what Jesus has already put in your hands, and whether he might be testing you with this need as he tested Philip. Sometimes the right answer really is to refer someone elsewhere. But it should be the answer of prayer and love, not of convenience. The church’s first instinct toward the hungry, the lonely and the lost should be to bring them closer to Jesus, not to move them along.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "We have only five loaves here and two fish." And he said, "Bring them here to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have only five loaves here and two fish. John’s account adds the detail that changes the arithmetic from small to almost comical. The loaves and fish were not the disciples’ rations. Andrew found them: there is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:9). Barley was the cheap grain, the poor man’s bread. And John’s word for the fish is a diminutive: little fish, the dried or salted sort eaten as a relish with bread rather than as a meal. So what is brought to Jesus is a child’s packed lunch, five small barley rolls and a couple of dried fish, against a crowd of perhaps fifteen thousand. Andrew’s own comment on it is the honest one: but what are they for so many?

And he said, “Bring them here to me”. Four words in the Greek, and they do not ask for more. He asks for the ridiculous thing they have already assessed and dismissed. The miracle does not happen in the disciples’ hands; it happens in his. But their obedience in bringing what seems useless is the first step.

The arithmetic. Most of us do the disciples’ sums by instinct: measure the need, measure the resource, and look for a way to reduce the need. The five loaves were genuinely inadequate, and genuinely all that was required, because the multiplying happened in neither the boy’s basket nor Andrew’s hands. The instruction is not to pretend the loaves are enough. It is to hand them over anyway.

Barley loaves and a greater prophet. Barley loaves have been in this situation before. A man once brought Elisha twenty loaves of barley, and Elisha said, give to the men, that they may eat. His servant said, how can I set this before a hundred men? And the prophet answered, thus says the LORD, they shall eat and have some left (2 Kings 4:42–44). Andrew’s question is the servant’s question. But the answer is different. Elisha has to quote the word of the LORD. Jesus quotes nobody. He takes the loaves into his own hands, blesses and breaks them, and a hundred becomes thousands. The prophet passed on God’s promise of bread. Jesus is the Lord who keeps it.

What it does not mean. Not that if we give God something he is obliged to multiply it into whatever result we want, or that giving is a technique for getting. The boy did not give his lunch as an investment.

But what can my little actually do? Probably much less than you would like, if you mean what it can do by itself. That is the point. The question Jesus asks is not how much you have but whether you will put it in his hands. A widow’s two small coins, a cup of cold water, an hour of listening, a short prayer, a Sunday school class of four children: Scripture is full of tiny things that God made great. You will often never see the multiplication; the boy only saw it because he was there. Give what you have, faithfully and without measuring, and leave the arithmetic to the Lord who owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10).
verseByVerse.note: John adds that the loaves were barley loaves, the bread of the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass. Mark adds that it was green grass, and that they sat in groups by hundreds and by fifties (Mark 6:39–40). Spring, near Passover (John 6:4). And the scene would have reminded any Israelite of a psalm: he makes me lie down in green pastures (Psalm 23:2). The Good Shepherd, who had seen them as sheep without a shepherd (9:36), is making his flock lie down and feeding them.

And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. As the head of a Jewish household did at every meal, Jesus thanked God for the food. The Jewish blessing over bread, in the form later recorded in the Mishnah, ran: blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. The Son of God looks up to his Father before he does what only God can do.

Took, blessed, broke, gave. Matthew’s readers would have recognised the four verbs at once, for Matthew records the sequence again, in the same order and almost the same words, in an upper room on the last night: Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples (26:26). And Luke records them a third time, at a table in Emmaus, where two men who had walked seven miles with a stranger recognised him at the moment he did this, and their eyes were opened (Luke 24:30–31). Three meals, a hillside, an upper room, an inn, and on the third the four movements were enough to identify him without a word. The feeding looks forward to the Lord’s Supper and beyond it to the great banquet of the kingdom (8:11).

And the disciples gave them to the crowds. He could have distributed it himself. What actually happened is that twelve men who had just said the thing was impossible spent the next hour walking up and down a hillside handing out food that would not stop coming out of their own hands. The supply ran through them and did not come from them. That is the shape of all ministry since. Christ provides; his servants carry.

And they all ate and were satisfied. Not a taste, but a full meal. The verb (chortazō) means to eat your fill, the word of the Beatitude: those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be satisfied (5:6).

And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Twelve baskets: perhaps one for each of the disciples who had doubted, or a sign of provision for the twelve tribes of Israel. The baskets (kophinoi) were the wicker baskets Jews carried for food on a journey. And the surplus at the end was far larger than the supply at the beginning. God’s provision is not barely enough. It overflows.

The background. God fed Israel with manna (Exodus 16); Elisha fed a hundred with twenty loaves; Jesus feeds thousands with five, the greater Moses and the greater Elisha. The next morning he said: I am the bread of life (John 6:35). The manna kept a nation alive for forty years and then it stopped, and everyone who ate it died anyway (John 6:49). This bread does not run out, and neither do those who feed on it.

What it does not mean. Not that the people simply shared lunches they had hidden, as some interpreters have suggested. They were in a desolate place, the disciples had only five loaves and two fish, twelve baskets were left over, and the crowd wanted to make Jesus king because of what they had seen (John 6:14–15). That is a response to a sign, not to a picnic. The Gospel writers describe a miracle of creation.

Does this mean God will always give me what I need materially? God has promised to care for his children, and Jesus tells us not to be anxious about food and clothing, because our Father knows we need them (6:25–33). He does provide, usually through ordinary means: work, family, the generosity of the church. But this miracle is not a guarantee that believers will never go hungry; Paul knew hunger and plenty (Philippians 4:12), and Christians in famine and persecution have died poor. What it guarantees is something larger: that the Lord who feeds is present with his people, that he is never short of resources, and that he will give us everything we truly need, above all himself, the bread that lasts to eternal life (John 6:27). Pray for daily bread, work for it, share it, and trust him with the rest.

How does this meal relate to the Lord’s Supper? The feeding is not the Supper, but it points to it. At the Lord’s Table the same Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives, and believers receive him, not in the bread as though it were changed, but truly and spiritually by faith, feeding on his body broken and his blood shed for us (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23–26). To feed on him by faith means this: as you eat the bread, you trust that his body really was given for you, and the Spirit uses that trust to strengthen your union with the living Christ. The hillside teaches us how to come to the Table: hungry, empty-handed, sitting down where we are told, and receiving from his hands. And it teaches us what the Table promises: a day when the whole people of God will sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (8:11), all fed, all satisfied, with baskets to spare.

Can a thinking person really believe this happened? The question is fair, and the answer is not to pretend that miracles are ordinary. They are not, and the disciples knew it as well as we do, which is why they remembered the baskets (16:9–10). But if there is a God who made grain, the earth that grows it and the sun that ripens it, then bread for a crowd is not hard for him; the only real question is whether he was present on that hillside. The Gospels say he was, and they were written within a lifetime of the event, while people who had been there could still be asked. For many people the deeper obstacle is not only the evidence. It is that a Jesus who can do this has a claim on us that a mere teacher does not.

For worship. The same hands that took and blessed and broke the loaves on the hillside would be taken and broken on the cross, and from them flows a supply that a world of sinners has never exhausted. They all ate and were satisfied. One day every child of God will say the same, at the marriage supper of the Lamb, and there will be twelve baskets left over.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with some left over
he took bread, blessed and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. Men (andres) means adult males, the unit normally counted for an assembly in that culture, and Mark, Luke and John all give five thousand men. Matthew alone adds the last four words, and they are not dismissive. The others count men, as was normal; Matthew makes explicit that the real number was considerably higher. He is guarding against an undercount, not making one. The women and children ate too, and the Lord who fed them wanted it recorded.

The scale. The total may have been fifteen or twenty thousand people. That is not a large meeting; it is a city, probably larger than any town on the lake (Tiberias, Herod’s new capital, held perhaps eight or ten thousand), gathered with no notice, on foot, in a place with no food, because they had heard where he had gone. And every one of them ate.

The uncounted at the cross. The people left out of the headcount are the ones Jesus never left out. He took children in his arms and said the kingdom belongs to such as these (19:14). And when the counted men had scattered, it was women who stayed at the cross, looking on from a distance (27:55–56), and women who came first to the empty tomb and were the first to be told he is risen (28:1–7). Matthew’s four extra words on the hillside are a small sign of a large truth about his Lord: the Shepherd who fed the crowd fed every one of them, and those the world’s arithmetic omits were the first witnesses of his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — Walking on Water and Healings at Gennesaret
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight after the feeding, Jesus makes the disciples go ahead by boat and goes up the mountain alone to pray. Through the night they struggle against the wind, and in the early morning Jesus comes to them walking on the sea. Peter walks on the water towards him, sinks when he looks at the wind, is caught, and the disciples worship. They land at Gennesaret, where all who touch the fringe of his garment are healed. He compelled them into the boat because the crowd was about to make him king (John 6:15), and they were struggling exactly where he had sent them.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus walking on the sea shows his lordship over creation: the one who stilled the storm (8:26) now treads on the waves, which the Old Testament says God alone does (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19). Peter walks on the water not by his own power but at Jesus’ word, Come. His sinking and rescue trace the pattern of every disciple’s faith: a bold first step, fear when we look at the circumstances, a cry for help, and rescue by the one who is always within reach.
verseByVerse.examples: After the earlier storm the disciples asked what sort of man this was (8:27); now, on their knees in the boat, they tell him he is truly the Son of God. It is the first time in Matthew that his disciples make this confession, and it looks ahead to Peter’s at Caesarea Philippi (16:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat. The verb (anankazō) is the word for force: compelled, the word Paul uses of forcing people to blaspheme (Acts 26:11). John gives the reason: perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself (John 6:15). Thousands who had just watched a man produce dinner out of nothing could have become an armed rising within the hour, and he got twelve very willing lieutenants off the beach before the crowd could reach them.

While he dismissed the crowds. He refused the crown they offered. Satan had offered him all the kingdoms of the world without a cross (4:8–10); now the crowd offers him Galilee without one. His kingdom would come by way of the cross, not by an uprising, and the crown he would wear in Jerusalem was made of thorns.

He went up on the mountain by himself to pray. Consider the day: the news of John, the crowds round the lake, the healing, the feeding, a movement that wanted to crown him. Then at last he got what he had set out for that morning, and used it to pray. The feeding of a city did not replace his need for communion with his Father; it increased it.

In the flow. The walk on the sea follows straight on from the feeding, and Matthew means the two to be read together. On the hillside Jesus did what the LORD did for Israel in the wilderness, giving bread; on the lake he does what only the LORD does, treading the waters. The crowd wanted a king who would feed them; the disciples are about to meet the King who is God.

Why would Jesus refuse to be made king? Was he not the King? He was, and is. But the crowd wanted a king on their terms: one who would fill their stomachs and drive out the Romans, a Messiah without a cross and a kingdom without repentance. To accept their crown would have been to become a different kind of Messiah from the one the Father sent, and to leave their real enemy, sin and death, untouched. He would be enthroned, but through suffering, and his throne would be at the right hand of God (26:64). The same temptation comes to us whenever we want Jesus for what he can give us in this life rather than for who he is. He will not be that kind of king, because he loves us too much to be so small.

For worship. While his friends were struggling on the sea below, he was on the mountain praying, as he still is: he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). Our safety in the night does not rest on our rowing but on his prayers.
verseByVerse.note: John says the crowd wanted to make him king by force.

verseByVerse.quote: but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves. John says they had rowed three or four miles (John 6:19), about halfway across. Beaten (basanizomenon) is a word for torture, used of the demons pleading not to be tormented (8:29).

For the wind was against them. They were struggling against a strong headwind for hours. Unlike the storm in 8:24, Jesus is not in the boat. And here is the detail that matters most: they were where he had sent them. He put them in that boat, over their objection, and pointed them at the far shore.

And in the fourth watch of the night. Matthew uses the Roman reckoning of four watches, so this is between three and six in the morning, the hours of lowest human resilience. They had got into the boat at evening: some nine hours of rowing into a headwind in the dark, going nowhere. Mark says they were making headway painfully (Mark 6:48).

He came to them, walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea. He alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea (Job 9:8); his way was through the sea, his path through the great waters, yet his footprints were unseen (Psalm 77:19). In Scripture the sea is the deep that only God can master, and Jesus walks on it as its Lord.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was unaware of their struggle during those hours. Mark says he saw them straining at the oars (Mark 6:48). His timing was deliberate. Nor does it mean he walked along the shore or on a sandbar, as some have suggested. The boat was a long way from the land, Peter also walked and sank, and the disciples worshipped.

If I am struggling, does that mean I have taken a wrong turn? Not necessarily, and this passage is the proof. It is a common and comfortable idea that difficulty means you are out of God’s will. On this occasion the headwind was blowing against men who were exactly where they had been told to be, and it blew for nine hours, and the one who sent them was on a hill watching. Hardship can be a sign that you need to repent of something, and it is right to ask. But it can equally be the ordinary weather of obedience. Keep rowing in the direction he gave you, keep praying, and do not read his apparent absence as his indifference. He sees you at the oars.

Why does Jesus so often seem to come so late? The fourth watch tells us he waited until they were at the end of their strength. He was not cruel and he was not careless. He was teaching them what they could not learn on a calm night: that their safety rested on him and not on their rowing. He came when coming would show them who he was. Most believers can look back on a long night when help came at the last possible moment, and see afterwards that it was the right moment. His delays are never desertions, and he is never late by his own clock.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch of the night ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.

parallels.desc: who alone trampled the waves of the sea
your way was through the sea

verseByVerse.quote: But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, "It is a ghost!" and they cried out in fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were terrified, and said, It is a ghost! Mark records a clause Matthew leaves out, among the strangest in the Gospels: he meant to pass by them (Mark 6:48). As ordinary narrative it is baffling. But passing by belongs to one kind of Old Testament scene. Moses asks to see God’s glory and is told God will put him in a cleft of the rock while his glory passes by (Exodus 33:19–22). At Horeb the LORD passed by Elijah (1 Kings 19:11). It is the vocabulary of a theophany, God making himself visible by going past. He came out on the water so that they would look up and see who was walking on it. They did, and concluded it was a ghost.

And they cried out in fear. The word is phantasma, and their reaction is not scepticism but terror. Experienced fishermen screamed, and men who had spent the night fighting a hopeless sea were more frightened by the sight of him than by the wind.

But immediately Jesus spoke to them. He did not leave them in their fear for a moment. What arrives first is a voice across black water: take heart, be of good courage, the word he spoke to the paralysed man and to the woman who touched his garment (9:2, 22).

It is I. In Greek, egō eimi, literally I am. It can simply mean it’s me, and it does. But it is also the name of God revealed to Moses at the burning bush: I AM WHO I AM (Exodus 3:14). And it is God’s own word in Isaiah: I am he; I, I am he who comforts you (Isaiah 43:10–13, 25; 51:12). In John’s Gospel the same two words will get him nearly stoned (John 8:58–59) and will throw an arresting party to the ground (John 18:5–6). Walking on the sea and saying I am, Jesus reveals himself as the LORD.

Do not be afraid. The word God so often speaks when he reveals himself to someone undone by the encounter: to Abraham (Genesis 15:1), to Joshua (Joshua 1:9), to Israel (Isaiah 41:10). First the voice, then the hand. Take heart, it is I, do not be afraid: three short sentences, and the middle one holds the other two up.

Was Jesus really claiming to be God? Taken alone, it is I could be an ordinary greeting. But nothing here is alone. He is doing what the Old Testament says only God does, walking on the sea; he is passing by, the language of God’s self-revelation to Moses and Elijah; he speaks the words of the divine name; and the scene ends with the disciples worshipping him, which he accepts, though every faithful Jew knew that worship belongs to God alone (4:10). Matthew is not leaving us to guess. Some suggest that this is the later church’s belief written back into the story; but Mark, usually thought the earliest Gospel, tells the same scene with the same words (Mark 6:45–52), within the lifetime of those who were in the boat. The man in the boat with them is the LORD who made the sea.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

parallels.desc: when you pass through the waters

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter answered him, "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water." He said, "Come." So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. Only Matthew tells this part of the story. The condition need not be a doubt: the Greek construction treats the thing as real for the sake of the request, so it can be heard as since it is you. Peter has heard the voice and believed it. And he asks for a command, the careful part of a reckless request. He does not ask for the ability or announce that he will try. He asks to be ordered, because he has grasped that a word from this man makes a thing possible, as he has just watched with five loaves.

He said, “Come”. One word, with all authority. The command created the ability to obey it, as Christ’s commands always do, now by the Spirit he has put within his people (Philippians 2:13).

So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. He walked on water. Not far, and not for long, but one man in the history of the world got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake.

Came to Jesus. The direction matters. He goes toward the person who called him, which is the only thing the water was ever going to be crossed for. For a brief moment Peter is doing what Jesus does, where Jesus does it, by Jesus’ word alone. That is the shape of all discipleship.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should demand miracles or take reckless risks to prove their faith. Peter acted on Jesus’ explicit command. Faith obeys Christ’s word; it does not invent its own tests (4:5–7). Wanting an adventure is not the same thing as being sent.

How do I know whether Christ is calling me to step out? Today Christ’s commands come to us in Scripture, not in voices across the water, and the canon is closed. (The canon is the list of books that make up Scripture. Reformed Christians hold that it is complete and that God now guides us through it rather than through new revelations; some believers expect God still to speak through prophecy, and even they agree that any such word must be tested by Scripture, 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21.) So begin there: is the step clearly required or clearly permitted by his word? Much of the time the boat we need to leave is not mysterious at all: the apology we have not made, the witness we have not given, the generosity we keep postponing. Those need no special guidance; he has already said Come. For larger choices that Scripture does not settle, such as a move, a job or a ministry, pray, weigh your gifts and circumstances honestly, seek the counsel of mature believers and your church, and then act in faith. You will not be given a voice, but you will not be left without wisdom (James 1:5).
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records Peter walking on the water.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, "Lord, save me." Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he saw the wind, he was afraid. What actually went wrong was not the getting out. Jesus had said Come. And it was not the wind either: the wind was already blowing when he climbed over the side, and nothing changed in the weather. He sank at the moment the storm became more real to him than the word that had sent him into it. Faith looks at Christ; fear looks at circumstances.

And beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me”. One of the shortest prayers in the Bible, and one of the best. Three words in English, from a man with his mouth full of water and no time to make it respectable, and it was enough. Do not wait until you can compose something better; you will drown politely. Cry out now, in the shape the panic actually takes.

Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him. Immediately: no delay, no lecture first. The rescue comes before the rebuke. The Psalms had sung of this hand: he sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters (Psalm 18:16; 144:7). The hand of God in the psalm is the hand of Jesus on the lake.

O you of little faith, why did you doubt? “Little faith” (see 6:30; 8:26). “Doubt” (distazō) means to waver, to be in two minds, pulled two ways. Peter had real faith, enough to step out of the boat, but it wavered. The order matters. Only after his grip was on him, above the water, with the sinking over, did Jesus say this. The rebuke is real, but that is the tone to hear it in. It is not contempt from the shore; it is the question of a man holding you up. And it is a real question: why? There was no reason to doubt. Nothing had changed except where Peter was looking.

Who sinks. The one man in that boat who failed is the one man who went. The other eleven had a dry night and no story. This particular humiliation is only available to people who attempted something, and the safety of never stepping out of the boat is often just refusal.

Was it presumption if I stepped out in obedience and it went wrong? Perhaps, but do not assume it. This is the passage for anyone who stepped out at Christ’s word and went under: the ministry that did not flourish, the costly obedience that has so far produced nothing but water round the ankles. Sinking is not evidence that the step was wrong. Before you conclude that, check where your eyes have been. Peter’s step was right; his gaze drifted. The remedy was not to climb back into the boat in shame but to cry to Jesus, and to be held. If you are sinking now, the prayer is the same and the hand is the same.

Does little faith mean I am not saved? No. Jesus calls Peter a man of little faith, not a man of no faith, and he catches him. Saving faith is not measured by its strength but by its object. A weak hand that grips a strong Saviour is safe, because the Saviour grips back. Many true believers waver, and Scripture is full of them; the man who cried I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24) was heard. Bring your little faith to him and ask him to increase it. He does not break a bruised reed (12:20).

On a Tuesday. What wind are you staring at today: the bank balance, the diagnosis, the hostile colleague, the news? It may be real, but it is not the most real thing in the picture. Turn your eyes back to Jesus, by opening his word and believing what he says there. And if you are sinking, pray Peter’s prayer: Lord, save me.

parallels.desc: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck
he drew me out of many waters

verseByVerse.quote: And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, "Truly, you are the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. In chapter 8, on this same lake, he was woken in a swamped boat and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (8:26). Here no command is recorded: he steps over the side and it stops. His presence is enough. John adds that immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going (John 6:21).

And those in the boat worshiped him. “Worshipped” (prosekynēsan) means bowed down before him, the word for prostration, the worship the magi gave him (2:11) and the worship Jesus told Satan belongs to God alone (4:10). He does not refuse it.

Saying, “Truly you are the Son of God”. Compare what the same men said after the earlier storm: what sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? (8:27). A question. Now: truly you are the Son of God. A statement, with truly in front of it, offered as worship. Two storms, two responses, and between them the disciples have moved from asking what sort of being he is to telling him what he is, on their faces, in a wet boat, at dawn. The centurion at the cross will say it too (27:54).

The first to say it. Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi is rightly called the turning point, since Jesus receives it formally and builds on it. But his disciples first say these words here, two chapters earlier, all of them together, and their ground is not an insight but a night of terror and rescue. Caesarea Philippi came out of a conversation; this came out of the water.

Still learning. Their understanding was not yet complete. They still did not understand that the Son of God must suffer (16:21–23), and Mark says their hearts were still hardened about the loaves (Mark 6:52). But they had seen enough to worship, and worship is where understanding grows.

What does Son of God mean here? In the Old Testament, Israel and its kings could be called God’s son, meaning chosen and beloved. But the disciples are not using it loosely. They say it while bowing down to a man who walks on the sea and speaks the divine name. Matthew means far more: Jesus is the eternal Son, sharing the nature of the Father, the one the Father himself called my beloved Son at his baptism (3:17). Only the Son knows the Father, and only he can reveal him (11:27). To call Jesus the Son of God is to confess that when you look at him, you are looking at God come to us.

For worship. He is the eternal Son who made the sea, and the Son who came into our boat, took our flesh, and went down into the deepest waters of all on the cross, so that the storm of God’s wrath might cease for us. One day his whole church will be brought safe to the land where they were going, and the confession first made in a wet boat at dawn will be sung for ever: worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:12).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to land at Gennesaret. A crescent of plain on the north-west shore, about three miles by one, between Capernaum and Magdala; the lake was sometimes named after it (Luke 5:1). Josephus calls its fertility extraordinary, with walnuts, palms, figs and olives side by side. And the men of that place recognised him.

The way of the sea. This shore had been named in prophecy. When Jesus first settled in Capernaum, Matthew quoted Isaiah about this very district: the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light (4:15–16). Gennesaret lies in that land. On this morning the light walks up the beach out of the night, and the people run to fetch their sick. Isaiah’s promise had a face and a cloak, and a whole plain came to it.

They sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick. Messengers went out, and what came back was all who were sick, carried on mats from every direction to a beach. Set it beside Nazareth, which asked where then did this man get all these things, and took offence, and Matthew’s verdict was that he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief (13:57–58). Gennesaret asked nothing. It sent runners. The difference between the two places is not information; Nazareth had more of it, years of it. The difference is what each did in the first hour after finding out he was there.

On a Tuesday. Who in your street, your office or your family is sick in body or soul and has never been brought? You cannot heal them, but you can carry them to him in prayer, as the men of Gennesaret carried their sick, and you can invite them to hear him.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. The woman with the bleeding had done exactly this (9:20–22), and the news had spread. Kraspedon is the tassel God commanded every Israelite to wear on the four corners of his outer garment, with a blue cord in it, to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD (Numbers 15:38–40; Deuteronomy 22:12). Jesus very probably wore them, keeping that law like any faithful Jew, and the sick of Gennesaret were reaching for a tassel on the corner of his cloak.

Healing in its wings. The Hebrew word for the corner of a garment, kanaph, is also the ordinary word for a wing. Ruth asks Boaz to spread his wings, his garment’s corner, over her (Ruth 3:9). Matthew does not draw the link himself, but it is a lovely one. The last page of the Old Testament, in the order of our English Bibles, promises: for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2). The crowds were reaching for the corners of the robe of the one Malachi said would rise with healing in them.
