And as many as touched it were made well. Made well (diesōthēsan) means brought safely through, built on the word for being saved. Not most: every one, including whoever got there by being carried. Faith that reaches for the edge of his garment is faith in its least impressive form, and it is enough.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ clothes had magical power, or that relics or objects carry healing power. The power was Jesus’ own, received through faith (9:22). The tassel was only the place where the hand met him.

In the flow. In the next verse a delegation arrives from Jerusalem to complain about unwashed hands (15:1–2). Matthew sets the two side by side: the sick reaching for the tassel of his cloak, and the experts inspecting his disciples’ hands. Both were concerned with touch and cleanness, and only the sick went home made clean.

Should I expect healings like these today? God still heals, and we should pray for the sick with real expectation, as James tells us to (James 5:14–15); many believers have seen remarkable recoveries in answer to prayer. But these mass healings belonged to the arrival of the King. Jesus’ miracles, and the signs given through the apostles, marked out the Messiah and confirmed the new revelation (Hebrews 2:3–4). We believe, as many Reformed Christians do, that the gift of working miracles at will passed with the apostles, and we hold that view charitably towards brothers and sisters who see it differently, including many Pentecostal and charismatic believers who love Christ and expect such gifts today. So pray for healing, boldly. Use doctors gratefully; they too are God’s gift. And when healing does not come, remember that every believer will be made completely well at the resurrection, when every touch of Gennesaret becomes permanent.

For worship. The tassel on his cloak was there to remind an Israelite of all the commandments of the LORD, and he is the only man who ever wore one and kept every commandment it stood for. The sick of Gennesaret reached for the corner of a perfect obedience, and healing came out of it. The same garment would be divided by soldiers at the cross, where he bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, and by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:4–5). His righteousness is the hem we hold, and as many as touch him are made whole.
verseByVerse.note: The fringe was the tassel the law required on the corners of a garment.

parallels.desc: the woman who touched the fringe

14.theology: Christ the true bread from heaven. John 6 says plainly what Matthew implies: the feeding points to Christ as the bread of life. The manna fed bodies for a time; he is the living bread who gives eternal life to all who feed on him by faith. The Lord’s Supper points the same way: at the Table believers receive Christ himself, spiritually and by faith, not in the bread as though it were changed. So the wilderness meal looks back to the exodus, across to the Supper, and forward to the great feast of the new creation. Until then Christ feeds his people in the wilderness of this age.
14.examples:
Then: Five loaves and two fish were laughably inadequate for five thousand men. The disciples knew it, and so did Jesus. He asked for them anyway. What he asks for is never the measure of what he can do with it.

Now: Every pastor, teacher, parent and missionary knows what it is to have too little time, energy, money or skill. This chapter does not promise that resources will always multiply visibly, but it calls us to bring what we have to Jesus and trust him with the rest. The twelve baskets testify that nothing given to Christ is wasted.

15.title: What Defiles a Person
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, <sup>2</sup>“Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat.” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? <sup>4</sup>For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>5</sup>But you say, ‘If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God,” <sup>6</sup>he need not honor his father.’ So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. <sup>7</sup>You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: <sup>8</sup>“‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>9</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’” <sup>10</sup>And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand: <sup>11</sup>it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person.” <sup>12</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” <sup>13</sup>He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. <sup>14</sup>Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” <sup>15</sup>But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us.” <sup>16</sup>And he said, “Are you also still without understanding? <sup>17</sup>Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? <sup>18</sup>But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person. <sup>19</sup>For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. <sup>20</sup>These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. <sup>22</sup>And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.” <sup>23</sup>But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us.” <sup>24</sup>He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” <sup>25</sup>But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.” <sup>26</sup>And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>27</sup>She said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” <sup>28</sup>Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed instantly. <sup>29</sup>Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. <sup>30</sup>And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them, <sup>31</sup>so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. <sup>32</sup>Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” <sup>33</sup>And the disciples said to him, “Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” <sup>35</sup>And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, <sup>36</sup>he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>37</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>38</sup>Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>39</sup>And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 confronts one of the oldest dangers in religion: putting human tradition in the place of the word of God. The Pharisees had built a careful system of ritual purity, with washings, food rules and oral traditions, and treated it as binding as God’s law. Jesus answers that defilement is not outside us but inside. The heart is the problem, and no ceremony can cleanse it; only Christ, by his blood and his Spirit, can.

Then Jesus goes into Gentile territory and meets a Canaanite woman whose persistent faith stands in sharp contrast to the Pharisees’ hypocrisy. She is a foreigner, a woman and from a pagan people, and Jesus commends her great faith, as he had commended the Gentile centurion in chapter 8. The chapter closes with a second feeding, of four thousand on the Gentile side of the lake: the bread of the kingdom is given to the nations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — What Defiles a Person: Tradition and the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem challenge Jesus because his disciples eat without the ritual washing of hands. Jesus answers by showing how their tradition cancels the command to honour father and mother, quotes Isaiah against worship of the lips without the heart, and then tells the crowd that defilement comes from within, not from food. In private he explains to the disciples that what comes out of the heart defiles a person: evil thoughts, murder, adultery and the rest. The washing was not about dirt but a ritual the law required only of priests before the altar (Exodus 30:17–21); the tradition had extended priestly purity to every meal.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy exposes the Pharisees’ deepest error: their oral tradition had come to override the written word of God. Jesus’ example is the Corban rule, by which a man could declare his property dedicated to God and so escape the duty to support his parents: a legal device that kept up the look of piety while breaking the fifth commandment. Isaiah’s word applies: this people honours God with their lips while their heart is far from him. Outward religion without a changed heart is hypocrisy.
verseByVerse.examples: The list in verses 19–20 searches the heart: evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These follow the order of the commandments about our neighbour. Clean hands matter far less than a clean heart, and a clean heart is what only God can give.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, "Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 15 asks where uncleanness really lives and who may come to God’s table. Defilement comes not from food going in but from sin coming out of the heart; then a Canaanite woman asking only for crumbs is praised for great faith, and four thousand are fed on the Gentile side of the lake. The experts who had everything went home offended; the outsiders who had nothing went home fed.

Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem. They came some eighty or ninety miles on foot to a lakeside district in Galilee. Nobody makes that journey to raise a question about hand hygiene. The religious capital has sent a deputation north, perhaps to investigate him, and the opposition that began in 12:14 is now organised.

Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? The tradition of the elders was the large body of oral rules that earlier teachers had built around the law of Moses, to apply it to every situation of life and to put a fence around it, so that no one would break it even by accident. Later rabbis taught, and many Pharisees probably already believed, that this oral law had been given to Moses at Sinai alongside the written law and handed down by word of mouth. It was later written down in the Mishnah, about AD 200. To break it was, in their framework, a serious charge.

For they do not wash their hands when they eat. It was not about hygiene. The washing was a ritual pouring of water over the hands, in a prescribed quantity and order, to remove ceremonial uncleanness picked up from the marketplace, from Gentiles, from unclean objects (Mark 7:3–4). The disciples are accused not of dirty hands but of eating without a rite. And the rite was for priests: the law commands Aaron and his sons to wash hands and feet before they approach the altar, on pain of death (Exodus 30:17–21). The tradition had extended priestly purity to everybody, at every meal, for ever.

A serious idea. The impulse behind it is not contemptible. If Israel was a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6), why should every table not be treated like the altar? And it took one true thing seriously: God is holy, and unclean people cannot stroll carelessly into his presence (Leviticus 10:3; Isaiah 6:5). Jesus will not lower that standard; he will move it from the hands to the heart, which is harder still. That is how human religion usually goes wrong: not by beginning in wickedness but by beginning in zeal and ending by putting its own careful additions in the place of God.

Clean hands and a pure heart. The psalm asked the question the Pharisees were trying to answer with water: who shall ascend the hill of the LORD, and who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart (Psalm 24:3–4). The Pharisees worked at the hands. Jesus will say the trouble lies in the heart. And only one man has ever answered the psalm truly. The one standing in front of the delegation, accused of keeping company with unwashed disciples, is the priest whose hands were clean and whose heart was pure all the way through. He has ascended the hill, and he did it to bring unwashed people with him (Hebrews 10:19–22).

How do I tell a good tradition from a bad one? Ask three questions. Does it come from Scripture, or only from us? Does it serve what God commands, or does it crowd it out? And are we binding it on other people’s consciences, so that someone who does not keep it is treated as less faithful? A church may sing certain hymns, meet at certain times, and follow certain orders of service, and these can be wise and helpful. But the moment they are treated as marks of true godliness, or used to look down on believers who do things differently, they have become the tradition of the elders. Hold your customs with an open hand and God’s commands with a closed one.
verseByVerse.note: The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law. The washing was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? The structure of the reply is exact and devastating. They ask why his disciples break the tradition of the elders; he asks why they break the commandment of God for the sake of their tradition. The same verb is thrown straight back with the nouns exchanged: not evasion, but the same charge at a higher level, putting them on trial in one sentence. And the possessive, used twice in this passage (vv. 3, 6): your tradition. They called it the tradition of the elders, a phrase with weight and distance, as though it belonged to nobody in particular. He calls it theirs. Human, not divine, and they will answer for it.

For God commanded. Jesus treats the words of Moses as God’s own command (compare Mark 7:10, where he says Moses said). What Scripture says, God says, and that is the whole ground on which Jesus judges their tradition.

Honor your father and your mother. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12), which Paul calls the first commandment with a promise (Ephesians 6:2), and the first of those that govern how we treat one another. Honour includes respect, obedience when young, and practical care in old age.

Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die. Exodus 21:17. “Revile” means to curse, to speak evil of, to treat with contempt. God took this so seriously that it was a capital crime in Israel. The two texts are chosen with care: the Ten Commandments, and then the death penalty behind it, so that nobody can suggest a small matter is being inflated.

The Son who kept it. The man who charged them with breaking the fifth commandment had kept it all his life. He grew up in Nazareth and was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51), the eternal Son obeying a carpenter and a village girl. And on the cross, in agony, he provided for his mother, giving her into the care of the beloved disciple (John 19:26–27). No Corban was ever spoken in that household. The one who exposes the Pharisees’ evasion is the only son who never needed one, and his obedience as a son is counted to every child of God who has failed at it.

Does that death penalty still apply? No. Jesus cites it to show how seriously God takes the fifth commandment, and how guilty the Pharisees were in evading it. The civil penalty belonged to Israel’s law as a nation under God, and it expired with that nation’s civil order (the Westminster Confession 19.4; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.4). The moral duty to honour parents still stands for Christians (Ephesians 6:1–3), and its seriousness has not changed. What has changed is that the penalty for breaking it does not now fall on the offender at the hands of the state, and for every repentant child of God it was borne by Christ.

On a Tuesday. How are you honouring your parents? If they are old, their care is a command of God, not an optional kindness. If they are difficult, honour still means respect in speech, patience, and practical help. If they are gone, honour their memory and thank God for what he gave you through them. And if your parents wronged you, honouring them never means pretending abuse was not abuse or putting yourself back in danger; it means refusing contempt and doing them what good you safely can.

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, "If anyone tells his father or his mother, 'What you would have gained from me is given to God,' he need not honor his father." So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God”. In Greek the sentence begins but you say, set against what God said (v. 4): God commanded; but you say. That is the whole controversy in five words. Mark gives the Aramaic word: Corban, an offering dedicated to God (Mark 7:11). Once a son declared his property Corban, it could not be used to support his parents, though, it seems, he could often keep using it himself during his lifetime. It became a legal loophole: a way to escape the duty of caring for ageing parents while appearing pious. The rule meant to honour God’s holiness had been used to dishonour God’s command.

So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. “Made void” means cancelled, nullified, made of no effect. Their human rule had overruled God’s clear command. Mark adds: and many such things you do (Mark 7:13). That is about as strong as language gets, and he says it to the most devout men of their generation, who would have been genuinely shocked to hear it.

The manoeuvre. A man owed his parents support and could not simply refuse, so he found a religious way of being unavailable: the money was dedicated, his hands tied by piety, the duty not neglected but outranked. It survives wherever a religious activity excuses a moral one. I am too committed at church to visit my mother. I am busy with the Lord’s work, which is why my children see so little of me. Each is Corban. The tell never changes: the thing done for God is precisely the thing that lets you off something costly, unglamorous and explicitly commanded.

The one true offering. There is one gift to God that did not rob anyone. Christ was wholly dedicated to his Father, Corban in the truest sense, and the dedication was the very way he loved his neighbour: he loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2). In Christ devotion to God and duty to people meet in one act. Every Corban excuse is exposed by a cross where giving to God and caring for the needy were the same thing.

The principle. Whenever human tradition contradicts Scripture, Scripture must win. This is the Reformation principle of sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority over the church’s traditions, and nothing is to be added to it, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or by the traditions of men (the Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10). The Reformers used this passage against medieval traditions they believed had overruled the word of God, such as the sale of indulgences.

What it does not mean. Not that giving to God is wrong, or that we should not give generously to the church. But no religious giving can replace the God-given duty to care for one’s family, and anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

What if caring for my parents conflicts with serving God? Usually it does not, because caring for them is serving God. Scripture never sets the two against each other. There may be real decisions to make, about money, time, where to live, whether a parent should move in or receive professional care, and faithful Christians will reach different answers. But the question is never whether to honour them; it is how. Talk to them, to your siblings and to your church. Share the load where you can. And if a parent opposes your faith or your obedience to Christ, you must obey God rather than man (10:37; Acts 5:29), while still showing them every honour and kindness you can.
verseByVerse.note: Mark gives the formula its Aramaic name, Corban — “given to God.” Property declared dedicated could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You hypocrites! Hypokritēs was a term of the Greek theatre: the actor speaking from behind a mask. The accusation is that what the audience sees is an exterior built to be read from a distance, while behind it the man’s own face is doing something else. Matthew uses the word far more than the rest of the New Testament together (6:2).

Well did Isaiah prophesy of you. Isaiah 29:13. Isaiah 29 is addressed to Jerusalem, to Ariel, the city where David encamped, in a chapter about a people who cannot read a sealed book. The complaint is not that they had abandoned religion. It is that they were performing it accurately and had gone somewhere else while doing so. Seven hundred years later, a deputation from that same city hears the prophet’s old words read back to them.

This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. They said the right words: prayers, praise, religious language, scrupulous and correct. But their inner life was not given to God. Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). God has never wanted lips without a heart. He has always wanted the heart, and lips that speak from it.

The sealed book opened. The chapter of Isaiah that Jesus quotes does not end in accusation. The same prophecy says that the vision has become like a sealed book to Jerusalem, and then promises: in that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see (Isaiah 29:11, 18). Matthew lets us watch it happen. A few verses after Jesus quotes Isaiah 29 against the experts, crowds bring him the lame, the blind and the mute, and he heals them, and they glorify the God of Israel (15:30–31). The one who exposes lip-service is the one who opens the sealed book and the closed ears.

Does this condemn all church tradition? No. Creeds, confessions and orders of worship can serve the church well, and there is great wisdom in the prayers and hymns of past generations. Traditions become wrong when they are bound on the conscience as if they were God’s commands, or when they override what God has plainly commanded. The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches give tradition authority alongside Scripture; Reformed churches hold that Scripture alone is the final rule, and that every tradition must answer to it. That is the stance of this commentary: we receive the wisdom of the church gratefully, and test all of it by the Bible.

How do I know if my worship is only lip-service? Everyone who sings in church has caught his mind wandering, and that alone does not make you a hypocrite. The danger Isaiah describes is settled, not momentary: religion that has become a performance, kept up for others, with no desire for God behind it. Some signs: you are more concerned with how worship looks than with whom it is for; you feel nothing about God from Sunday to Sunday; and the words you sing never touch what you do. If that frightens you, the remedy is not to stop worshipping but to ask God for a new heart (Psalm 51:10), and then to come honestly, telling him exactly where your heart is.

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." And he called the people to him and said to them, "Hear and understand:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In vain do they worship me. “In vain” is matēn, meaning to no purpose, without effect, uselessly. Not wrongly, and not insincerely. Useless. That is a colder verdict than hypocrisy. These men prayed at fixed hours, fasted twice a week and tithed their herb garden. And the verdict is that it accomplished nothing whatever.

Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. Nobody here has thrown Scripture out; the Pharisees revered it, memorised it and would have died for it. What went wrong is that human material had been promoted into the same category. Once a tradition is taught as doctrine it acquires the authority of the thing it was built to protect, and can then overrule it, as verses 5 and 6 show happening to the fifth commandment. The danger is not irreverence but reverence attached to the wrong object. Paul warns of the same (Colossians 2:20–23).

A note on the quotation. Matthew follows the Greek version of Isaiah 29:13, which reads in vain do they worship me. The Hebrew runs differently: their fear of me is a commandment taught by men. The Greek sharpens what the Hebrew implies. Isaiah’s complaint is that reverence for God had become a matter of learned human procedure, and the Greek states outright what that makes of the worship. Nothing is invented; the emphasis moves.

The LORD they honoured with their lips. Isaiah’s words are God speaking: they honour me, they worship me. Jesus applies them to men who are at that moment rejecting him, and the implication is enormous. The God they honoured with their lips was standing in front of them, and their hearts were far from him. That is why their worship was in vain. God has appointed one way to come to him, and it is through his Son: no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). Worship that goes round Christ, however correct, is the worship of Isaiah 29.

The regulative principle. The Reformed tradition draws from verses like this that God is to be worshipped only in the ways he has appointed in Scripture, and not according to human imaginations and inventions (the Westminster Confession 21.1). In practice that means the parts of a service, reading and preaching the Bible, prayer, singing, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, must come from Scripture, while things like the time of meeting or the shape of the building are left to wisdom. Others hold that whatever Scripture does not forbid is permitted in worship. Both agree that no human rule may be imposed on the conscience as if it were God’s command, and that worship must be shaped by God’s word rather than by our preferences.

And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand”. The turn in verse 10 is a deliberate public act. He has been answering a delegation from Jerusalem; he stops, summons the crowd, and says the next thing to them. The ordinary people, told all their lives that these were the men who understood, are given the answer directly, and asked to understand, the verb running since chapter 13 (13:13–15, 51).

What does it mean that worship can be in vain? It means God does not accept worship simply because it is offered, or because it is sincere, or because it is elaborate. He accepts worship that comes through Christ, from a heart that trusts him, in the way he has appointed. That should humble us and free us. It humbles us because we cannot impress God by effort, beauty or tradition. It frees us because the simplest prayer of a believing child, the plainest service of a small church reading Scripture, singing and praying in the name of Jesus, is not in vain. God is not looking for performance. He is looking for faith.

verseByVerse.quote: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person." Then the disciples came and said to him, "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person. “Defiles” (koinoi) means makes common, unclean, unfit for God’s presence. The Pharisees taught that eating with unwashed hands, or eating unclean food, made a person unclean before God. Jesus says food cannot make a person morally unclean.

But what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person. Words, and the heart from which they come (vv. 18–19; 12:34). Real uncleanness is moral and spiritual, not ritual. The Pharisees’ whole system of defilement faced outward, and the problem was inward.

The touch that runs backward. Under the law, uncleanness was contagious: touch a leper or a corpse and you became unclean. With Jesus it ran backward. He stretched out his hand and touched a leper, and the leper was made clean (8:3). A woman unclean for twelve years touched his garment and was healed (9:20–22). Defilement could not flow into him; holiness flowed out of him. That is why he can say that nothing going in defiles. In his kingdom holiness is no longer kept by distance from the unclean. It is given by contact with him.

Then the disciples came and said to him, Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying? “Offended” (eskandalisthēsan) means scandalised, made to stumble. Jesus had swept away a central part of their purity system in one sentence. The disciples seem anxious; it is never comfortable to watch your teacher offend the most respected men in the nation. Jesus’ response is not an apology but a deepening (vv. 13–14).

What about the food laws? The claim that Jesus is speaking only about handwashing needs qualifying, because Mark, telling the same scene, adds a sentence Matthew does not: thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). (The KJV reads this phrase as purging all meats, part of Jesus’ own sentence about digestion; most modern Bibles take it as Mark’s comment, which the Greek allows.) A reader with both Gospels open may feel the two pulling in different directions. They are not. What Jesus says here is the principle; Mark supplies the conclusion the principle was always going to force. And the conclusion was not obvious even to the men in the room. If Peter had understood that afternoon that all foods were clean, he would not have needed a sheet let down from heaven three times, years later, before he would eat with a Gentile, and he still argued with the voice that told him to (Acts 10:9–16). The church would take years, a vision, a council and a good deal of correspondence to work it through. So both writers are right, and the difference between them is the difference between a seed and its fruit. Matthew, probably writing for Jewish readers, records what Jesus said. Mark, probably writing for Gentiles among whom the question had become urgent, tells his readers where it led.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament food laws were wrong. They were God’s commands for Israel, teaching the difference between clean and unclean and setting Israel apart from the nations (Leviticus 11:44–47). But they were symbols pointing to inner purity, and they are fulfilled in Christ. They were not abolished but fulfilled: the picture has given way to the thing it pictured, for Christ now makes people clean within and sets them apart for God himself (Hebrews 9:9–14; Colossians 2:16–17). Christians are free to eat any food with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), while taking care not to make a weaker believer stumble (Romans 14).

Should I worry about offending religious people? Not when the offence comes from the truth. The disciples were troubled that the Pharisees were offended, and Jesus did not retract a word. We should never offend needlessly, by rudeness, pride or careless speech, and Paul tells us to give no offence to Jews or Greeks or to the church of God in matters of freedom (1 Corinthians 10:32). But the gospel itself offends people who are trusting in their own goodness, and no amount of tact will make it otherwise. The question to ask is not whether someone was offended, but whether what offended them was Christ’s word or our manner.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Israel was pictured as God’s planting, the branch of his planting, the planting of the LORD that he might be glorified (Isaiah 60:21; 61:3). The Pharisees and their teaching were not planted by God, however ancient and elaborate, and they will be removed in judgment. What God did not plant cannot last; what he plants cannot be uprooted.

The planting of the Father. Jesus says my heavenly Father. The planting that will stand is the Father’s, and Jesus will name its centre: I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser (John 15:1). Jesus is the Branch himself, and those planted by the Father are those grafted into him. So the question is not whether a teacher is ancient, learned or respected. It is whether he is rooted in the Son. Every system of religion that grows beside Christ instead of from him is a plant the Father did not set, and it will come up at the root.

Let them alone. Told that the Pharisees were offended, he does not explain or try again. Leave them. It is no licence to give up on people: the man saying it wept over Jerusalem and prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). But it means something. There is a point where further argument is not owed, where a man has seen enough and hardened. Paul says the same: after warning a divisive person once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him (Titus 3:10). It is a permission about religious leaders, not about the lost. For the disciples it means: do not follow them or seek their approval.

They are blind guides. The two words do not go together. A guide is hired precisely because he can see the road, and this one cannot. The Pharisees saw themselves as a guide to the blind (Romans 2:19). Jesus says they are blind themselves. Matthew will use the phrase again in chapter 23, where it becomes a refrain (23:16, 24).

And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit. A proverb, and the consequence is put with no cruelty at all. Not the guide only. The teacher of error is rarely its only casualty.

How do I know if my teacher is a blind guide? Test what he says by Scripture, as the Bereans tested even Paul (Acts 17:11). A faithful teacher points you to Christ and his finished work, not to himself or to a system of extra rules. He submits his own words to the Bible, explains it rather than adding to it, and lives in a way that matches what he teaches. Watch for warning signs: a teacher who is always adding requirements God did not give, who cannot bear to be questioned, who treats Scripture as a springboard for his own ideas, or who makes the gospel about something other than sin, grace and Christ. Read your Bible for yourself, belong to a church that is accountable, and do not follow anyone you could not follow with your Bible open.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "Explain the parable to us." And he said, "Are you also still without understanding?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us”. Peter calls it a parable. Verse 11 is not a story but a plain statement, with nothing hidden in it. Peter files it as a riddle because, raised on food laws God himself gave, he cannot believe it means what it appears to mean. He is wrong about the form and right about the size of it. Peter, as spokesman, asks for the meaning, and asking is good (13:36).

And he said, Are you also still without understanding? A gentle rebuke, and the word in it is the chapter 13 word. “Without understanding” (asynetoi) is built on the verb that ran through the parables: they do not understand; the one who hears the word and understands it; and at the end, have you understood all these things? To which the disciples had answered yes (13:51). That was two chapters ago. Here the same men are told they are still without understanding, and the adverb does the work. Their yes had been honest, and it had been thin. And the little word also puts them, for a moment, in the same column as the crowd and the Pharisees. After all his teaching, the disciples were still thinking about purity in the Pharisees’ way. Old habits of thought die hard. But Jesus explains, patiently.

Slow learners. It is a mercy that Matthew records this. These men were slow, and if, as the church has long held, Matthew was one of them, he put his own slowness in the book. The hero of his Gospel is the Teacher who would not give up on them. The Lord who could have chosen quick minds chose these, so that the church would know its understanding is his gift and not its talent.

Is it wrong to need things explained again? No. Jesus’ rebuke is real, because the disciples had been given so much, but he does not refuse to explain. He goes straight on to teach them. Some believers feel ashamed that they still do not understand parts of the faith they have heard for years, or are afraid to ask in Bible study in case they look foolish. Ask anyway. Ask your pastor, ask a mature friend, ask God as you read. The only thing worse than being slow to understand is pretending you understand when you do not.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled. The physiology is deliberately plain: in at the mouth, through the gut, out of the body. At no point does it pass through the heart. Whatever a food is, it never touches the part of a person where defilement happens.

The mouth in which no deceit was found. If the mouth shows the heart, there has been one mouth in history that showed a perfectly clean one. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22, quoting Isaiah 53:9). From that heart came words of eternal life (John 6:68), never a lie, never a slander, never a careless word. Jesus is not only diagnosing the human heart in these verses. He is the one exception to the diagnosis, and that is why he can cure it. The clean heart we lack he possessed, and his righteousness is credited to all who trust him. Scripture’s word for this is justification: the guilty are pronounced righteous before their hearts are clean, on the ground of Christ’s perfect record, which is counted as theirs (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). The cleansing of the heart then follows, as the Spirit begins to make them what God has declared them to be.

But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart. In Scripture the heart is not the seat of the emotions as against the head. It is the whole interior control room: thinking, willing, deciding, loving, remembering. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (Proverbs 4:23). The mouth is simply the outlet where it becomes audible (12:34).

The significance. The Pharisees located defilement outside the person and stayed pure by avoiding the unclean. Jesus says you cannot stay pure by avoiding the world, because you carry the source of impurity in your own heart (Ezekiel 36:25–26).

So should Christians not bother avoiding bad influences? We should, but for the right reason. Scripture tells us to flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22) and warns that bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33). Avoiding temptation is wise, because temptation feeds what is already in the heart. But it is not what makes us clean. The person who has cut out every bad film and every worldly friend can still be proud, bitter and unloving, because the root was never outside. So guard your eyes and your company, yes, and do not mistake that for holiness. Holiness begins with a heart made new by the Spirit and kept close to Christ.

Is Jesus not simply saying that the inside matters more than religion, as many people now believe? He is saying something far more searching. Many today agree that rituals do not make a person good and that what counts is the heart. Jesus agrees about the rituals, and then turns the argument round: the heart is not the good part of us that religion gets in the way of; it is the source of the trouble (15:19). That is hard news for the religious person who trusts his observances, and just as hard for the irreligious person who trusts his sincerity. Both are looking for something in themselves to rest on. Jesus offers neither of them a better technique. He offers himself, the one who makes the heart new.

On a Tuesday. When you sin this week, resist the instinct to blame what was around you, the traffic, the tired children, the colleague, and ask instead what it showed you about your heart. Then ask God for a clean one.
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean.”

parallels.desc: out of the abundance of the heart

verseByVerse.quote: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For out of the heart come evil thoughts. First, and the source of all the rest: evil thoughts, the inner reasonings, plans and intentions of the heart. Sin begins in the mind before it becomes action (James 1:14–15). The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? (Jeremiah 17:9).

Murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. The list follows the order of the second table of the Ten Commandments (the commandments about our neighbour): the sixth (murder), the seventh (adultery and sexual immorality), the eighth (theft) and the ninth (false witness and slander). Sexual immorality (porneia) is every kind of sexual sin outside the marriage of one man and one woman (5:32), the marriage Jesus himself grounds in God’s making of us male and female (19:4–6). Slander (blasphēmiai) is speech that damages others or insults God: the tongue that never touched an unwashed loaf can be defiled by a single sentence.

But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone. These are what defile a person: not food, but sin. Clean hands and a dirty heart are defiled; unwashed hands and a heart made new are not. The whole elaborate handwashing tradition could not address the real problem of human defilement, because it addressed the wrong organ.

In the flow. Matthew at once puts the argument to the test. The very next scene takes Jesus to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman, everything the purity rules taught a Jew to keep away from, comes to him (15:21–22). If uncleanness came from outside, he should avoid her. Because it comes from the heart, and he is the one who cleanses hearts, he can meet her, and he finds in her great faith.

If the trouble is my heart, how can it ever be changed? This is the hardest question in the chapter, and it must not be left hanging. If the heart is the very thing doing the wanting, I cannot repair it with itself. This is what the older theologians meant by total depravity, and the term is often misheard. It does not mean every person is as wicked as he could possibly be; it means there is no part of us, mind, will or affections, that the corruption has not reached, so there is no clean corner left to start the repairs from. So the cure cannot be a better tradition, a stricter rule or a firmer resolution. It has to be a replacement. And God promised exactly that, centuries before this argument: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezekiel 36:26). That is not reform; it is transplant. It is the Spirit’s work, purchased at the cross toward which this whole Gospel is walking. Jesus is not telling you to try harder at the impossible. He is telling you where the disease is, so that you will stop treating your hands and bring him your heart.

Am I really changed if I still find these things in my heart? Yes, if you hate them and fight them. A new heart is not yet a perfect heart. The old sinful nature remains in believers until death, and the Christian life is a lifelong war between the flesh and the Spirit (Galatians 5:17; the Westminster Confession 13.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.2). What changes at new birth is that sin no longer reigns: you now grieve over what once pleased you, confess what you once excused, and want God more than you want the sin. Finding evil thoughts in yourself does not prove you are unconverted. Being untroubled by them would be far more worrying. Keep confessing, keep fighting, and keep looking to Christ, whose righteousness, not your progress, is your standing before God.

For worship. The Lord who sees every evil thought in us did not stand at a distance with a list. He took that list upon himself. He who knew no sin was made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that hearts which produced murder, adultery, theft and slander might be washed, sanctified and justified in his name (1 Corinthians 6:11). He did not come to wash our hands. He came to give us new hearts, and he paid for them with his own.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–39 — The Canaanite Woman and the Feeding of the Four Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman cries out for her demon-oppressed daughter. After testing her faith with silence and a hard saying, he heals her daughter and commends her great faith. Then, on the Gentile side of the lake, he heals many on a mountain and feeds four thousand from seven loaves and a few fish. Matthew calls the woman a Canaanite, the old name of the nations Israel was to drive out, so that the reader feels the distance before she cries Son of David. The second feeding is not the first told twice: Jesus himself distinguishes the two (16:9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus’ apparent reluctance toward the Canaanite woman, his silence, his word about being sent to the lost sheep of Israel, and the hard saying about dogs, is best understood as a test that draws out her faith, not as real exclusion. Her answer, yes, Lord, asking only for crumbs, is a model of faith: it does not demand or claim rights, but presses through apparent refusal on the strength of the Saviour’s character. Jesus calls it great faith.
verseByVerse.examples: The second feeding parallels the first but takes place in the largely Gentile Decapolis. The first fed a Jewish crowd, with twelve baskets left over, perhaps recalling Israel’s tribes; the second feeds a crowd of the nations, with seven baskets, a number that may suggest completeness. The Messiah who came first to the lost sheep of Israel is already spreading his table for the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. Gentile territory on the Mediterranean coast, in modern Lebanon (11:21). This is the furthest Jesus goes from Jewish territory in the Gospels. Tyre and Sidon are Phoenicia, old pagan soil that Israel had never really possessed. In the Old Testament they are bywords: Jezebel, the Sidonian princess, brought Baal into Israel. Straight after the Jerusalem delegation’s complaint about handwashing, and having declared that food does not make people unclean, he goes among the people Israel considered unclean.

Greater than Elijah in Sidon. Jesus had already pointed to this region in his first sermon at Nazareth: there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, but he was sent to none of them except a widow of Zarephath, in the land of Sidon (Luke 4:25–26; 1 Kings 17). That woman was a Gentile mother in a famine, with a handful of flour and a son who later died, and the prophet gave her bread that did not run out and gave her son back alive. Now one greater than Elijah walks into the same country, and another Gentile mother comes to him for her child. Elijah had to stretch himself on the boy and cry to the LORD. Jesus will heal at a distance, with a word.

And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out. Matthew’s word for her is deliberately archaic. Mark calls her a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth (Mark 7:26), the ordinary description. Matthew calls her a Canaanite, the Old Testament name of the nations Israel was commanded to drive out. Matthew wants the reader to feel the full distance between this woman and the covenant before she opens her mouth. And yet Rahab, another Canaanite woman, is already in Jesus’ family tree (1:5).

And was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David”. A Canaanite, using Israel’s messianic title, correctly, in Gentile country, while back in Galilee the scribes who owned that title were arguing about whether his men had washed properly. She recognises who Jesus is, as the blind men did (9:27). And have mercy: she knows she has no claim on him. Her faith begins with who he is, not with any merit of her own.

My daughter is severely oppressed by a demon. She pleads for her daughter, not for herself. She does not argue about whether she deserves help; she simply names him and names the need. That is always the starting point of prayer.

What does severely oppressed by a demon mean? The Gospels describe people under the cruel control of evil spirits, often with physical or mental suffering as a result, and Jesus always treated this as real and always had authority over it (4:24; 8:28–34). It is not simply an old word for illness, for the Gospels distinguish the two (4:24). Nor should we think every trouble today is demonic. The New Testament warns us that we wrestle against spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12), but it gives believers armour, not anxiety: the truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, the word and prayer. A Christian indwelt by the Holy Spirit cannot be owned by a demon, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast north of Galilee. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician; Matthew uses the old name Canaanite, Israel’s ancient enemies.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, "Send her away, for she is crying out after us." He answered, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he did not answer her a word. A startling silence, the hardest moment in the episode. She asks and receives nothing; she asks again and gets what sounds like a closed door. His silence was not a refusal but a test that would make her faith shine, and the outcome proves it. And the Lord who kept silent toward her would one day cry to his own Father, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? and receive no answer (27:46). He bore the final silence of God himself, so that no one who cries to him will ever meet it.

And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us”. They found her annoying and embarrassing. Whether they meant grant it or simply be rid of her, they had no compassion for her. It is the same instinct as the evening of the five thousand: send them away (14:15). Persistent need that complicates the journey is always tempting to dismiss.

He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”. The same principle as 10:6. Jesus’ mission during his earthly ministry was first to Israel, the people of the covenant. This was God’s order: to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16). The woman was outside that mission. And yet the statement of the mission is a context, not a ceiling. She will press past both the silence and the mission statement.

Did Jesus come only for the Jews? His earthly ministry was directed to Israel, as he told the Twelve (10:5–6), because God’s promises came first to them. The mission to all nations came after the resurrection, when he sent his disciples to make disciples of all nations (28:19). Yet even here he blesses a Gentile woman, a foretaste of the other sheep he must also bring, so that there will be one flock, one shepherd (John 10:16). From the very beginning God promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Israel first was always the road to the world, never a wall against it.

How do I keep praying when God is silent? Watch what she does, because it is the most instructive thing in the chapter. She does not withdraw offended, which most of us would call self-respect. She does not argue that the arrangement is unfair. She keeps coming, and she never once rests her case on herself. There is no protest that she deserves better, no account of how long she has waited. Her whole argument is about what he is like. If you are praying into silence, that is the shape to copy: not louder, and not a better case for your own deserving, but persistence, with the plea fastened to his character rather than your merit. Jesus told a parable precisely so that we would always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Silence is not his last word.

On a Tuesday. Take the disciples’ side of the scene: the person whose need is inconvenient to us may be the one Christ has come north to find.

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel
a servant to the circumcised, that the Gentiles might glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: But she came and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, help me." And he answered, "It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But she came and knelt before him. She would not be put off. She came closer, past the silence and past the disciples, and bowed down before him. The verb is the worship word, prosekynei. A Canaanite woman on her knees in Phoenicia, doing what the Pharisees of Jerusalem had never done.

Saying, “Lord, help me”. The simplest prayer, stripped of all argument and claim. She drops the title Son of David, which belonged to Israel and had not moved him, and appeals simply to him as Lord. She does not dispute his mission; she simply keeps her need in front of him.

And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs”. A hard saying. The children are Israel; the bread is the blessing of the Messiah’s ministry; the dogs are Gentiles, and Jews sometimes called Gentiles dogs as an insult. But the diminutive matters. Kyōn is the dog of the streets, a scavenger, and that is the word used when dog is an insult: do not give what is holy to the dogs (7:6). Jesus uses kynarion, a diminutive, probably the little dog that lives in the house. This is not a pack outside the gate but a family at a meal with a pet under the table. What is said is not you are vermin but the children eat first, a statement about order, not worth. Mark adds the word: let the children be fed first (Mark 7:27). The woman hears it instantly, which is why her reply works.

The difficulty, honestly. The difficulty should not be dissolved entirely. He ignored her; he told her his commission did not extend to her; and when she knelt and said Lord, help me, he answered with a proverb about dogs. No word study makes that gentle, and readers who feel the shock are reading correctly. What resolves it is the outcome: within two verses he calls her faith great, grants her request without qualification, and heals the girl that hour. He was not refusing her. He was drawing something out of her, and what came out is the finest reply anybody gives him in the Gospel. And the one who spoke of children and little dogs is the one who turns outsiders into children: to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God (John 1:12).

Why would Jesus test someone who was already desperate? Because the test was for her good and for ours. Gold is tested by fire not to destroy it but to show it is gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). Her faith was already there, given by God; the test brought it into the open, strengthened it, and made her an example to every generation of the church. And the test was never as hard as it sounded, because the one testing her already intended to give her everything. When God allows hard things in the lives of his people, he is not looking for an excuse to say no. He is preparing a greater yes. We do not always see the purpose at the time, but we can trust the heart of the one who sets the test.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table.

verseByVerse.quote: She said, "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." Then Jesus answered her, "O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed instantly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, Lord. Her reply begins with one small word, and everything turns on it. Nai, kyrie: yes, Lord. She agrees, and that is the whole foundation of her argument. She does not dispute the order he has described or claim it is unfair. She accepts his words and takes the place he has given her.

Yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. She has stayed inside the picture he offered and found that it contains her. If the household is as he says, there is a floor under the table, things fall onto it, and the little dog that lives there eats them. Nothing has to be taken from the children. She asks only for what drops, and she understands that his power is so great that a crumb of it will heal her daughter.

Twice in this Gospel. Twice somebody argues with Jesus and wins, and both times it is a Gentile. Neither wins by disputing him: the centurion accepts that he is unworthy (8:8), this woman that she is not a child of the house, and both press through on what they have grasped about him.

Then Jesus answered her, O woman, great is your faith! In the Gospels Jesus speaks of great faith in exactly two people: this woman, and the centurion, of whom he said that not even in Israel had he found such faith (8:10). Both are Gentiles, both are pleading for somebody else, and neither sees Jesus perform the healing. The disciples were often called men of little faith (8:26; 14:31; 16:8). This woman’s faith was great because it was humble (she claimed nothing), persistent (she would not give up), and confident in Jesus’ power and mercy (she was sure that a crumb would do). Matthew does not say why he went north to Phoenicia, but by the end of the scene a reader may well think it was to find her.

Be it done for you as you desire. Jesus gives her exactly what she asked, without qualification, and her daughter was healed instantly, at a distance, like the centurion’s servant, from that hour.

Does great faith mean I will always get what I ask? No. Her faith was great not because it forced Jesus’ hand but because it trusted his heart. Faith is not a technique for obtaining outcomes; it is reliance on Christ. She asked for something that was in line with his compassion and his power, and he granted it. Sometimes believers with great faith pray for healing and do not receive it in this life, as Paul did not have his thorn removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). That is not proof of weak faith. Great faith asks boldly, humbly and persistently, and then trusts the Lord with his answer, knowing that whatever he gives will be good.

Is it wrong to argue with God in prayer? Not when, like this woman, we agree with his word and plead his own character rather than our deserving: Lord, you are like this, so please do this. (See Acts 22:19 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. His table is so rich that its crumbs heal, his mercy so wide that there is more than enough for outsiders like us, and he delights to praise the faith he himself has given. We who were once far off, without hope and without God in the world, have been seated not under the table but at it, as children, by the grace of the Son of David.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. Mark places this in the Decapolis, the mainly Gentile region east of the lake (Mark 7:31). He had left Jewish territory at verse 21 and has not come back. The crowd that follows was probably largely Gentile.

In the flow. Chapter 15 now repeats the pattern of chapter 14 on the far side of the border: crowds healed, then a feeding in a desolate place (14:14–21; 15:30–38). She asked for crumbs from the table; on this mountain the Gentiles are given the whole meal.

And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. Matthew has used that pairing once before, at the opening of the Sermon on the Mount (5:1): the same two verbs, the same posture of authoritative teaching. On that mountain he taught. On this one he heals, and Matthew records no word at all.

And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others. The list is Isaiah’s in substance: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isaiah 35:5–6). Jesus sent that passage back to John in prison as evidence that the promised age had begun (11:5). Here it happens in bulk on a hillside, on the wrong side of the lake, among the nations.

And they put them at his feet, and he healed them. Not brought them to him, which is what Matthew usually writes. They were put down, which tells you these were people who could not stand, carried some distance by others, and laid on the ground in front of a seated man. No preaching is recorded and nobody is asked anything. They were put down at his feet, and picked up again whole.

Why did Jesus heal so many, when he does not heal everyone today? These healings were signs that the King had come and the new creation had begun, exactly as Isaiah promised. They were previews of the resurrection, when there will be no lame, blind or mute at all. God still heals in answer to prayer, but he has not promised to heal every illness now, and believers still suffer and die. We do not believe the gift of miraculous healing at will continues in the church as it was given to Christ and the apostles, though we hold that view charitably towards brothers who differ. The reason is that in the New Testament such signs are tied to Christ and his apostles and to the confirming of their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). What does continue is what these healings pointed to: the King who has authority over every disease, and the promise that every one of his people will be raised whole.

On a Tuesday. Lay your needs at Jesus’ feet today in prayer, and the needs of those who cannot bring themselves. Some people will only come to him if they are carried. Whom could you carry?
verseByVerse.note: Mark places this in the Decapolis, the Gentile region east of the lake.

parallels.desc: the lame leap and the mute sing

verseByVerse.quote: so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, "I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that the crowd wondered, and they glorified the God of Israel. The words of praise suggest who they were. The qualifier of Israel is what an outsider adds, distinguishing this God from the gods he grew up with. So the people on that mountain were very likely Gentiles, and Matthew signals it by the way they worship rather than by stating it. It is the moment the prophets foresaw: many peoples saying, come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob (Isaiah 2:2–3).

Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd”. The word is physical (splanchnizomai, 14:14), not pity considered at a distance. Outside the parables, the Gospels use it only of Jesus, and here it is used of a Gentile crowd.

Because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. These people had camped on a hillside in Gentile country for three days, and whatever food they brought ran out. Some had come a long way (Mark 8:3). Their hunger for him had outlasted their bread.

And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way. The concern is not spiritual and he does not dress it up as such. He is thinking about people collapsing on the walk home. The last thing on his mind before they disperse is whether they will get home without falling over. Jesus cares about bodies.

Does Jesus care about my ordinary practical needs? Yes. This verse is one of the plainest proofs. The Son of God, who had just healed every kind of disease, was concerned about whether people had enough to eat for a walk. Our Father knows what we need before we ask him (6:8), and we are told to cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). Nothing in your life is too small or too ordinary to bring to him: the bills, the car, the meals, the long walk home. That does not mean he will always provide in the way we expect. It does mean he is never indifferent.
verseByVerse.note: “The God of Israel” may suggest a largely Gentile crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples said to him, "Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?" And Jesus said to them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven, and a few small fish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd? One of the most astonishing sentences in the chapter, and it should not be smoothed over. These are the same men, the same twelve who, not long before, had gathered twelve baskets of leftovers on a hillside where five loaves had fed a crowd of much the same size. And they ask the question as though it had never happened.

Two feedings, not one. Some have found this so implausible that they argue the two feedings are one story told twice. Matthew’s answer is that Jesus himself distinguished them: a chapter later he asks whether they remember the five loaves for the five thousand and the seven for the four thousand, and how many baskets each time (16:9–10), and rebukes them for learning from neither. The implausibility is real, and it is in the men rather than the record. That is a quiet argument for the Gospels’ honesty. If, as the early church said, Matthew was one of the Twelve, he describes his own lapse of memory without softening it.

Is the LORD’s hand shortened? The disciples’ question has been asked before, in the wilderness. Moses, faced with a hungry nation, said to God, where am I to get meat to give to all this people? And the LORD answered him: is the LORD’s hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not (Numbers 11:13, 23). The disciples stand where Moses stood, and the one they are asking is the LORD who answered him. His hand is not shortened. It has just been laid on the lame, the blind and the mute of the Decapolis, and in a moment it will take seven loaves and break them for thousands.

How many loaves do you have? As at the first feeding, Jesus starts with what they have, not with what they lack; the rebuke comes later (16:8–11). (See Mark 8:5 for the fuller answer.)

They said, “Seven, and a few small fish”. More than last time, and a smaller crowd, and still nothing like enough. They had improved slightly on the arithmetic and not at all on the conclusion.

Why do I forget God’s past help so quickly? Because we are like these disciples. We believe after the miracle and doubt before the next one; each new need feels as if there had never been any previous provision. The remedy Scripture gives is deliberate remembering. Israel was commanded to remember the way the LORD had led them (Deuteronomy 8:2), to set up stones as memorials, to teach their children. The Lord’s Supper is itself a commanded act of remembrance. Keep a record of answered prayers and past mercies, tell them to others, and when a new crisis comes, read them back to yourself before you start to calculate. Faith remembers what grace has done; unbelief only counts what is in the bag.

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground. As at the feeding of the five thousand (14:19), though there is no mention of green grass this time; perhaps it was later in the year. The same Shepherd seats his flock.

He took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples. Then the sequence, the same as before and the same as it will be at the Last Supper: took, gave thanks, broke, gave (14:19; 26:26). The second verb here is eucharisteō, giving thanks, rather than the blessing of chapter 14. It is the word from which the church later took the name Eucharist for the Lord’s Supper. Before he does what only God can do, the Son thanks his Father.

And the disciples gave them to the crowds. Again the men who had just asked where bread could possibly come from spent the next hour handing it out. They distribute what they cannot produce.

What it does not mean. Not that this meal was itself the Lord’s Supper, or that the bread became something other than bread. The pattern points forward to the Table, where believers receive Christ spiritually by faith, and backward to the manna in the wilderness. Every meal Jesus gives is a sign of the greater gift of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they all ate and were satisfied, and they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. The two feedings differ in a way invisible in English and decisive in Greek. At the five thousand the twelve baskets are kophinoi, small stiff wicker baskets of the sort a Jew carried his own food in when travelling, so as not to depend on Gentile provisions. Here the seven are spyrides, large hampers, big enough to hold a man: the basket Paul was let down the wall of Damascus in (Acts 9:25). The two words are used consistently, in Matthew and in Mark, and in Jesus’ own recollection at 16:9–10. That is not how a duplicated story behaves. And the numbers may be saying something too. Twelve may recall Israel’s tribes. Seven may suggest completeness, and some have seen in it the seven nations of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:1). Twelve baskets on the Jewish shore; seven on the Gentile one.

Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. Matthew adds the same four words he added at the first feeding (14:21), and both times he is spelling out what the round number leaves out. The actual crowd was perhaps eight or ten thousand people.

Why does it matter that there were two feedings? Because it shows the heart of Jesus is the same for Gentiles as for Jews. The first feeding fed Israel in the wilderness, as the manna had; the second fed the nations, on the far shore, after a Canaanite woman had asked for crumbs and been given far more. Together they say that Christ is the bread of life for the whole world, and that the table of the kingdom has room for every people. If you are not Jewish, this is your feeding. You were the crowd on the far side of the lake, and he would not send you away hungry.
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets is different from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand, and could mean a large hamper.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after sending away the crowds. This time he dismissed them with their needs met: healed, taught and fed. He sent them away only when they were ready to go.

He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan. Matthew has Magadan, Mark has Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10), and some later manuscripts of Matthew, followed by the KJV, read Magdala. None can be identified with certainty. The likeliest account is a stretch of shoreline with more than one landmark, named differently by different people. Nothing hangs on it.

The end of an arc. He left Jewish territory at verse 21; now he crosses back, and the first thing on the other side is the Pharisees and Sadducees asking for a sign (16:1). Gentiles who had nothing glorified the God of Israel; the men who had everything met the boat and asked for evidence. The great commission of chapter 28 is not a new idea. It is the conclusion of what these chapters have been showing all along.

For worship. The Lord crossed the lake and crossed the boundaries, and his compassion had no ethnic limit. The boundary between Jew and Gentile that the Pharisees guarded so carefully was already giving way under the feet of the Messiah, who would soon tear it down in his flesh and make the two one new people (Ephesians 2:14–16). He is the Shepherd who has other sheep, and he will not rest until every one of them is home.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Magadan is uncertain; Mark names it Dalmanutha.

15.theology: The corrupt heart and the new heart. Matthew 15:18–19 is one of the plainest statements in the Gospels that the evil which defiles comes from within, from the heart that Jeremiah called deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9). Reformed theology calls this total depravity, meaning not that every person is as wicked as possible, but that sin has reached every part of us, mind, will and affections, while God’s common kindness restrains it. So the remedy must go as deep as the disease: not education, ceremony or moral effort, but the new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26. That is the Spirit’s work of new birth, purchased by the cross of Christ.
15.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ tradition had become a way of looking devout while avoiding the cost of obedience. The Corban rule let a man appear generous to God while neglecting his parents. Jesus shut the loophole.

Now: Every generation finds ways to honour God with the lips while keeping the heart back: sound doctrine without holiness, church attendance without costly love, giving without generosity. The Canaanite woman shows the way back: no credentials and no performance, only humble faith in the mercy of Christ. That is always enough.

16.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. <sup>2</sup>He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’ <sup>3</sup>And in the morning, ‘It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. <sup>4</sup>An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” So he left them and departed. <sup>5</sup>When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. <sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>7</sup>And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” <sup>8</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said, “O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? <sup>9</sup>Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>10</sup>Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>11</sup>How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>12</sup>Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” <sup>14</sup>And they said, “Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” <sup>15</sup>He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” <sup>16</sup>Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah!
