For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. <sup>18</sup>And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. <sup>19</sup>I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” <sup>20</sup>Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. <sup>21</sup>From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. <sup>22</sup>And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” <sup>23</sup>But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>24</sup>Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>25</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>26</sup>For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? <sup>27</sup>For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. <sup>28</sup>Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Peter confesses Jesus as “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, and Jesus calls the confession a gift of the Father and promises to build his church on the confessing apostle. Then he turns at once to the cross: the Christ must go to Jerusalem and die, and Peter, who has just made the highest confession in the Gospel, is called Satan for refusing it.

The pairing is deliberate. You cannot confess Jesus as the Christ without receiving the cross. The church advances not by cultural power but behind a King who goes to a cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Sign of Jonah, Peter's Confession, and the Keys of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven. Jesus refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah, and warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus blesses him, declares he will build his church on this rock, gives him the keys, and then forbids them to repeat the confession until the cross can show what kind of Christ he is (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The section is a study in reading. Men who can forecast the weather cannot read the moment they are standing in (vv. 1-4), and the only sign they will get is a grave and an empty tomb. The leaven warning (vv. 5-12) names two ways a faith is brought under human management: the Pharisees added to God's word until their tradition outranked it, the Sadducees subtracted from it until nothing supernatural was left, and verse 12 calls the two one teaching. Then Peter gives the answer that fits what they have seen, and Jesus promises that he himself will build his church on that confession.
verseByVerse.examples: The crowds reach for the biggest names they have, John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, and every one is a forerunner, a signpost rather than the destination. Peter offers the only category that fits the evidence. And the leaven warning is spoken to the Twelve about themselves: not a licence to hunt heresy in other people but a question about which way your own faith drifts.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. He answered them, "When it is evening, you say, 'It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 16 is the hinge of the Gospel. Men who can read the sky but not the Son of God are promised only the sign of Jonah: a grave and an empty tomb. The disciples are warned about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees; Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ; and Jesus begins to say plainly that he must suffer, and calls every disciple to take up his cross. A crucified King, a church that cannot die, and a life found by being given away for him.

And the Pharisees and Sadducees came. Normally rivals (see 3:7), they now join forces against Jesus. They agreed on almost nothing (Acts 23:6–9; see v. 12), and shared opposition to Jesus united them.

And to test him. “Test” (peirazontes) is the word used of the devil tempting Jesus in the wilderness (4:1, 3). It was the devil’s own kind of request: prove yourself on our terms.

They asked him to show them a sign from heaven. Not another healing, which they had already explained away (12:24), but a spectacular sign in the sky, too large to be disputed: Elijah calling down fire (1 Kings 18:38), or manna falling again. They had already asked for a sign and been refused (12:38–39). What they wanted was one that would compel belief without requiring trust.

Come down from the cross. The devil set him on the pinnacle of the temple and told him to throw himself down, so that angels would catch him (4:5–7). He refused then, and he refuses now. And the demand will come once more, at the very end, from the same leaders: let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him (27:42). He stayed on the cross, and that refusal was our salvation. The sign from heaven they wanted would have proved his power and saved no one. The sign he chose was to stay where he was until the work was finished, and then to be raised by the Father on the third day.

He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’”. A red sky in the evening meant good weather the next day. The capacity to read signs is not missing in these men; what is missing is the willingness to read the one in front of them.

Textual note. Verses 2b–3 (“When it is evening … the signs of the times”) are missing in some important early manuscripts. A reader with an open Bible will notice the brackets. Two of the oldest and best copies of Matthew, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have these words, nor do several early translations, and Jerome in the fourth century remarked that most of the copies in front of him lacked them. Many later manuscripts do have them. One likely explanation is that a copyist who knew the similar saying in Luke (Luke 12:54–56) filled in what looked to him like a gap in Matthew, the same movement of a scribe’s hand that we meet at Matthew 17:21 and 18:11. Others argue the other way: that copyists in Egypt, where a red morning sky does not forecast a storm as it does in Palestine, dropped a line of weather lore that made no sense where they lived. This commentary’s view: the evidence is divided; the saying is certainly authentic as Jesus’ teaching (Luke has a parallel), whether or not Matthew wrote it here. The ESV includes it.

How much is at stake? Very little, which is the usual outcome of these questions. Every word of the exchange that carries the weight stands in undisputed text: they came to test him, they demanded a sign from heaven, and he answered that an evil and adulterous generation would be given none but the sign of Jonah. Matthew has already given us the same refusal in full (12:38–39), and the rebuke about reading the sky is beyond dispute in Luke. Not one thing taught in this chapter depends on the answer. The bracket marks a question about a copyist. It does not mark a doubt about the Lord’s words. And it is a mark of the care with which God has preserved his word that we can see the evidence so plainly and lose nothing by it.

Would one undeniable sign not settle it? It sounds reasonable, but Scripture says no. These men had already seen the sick healed and the hungry fed, and explained it away (12:24). John tells us that when Lazarus was raised, the council’s answer was to plan his death and the death of Jesus (John 11:47–53; 12:10). In one of his parables Jesus has Abraham say that those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31). The problem is not a shortage of evidence but a heart that has already decided. A sign can force a man to admit that something happened. It cannot make him love the one who did it. Only God can do that, and he does it through the word about his Son.

parallels.desc: reading the sky but not the times

verseByVerse.quote: "And in the morning, 'It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.' You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah." So he left them and departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the morning, “It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening”. A red sky in the morning warned of storms. The English proverb says the same: red sky at night, shepherd’s delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd’s warning.

You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. The signs of the times were all around them: the healings, the feedings, the teaching with authority, the fulfilment of prophecy, the ministry of John. The kingdom had arrived, and they could not see it, because they did not want to (13:13–15).

An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign. The same words as 12:39. Adultery here is not a charge about their morals but about their marriage. The prophets described God’s covenant with Israel as a wedding, and every turning to another god as a wife’s unfaithfulness (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3). They were bound to God in covenant and were standing in front of his Son asking him to prove himself, the way a wife asks for one more piece of evidence from a husband she has already decided to leave. The request sounds neutral; it comes from inside a marriage gone cold.

Only the sign of Jonah. Matthew has already told us what it is: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (12:40). His death and resurrection. They asked for a sign from heaven, something in the sky, beyond dispute. What they are promised is a sign from underneath: a grave. God answers the demand for overwhelming proof with a corpse and an empty tomb. There is a second edge to Jonah too. Nineveh repented at a preacher who worked no miracle among them, whose only sign was himself, a man given back from the deep (Luke 11:30), and the men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment beside men who were given every sign and wanted one more (12:41).

So he left them and departed. The last six words. He does not argue or perform. He walks away from men still waiting to be impressed. A judgment can be very quiet. To be contradicted by Christ is a mercy; Peter is about to receive one of the hardest contradictions in the Gospels and be kept. To be left by him is something else entirely. These men got exactly what they had asked for, an end to the conversation, and the getting of it was the punishment. Those men did not care that he had gone. A person who fears that he has been left, and grieves at the thought, is showing the very concern they lacked, and that concern is the mark of a Lord still at work in him.

Is it wrong to ask God for a sign? Most believers have at some point said, in a hospital corridor or at two in the morning, Lord, if this is really you, show me something. Is that person under this rebuke? Almost certainly not, and it matters that he knows it. Scripture is not against asking. Gideon asked twice, with a fleece, and was answered twice without reproach (Judges 6:36–40). Ahaz was told to ask for a sign, refused out of false piety, and was given the greatest sign in the Old Testament anyway (Isaiah 7:10–14). In this very Gospel, John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, and received no rebuke, only the evidence and then a public commendation (11:2–11). The difference is never the asking. It is what the asking is for. These men had watched the healings and filed them under demonic power; they were not gathering evidence but auditioning a candidate they had resolved to reject. The frightened believer who asks for help is doing the opposite: he wants the evidence to work. Even so, the normal way God guides and assures us now is through his written word, applied by his Spirit, not through signs. Ask for help, and then open your Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. Jesus said to them, "Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. Mark says they had only one loaf with them in the boat (Mark 8:14). After two feedings with baskets to spare, they were down to one loaf, and worried.

Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees”. Leaven in that world was not a sachet bought at a shop; it was a lump of last week’s dough, gone sour, kept back and worked into the new batch. The dough is changed quietly from the inside, and by the time the difference can be tasted there is no separating it out again. In Scripture leaven often pictures a corrupting influence that spreads quietly: a little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Galatians 5:9). And the verb is watch: keep watching, a standing habit, not a single inspection. Jesus warns his disciples that the teaching and attitudes of the religious leaders could spread into their own hearts without their noticing.

The guard. This is not a commission to go looking for heresy in other people. He says it to the Twelve, about themselves, when there is not a Pharisee in sight. Leaven is not what you detect in someone else’s loaf; it is what is already working in yours. False teaching must be named and resisted in the church, but this warning begins at home.

The other leaven. Only three chapters earlier Jesus had used the same picture for his own kingdom: it is like leaven that a woman hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened (13:33). So there are two leavens at work in the world, and both work from the inside. The Pharisees’ teaching spreads by quiet habit until a man’s whole religion tastes of pride. Christ’s word spreads by the quiet work of his Spirit until a whole life tastes of him. The only protection against a hidden corruption is not suspicion but a stronger presence: the words of the one who has authority, folded into the heart until they have worked through all of it. The disciples are not kept by their own vigilance. They are kept by the Teacher who is in the boat with them.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; it often pictures a corrupting influence.

parallels.desc: a little leaven leavens the whole lump

verseByVerse.quote: And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, "We brought no bread." But Jesus, aware of this, said, "O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread”. He said one word, leaven, and what they heard was bread. They thought he was rebuking them for forgetting it, or warning them not to buy bread from Pharisees. They were not disputing with him. They simply were not listening, because their heads were full of an empty bag, and a man with an empty bag hears every subject as a comment on his bag.

The preoccupied mind. Think of the last sermon you heard, or the last chapter you read, and ask what it had turned into by the time you reached the car. A man worried about money will hear a sermon on the sovereignty of God and come out thinking about his mortgage. It is what a preoccupied mind does with everything it is handed, and it is why the Twelve could be given a warning about false teaching and come away discussing catering.

But Jesus, aware of this, said, O you of little faith. Again he knows their thoughts (9:4; 12:25); nothing said in the boat is hidden from him. One word in Greek, oligopistoi, very nearly Matthew’s own word (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 17:20), and it is spoken every time to disciples. He never once calls a Pharisee a man of little faith. It is a family word, spoken only to people who are already inside. Why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? The Lord of the harvest, sitting with them in the boat, does not run out.

Does little faith mean I am not really a Christian? No, and this is where the mercy hides. He does not say you of no faith, or you unbelievers, though he has that vocabulary and uses it of other men. He weighed what they had, found it small, said so, and then kept them in the boat, took them north to Caesarea Philippi, and within days called one of them blessed and took three of them up a mountain. Little faith is not a verdict of exclusion. It is a diagnosis delivered by a physician who has no intention of discharging the patient. And see what the cure turns out to be. He does not tell them to try harder, or to generate more confidence, or to stop feeling anxious. He asks them a question about the past. The opposite of little faith, in this scene, is memory.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not yet perceive? The yet implies a growth he expected and had not seen. Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Twelve baskets (14:20). He asks two questions with the numbers left in: five loaves, five thousand, how many baskets; seven loaves, four thousand, how many baskets. Those men had carried the baskets. The arithmetic had gone through their own arms. He is not saying remember that I am generous. He is saying count.

Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Seven baskets (15:37). Jesus reminds them of both feedings separately, and Matthew has kept even the detail that the two sets of baskets were different: twelve hand baskets at the first and seven baskets of another kind at the second, probably larger hampers, a different word each time. Their memory of God’s past provision should have removed their anxiety. Forgetting what God has done lies at the root of much unbelief: Israel forgot his works and the wonders he had shown them (Psalm 78:11, 42). Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits (Psalm 103:2): David had to command his own soul not to forget, because forgetting comes as naturally to us as worrying.

Keep the record. Somewhere behind you on the road is a fear that never came true, or came true and was carried. We carry the fears forward and leave the answers behind us, which is why a written page at the back of a Bible, dated and specific, what was asked and what happened, is worth more to a frightened man at three in the morning than a shelf of resolutions.

What if I remember and I am still afraid? Then hold this honestly, or remembering becomes another burden. Remembering is not a technique that makes anxiety disappear; it did not work that way for the Twelve. They will fail again at the foot of the next mountain, and in the end every one of them will run. So a person who does his remembering faithfully and is still afraid has not fallen out of the story; he is standing exactly where the apostles stood. Keep remembering anyway, and pray your fear to God rather than about him (Philippians 4:6–7). And see what their Lord does with a memory as poor as theirs. He puts the question to them, gets no good answer, and then walks them north and asks them who he is, and when one of them gets it right he calls him blessed. He rebuked their memory. He did not revise his plans for them.

Bread taken, blessed and broken. Look at the hands that fed both crowds. Each time Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, broke them and gave them to the disciples (14:19; 15:36). Matthew will use those same four actions once more, in an upper room, when Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and says, take, eat; this is my body (26:26). The Supper is that same Shepherd giving himself. And he gave it to his church precisely because he knew how badly we remember. A Lord with forgetful disciples did not merely scold their memory; he gave them a meal to eat until he comes again, so that the greatest of all his provisions would be set in front of them, broken and visible, week after week.

verseByVerse.quote: How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Jesus speaks in pictures, and they must learn to think spiritually. And count how often he has to say it. He gives the warning in verse 6. They mishear it. He asks them a string of questions. Then he gives the same warning again in almost the same words, and only after that does Matthew write, then they understood. He was not too grand to repeat himself, and nothing in the text suggests he found it beneath him.

Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. The Pharisees added. They built a fence of tradition around the law to keep people from breaking it, and the fence ended up outranking the law it was built to protect. Matthew has just shown it working with Corban (15:6). Luke calls their leaven hypocrisy (Luke 12:1), and with it came the demand for signs while rejecting the evidence. The Sadducees subtracted. They held only the five books of Moses, denied the resurrection, denied angels and spirits (Acts 23:8; 22:23), ran the temple, and had made their peace with Rome. What is left after that subtraction is a religion with nothing supernatural in it at all, competently administered and politically safe. Mark adds the leaven of Herod (Mark 8:15): political worldliness.

One teaching. It does not say the teachings of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees. It says the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees: one warning covering two parties who agreed on almost nothing. That is the diagnosis, and it is sharper than either party alone. Adding to God’s word and subtracting from it arrive at the same place: a faith that has been brought under human management. One puts man’s word alongside God’s; the other takes God’s word out of God’s hands. Either way you end up with a religion no larger than the men running it. And underneath both lies the same wish of the heart: to stay in control. The man who adds rules keeps a ledger and feels that God owes him; the man who removes the supernatural keeps a God too small to interrupt his life. Both are ways of saving ourselves from having to be saved.

Nothing added and nothing missing. Both leavens are answered by one person. To the Pharisees, who loaded heavy burdens on men’s shoulders, Jesus says, come to me, and my yoke is easy (11:28–30): he does not add a fence to the law, he fulfils it (5:17) and carries its weight himself. To the Sadducees, who had taken the supernatural out of their Bible, he will answer that they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God (22:29), and then he will walk out of a tomb they had sealed. The cure for both is Christ himself, the whole Word of God in person, nothing added to him and nothing missing.

Which way do I drift? Both leavens are still in production, and each has a congregation that finds it comfortable. So put the question to yourself rather than to the church down the road. Which way does your own faith drift when nobody is checking? Toward a list of things you are careful about, which you could keep whether or not God were alive? Or toward a quiet, respectable removal of everything in the Bible that would be embarrassing to say out loud at work: miracles, judgment, the exclusive claims of Christ, the parts of his ethics your friends find old-fashioned? Answer honestly. Nobody drifts toward both at once, and almost nobody drifts toward neither. The cure for both is the same: let Scripture be the whole word of God, no more and no less, and let it judge you.

The difference between them. The difference between the Pharisees and the Twelve here is not intelligence or performance. Both groups failed to read what was in front of them. The Pharisees demanded evidence with the evidence already in their hands; the disciples had watched two crowds fed and were still counting loaves. The difference is one thing only: one group could still be told. That is why verse 4 ends with him departing and verse 12 ends with them understanding. He walked away from the closed mind. He stayed in the boat with the slow one.

What it does not mean. Not that every Pharisee or Sadducee taught nothing true. Jesus says elsewhere to do what the scribes teach from Moses, but not what they do (23:2–3). The danger was their characteristic errors, which could spread unnoticed.

How teachable am I? The question to bring away from this is not whether you understand your Bible well. It is what happened the last time somebody showed you that you had a passage wrong: a preacher, a book, a friend who loved you enough to risk it. Not whether you turned out to be right, but whether you could be told. A Christian who is often wrong and always teachable is in the boat. A Christian who is usually right and cannot be corrected is standing on the shore.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that the Son of Man is?" And they said, "Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi. A Gentile city about twenty-five miles (forty kilometres) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon by a source of the Jordan, among the farthest points from Jerusalem that Jesus reached with his disciples. It was a centre of the worship of the god Pan, with a great cave and spring at the foot of a cliff and shrines cut into the rock. Herod the Great built a white marble temple there to Caesar Augustus, and his son Philip named the town after Caesar and himself. Against pagan gods, emperor worship and a great rock, Jesus asks who he is.

Who do people say that the Son of Man is? The turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Jesus has taught and worked for months. Now he asks what people have concluded. And he uses his own favourite title for himself, Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7 who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom (see 8:20).

Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah. John, as Herod feared (14:2); Elijah, the prophet whose coming was promised before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5).

And others Jeremiah. Only Matthew mentions Jeremiah; Mark and Luke say only one of the prophets. Of all the names available, why that one? Jeremiah told the worshippers that the temple they trusted in would be pulled down, was dropped into a cistern for it, wept over a city that would not hear him, and announced a new covenant written on hearts (Jeremiah 7; 31:31–34; 38:6). Some Jewish traditions also expected Jeremiah to return before the Messiah. It is the shrewdest guess of the three, and it is nearer the mark than the man who made it can have known, for every part of that description is about to happen. Or one of the prophets: every opinion was a compliment, and none was high enough.

What the answers share. Every one of them belongs to the past. John had been beheaded two chapters ago (14:10); Elijah was taken up centuries before; Jeremiah had been in his grave six hundred years. No ordinary category was large enough. And they share something sharper still. John was the forerunner. Elijah was the herald. Jeremiah and the prophets pointed forward. Every popular answer makes Jesus the signpost and not the destination, a very great man on the road to someone greater. The answers were not wicked; the crowd was paying him the highest compliment its vocabulary allowed. But a person can hold Christ in the highest regard his categories permit, speak of him with real warmth, and still have missed him altogether, perfectly politely.

Why is a great teacher not enough? Because Jesus did not leave that option open. A mere teacher does not forgive sins against God (9:2–6), accept worship (14:33), claim to be the only one who knows the Father (11:27), or say he will judge the world (16:27). If those claims are false, he is not a great teacher but a deceived or deceiving one. If they are true, he is far more than a teacher. The one answer that does not fit the evidence is the polite one. Some reply that the church put these claims into his mouth later; but they run through every layer of the earliest Gospels, and the great-teacher picture is drawn from those same sources. When a friend says Jesus was a good man, you can agree warmly, and then ask what they make of the things he said about himself.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee, with a shrine to the god Pan.

parallels.desc: Herod thinks he is John raised

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "But who do you say that I am?" Simon Peter replied, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But who do you say that I am? In Greek the pronoun is plural, emphatic and put at the front: you, as against all of them, who do you say that I am? Reported answers will not do. He is asking what these men, who have eaten with him and watched him and been rebuked by him, will now say for themselves.

The question behind every pew. It is the one question in the Bible that a lifetime of church attendance can be conducted without ever answering. A man may attend for forty years, recite a creed and sing every hymn, and hold all of it as information received rather than as something he has ever once said. If the question were put to you with nothing to recite and nobody else’s phrasing to borrow, what would you say? This is not a demand for eloquence. Nor must your life have already caught up with it, as Peter’s had not. The question is not whether you can say it beautifully. It is only whether it is yours.

Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ”. He speaks, as so often, for the Twelve. The Christ is the Messiah, the Anointed One, the promised King of David’s line (see 1:1). Not merely a prophet who points to the Messiah, but the Messiah himself, the one all the prophets were pointing to.

The Son of the living God. Not only a title of the Davidic king (Psalm 2:7), but more. Not a son of God in the general sense in which Israel was called God’s son, but the Son, in a relationship with the Father that belongs to him alone (11:27). It does not mean that Jesus began to exist at Bethlehem; he shares the Father’s own nature and has been with him from eternity: the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made (John 1:1–3). And the living God is not a decorative phrase. It is the Old Testament title that sets the true God against dead idols (Joshua 3:10; Psalm 42:2; Jeremiah 10:10), especially fitting here, surrounded by the shrines of Pan and the temple of Caesar. Peter confesses that Jesus belongs to the one true, living God as his unique Son.

The same words at the trial. The phrase has one more appearance in this Gospel that should make a reader sit still. At the trial the high priest stands up and says: I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God (26:63). The question is almost word for word what Peter says here. Peter says it and is called blessed; Jesus agrees to it and is condemned to die for it. The very sentence that opens heaven to a fisherman is the sentence that sends the Son of God to a cross. He knew that when he asked the question.

Had Peter not already said something like this? Andrew had told him, we have found the Messiah (John 1:41), and Peter later confessed Jesus as the Holy One of God (John 6:69; the King James Version reads the Christ, the Son of the living God there, following later manuscripts that borrowed the words from this verse). Those confessions were real but partial; the disciples’ idea of the Messiah was still shaped by hopes of a political deliverer, as Peter’s rebuke in verse 22 shows. What is new here is the full content, the Son of the living God, given by the Father after all they had seen, and received by Jesus as the foundation of his church.

parallels.desc: “you are the Holy One of God”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! “Bar-Jonah” is Aramaic for son of Jonah (John calls his father John, John 1:42; 21:15, perhaps a variant of the same name). Jesus calls him blessed: favoured by God, the word of the Beatitudes (see 5:3). It is the only time in this Gospel that Jesus pronounces a beatitude on a named individual.

For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. “Flesh and blood” means human beings, human reasoning. Peter did not reach this by his own cleverness; the crowd had the same evidence and settled for a prophet of the past. It was his Father in heaven who revealed it to him. Saving knowledge of Christ is always a gift of God’s grace (11:25–27; 1 Corinthians 12:3). Such revelation is usually not a voice or a vision. God opened Peter’s eyes, so that the same facts the crowd had shrugged at became, to him, plainly true and precious. The God who first commanded light to shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to show us his glory in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

If faith is a gift, can I take any credit for believing? None at all, and that is the joy of it. If your faith were your own achievement, it would be as fragile as you are, and you could boast of it. Because it was revealed to you by the Father, it rests on his purpose, not your cleverness (Ephesians 2:8–9). That does not make your believing unreal; Peter really spoke, and you really trust. It means that when you confess Christ you are not displaying your insight but receiving his grace. And it is a reason to pray for those who do not yet see: the same Father who opened Peter’s eyes can open theirs.

And I tell you, you are Peter. “Peter” (Petros) means rock or stone. Jesus had given Simon this name when they first met (John 1:42); now he explains it. Peter has said who Jesus is; now Jesus says who Peter is.

And on this rock I will build my church. A wordplay: Petros (Peter) and petra (rock). In Aramaic, which Jesus probably spoke, both would be Kepha (Cephas). What is this rock? The main views:

1. Peter himself. Peter, as the first to confess Christ and the leader of the apostles, is the foundation stone on which Christ builds his church. This fits the wordplay best. It does not exclude the other apostles: the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20; Revelation 21:14), with Peter first among them. Peter did lead the early church: he preached at Pentecost (Acts 2) and opened the door to the Gentiles (Acts 10).

2. Peter’s confession. The truth Peter confessed, that Jesus is the Christ, is the rock. Many Reformers held this.

3. Christ himself. Christ is the rock and the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8).

The argument from the Greek. Older Protestants often pressed the Greek: you are Petros, a stone, and on this petra, bedrock, I will build, as though Jesus deliberately distinguished the man from the confession. That argument is weaker than it looks, for in Aramaic both words are the one word Kepha, and Petros is masculine only because it has become a man’s name. Honesty admits that Peter himself is most likely the rock. The real answer to Rome is not to deny that, but to see how Peter is the rock. This commentary’s view: the most natural reading is Peter himself, as the confessing apostle, the first stone of the foundation. But this gives no support to the papacy. Nothing in the text speaks of successors, of Rome, or of a supreme authority over the other apostles. Peter’s foundational role, like that of all the apostles, was unique and unrepeatable: a foundation is laid only once. The rock is Peter as the confessor of Christ: Peter and his confession cannot be separated.

The place. Some ancient writers spoke of Pan’s cave at Caesarea as a way down to the underworld. It is in front of that rock, crowded with the shrines of dead gods, that Jesus announces the building of his church on a living confession and declares that the gates of death will not prevail against it. Matthew does not draw out the setting, and we should not lean on it too heavily.

I will build my church. “Church” (ekklēsia) means assembly, the gathered people of God. It occurs only here and at 18:17 in all four Gospels. The Greek Old Testament used it for the assembly of Israel gathered before God at the mountain (Deuteronomy 4:10). He is not founding a society. He is claiming a very old one and building it on himself. My church, and I will build: it is his work, not ours.

And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. “Hell” here is Hades, the realm of the dead (ESV footnote), not Gehenna, the place of judgment, which Matthew uses freely elsewhere (5:22; 10:28; 23:33). “Gates” stand for the power of a city, and the gates of Hades is an ordinary Hebrew way of speaking of the power of death itself (Job 38:17; Isaiah 38:10). Death will not overcome Christ’s church. And consider who is saying it: a man who a few verses later tells these same friends that he is going to Jerusalem to be killed, and that on the third day he will be raised. The gates of death will not prevail against his church because they will not prevail against him. Christ, who will rise from the dead, holds the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The church is not a garrison pinned behind its walls; it is the people of the risen Christ, and the gates of death will open before them on the last day.

Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter the head of the whole church, that Peter was the first bishop of Rome, and that his authority passes to each pope as his successor. Orthodox and Protestant churches reject this. Peter was a leader among the apostles, but Paul rebuked him publicly (Galatians 2:11–14); James led the council at Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21); and Peter called himself a fellow elder (1 Peter 5:1). The New Testament says nothing about successors to Peter’s role or about Rome. This commentary’s view: Peter had a unique foundational role, which no successor inherits. The church’s authority now rests on the apostolic teaching preserved in Scripture.

The Roman case at full strength. The Roman case deserves a proper hearing. Peter is not prominent by accident of temperament. Matthew numbers him and nobody else: first, Simon, who is called Peter (10:2). He is named, it is often pointed out, more often than all the other apostles together. And three times, in three different Gospels, our Lord speaks to him alone in terms he uses of no one else: here he is given a new name and the keys; in the upper room he is told that Jesus has prayed for him in particular, and that when he has turned again he is to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:31–32); and by the lakeside after the resurrection he alone is charged three times to feed the sheep (John 21:15–17). Rock, keys, shepherd. The strongest piece: a foundation is a permanent fact. If Christ founded a visible church on a man, and that church is to stand until he returns, then surely the office outlives the man who first held it, as offices do in Scripture, from Aaron to his sons, and from Judas to Matthias (Acts 1:20).

The answer. Three things answer it. First, the one apostolic vacancy the New Testament actually fills is filled on a condition that closes the category. The replacement had to be a man who had been with them from John’s baptism to the ascension, and a witness of the resurrection (Acts 1:21–22). Only one generation could ever meet that, and when James the brother of John is put to the sword a few chapters later, nobody replaces him at all (Acts 12:2). The New Testament’s own precedent for apostolic succession is a door that shuts by design. Second, the foundation argument proves less than it needs to. Grant that a foundation is permanent; that is the Protestant point. But Paul says the household is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). If a permanent foundation required a living succession of foundation stones, we should need successors to the prophets too, and nobody argues that. A foundation is permanent by staying laid, not by being laid again every generation. The apostles hold the church up still, and we meet them where they are: in what they wrote. Third, everything the New Testament singles Peter out for is a first, not a permanence: first to confess, first to preach when the Spirit fell, first through the door into a Gentile house. And most telling of all, five verses on, this same rock is called Satan. The honour is real, and it is grace; but it is the honour of a forgiven confessor, not the founding of a throne.

If the church cannot be defeated, why do churches close? This has to be said carefully, because a confident sentence here sits one step from a cruelty. This is a promise about the church, and it is not a promise that your congregation or your denomination will survive. Congregations close. Denominations grow proud and cold and are buried. Seven churches in Asia received letters from the risen Christ himself, and those congregations have long since gone; Ephesus had Paul for three years and, by early tradition, John in his old age, and in time its lampstand went out, as it had been warned it could (Revelation 2:5). So if you have watched your own fellowship shrink to nine people and then to none, and quietly wondered whether this verse failed, be told plainly that it did not, and that nothing here is aimed at you. What is guaranteed is that Christ will never be without a church, that he is the one building it, and that death will never get the doors shut. Two thousand years on, having outlived every empire that set out to finish it, the promise has held in precisely the terms it was made.

On a Tuesday. When you are discouraged about the church, its failures, its smallness, its quarrels, remember whose church it is and who is building it. Then take your place in it: a living stone in a real congregation, not a spectator of the building site.
verseByVerse.note: Bar-Jonah means “son of Jonah.” Peter means “rock.” The ESV notes that “hell” here renders Hades, the realm of the dead; its gates stand for the power of death. A play on words: “Peter” (Petros) and “rock” (petra) are closely related Greek words.

parallels.desc: built on the foundation of the apostles

verseByVerse.quote: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Keys represent authority: to open and shut, to admit and exclude. Isaiah 22 is the passage in view. Shebna is steward over King Hezekiah’s household, a self-important official caught cutting himself a splendid tomb in the rock, and God announces that he will be removed and another man, Eliakim, installed. The words of installation are these: I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open (Isaiah 22:22). The key on the shoulder was the badge of the office. The steward is not the king. He is the man who runs the king’s house and decides who is brought into the king’s presence. And the risen Christ takes that very sentence for himself: the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut (Revelation 3:7). The key is his. He hands a servant the use of it. He does not hand over the house.

Peter using the keys. Luke shows Peter using the keys: he opens three doors. At Pentecost he preaches and three thousand Jews enter (Acts 2:14–41). In Samaria, where Philip had already preached, Peter and John pray for the despised Samaritans, and they receive the Spirit (Acts 8:14–17). On a rooftop in Joppa he is argued out of a lifetime’s revulsion, walks into a Gentile house, and the door to the nations stands open from that day to this (Acts 10). Three doors, each opened once and never needing to be opened again. After Acts 15 Peter disappears from Luke’s account. That is not the career of a man administering a permanent office. It is the career of a doorkeeper who has finished with the doors. The keys are the preaching of the gospel, which opens the kingdom to those who believe and shuts it to those who refuse.

The Isaiah argument. This is where the Roman argument is at its most impressive. Isaiah 22 is about a post, not a man: Shebna is removed and Eliakim installed, and the stewardship continues while the king’s house continues. So, the argument runs, if Jesus reached for this text, he instituted a stewardship that is filled again when its holder dies. But the oracle does not end where the argument stops quoting it. Three verses later the picture is reversed: the peg fastened in a secure place will give way, and be cut down and fall, and the load on it will be cut off (Isaiah 22:25). On a common reading, Eliakim himself comes down and takes the household with him. That is a strange charter for an office that cannot fail. Isaiah gives a stewardship with the steward’s collapse written into the same paragraph, which is close to what happens here, four verses later, when the man holding the keys is called Satan.

And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. “Bind” and “loose” were rabbinic terms meaning to forbid and permit, and also to condemn and acquit. The Greek tense is a future perfect: “shall have been bound in heaven”. The apostles do not decide things that heaven then must follow; they declare on earth what God has already decided in heaven. Their authority is to declare God’s will, not to create it. Some reply that the construction is an idiom and will not bear so much weight, and the grammar alone may not settle it. But the rest of the New Testament settles the direction, because the apostles never once invent terms of admission. The key does not make the door. It opens the one the King built. And to loose is to declare what is permitted, and to pronounce forgiveness to those who repent (John 20:23).

The same authority given to all. In 18:18, Jesus gives the same authority to bind and loose to all the disciples, and to the church in its discipline. After the resurrection the authority to forgive and to retain is breathed on the gathered disciples together (John 20:23). Whatever the keys are, Jesus distributes them almost at once. The keys belong to the church, exercised through the preaching of the gospel and its discipline. Churches order this differently, some through elders (the Westminster Confession 30.2), some through the gathered congregation with its elders (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 26.7). All agree that the keys work only through the word.

What this means on an ordinary Sunday. When a church hears someone confess Christ, baptises him and receives him to the Lord’s Table, it is not offering an opinion about his prospects; it is doing on earth a thing Christ authorised, and heaven is not indifferent to it. When a church, after long patience, must finally tell an unrepentant member that his life and his profession no longer agree (18:15–17), that is not a committee being unkind; it is the same key turned the other way, in the hope of his return. This is why belonging to a real congregation is not optional: the keys were given to a church, not to individuals with Bibles and strong opinions. And it is why the keys are terrible in the wrong hands, which is the substance of what the Reformers said when forgiveness was being sold at a church door. The abuse of the keys does not abolish them. It makes their right use urgent.

Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. He has just called Peter blessed for saying it, and now forbids them to say it to anybody. Why put a true confession under guard? Because the word was true and the definition in the hearers’ heads was false. Christ, in many Galilean mouths, meant a son of David with an army who would clear the Romans out of the country (see 8:4; 14:22). A man misunderstood in silence can still be explained later; a man acclaimed on the wrong terms cannot, because every cheer makes the correction more expensive. Only after the cross and resurrection could the title be proclaimed without misunderstanding.

The seal lifted. The seal and the explanation arrive together: in verse 21 he begins for the first time to tell them plainly that he must go to Jerusalem and be killed. Nor does the seal stay on. At the trial, put on oath and asked whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, he answers openly (26:63–64), because by then the cross is close enough that the word cannot be misheard. And after the resurrection the charge is reversed: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19). What was forbidden in a Galilean village is commanded to the ends of the earth. There is a warning here for anyone impatient for results: it is possible to get someone to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs. Our Lord had that option, with a crowd ready to take it, and chose silence.

What it does not mean. Not that a church or minister can forgive or condemn arbitrarily; the keys work only in line with God’s word.

Can my pastor forgive my sins? Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7), and he does so through Christ, when we repent and believe. What a minister can do, and must do, is declare that forgiveness with authority: tell a repentant sinner, on the basis of God’s word, that his sins are forgiven in Christ. That declaration is not a power of its own; it is the gospel spoken to you personally, and it is meant to be believed. You do not need a priest to confess to before God will hear you; you may go straight to him through Jesus (1 John 1:9; Hebrews 4:16). But there is real help in confessing to a trusted fellow believer and hearing God’s promise spoken aloud (James 5:16).
verseByVerse.note: Keys give authority to open and shut. “Bind” and “loose” were used of forbidding and permitting.

parallels.desc: the key of the house of David
the same authority given to all the disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — The First Passion Prediction and the Call to Cross-Bearing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the moment of Peter's confession, Jesus begins to teach that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day. Peter rebukes him, and Jesus rebukes Peter: "Get behind me, Satan!" He then calls every disciple to deny himself and take up his cross, asks what a man could give in exchange for his soul (v. 26), and promises that some standing there will see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (v. 28), a promise first kept six days later on the mountain.
verseByVerse.theology: The cross is not an unexpected tragedy but the appointed path. Peter's protest is the most natural human response and the most dangerous: it puts human preference in place of God's purpose, and it is the diagnosis of every Christianity that wants no cross. Verse 26 asks what sum could buy back a soul, and the question is left unanswered until 20:28, where the Son of Man gives his own life as the ransom. Verse 27 says he will repay each person according to what he has done; Matthew rules out a scoreboard (7:21-23; 25:31-46), for works are the evidence of a righteousness received, never its ground.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciple's cross is not every hardship; it is the cost of belonging to a man under sentence, the losing of a life organised around self in order to find one organised around Christ. And verse 28 shows how this Master treats frightened followers: the call to carry a cross is followed within a week by three of them being taken up a mountain and shown where the road ends.

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that time Jesus began. The second great turning point in Matthew. The same phrase opened his public ministry: from that time Jesus began to preach, repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (4:17). Now it opens his teaching about the cross. From here on, Jesus’ face is set toward Jerusalem.

To show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem. “Must” (dei): it is necessary, by God’s plan. It is the purpose for which he came: to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). The Scriptures required it (26:54; Luke 24:26). He was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

And suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes. The three groups who made up the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council. The builders would reject the stone (21:42). And be killed: a shocking statement, for the Messiah was expected to conquer, not to die.

And on the third day be raised. The resurrection is part of the plan from the start, not an afterthought. Jesus predicted his death and resurrection three times (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:18–19). The disciples heard the death, but apparently not the resurrection.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. Peter, who had just confessed Jesus as the Christ, now presumes to correct him. “Rebuke” is a strong word, the word Jesus uses against demons and the wind (8:26; 17:18). The man who confessed the Son of the living God is now trying to redirect the living God from his stated purpose.

Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you. Literally mercy to you, meaning God forbid! His idea of the Messiah had no room for suffering. A Messiah who dies is a defeated Messiah.

The same mouth. In verse 16 Peter says one of the most exalted sentences yet spoken in this Gospel, and Jesus tells him no man taught it to him; the Father did. Seven verses later the same man is called Satan. Revelation received does not immunise you against the next hour. If your walk with God consists of genuine heights followed by collapses that embarrass you, you have not discovered that you are a special case. You are Peter, and Peter is the normal one.

Love that tempts. Peter is not being wicked here. He is being protective. Far be it from you, Lord is affection talking; it is what you say to someone you love who has just told you he is going to die. That is precisely what makes it dangerous: advice that would turn us from a costly obedience often comes from people who love us and cannot bear to see us suffer, or from our own hearts dressed as care. Satan did not need to find an enemy for this errand. A devoted friend did it for him, sincerely, out of love.

Why did Jesus have to die? Could God not simply forgive? God is merciful, and he is also just. He cannot pretend sin does not matter, any more than a good judge can wave away a crime. The Old Testament sacrifices taught Israel that sin brings death and that forgiveness comes through a substitute’s blood (Leviticus 17:11). Jesus is the true substitute. He bore the penalty our sins deserved, the curse of God’s law, in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24), so that God might be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). To justify means to declare someone righteous in God’s court: not to make him good overnight, but to acquit him and count him right with God, because his sins have been paid for and Christ’s righteousness is credited to him (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is why he must go to Jerusalem. The must is not a cruel necessity laid on him from outside; it is the necessity of love determined to save sinners without denying justice.

verseByVerse.quote: But he turned and said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man." Then Jesus told his disciples, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he turned and said to Peter, Get behind me, Satan! Peter was speaking Satan’s words: the same temptation Satan offered in the wilderness, the crown without the cross (4:8–10). “Get behind me” may also mean: get back in your place as a follower, behind me, not in front, not steering.

You are a hindrance to me. “Hindrance” is skandalon, a stumbling block, a trap. A wordplay: The rock has become a stone to trip over. The same stone can be a foundation or an obstacle, depending on whether it stays where Christ has put it.

The things of God and the things of man. Peter was thinking by human standards: success, safety, power, a Messiah who wins without bleeding. God’s way was the way of the cross.

Severity and commitment together. He rebukes Peter about as hard as anyone is rebuked in the Gospels, and he does not dismiss him. Six days later Peter is one of the three taken up the mountain (17:1). He will go on to deny his Lord outright, with oaths, in a courtyard, and will be restored and commissioned by a charcoal fire (John 21:15–19). Full severity and unbroken commitment, held together at the same moment. Do not read your worst moment as your verdict.

Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me”. Not only for the Twelve, but for anyone. Deny, take up, follow, and the following is behind him, on a road he walks first. He is not asking for anything he declined to do himself.

Let him deny himself. Not deny himself things (like chocolate in Lent), but deny his self: say no to self as the master of his life. It is the word Jesus uses when he foretells what Peter will do in the courtyard, and the word Peter remembers there after he has said I do not know the man (26:34, 72–75). To deny is to disown, to refuse to be identified with, to decline to take someone’s side. So to deny yourself is to do to your own claims what Peter did to Jesus: to hear the demand of your own comfort, your own reputation, your own being in the right, and answer, I do not know him. Not to despise yourself, but to stop automatically taking your own side.

And take up his cross. Like a condemned man carrying his crossbeam to execution (see 10:38). The phrase has been flattened until it means anything one has to put up with. A cross is not a weight you carry. It is a death you have agreed to: a willingness to die, to self and if necessary physically, for Jesus.

Is my illness my cross? Not in the sense Jesus means, and the distinction is worth keeping. Your illness, your difficult marriage, your bad back, your awkward colleague, your ageing parents: these are afflictions, and Scripture has a great deal to say about them, and God is deeply present in them. But your cross is the specific cost of following Jesus, the thing you would not be bearing if you were not his. The promotion refused because the figures would have to be wrong. The relationship ended because it could not continue in obedience. The truth told when silence would have been cheaper. The money given that you had other plans for. The reputation you have quietly lost among people whose good opinion you wanted. The reason for insisting on this is not pedantry. Calling an ordinary hardship a cross is a way of feeling that discipleship is costing us something when it may be costing us nothing at all. Luke adds one word that settles the shape of it: daily (Luke 9:23). It is not one dramatic renunciation, remembered for years. It is a small repeated decision, most of which nobody sees. None of this makes your suffering smaller in God’s sight: he keeps count of your sleepless nights and stores up your tears (Psalm 56:8), and bearing an illness with trust is itself a way of following him.

And follow me. Walk behind him, on the road he walks, which leads to the cross and through it to resurrection. And six days later he takes three of them up a mountain and lets them see the far side of it.

In the flow. The order of the chapter is the order of the gospel: who Jesus is (16:16), what he must do (16:21), and only then what it means to follow him (16:24). The call to carry a cross is built on his cross, not the other way round.

What it does not mean. Not that self-denial earns salvation, or that Christians should hate themselves; self-denial is the response of those who have been loved and saved. Nor was Peter demon-possessed or a false disciple: he was a true disciple who, in that moment, spoke Satan’s thoughts.

On a Tuesday. Most self-denial happens in small moments nobody sees: the reply you do not send, the credit you let someone else have, the evening given up without anyone knowing. None of them earns anything, and none is done perfectly. Each is one step behind a Lord who went first and never once took his own side against the Father; his perfect self-denial is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and his Spirit in you gives strength for the next step (Galatians 5:25).

For worship. The one who said get behind me to a frightened friend was not pushing him away; he was putting him in the safest place in the world, one step behind the Son of God. The Lord did not please himself (Romans 15:3). He carried his own beam out of the city to the place of the skull, and died on it for the very man who had tried to stop him.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever would save his life will lose it. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the soul, life itself. Those who protect their life and comfort by avoiding the cross will lose what matters most (see 10:39). But whoever loses his life for Christ’s sake will find true and eternal life. Self-surrender, for him, saves.

One word, four times. Life in verse 25 and soul in verse 26 are the same word, psychē, and it occurs four times in three sentences. One word runs through one argument: the self you clutch, you lose; the self you hand over, you get back; the self cannot be bought at any price; and there is not a second one available for another attempt. You have one self, and every day you are spending it on something.

For my sake. One guard, because the sentence is used to bully decent people. Nothing here forbids ambition. A person is not more spiritual for wanting less. And note the three words that keep this from being a general commendation of sacrifice: for my sake. Jesus does not praise losing your life as such. People lose their lives for a country, a company, a cause, a reputation, and lose them altogether. The clause that turns a loss into a finding is not the size of the sacrifice but the name of the person it is made for. Self-denial is not the point of Christianity. He is.

For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? A business question: what is the profit? Imagine gaining everything the world offers: wealth, power, fame, pleasure. If you lose your soul, you have made the worst trade in history. The devil offered Jesus the whole world (4:8–9); Jesus refused.

Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? The word behind in return is antallagma, the sum handed over in an exchange, the price. So he is inviting a bid: name the figure. And the terrible thing about the question is not that the price is high; it is that there is no price at all. Everything else a man owns converts into something else. A house converts into money, money into time, time into comfort. There is exactly one item in his possession that no market will quote, and it is himself. Nothing can buy back a lost soul. Psalm 49:7–9 says that no one can ransom another, for the ransom of their life is costly. Only Christ can pay that price (20:28).

The answer to the question. Left there, it is a lecture on prudence. But four chapters later the same Gospel supplies the only answer ever given: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). The word for the life he gives is psychē, the same word as here, and the ransom is the price paid to buy a person out. The questioner answers his own question, and not with a sum. He walked from this conversation to Jerusalem, carried the price to the counter himself, and paid it in the only currency the exchange would accept, which was his own life.

How do I know if I am trading my soul? Not usually by one dramatic bargain, but by a hundred small ones. Ask what you will not give up for Christ; that is where your price is set. Ask what you think about when your mind is free, what you would be most devastated to lose, what you sacrifice your time with God and your family for. If the answer is a career, an image, a relationship, a comfort, take it to Christ honestly. The remedy is not to despise those good things but to hold them under him, and to receive them back from his hand. And if you see that you have been selling yourself cheaply for years, the good news is the answer this Gospel gives to verse 26: Christ came to buy back exactly such people (20:28).

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father. The one who must suffer (v. 21) will come in glory. The suffering Servant is also the glorious Judge of Daniel 7:13–14 (see 8:20). The glory comes through and because of the cross.

And then he will repay each person according to what he has done. From Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12: God judges each person according to their works. At the final judgment, Christ will judge (25:31–46). Our works will show whether we truly followed him (7:21–23).

Judgment by works? An honest Protestant reader stops dead at this clause. Judgment by works, on the lips of Jesus, in the same paragraph as the cross. Say the awkward thing first: the New Testament teaches this everywhere and never apologises for it, and Matthew insists on it most of all: the men turned away in 7:21–23, the account rendered for every careless word in 12:36–37, the sheep and the goats separated by what was and was not done in 25:31–46. The resolution is not a softening of the words but a question about what a court is for. Two different questions are asked at any trial: on what ground is this person received, and what was this person actually like? Righteousness is received and never earned; that is settled at the cross. But a righteousness that has been received always shows, and faith in itself is invisible. God does not hold an invisible judgment. The deeds are the visible form of the thing, produced in evidence, the way a man’s handwriting is produced to show whose hand it was.

Not an audit. Matthew rules out a scoreboard twice over. In 7:21–23 the people rejected are not rejected for a low total; their works are impressive, prophecies and exorcisms and mighty deeds, and the verdict against them is not that they did too little but that they were never known: I never knew you. Works could not supply the relationship. In 25:31–46 the sheep are astonished by their own record and cannot remember any of it: when did we see you hungry? On a scoreboard, nobody is surprised by his own score. It is not an audit. It is a recognition.

Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. A puzzling verse, often produced as proof that Jesus was mistaken, as though he promised to return before his hearers died. “Taste death” means die. What coming did Jesus mean? Several views:

1. The transfiguration. Six days later, three of the disciples saw Jesus in his glory (17:1–8). All three Synoptic Gospels place this saying immediately before the transfiguration, suggesting a link. Peter later described the transfiguration as seeing the power and coming of the Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 1:16–18).

2. The resurrection and ascension. Jesus received all authority and came into his kingly reign (28:18).

3. Pentecost and the spread of the church. The kingdom came with power (Mark 9:1).

4. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A coming in judgment within that generation (24:34).

Coronation, not arrival. The phrase itself matters. The Son of Man coming in his kingdom is throne-room language borrowed from Daniel, where the figure moves toward the Ancient of Days to be crowned, rather than toward earth to be seen (Daniel 7:13–14). So the sentence need not be about the last day at all. Matthew raises the same question at 10:23 and 24:34. And the objection usually pressed against the transfiguration reading deserves an answer: if Jesus meant an event six days away, why speak so solemnly of some not tasting death, as though the interval were long? First, the emphasis falls on some: he has just spoken of the last day in verse 27, and now he distinguishes; that day is not what you are about to see, but a few of you are about to see something of it. Second, all three Gospels place the saying right before the transfiguration and then date the transfiguration to the following week, which is as loud a piece of arrangement as the Evangelists ever make. Third, and best, one of the men standing there tells us what he thought he had seen. Writing near the end of his life, Peter defends the promise of Christ’s coming by appealing to that mountain: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, for we were with him on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:16–18). The man who heard the promise cites its fulfilment. (Some scholars doubt that Peter wrote this letter; the church received it as his, and at the very least it shows how the earliest Christians read this saying.) This commentary’s view: the transfiguration, which follows at once, is the first fulfilment: a preview of his glory seen by some of those standing there. The promise is fulfilled further in his resurrection and enthronement, at Pentecost, and in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. On any of these readings, Jesus was not mistaken about his return: he was speaking of events within his disciples’ lifetimes.

Should the judgment frighten me? Look at whom he is saying it to. These are men who could not follow a warning about bread that morning, one of whom has just been called Satan and will in due course deny him with oaths. He tells them about the judgment not to terrify them but to steady them, as the reason they can afford to lose their lives: the Son of Man is coming in his Father’s glory, and nothing spent on him will be mislaid. A believer who examines his own deeds and finds them thin has not thereby discovered that he is lost. There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1): for the one who is in Christ the verdict has already been given. The question at that day is not how much was done. It is whose you were, and the deeds are only how that shows. If you belong to him, the Judge is your Saviour, and his coming is your hope. If you do not, the right response to this verse is not despair but to come to him today, while the door is open.

On a Tuesday. Live today as one who will stand before Christ the Judge, and as one who belongs to him. Do one thing this week that only makes sense if he is really coming back: a gift no one will repay, a kindness no one will see, a truth spoken that costs you.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

16.theology: The church and the confession. Matthew is the only Gospel that records Jesus using the word “church” (the gathered assembly of God’s people), and only twice: here, and in the discipline of 18:17. The promise is remarkably confident: he will build it, not we, and death will not overcome it. The church endures not because of its institutional strength or cultural influence but because of who its Lord is and the truth of its confession. A church that loses the confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, has lost the rock on which it stands.
16.examples:
Then: Caesarea Philippi was an unlikely place to announce the church: a pagan city, far from Jerusalem’s religious centre. The church is announced at the margins, by a confession no human calculation produced.

Now: “Who do you say that I am?” is not a quiz but a question every hearer of the gospel must answer for himself. Calling Jesus a great teacher, a moral example or a historical figure falls short of Peter’s confession. The church is built of those who answer as Peter answered, by the same Father who revealed it to him.

17.title: The Transfiguration
17.text: <sup>1</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. <sup>2</sup>And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light. <sup>3</sup>And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. <sup>4</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>5</sup>He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” <sup>6</sup>When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified. <sup>7</sup>But Jesus came and touched them, saying, “Rise, and have no fear.” <sup>8</sup>And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man is raised from the dead.” <sup>10</sup>And the disciples asked him, “Then why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>11</sup>He answered, “Elijah does come, and he will restore all things. <sup>12</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands.” <sup>13</sup>Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist. <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the crowd, a man came up to him and, kneeling before him, <sup>15</sup>said, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and he suffers terribly. For often he falls into the fire, and often into the water. <sup>16</sup>And I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him here to me.” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed instantly. <sup>19</sup>Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “Because of your little faith. For truly, I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.” <sup>22</sup>As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men, <sup>23</sup>and they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day.” And they were greatly distressed. <sup>24</sup>When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax went up to Peter and said, “Does your teacher not pay the tax?” <sup>25</sup>He said, “Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do kings of the earth take toll or tax? From their sons or from others?” <sup>26</sup>And when he said, “From others,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free. <sup>27</sup>However, not to give offense to them, go to the sea and cast a hook and take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a shekel. Take that and give it to them for me and for yourself.”
17.overview:
On a mountain, for a short while, three disciples see who Jesus is. His face shines like the sun and his clothes become white as light: nothing is added to him; his own glory stops being hidden. Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, speak with him about the departure he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), and the Father speaks from the cloud, as at the baptism: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

The mountain answers Peter’s refusal of the cross in chapter 16. The one who will be crucified is the radiant Son of God, and the cross does not contradict his glory; it is the road by which it reaches the world. Then the disciples come down to a boy they could not help, and from the height to the valley of need is where the church must work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain and is transfigured before them. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him; a cloud overshadows them and the Father speaks from it; the disciples fall on their faces, and Jesus touches them, and they see no one but Jesus only. Coming down, he forbids them to speak of the vision until he is raised from the dead, and tells them that Elijah has already come, in John the Baptist, and was treated however his enemies pleased, as the Son of Man will be.
verseByVerse.theology: The mountain confirms Peter's confession: the Son whose glory was hidden in flesh is unveiled.
