verseByVerse.quote: And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery." The disciples said to him, "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I say to you. Not as the scribes, quoting the schools, but as the Lord of the law. The authority that made marriage rules on it, and the same authority forgives the adulterer who comes to him in repentance (1 John 1:9).

Whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery. Divorce for “any cause” does not dissolve the marriage in God’s eyes, so a second marriage after it is adultery. The exception is “sexual immorality” (porneia), sexual unfaithfulness, which breaks the marriage covenant. In that case, the innocent party may divorce and remarry (see 5:32). Jesus stands nearer to Shammai, but argues from creation, not from the wording of Deuteronomy.

The disciples said to him, If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry. The disciples had assumed the easy divorce of their culture. Their conclusion misses the point but captures the weight, even if their response is flight rather than faithfulness.

Where Christians differ: may the innocent party remarry? Those who hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives have serious reasons: Mark and Luke record no exception (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18), Paul says a wife is bound while her husband lives (Romans 7:2–3), and many in the early church held this view. Others read the exception only of unfaithfulness during betrothal. The historic Reformed reading is the more likely, because Jesus’ exception is a real exception, and Paul shows that the bond can be released (1 Corinthians 7:15). Sexual immorality covers adultery and sexual sin of the same gravity. And the exception permits divorce; it does not command it. Where there is repentance, reconciliation is the better path. This commentary’s view: marriage is for life, and divorce is always a tragedy; Scripture permits it on two grounds only, sexual unfaithfulness (Matthew 19:9) and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied (1 Corinthians 7:15), and in those cases the innocent party is free to remarry (the Westminster Confession 24.5–6). Persistent, serious abuse can amount to such desertion, and the elders help judge each case; but the abused should seek safety at once, no one is ever required to stay where they or their children are in danger, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered.

Two grounds and no others. None of this is a loophole to be worked but a protection for something holy: Jesus’ aim is not to license divorce but to guard the one-flesh covenant.

Why Mark and Luke have no exception. Matthew twice records an exception (5:32; 19:9), and Mark and Luke record none (Mark 10:11; Luke 16:18). The likely explanation is that this is how people have always spoken: a father who says, we do not lend the car out, is not lying when he lends it to his son in an emergency. Mark and Luke give the principle in its blunt form; Matthew, writing for Jewish readers to whom the quarrel was live, records the qualification Jesus made.

What about a marriage that is destroying somebody? For some readers this is the only question in the chapter: the husband who is violent, the wife whose rage has made the house unsafe, the parent whose drinking has turned a home into somewhere the children brace themselves to enter. Matthew names one ground and Paul a second, and neither uses the word. Does Christ require a battered woman to stay? He does not, and it will not do to be vague about it, because vagueness here has cost real people a great deal. Three things are true, and the order matters.

Separation for safety. First, before any question of divorce: separation for safety is nowhere forbidden in Scripture, and Paul attaches no shame to it (1 Corinthians 7:11). Getting out of reach of a dangerous man is a step toward not being killed, and often the only thing that has ever made his repentance a live possibility. Violence and threats are crimes, and they should be reported to the police.

The children. Second, a parent who removes the children from a violent house is obeying the Lord who spoke of the millstone (18:6), not disobeying him.

Desertion judged by its substance. Third, on the bond itself. A husband whose cruelty makes the home unsafe has abandoned the marriage as truly as one who leaves it; he has simply arranged for his wife to do the walking. Many older Reformed pastors judged desertion by its substance, not by who physically left the house.

Not settled alone. This is a matter to be taken to the church rather than settled alone (18:15–20). A church that answers such a case by sending a woman home to try harder, or by weighing a man’s standing in the congregation against what she has described, has been careless with a life. Abuse is never to be handled privately: the authorities must be told.

What of someone who divorced without biblical grounds, or who divorced and remarried before becoming a Christian? The guilty party who repents is called to remain single or be reconciled (1 Corinthians 7:11), though Reformed churches differ on remarriage in that case. Those already remarried are not to break up the second marriage; it is a real marriage, and the call is to repent of how it began and to live faithfully in it. The phrase commits adultery describes how the second marriage began, not a sin repeated every day it continues.

A fence, not a cage. Every stroke of this passage, the one flesh, the yoking, the refusal of the convenient exit, is meant to make a marriage the one place on earth where a human being is safe for life. A reading of it that shuts somebody inside cruelty has taken the fence he built around a person and used it as a cage.

If my own marriage has already broken, is there hope for me? Yes. To any reader whose marriage has already broken, through your sin, or another’s, or a tangle of both: there is no sin here that the blood of Christ does not cover, and no past so broken that grace cannot make something new of what remains. The gospel meets us not in the marriage we should have had but in the life we actually have. If you sinned, confess it plainly to God and, where it is wise, to those you wronged, and receive his forgiveness. If you were sinned against, bring your grief to the one who was himself betrayed. And find a church that will walk with you rather than define you by it.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, "Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this, receive it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. This saying is probably the disciples’ remark that it is better not to marry (v. 10). Single life is a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7), a calling for some, not a command for all.

For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth. A eunuch was a man unable to father children, and so, in that world, usually unmarried. Some were born unable, because of physical conditions.

And there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men. Men castrated as servants for royal courts (Acts 8:27). Under the law of Moses, eunuchs were excluded from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1), but God promised them an everlasting name in his house (Isaiah 56:3–5). This middle category is nearly always skipped: people made this way by others, often by cruelty.

And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. People who choose to remain unmarried to serve God’s kingdom more fully, with undivided devotion (1 Corinthians 7:32–35). Jesus names all three kinds in one breath; the calling’s dignity is not reserved for those who volunteered.

Ministers may marry. Nor does the third kind require ministers to be unmarried: Peter had a wife (8:14; 1 Corinthians 9:5), and Paul expects overseers to be husbands (1 Timothy 3:2).

A eunuch reading Isaiah. The most famous eunuch in the New Testament sat in a chariot reading Isaiah 53: Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth (Acts 8:33). He was reading about a man who would die with no descendants, and Philip told him that the man was Jesus. Three chapters on in the same scroll stood the promise to eunuchs of an everlasting name (Isaiah 56:3–5). The Lord who honours eunuchs here died unmarried and childless, his line apparently ended at a cross, so that those cut off from family and future might be grafted into his. He shall see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10), and gives the cut-off an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:5).

What it does not mean. Not that marriage is less holy than singleness, or that single people are second-class Christians: both are callings from God (1 Corinthians 7:7). The Reformers rightly rejected the medieval idea that celibacy is a higher state (1 Timothy 4:1–3). Nor does it mean literal castration: Origen is reported to have done so, a tragic misreading. Some today read eunuchs from birth as a reference to people with same-sex attraction, but the word refers to physical inability to father children. Christians who remain single and celibate out of faithfulness to Christ, including those who experience same-sex attraction, are following a path Jesus honours here.

If I did not choose to be single, how can it be a gift? The objection is entirely fair. A gift is normally something you wanted and unwrapped. Many single Christians did not choose this and would exchange it tomorrow: the woman who hoped to marry and is now fifty, the widower, the person whose marriage ended and who will not remarry, the believer whose convictions about sexuality mean marriage is not open to him. Told that their situation is a gift, they may feel asked to be grateful for a loss. But in the New Testament a gift (charisma) is grace given for a purpose, not a pleasure guaranteed. Paul’s thorn was no delight either, and what he was promised in it was not enjoyment but sufficient grace (2 Corinthians 12:9). So what is promised is not that you will like it. It is that there is grace enough for it; that it is a genuine vocation rather than a waiting room for real life to begin; and that it is not a lesser existence. The most completely human being who ever lived was single, and so, when he wrote, was the apostle who wrote more of the New Testament’s letters than anyone else.

What the church owes. Jesus says later in this chapter that everyone who has left houses or family for his sake will receive a hundredfold (v. 29), which Mark spells out as brothers, sisters, mothers and children now in this time (Mark 10:30). That is a debt. A congregation that preaches marriage constantly and has no place at its tables for the unmarried has left half its members outside the promise its Lord made. If you carry singleness as a grief, say so plainly to God and to somebody who will not rush you; Scripture has room for people who wanted a good thing and did not receive it, and it never calls that unbelief.
verseByVerse.note: A eunuch was a man unable to marry or father children. Some, like Paul, remained single to serve the kingdom.

parallels.desc: a name better than sons and daughters

verseByVerse.quote: Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, but Jesus said, "Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. Luke says they were infants (Luke 18:15). Jewish parents brought children to rabbis and elders to be blessed (compare Genesis 48:14).

The disciples rebuked the people. They thought they were protecting him. They had forgotten the lesson of 18:1–5, given a chapter before, with a child standing in the middle of them.

But Jesus said, Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them. Mark says Jesus was indignant (Mark 10:14). The disciples are putting a fence where Jesus wants a door.

The King who had been a child. The one who says let the little children come was himself carried once in a mother’s arms into the temple, and lifted by an old man who blessed God for him (Luke 2:28). The eternal Son did not skip infancy on his way to the cross; he knows from the inside what it is to be small and dependent. The kingdom is not a prize for adults who have achieved something. It is the gift of a King who came down to the size of the people he welcomes.

For to such belongs the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom belongs to those who receive it like children, as a gift (18:3–4). Not they will eventually be admitted, but theirs is the kingdom.

In the flow. These children stand between a debate about how much a husband may keep and a rich man who would not let go. The young man will ask what good deed he must do, and the answer has already been given here, to people too small to do anything.

What it does not mean. Not that children are saved by being children, or that they do not need Christ. They are sinners by nature too (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3). But Jesus welcomes them and blesses them.

Where Christians differ: infant baptism. Paedobaptists (Christians who baptise the infants of believers) often cite this passage in support of baptising infants: if the kingdom belongs to children, they should receive the sign of the covenant. They set it beside the covenant sign given to Abraham’s children (Genesis 17:7), Peter’s word that the promise is for you and for your children (Acts 2:39), and the whole households baptised in Acts. Credobaptists (who baptise those who profess faith) respond that this passage says nothing about baptism; Jesus blessed the children and prayed for them, he did not baptise them; and baptism signifies faith and union with Christ, which a person must profess. Every baptism the New Testament describes follows a profession of faith. Honesty requires admitting that this point lands: a case for infant baptism has to be built from the shape of the covenant across both Testaments rather than from these verses, and to us that wider case is less convincing than the plain New Testament pattern of baptism after faith. Many godly Reformed believers find it persuasive, and a reader baptised as an infant by believing parents was brought to Christ in love, and is a brother or sister, not an opponent. This commentary’s view: credobaptist, held charitably. The passage teaches that children are welcome to Christ and should be brought to him in prayer and teaching, but it does not mandate infant baptism. Both sides agree that Christian parents must bring their children to Jesus.

What both sides can take home. The only people rebuked in the story are the ones who thought children were a distraction from the real work. When children are noisy in church, it is worth remembering who was rebuked here.

Do children who die in infancy go to heaven? This verse does not say that children are innocent; Jesus has just warned that we must become like them, not that they are sinless (18:3). But it shows his welcome to them, and Scripture gives grieving parents real hope. David said of his dead infant, I shall go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and the historic Reformed confessions teach that elect infants who die in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Many Christians are confident that God, the Judge of all the earth, will do right by every child who dies before it can believe. We do not have a verse that says so in plain words, but we have the character of the God who said, let the little children come to me.

So should I wait for my children to choose for themselves? No. Credobaptists wait for a credible profession of faith before baptism, but no one should wait to bring children to Christ. Pray for them and with them from the day they are born; read them the Bible; bring them to worship; tell them the gospel plainly and often; and call them to trust Christ for themselves. Children can truly believe, and Jesus wants them near him. A child who asks to follow Jesus should be taken seriously and gently helped, and when his faith is credible, he may be baptised.

verseByVerse.quote: And he laid his hands on them and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he laid his hands on them. Mark says he took them in his arms (Mark 10:16). The parents who had been told off by the inner circle watched him bless their children one by one.

Bring them. Somebody thought it worth the walk, and declined to be embarrassed out of the queue. Put them where Christ is, week after week, when it is inconvenient. Pray with your hand on them, out loud, using their name, which is as nearly as we can manage the thing happening in this verse. And do not be argued out of it by anyone who implies that the serious work of the church is going on elsewhere; that argument was made once already in this passage, and it was publicly overruled.

Does this promise that my children will become Christians? No, and the verse is quietly used to wound. Scripture is honest about godly parents whose children went their own way, and so is every congregation that has been going long enough. A mother or father grieving over a grown son who wants nothing to do with any of it must not read these verses as a verdict on their parenting or as a promise that failed. What is here is a picture of Christ’s disposition toward children, warm, unhurried and personally given, and an instruction about the church’s. That disposition has not altered for a man of forty who was once carried up to him. Keep praying; the arms that held these children are still open.

And went away. He blessed them, and left, on the road to Jerusalem. In the old covenant the priest lifted his hands and put God’s name on the people (Numbers 6:23–27), and the blessing rested on the sacrifice he had offered. Here the Priest blesses first and goes away to become the sacrifice. Luke ends his Gospel with the same gesture: he lifted up his hands and blessed them (Luke 24:50).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Rich Young Man and the Great Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young man asks what good deed will earn eternal life. Jesus directs him to the commandments, then tells him to sell his possessions and follow him, and he goes away sorrowful. The camel and the needle leave the disciples asking who then can be saved. Peter asks what the Twelve will have for leaving everything; Jesus promises thrones and a hundredfold, and attaches a warning: many who are first will be last.
verseByVerse.theology: The young man kept the commandments in their visible form but not in their heart: he had another god, and his love for his neighbour cost him nothing. Jesus’ command to sell everything exposes the one thing that stood between him and eternal life. Verse 17 does not deny that Jesus is God: he asks a question that invites the man to see whom he is addressing, and the rest of the Gospel shows him forgiving sins as only God can (9:2–6) and claiming all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18).
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples assumed that wealth was a sign of God’s blessing. Jesus treats it as an obstacle, and the camel and the needle picture impossibility. The only answer is that with God all things are possible. That promise is about the salvation of a rich man, not a general assurance that whatever we want can be had; and Matthew shows it kept when a rich disciple, Joseph of Arimathea, comes for the body of Jesus (27:57).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man came up to him, saying, "Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?" And he said to him, "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a man came up to him. Young (v. 20), a ruler (Luke 18:18) and wealthy (v. 22): he had everything his culture valued, including religious seriousness.

Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life? “Eternal life” means the life of the age to come, life in God’s kingdom (v. 23). His question assumes that eternal life is earned by doing something good: one more deed, one more achievement. It frames eternal life as a transaction: what can I perform to secure it?

Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. Mark and Luke record his question as “Good Teacher” and Jesus’ answer as “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:17–18). Jesus is not denying that he is good or that he is God. He is making the man think. Only God is truly good. If the man calls Jesus good, does he realise what he is saying? And goodness is not found in doing one good deed, but in God himself. Good here does not mean pleasant or decent. It means the perfect, unmixed goodness of the holy God, beside which even our best deeds are stained (Isaiah 64:6), and a man who has glimpsed that goodness stops asking which deed will be enough.

Did Jesus deny being God? No, though this verse is regularly produced as proof that he did. Read the sentence again and see what it does. Jesus does not say, I am not good. He asks a question, and the question is a door: you have called goodness a thing you can do and me a teacher who can tell you the trick; there is only One who is good, so think again about what you are asking, and whom you are asking. He is not refusing the title. He is telling a man who used it casually that he has no idea what he has just said. And the rest of the Gospel refuses to let the denial stand: this is the man who forgives sins as only God can (9:2–6), who calls himself lord of the Sabbath (12:8), who receives worship without once waving it away (14:33), and who at the end claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). A man building a case against his own deity does not talk like that.

Matthew’s wording. Matthew gives the exchange in compressed form, as he does elsewhere (compare 9:18 with Mark 5:23); the reply is the same: goodness is not a deed in your hand but a property of God.

If you would enter life, keep the commandments. Not because the law can save, but because it shows us our sin (Romans 3:20; 7:7).

Does this teach salvation by works? No. Perfect obedience would bring life, but no sinner can offer it (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10–12). Jesus uses the law here to expose the young man’s need, which is why he goes on to say that salvation is impossible with man but possible with God (v. 26).
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke record the question as “Good Teacher.” Luke calls him a ruler.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, "Which ones?" And Jesus said, "You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to him, Which ones? Perhaps he wanted to know which ones mattered most, or to check that he had kept them. His question gives him away. A man who asks which commandments has already turned the law into a syllabus and is asking what is on the examination. He is not asking how to love God; he is asking which items he will be marked on, so that he can tick them off and know where he stands. It is the most common way there is of holding a religion, and it is comfortable precisely because a list can be finished.

You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother. The fifth to ninth commandments, about how we treat others (Exodus 20:12–16).

And, You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18, which sums up the second half of the law (22:39; Romans 13:9). Every other item on his list can be obeyed by sitting still; a man asleep is keeping five of them. This one cannot be kept by not doing something, and it has no upper limit.

What is missing. Jesus does not mention the tenth commandment, you shall not covet (Exodus 20:17), nor the first, you shall have no other gods. These are the ones the young man will be shown to have broken: his wealth was his god, and he coveted it. Jesus recites a list with the man’s own sin removed, lets him answer all these I have kept, and then asks him for the one thing the missing commandments were about. It is the method Nathan used on David (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

The list kept to the last line. There was one man on that road who had kept every line of the list, including the one with no upper limit. Jesus honoured his mother from the cross (John 19:26–27), never lied, never took, never lusted, and loved his neighbour more than himself: he laid down his life for friends who ran and enemies who mocked (Romans 5:8–10). That is the gospel the young man had not yet heard. We never keep the list perfectly, not even on our best day; but the obedience God requires has been offered in full by the Son, and it is counted as ours when we trust him (Romans 5:19). This is justification: the verdict of righteousness pronounced over people who have broken every line, resting wholly on the obedience of another.

A conscience made of prohibitions. Asked what we got wrong last week, we tend to name things we did: a temper lost, a lie about why we were late. We rarely name the person we did not visit, the money we did not give, the conversation we avoided because it would have cost an evening. A conscience built entirely out of prohibitions can be satisfied by half past ten in the morning, and that is exactly what recommends it.

Why does Jesus list the commandments if no one can keep them? Because the law is a mirror before it is a ladder. Its first work for a sinner is to show him what he is, so that he will look for a Saviour (Galatians 3:24). But the law is not thrown away after that. For the believer, the commandments remain God’s good guide to a life of love (Romans 13:8–10), kept now not to earn life but out of gratitude for life freely given. Read them both ways: as the verdict that sends you to Christ, and as the shape of the life Christ is producing in you.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour and adds Leviticus 19:18.

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: The young man said to him, "All these I have kept. What do I still lack?" Jesus said to him, "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these I have kept. He was sincere, and outwardly had kept them from his youth (Mark 10:20), but had not understood the depth of the law (5:21–48). He is a decent, careful, religious man who had done everything he understood himself to have been asked, and that is the most frightening thing about him.

What do I still lack? He knew something was missing. Despite his morality, he had no assurance of eternal life. His honest question is the most hopeful thing about him. And nobody asks it unless something has been nagging at him. He did not need information; he needed to hear it said aloud by someone with the authority to say it.

If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor. Perfect means complete, whole. Jesus puts his finger on the one thing that held his heart. He gives no rule about percentages. He names the specific object that had this specific man, and asks for exactly that.

And you will have treasure in heaven. Treasure where moth and rust do not destroy (6:19–20). Jesus is not confiscating. He is prising the man’s fingers off something small so that his hands are free for something enormous.

And come, follow me. The removal exists for the sake of this last clause. The cure Jesus offers is not a better attitude to money but himself. Only God may say, put away your idol and give your heart to me, and that is exactly what Jesus says. He puts himself where the first commandment puts God.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must sell everything. Zacchaeus gave away half (Luke 19:8), and Joseph of Arimathea remained rich (27:57). The principle for all is that nothing may come before Christ: Christians may own property and save wisely, but must hold it as God’s and be willing to give it up if he asks. Nor does giving away possessions earn eternal life.

Where Christians differ: counsels of perfection. Medieval Catholic teaching distinguished between commands for all Christians and “counsels of perfection” (poverty, celibacy, obedience) for those seeking a higher spiritual state, especially monks and nuns. The Reformers rejected this two-level Christianity: every Christian is called to total devotion, in whatever calling God gives. This commentary’s view: there is one standard of discipleship for all; Jesus addressed this man’s particular idol. Does if you would be perfect mean there is a higher class of Christian, as some teach of vows of poverty and celibacy? No. Jesus means complete, wholehearted devotion, the same word he used in 5:48, and he calls this man to it because wealth was his rival god. The call is to every disciple; what it costs varies from person to person.

How do I find my one thing? Sit still for a minute and most people can name the thing they would least like Christ to ask them for. It is not always money. It may be a relationship you know is pulling you away, a career you have quietly made the point of your life, your reputation, a plan for your children, an addiction you manage rather than end, a grudge you have decided to keep, or simply the fear of what people would say. The tell is the flinch. And the test is not whether you would be willing in principle, because principle costs nothing. It is what happens when the thing is actually named, out loud, and asked for.

What if I find my one thing and cannot let it go? Then you have not failed the test; you have arrived where the gospel starts. When the disciples ask who then can be saved, Jesus does not say, those with the strength to let go. He says that with man it is impossible, and with God all things are possible (v. 26). Bring the clenched hand to him, honestly, and ask him to open it. He does not wait for you to free yourself before he receives you. He frees those who come.

verseByVerse.quote: When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. And Jesus said to his disciples, "Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful. The only person in the Gospels said to have walked away sad from Jesus’ personal call. The same words emptied a fishing boat and a tax booth; this man went home.

Grief is not repentance. He was not scornful. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew Jesus was right: he felt everything a man ought to feel, and did nothing. A person can be moved almost to tears by a sermon on Sunday, know that it describes his own life, have altered nothing by Wednesday, and mistake being moved for being changed. But if you read that and fear it describes you, see the difference: he went away, and you are still listening. The Lord who looked at this man and loved him (Mark 10:21) casts out no one who comes to him (John 6:37).

For he had great possessions. Or rather, his possessions had him. They were not his property but his prison, and he chose to stay in it.

The rich man who went the other way. The Son had the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5), and he let it all go (2 Corinthians 8:9). One man walked away from treasure because it held him. The other walked toward a cross because we did.

Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven. Wealth competes for the heart’s loyalty (6:24) and chokes the word (13:22); it is hard for someone with much to come as a child with nothing (18:3).

The danger named precisely. The trouble with money is not that it is evil; it is that it quietly removes the daily experience of dependence. A man who can solve most of his problems by paying for them will, across twenty years, gradually stop asking anyone for anything, and never notice, because every decision along the way was sensible. He did not rebel against God. He simply stopped needing him for anything specific. Illness and bereavement are often where such a man finally meets God: they are the rooms in a wealthy life where a cheque does nothing at all.

What it does not mean. Not that rich people cannot be saved, or that poverty earns salvation: Jesus will immediately say that with God all things are possible (v. 26). By world standards, most people in Western countries are rich. Scripture has wealthy believers: Abraham, Job, and the women who paid for this very ministry out of their means and stayed to the end when the men had gone (27:55–56; Luke 8:3). This is a warning about a specific danger. It is not a sentence.

How much should I give? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage for Christians, though many find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point. It gives principles instead: give regularly and in proportion to what you have (1 Corinthians 16:2), give generously and cheerfully, not reluctantly (2 Corinthians 9:6–7), care for your own household (1 Timothy 5:8), support those who teach you the word (Galatians 6:6), and do not forget the poor (Galatians 2:10). A useful test is whether your giving costs you anything you notice. If it never does, it is probably not yet generous. Above all, give as one who belongs to Christ, because the giving is the opening of a hand, and the hand is the heart’s. When Jesus told this young man to sell everything, he was not setting a figure for every Christian but exposing the one thing this man loved more than God.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God." When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, "Who then can be saved?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The largest animal in Palestine and the smallest opening: a deliberately absurd picture.

Softenings. There is no evidence for a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle’s Eye, and the reading rope for camel in a few late manuscripts is a scribe’s improvement. Both softenings try to make the sentence survivable. Jesus means it is humanly impossible.

When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished. Wealth was often seen as a sign of God’s blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and this young, serious man was the strongest candidate any of them had ever seen.

Saying, Who then can be saved? Exactly the right question. If salvation depends on human ability, no one can be saved. Almost nobody asks it honestly, because almost everybody keeps a private category of people who obviously qualify: the missionary, the pastor’s wife, the old woman in the third row who has prayed for forty years and never said a sharp word. As long as that category exists, salvation remains comfortably plausible and somebody else’s problem. Jesus has just abolished the category. Not one name survives it.

The answer was standing beside them. Only one way into the kingdom remains: not a man squeezing through, but God coming down. The Son of God opened by his death the door that no rich man or poor man could open from this side.

What it does not mean. Not that wealth is a sign of God’s favour, as the prosperity gospel teaches. Wealth is not a proof of blessing, and it can be a great obstacle.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus looked at them and said, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." Then Peter said in reply, "See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus looked at them and said, With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. The heart of the passage. No one can save himself, but God can save anyone by changing the heart (Jeremiah 32:17). That is what Jesus calls being born again (John 3:3–8): the Holy Spirit gives a new heart that loves God (Ezekiel 36:26), so that a man who could not let go of his money finds that he wants Christ more. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish (Ephesians 2:8–9). Matthew keeps the detail that he looked at them first.

The staircase removed. Everything up to here has been about what a man must do. And now: with man this is impossible. The young man arrived asking what good deed he must do, and the final answer is that there is no deed. He asked exactly the right person, and went home a few verses before the answer came.

What this promise covers. The word this has an antecedent, the salvation of a rich man. It is not a general assurance that anything you want is obtainable if you believe hard enough. It is the promise that the one thing which genuinely cannot be done, the unfastening of a heart welded to its possessions, is the thing God does. When Sarah laughed at the promise of a son, the LORD asked, is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). The impossibility there was a settled fact too, and the answer was a baby.

The rich man at the tomb. Matthew has left the proof at the far end of his book. When the disciples have scattered, a man Matthew alone calls rich comes to Pilate for the body (27:57): a rich disciple, spending his money, his position and his new tomb on a body nobody else would claim. The needle did not widen and the camel did not shrink; God did what he had said only God could do.

Then Peter said in reply, See, we have left everything and followed you. They did what the young man would not: they left their boats, nets and families (4:20, 22; 9:9).

What then will we have? An honest question, perhaps with a trace of self-interest. What is the reward for leaving everything? And the striking thing is that it is not rebuked. Jesus answers it, at length. Christianity is not indifferent to reward, and a piety that claims to want nothing at all is not more spiritual than Peter but less truthful; this Gospel has already told these men to lay up treasure in heaven (6:19–21), which is an instruction to want something. The trouble in Peter’s sentence is not the wanting. It is the small word we. He has just watched another man fail the test, and he has begun to compare.

If salvation is God’s work, does it matter what I do? Yes, though not in the way the young man thought. God saves by changing the heart, and a changed heart follows Christ, repents, gives and obeys (Philippians 2:12–13). Our actions do not earn salvation; they are what salvation looks like when God has done his work. And the impossibility of saving ourselves is exactly what frees us to come: you do not have to manage it, only to ask. Anyone, however far gone, may call on him today, and he who began the work will finish it (Philippians 1:6).

On a Tuesday. Somewhere there is a person you have quietly given up on: a son, a colleague, a hard old neighbour. This verse was spoken about exactly that kind of impossibility, and it covers the person you stopped praying for.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, in the new world. The new world (literally rebirth) means the renewal of all things at Christ’s return (Acts 3:21; Romans 8:19–23). Matthew uses of the creation the word Paul uses of the new birth of a person (Titus 3:5). Whatever happens to a Christian is going to happen to the world.

When the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne. From Daniel 7:9–14. Jesus says it on the road to a cross: the Son of Man who will sit on the throne of glory will first be mocked and flogged and crucified (20:18–19). The thrones he promises his followers are not prizes for their sacrifice but a share in his victory, given by the King who was crowned with thorns first.

You who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. The apostles will share Christ’s rule over the renewed people of God. “Judging” may mean ruling, as Israel’s judges governed and rescued. Paul says all the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2).

Judas in the room. Judas Iscariot is standing in it when this is said. Acts shows his vacant seat filled (Acts 1:20–26). It is possible to stand inside the circle to whom the promise is made, to hear it addressed to you, and not to be in it. That is a warning to the careless, not a torment for the anxious: Judas schemed and did not grieve, while Peter, who failed badly within the week, wept and was restored.

Who are the twelve tribes of Israel, and when will this happen? Premillennial readers, who expect Christ to reign on this earth for a thousand years after his return, take it of ethnic Israel in that future kingdom, and they take the promise with real seriousness. The more likely reading is that it describes the renewal of all things at Christ’s return (the new world), and that the twelve tribes stand for the whole people of God, as the twelve gates and twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem suggest (Revelation 21:12–14). Christians who agree on this still differ on whether Scripture promises a future turning of the Jewish people as a whole to Christ (Romans 11:25–29); that question is not settled by this verse.

And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name’s sake. Not only the Twelve, but every disciple who gives up things for Jesus.

Will receive a hundredfold. In this life, in the family of God (Mark 10:30 adds with persecutions). The hundredfold is made of the same items as the list surrendered. It is not a promise of a hundred houses. It is a promise that a man who loses a family receives a family a hundred times its size, which is a plain description of the church whenever it is working properly.

Somebody is paying this cost today. The convert whose family holds a funeral for him while he is alive; the young woman whose marriage, inheritance and place at the table all go on the day she is baptised. The only place on earth where their hundredfold can be handed over is a congregation. So the question for the reader who has surrendered little is whether anybody is receiving their hundredfold through you.

And will inherit eternal life. The very thing the rich young man wanted (v. 16) and walked away from, given as an inheritance, not a wage.

Does this mean I may neglect my family for Christ? No. This does not license a believer to neglect his family; Jesus condemned that (15:3–6), and Paul says it denies the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). It describes the cost when loyalty to Christ and loyalty to family conflict.
verseByVerse.note: “The new world” is the renewal of all things at Christ’s return.

parallels.desc: I am making all things new

verseByVerse.quote: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But many who are first will be last. The rich young man was first in the eyes of the world, and ended last. The word many is doing careful work: a mechanical inversion, in which being at the front automatically damns and being at the back automatically saves, would only be the same league table turned upside down. It is a warning, not a formula.

And the last first. The disciples, fishermen and a tax collector, were last in the world’s eyes. They will be first, sitting on thrones.

A warning too. The parable that follows ends with the same words (20:1–16), and the saying falls after Peter’s what then will we have? The men most in danger of finishing last are the men who have just been promised that they will be first.

The long-serving. It lands on the man who has given thirty years and cannot rejoice when the convert of six months is asked to do the thing he had assumed would come to him; the unwritten order of seniority no church admits to having. Length of service is real and God does not forget it (v. 29 has just said so). It simply does not establish a position in the queue.

The comfort in it. The reader who came late, who wasted the years, who is privately certain he belongs at the back, is the one this sentence was spoken to encourage. He is not told his lateness does not matter. He is told who decides the order.

The firstborn among many brothers. Only one person in the kingdom is first by right (Colossians 1:18), and he is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). The Son of God took the last place, the servant’s towel and the criminal’s cross, and the last are made first because the First shares what is his with them. No one at his table sits there by seniority, only by being his.

Will there be ranks in heaven, then? Scripture speaks of rewards differing according to faithfulness (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Luke 19:17–19), so there is some sense in which God honours his servants differently. But no one in heaven will be there by merit, everyone will be there by grace, and no one will be resentful. The joy of each will be full, and every crown will be cast before the throne (Revelation 4:10). The point of this verse is not to help us calculate our place but to stop us calculating at all.

The shape of the chapter. Children with nothing, nearly turned away; a young man with everything, who went home; twelve who had left everything, already counting what it was worth. The chapter opened with a question about how much a man is permitted to keep. It closes with a warning about how much a man can lose by being sure he is near the front.

parallels.desc: the same saying ends the next parable

19.theology: Salvation is God’s work. Matthew 19:26 says plainly what the Reformed churches mean by grace: God alone brings a sinner to life, and the unaided human will cannot do it. The rich young man is not an extreme case; every person has something that competes with Christ. The new birth, God’s gracious work that overcomes the resistance of the sinful will, is what makes it possible for anyone to let go and follow Christ.
19.examples:
Then: The rich young man came running (Mark 10:17), eager and morally serious, and went away sorrowful.

Now: Every generation has its version of his idol: wealth, reputation, career, family, comfort. The question Jesus puts is what we are least willing to surrender. The command shows where grace needs to go, and the God who makes the impossible possible is the one who opens the hand.

20.title: First and Last
20.text: <sup>1</sup>“For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. <sup>2</sup>After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, <sup>4</sup>and to them he said, ‘You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you.’ <sup>5</sup>So they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. <sup>6</sup>And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, ‘Why do you stand here idle all day?’ <sup>7</sup>They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’ <sup>8</sup>And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first.’ <sup>9</sup>And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. <sup>10</sup>Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more, but each of them also received a denarius. <sup>11</sup>And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, <sup>12</sup>saying, ‘These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’ <sup>13</sup>But he replied to one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? <sup>14</sup>Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. <sup>15</sup>Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?’ <sup>16</sup>So the last will be first, and the first last.” <sup>17</sup>And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, <sup>18</sup>“See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death <sup>19</sup>and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.” <sup>20</sup>Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. <sup>21</sup>And he said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?” They said to him, “We are able.” <sup>23</sup>He said to them, “You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” <sup>24</sup>And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. <sup>25</sup>But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>26</sup>It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>27</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be your slave, <sup>28</sup>even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>29</sup>And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. <sup>30</sup>And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>31</sup>The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>32</sup>And stopping, Jesus called them and said, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>33</sup>They said to him, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 turns the world’s values over. In the parable of the workers in the vineyard, those hired at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who worked all day; the owner pays what was agreed, but his generosity offends their sense of merit. The parable is about grace: God owes nothing to anyone, and salvation is mercy.

Then comes the third prediction of the cross (vv. 17–19), and at once the mother of James and John asks for the seats of honour. Jesus answers that the leader is the servant and the first is the slave, and grounds it in his own mission: the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. The chapter closes on the Jericho road, where two blind men call him Son of David, receive their sight and follow him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Workers are hired at dawn, nine, noon, three and five, and all receive the same denarius at day’s end. Those hired first complain. Only the dawn workers agree a figure; everyone hired later goes on the owner’s word alone. And he has the last paid first, so that the first see it.
verseByVerse.theology: The owner paid what was agreed, and his generosity to others takes nothing from them. The problem is not injustice but envy: is your eye evil because I am good? The wage is set by need rather than output, since a denarius was a day’s keep for a household, and there is only one wage because eternal life does not come in grades.
verseByVerse.examples: The deathbed convert and the lifelong believer receive the same eternal life, because it is a gift, not a wage proportional to service. And no labourer in the parable finds his own way to the vineyard: each is there because the owner came down to the market and found him.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 20 is the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem, held together by one question: what is God like when he gives? A landowner keeps going out to the marketplace all day, until at five in the afternoon he is still finding men nobody wanted, and at evening every one receives a full day’s wage: salvation is a gift, and only the man who was counting goes home bitter. Then Jesus foretells his death and resurrection in the plainest words yet; James and John ask for the best seats; and he defines greatness as service and his death as a ransom for many. At Jericho two blind beggars cry for mercy, are healed, and follow him.

The connection. For ties this parable to the saying just before it: many who are first will be last, and the last first (19:30). So that the promise of thrones and a hundredfold (19:28–29) would not be turned into a ledger, he tells this story, and ends it with the same saying turned round (v. 16).

Stand in the marketplace at first light. A day labourer owned nothing but his hands. If a landowner picked him at dawn his children ate that night, and if nobody picked him they did not. The law assumed the knife edge he lived on: the hired worker was to be paid before the sun went down, for he is poor and counts on it (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). That is why standing unhired at five in the afternoon is a disaster with a family attached to it.

For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house. Not like a wage system but like a person: the landowner pictures God. Every question the parable raises about fairness is answered not with a principle but with a man, and by the end the only question left is what sort of man he is.

Who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. The parable repeats one detail until it cannot be missed: he went out. This man has a foreman (v. 8), and he does not send him. He walks down to the market himself at dawn, and again at nine, at noon, at three, and at five, when no sane employer is still hiring. The urgency fits the grape harvest of late summer, when extra hands were needed before the autumn rains.

The master who would not send the foreman. God did not stay in heaven and send a deputy to the square. The Word became flesh (John 1:14). The man on the road to Jerusalem is the Master going out in person, at the cost of his own life.

His vineyard. Israel was God’s vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), so the field is the people of God. That matters when the grumbling starts: the men who complain are not outsiders. They are inside the vineyard, and have been working in it since dawn.

After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day. A denarius was the standard day’s wage, about enough to feed a family for a day. The master pays the market rate for a working day of about twelve hours. The story opens as an ordinary piece of business, which is why its end lands as hard as it does.

Is a deathbed conversion real? Yes. The thief on the cross received the whole of salvation in his last hours: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). And in this parable the men hired at the eleventh hour receive exactly the same wage as the men hired at dawn. A person who turns to Christ at eighty, or in a hospital bed, is not given a smaller salvation or a back seat. But nothing here licenses delay. The late workers were hired the moment they were called and went at once, and nobody in the parable chose to wait until five because he had heard the pay was the same. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and the man who plans to come at the last hour has no promise that he will be offered one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. The working day ran from sunrise to sunset.

parallels.desc: do not hold back a hired worker’s wages overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and to them he said, "You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you." So they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And going out about the third hour. About nine in the morning. Idle does not mean lazy but without work.

Whatever is right I will give you. Something changes at nine in the morning, and everything later depends on it. The dawn men had negotiated: a denarius, agreed, settled before a foot went into the vineyard. These men are offered no figure at all. Whatever is right, whatever is just, I will give you. They have a promise and a person, and no number.

So they went. For a man with nothing in the house, going to work on a stranger’s word is no small thing. Every group after the first goes into the vineyard on the character of the owner rather than on terms, and that turns out to be the difference between the men who end the day content and the men who end it bitter. The dawn workers were the only men on the estate with a figure in their heads, and by evening the figure had become a grievance.

Whatever is right, sealed in blood. The nine o’clock men had only a person’s word, and so do we, but we know far more of the person. All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). To walk into the vineyard on his word is to trust the one who has already shown, at Calvary, what he thinks is right to give.

Is it wrong to make agreements, or to want to know where I stand? No. The parable is not against agreements. The dawn men did nothing wrong in accepting a denarius, and the master never suggests they did; he will treat the agreement as binding and honour it to the coin. Contracts are good and proper among men, and God himself binds himself by covenant promises you may hold him to. The trouble comes when a man carries a wage contract into a relationship that was never a wage arrangement, and then reads every kindness God shows to somebody else as a clause he has been denied. God’s promises are to be trusted, not invoiced.

On a Tuesday. Recall the last time God did not do what you expected, and the first sentence that came into your head. If it was something like I deserved better than this, you were holding a contract. Lay it down, and go back to today’s work on his word.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m.

verseByVerse.quote: Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, "Why do you stand here idle all day?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. Noon, and then three, and the master is still coming out to bring more people in.

And about the eleventh hour. About five in the afternoon, with the working day ending at six. He found others standing: perhaps the weakest, the oldest or the least wanted.

What that standing had been like. Four times they had watched an employer walk in, look along the line, choose other men, and walk out. By the middle of the afternoon a man in that line is not hoping any more; he is standing there because going home is worse.

Why do you stand here idle all day? Read the master’s question in the tone the next verse requires, not the tone we expect. It sounds like an accusation and is nothing of the kind: their answer will satisfy him completely and he will hire them on the spot. It is the question of a man who has walked up to people nobody else has spoken to all day and asked them what happened.

These men have a name in every congregation. The one out of work long enough that the sympathy has run out; the believer converted at sixty who thinks he has nothing to bring; the chronically ill Christian who cannot do any of the things his church visibly counts. If you have thought that you arrived too late to matter, this is the hour you were hired in.

The Unchosen who chooses. The one telling this parable knew that square from the inside. He was despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3), the stone the builders rejected (21:42). A crowd offered a choice picked Barabbas (27:21). The Lord who walks up to the unchosen at five in the afternoon was passed over himself, so that those passed over might be picked.

What do I do with the years I wasted before I came to Christ? Grieve them honestly, because the years were real and some of what was lost cannot be recovered. But do not let the grief tell you a lie about the present. The eleventh-hour men did not spend their one hour lamenting the eleven; they worked, and at evening they were paid in full. God says he will restore the years the locust has eaten (Joel 2:25), and he does it not by giving the years back but by making what is left fruitful far beyond its length. Serve gladly in the hour you have, and leave the arithmetic to the Master.

On a Tuesday. Someone in your church is plainly standing in the square: overlooked, unchosen, slightly hard work. Go out to him this week the way the Master went out for you: ask a real question and wait for the answer.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m., the eleventh about 5 p.m. — an hour before the day ended.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Because no one has hired us." He said to them, "You go into the vineyard too." And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, "Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because no one has hired us. That is the whole answer, and the parable lets it stand. The master refuses to blame them for a condition that was done to them, and puts them in the vineyard for the last hour of the light.

You go into the vineyard too. No interview, no terms: they are simply welcomed.

And when evening came. Sunset, the time the law set for paying wages (Deuteronomy 24:15). Evening pictures the end of the age. The one who will settle accounts is Jesus himself, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22), and that is why the reckoning holds no terror for those he hired: the Judge at the pay table is the one who came to the square.

Beginning with the last, up to the first. The most deliberate sentence in the parable. Pay the dawn men first, and they take their denarius and walk home satisfied, never learning what happened at the far end of the queue. He has the last men paid first, in full view, while the men who have been there since dawn stand in the line and do the arithmetic.

Diagnosis, not cruelty. That order is not meant to wound. God lets us see what he has given somebody else, because what rises in us when we see it tells the truth about us, and until it rises it cannot be healed. When you hear of someone else’s blessing and feel a small cold drop of something other than gladness, it was sent the way a doctor sends a man for a scan.

Does every detail, like the foreman, stand for something? No. A parable is a story with one main point and a few telling details, not a code in which every item has a hidden meaning. The foreman is there because a real estate had one, and because the payroll had to be handled by someone. The master, the vineyard, the hiring and the pay plainly carry the meaning; the foreman, the hours and the marketplace furnish the scene. Reading too much into the furniture is how parables have been made to say almost anything, so hold on to what Jesus himself draws out in verse 16.

parallels.desc: give him his wages on the same day

verseByVerse.quote: And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. A full day’s wage for one hour’s work.

What the master was doing with that coin. A denarius was a day’s keep. The eleventh-hour man had earned a twelfth of it, which would have fed nobody. So the master pays him not what his hour was worth but what his household needs. The wage in this parable is set by need and by the master’s goodness, and in that coin the shape of the whole gospel is standing.

Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. One hour has been paid a denarius, so twelve should bring twelve. But they supposed it; nobody had told them so. The extra eleven denarii existed nowhere but in their own heads.

But each of them also received a denarius. Exactly what they had agreed (v. 2). There is only one wage in this story, and it is the whole of what the master has to give. Eternal life does not come in grades, because God is not a quantity you accumulate: eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (John 17:3). It felt like an insult only because they had been thinking of it as pay. So it is with Christ. Everyone who is in him has all of him: the same adoption, the same inheritance, the same righteousness (Philippians 3:9). None of us obeys perfectly, but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, and God counts his obedience as ours, so the newest believer stands before the holy God as fully accepted as the oldest, because neither stands there in his own record.

Disappointment over things he never said. A great deal of the disappointment Christians carry with God is over things he never promised: that the marriage would be easy because you waited, that the child raised in the faith would keep it, that the years of service would be recognised. The grief over a wayward child or a hard diagnosis is real, and he receives it; what needs laying down is the bitterness, and the list of things he never said is usually shorter than the grievance.

But does God not promise to bless obedience? He does, and those promises are real (Psalm 1; Galatians 6:9). But look at what he actually promises: his presence, his care, a harvest in due season, and a reward that is itself his gift. He does not promise a particular outcome on a particular timetable, measured against what other people receive. The sting in this verse is not that the dawn men were promised nothing. It is that they added to what they were promised, and then held the master to their additions.

On a Tuesday. Would you be glad if someone who came to faith on his deathbed received the same eternal life as you? Try it with a real name: the relative who mocked your faith for forty years, the man who did real harm and then repented in prison. If resentment rises, bring it to the Master who put the full wage into your hand when you had earned none of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, saying, "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house. Grumbled is the word used of Israel murmuring in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; 1 Corinthians 10:10): a people fed with bread from heaven every morning, complaining about the menu.

These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us. By human standards the complaint is fair: twelve hours of summer work, the scorching heat perhaps the burning east wind, against one hour in the cool of the evening. But listen to what they say. Their complaint is not that they had been cheated, but that others had been made equal to them.

Nothing had happened to them. Their wage had not been cut. One thing changed: they saw somebody else’s pay. That is the whole mechanism of envy. It cannot take anything from anyone; it can only alter how you feel about what you have. A man happy at dawn is bitter by dusk with the same denarius in his pocket.

Who are they? They are like the Pharisees, who grumbled that Jesus welcomed tax collectors and sinners (9:11; Luke 15:2), and like the elder brother in the parable of the prodigal son, standing outside while the fatted calf was killed for the younger (Luke 15:28–30). In Matthew’s setting they also fit Israel’s leaders, resenting the Gentiles and outcasts being brought in on equal terms. And they are like Peter, who had just asked what he would get for leaving everything (19:27). Anyone who serves God for a long time can fall into this attitude, which is why the parable is told to disciples.

How do I break envy when I find it in myself? The master’s cure is a question, and it can be borrowed: did you not agree with me for a denarius? Go back to what you were actually given, and say it out loud if it helps. Then do three things. Name it to God as sin rather than as a grievance, since it will always present itself as a grievance; that is its disguise, and the disguise is why it survives so long in respectable people. Thank him deliberately and specifically for your own denarius. And pray for the person by name, asking God to give him more of the very thing you envy. It is close to impossible at first, and it works.

For worship. The grumblers said they had borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat. One man truly bore it. From the sixth hour to the ninth hour darkness lay over the land (27:45), and in that darkness the Son carried the whole weight of his people’s sin, and opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). He bore the burden so that latecomers could share his wage. When the crowd grumbled at him as Israel had over the manna (John 6:41), he gave himself as bread for the murmurers.

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to one of them, "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Friend. But he replied to one of them, Friend: not the warm word we hear in English. It is a polite but cool address, and Matthew uses it three times: here, to the man grumbling at the pay table; at 22:12, to the guest without a wedding garment; and at 26:50, from Jesus to Judas with the kiss still on his face. Every one is addressed to a man in the wrong, and every one is courteous.

I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Every fact is on the master’s side. The grievance is not that the man received too little but that somebody else received the same.

Take what belongs to you and go. There is an edge under the courtesy: he gets exactly what he bargained for. A man who insists on strict justice from God will receive strict justice, and nothing is more frightening to be granted. The eleventh-hour men went home with the same coin and something the grumbler never got near: they knew it was a gift.

I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. I will, I want to: not I am obliged. That is the only reason given in the whole parable for the eleventh-hour denarius, and Scripture never finds the reason God saves anybody in the person saved. He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, according to the purpose of his will (Ephesians 1:4–5). That free decision to save particular sinners is what Scripture calls election. It is not a cold list; it is the reason the master went down to the square at all.

The warmer word. Hold this cool word beside the upper room: I have called you friends (John 15:15), and there the word is one of real affection. He made the warm word true in the only way it could be made true for sinners: greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends (John 15:13). The grumbler is kept at a courteous distance by his own contract. The friends of Jesus are brought near by his blood.

Is God being cold to the grumbler? No, and the scene is worth reading again for how he handles him. He does not have him removed. He does not answer him through the foreman. He comes to him personally, calls him by a courteous name, sets out the reasoning step by step, and asks him two questions, which is more than the complaint deserved and more patience than most of us would show. The coolness of the word friend is a warning, not a rejection: it tells the man he is standing in a dangerous place. But the master is still standing there talking to him, and the conversation is an invitation to see the gift for what it is.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" So the last will be first, and the first last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Here is the sovereignty of God, and it needs its guard on both sides. This is not a God who does as he likes and calls it righteousness. The master has just shown, point by point, that he has wronged nobody, and he does not appeal to his rights until after he has cleared himself on justice. Sovereign generosity is not caprice. But nor is it negotiable. Salvation and its rewards are his to give as he wills: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Romans 9:15–16). He owes no one more than justice, and he is free to give grace. And justice, for sinners, would mean condemnation: the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). The sovereignty of the master is not a threat hanging over the latecomers; it is the only reason anyone in the line is paid at all. What is his is his, and grace is not a substance that gets thinner when it is shared. Nobody in that line was given less because somebody else was given something.

Or do you begrudge my generosity? The English hides how sharp this is. Word for word it reads: is your eye evil because I am good? An evil eye was the Jewish idiom for envy and stinginess: a man with a good eye is open-handed, and a man with an evil eye is the grudging one who cannot bear to give or to see giving (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 23:6; 28:22). Matthew’s readers had met it already in the Sermon on the Mount: if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness (6:22–23), set in the middle of a passage about money and treasure. So the master’s question is a diagnosis of an organ. The problem is not the wage; it is the eye that looked down the line.

Because I am good. He does not say, is your eye evil because they are undeserving. He says, because I am good. That is more searching than a charge of greed: something in a fallen man can be made bitter by God being kind where he did not expect him to be. Jonah had it, outside Nineveh, angry enough to die because God was gracious and merciful (Jonah 4:1–3).

The Good One telling the story. Jesus had just told the rich young man, There is only one who is good (19:17). Now he tells a story whose master says, I am good, and the man telling it is the one in whom that goodness walked the roads. When we resent God’s goodness to someone else, it is finally Christ we resent: his welcome to tax collectors, his meals with sinners, his ransom paid for people we would have left in the square.

So the last will be first, and the first last. The saying of 19:30, turned round, closing the brackets around the parable. Some later manuscripts add here, for many are called, but few are chosen; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it (Jesus certainly says it at 22:14).

The meaning. Eternal life is not a wage earned in proportion to work, but a gift given equally to all who are called, early or late. Grace offends those who think in terms of merit, and delights those who know they have none.

Does the one denarius mean there are no differences of reward in heaven? The wage everyone receives is eternal life, God himself, and that is the same for all. Other passages speak of different rewards and responsibilities (Luke 19:17–19; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but those rewards are themselves grace, God crowning his own gifts, and no one in heaven will envy another. A thimble and a bucket can both be full. The saint with the larger capacity will not look down on the other, and the other will not look up in resentment, because envy is one of the things that does not get through the gate.

Then why work hard for Christ, if the late convert gets the same? Because the work was never the price. The dawn men had the privilege of a whole day in the vineyard: the Master’s company, his purpose, the joy of fruit, and freedom from the misery of the square. Paul worked harder than all the apostles and called it the grace of God that was with him (1 Corinthians 15:10). Those who serve longest are not the most owed but the most blessed. If you resent the hours, you were treating them as payment; if you see them as a gift, you will wish the late arrivals had come sooner, not that they had been paid less.

The mercy in the arithmetic. If the kingdom paid by the hour, the latecomer would have almost nothing, and the dawn man would spend eternity knowing exactly how much he had earned. The master hands every one of them the entire day’s keep and shuts the ledger, and the only man who goes home unhappy is the one who kept it open.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “do you begrudge” is literally “is your eye bad” — an idiom for envy.

parallels.desc: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–34 — The Third Passion Prediction, the Mother's Request, and Two Blind Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus gives his fullest prediction yet: delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, crucified, raised. At once James and John, through their mother, ask for the seats at his right and left, and Jesus answers all twelve: greatness is service, and the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many. At Jericho two blind men cry out to the Son of David and receive their sight.
verseByVerse.theology: He has announced crucifixion, and she asks for thrones. Jesus answers with patience: the cup he must drink is suffering and the wrath of God against sin, and the places at his right and left are the Father’s to give. He does not abolish ambition but changes its object, and the standard he sets is not an attitude but his own cross. The many of verse 28 is Isaiah’s word for a multitude (Isaiah 53:11–12), not a word that fences people out.
