verseByVerse.examples: The two blind men at Jericho recall the two blind men of 9:27–31, and the cry to the Son of David prepares for the crowds’ Hosanna at Jerusalem. Matthew asks the same question twice in this chapter: what do you want, to the mother of James and John (v. 21), and what do you want me to do for you, to the beggars (v. 32). One asks for the best seats in the kingdom; the other asks for eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem. Going up is not a figure of speech. From Jericho the road climbs about a kilometre in some fifteen miles of bare rock, in a Passover crowd, and the man at the front of the column knows what is waiting at the top. Mark says he walked ahead of them, and they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid (Mark 10:32).

He took the twelve disciples aside. On a packed festival road he tells the Twelve, quietly and on the move, that he is going up to be killed.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. The third telling, and the most exact (16:21; 17:22–23): now it is condemnation, the Gentiles, mocking, flogging, and crucifixion, named for the first time.

In the flow. The parable has said that the last will be first; now the one who is truly first says he is going up to be made last; and in the next scene two of his friends ask to be first.

He looked straight at it. Most of us manage dread by not looking at it: not asking the consultant the second question, leaving the letter unopened. Jesus named what was coming, three times, to people who did not want to hear it, and set his face to the hill and kept climbing. He walked toward suffering on purpose, for us, and he walks with his people toward whatever they dread.

And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. Delivered by whom? Judas, the Jewish ruling council and Pilate, every one of them answerable. But at Pentecost Peter will say who stood behind the passive: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). And they will condemn him to death: the council would pass the sentence, he deserves death (26:66).

If God planned the cross, how could Judas and the leaders be guilty? Scripture holds both together without embarrassment, and so must we. God ordains all that comes to pass, yet he is not the author of sin, and the will of the creatures is not violated (the Westminster Confession 3.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1). Judas acted freely, out of his own greed and unbelief, and was fully responsible; God, in the same events, was working out the salvation of the world. Joseph said it to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The brothers who sold Joseph into Egypt are the old pattern of it: their evil was wholly theirs, and the good God brought out of it was wholly his, and here the pattern reaches its height in the betrayal of the one Joseph foreshadowed. You cannot fully see how the two fit, but you can see why it matters: the worst thing human beings ever did was not outside God’s hand, and so nothing done to you is either.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And deliver him over to the Gentiles. The council could not carry out the death penalty itself (John 18:31). Jew and Gentile each contribute their portion to the same crucifixion, and nobody in the story stands outside it.

To be mocked and flogged and crucified. Mocked is not teasing: a scarlet robe over a torn back, a crown of thorns, soldiers kneeling before they spat on him (27:27–31). Flogged is the Roman scourge, a whip with bone and metal tied into its thongs (27:26). And crucified (27:35) was the cruellest and most shameful Roman death, so far beneath a citizen that Cicero said the very word should be kept away from Roman ears. It was the death kept for slaves and rebels, worth remembering at verse 27.

And he will be raised on the third day. The last verb, which he has never once left out. When the women come to the tomb, the angel does not break news to them; he reminds them: he is not here, for he has risen, as he said (28:6).

A strange comfort. The men closest to him heard all three predictions and fell apart when it happened, and it did not derail a single detail. He was not depending on their understanding to get it done, and he is not depending on yours: your salvation rests on what he did, not on how well you grasp it.

Why did the disciples not understand something said so plainly? Because it did not fit what they already believed. They expected a Messiah who would conquer, and a crucified Messiah was a contradiction in terms, a stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23). Luke says the saying was hidden from them (Luke 18:34). We do the same: we hear the parts of Scripture that fit our hopes and quietly file away the parts that do not. The remedy is to read what is actually there, and to ask the Spirit to open our eyes, as Jesus later opened theirs when he explained from all the Scriptures that the Christ must suffer and enter his glory (Luke 24:26–27, 45).
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the first to name crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. And he said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons. She was probably Salome, present at the crucifixion (27:56; Mark 15:40), and possibly the sister of Jesus’ mother (John 19:25), which would make James and John his cousins: family has claims.

And kneeling before him she asked him for something. The timing is the shock: Jesus has just announced that he is going up to be crucified, and the family of Zebedee responds with a request for thrones.

Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom. The places of highest honour and power. They took the promise of twelve thrones (19:28) and wanted the best two, still imagining an earthly kingdom, coming soon.

Mother or sons? A reader with Mark open will stop here, because there the brothers make the request themselves (Mark 10:35). Which was it? It is often said that Matthew moved the words onto their mother to spare the two apostles. That explanation is worth resisting, for two reasons. First, Matthew is not a man who spares people: he records Peter called Satan (16:23), the disciples fleeing (26:56), and his own name in the list as Matthew the tax collector (10:3). Second, and decisively, look at the very next verse. Jesus does not answer the mother. He says, you do not know what you are asking, and in the Greek every you is plural, addressed to the sons; it is the sons who reply, we are able. Three verses later the ten are indignant, and not with her: they are indignant at the two brothers (v. 24). Matthew’s own account, read to the end, has James and John behind the request, exactly as Mark says. So both are true, and the likeliest picture is one anyone who has watched a family will recognise: the sons wanted the thrones and their mother made the request. Matthew tells you who spoke; Mark tells you whose ambition it was.

The throne they did not see. The ones at Jesus’ right and left when he was proclaimed King of the Jews were two criminals crucified with him (27:38), under a sign that gave him exactly that title (27:37). Yet the throne was real, and the way to it ran through that hill: after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3). That seat was his, won by the cross, and from it he shares his reign with those who share his cup. Within days their mother stood among the women watching him die (27:55–56), and on the third day she saw the rest.

Is it wrong to want to be great, or to pray for my children’s success? Not in itself. Jesus does not rebuke the wanting to be great; in verse 26 he redirects it. And a mother’s prayer for her sons is a beautiful thing. What was wrong here was the object and the motive: honour above others, sought by influence, in a kingdom misunderstood. Pray for your children to be near Christ, to be faithful and fruitful and to serve; pray that they will be great in the only way the kingdom counts greatness. Pray less for their position and more for their character, and leave their place to the Father. Underneath the request was something most of us share: the wish to feel secure by being ranked above others. Jesus offers a better security, a place prepared by the Father that nobody can lobby away from you (v. 23).
verseByVerse.note: In Mark the brothers ask for themselves. Comparing the women at the cross, their mother may be Salome.

parallels.desc: the mother of the sons of Zebedee at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?" They said to him, "We are able." He said to them, "You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You do not know what you are asking. They did not understand that the way to glory was through suffering.

Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink? Unless we understand the cup, his question makes no sense. In the prophets the cup is not an image of hardship in general; it is a very specific vessel. Asaph sees it in the LORD’s own hand: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Psalm 75:8). Isaiah calls it the cup of his wrath and pictures Jerusalem staggering after drinking it (Isaiah 51:17). Jeremiah is handed it and made to take it round the nations (Jeremiah 25:15–16). So when Jesus asks two ambitious young men whether they can drink the cup he is about to drink, he is not asking whether they can cope with a hard road. He is telling them what he is going up to Jerusalem to receive, and it is not chiefly nails. It is the wrath of God against sin, poured out and drained to the bottom by somebody who never earned a drop of it. Jesus would drink this cup at the cross, bearing God’s judgment on sin in his people’s place. In Gethsemane he prayed that it might pass from him, if possible (26:39), and then took it. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add here and in verse 23 the words about being baptised with his baptism; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit them (they are certainly part of Mark’s account, Mark 10:38–39).

We are able. Brave, sincere and ignorant. Within days they would be asleep in the garden and then running away in the dark.

You will drink my cup. He does not call them liars. They would share his sufferings, though not his atoning work, and they did, in two very different shapes. James was the first apostle to be martyred (Acts 12:2). John, by the early church’s memory, outlived them all, exiled on Patmos (Revelation 1:9), watching his friends die one by one. A short violent cup and a long lonely one. A Christian who has been given the slow version, a caring role that never ends or an illness that never lifts, should not conclude he was given the easy one.

But to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant. This is not Jesus disclaiming authority: he ends the book saying all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (28:18). It is the Son, equal with the Father, declining to act outside the Father’s arrangement, the pattern of his whole earthly life (John 5:19, 30).

But it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father. Rewards in the kingdom are God’s gift, prepared in advance, not won by ambition (25:34). Position in the kingdom is not open to lobbying, which frees a Christian from a great deal of exhausting comparison: if your place cannot be secured by asking, it cannot be lost by somebody else asking either.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples’ sufferings atone for sin. Only Christ drank the cup of God’s wrath; his followers share in suffering for his sake (Colossians 1:24; 1 Peter 4:13).

If Jesus drank the cup of wrath, why do Christians still suffer? Because there are two cups, and only one of them was his alone. The cup of wrath, God’s judgment on sin, he drained completely; not a drop of it is left for those who are in him (Romans 8:1). The cup his disciples share is the cup of suffering for his sake: opposition, loss, hardship, sometimes death, borne in fellowship with him. Your suffering is never God punishing you for sins Christ already paid for. It is the road the Master walked, now walked with him, and it ends where his ended, in glory (Romans 8:17).
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is an Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. But Jesus called them to him and said, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. Not out of moral superiority: they wanted the same places themselves.

But Jesus called them to him. All of them. Nobody in the room got to hear this as advice for somebody else.

You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. Both verbs carry the prefix down upon. The disciples had seen it in the Herods and the Roman governors. Greatness in the world means having others under you, and Jesus describes it without a flicker of admiration.

Authority that comes down underneath. The one true Lord also came down, from heaven (John 6:38), but he came down to go underneath. He took the form of a servant and humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8). The shape of his power is a man stooping under a beam. So no pastor, elder or church member may use a place in the church to get his own way, to frighten people, or to be waited on.

Where does this show up today? Not only in tyrants. It appears in the husband who uses his headship to get his own way, which is the very opposite of the self-giving love Scripture means by headship (Ephesians 5:25), and abuse is never to be tolerated under any name. It appears in the pastor who treats disagreement as rebellion, the manager who enjoys making people wait, the parent who rules by temper, the committee member who guards his territory. The question is never whether you have authority, but which way it presses: down on people, for your sake, or under them, for theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: "It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be your slave," "even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It shall not be so among you. Leadership in Christ’s community is not domination. Servant leadership has become a slogan, so it is worth pinning down what Jesus actually says.

But whoever would be great among you must be your servant. He does not abolish ambition; he changes its object. James and John have misunderstood what mattering is, which turns out to be a towel rather than a throne. Servant is the word for someone who waits at table.

And whoever would be first among you must be your slave. Slave goes further: someone with no rights, who belongs to another, not his time, not his reputation, not his plans for the afternoon. The two words come in ascending order, the opposite direction from the one careers normally travel.

How do I tell a servant from someone using the word? The tests are uncomfortable. A servant is available: he does not control his own diary the way a master does. A servant does work that nobody sees and nobody thanks him for, and keeps doing it when the thanks do not come. A servant can be interrupted. And the sharpest test of all: you can tell a servant by how he behaves when he is treated like one. Anyone can adopt the language while quietly requiring the deference; the moment of truth is when the deference is not given.

Even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. He does not say be like a servant; he says this is what I came to do. The Son of Man of Daniel 7 is the one whom all peoples, nations and languages should serve (Daniel 7:14), and he came to be the servant of the world. At the Last Supper he would take a towel and wash his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17).

And to give his life as a ransom for many. The heart of the gospel, in Jesus’ own words. A ransom was the price paid to set a slave or prisoner free, or to redeem a forfeit life (Exodus 21:30). Jesus gives his life to set his people free from sin, death and God’s judgment. For means in place of: a substitute. This echoes Isaiah 53:10–12, where the Servant makes his soul an offering for guilt and bears the sin of many. The cross is the supreme act of service, and the service that makes every other service possible.

In the flow. Verse 28 is the summit of the chapter. It explains the third prediction (vv. 18–19) as a payment he makes rather than a tragedy that overtakes him. The angel said that he would save his people from their sins (1:21); here Jesus says how.

For many. Christ died for his people (1:21), the many, and actually secured their redemption; the gospel offer goes to all (28:19). Christians differ on the extent of the atonement, as the next paragraph explains.

Does many mean not all? Begin where the objection is weakest. In Hebrew and Aramaic “the many” is not a word that shuts people out; it means the multitude, the great mass. Isaiah uses it exactly so of the Servant who makes many to be accounted righteous and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:11–12), the passage Jesus is echoing, and Paul can move between “the many” and “all” without feeling he has changed the subject (Romans 5:15–19). So the word itself is not a fence; it is a word for a crowd nobody could count. Underneath, though, is a real question Christians have long divided over. Scripture also says Christ gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6; see 1 John 2:2). Reformed churches answer that the key is what a ransom does. A ransom is not an offer; it is a payment. Money laid on the table for a hundred prisoners does not make a hundred men releasable; it releases them. If Christ’s death merely made salvation possible for everyone and certain for no one, it would be the one ransom in history that might be paid and leave the captive in his cell. So the cross actually secured the freedom of those it was given for, which is why the New Testament speaks of it as purchasing a people and not merely an opportunity (Acts 20:28; Ephesians 5:25). The “all” texts are read as all kinds of people, Jew and Gentile, rulers and subjects. Other believers who love the same Lord read those texts more broadly, and they should be heard with respect and never caricatured.

Then how do I know I am one of the many? Not by working it out first. This doctrine has sometimes been used to frighten people it was meant to comfort, and no one in Scripture is ever sent to look for his name on a list before coming. The invitation is unrestricted: let the one who desires take the water of life without price (Revelation 22:17), and there is no small print under it. You find out you were among the many the way the eleventh-hour workers found out they were in the vineyard: by coming when called, and being handed the wage. Whoever comes to Christ will never be cast out (John 6:37). The doctrine is not a gate to be checked before you approach. It is the discovery, afterwards, that the price of your freedom was paid before you ever thought to ask.

Is a God who requires a ransom in blood not cruel? Only if the ransom were wrung out of an unwilling victim to satisfy someone else. But look at who pays. The Son of Man gives his own life; nobody takes it from him. And the God whose justice is satisfied is the same God who provides the price: Paul calls the church the flock God obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). Sin is not a small debt a holy God could quietly write off, any more than a just judge could shrug at murder. At the cross God takes his own holiness with full seriousness and pays its demand himself. That is not cruelty. It is love that spared itself nothing.

What it does not mean. Not that the ransom was paid to Satan, as some early church writers suggested. Scripture does not say to whom the ransom was paid, but its broader teaching shows that Christ satisfied God’s justice by bearing the penalty for sin (Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21). This is penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty our sin deserved, in our place.

Two guards on servant leadership. This is not the abolition of authority: a leader who will not lead is not being humble but leaving people unshepherded (Hebrews 13:17). Servant leadership is authority used for the good of those under it. But the commoner failure is the other: a man who wears the phrase as a title while making every decision alone and requiring loyalty from everyone beneath him has kept the substance of what Jesus forbade and taken the vocabulary of what he commanded. The elder is to shepherd not domineering over those in his charge, but being an example to the flock (1 Peter 5:3).

Where Christians differ: the atonement. Some see Christ’s death mainly as an example of self-giving love (the moral influence view), or as a victory over evil powers (Christus Victor). These contain truth: the cross does show love (1 John 4:10) and defeat Satan (Colossians 2:15). But Jesus’ word “ransom … in place of many” points to substitution at the centre. This commentary’s view: penal substitution is the heart of the atonement, with example and victory flowing from it.

On a Tuesday. You were ransomed by a Servant who spared himself nothing. Look for the job in your home or church that nobody wants and nobody will notice, and do it without mentioning it. You will serve unevenly, but the Servant served perfectly in your place, and his Spirit in you makes today’s small service possible.
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!" The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they went out of Jericho. The last stop on the pilgrim road. A great crowd followed him: pilgrims heading up for Passover.

Leaving or entering? Matthew and Mark place the healing as Jesus was leaving Jericho, but Luke sets it as he drew near (Luke 18:35). The likeliest answer is simple once you know the ground. There were two Jerichos about a mile apart: the old ruined mound of Joshua’s city, and the new Jericho that Herod had built beside it, with its palaces and gardens. Jesus could be leaving the one and approaching the other at the same moment, so both descriptions could be literally true of one scene seen from two sides. That is one likely explanation among several offered, and none requires a contradiction.

And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside. Mark names one, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). Matthew mentions two, as at Gadara (8:28); one never denies a second. They seized their only chance: he would not come this way again.

Mercy at Jericho again. When Joshua came to Jericho, one household was spared: Rahab’s, an ancestor of Jesus (1:5). Now the one who bears Joshua’s name, the LORD saves, comes through Jericho, and again what comes out of the city is mercy for the outcast. The first Joshua brought down walls. The second opens eyes.

They cried out, Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David! They recognise him as the Messiah (see 9:27; 15:22), the title the crowds will shout at the entry into Jerusalem days later (21:9). Two men who could not see shouted the one true title on that road, while a crowd with perfect eyesight told them to stop.

The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent. Not the officials, but the people following Jesus, as the disciples turned away the children (19:13). Twice in two chapters the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the group already committed to him.

Who has learned to keep quiet in our church? Every congregation has ways of signalling that a particular sort of person is making things difficult: the man whose questions hold everything up, the woman whose crisis has gone on too long, the family whose children are loud, the person whose need is chronic and will not resolve into a tidy testimony. Nobody says be quiet. The crowd in this story probably thought it was being helpful, keeping the road clear for an important man on important business. Ask seriously who has learned to keep his voice down in your church, and who taught him; then make room for him to cry out.

But they cried out all the more. The opposition made them louder (15:22–28).

Does persistent prayer twist God’s arm? No, and this passage is often turned into a technique. Their persistence is not what obtained the miracle, and shouting longer is not a lever that moves God. Jesus is not worn down here; he is not reluctant at any point, and there is no hint that a quieter pair would have been left blind. Persistence in prayer is not leverage. It is what real need looks like from the outside. They kept calling because they had no alternative, and they had worked out who was walking past. So keep praying, not to change his heart, which is already kind, but because he is the only one who can help.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Mark names one of the men, Bartimaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: And stopping, Jesus called them and said, "What do you want me to do for you?" They said to him, "Lord, let our eyes be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And stopping, Jesus called them. He is going up to the Passover at which he will be executed, and he stops the whole procession for two men everybody else had classified as an interruption. Under the heaviest pressure a human being has ever carried, he stops.

What do you want me to do for you? Matthew has put the same question twice in one chapter, and it is the spine of the whole thing. To the mother of James and John, in verse 21: what do you want? To two beggars on the Jericho road: what do you want me to do for you? Same questioner, same chapter, same courtesy, and two answers that could not be further apart. One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom. The other asks for eyes. The brothers asked for status; the blind men asked for mercy.

He asks anyway. He asks because he will not treat a man as a case to be processed, and wants them to voice their need and their faith.

Lord, let our eyes be opened. A specific request, for something they could not obtain anywhere else and could not pretend to have. Nobody fakes sight. It was not a modest request: the Old Testament speaks of opening the eyes of the blind as the work of God himself (Psalm 146:8; Isaiah 35:5). It was enormous, and it was honest.

Should I ask God for specific things, or only pray “your will be done”? Both, and this scene shows how they fit. Jesus invites a specific answer, and the blind men give one. Vague prayers are often a way of protecting ourselves from disappointment, or of hiding what we really want. Tell him plainly what you want, as a child tells his father, and then entrust the answer to his wisdom, as Jesus himself did in Gethsemane: let this cup pass, yet not as I will (26:39). Specific asking and humble yielding belong together in the same prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus in pity touched their eyes. Matthew tells us what moved before he tells us what happened: compassion felt deep inside (9:36; 15:32).

He touched them. He did not have to (8:13; 15:28). The touch was not for the miracle; it was for the men. Two beggars who had spent the morning being told to be quiet, and the first thing that happens to them is a pair of hands on their faces.

And immediately they recovered their sight. Isaiah’s sign of the messianic age: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened (Isaiah 35:5; see 11:5). The kingdom had come near enough to touch.

And followed him. Their first act as seeing men was to fall in behind somebody walking to a flogging and a cross. The Twelve had been told three times where this was going and were arguing about seats; two beggars, blind an hour earlier, saw who he was and went with him.

The whole chapter in one movement. It opens with a landowner who walks down to the market himself, again and again, for men nobody had chosen. It closes with the Son of Man stopping a procession on the way to his own execution because two beggars the crowd had silenced were shouting for mercy. The parable said that is what the owner of the vineyard is like. The Jericho road shows him doing it.

Does Jesus still open blind eyes? He still does the greater thing these healings pointed to. Physical healing is in his hands, and he sometimes grants it in answer to prayer, though he does not promise it to every believer in this life. But every Christian is a blind man who has been given sight: the god of this world had blinded our minds, and God shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4–6). If you can see who Jesus is and want to follow him, that is the miracle of this verse, done in you.

For worship. His heart turned over at the sight of two beggars; his hands touched faces the town had stopped looking at; his road led to a cross where he would be the one left alone, so that the blind could see and the outcast could follow. Once we were blind, and now we see, and what we see is him, walking ahead of us up the road.

20.theology: The atonement as ransom. Matthew 20:28 is Matthew’s clearest statement that Christ died in our place. A ransom was a payment that secured release, and Jesus gives his life as the price that sets the many free from sin, death and judgment. Reformed theology holds that the cross first accomplishes something before God, paying the debt and satisfying his justice, and only then moves and changes us. The ransom is paid; the captives are free.
20.examples:
Then: James and John had left everything (19:27) and wanted the best seats. Jesus redefines greatness as service and suffering, and the Twelve spent the rest of their lives learning it.

Now: The parable of the workers answers the idea that longer service or greater sacrifice earns a larger share of God’s favour. Grace can only be received. The fitting response is gratitude, not calculation.

21.title: The King Enters Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, <sup>2</sup>saying to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them at once.” <sup>4</sup>This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying, <sup>5</sup>“Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’” <sup>6</sup>The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. <sup>7</sup>They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. <sup>8</sup>Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. <sup>9</sup>And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>10</sup>And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?” <sup>11</sup>And the crowds said, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” <sup>12</sup>And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>13</sup>He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a den of robbers.” <sup>14</sup>And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. <sup>15</sup>But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” they were indignant, <sup>16</sup>and they said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” And Jesus said to them, “Yes; have you never read, “‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise’?” <sup>17</sup>And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. <sup>18</sup>In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. <sup>19</sup>And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once. <sup>20</sup>When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree wither at once?” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. <sup>22</sup>And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.” <sup>23</sup>And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” <sup>24</sup>Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>25</sup>The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?” And they discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>26</sup>But if we say, ‘From man,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.” <sup>27</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And he said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>28</sup>“What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’ <sup>29</sup>And he answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went. <sup>30</sup>And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, ‘I will, sir,’ but did not go. <sup>31</sup>Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. <sup>32</sup>For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. <sup>33</sup>“Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. <sup>34</sup>When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. <sup>35</sup>And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. <sup>36</sup>Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them. <sup>37</sup>Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>38</sup>But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’ <sup>39</sup>And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. <sup>40</sup>When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” <sup>41</sup>They said to him, “He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons.” <sup>42</sup>Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: “‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? <sup>43</sup>Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. <sup>44</sup>And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>45</sup>When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. <sup>46</sup>And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 opens the last week of Jesus’ life. He enters Jerusalem not on a warhorse but as a humble king on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 on purpose. The crowds shout Hosanna, hoping for a liberation from Rome; he has come for a deeper one.

The entry (vv. 1–11), the cleansing of the temple (vv. 12–17) and the cursing of the fig tree (vv. 18–22) interpret each other: the temple, like the tree, has leaves of religious activity but no fruit. When his authority is challenged (vv. 23–27), Jesus answers with a question about John and two parables, the two sons (vv. 28–32) and the tenants (vv. 33–46), which declare that the kingdom will be taken from the present tenants and given to a people who produce its fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Triumphal Entry, Cleansing of the Temple, and the Withered Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus enters Jerusalem to the crowd’s Hosannas, drives the traders from the temple, heals the blind and the lame there, and defends the children’s praise with Psalm 8. He returns to Bethany, and the next morning curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit, and teaches the disciples about faith that moves mountains.
verseByVerse.theology: The entry fulfils Zechariah 9:9: the king comes humble, mounted on a donkey, not a warhorse. Hosanna, from Psalm 118:25, is a prayer, save now, and the crowd prayed it with the wrong emergency in mind. The pilgrims shout Psalm 118:26 on the way in (v. 9), and Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone, to the men who run the temple (v. 42). Between two verses of one psalm lies the whole week.
verseByVerse.examples: The cleansing of the temple is a sign of judgment: the Court of the Gentiles, where non-Jews could pray, had become a market. The withered fig tree is an acted parable of the same thing, in the tradition of the prophets’ sign-acts. Its charge is pretence, not weakness: a tree in full leaf promised fruit it did not have, and the same Gospel says a bruised reed he will not break (12:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 21 is the day the King comes to his city and his house. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, acting out Zechariah’s prophecy of a humble king, while pilgrims shout Hosanna, save now, to the Son of David. In the temple he drives out the traders and heals the blind and the lame while children sing his praise. He curses a fig tree that is all leaves and no fruit, a sign of judgment on a busy, fruitless religion. Asked by what authority he acts, he answers with a question about John and two parables: two sons, and wicked tenants who kill the owner’s son. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and every reader must decide what he will do with him.

The setting. This is the beginning of the last week of Jesus’ life. Matthew gives it eight chapters, nearly a third of his Gospel. Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims for Passover.

Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives is the ridge east of Jerusalem, looking down on the city and the temple; Bethphage was a village on its slope. Zechariah had said that on the day of the LORD his feet would stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4), and Jewish hope had settled on this ridge. Jesus does not stumble into the fulfilment. He stops at the right hill, sends for the right animal, and rides down it.

The only journey he would not walk. He had walked everywhere for some three years. This is the only journey in the Gospels on which he chooses to ride, and he chooses it for the mile or so into his own capital, as her king.

Then Jesus sent two disciples, saying, Immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Whether by divine knowledge or prior arrangement, Matthew does not say. Nothing about the next five days is happening to Jesus; he is setting it up. Mark says the colt had never been ridden (Mark 11:2), a mark of an animal set apart for a sacred purpose (Numbers 19:2; 1 Samuel 6:7).

A royal mount. This is not a story about a man too poor for a horse. In Israel the donkey could be a royal mount. When David wanted the succession settled he had Solomon set on the king’s own mule and led down to Gihon, and the people came up after him rejoicing (1 Kings 1:33–40). A king’s son, a royal beast, a descent from a hill, a shouting crowd: many on that road would have known what they were watching.

Untie them and bring them to me. Genesis 49:11 speaks of the ruler from Judah tying his donkey’s colt to the vine, a messianic image. The sceptre was promised to Judah until the one should come to whom it belongs, and here he is, untying the colt.

Why does it matter that Jesus planned this so carefully? Because it shows that the cross was not an accident that overtook a good man. Jesus chose the day, the hill, the animal and the prophecy, and in doing so he publicly claimed to be Israel’s King, knowing it would bring the authorities down on him within the week. He was not swept along by events. He was laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). That is the comfort of it: the One who arranged this procession is the same One who arranges the days of those who belong to him.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, near Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, 'The Lord needs them,' and he will send them at once." This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord needs them. If anyone says anything to you, you shall say this. The Lord may refer to Jesus himself or to God. Either way, the title is the whole of his credentials: everything belongs to him.

Needs. It is a rare moment when Jesus says he needs anything, and what he needs is the loan of a young donkey. He had nowhere to lay his head (8:20); he will borrow an upper room and be laid in another man’s tomb (27:60). He owns everything, and he arrives owning nothing and asking for a colt.

This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet. Zechariah 9:9, with the opening words from Isaiah 62:11. Jesus deliberately acts out the prophecy, presenting himself publicly, for the first time, as the King.

Does the Lord really need anything from me? Not in the sense of lacking anything; God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25). But he chooses to use what his people have, and to give them the honour of lending it. The donkey’s owner was not making up a deficit in God. He was being let in on the coronation. So when you give your home, your time or your skill to Christ, you are not propping him up; you are being given a part in what he is doing, which is a gift to you before it is a gift to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.'" The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say to the daughter of Zion. From Isaiah 62:11: a tender, poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

Behold, your king is coming to you. Zechariah 9:9. Your king, coming to you: She does not have to go looking for him.

Humble. The same word as meek in the Beatitudes (5:5) and gentle in Jesus’ invitation to the weary: I am gentle and lowly in heart (11:29). It does not mean weak. Greek writers could use the word of a horse that has been broken in: all the strength still there, and every ounce of it under control.

And mounted on a donkey. Kings went to war on horses; a king on a donkey came in peace. Zechariah’s next verse cuts off the chariot and the war horse, and he shall speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). The animal is the king’s policy. He comes not as a military Messiah to overthrow Rome but as the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who will make peace through his death.

Not a Roman triumph. A Roman triumph had the general in a four-horse chariot, spoils before him, captured leaders in chains behind, and at the end prisoners executed and bulls sacrificed. This king has no chariot and no spoils. He drags no prisoners, having spent three years setting them free. And at the end of his route there is indeed a sacrifice, and it is him.

On a colt, the foal of a beast of burden. In Zechariah’s parallel lines on a donkey, on a colt describes one animal. Matthew mentions two because there were two: the colt, with its mother walking alongside.

The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. They were not asked to understand the Zechariah citation. They were asked to walk into a village and fetch a donkey, and they did. A great deal of obedience is that size.

Did Jesus accept the crowd’s idea of kingship? He accepted the crown in the one form nobody wanted. The crowd was shouting for a king who would deal with Rome, and the King they were shouting at had come to deal with something they had not asked him to touch: sin, death and the wrath of God. He let them cheer. He did not turn down the volume; he corrected the meaning, and he did it by choosing his transport. So do not be surprised if Christ, coming into your life, does not do first what you most wanted done. He has come to deal with the deeper thing.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse. Matthew mentions both the donkey and her colt.

parallels.desc: your king comes, humble and mounted on a donkey
say to the daughter of Zion

verseByVerse.quote: They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks. As a saddle for the King.

And he sat on them. On the cloaks; he rode the colt. Scoffers have asked whether Jesus straddled two animals. The nearest plural is the cloaks, and he sat on those on the colt (Mark 11:7). An unbroken colt was likely steadier with its mother beside it; Matthew has not misread Zechariah, he saw the real scene match even the prophet’s parallel lines.

Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road. Homage to a king, as when Jehu was proclaimed and the people put their garments under him (2 Kings 9:13). For a poor man a cloak was his coat by day and his blanket by night, so precious that the law forbade keeping it overnight as a pledge (Exodus 22:26–27). They laid in the dust the most valuable thing most of them owned.

And others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. John says palm branches (John 12:13), symbols of victory and national hope, waved when Simon Maccabeus took Jerusalem’s citadel (1 Maccabees 13:51). The crowd was greeting a liberator.

Palms before the Lamb. John saw the same welcome at the end of all things: a great multitude from every nation before the throne and before the Lamb, with palm branches in their hands (Revelation 7:9–10). The crowd on the Mount of Olives waved palms for a king they half understood, and within a week many had gone quiet. The crowd before the throne waves them for the King who was slain, and will never go quiet.

Were they right or wrong to welcome him as king? Right in what they did, mistaken in what they expected. He was the King, and homage was exactly what he deserved; Jesus did not stop them. But many wanted a deliverer from Rome, and their welcome would cool when he would not be that. It is possible to honour Christ sincerely with the right gestures and still want him for the wrong reasons. The cure is not to stop the gestures but to learn who he really is, so that the homage stays when the expectations are disappointed.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, "Who is this?" And the crowds said, "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
## And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting.

Hosanna to the Son of David! Hosanna is Hebrew for Save, we pray, from Psalm 118:25. By Jesus’ time it had become a shout of praise, but it began as a cry for help to God. Son of David is the Messiah (1:1).

The right prayer with the wrong emergency in mind. Ask that crowd what they wanted saving from, and many would have said Rome: the garrison, the taxes, the humiliation of occupation. He did nothing about it. He had come to save his people from their sins (1:21), and the rescue they asked for was smaller than the one he was carrying up that hill. They were more right than they knew and less right than they thought, which is the usual condition of anybody praying.

The psalm of the king at the gate. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord is Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims at Passover, the psalm of a king received at the temple gates. Before the chapter is over, Jesus will quote another line of this psalm at the men who run the temple (v. 42).

And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up. Stirred means shaken, the root that gives us seismic; Matthew uses it again when the earth shakes at his death (27:51) and on the third day (28:2). And the city asks, Who is this? The question of the whole Gospel.

This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee. True but incomplete (Deuteronomy 18:15; 16:14): a great category that is still the wrong one. Within five days a crowd in the same city would shout, let him be crucified (27:22).

Was it the same crowd that shouted Crucify? Partly, perhaps, but probably not mostly. The crowd on the road was chiefly pilgrims, many of them Galileans who had followed Jesus for months. The crowd at the trial gathered early in the morning inside the city, at the governor’s headquarters, and Matthew says the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas (27:20). So the lesson is less tidy than the usual sermon, and sharper. It was not simply that everyone turned. It was that when it mattered, many who had cheered him were nowhere to be found, and a crowd that had been worked on was. Enthusiasm that is not faith either changes sides or goes quiet.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He said to them, "It is written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer,' but you make it a den of robbers." And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus entered the temple. Malachi 3:1 promised that the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. Mark puts the cleansing the next day (Mark 11:11, 15); Matthew tells it compactly.

And drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and overturned the tables. The trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one area where Gentiles could pray. Money-changers took a fee for the coin of the temple tax (17:24). Pigeons were the sacrifices of the poor (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8), as Jesus’ own mother offered at his birth (Luke 2:24), and the sellers may well have been fleecing the poorest worshippers in the building.

My house shall be called a house of prayer. From Isaiah 56:7, which continues: for all peoples. The trading had pushed foreigners out of the one court that was theirs.

But you make it a den of robbers. From Jeremiah 7:11, where the people thought the temple would protect them while they lived wickedly, as robbers hide in a cave between raids, and God warned that he would destroy it, as he destroyed Shiloh. Jesus’ action is a sign of judgment: the temple will be destroyed (24:2), as it was in AD 70.

And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. When David captured Jerusalem, a saying arose that the blind and the lame shall not come into the house (2 Samuel 5:8). The Son of David welcomes them in. The tables go over and the sick come in. If a man’s zeal clears a space and nothing tender happens in it, he has done half the scene and the wrong half.

The true temple standing in the court. The temple was where God dwelt, sacrifice was offered and prayer went up. The man among the overturned tables is Immanuel (1:23), days from the sacrifice that ends every other one. John records him saying, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and adds that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). When the building fell in AD 70, it took nothing from the people of God that they had not already been given in Christ. The house of prayer for all nations turned out to be a Person.

Did Jesus cleanse the temple once or twice? John places a cleansing at the beginning of the ministry (John 2:13–22), while Matthew, Mark and Luke place it in the last week. Christians who take Scripture with equal seriousness answer in two ways. Some think there was one cleansing and John arranged his Gospel by theme, putting it early. But the simpler answer is that it happened twice, and the details suggest it: in John there are oxen and sheep and a whip of cords, here the dove sellers and money-changers; in John the leaders ask for a sign, here they ask by what authority. And trades grow back. Jesus confronted the temple when he began and when he finished: an opening statement and a closing verdict. Nothing in the meaning hangs on the answer.

Does this passage justify angry confrontation? No passage is quoted more often to excuse the furious post or the scorching email. See first who is acting and in whose house: the Lord of the temple, exercising an authority that belongs to him alone, over abuses in his own courts. It is the owner closing a market that had set up in his front room, not a worshipper losing his temper about the church. Notice next what the anger is about. Not a slight to himself; he had been mocked and plotted against without overturning anything. He was moved because the poor were being fleeced and the Gentiles crowded out. His anger ran entirely on behalf of others, the ones with least power in the building. Anger that flares when I am disrespected and stays seated when the weak are exploited is not this anger, whatever it calls itself. Holy anger is slow, aimed at the wrong rather than at the wrongdoer’s face, and ready to heal in the same hour, as his was.

Does this forbid selling things in a church building? A church building is not the temple, which was the unique place of sacrifice, so the comparison must be made carefully. What Jesus condemned was exploitation and the crowding out of prayer, especially for the outsiders who had nowhere else to pray. A bookstall or a coffee table is not wrong in itself. The test is whether anyone is being fleeced, and whether the business is getting in the way of worship or keeping the outsider from finding room.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples
pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David!" they were indignant, and they said to him, "Do you hear what these are saying?" And Jesus said to them, "Yes; have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did. The healings (v. 14). The priests watched the blind receive sight in their own courts, and the identical evidence produced worship in the children and indignation in the men trained to interpret it.

And the children crying out in the temple. Hosanna to the Son of David! The children had picked up the crowd’s cry inside the temple courts, where the chief priests were in charge.

They were indignant. They said, Do you hear what these are saying? They knew the children were calling Jesus the Messiah, and they expected him to stop them. Their indignation is at his silence as much as at the words.

Yes; have you never read, “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise”? Psalm 8:2, in its Greek form; the Hebrew has a word closer to strength, and either way God establishes something formidable out of the smallest voices there are. Psalm 8 is about praise to God; Jesus applies it to praise of himself. The children are praising God by praising Jesus. Once again Jesus claims what belongs to God. The children see what the experts cannot (11:25). And the rest of the line, which he did not need to say aloud to men who knew the psalter by heart, speaks of strength established because of God’s foes, to still the enemy and the avenger. By quotation he has told the chief priests which part of the psalm they are standing in.

Have you never read? The question he keeps putting to the professional readers of Scripture (12:3, 5; 19:4; 21:42; 22:31). It is put to men who knew the text well and had kept it at a safe distance, a danger for anyone who has owned a Bible for a long time. These men had sung Psalm 8 in this very building. Their trouble was not that they had never read it, but that they had never expected it to come true in front of them, out of the mouths of children, about a Galilean.

Is this a sneer at learning? No. The problem with these men was never that they had studied. It was that their study had become the property of their position, so that a conclusion which would cost them the position had become unthinkable. A child had nothing to lose by saying Son of David out loud. Learning that bows to Christ is a gift to the church; learning that guards its own standing is blindness with a library. Study hard, and stay a child before the text.

For worship. The same psalm asks, What is man, that you are mindful of him? Hebrews reads it of Jesus, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). The children were singing to the Man of Psalm 8, a week from his suffering, and he gladly took their praise as his due.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus quotes the psalm in its Greek form.

parallels.desc: out of the mouth of babies and infants

verseByVerse.quote: And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany. On the evening he entered Jerusalem as her King, he walked back over the Mount of Olives to Bethany, about two miles east, the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1; Luke 21:37). The city that had quaked at his arrival did not offer him a bed.

And lodged there. A man who sleeps outside the walls is harder to arrest quietly. He comes in each morning to teach and goes out each evening, and the last night he spends near it he will spend in a garden on that same hillside, awake.

In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. This is the man who had multiplied loaves for five thousand and refused to turn stones into bread when he was far hungrier (4:2–4); the power was never for himself. The eternal Son in a real human body, at an ordinary hour on an ordinary road.

Why does Matthew mention that Jesus was hungry? Partly to lead into the fig tree: the sign does not begin as a lesson looking for an illustration but with a hungry man walking toward a tree that looked, from the road, as though it had something on it. But it also guards a truth the church has always had to defend: Jesus is truly man as well as truly God, with a real body and real needs. He did not merely appear human. That is why he can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and why his obedience and death count for human beings: he was one of us.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem, home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus.

verseByVerse.quote: And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, "May no fruit ever come from you again!" And the fig tree withered at once. When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, "How did the fig tree wither at once?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. Fig trees are usually said to produce small early knobs of fruit with their leaves in spring, before the main crop (Mark 11:13 says it was not the season for figs). A tree in full leaf with no early fruit at all was barren: its leaves promised what it did not have.

May no fruit ever come from you again! An acted parable. In the Old Testament the fig tree was a picture of Israel: when I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree (Jeremiah 8:13; see Hosea 9:10). The tree was like the temple Jesus had just cleansed: religious activity at full volume, without the fruit God looked for, justice, mercy and faith. The withering pictures God’s judgment on fruitless religion, which fell on the temple in AD 70.

The hungry Lord at the tree. Micah had put the scene into God’s own mouth: Woe is me! For I have become as when the summer fruit has been gathered; there is no cluster to eat, no first-ripe fig that my soul desires (Micah 7:1). The God of Israel had always come to his people hungry for fruit and found leaves. Now that hunger walks up the road from Bethany in a human body: the LORD of the prophets come in person to inspect his planting.

Why curse a tree? It is the only miracle in the Gospels in which Jesus’ own word destroys something, and anyone who has felt uneasy here is reading attentively: on the face of it, a hungry man does not find breakfast and kills the tree. But this is not a miracle of temper. It is a prophet’s sign-act, a genre Israel had seen for centuries. Jeremiah smashed a clay jar in front of the elders (Jeremiah 19:1–13). Ezekiel lay on his side for months beside a brick with the city drawn on it (Ezekiel 4). Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces and handed ten to Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:30–31). The prophets acted their message when words had stopped landing. And see the mercy in the choice. In a life in which he raised the dead and refused every chance to harm a soul, the only thing he ever destroyed in a sign of his own was a plant. He could have made the point on the temple itself. He made it on a tree by the roadside where nobody was hurt.

And the fig tree withered at once. In Mark the disciples notice it withered the next morning (Mark 11:20–21). Matthew tells it as one episode, his interest being the sign and not the schedule: he says when the tree died, Mark says when the disciples saw it.

When the disciples saw it, they marveled. They said, how did the fig tree wither at once? They asked about the mechanics; the meaning was standing across the valley, on the temple mount.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people for ever. The judgment fell on the temple system and the leaders who rejected the Messiah, and Paul shows that God has not finished with Israel (Romans 11).

I look at my life and see very little fruit. Is this verse about me? Read what was actually condemned. Not smallness, not slowness, not a poor year. The tree was judged for displaying what it did not have: full leaf and no fruit at all. That is a charge against pretence, not against weakness, and the same Gospel has told you how this Lord handles the genuinely feeble: a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench (12:20). He is severe with advertising and unfailingly gentle with frailty. If you grieve your fruitlessness and long for more, that longing is itself fruit of his Spirit. Abide in him, and fruit comes (John 15:5).

For worship. The One who withered the fruitless tree was himself hung on a tree, bearing the curse that fruitless people deserved (Galatians 3:13), so that we might be grafted into the true vine and bear fruit that lasts.
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds that “it was not the season for figs”; leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt. The disciples ask how it was done and are told what they will be doing. Doubt means to be divided, to waver between two minds (James 1:6–8): not the honest question of a struggling believer, but a heart split between trusting God and not.

You will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain. Probably the Mount of Olives, which Zechariah says will be split on the day of the LORD (Zechariah 14:4), or the temple mount across the valley, the thing the withered tree has just been a parable about.

Be taken up and thrown into the sea, it will happen. A picture of doing the impossible, as with faith like a grain of mustard seed (17:20).

The mountain that moved. These men were never promised authority over fig trees: none of them ever withered anything. Within a generation, a handful of provincial men with no money and no army had carried this message into the great cities between Jerusalem and Rome, against the Sanhedrin and the empire, and it did not slow down. That is the mountain. It went into the sea.

The stone that became a mountain. Daniel saw a stone cut out by no human hand strike the kingdoms of the world, and the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:34–35). Before this chapter ends Jesus will call himself the stone (vv. 42, 44). The old mountain of the temple is passing away; a new one is rising. The faith Jesus asks for is not a force of its own. It is reliance on him.

And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith. A great promise, to be read with the rest of Scripture: asking in Jesus’ name, according to God’s will (John 14:13–14; 1 John 5:14–15), from a heart that forgives (Mark 11:25). Spoken to men about to be sent out, it means their work will never fail for want of supply.

Is this a promise that anything I ask with enough faith will be given? No. Prayer is answered according to God’s will (1 John 5:14), not according to wrong motives (James 4:3), and Paul’s own prayer for healing was answered no, with the better gift of grace sufficient for him (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). The mountain is a picture of what seems impossible, not a literal mountain to be moved for show. Faith is trust in God, not confidence in a particular outcome. If a prayer of yours has not been answered as you asked, it does not mean your faith failed; it may mean your Father has something better, or a different time.

What we ask for. We ask whether we have enough faith for what we want; the passage asks what we are asking for. These men were told to expect the impossible because they had been given something impossible to do: to make disciples of all nations. So add one prayer that is mountain-sized: for a friend far from God, for your town, for a people with no church.

For worship. The greatest mountain ever thrown into the sea was the mountain of our sins. You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea, the prophet sang (Micah 7:19), and at the cross Christ did it. The God who did that will not find any prayer of his children too large.

parallels.desc: ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Authority Questioned: Three Parables of Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chief priests and elders challenge Jesus’ authority. He answers with a question about John’s baptism that they refuse to answer, then tells the parables of the two sons and of the tenants who killed the owner’s son. He closes with Psalm 118’s rejected stone. The sharpest sentence comes between the parables: the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom ahead of them (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology: The leaders do not want to know the source of Jesus’ authority; they want to discredit him, and their huddle over John shows them governed by the crowd rather than the truth. In the tenants he takes up Isaiah’s song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–2) and changes it: the vine is not blamed, the tenants are. And they kill the son not by mistake but because they recognise him as the heir, which is why unbelief in this chapter is never a shortage of information.
verseByVerse.examples: The rejected stone, from the psalm shouted at the entry, completes the argument: what the leaders reject, God makes the foundation of his house. Verse 43 is about the tenancy, not race: the vineyard is let to a people whose first members were Jews (see the notes on vv. 43–44). And verse 45 sobers anyone who reads the Bible well: they understood perfectly that he was speaking about them, and their understanding produced not repentance but an arrest plan.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" Jesus answered them, "I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching. An official delegation of the council that controlled the temple, and Israel’s law did require anyone who acted as a prophet to be tested (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22). On the face of it they are doing their job.

By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority? “These things”: the triumphal entry, the cleansing of the temple, the healings, the teaching. In the space of a few days he had ridden into the city like a king being crowned, cleared the temple court by force, healed in the temple courts, and let children call him Messiah without correcting them. Every one is an act of ownership. They were the official authorities over the temple; Jesus had no official position. Who did he think he was? It was a trap. If he said “from God”, they could charge him with blasphemy; if he said “my own”, they could dismiss him.

I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you. Rabbis often answered a question with a question. It was not a dodge: his question will reveal the answer to theirs.

In the flow. He answers with a question about John and then three parables (21:28–22:14), and the authority question runs through every debate in the temple courts until no one dares to ask him anything more (22:46). Matthew gives the final answer on a mountain in Galilee: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (28:18).

Why answer with a question? Because the question about John is the authority question, handed back in the one form they cannot answer without convicting themselves. John was the one man in Israel who had already answered it publicly. He had pointed to Jesus as the one coming after him, whose sandals he was not worthy to carry; he had baptised him and seen the Spirit descend while the voice from heaven spoke (3:11–17). If John was from heaven, they had their answer already. Christ often does this: he answers not the question we put but the one underneath it, and points us back to the evidence we have already declined to act on.

verseByVerse.quote: The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" And they discussed it among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say, 'From man,' we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man? “Baptism” stands for John’s whole ministry; “from heaven” means from God. At Jesus’ baptism heaven had already spoken, out loud (3:16–17), so to call John’s baptism heavenly was to confess the Son. The answer to Jesus’ question is the answer to theirs: Jesus’ authority comes from the same God who sent John.

And they discussed it among themselves. Matthew takes us inside the huddle of the most senior religious men in Israel, deciding what to say about a prophet of God. They did not ask what was true, but what was safe.

If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him? They had rejected John (21:32; Luke 7:30). Read the minutes and notice what is missing. Two options, each assessed purely for what it will cost. Not one syllable about whether John was in fact from heaven. The question of truth is not raised, not dismissed, not even avoided: it never occurs to anyone to bring it up. That is the difference between a man who is wrong and a man who is corrupt. Being mistaken about John would have been forgivable and correctable. These men are not weighing evidence badly; they have stopped weighing it.

But if we say, From man, we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet. Luke adds that they feared being stoned (Luke 20:6). Men who could rouse a Roman governor feared the street. The men in charge of Israel’s conscience were taking their instructions from Israel’s mood.

The question that changes. We rarely fail the way they did, out loud. The danger is the moment when the question in our mind silently changes from what is true here to what will this cost me to say: in a staffroom when somebody sneers at Christians, or when a group settles on an unfair view of someone we know. The calculation is so fast it does not feel like a decision at all.

Is it always wrong to keep quiet? No. Prudence is not cowardice. Jesus told his followers to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (10:16); there are things not to say yet, and moments badly chosen, and the Lord himself sometimes kept silent. The difference is what sits in the driving seat. Wisdom asks how and when to say the true thing, and plans to say it. What was happening in this huddle was not wisdom deciding the timing; it was safety deciding the content. If you find you never seem to find the right moment, safety may be driving.
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And he said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not know. So they answered Jesus. These are the men whose office was to rule on prophet and fraud. What they were really saying was: we have an answer and we cannot afford it. That is more dangerous than ignorance, because ignorance can be cured by information, and this only by repentance.

His silence keeps his word. Neither will I tell you, he says. He declines, and the declining is itself a judgment. To a man who will not act on what he has, more light is only more to answer for (7:6; 13:12). But the silence is not the last word. The parables that follow answer the question indirectly: the owner has sent last of all his son (v. 37). And within the week the answer will be given on a cross, under a notice that says who he claimed to be (27:37).

What do you think? A man had two sons. Without a pause, he begins to tell them a story. They have refused his question; he will not answer theirs. But he has not finished with them. The first of three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14), each aimed at them, each still giving them a way to see themselves and turn. He is being more patient than they deserve, and far more patient than they will be with him. The father pictures God.

Son, go and work in the vineyard today. The vineyard again pictures God’s kingdom (20:1; Isaiah 5:1–7). And the word today: the call is to a day’s work now.

What if I sincerely do not know what I believe about Jesus? Then this passage is not a condemnation but an invitation. The leaders did know and would not say; honest uncertainty is a different thing. Ask God plainly to show you who Jesus is. Read one of the Gospels through, asking at each page, who is this man? Talk with a Christian you trust. But be honest with yourself about one question: if it became clear, what would it cost me? If the answer frightens you, that fear may be the real obstacle, and it can be brought to God too.
