verseByVerse.quote: "And he answered, 'I will not,' but afterward he changed his mind and went. And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, 'I will, sir,' but did not go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he answered, “I will not,” but afterward he changed his mind and went. A rude refusal, followed by repentance: a mind changed and then a road changed. The first son was insolent; what commends him is that he changed his mind and went. The parable asks only who ended up in the field.

And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, “I go, sir,” but did not go. Sir is literally Lord: a polite answer with no obedience (7:21). He says the right thing, in the right tone, with the right title, and his failure is invisible until you go and look at the vineyard. That is the shape of a great deal of respectable Christianity: the yes given years ago, the language still fluent, the vineyard unvisited.

A third son behind the story. Both sons fail their father, one at the start and one at the end. The one telling the story is the Son who never failed at either. I always do the things that are pleasing to him, he said of his Father (John 8:29), and he said yes and went, and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). His obedience is the only reason either son in this parable can be welcomed home.

Textual note. Some manuscripts reverse the order of the two sons, and the leaders’ answer in verse 31 then varies. This commentary’s view: the ESV’s order is best supported; the meaning is the same either way.

Which son am I? Most people who read a commentary are in more danger of being the second than the first. So take it as a question with a date on it. Not did I once say yes, but: since the last time I said yes to God about something specific, have I actually gone? There is usually one thing in view: a conversation to have, a debt to repay, a habit to end, a person to forgive, money to give, a reconciliation to attempt. You will know it as you read this, because it is the thing that came to mind before the sentence finished.

I have been the second son for years. Is it too late? No, and the first son’s story is the better news of the two, because it means a bad start is not a settled verdict. Nothing prevents a man who said no this morning from being in the vineyard by the afternoon. And notice that the father in this parable does not require a speech first. He requires a son in the field. If you have been the second son for twenty years, the way out is not despair or a better promise; it is a change of direction today, in one thing, trusting the Father’s welcome. The vineyard gate is still open.

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of the two did the will of his father? The answer is obvious. Jesus asks the question himself, so it is plainly meant to be answered by every reader and not only by the men in front of him.

They said, The first. They condemn themselves. The parable was too plain to get wrong and too small to feel dangerous. Then he tells them what they have agreed to.

Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. Tax collectors were collaborators who squeezed their neighbours for Rome (9:9); prostitutes, many likely driven there by a man who discarded them or by hunger, were beyond the edge of respectable society. Jesus names these two groups, in the temple, to the highest religious authorities in the nation, and puts them in front. They had said no to God by their lives, but repented when John preached. The leaders had said yes by their words, and refused to repent.

The door is still open. The verb is present tense: they are going in ahead of you. That is the order of a procession, and a procession is something you can still join. Even at the sharpest moment of the confrontation, the door is held open while they are told who is walking through it first. And many priests did join it: a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (Acts 6:7).

The forerunner at the head of the line. Jesus is our forerunner (Hebrews 6:20). The tax collectors and prostitutes are following the man who walked in ahead of them by way of a cross, and who is telling the high priests that there is still room behind him.

For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. John preached repentance and a changed life (3:1–12), and tax collectors came to him to be baptised (Luke 3:12; 7:29–30). The charge is precise: not that they disliked him, but that they did not believe him.

And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. The same word as the first son (v. 29): he changed his mind; they did not. And the last clause names the hardest condition in the chapter: even when you saw it. They watched collaborators turn honest and ruined women come up out of the Jordan new, and it moved them not at all. That state is reached by a long series of moments in which the honest answer was known and not acted on. If you fear you are in it, the fear itself is a good sign: your heart is still being troubled, and the door is still open.

Why can religion make repentance harder? Because repentance begins with admitting you are in the wrong, and a respectable life gives a man a great deal to hide behind. The tax collector had nothing to protect; his sin was public, and so his need was obvious to him. The religious man has a reputation, a record of attendance, a vocabulary, and the habit of being the one who is right. Every one of those can become a wall between him and the plain prayer, God, be merciful to me, a sinner (Luke 18:13). The cure is to let God’s word search the respectable sins: pride, coldness, contempt, self-righteousness.

parallels.desc: the tax collectors baptized, the Pharisees refusing

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower. The second of three parables aimed at the temple leaders, and every man listening recognised it within a few words: Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, the house of Israel, which ends with the hedge removed and the vineyard trampled (Isaiah 5:1–7). Every advantage the tenants enjoy came from the hands of the man they are about to rob.

The change Jesus makes. In Isaiah the fault is in the vine. Here the vine is not blamed at all; what has gone wrong is the tenants. Jesus has taken the best-known indictment of the nation in the prophets and narrowed it, off the people and onto the men given charge of them: a far more dangerous parable to tell in the temple, and to an ordinary Israelite in that crowd, a more merciful one.

And leased it to tenants, and went into another country. The crowd’s instinctive sympathy was with tenants against absentee landlords, right up to the moment these tenants start killing people. It is the method of the two sons: get the hearers to take a side, then show them which side they took. The tenants are Israel’s leaders (v. 45).

When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. The servants are the prophets. And he sends not for rent in coin but for his fruit, the thing the vineyard exists to produce. That is the standing question of this chapter, put to the fig tree, the temple and the men in charge of both: not whether the operation is busy, but whether anything is growing.

The vine that bore fruit. Isaiah’s song ends with a vineyard that failed. But it had a sequel: I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser (John 15:1). Where Israel yielded wild grapes, the Son yielded exactly the fruit the Owner had been looking for, grown in human flesh. We never bear that fruit perfectly; but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours, and so the uneven crop of those joined to him is accepted for his sake. The fruit the Owner now seeks grows only from that vine (John 15:8). The vineyard is not abandoned. It has a new root.

Who are the tenants today? In the first place, the leaders of Israel who rejected Jesus; Matthew says they knew it (v. 45). But the principle reaches every generation of those entrusted with God’s people: pastors, elders, teachers, parents. The vineyard is never theirs. They are stewards, and the Owner will ask for his fruit. In a wider sense every Christian is a tenant of what God has given: life, gifts, time, family, church. None of it is ours to keep for ourselves, and all of it is meant to bear fruit for him.
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. The listeners knew what happened to men God sent to Israel. Jeremiah was beaten and lowered into a cistern (Jeremiah 20:2; 38:6); Uriah was killed with the sword (Jeremiah 26:20–23); Zechariah was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). This is not exaggeration. It is a summary.

Again he sent other servants, more than the first. A normal landlord would have sent soldiers. This is the patience of God across centuries, and the Chronicler wrote it in one sentence: the LORD sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people, but they kept mocking the messengers of God, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:15–16).

Both halves are true. And they did the same to them. The patience is real, and so is the Chronicler’s last clause: until there was no remedy. Patience is not indifference, and it is not permanent, and after all the servants there is one more figure standing at the estate gate.

The sender among the sent. Two chapters later Jesus says, Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify (23:34). I send. As the eternal Word he had been sending all along; it was the Spirit of Christ in the prophets who foretold his sufferings (1 Peter 1:10–11). Every rejection of the servants was a rehearsal for the rejection of him. The parable is God’s patience told by God.

Does God still send messengers today? Not new prophets adding to Scripture; the canon is closed, and God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). But he still sends his word, through faithful preaching, through the Bible open on a table, through a friend who tells you the truth, through a parent’s prayers. Every time Scripture is faithfully explained to you, the Owner is sending to collect his fruit. The question this verse asks is not whether he sends, but what we do with the messenger.

verseByVerse.quote: "Finally he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally he sent his son to them. The story has run out of servants. Mark says a beloved son (Mark 12:6). This is the answer to the question about his authority (v. 23): he comes from the Father, as the Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).

Did God not know what they would do? He did. The owner’s hope, they will respect my son, shows the depth of God’s patience and love, not a gap in his knowledge. Jesus had told his disciples plainly, more than once, that he would be handed over, mocked and crucified (16:21; 20:18–19). But this is a parable, and it speaks the way a father speaks. It is not a report on the limits of God’s foreknowledge; it is a way of making you feel the size of what is about to be done. The owner sends his boy to men who have killed his servants, and the sentence lets you hear him hoping. God is not cold in sending his Son. He is not ignorant either. He knew, and sent him anyway, for us.

But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, This is the heir. They kill him not because they mistake him for someone else but because they know who he is. If he had been another servant they would have beaten him and sent him back; it is his being the son that makes the murder worth committing.

Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance. Their reasoning was absurd, since the owner was alive, but it shows the motive: to keep control of the vineyard (John 11:48). Within days the chief priests and elders gather in the high priest’s palace and plot to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him (26:3–4). They walked out of the temple and did it.

Is unbelief just a lack of information? Sometimes. But this parable says the deepest form of it is not confusion at all. It is a clear-eyed calculation that this man’s rightful claim is incompatible with keeping what I have, and a decision to keep it. The tenants’ problem was never that they did not know whose vineyard it was. It was that they did. That is why more arguments rarely convert anyone on their own: what is needed is a new heart that is willing to give up the vineyard. And that is why we pray for unbelievers as well as reason with them.

parallels.desc: God has spoken by his Son

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Note the order in Matthew (Mark has the other): he is put outside first and killed outside. He was crucified outside the city walls (John 19:17), and Hebrews makes the point: Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp (Hebrews 13:11–13). The tenants threw the son over the wall to be rid of him, and put him precisely where the sacrifice belonged.

When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants? Jesus asks his hearers to pronounce the judgment, as Nathan made David pronounce judgment on himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7). It is the second time in a few minutes that he has invited these men to judge a case that is their own. He did it with the two sons, and they answered correctly and were told what they had said. Now he does it again with a heavier case and lets them dictate the sentence.

A mirror, not a snare. It is not a trap set to destroy them; it is a mirror set where they cannot avoid it, and recognition is the only thing that could have saved them.

How do I avoid reading the Bible like these men? Ask, every time, where am I in this passage? You can read with real attention, form a confident judgment about the people in the story, and never notice that the judgment applies to you. These men were not bad listeners; they understood the parable perfectly (v. 45). They simply assumed, until the last second, that it was about somebody else. So when you find yourself thinking how blind they were, stop and ask where you are blind in the same way, and pray, search me, O God, and know my heart (Psalm 139:23).

For worship. The tenants threw the Son over the wall to keep the vineyard, and the Father answered by giving him the world: Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession (Psalm 2:8). The one they put outside now decides who comes in, and he uses that authority to bring in outsiders like us. His rejection was our welcome.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus was crucified outside the city walls.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons." Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will put those wretches to a miserable death. They answer without hesitating, with a hard play on words in Greek, bad men badly: the phrase a man produces when he is enjoying his indignation. The judgment came in AD 70, when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and ended the rule of the priestly leaders. And the vineyard itself is not destroyed but let to other tenants, a people producing its fruit (v. 43).

Have you never read in the Scriptures. Psalm 118:22–23. The pilgrims had shouted verse 26 (v. 9); now he quotes verse 22, and between them, in the events of that week, lies the welcome, the refusal, the trial, the cross and the empty tomb.

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The picture changes to a building. The builders, Israel’s leaders, rejected a stone as useless, but God made it the cornerstone (see Ephesians 2:20), the stone the whole building rests on. Jesus, rejected and killed, will be raised and exalted to be the foundation of God’s new temple, his people (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8). Assessing stone was the builders’ whole competence. They were experts, they inspected him, and they got it exactly wrong.

The Lord’s doing, and a marvel. The rejection itself was taken up into the Lord’s doing. The builders threw the stone off the site and were, in that very act, laying the foundation of a building they did not know was going up. Nothing excuses them; the parable has shown that they knew what they were doing. The children had it right (v. 15). It is a wonder.

What comfort is there here for my own rejections? A real one, but it must be offered carefully. The stone did not become the cornerstone in spite of being thrown away; it became the cornerstone by being thrown away. That cannot be turned into a technique or promised cheaply over every sorrow, to someone still bleeding. But it happened once, publicly, in the most important week in history, and it means that the worst thing men ever did was in the hand of God. If you belong to Christ, your rejections are not outside his hand either. He who brought the cornerstone out of the rubbish heap can bring good out of what was done to you (Romans 8:28), even when you cannot yet see how.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you. You means the leaders and those who follow them (v. 45). It is the tenancy that is being revoked.

And given to a people producing its fruits. People is singular: a nation. It is the new people of God, the church, of believing Jews and Gentiles, the holy nation of 1 Peter 2:9. And its first thousands were Jews.

In the flow. Verse 43 is the one place where Jesus steps out of the parable and says plainly what it means. The fruitless fig tree, the busy temple and the tenants all meet in this verdict, which reaches forward to the risen Lord sending his disciples to all nations (28:19).

And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces. Isaiah 8:14–15: a stone of stumbling, over which many will fall and be broken.

And when it falls on anyone, it will crush him. Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45: the stone cut without hands that crushes the kingdoms of the world. The stone of judgment is the same stone as the stone of salvation: the cornerstone for believers is the crushing stone for those who refuse him. There is no neutral way to stand near this stone.

Is it fair that everything hangs on what I do with Jesus? It would not be, if he were one teacher among many. But this verse says he is the stone God himself has laid, and to stand near the foundation of God’s house and decline to build on it is already a decision. Nor is God quick to crush. The parable has just shown servant after servant sent, and last of all the son; the stone is offered as a foundation long before it falls as a judgment. The God who warns this plainly is not hunting for reasons to condemn. He is pleading with people to come in while the door is open (2 Peter 3:9).

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit verse 44. It may have been added from Luke 20:18. This commentary’s view: the evidence is divided; it is probably original, and Luke confirms that Jesus said it.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people as a race and replaced them with Gentiles (a crude form of replacement theology). The leaders who rejected Jesus lost their stewardship; the new people includes believing Jews, starting with the Twelve. There is one people of God in Christ, the one olive tree, into which Gentiles are grafted and into which Jews who believe will be grafted again (Romans 11:17–24).

Why does this matter so much? Because this verse has been made to carry a weight it will not bear, and across some dark centuries it was used to teach that God had finished with the Jewish people and that Christians were free to despise them. Worse was done in the name of that idea than can be written here. Paul, who knew this saying, asks the question in so many words: has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite (Romans 11:1). Christians differ on exactly what Paul means when he says all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:26), whether a great turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end or the full number of believing Israel gathered through the ages, but no reading of Scripture permits contempt. And Paul turned the warning on the Gentile church at once: do not become proud, but fear (Romans 11:20). A church that keeps the leaves and yields no fruit has been told, in this very chapter, what happens to trees like that.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verse 44.

parallels.desc: the stone that breaks the kingdoms

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. There was no failure of communication anywhere in this chapter.

And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds. Perfect understanding produced no repentance whatever, only the plan the parable described. And there is the fear again, the fear that decided their answer about John (v. 26) and would keep them from arresting him openly during the feast (26:5).

Because they held him to be a prophet. The crowds’ opinion (v. 11) protected Jesus for now, and the protection was thin: within days the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas (27:20). But the real wall around him was never a crowd. No one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30); when it came, he would hand himself over in a garden.

How do I know whether my Bible knowledge is helping me or hardening me? Ask what it produces. Knowledge that is helping you leads you to confess sin, to love Christ more, to be gentler with others, and to obey in specific things. Knowledge that is hardening you makes you quicker to judge, slower to repent, more confident that the hard passages are about other people, and more irritated when a sermon comes close. The test is not how much you know but whether what you know is bending you toward Christ. If you see signs of hardening, the remedy is the one these men refused: humble yourself before the word, and repent.

For worship. The chapter closes on the question of who this is: a crowd that half knows, a leadership that fully knows and will not have it, and a King who does not run or soften it. He laid down his life of his own accord, with the very men plotting to take it listening to every word.

21.theology: Christ the true temple. The temple was where God dwelt with his people, where sacrifice was made and through which prayer went up. Jesus fulfils all three: he is Immanuel, God with us; he is the Lamb whose offering ends the sacrifices; and he is the one through whom prayer reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John says it plainly: he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:21). When the temple fell in AD 70, the picture had given way to the reality it pointed to.
21.examples:
Then: The crowds welcomed Jesus with real excitement and the wrong expectations. It is possible to praise Jesus loudly while misunderstanding who he is and what he came to do.

Now: The fig tree warns against keeping the form of Christian practice without the faith, repentance and love it is meant to bear. The question Jesus asks of every church and every believer is where the fruit is, and the fruit grows only from union with him.

22.title: The Great Banquet and the Hard Questions
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, <sup>2</sup>“The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son, <sup>3</sup>and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent other servants, saying, ‘Tell those who are invited, “See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.”’ <sup>5</sup>But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, <sup>6</sup>while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. <sup>7</sup>The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. <sup>8</sup>Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. <sup>9</sup>Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find.’ <sup>10</sup>And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests. <sup>11</sup>“But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. <sup>12</sup>And he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?’ And he was speechless. <sup>13</sup>Then the king said to the attendants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ <sup>14</sup>For many are called, but few are chosen.” <sup>15</sup>Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. <sup>16</sup>And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. <sup>17</sup>Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” <sup>18</sup>But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, “Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? <sup>19</sup>Show me the coin for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius. <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” <sup>21</sup>They said, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” <sup>22</sup>When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away. <sup>23</sup>The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, <sup>24</sup>saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.’ <sup>25</sup>Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. <sup>26</sup>So too the second and third, down to the seventh. <sup>27</sup>After them all, the woman died. <sup>28</sup>In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her.” <sup>29</sup>But Jesus answered them, “You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. <sup>30</sup>For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>31</sup>And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” <sup>33</sup>And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. <sup>34</sup>But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. <sup>35</sup>And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him. <sup>36</sup>“Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” <sup>37</sup>And he said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. <sup>38</sup>This is the great and first commandment. <sup>39</sup>And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. <sup>40</sup>On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.” <sup>41</sup>Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, <sup>42</sup>saying, “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “The son of David.” <sup>43</sup>He said to them, “How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, <sup>44</sup>“‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet”’? <sup>45</sup>If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” <sup>46</sup>And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
22.overview: Chapter 22 is Tuesday of the last week, a day of questions in the temple courts. Jesus first tells the parable of the wedding feast: the invited guests refuse the king’s invitation, the hall is filled from the road junctions with bad and good, and a guest without a wedding garment is thrown out, for many are called, but few are chosen. Then three groups come to trap him: Pharisees and Herodians on Caesar’s tax, Sadducees on the resurrection, a lawyer on the greatest commandment. He answers each, then asks whose son the Christ is, if David calls him Lord. After that no one dares ask him anything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Parable of the Wedding Banquet and the Question about Taxes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells the parable of the wedding feast: the invited guests refuse, some kill the king’s servants, their city is burned, and the hall is filled with whoever is found at the road junctions, bad and good. A guest without a wedding garment is thrown out. Then Pharisees and Herodians try to trap him on Caesar’s tax; he asks for a coin, and tells them to give Caesar what bears Caesar’s image and God what bears God’s. They marvel, and leave him.
verseByVerse.theology: The invitation is free, finished and urgent: the oxen are slaughtered, everything is ready, and nothing is outstanding but coming. Grace then reaches the road junctions and gathers bad and good alike, a picture of the gospel going to the Gentiles. But grace is not a free pass: the king walks the room, and the man without the garment is speechless because what he needed had been offered and he did not take it. On the tax, the coin bears Caesar’s image and may be given back to him; the person bears God’s image, and Caesar may never have that.
verseByVerse.examples: The first guests went off to a farm and a business: not vice, but respectable occupation, which crowds God out precisely because nobody has to defend it. The busy and the violent end in the same place. In the tax scene, men with scruples about Caesar’s tribute had his coin in a purse on the temple mount. And verse 22 shows the most respectable way of rejecting Christ: they marvelled, and they left him.

verseByVerse.quote: And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The whole chapter displays the King’s Son in his wisdom and authority: refused as the Bridegroom, tested by every party in turn, and finally silencing them with the question of who the Christ is.

And again Jesus spoke to them in parables. The third of three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14). The first showed their refusal to repent; the second their rejection of the Son; this one their refusal of God’s invitation, and God’s invitation going to others. A story gets past defences that an argument would only harden.

The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son. The king is God; the son is Jesus. A royal wedding could last a week, and its whole point was the honouring of the king’s son. To decline an invitation of that kind was not a social lapse. It was a public verdict on the son.

The Bridegroom tells his own wedding. The man telling this story is the son in it. He stands in the temple courts, three days from the cross, describing the feast his Father has prepared in his honour, and the men listening are the guests who are refusing. He had warned that the bridegroom would be taken away (9:15), and that day is close. This wedding will not be paid for out of the royal stores alone: Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The bride is won at the cost of the Bridegroom’s life, and every honour of the feast is honour paid to him.

A feast, not a courtroom. In Scripture the age to come is a great feast and God’s bond with his people a marriage (Hosea 2:19–20), consummated at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). Isaiah’s picture: on this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, and he will swallow up death for ever and wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:6–8). The prophet’s word for the end is not a cloud or a silence. It is food, and company, and wine kept a long time for a particular occasion.

Is this the same parable as the great banquet in Luke 14? Most likely not. Luke 14:16–24 has a similar shape, but here it is a king and his son’s wedding, with murdered servants, a burned city and a guest without a garment, and it is told in the temple in the last week rather than at a meal in a Pharisee’s house. Jesus often taught similar themes on different occasions, and a preacher who travelled for about three years would naturally use a strong story more than once, shaped for each audience.
verseByVerse.note: A royal wedding feast could last a week.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants, saying, "Tell those who are invited, See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast. In the ancient world, guests were invited in advance, and then summoned again when the feast was ready (Esther 6:14; Luke 14:17). The first invitation is God’s call to Israel through the Old Testament prophets and John; the guests had been told the feast was coming. Now the servants announce that it has come.

But they would not come. A deliberate refusal, and a grave insult to a king. They were not willing. The obstacle in this parable is never circumstance; it is the will.

Again he sent other servants. The king’s patience, as with the tenants (21:36). Publicly snubbed, he sends another delegation with a warmer message.

See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. A lavish feast, with meat ordinary people rarely ate. Prepared, slaughtered, ready: nothing is pending. In a world without refrigeration, once the animals are killed the king is committed and the cost is spent: he has made himself vulnerable to their refusal before they refuse. This is grace: the gospel announces that God has prepared everything in Christ.

Come to the wedding feast. The church is not sent to persuade God to be gracious. It is sent to say that everything is ready, and that the only thing outstanding is attendance. What was still to be done when Jesus told this parable would be done within the week, and his last word from the cross would be the word this message rests on: it is finished (John 19:30).

What am I waiting for? Most people who are not at the feast imagine they are waiting for something: to understand more, to feel differently, to get a part of their life straightened out first, to become the kind of person who belongs at such a table. Read the message again. There is nothing on the list. The oxen are killed, the tables are laid, and the only word left in the invitation is come. You do not tidy yourself before you accept a king’s invitation; you come, and the King himself provides what you need to wear. If you have been meaning to settle this for years, the invitation is not asking you to be ready. It is telling you that he is.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they paid no attention. They made light of it. Nobody argues. They simply have something on.

And went off, one to his farm, another to his business. Two kinds of rejection. Some were indifferent, and here the parable stops being only about Jerusalem: not vice, not a rival religion, but a field that needed walking and a business that needed running. These were not wrong in themselves, but they put them before the king (13:22). The most effective rival to God in most lives has never been wickedness. It is respectable occupation, and it works because nobody has to defend it. A man who misses the feast for a mistress knows he has done something. A man who misses it for the farm has merely been busy.

While the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. Others were violent, as the tenants were (21:35). God’s messengers, the prophets, John and later the apostles, were persecuted and killed (23:34).

The same end for both. The violent and the busy are dealt with in the same sentence and end in the same place: outside, with the feast going on without them. Not being hostile is not the same as being safe. The busy never opposed the king; they are condemned, with the violent, for not coming.

Made light of to his face. The snub in this parable falls on the son, because the feast is his. Jesus tells it about himself, and within three days it happened to him in the flesh. Herod’s soldiers mocked him (Luke 23:11), Pilate’s knelt in mock homage, and passers-by wagged their heads. Isaiah had seen it centuries before: he was despised, and we esteemed him not (Isaiah 53:3). Not esteeming him is exactly the sin of the farm and the shop, done politely. And he bore all of it in silence, like a lamb before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7).

But I have real responsibilities. Am I supposed to neglect them? No. Farms must be worked and businesses run, and Scripture honours diligent work (Proverbs 6:6–11; 2 Thessalonians 3:10). The fault was not that they had work but that the work came first when the king called. The question is one of order: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (6:33). In practice that means Christ’s claims are not fitted into the gaps the farm leaves. The Lord’s Day, prayer, Scripture and his people are given their place first, and the farm is worked as service to him.

parallels.desc: the servants in the vineyard beaten and killed

verseByVerse.quote: The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king was angry. God’s just anger at those who reject his grace and kill his messengers. It should not be softened. But read the offence carefully: this is not a monarch burning a town over a declined invitation. The men of verse 6 seized the king’s envoys, humiliated them and killed them. In the ancient world the murder of a royal embassy was an act of war, and everyone understood it so.

And he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. An unusual detail in a story about a wedding: a war in the middle of the preparations. It points to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Roman army in AD 70, which burned the city and the temple. Jesus is speaking prophetically of judgment on the city that rejected him (23:37–38; 24:2). God can use pagan armies as instruments of his judgment (Isaiah 10:5–6).

The guard that matters most. This is not a word that God hates the Jewish people, or that Christians may. Christians have too often misused it to justify anti-Semitism, and Jesus himself wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44). It is addressed to the leadership who had the vineyard on lease (21:45), not a race. And remember who the church in Jerusalem was: Jewish believers, warned by Jesus to flee when they saw the armies coming (Luke 21:20–21). There is no reading of this verse in which a Gentile Christian gets to feel superior.

Is it right for God to be angry? Yes, and it would be wrong for him not to be. What the verse says, without apology, is that patience has an end. A God who could be refused for ever with no consequence would not be a God who cared what happened. The anger exists because the invitation was real, the Son was real and the murders were real. God’s anger is not a temper; it is his settled, holy opposition to evil, and it is always just. And it is the measure of the cross: this is the anger that Christ bore for his people, so that it would never fall on them.
verseByVerse.note: Many see here a pointer to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to his servants, "The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Not worthy because they refused. In this parable the only unworthiness that matters is refusal, and the only worthiness on offer is a willingness to come hungry.

Go therefore to the main roads. Literally “the partings of the ways”: where a city street leads out into the country roads, where travellers, beggars and all kinds of people gathered. The invitation goes out beyond the original guests.

And invite to the wedding feast as many as you find. No restrictions. This is the gospel going to the Gentiles and to the outcasts of Israel (8:11; 21:31; 28:19). The feast will be full. And the second group is not let in at the back to watch: they are guests at the same tables, with the same food.

You are the person at the junction. If you are not Jewish, you are the person at the road junction, with no claim on the God of Israel and nothing to bring. Paul writes of Gentiles who were once without hope and without God in the world, and now brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:12–13), and he never quite gets over it. Neither should we.

Worthy is the Lamb. The first guests were not worthy, and the people from the junctions were no worthier. In the whole parable only one person is worthy of the wedding, and it is the son whose wedding it is. John heard heaven say so: the Lamb is worthy because he was slain, and by his blood he ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9). That is the guest list of the main roads, and how it was paid for. Their worthiness is borrowed, and it is enough.

Who should my church be inviting? The king’s instruction is not invite the people most likely to accept, or the ones who will fit in. It is: go to the junctions and bring in whoever is there. A church whose members all come from one part of one town has not been to the main roads; it has been to the people it already knew. Ask where the junctions are in your area: the estate, the students, the newcomers, the lonely, the people of other languages. Then go there with the invitation, not waiting for them to find the door.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.quote: And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found. The servants obeyed.

Both bad and good. Matthew puts the bad first, and it is the point: there is no screening at the door (13:47–48). And the good are there on exactly the same terms. The decent man was gathered from the road too, and his decency did not earn him a better seat. That is hard on the respectable heart, which would quite like grace for other people and wages for itself.

So the wedding hall was filled with guests. God’s purpose will not fail (Luke 14:23). Not one seat the King has prepared will stand empty, for all that the Father gives the Son will come to him (John 6:37).

The host who eats with sinners. The servants gather the bad with the good because their master did it first. Jesus was known as a friend of tax collectors and sinners (11:19). He came to call not the righteous but sinners (9:12–13). The King’s Son did not wait at the palace for decent people to arrive. He went out to the roads himself, and he went the whole way, to a cross between two criminals, so that the bad could be brought in.

Come as you are, stay as you are? No. The same parable goes straight on to a man who came as he was and was not clothed, and the parable that welcomes the bad without a question at the door also has a king who walks the room. Both halves are in the story: nothing whatever is required to get in, and something is required to be there. The bad are brought in. They are not left as they were found. Grace receives sinners exactly as they are, and then, by the same grace, makes them new.

parallels.desc: the net gathers fish of every kind

verseByVerse.quote: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. And he said to him, "Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?" And he was speechless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the king came in to look at the guests. The parable turns without warning: a picture of God’s final judgment. Everything so far has been about getting people through the door; now the host walks the room. What is wrong was not detectable at the door. It is detected by the king.

He saw there a man who had no wedding garment. Guests wore clean, festive clothing, and to come in dirty clothes insulted the host. (That kings provided garments is suggested but not well attested.) Either way, this man came on his own terms, without the clothing the occasion required.

What is the wedding garment? Jesus does not say. So start with the story and with Matthew. In the story, the man accepted the invitation but came as he was, without what the occasion required. In Matthew, righteousness is the life God requires: a righteousness greater than the scribes’ (5:20), fruit in keeping with repentance (3:8), and, in the parable just before, a people producing the kingdom’s fruits (21:43). So the first meaning is clear: the man wanted the feast without the change. He had not repented.

Who provides the garment? The Old Testament background points to God. Isaiah rejoices that God has clothed him with the garments of salvation and covered him with the robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). Zechariah saw the high priest’s filthy garments removed and replaced with clean ones, a picture of forgiveness (Zechariah 3:3–5). And the bride of the Lamb is given fine linen to wear, which is the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). The rest of the New Testament then explains how God clothes sinners: with Christ’s righteousness credited to those who trust him (Philippians 3:9; Galatians 3:27), and with the new life that follows, as they put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:14). Credited means counted to your account. God declares the believer righteous, not because he has become perfect, but because Christ’s perfect obedience is reckoned as his, as a debt is cleared when someone else’s payment is entered against it (Romans 4:5–6). That declaration is what Scripture calls justification. This commentary’s view: in the parable, the garment is the repentant, changed life that the kingdom requires. The rest of Scripture shows that this too is God’s gift: forgiveness and righteousness in Christ, and a new life that grows from it. It is not one without the other.

Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? “Friend” is a cool, polite address (see 20:13). Matthew uses hetairos as a form of address three times, and this is the middle one: to the labourer grumbling at the pay table (20:13), here to a man about to be thrown out, and in a garden by torchlight to Judas (26:50). Every occurrence is addressed to someone in the wrong, and every one is courteous: the address of a man who has not raised his voice and has stopped pretending. And the question is an enquiry, not a tirade. The king gives him the chance to explain.

And he was speechless. He had no excuse. On the day of judgment, every mouth will be stopped (Romans 3:19). The verb is the one for muzzling an ox. A man pulled in off a road junction at an hour’s notice could hardly be blamed for his clothes unless something had been open to him that he did not take. He is speechless because he has no grievance. His silence is the admission.

Was the man a believer who lost his salvation? Some read it that way. The more likely reading is that he was a professing guest who never truly came on the king’s terms, someone who wanted the feast and not the King, like those who say Lord, Lord, and whom Jesus never knew (7:21–23). Those whom God truly clothes he keeps: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). The warning is not meant to make true believers doubt whether they will be kept. It is meant to make everyone who sits in the hall ask whether he has truly come.

How do I know whether I have the garment? Not by inspecting yourself until you feel worthy; no one does. Ask instead two plain questions. Have you come to Christ, trusting him and not your own record to make you acceptable to God? And is there in you, however weak, a turning from sin and a desire to please him, the repentance the parable looks for? If both are there, even faintly, the King has clothed you, and the new life will grow. If you find that you want the feast but not the change, that is the warning, and the remedy is still open: come to him now, confess it, and ask him to clothe you.
verseByVerse.note: The wedding garment stands for the fitting clothing the host requires — the righteousness God gives and the life that matches it.

parallels.desc: clothed with the garments of salvation
fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the attendants, "Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." For many are called, but few are chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king said to the attendants, Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. Thrown out of the lit hall into the darkness outside: in Matthew, final exclusion from the kingdom (8:12; 25:30).

Where the weeping is. The anguish of final judgment (13:42). Jesus speaks of it more often than anyone else in Scripture, and never with satisfaction. The binding and the darkness come not from dramatic wickedness but from refusing the King’s provision while sitting at his table.

Bound and cast out in our place. Within three days the words of this verse were carried out on the King’s own Son. The leaders bound Jesus and led him away to Pilate (27:2). At noon darkness came over all the land, and out of it he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (27:45–46). The one man in history who had every right to the wedding garment was treated as the man without one: bound, put outside the city, left in the dark. He went out into the darkness so that they would never be thrown into it.

For many are called, but few are chosen. The key saying. “Called” (klētoi) here means invited: the gospel invitation goes out to many, to everyone (v. 9). “Chosen” (eklektoi) means elect: those whom God has chosen, who respond to the invitation with true faith and are clothed in righteousness. The gospel call is universal; God’s election is particular. “Few” is not a number; it means fewer than those invited. Those who are not chosen are those who refuse (vv. 3–6) or come without the garment (v. 12), and they are responsible for their response.

The two callings. Reformed theology distinguishes the external call of the gospel, which goes to all who hear it, from the effectual or inward call by which the Spirit brings the elect to faith (Romans 8:30; 1 Corinthians 1:23–24). Matthew’s “called” here is the external call; Paul often uses the word for the effectual one. Put simply: the outward call is the preacher’s voice reaching the ear; the inward call is God’s voice reaching the heart. Lydia heard Paul with the other women by the river, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what he said (Acts 16:14). So preach to everyone, because the outward call is genuine; and rest, because God secures his own.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminian Christians hold that God chooses those he foresees will believe, so that election follows human decision. Reformed theology reads it as God’s prior choice, which produces the response (John 6:44; Ephesians 1:4–5; Acts 13:48). This commentary’s view: unconditional election. The reason is that Scripture traces faith itself to God’s choosing: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48), not the other way round. Many faithful Christians read these texts differently, and they love the same Saviour and preach the same invitation. But the invitation goes to all, and everyone who comes will be received (11:28; John 6:37).

What if I want to come and I am not one of the chosen? That fear has kept people from Christ for centuries, which is a bitter irony, since the doctrine was given to settle fear and not to create it. Notice first that nobody in Scripture is ever told to establish that he is elect before coming. In this very parable the servants are told to invite as many as they find: no list, no enquiry into anyone’s eternal status. They were not given the names; they were given the invitation. And election is not meant to be looked at from the front. Paul writes about it to people already inside, as an explanation of how they got there and a guarantee that they will be kept. It is the foundation under the house, not the door of it. Calvin’s counsel is still the best: Christ is the mirror in which we see our election. Look at him and come to him, and you are looking at the evidence. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37), and no one has ever found an exception.

Is my wanting to come a sign of anything? Yes, and a hopeful one. No one drags himself toward God unaided; no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). So if you find in yourself a real desire to be at the feast, to be forgiven, to know Christ, you did not manufacture it. That desire is the surest sign that the One who does the choosing has already been at work. Do not sit and analyse it. Act on it: come.

Is the outer darkness not far too severe for a missing garment? Yes, if the garment were a dress code. But the man is not thrown out for poor taste in clothes. He sat at the wedding of the King’s Son while refusing what the King provides, wanting the feast and not the King. That is not a small slip against a minor host. It is contempt for the Son, offered to the holy God whose worth has no limit, and the seriousness of an offence is measured by the one it is against (Psalm 51:4). Notice too what the sentence is: to be put outside the light of the one he did not want. The King’s judgment is just, and it is also the one thing the man had chosen, given to him for ever. The remedy was free, and it was offered to him at the door.

For worship. Salvation belongs to the LORD from first to last: he prepared the feast, chose his guests, draws them by his Spirit, clothes them in his Son and will keep them for ever. And the call that goes out to all is no pretence; it is the voice of a King who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, saying to every sinner, come.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. Unable to arrest him openly (21:46), they try to trap him into saying something that would turn the crowds against him, or give them grounds to accuse him to the Romans. The verb comes from the word for a snare.

In the flow. The parable said the invited guests would not come; now they refuse in person. Three tests follow, and the King who could not be trapped in argument will later give himself up to be taken (26:53–54).

And they sent their disciples to him. They sent their students, perhaps to make the trap look innocent, while the seniors kept their distance from whatever happened.

Along with the Herodians. Supporters of Herod Antipas and his family, who cooperated with Rome. The Pharisees resented Roman rule; the Herodians supported it. Natural enemies, united against Jesus (Mark 3:6): whatever he said about taxes, one group would accuse him.

Enemies made friends against him. This odd alliance is a small rehearsal of the week’s end. On Friday Herod and Pilate, who had been at enmity, became friends over the prisoner they passed between them (Luke 23:12). The Pharisee and the Herodian thought they were laying a snare. They were walking into a counsel older than either party, in which the Anointed One would be handed over according to the definite plan of God (Acts 2:23), and would win.

Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully. Flattery, intended to make him answer boldly. Everything they say is true, and they do not believe a word of it.

And you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. Literally “you do not look at the face of people”. The purpose is to build a box out of his own reputation and shut him in it: you fear nobody, so prove it by answering recklessly. Scripture treats flattery as a form of attack: a flattering mouth works ruin (Proverbs 26:28).

How do I recognise flattery? It usually arrives dressed as respect. You are the only one round here who says what he really thinks. You are not like the others. I knew you would understand; you have always been more open-minded than they are. Each is a door held open in a particular direction, and the compliment is the hinge. The test is simple: notice whether the praise is describing you or steering you, and whether it arrived just before a request. Genuine encouragement leaves you freer to do right; flattery leaves you more obliged to do what the flatterer wants.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. Their alliance was a trap.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? “Lawful” means according to God’s law. The tax was the poll tax, a yearly denarius per person paid directly to the Roman emperor. It was not the amount that stung but what it meant: a yearly admission of who ruled God’s land. When it was introduced in AD 6, Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it (Acts 5:37) under the cry that God alone was Israel’s king. Men had died over this question within living memory.

The trap. If Jesus said “Yes, pay”, he would lose the support of the crowds, who hated the tax and hoped the Messiah would end Roman rule. If he said “No”, the Herodians could report him to the Romans as a rebel, and he would be arrested for sedition. And they put it as a question of conscience, so that refusing to answer would look like evading a religious duty.

The charge that came back on Friday. The trap failed on Tuesday, and its bait was used anyway. When the council brought Jesus to Pilate, the first accusation was this very question, turned into a lie: we found this man forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king (Luke 23:2). He had said the opposite, in public, with a coin in his hand. So the King who would not be trapped into rebellion against Caesar died as a rebel against Caesar, carrying an accusation that was false, as he carried the guilt of his people that was not his own.

What do I do with questions designed to trap? Almost every generation produces a question shaped so that a Christian must offend one group or another, and the questioner’s interest is not in the answer but in the offence. Do not be rushed into the alternatives you are handed. Ask what the real question underneath is, and answer that, truthfully and with grace. Sometimes the wisest reply is a question back (21:24). Pray for wisdom, which God gives generously (James 1:5), and remember that you do not need to win the exchange; you need to be faithful in it.
verseByVerse.note: This was the poll tax paid directly to Rome, bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus, aware of their malice. He sees the evil intent behind the flattery. They told him he was not swayed by appearances, and discovered that he was not swayed by appearances.

Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? They pretended to seek his opinion; they wanted to destroy him. He names them to their faces before answering a word.

Show me the coin for the tax. He does not produce one. He asks them, and the request wins the argument before it starts.

And they brought him a denarius. A silver coin, a day’s wage (20:2). Men troubled in conscience about Caesar’s tax had his coin in a purse, on the temple mount, and handed it over without a flicker: they were already using his money and benefiting from his rule.

The scruple and the purse. The quiet accusation lands near home. It is easy to hold a principled objection to a thing while living comfortably inside it, unaware of the gap. Think of one conviction you hold firmly, about money, honesty or the poor, and ask what your bank statement or your diary would show if he said, show me. Then be honest with him: the One who sees through every pretence went on to die for sinners whose hearts were open books to him.

The image of God holding Caesar’s coin. Every other hand that ever turned that coin over belonged to someone who bears God’s image and has defaced it. This one belongs to the image of the invisible God himself (Colossians 1:15), the one man who has always given God everything that is God’s: his will, his body, his life, down to the last cup in Gethsemane. Not my will, but yours, he would pray two nights later (26:39). When he says render to God the things that are God’s, he is the only person in history who has ever done it perfectly, and he did it in the place of all who have not.
verseByVerse.note: The denarius was a silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whose likeness and inscription is this? The denarius most likely bore the head of the emperor Tiberius (AD 14–37), with an inscription reading “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Augustus”, and on the reverse “High Priest”. To devout Jews the image and the claim to divinity broke the second commandment. So the coin handed to Jesus in the temple announced that another man was the son of a god.

They said, Caesar’s. Their own answer settles it.

Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. Render means to give back what is owed. Governments are established by God and have a right to taxes (Romans 13:1–7). That holds even for a pagan, oppressive government. Give it back, and do not make a religion of resenting it.

And to God the things that are God’s. The deeper point. The coin bears Caesar’s image; human beings bear God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27). An image declares ownership. Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, your whole life. Caesar may have your taxes, your obedience in his own sphere, your honour and your prayers. He may never have the thing that bears the other image, and that is not a small reservation; it is everything. Christians have given tyrants the coin all day and would not give them that.

What it does not mean. Not that life divides into religious and secular areas, with God ruling only the first. Everything belongs to God (Psalm 24:1), including Caesar.

When exactly should a Christian disobey the government? Only when obeying would mean sinning. Paul wrote let every person be subject to the governing authorities, and Peter wrote honour the emperor, both under Nero, who would kill them (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:17). So a government being unjust, corrupt or hostile to the faith is not by itself grounds for disobedience. The line is crossed not when the state is wicked but when it requires you to be. Then Scripture is clear: the Hebrew midwives refused Pharaoh’s order to kill the boys (Exodus 1:17), the three young men would not bow to the statue (Daniel 3:16–18), Daniel kept praying at his open window (Daniel 6:10), and Peter told the council, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). And notice the manner: they refused openly, without rebellion or contempt, and accepted the cost. Christian disobedience is the refusal to sin, with the punishment borne.

Where Christians differ: church and state. Some Christians want the state to enforce the civil laws of Moses or a Christian nationalism. Others want complete separation of religion from public life. The Reformed tradition has generally held that the state and the church are distinct institutions, each under God, with different roles: the state bears the sword for justice; the church bears the keys of the kingdom (Romans 13; Matthew 16:19). This commentary’s view: Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes, praying for rulers, and seeking justice, while giving ultimate loyalty only to God.

Is it wrong to cut my tax bill, or to complain about how taxes are spent? Arranging your affairs lawfully to pay what is actually owed, and no more, is not wrong; render means pay what is due. Evading what is due, by hiding income or cash-in-hand work, is. And Christians may speak, vote and campaign for wise and just use of public money, since they are citizens as well as believers. What Jesus rules out is treating the tax as a reason to withhold honour from the authorities God has set over us, or making a cause of resentment the centre of our lives.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those in authority by name this week (1 Timothy 2:1–2), including the ones you did not vote for. Then look for one place where you have quietly given Caesar, or your career, or the crowd, something that bears God’s image and belongs only to him.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

parallels.desc: be subject to the governing authorities

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard it, they marveled. His answer escaped their trap and went deeper than their question. Among his enemies the marvelling never once ends in worship.

And they left him and went away. Defeated, but not converted: impressed, and nothing had happened to them. The next time these men are in a room with Jesus they will not be asking questions; they will be looking for witnesses against him (26:59). Admiration that refuses to become allegiance does not stay neutral for long.

Can I admire Jesus and still be lost? Yes, and it is perhaps the most respectable way of rejecting him. It is possible to find Jesus intellectually magnificent, to enjoy the way he handles opponents, to admire the answer about Caesar as a piece of reasoning, to recommend the passage to others, and to have moved not an inch. Admiration costs nothing and flatters the admirer. Faith is different: it bows, trusts and follows. The question is not whether you think highly of Jesus, but whether you have given yourself to him. And if you fear that you have only admired, that fear is not a closed door: admiration is where many disciples began, and he receives anyone who moves from applause to asking.

Something greater than Solomon. Jesus had already told these men how their marvelling would be judged. The queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and something greater than Solomon is here (12:42). She heard Solomon and blessed the LORD (1 Kings 10:9). These men hear Solomon’s greater Son from a few yards away and go home. What they cannot fault is the wisdom of the One who is himself the wisdom of God, and the right response to him is not applause but bowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Resurrection, the Great Commandment, and David's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sadducees make up a story of a woman married to seven brothers to make the resurrection look absurd, and are told they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God; Jesus proves the resurrection from the books of Moses they accepted. The crowd is astonished. A lawyer asks which commandment is greatest, and Jesus answers with love for God and love for neighbour, on which the whole Law and the Prophets hang. Then Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, quotes Psalm 110, and no one can answer him a word.
verseByVerse.theology: Many errors come under one of the two failures Jesus names: not knowing the Scriptures, and not knowing the power of God. The Sadducees knew the Torah and believed in a God too small to raise the dead. The resurrection argument rests on the covenant: God binds himself by name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and he does not attach his name to dust. The law hangs on two hinges. And Psalm 110 closes the day: the Christ is David’s son by birth and David’s Lord as the eternal Son, which is Matthew’s first chapter put as a riddle (1:23).
verseByVerse.examples: Like angels in heaven means only that they do not marry: what ends is the institution, not love. Notice the woman in the Sadducees’ story, whom no one in it notices: she has buried seven husbands and appears only as a question of ownership. As yourself is a measure: you never need reminding to care about your own toothache, and that attention is the standard for your neighbour. And verse 33 warns that astonishment is not allegiance.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses said, 'If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same day Sadducees came to him. The second test. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy: the high priest belonged to them, they controlled the temple and its revenues, and they had their working arrangement with Rome. They are often said to have accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative.

Who say that there is no resurrection. They denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). A party with wealth and office in the present world has perhaps the least reason to want a world to come: if this life is where the accounts are settled, they have already won.

Teacher, Moses said, If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. The law of levirate marriage, from the old word for a husband’s brother (Deuteronomy 25:5–6; compare Genesis 38:8). The first son would carry on the dead man’s name and land, and the widow would have a protector.

Do my desires shape what I believe? More than we like to admit. The Sadducees are a warning that we tend to find persuasive the arguments for what suits us, and weak the arguments for what would cost us. That does not make every conviction suspect, but it does mean we should be most careful where a doctrine is most inconvenient. Ask, when you resist a teaching of Scripture: is my objection really from the text, or from what it would require of me? Let God’s word judge your desires, not the other way round.

The question Easter would answer. In this same temple Jesus had said, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, speaking of his body (John 2:19–21). The Sadducees came to argue that no one rises. Within the week the answer was given not as an argument but as an empty tomb. When the apostles preached it in these courts, the Sadducees had them arrested (Acts 4:1–3). The doctrine they mocked on Tuesday walked out of a grave on Sunday, and it has a name.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture and denied the resurrection. The law of levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

parallels.desc: Sadducees say there is no resurrection

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. So too the second and third, down to the seventh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were seven brothers among us. A hypothetical story, designed to make the resurrection look absurd.

The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. So on down to the seventh.

The logic of the trap. If your doctrine is true, this absurd situation follows; the situation is absurd; so your doctrine is false. Everything depends on the hidden premise. Here the premise is that resurrection means the resumption of this life exactly as it stands, with the same arrangements and the same property law. Jesus will deny the premise rather than the conclusion, which is usually where such arguments break.

The woman nobody sees. Nobody in the story looks at her. She has buried seven husbands, been handed on from brother to brother as a legal obligation, borne no children in a society where a childless widow had no protection, and died. And she appears in the argument purely as a difficulty, an object whose ownership must be decided. The Sadducees have taken a law that existed to protect widows and used it to mock the one hope that would have comforted her. Behind every hard case in an argument is a person with a name.

The one who sees the widow. The Sadducees did not see her. Jesus always did. At the gate of Nain he saw a widow following her only son’s coffin, had compassion on her, and gave the young man back to his mother (Luke 7:12–15). The man the Sadducees are trying to trap is the only person in the conversation who would have known her name, and the resurrection they mock is the gift he would give her.

verseByVerse.quote: "After them all, the woman died. In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After them all, the woman died. Then comes the question: in the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be?

For they all had her. The question assumes the life to come simply continues this one, so that seven men would each have a claim on her. The Pharisees taught the resurrection, some in very earthly terms; Jesus exposes the assumption itself.

This life, improved? The error is not confined to Sadducees. Ask most people, including many Christians, what they expect of heaven, and you hear the present world improved: the same house without the mortgage, the same work without Monday, the same relationships without the friction. It is natural, since this world is the only material we have. But it is an extension, not a transformation, and it is why heaven strikes many people as faintly boring. Paul answers the same confusion with a seed: what you sow is not the body that is to be (1 Corinthians 15:37). The plant is truly continuous with the seed, and not remotely predictable from it. Nobody holding an acorn would guess an oak.

So will my resurrection body be real? Yes: real, physical and recognisable, and also transformed beyond anything we can extrapolate. The risen Christ ate fish in front of his friends and invited Thomas to touch his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27); his body was truly his. Yet it was raised imperishable, in glory and power (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Both halves must be held. Drop the first and you get a vague spiritual mist that Scripture never promises. Drop the second and you get the Sadducees’ question. We will be ourselves, body and soul, made fit at last for the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered them, "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are wrong. Literally “you have gone astray”: said to the priestly aristocracy in public.

Neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Two errors. They did not understand the Scriptures, which teach the resurrection (vv. 31–32; Daniel 12:2; Job 19:25–27). And they underestimated God’s power: the God who created life can raise the dead and create a new kind of life, not merely restore the old one (1 Corinthians 15:35–44). Knowing the words is not the same as knowing what they say. And the second charge is worse.
