They believed in God and did not believe he could do anything; their God had been quietly cut down to the size of the arrangements they already understood.

For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. The Sadducees’ question does not get solved; it stops applying. Marriage belongs to this age. With no death there is no need to continue a family line, the whole purpose of levirate marriage, and the marriage earthly marriage pictured, between Christ and his people, will be complete (Ephesians 5:31–32; Revelation 19:7–9).

But are like angels in heaven. Like angels in not marrying, and in being immortal (Luke 20:36). The Sadducees did not believe in angels either (Acts 23:8), so Jesus is answering two of their denials at once.

Will I be with my husband or wife in heaven? If you are both in Christ, yes, and you will know each other better than you ever did here. What ends is the institution: the exclusive covenant of marriage, with its vows until death, which belonged to this age and to the raising of families. Love itself is not abolished; it is perfected. You will not know your beloved less in that day but far more, no longer through the narrow channel of one exclusive bond, but in the open light of a love with nothing in it left to fear or forgive. Marriage was always a signpost, not the destination: a picture of Christ and his church, and when the Bridegroom comes the picture gives way to what it was painting all along. We are not told every detail. It is enough to know that nothing good is lost in that country; it is taken up and made everlasting, with Christ at the centre of it.

What about someone who never married, or whose marriage was unhappy? This verse is good news for you too. The single person is not a lesser guest at the wedding of the Lamb; in the age to come no one is married to anyone but Christ, and his love is wholly theirs. And the one whose marriage brought grief or harm need not fear that it is fastened to them for ever. In the resurrection every relationship is healed or set free, and every believer belongs first and fully to the Bridegroom.

On a Tuesday. When you face something that seems impossible, a death, a ruined relationship, your own stubborn sin, ask which you are forgetting: what God has said, or what God can do.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees accepted. He argues on the only ground they acknowledged. “Said to you”: Scripture is God speaking to every generation, not merely an old record.

The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Exodus 3:6, God’s words to Moses at the burning bush, centuries after the patriarchs had died.

God of the living. How does this prove the resurrection? Not from the present tense of the verb, which is not actually in the Hebrew. The argument rests on the covenant. God names himself by his covenant with Abraham, and that covenant included promises to Abraham himself: a land, a seed, a blessing, and God being his God (Genesis 17:7–8). Abraham died without receiving them (Hebrews 11:13). If death were the end of Abraham, God’s covenant would have been with a corpse. A God who calls himself “the God of Abraham” must keep Abraham alive to enjoy the promises, and keep him whole, body and soul, since God made him a body-and-soul creature. So the covenant guarantees the resurrection. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are alive to God (Luke 20:38), and their bodies will be raised.

Where are believers who have died now? With the Lord, consciously, in joy. Their souls do not sleep or drift; to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and Paul calls departing to be with Christ far better (Philippians 1:23). The thief went to paradise that very day (Luke 23:43). There is no purgatory in between, for the blood of Christ has already cleansed them. Yet they wait for something more: the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return, when they and we will be raised together, whole (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

What God does with names. At the bush God chose to be named, for the rest of the Bible, as the God of three men. One lied about his wife twice. One was a passive father who favoured one son over the other. One cheated his brother, wrestled with God and limped afterwards. God took their names into his own and is not ashamed to be called their God (Hebrews 11:16), and on the strength of that bond Jesus tells a hostile audience that the grave does not get them.

Every promise kept in the Seed. The promises God made to Abraham were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and Paul says the offspring is one man: Christ (Galatians 3:16). So the covenant that guarantees Abraham’s resurrection runs through the man answering the Sadducees. Within the week he would die, and on the third day God would raise him as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will rise because the Seed of Abraham rose first.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to God, death cannot break that bond. Put your own name where Abraham’s stands: the God of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and you. Say it at a graveside, and say it on the morning you are afraid of dying.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held highest.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. Jesus had silenced the most powerful religious leaders with the Scriptures they claimed to know. The word is built on a verb for striking: they were knocked sideways, as after the Sermon on the Mount (7:28).

A warning inside a victory. Many were ordinary pilgrims, delighted to see their teachers beaten by a Galilean. By Friday a crowd gathered at the governor’s headquarters, worked on by the men who had just lost this argument, would shout for a murderer to be released instead of him (27:20–23). Astonishment is not allegiance. The difference between crowd and disciples in this Gospel is whether anybody follows him out of the building.

Scripture opened by its Author. What struck them was a man who handled the Scriptures as though he had written them. He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes (7:29). The scribes quoted authorities. Jesus was one. After his resurrection he would do the same on the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets and interpreting in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The crowd was watching the Word explaining the word.

Is it wrong to be moved in church? Not at all. God gave us the capacity, and the Psalms are full of it. Being moved by the truth is a good gift. But it is meant to lead somewhere: to repentance, trust, obedience and love. Ask what the last thing was that moved you deeply, and what it changed. If you must admit that it was a very good hour and nothing came of it, that is not a reason to despair. It is a reason to ask him for more than astonishment, and to act on the next thing he shows you.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. “Silenced” is the verb used of the speechless guest (v. 12). Their rivals had been defeated by a man defending the Pharisees’ own belief in the resurrection. Instead of delight, they close ranks and send in another questioner. Opposition to Christ is not, at bottom, a set of convictions that a better argument will correct. It is a disposition that survives every argument, including the ones it wins.

They gathered together against his Anointed. Perhaps an echo of Psalm 2:2, the rulers take counsel together against the LORD and his Anointed, a psalm the early church prayed over Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:25–27). The men regrouping in the temple court are standing inside a psalm, playing the part the psalm assigned them, and the psalm’s verdict on the whole enterprise is that the One enthroned in heaven laughs.

And one of them, a lawyer. An expert in the law of Moses, a scribe (Mark 12:28), brought forward because the question is technical and they want it asked properly.

Asked him a question to test him. The third test, with the word Matthew used of the devil in the wilderness (4:1). Mark presents this scribe more favourably: Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God (Mark 12:34). What follows is an answer about the law that has never been bettered, drawn out by a test. God has never been prevented from saying something glorious by the poor motives of the person who asked.

Should I bother answering people who only want to argue? Usually, yes, with care. You do not know what is happening in the questioner’s heart; this scribe, sent to test, went away not far from the kingdom. Answer the question honestly and kindly, without trying to win, and let the truth do its work. There are times to decline, when someone is only mocking (7:6), but more often a hostile question is an open door. Jesus answered every one of these tests, and he answered them with the deepest truths he had.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law? The rabbis debated which commandments were “heavy” and which were “light”, and whether one could sum up the law in a single principle. Later rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments.

A trap with three jaws. Name one commandment great and you imply the others are small, a charge to take to the crowd. Refuse to answer and you are not the teacher you claim to be. And underneath sits an assumption: that the law is an inventory a careful man might sort by importance. That way of holding God’s commands leaves the man himself untouched: however scrupulous, he is managing a portfolio.

The law written out in a life. The lawyer treats the law as a list because he has never seen it any other way. But the commands came from one holy and loving heart, and that heart was standing in front of him in a human body. The Son is the exact imprint of his nature (Hebrews 1:3), and the best answer in the room to which commandment is greatest was the man who had kept every one.

What is my own list? Almost every Christian has a working list of the things that really matter and the things that are technically commanded, and almost nobody has written it down or would defend it out loud. The list is usually shaped to be keepable. That is the instinct this lawyer brought into the temple. Jesus answers it by naming not one item from the list but the thing every item is made of, and you cannot manage a portfolio of love with all your heart. There is nothing left over to do the managing with.
verseByVerse.note: Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the law; teachers debated which were weightiest.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. From Deuteronomy 6:5, part of the Shema (“Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one”, Deuteronomy 6:4), which devout Jews recited twice daily. The command is love, not merely obedience. Love for God is not an emotion added on top of religious duty; it is the life without which no commandment is really kept at all.

Heart, soul, mind. Not three separate parts of a person, but a way of saying “with everything you are”.

Why do the Gospels give different lists? Matthew has three terms, Mark and Luke four (Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27), and Deuteronomy its own three: heart, soul and might. The question dissolves once you see what kind of list this is. It is not an inventory dividing a person into drawers; it is a Hebrew way of saying all of you, and the terms deliberately overlap and pile up. Jesus, like any teacher with a text everyone knew by heart, gives its full sense, not a word count. And the sense is the one thing all the versions agree on perfectly: the list has no edge you can stand outside of. Whatever you were about to hold back is named in it somewhere.

This is the great and first commandment. First in importance, and the source of all the others. To keep every rule without loving God is to miss the point (15:8).

Why love? Because God first loved us (1 John 4:19; Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Love cannot be commanded into existence by willpower alone; it grows in response to love received. The gospel, showing us God’s love in Christ, is what makes this command possible.

I do not feel much love for God. What do I do? First, do not measure love by your emotional temperature on a given morning. Biblical love is more than feeling, though never less: the Psalms are full of longing. But it is chiefly the settled direction of the whole person, which is why it can be commanded. Jesus gives a usable test: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15). Obedience is not a substitute for love; it is its most reliable evidence, available on days when feeling is not. Second, do not try to work on the love directly, which is like trying to feel warm by concentrating. Love is a response, and it rises with what is seen. Look longer at what God has done: read Scripture slowly rather than quickly, come to the Lord’s Supper, sing with God’s people, and remember particular mercies rather than mercy in general. And obey in the meantime. Feelings very often follow the feet.

The command no one has kept. Jesus hands the lawyer the one no one else in the room has kept for a single hour. You are commanded to love God with all your heart and soul and mind; you have not; and the one who tells you so did exactly that, all the way to a cross, in your place. His perfect love is counted as yours, so your own failing love does not undo your standing. Start there, and the loving becomes possible, because it is no longer the price of anything, and because the Spirit he gives pours the love of God into our hearts (Romans 5:5).

parallels.desc: love the LORD your God with all your heart

verseByVerse.quote: "And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a second is like it. The questioner asked for one; Jesus gives two, because they belong together. “Like it”: of the same nature and importance. Love for God shows itself in love for others (1 John 4:20–21).

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18. Jesus joins two verses that stand far apart in the law. A few Jewish teachers had set love for God and love for neighbour side by side before, but no one, as far as we know, had made them so plainly the two hinges of everything.

As yourself. A far harder command than being nice. You do not have to remember to take an interest in your own toothache. That automatic, ever-present attention to your own case is the standard: give the same to the person next to you. Or take the excuses. When something goes wrong for you, the mind produces context at once: I was tired, it was difficult, anyone would have. When the same goes wrong at someone else’s hands, the mind produces character: he is careless, she is like that. Loving your neighbour as yourself means giving him the same generous supply of excuses you make for yourself. Christ loved you more than himself while you were failing him, and that is where the strength to begin comes from.

As I have loved you. Two nights after this conversation, Jesus took the second commandment and raised its measure. A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another (John 13:34). As yourself is the measure of the law; as I have loved you is the measure of the cross. He washed the feet of the men who would desert him and died for them: the neighbour command shown at its full height, in the one man who loved others not as much as himself but more.

Who is my neighbour? The command comes from Leviticus 19:18, where it applies first to fellow Israelites, and then in the same chapter to the foreigner: you shall love him as yourself (Leviticus 19:34). When a lawyer asked Jesus this question, he answered with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37): your neighbour is anyone in need whom you can help. And Jesus has already said it includes enemies (5:43–48). In practice it begins with the people nearest you, your family, the people in your street, your church, your workplace, and reaches out to whoever God puts in your path.

On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets. “Depend” literally means “hang”, as a door hangs on its hinges: take them out and the whole structure is on the floor. Love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8–10). So the 613 items the lawyer wanted ranked are not 613 separate obligations at all. They are the outworking of two.

In the flow. Render to God the things that are God’s (v. 21) is spelt out here: what God is owed is all of you, in love. And the next chapter shows what happens when it is forgotten (23:23).

What it does not mean. Not that the specific commands of the law can be ignored as long as we have loving feelings. Love does not replace God’s law; it fulfils it. Love tells us why we obey; the law tells us how love behaves. Nor does “as yourself” command self-love as a separate duty; it assumes it.

Can I love God and not my neighbour? No. John puts it as bluntly as it can be put: if anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar (1 John 4:20). Not mistaken, not inconsistent: a liar. The love of God is not a private arrangement between a man and heaven that leaves the people in his house untouched. It comes down the stairs, or it was never on the roof. And the reverse holds too: love of neighbour cut off from love of God soon becomes either sentiment or self-congratulation. The two hinges hold the one door.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, saying, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "The son of David."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question. Now he puts one question of his own.

What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he? The question that matters most. It is close to the question at Caesarea Philippi, where he had asked twelve friends, who do you say that I am? (16:15). Here, in the temple, surrounded by the men arranging his death, he asks it in the third person. It is the question this Gospel has been walking toward since the genealogy, and one after another the people in Matthew answer it: Peter, the high priest, Pilate, the centurion at the cross.

They said to him, The son of David. The standard answer, and a correct one (1:1; 2 Samuel 7:12–16). Most expected a human king who would restore Israel. These men are not caught in an error. They are caught in an answer that is true and has stopped short.

Is a correct answer about Jesus enough? No. It is possible to hold an entirely correct doctrinal position about Jesus Christ and to have got no further than the position. These Pharisees could have passed an examination on the Messiah’s lineage. What they could not do was follow their own answer far enough to notice who was asking. A right answer is precious, and we must never despise sound doctrine. But it is meant to lead to the Person: to trust him, worship him and follow him. Jesus does not correct their answer. He asks them to keep reading.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord. “In the Spirit”: inspired by the Holy Spirit. Jesus affirms that David wrote Psalm 110 and that it is God’s word.

The Lord said to my Lord. Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew the first title is the divine name, Yahweh, printed LORD, and the second is adoni, my lord, the word a subject uses of his king or master. David, Israel’s greatest king, calls the Messiah his Lord. No Jewish father would address his own descendant so.

Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. The right hand is the place of highest honour and authority, beside God himself. The Messiah will reign until every enemy is defeated (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). It is the Old Testament verse the New Testament cites most often (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13), of Christ’s ascension and present reign.

In the flow. The verse will come back. Two nights later, on oath before the high priest, Jesus will answer with the same psalm: you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power (26:64). The riddle he sets in the temple is the claim for which he will be condemned, and the throne it describes is the one he takes when he rises and ascends (28:18).

Did David really write Psalm 110? Everything in the argument hangs on it, and it is widely denied: much modern scholarship assigns the psalm to a later court poet writing about a king, in which case there is no puzzle at all. Three things are worth weighing. The psalm carries its own heading, a Psalm of David, the oldest testimony we have about it. What happens in the room also counts: these were hostile experts who wanted nothing so much as to catch him in a mistake, and they did not dispute the premise, since Jewish teachers of the day, like Jesus, took the heading at its word; no one was able to answer him a word (v. 46). Scholars will go on debating the psalm’s date, and a believer can admit that the question is argued without being unsettled by it. And for a Christian the third consideration settles it. Jesus stakes a public argument about his own identity on David’s authorship, and says David spoke in the Spirit. A Lord who built his case on a premise he knew to be false would not be a Lord to trust on anything else. The authorship is not a detail on the edge of the passage; it is holding it up.

On a Tuesday. Christ is reigning now, at God’s right hand, until every enemy is under his feet. When the news, or your own life, makes it look as though evil is winning, read Psalm 110 and say it out loud: he is seated, and he is reigning, and the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son? A father would never call his son “Lord”. How can the Messiah be both David’s son (his descendant) and David’s Lord (his superior)? The only answer: the Messiah is more than a human descendant of David. He is a man, born in David’s line (1:1), and he is God’s Son, the eternal Lord (16:16; Romans 1:3–4).

One person, truly God and truly man. It took the church centuries to state it: the Christ is David’s son according to the flesh and David’s Lord according to his eternal nature, one person, truly God and truly man (Westminster Confession 8.2). That does not mean half God and half man, or a man whom God lived inside for a while. It means that the eternal Son of God took a full human nature to himself, body and soul, and never laid it down: the Word became flesh (John 1:14). Matthew has been saying it since his first chapter, where the child in the genealogy of David is also the one called Immanuel, God with us (1:23). The riddle in the temple is his Gospel’s first chapter, put as a question.

And no one was able to answer him a word. The answer was standing in front of them, and they would not accept it.

Nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions. The tests are over. Now he will speak against them (chapter 23), and then they will act against him (26:3–5). When argument has been exhausted, what remains is not always agreement. Sometimes it is the plot.

Three kinds of silence. The man without the wedding garment was speechless because he had no defence (v. 12). These men are speechless because they will not say what they can see. And there is a third kind, which the psalm Jesus quoted points to: the silence of a man who stops arguing because he has finally understood who he is talking to. Let the silence of this verse be the right kind in you: stop arguing with him where you have been resisting, and bow.

Why does it matter that Jesus is both God and man? Because only such a Saviour could save us. As man, he could take our place, obey the law we broke and die the death we deserved. As God, his obedience and death have infinite worth, enough to pay for all the sins of all his people, and he could not be held by death. A Saviour who was only man could not save; a Saviour who was not man could not stand in our place. That is why the answer to Jesus’ riddle is not a puzzle for scholars but the ground of every Christian’s hope.

For worship. Great is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3:16). David’s root and descendant (Revelation 22:16), the child of Bethlehem and the eternal Son enthroned: this is our Saviour. The only fitting answer left is the one Thomas gave: my Lord and my God.

22.theology: Election and the free offer of the gospel. Many are called, but few are chosen holds two truths together. The invitation goes out to all without exception, a genuine offer to be preached without restriction, and God’s own choice secures who will come. The preacher does not know who the chosen are; he opens the doors as wide as the gospel goes and trusts God with the result.
22.examples:
Then: The leaders tried to trap Jesus on politics, doctrine and law. He answered all three from Scripture.

Now: His answers still hold. Give Caesar his coin, and give God yourself, since you bear his image. The resurrection rests on the faithful God of the covenant. Love God with everything, and your neighbour as yourself. And the Christ is David’s son and David’s Lord, truly God and truly man, the Saviour we need.

23.title: Woe to You, Scribes and Pharisees
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, <sup>2</sup>“The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat, <sup>3</sup>so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. <sup>4</sup>They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. <sup>5</sup>They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, <sup>6</sup>and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues <sup>7</sup>and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. <sup>8</sup>But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers. <sup>9</sup>And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. <sup>10</sup>Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ. <sup>11</sup>The greatest among you shall be your servant. <sup>12</sup>Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. <sup>13</sup>“But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. <sup>15</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. <sup>16</sup>“Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>17</sup>You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? <sup>18</sup>And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>19</sup>You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? <sup>20</sup>So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. <sup>21</sup>And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. <sup>22</sup>And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. <sup>23</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>24</sup>You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! <sup>25</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. <sup>26</sup>You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. <sup>27</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. <sup>28</sup>So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness. <sup>29</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, <sup>30</sup>saying, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.’ <sup>31</sup>Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. <sup>32</sup>Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. <sup>33</sup>You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? <sup>34</sup>Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town, <sup>35</sup>so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. <sup>36</sup>Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. <sup>37</sup>“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>38</sup>See, your house is left to you desolate. <sup>39</sup>For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”
23.overview:
Chapter 23 is Jesus’ last public sermon. He warns the crowds about the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 1–12), pronounces seven woes on them (vv. 13–36), and laments over Jerusalem (vv. 37–39). The woes are a diagnosis, not an outburst: religion that performs outside while the inside is unchanged, leaders who load burdens instead of shepherding, and teachers who stand in the doorway of the kingdom keeping others out.

The lament shows the heart behind the woes. Jesus pronounces judgment with the grief of a hen who would have gathered her chicks under her wings, and they would not come. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and he judges hardness that will not repent; within days, at the cross, both truths meet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Seven Woes: The Hypocrisy of Scribes and Pharisees (Part One)
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus turns from silencing his opponents to warning the crowds about them. He grants the office (Moses’ seat) before he indicts the men: burdens tied on others and not lifted with a finger, phylacteries widened and fringes lengthened to be seen, titles, seats and greetings craved. The disciples are all brothers under one Teacher and one Father. The first three woes follow: shutting the kingdom in people’s faces, making converts twice as much children of hell, and the system of binding and non-binding oaths.
verseByVerse.theology: The authority of a pulpit is borrowed. What is read from Moses’ seat binds the hearer whatever the reader’s life; when he steps off that seat, the conscience is free. So do and observe whatever they tell you is not a blank endorsement of teaching this same Gospel calls leaven (16:12). No disciple is to be called rabbi because there is one Teacher, the Christ. And the first woe heads all seven, because it describes men standing between other people and the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: The burdens were concrete: thirty-nine categories of forbidden Sabbath work, each subdivided. They were produced by serious people trying to be careful. Matthew uses the same noun for the heavy burdens here and for Christ’s light burden at 11:30. The phylacteries and fringes were commanded, and Jesus wore the fringes himself (9:20); the objection is to the width and the length, which lies in who is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The chapter exposes religion that is all outside and no inside: teaching without doing, burdens without help, display without love, careful rules that dodge God himself. But it is not the speech of an angry man. It is the grief of the Son of God, who longed to gather his people under his wings, and who walked out of that temple to die for sinners, Pharisees included.

The setting. Chapter 23 is given in the temple on the Tuesday of the last week. After it he will speak to the crowds only once more, a single sentence at his arrest (26:55). So this is his last public sermon, spoken days before he is killed by the men he is describing, and he spends it warning ordinary people about their religious leaders and then weeping over the city.

Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples. The audience is not who we assume. For the first twelve verses the scribes and Pharisees are talked about in the third person: he is warning the congregation about its clergy, in public, with the clergy listening. The seven woes that follow, in the harshest language he ever used, are spoken to the flock, about the shepherds, by someone who is about to die for both.

The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Moses’ seat was a real piece of furniture. Excavated synagogues at Chorazin and elsewhere have a stone chair at the front, facing the congregation. The phrase stands for the authority to teach and interpret the law of Moses, and the scribes and Pharisees were the recognised teachers who filled that place. The word sit may hint that they had taken the seat for themselves.

Conceding the seat. Jesus begins by granting it. Before a syllable of criticism he admits that what is read from that chair binds Israel. He separates the chair from the men in it.

Who were the scribes and Pharisees? The scribes were the professional scholars of the law, trained to copy, interpret and apply it; many of them were Pharisees. The Pharisees were a lay movement, a little over six thousand strong in Herod’s day according to Josephus, devoted to keeping the law with great precision, including a large body of oral tradition about how to keep it. They were the most respected religious people in the nation, not its villains. They were serious about Scripture, prayer, fasting, tithing and purity. That is exactly why this chapter is so searching. Jesus is not exposing the irreligious. He is exposing the very best religion can do without a new heart, which is why the warning reaches every church.

What it does not mean. Not that every scribe and Pharisee was a hypocrite. Nicodemus, Gamaliel and Paul came from among them. Nor is this chapter a licence for Christians to despise Jews. Its warnings apply above all to religious people today, including Christians and church leaders.

On a Tuesday. Read this chapter as a mirror, not a window. The question is not how bad the Pharisees were but where I am like them. One of the seven woes will probably sting more than the others, and that sting is not an enemy: it is the Shepherd putting his finger on the place he means to heal.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses’ seat” stands for the authority to teach the law; synagogues may have had a stone chair for the teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: "so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do and observe whatever they tell you. In so far as they teach the law of Moses faithfully, it should be obeyed.

Whatever? But there is a difficulty here that a careful reader will not get past. This is the same Gospel in which Jesus tells the disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and Matthew explains that he meant their teaching (16:12); the same Gospel in which their tradition is said to have made void the word of God (15:6); and in this very chapter he is about to call their teaching on oaths the reasoning of blind fools (vv. 16–22). So he cannot be handing them a blank endorsement, and it will not do to quietly insert the word correct into his sentence and move on.

The answer is in the seat. The clause just before it says they sit on Moses’ seat, and that seat is the point. The authority in the room is not theirs; it is Moses’, that is, the Scripture they are reading out. When they open the law and tell Israel what God has said, the people are bound, and the messenger’s hypocrisy does not release them, because the word is God’s and not his. When they leave that seat and start building fences and loopholes of their own, they have stepped off the only ground that gave them a claim on anyone’s conscience. Jesus is not commanding obedience to Pharisees. He is commanding obedience to Moses, even from the mouth of a Pharisee.

A borrowed authority. The authority of any pulpit is borrowed, every word of it. A congregation is bound to the word read to them, not to the man who reads it, which protects them both from the preacher whose life is worse than his sermon and from the one whose opinions have replaced it. Here, in seed, is the principle of Scripture alone: Scripture is the one rule that has authority over the conscience; pastors, councils and traditions are bound by it and are to be tested by it, as the Bereans tested even Paul by the Scriptures (Acts 17:11).

The greater Moses on the mountain. On the mountain Jesus sat and taught (5:1–2), and six times set the law beside his own word: but I say to you. No scribe ever spoke so. Moses had promised that God would raise up a prophet like him, and that Israel must listen to him (Deuteronomy 18:15). That prophet is the man in the temple courts. The scribes sit on Moses’ seat; the one who gave Moses his words is standing in front of them.

But not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. The heart of hypocrisy: saying without doing. Paul makes the same charge: you who teach others, do you not teach yourself (Romans 2:21–23)? Every man who stands up to explain God’s word stands under this indictment the moment his pulpit and his life diverge.

What if my pastor’s life does not match his preaching? Separate the two questions, as Jesus does. First, the word: if he preaches what Scripture says, it binds you, and his failures do not give you permission to ignore it. Do not let another man’s sin become your excuse. Second, the life: if the inconsistency is a serious and continuing sin, not merely an ordinary weakness you have noticed, it should be raised, privately and humbly first (Matthew 18:15), and if it continues, with the elders, because Scripture holds teachers to a stricter standard (1 Timothy 5:19–20; James 3:1). What you must not do is either of the easy things: swallow everything because of his position, or throw out the Bible because of his conduct.

For worship. There has been one Teacher whose sermon and life never diverged by a hair. He told us to love our enemies and prayed for the men driving in the nails. He is the Word made flesh, in whom saying and doing are one, and his perfect obedience is counted to those who have only ever preached better than they lived.

parallels.desc: you who teach others, do you not teach yourself?

verseByVerse.quote: "They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders. A load tied in a bundle and placed on a porter. The burdens were the many rules the Pharisees added to the law: Sabbath regulations, purity rules, tithing details (12:1–14; 15:1–9). Peter called such a load a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10).

Put some weight in the burden. The written law said: remember the Sabbath day and do no work. The oral tradition specified thirty-nine categories of prohibited labour, each subdivided: how far a man might walk, how much he might carry, whether a chair could be dragged across a floor, since dragging might scratch a furrow and furrowing is ploughing. Much of this was written down later, from about AD 200, but it grew from a tradition already at work in his time. None of it was invented by wicked men. It was produced by serious people trying to be careful, which is how such systems are always produced.

But they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. Two meanings, both true: they did not keep the rules themselves, finding loopholes, as with Corban (15:5), and they gave no help to those weighed down by them. The same tradition that generated the rules generated devices for living with them, such as declaring a courtyard a single household so that carrying within it was permitted. Men who knew the system could move within it. The ones crushed by it were the ones who only knew that they were failing.

Two burdens in one Gospel. Matthew uses the same noun twice. Twelve chapters earlier Jesus had said: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (11:28–30). Two teachers offering to load your shoulders. Christ’s yoke is real. But he carries it with you, and he has first carried the one load that would have crushed you.

We still build it. Every generation rebuilds some version of this, from real commands. God says pray; the tradition specifies the hour and the minimum. God says teach your children; the tradition produces a schooling decision that sorts the faithful from the rest. Not one addition is wicked in itself. Together they produce a Christian who is quietly certain he is behind and does not know where the line is.

The tell. Look at who is setting the standard. A man with a study, a quiet house and no shift work will describe an early-morning devotional discipline as the mark of a serious believer, and he has never once tried it with a newborn, two jobs and a bus at six. The man laying the burden on has never had to move it with his finger.

How can I tell God’s commands from human burdens? Ask where it is written. A true command of God can be shown from Scripture, read in its context, and it binds every Christian in every place. A human rule may be wise for a person or a family (a set time for prayer, a budget for giving), but it is a tool, not a law, and it must never be used to measure another believer’s faithfulness. Ask also whether the rule drives you to Christ or away from him. God’s law, rightly heard, shows us our need and then shapes a grateful life. Man-made burdens produce either pride in those who keep them or despair in those who cannot. The Westminster Confession says God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster 20.2; 1689 21.2).

On a Tuesday. Christ has carried your heaviest load; look around your church for the one most obviously struggling, the young mother, the man between jobs, the carer worn thin, and ask what you could carry for them this week with more than a finger.

parallels.desc: a yoke our fathers could not bear

verseByVerse.quote: "They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do all their deeds to be seen by others. Their religion was a performance, the charge of the Sermon on the Mount: beware of practising your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them (6:1). This chapter shows what happened to men who had been doing it for a lifetime.

For they make their phylacteries broad. Phylacteries were small leather boxes containing tiny scrolls of Scripture, strapped to the forehead and left arm during prayer, from a literal reading of God’s command to bind his words as a sign on your hand and as frontlets between your eyes (Deuteronomy 6:8). To make yours broad was to make it seen across a courtyard.

And their fringes long. The tassels on the corners of the outer garment, with a cord of blue, commanded by God to remind Israel of his commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). Jesus himself wore them: it was the fringe of his garment that the woman with the haemorrhage reached for in the crowd (9:20). He is not objecting to the tassel but to the length. When she touched it he turned, not to be admired, but so that she would hear him say, take heart, daughter (9:22). The Pharisees lengthened their fringes to be seen. The Son of God wore his for a sick woman to reach.

Nothing that could be forbidden. That is the awkward genius of this woe. You cannot legislate against a wide phylactery, because the phylactery is commanded and the width is a matter of taste. Everything visible here is defensible, and the whole of it is rotten, because of a motive no committee could assess.

And they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues. The same appetite with the religion stripped off: the couch nearest the host, from which everyone could read the rankings (Luke 14:7–11), and the bench at the front of the synagogue, facing the congregation, where you spend the service being looked at.

Who is watching. Take some part of your religious life that is genuinely good: a discipline, a habit of giving, a service you perform. Suppose nobody would ever find out about it. Whatever in it quietly deflates was the part being worn broad. Do one good thing this week that only your Father will know about. And when you find the broad phylactery in yourself, as every believer does, take it to the One who sought no glory from men, and whose hidden obedience is counted as yours.

But did Jesus not say, let your light shine before others? He did, and the two sayings fit exactly. Let your light shine so that people may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (5:16). Beware of practising your righteousness to be seen by them (6:1). The difference is not whether people see but whom the seeing is for. Light shines on the thing it illuminates; it does not draw attention to the lamp. So do good openly when love requires it (help the neighbour, speak of Christ, stand with the weak), and keep hidden what is between you and God (your private prayer, much of your giving, your fasting). And when you are noticed, pass the praise upward quickly.
verseByVerse.note: Phylacteries were small leather boxes holding verses of Scripture, strapped to the forehead and arm. Fringes were the tassels on a garment’s corners.

parallels.desc: bind them on your hand and between your eyes

verseByVerse.quote: "and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And greetings in the marketplaces. Harmless until you know the protocol: you rose when a teacher passed, greeted him first, used his title. It was a daily, public administering of status, and men came to need it the way they needed breakfast.

And being called rabbi by others. Rabbi means, literally, my great one.

But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher. The reason he gives is not the one we would give. He does not say titles are worldly; he says you have one teacher, and two verses later names him, the Christ. The position of Teacher is filled, permanently, by the man saying so. Every Christian teacher is a student of the one Teacher, with no independent authority.

And you are all brothers. If there is one Teacher, the only relation left among the learners is brotherhood. Not equality of gift or of office: Matthew’s Gospel ends with commissioned apostles, and the New Testament has elders and overseers with real authority. But equality of standing. The senior man and the newest convert are at the same distance from the chair.

The appetite survives the noun. This is not a rule about vocabulary: the New Testament names teachers and elders (Ephesians 4:11), and Paul calls himself a teacher (1 Timothy 2:7). What is forbidden is the appetite, and the appetite survives the abolition of the noun perfectly well. Congregations proud of having no titles can develop an informal pecking order that is written down nowhere and harder to challenge than a formal one. A hierarchy you can name can be questioned. The other kind just is.

The real test. The question is not what people call you, but what happens inside when the deference does not arrive: when the newcomer does not know who you are, when your opinion is passed over, when somebody less experienced is asked instead. The Pharisees’ problem was that by now they could not have done without it. The respect of other people had taken the place that belongs to God’s verdict. The gospel breaks it from the inside, because the one whose verdict matters most has already spoken it over every believer, no condemnation (Romans 8:1), and a man already accepted by God in Christ no longer has to collect his worth in the marketplace.

If we are all brothers, does anyone have authority in the church? Yes. Brotherhood describes our standing before God, not the absence of order. Christ gives elders to shepherd his flock, and Scripture tells the church to respect and follow them (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13; Hebrews 13:17). But their authority is a servant’s authority, exercised under the word and for the good of the flock, never for their own honour (1 Peter 5:1–4). An elder is a brother with a task, not a superior with a title. And the newest believer has the same Father, the same Saviour and the same access to the throne of grace as the most senior man in the room.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabbi” means “my great one,” a title of respect for a teacher.

parallels.desc: not many of you should become teachers

verseByVerse.quote: "And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And call no man your father on earth. Father was used of revered teachers, the fathers of tradition. Jesus forbids giving any human being the spiritual authority that belongs only to God.

For you have one Father, who is in heaven. God alone is our Father in the ultimate sense (6:9), and the prohibition protects a relationship. In Matthew your Father knows what you need before you ask and sees in secret (6:6, 8), and every such sentence would be weakened if there were an intermediate father standing in the room. The command is jealous on the reader’s behalf.

Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ. The word for instructor occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: the guide who goes ahead and shows the way. Jesus uses it only here, of himself, and so claims an authority equal to the Father’s.

Handling it honestly. This verse is often thrown across the table between Protestants and Roman Catholics, so handle it with care. It cannot be a flat ban on the word, since Jesus himself honoured father and mother (15:4), or Scripture would contradict itself. Paul says he became the Corinthians’ father in Christ Jesus through the gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15), and Stephen addresses the Sanhedrin as fathers (Acts 7:2). So the Bible plainly permits both the natural word and the affectionate sense of a spiritual mentor. What Jesus forbids is giving a man the place that belongs to God alone, as though a human being were the source of one’s spiritual life or the required channel of grace. So the real question is not the word a Catholic uses for his priest but whether any man is treated as the indispensable go-between for the soul and God. There Scripture is jealous: the only go-between it allows is the man who said these words, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:5–6). The Reformers pressed this point against the claims then made for the papacy, and many Catholic believers today would themselves say that only Christ saves.

Protestants should not feel comfortable. The thing forbidden arrives just as easily without a title. It is the pastor whose approval has quietly become the measure of whether you are acceptable. The mentor whose opinion functions as your conscience, so that you cannot tell whether you believe something or he does. The teacher, dead or living, or heard weekly through headphones, whom you cannot disagree with. None of those men is called father. Every one of them can end up sitting in the chair.

The test. It is not what you call anyone. It is what happens when the man you respect most is wrong. If you can see it, say it, and go on loving him, he is a brother and a teacher. If the possibility cannot be entertained, then whatever his title, the seat is occupied.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?
one God, the Father, and one Lord

verseByVerse.quote: "The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest among you shall be your servant. As in 20:26–28, true greatness is service, the shape of the gospel itself: the Son of God humbled himself to a servant’s death and was exalted to the name above every name (Philippians 2:5–11).

Whoever exalts himself will be humbled. God brings down the proud (Proverbs 3:34; Luke 1:51–52). Self-exaltation ends in humiliation, if not now, then at the judgment.

And whoever humbles himself will be exalted. The passive means by God (James 4:10): the man who takes the lowest place will be raised, and the man who takes the highest will find it was never his to take.

In the flow. Verse 12 states the principle over the first half of the chapter, God reverses human rankings, and is the bridge into the seven woes. It also states in a single sentence the path of Jesus himself, who will be humbled to the cross within days and given all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18).

The trap in this verse. This is the verse where a reader falls into the chapter’s trap. After portrait after portrait of religious pride, you may feel rather pleased at having recognised them. That is the whole difficulty with humility: it is the one virtue that evaporates the moment you notice you have it. You succeed, you observe your success, and the success is gone.

A position, not a mood. Jesus does not command a feeling here. He states how God deals with people, and in the verse before gives the mechanism: the greatest among you shall be your servant. Humility is not a mood to be worked up. It is a position to be taken, and positions can be taken on days when the mood is entirely absent. You cannot decide to feel small. You can do the job nobody wants and not mention it; let someone else be right about something that does not matter; take the seat further down; ask a question instead of delivering a verdict. The inner state tends to arrive later, quietly, by the back door, as the Spirit’s work in people who stopped monitoring for it.

Thinking of yourself less. Most self-examination about humility is simply pride holding a mirror. The deeper cure is not thinking less of yourself but thinking about yourself less, which happens only when something better has your attention. Look where this chapter finally goes: not to a call for us to be humbler, but to a man standing over a city that is about to kill him, saying how often would I have gathered your children (v. 37). Spend long enough looking at that, and the arithmetic of who ranks where in the room stops being interesting.

What it does not mean. Not that we should humble ourselves as a strategy to get exalted. The promise does not say that humility earns exaltation, which would make it one more way of climbing. It says God does the lifting, and he has never once been fooled about which of the two he is looking at.

Is it wrong to want to lead, or to want a promotion? No, not in itself. Paul says that if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task (1 Timothy 3:1), and doing your work well, even rising in it, can glorify God. The question is what the position is for. If you want it so that you can serve more people, carry more weight and use your gifts for others, that desire can be holy. If you want it so that people will look up to you, or because you cannot bear someone else having it, that is the Pharisee’s appetite. A useful check: would you be content to serve faithfully if the promotion never came? And when it does come, do you treat those under you as brothers?

For worship. The highest took the lowest place, all the way down: from the Father’s side to a manger, a basin and a towel, a cross and a borrowed grave. No one has ever gone as low as he went, and no one has ever been lifted as high. Every lifting of the lowly is a preview of the day when the universe bows to the Servant who would not exalt himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! The first of seven woes, the opposite of blessed: the seven woes may deliberately answer the Beatitudes (5:3–12).

In the flow. At verse 13 Jesus turns from speaking about the scribes and Pharisees to speaking to them, and does not stop until he has named seven woes and the blood of every martyr (vv. 13–36).

Woe is not a curse. A woe is the sound a person makes over a disaster: the prophets’ cry, closer to alas than to damn you. Isaiah stacked six of them and then turned the seventh on himself: woe is me, for I am lost (Isaiah 5:8–22; 6:5). If you read these seven as a man losing his temper, you will not be able to account for verse 37, where the same voice breaks.

Hypocrites. In ordinary Greek the word meant an actor, speaking through a mask. That is the whole charge: there was a face and there was a man behind it, and the two were not the same.

For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. The first woe is the head of all seven: a doorway with men standing in it, the very men who held the key of knowledge (Luke 11:52). The men appointed to open the door had positioned themselves in the gap. By rejecting Jesus and teaching a religion of human merit, they slammed it shut.

Those who would enter. The last clause is heartbreaking: you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. People were trying, and the professionals stood in the way (John 9:22). That is why this woe comes first and is the worst. The others describe men damaging themselves. This one describes men damaging somebody else’s only hope.

The Door a few yards away. The men in the doorway were blocking the way to someone standing within earshot. Jesus had called himself the door of the sheep, through whom anyone who enters will be saved (John 10:7–9). He is not guarding a door jealously; he is the door, standing in the temple courts wide open in his own person, and the scribes were between the people and him.

Can anyone really keep out a person God has chosen? No, not in the end. Jesus says all that the Father gives me will come to me (John 6:37), and no false teacher can snatch his sheep from his hand (John 10:28–29). God’s purpose cannot be defeated. But that does not make the false teacher innocent. Scripture holds both together: God is sovereign, and men are fully responsible for the harm they do (Acts 2:23). The scribes really did stand in the doorway, and many really were hindered, and they will answer for it. So a church cannot excuse its coldness by saying God will save his own anyway. God saves his own through faithful witnesses, and he calls us to be the open door and never the obstacle.

On a Tuesday. Picture a stranger walking into your church next Sunday with a broken life and no church background. What would he have to get past before he heard that Christ receives sinners?
verseByVerse.note: A woe is a solemn lament and warning of judgment, used by the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 14: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows’ houses and for a pretence you make long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater condemnation. It is missing in the earliest manuscripts and was probably copied from Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. This commentary’s view: not original in Matthew, though Jesus did say it.

Why the verse is missing. The sentence is absent from the oldest and best copies of Matthew, including the two great fourth-century manuscripts, and later copies put it in two different places, before verse 13 or after: a classic sign of an insertion, here by a copyist who knew Mark and Luke. So the words are the Lord’s, and their home is Mark and Luke. Nothing is lost.

Widows’ houses. The charge probably names a real abuse: religious men acting as trustees of widows’ estates, taking fees, and covered by a reputation for lengthy prayer. The long prayers were not a distraction from the fees; they were the security on which the fees depended.

Does a missing verse mean the Bible has errors? No. What God inspired is what the apostles and evangelists wrote, and the thousands of manuscripts we possess let us see, with remarkable clarity, where later copyists added something. Verse 14 is not a hidden truth that was lost but an addition that has been found out, and its words are kept safely in Mark and Luke where they belong. No doctrine of the faith depends on a disputed reading. The care with which these few places are marked in your Bible is a sign of honesty, not weakness, and of God’s providence in preserving his word through the centuries (Westminster Confession 1.8; 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.8).

For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte. A proselyte was a Gentile who converted fully to Judaism, through circumcision, ritual washing and sacrifice. This is not sarcasm about effort: the effort was genuine.

And when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. The most disturbing sentence in the chapter. Child of hell means someone who belongs to hell. Not as bad. Twice as bad. The man who has crossed over has staked something on it, and holds the position with a fierceness the people born into it never needed. Zeal passed on without truth does not arrive diluted. It arrives concentrated.

Converted to a Person. The difference between a proselyte and a disciple is who the convert is brought to. The Pharisee brought a Gentile to a system and left him alone with it, so that he could only prove himself by keeping it harder. Jesus calls people to himself: follow me, come to me (11:28). A tax collector, a Canaanite mother, a centurion: none was handed a programme. A convert to a system has to hold the system up. A convert to Christ is held by him.

What it does not mean. Not that zeal for converts is wrong: the Lord who spoke this woe gave the Great Commission (28:19). The question he raises is not whether to go, but what people find when we arrive.

How do I know I am pointing people to Christ and not to my tribe? Listen to what you talk about most. If the conversations keep coming back to your church’s distinctives, your favourite teacher, your politics or your style of worship, you may be making proselytes. If they keep coming back to who Jesus is, what he has done, and how a sinner can be forgiven, you are making disciples. Watch the fruit as well. A person converted to Christ grows in humility, love and dependence on grace. A person converted to a party grows in certainty about other people’s errors. Secondary convictions matter, and we should teach them; but they are the furniture of the house, and Christ is the door.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 14, a woe about devouring widows’ houses and long prayers for a pretence. A proselyte was a Gentile convert to Judaism.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, blind guides, who say, 'If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.' You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, blind guides. The third woe. A blind guide leads those behind him into the pit (15:14).

Who say, If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing. Nothing means it is not binding (see 5:33–37). An oath by the temple could be broken; an oath by the temple’s gold was binding.

But if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath. The system sounds absurd until you see what it was for: a man could invoke the sanctuary of God, satisfy the person he was dealing with, and walk away bound to nothing. Legalised lying, practised by the scrupulous. Nobody has lied, and somebody has been robbed.

You blind fools! Morally foolish: people who reject God’s wisdom.

Has he broken his own command? Most readers trip over this. In this same Gospel Jesus said that whoever says You fool! will be liable to the hell of fire (5:22). No, and the reasons matter. What 5:22 forbids is contemptuous anger against a brother: the word thrown in a quarrel to dismiss another human being as worthless. That is not what is happening here. This is a judicial pronouncement by the one appointed to judge, delivered publicly about men holding public office, and it is a statement of fact rather than an insult: they were teaching, and they could not see. And the biblical fool is not a man of low intelligence. From the Psalms onward he is a moral category, the man who has arranged his thinking so as not to have to reckon with God: the fool says in his heart, There is no God (Psalm 14:1). These men were formidably clever. That is precisely what made them blind.

For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? The argument is one sentence long. The gold was holy only because it belonged to the temple, God’s house; it was ordinary metal until it was brought inside, and the temple did not derive its holiness from the gold. They had the logic exactly upside down, valuing the gold more than the God it was dedicated to. Once the question is asked the system collapses, which is why he asks it rather than arguing.

The one oath he kept to the death. Two days later the high priest put Jesus under oath: I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God (26:63). Jesus answered plainly, you have said so (26:64), and that plain yes condemned him. The one man in Jerusalem who never needed an oath to make his word binding told the truth under oath, knowing it would kill him, and his yes was the beginning of our salvation.

May a Christian swear an oath in court or make marriage vows? Yes. Jesus is exposing the evasions of those who used oaths to deceive, not forbidding every solemn oath. God himself swears (Hebrews 6:13–17), Paul calls God to witness (2 Corinthians 1:23), and Jesus answered under oath before the high priest (26:63–64). Some Christians, especially in the Anabaptist tradition, refuse all oaths on the basis of 5:34. The more likely reading is that lawful oaths and vows are permitted; what is forbidden is casual or evasive swearing (Westminster Confession 22.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 23.2).

Not a vocabulary to borrow. Jesus can say this because he reads hearts and will judge them; we cannot and will not. The right use of a verse like this is to examine our own words, not to acquire vocabulary for our opponents.
verseByVerse.note: These rules let a man decide which of his oaths were binding.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you say, 'If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.' You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you say, If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing. The same evasion again: not one odd ruling but a settled habit of mind.

But if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath. You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? The altar made the gift holy (Exodus 29:37). Again, they valued the lesser thing above the greater.

The measurable and the meaningful. Now the pattern can be named: gold over the temple, the gift over the altar. In each pair the thing they took seriously is the thing that can be weighed, counted, valued and carried; the thing they treated as nothing is the thing that gives it meaning and cannot be measured at all. Gold has a market price; a sanctuary does not.

The key to all seven. That logic accounts for the rest of the woes. Tithed dill can be measured, so it received meticulous attention; justice and mercy and faithfulness cannot, so they were neglected (v. 23). The outside of a cup can be inspected; greed cannot (v. 25). A phylactery’s width is a fact; the motive behind it is not (v. 5). Give a religious man a system and he will drift, without noticing, toward the parts that can be assessed, because those are the parts at which he can succeed and be seen to succeed.

Still a live danger. Attendance can be counted; love for the people attending cannot. Doctrinal precision can be examined line by line; whether a man is kind to his wife at nine on a Tuesday night cannot. The countable offers the one thing the proud heart wants, which is a score.

The altar that makes us acceptable. The principle did not stop at the temple. We have an altar (Hebrews 13:10): Christ, who suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (13:12). A Christian’s worship, money and service are acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5), laid on him. God does not weigh a believer’s gift to decide whether it is worthy. He receives it because the giver belongs to Christ, whose sacrifice has already made the giver acceptable (Ephesians 1:6), which is why a widow’s two small coins could be worth more to him than a rich man’s thousands (Mark 12:41–44). The Pharisees made the gift the important thing. The gospel makes the gift holy by what it is laid upon.

So should I stop keeping track of my Bible reading or giving? Not necessarily. Measuring can be a servant: a reading plan helps many people get through Scripture, and a budget helps us give faithfully. The danger is when the measure becomes the master, when the ticked box replaces the meeting with God, or the number on the giving statement replaces love for the poor. Keep the tools if they help, but every so often ask the questions no chart can answer. Has my reading made me love Christ more? Has my giving made me more generous in spirit? Am I kinder at home? Those are the altar; the rest is the gift.

parallels.desc: whatever touches the altar shall become holy

verseByVerse.quote: "So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. You cannot separate the altar from its gifts.

And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. God himself dwells in the temple (1 Kings 8:13; Psalm 26:8), so every oath by the temple is an oath by God. The Pharisaic system depended on being able to reach for the sacred and leave God out of it, and Jesus’ answer is that there is no such transaction available anywhere in creation.

Holy things at arm’s length. A great deal of religion consists of handling holy things at arm’s length from the one who made them holy: going through a liturgy without addressing anyone, treating a building as sacred while its Lord is not consulted, valuing the Bible as an object and not reading it, taking the bread and the cup as a custom. In each case the Person is edited out, and the editing does not work. What is holy is holy because of somebody, and touching it touches him.

Something greater than the temple. Jesus had said, something greater than the temple is here (12:6): the God who filled Solomon’s house had come in flesh and was walking its courts. So the men who swore by the temple and meant nothing by it were doing so within sight of the Resident himself, treating his name as small change.

The Sermon from the other side. The Sermon on the Mount already said: do not take an oath at all, either by heaven or by the earth or by your head, but let what you say be simply Yes or No (5:34–37). If every oath invokes God, then the whole apparatus of graded oaths is not merely dishonest, it is unnecessary, because a Christian who understands that every word he speaks is spoken in God’s hearing has no use for a device that makes some of his words more binding than others.

parallels.desc: a place for you to dwell in forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. Heaven is God’s throne (5:34; Isaiah 66:1). Every oath is sworn in his hearing whether or not his name is used.

No neutral ground. Many of us live as if words spoken in church carry a weight that words spoken in the car do not, with two registers: statements made carefully where it matters, and the promise to a child or the assurance given to end a conversation, never meant to be held to. These men built that distinction into a system, and it does not exist. There is no hour of the week in which we speak merely to other people.

Oppressive or liberating? That sounds oppressive and is meant to be liberating, and the difference lies in who is on the throne. If the constant hearer were an inspector, the doctrine would be unbearable. Jesus has spent this chapter describing men for whom God had become exactly that, an auditor to be satisfied and, where possible, out-manoeuvred, and their religion had rotted under the weight of it. But the One who hears everything is the Father who feeds the birds and numbers the hairs of your head (6:26; 10:30), and who is described three times in the Sermon as the one who sees in secret and rewards (6:4, 6, 18). The same total attention that makes hypocrisy impossible makes hiddenness safe.

The Son at the right hand of the throne. The throne is not an inspector’s desk: the risen Jesus is seated at its right hand (Hebrews 8:1), interceding for us (Romans 8:34). The Judge who hears every word has at his right hand the Saviour who bore every false word his people ever spoke. For them, the throne that hears everything is the throne where their Advocate is seated.

The respectable lies. The fruit of this teaching is plainer speech, and the alternatives are worth naming because they are so respectable. The sentence that is accurate and designed to mislead. The commitment worded loosely enough to be escaped later. The silence held while somebody forms a false impression you could correct in four words. The technically true answer to a question you knew was really asking something else. Not one of those is a lie by the rules, and every one of them is an oath sworn by the gold rather than by the temple.

Is it wrong to say I swear or honestly in ordinary speech? Saying I swear to it, or swearing on your mother’s life, to make a casual statement sound more convincing is exactly the habit Jesus forbids, because it implies your ordinary words are less reliable. Words like honestly or to be frank are not oaths, but notice why you reach for them. If people need a signal that this time you mean it, something has gone wrong with the rest of the time. The goal is to be the kind of person whose plain word is enough. And of course using God’s name lightly as an exclamation breaks the third commandment and should go altogether.

The cure. Simple and hard: let your yes be yes (5:37). Say what you mean and do it; if you cannot, decline. And when you catch yourself in the sentence that was technically true and meant to mislead, go back and correct it, before the throne where your Advocate sits.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — Seven Woes Concluded and the Lament over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last four woes move from the outside inward: herbs tithed while justice, mercy and faithfulness are neglected; a cup scoured outside and full of plunder within; whitewashed tombs; and monuments built to murdered prophets by men arranging a murder. Then the blood of the righteous from Abel to Zechariah is laid on that generation. Then the voice breaks over Jerusalem, the hen and her brood, and you were not willing. The chapter ends not on desolation but on one word: until.
verseByVerse.theology: Woe and lament belong together. A woe is the prophets’ cry of grief, not a curse, and it is aimed with precision: not at sinners, for no harsh word in this Gospel falls on a tax collector or a dying thief, but at men shutting the door on them. The remedy is the clause for anyone who reads the seven and wants out: first clean the inside of the cup, that the outside also may be clean. That order is the difference between the gospel and moralism, and no one can do it for himself, which is why the honest prayer is David’s: create in me a clean heart (Psalm 51:10).
