The measure of verse 32 explains God’s patience (judgment waited four hundred years for the Amorites, Genesis 15:16) without promising that the delay is permanent.
verseByVerse.examples: The gnat and the camel is a joke: wine was strained to catch unclean insects, and the camel was the largest unclean animal. The whitewashed tombs were marked before Passover as a warning, since touching a grave barred a pilgrim from the feast (Numbers 19:16). And if we had lived in the days of our fathers is an easy sentence to say, because the sins of a past age are labelled and ours still look like normal life. The seven in their modern forms, and whether we may speak as Jesus does here, are set out at verses 33–34.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you tithe mint and dill and cumin. The fourth woe. The law required a tenth of grain, wine and oil (Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 14:22–23). The Pharisees extended it to the smallest garden herbs.

Start with what is praised. Tithing herbs was not the sin. Whether kitchen herbs fell under the requirement was disputed, and these men tithed them in case. That is scruple, not hypocrisy, and Jesus does not withdraw it: these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. He is not asking for less carefulness about small things. He is asking why the carefulness stopped where it did.

And have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. Justice is fairness, especially to the poor and powerless; mercy is compassion; faithfulness is loyalty to God and others. The prophets summed up God’s requirements this way: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8). It is a particular kind of failure: not a collapse into obvious wickedness, but a religion that had become entirely accurate about everything that could be checked and had quietly dropped everything else.

These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. They should have done both, but the weightier matters come first.

You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! A comic picture. Wine was strained because insects were unclean (Leviticus 11:20–23); the gnat was the smallest unclean creature and the camel the largest (Leviticus 11:4). A man filters his cup with great care to catch anything the size of a pinhead, and then swallows a camel whole. In Aramaic the two words may chime.

The two lists. Make two lists: what you are meticulous about in your Christian life, and what you have made a settled peace with failing at. Read them against the three words in this verse. Justice: whether the people who depend on you are dealt with fairly. Mercy: whether anyone gets a second chance from you. Faithfulness: whether you can be relied on when it costs. If those three keep turning up on the second list, this woe has your name on it. But Christ kept both columns for you, and his mercy covers what you neglected; the next woe names the cure, an inside that he himself makes clean (v. 26). Then choose one thing from the weightier column to act on before Sunday: a debt to pay, a wrong to put right, a person to forgive.

The weightier matters in person. Twice Jesus quoted Hosea against the Pharisees, I desire mercy (9:13; 12:7), and Matthew applied Isaiah to him: he will not break a bruised reed, until he brings justice to victory (12:18–20). Justice that does not crush the weak, mercy that eats with sinners, faithfulness that goes to the cross rather than break his Father’s word: what the Pharisees neglected, Jesus is. The weightier matters are a portrait, and the face in it is his.

Should Christians tithe? Jesus was speaking to Jews still under the law, before the cross, so this verse does not bind Christians to the tenth. The New Testament calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8–9), and many Christians find the tenth a useful starting point rather than a law. What Jesus says applies to everyone: careful giving is good, but it must go together with justice, mercy and faithfulness.

Is caring about sound doctrine a gnat? No. Truth about God is never small, and Jesus himself is about to teach his disciples with great precision. The gnat is not doctrine but the trivial added to doctrine, and the camel is not doctrine either but the hard-heartedness that can sit alongside it. A man can be exact about the Trinity and cruel to his wife, precise about justification and dishonest with his employer. The cure is not to care less about truth but to let truth do its work, because the doctrines of grace (the Reformed teaching that salvation is God’s free gift from first to last), rightly held, produce justice, mercy and faithfulness. If your theology is making you harder rather than kinder, it is not the theology that is wrong but the way you are holding it.

Why a woe and not advice? The reason it is a woe is worth noting. A man in this condition is not miserable. He is doing well by his own measurements and has the receipts. That is why somebody had to say it out loud to him. And underneath the drift toward the measurable lies a deeper motive: what can be counted lets a man keep score with God, and keeping score is a way of saving yourself. Grace ends the scorekeeping, because Christ has already paid in full what we owe.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to kitchen herbs. Both gnats and camels were unclean; wine was strained through cloth to remove insects.

parallels.desc: a tithe of the seed of the land
do justice, love kindness, walk humbly

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate. The fifth woe. The schools disputed whether a vessel’s outside could be clean while its inside was unclean (Mark 7:4). He answers by applying it to the men holding the cups.

But inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. Greed here is the word for plunder; self-indulgence is appetite with nothing holding it. The widows’ houses were in there (Mark 12:40).

You blind Pharisee! The singular addresses each one personally: first clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. This is the sentence for anybody who reads the woes and wants out. It has an order and a promise: inside first, which no religion of performance can manage, and the outside follows. Moralism scrubs the exterior and hopes something happens within. Christ starts at the centre, and the surface follows.

How does a man clean his own inside? He cannot, and that is not a discouragement but the doorway. Only God can cleanse the heart (Psalm 51:10; Ezekiel 36:25–26). It is the thing David asked for after his sin with Bathsheba, when the outside had been managed for months and the inside was rotten: behold, you delight in truth in the inward being; create in me a clean heart, O God (Psalm 51:6, 10). He does not offer to do it. He asks. The one thing needed is the one thing that has to be given, and the men in this chapter never asked because they never believed the inside was the problem. God promises it: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean; a new heart I will give you (Ezekiel 36:25–26). He does it in regeneration, once for all, and goes on doing it in sanctification, as we confess our sins and he cleanses us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Regeneration is the new birth, the moment the Spirit gives a dead heart life (John 3:5–8); sanctification is his patient work, all life long, of making that new heart more and more like Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Should I stop doing good things until my heart is right? No. Jesus is not telling hypocrites to stop praying or giving; he is telling them to bring their hearts to God. If you wait to obey until your motives are pure, you will wait for ever, because no believer’s motives are perfectly pure this side of glory. Keep doing what God commands, and at the same time bring the inside to him honestly: confess the mixed motives, ask him to change what you cannot, and trust that he accepts your imperfect works for Christ’s sake (Westminster Confession 16.6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.6). The difference between a struggling believer and a hypocrite is not that one has a clean cup. It is that one knows the inside is dirty and keeps bringing it to be washed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness. So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you are like whitewashed tombs. The sixth woe. Tombs were whitewashed each spring before Passover as a warning: touching one made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16) and barred him from the feast. At this very time they would have been gleaming in the sun.

Which outwardly appear beautiful. The irony: a thing painted to say danger was the most striking object in the landscape.

But within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. A tomb is contagious: touch it and you cannot go to the feast. So the charge is not only that their outsides and insides did not match, but that contact with them and their teaching left people unfit for the presence of God. The safest-looking men in the city were the ones you could not afford to touch.

So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness. Hypocrisy we expect by now. Lawlessness we do not: for all their law-keeping, underneath the performance there was no keeping of it at all. And Matthew has used that word before, in a sobering paragraph of the Sermon on the Mount, spoken to men who had prophesied and cast out demons in his name: I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness (7:23). The same noun. It is possible to have a ministry and be described by that word.

The one whose touch makes clean. Touch these men and you were made unclean. Jesus reached out and touched a leper, and the leprosy left him (8:3). He took a dead girl by the hand, and she rose (9:25). A woman unclean for twelve years touched the fringe of his garment and was healed (9:20–22). His holiness is stronger than our corruption. The whitewashed tomb spreads death to anyone who comes near. He spreads life.

Not a rare condition. What Jesus describes here is not peculiar to first-century Judaism. It is the natural state of the human heart wherever religion is available and regeneration is not. These men are not uniquely wicked; they are uniquely exposed. Their hearts were unchanged, which is the condition of every heart, religious or not, until God makes it new (Jeremiah 17:9). The moralist and the sceptic need the same thing, and the same Christ offers it to both.

How can I tell whether I am a whitewashed tomb? Ask what you do with what is inside. The hypocrite hides his sin from God and from himself and works on his appearance; the believer brings his sin into the light, confesses it and hates it, even while he still struggles with it (1 John 1:7–9; Psalm 32:3–5). A tender conscience that grieves over hidden sin is a mark of life, not death; tombs feel nothing. If this verse frightens you, that fear is itself a sign that the Spirit is at work. Do not try to prove you are clean. Go to Christ as one who needs cleansing, because he did not come for the healthy but for the sick, and no one who comes to him is cast out.

On a Tuesday. Hiddenness is what keeps a tomb a tomb, and light is where the cleaning starts: tell one trusted believer the truth about the part of you nobody sees.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were whitewashed so that passers-by would not touch them by accident and become unclean.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, saying, 'If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous. The seventh woe, and perhaps the most searching, because on the surface it is admirable: building monuments to the prophets was a fashion (Herod built one at David’s tomb). Nobody watching would have called it sin.

Saying, If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets. That sentence is the woe. They meant it, and it is self-deception in its purest form, because the men saying it were at that moment arranging the death of the greatest prophet who ever came, and the arrangement did not feel to them like killing a prophet. It felt like protecting the nation from a dangerous Galilean (John 11:47–50). It is easy to honour prophets who are safely dead.

Why the past is always clearer. A previous generation’s sins have been sorted, labelled and agreed upon; ours are still disguised as common sense.

The cheapest currency there is. It is easy to be sure we would have hidden Jews in 1942 or spoken up when others stayed quiet. The certainty costs nothing: the people who did not were ordinary churchgoers to whom the wrong was not apparent. The only evidence of what you would have done then is what you are doing now about the things your own age finds it convenient not to see.

Last of all, the Son. The men building the tombs were days from killing the one to whom every prophet had pointed. Last of all he sent his son (21:37). The woe is not only that they would repeat their fathers’ sin. It is that they would carry it to its summit, against the Word himself, while decorating the graves of the men who had announced him.

What then should I do with this woe? Not admire its aim. Ask what living correction you are currently resisting: whose voice, in your church or your family, you have quietly filed under difficult, unbalanced, or not to be taken too seriously. It is always easier to build a monument to a dead prophet than to listen to a live one, and it has the additional advantage of being extremely good for your reputation. That does not mean every critic is a prophet. Test what is said by Scripture. But if the Bible agrees with the uncomfortable voice, the discomfort is yours to deal with, not his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. He takes the sentence they were proud of and turns it over. By calling the murderers our fathers, they admitted descent, and in Hebrew thought a son shares his father’s character.

Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. Irony and judgment at once. Their ancestors had filled the cup of guilt partly; they would fill it to the brim by killing Jesus. Sin accumulates until judgment falls (Genesis 15:16; 1 Thessalonians 2:16).

Not a command to sin. Nor is it mere sarcasm. It belongs to a form of speech Scripture uses when God addresses the settled and determined, the moment at which he stops arguing and says, in effect, proceed. It is the voice of let the evildoer still do evil (Revelation 22:11). Few things are more frightening than God ceasing to restrain a man. He is not being given permission. He is being given over (Romans 1:24). But being given over looks like no longer caring; a believer who hates his sin and keeps fighting it, however often he falls, is showing the opposite, for that fight is the Spirit’s work in him (Galatians 5:17).

The measure. God told Abraham that his descendants would not possess Canaan for four hundred years, because the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Genesis 15:16). That is the patience of God: not indifference, but a delay with a limit built into it. The time was real, and so was the cup.

For the impatient and the afraid. To the person who concludes from the delay that nothing is ever going to be said: the measure explains the silence, and it does not promise that the silence is permanent. To the person frightened by the severity of it: notice that the delay was four hundred years long, and that the same chapter which announces the cup full ends a few verses later with a man weeping over the city.

Does God make people sin when he says fill up? No. God is never the author of sin, and no one can blame him for his own wickedness (James 1:13; Westminster Confession 3.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1). These men had already chosen their path and were already plotting his death (26:3–4). When God gives people over, he withdraws restraint and lets them go where their hearts are already set. The sin is wholly theirs. Yet God remains sovereign even over that sin, so that the worst thing men ever did, killing his Son, was the very means he had planned to save the world (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). That is the deepest comfort in the darkest sentence.

He stayed. He is standing in front of the men who will kill him, describing it days in advance, and then going up the hill anyway. Nobody took his life from him; he laid it down of his own accord (John 10:18). He knew the measure was full, and he stayed.

For worship. The cup they filled, he drank. In Gethsemane he asked if it might pass, and then took it. My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done (26:42). The patience that waited centuries for the Amorites was the same patience that waited for us, and at the end of it was not our judgment but his cross.

parallels.desc: which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?

verseByVerse.quote: "You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You serpents, you brood of vipers. John’s words (3:7), and Jesus’ before (12:34). Children of the serpent, the devil (John 8:44).

How are you to escape being sentenced to hell? Hell is Gehenna (5:22), named after the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children had once been burned as sacrifices (Jeremiah 7:31), and which the prophets turned into a picture of God’s judgment (Jeremiah 7:32). The often-repeated idea that it was the city’s burning rubbish dump comes from a medieval writer and is doubtful. It is not exaggeration but judicial reality. If they continue to reject him, they cannot escape judgment.

Is this the same Jesus? Many readers reach this verse and flinch. You serpents, from the man who said love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, turn the other cheek; who called himself gentle and lowly in heart (5:39, 44; 11:29). Is this the same person? And may I speak like this? Both questions deserve an answer, because the chapter is unreadable without one.

The pattern of his severity. His severity is not random. Look, across the Gospels, at who never gets spoken to this way: the sinful woman at the Pharisee’s house, the tax collector up a tree, the woman taken in adultery, the thief dying beside him, Peter after he denied him three times. Not one harsh word to any of them. (The story of the woman taken in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is missing from the earliest manuscripts, so many modern Bibles bracket it, though many believe it records a true event.) Now look at who does, and at the first woe: you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces (v. 13). The ferocity is not aimed at sinners; it is aimed at men who stand in the doorway keeping sinners out. He is tender with the broken and terrible toward the proud who break them: the same love facing two directions. A father who spoke gently to the man harming his children would not be gentle; he would be indifferent.

The warning and the wings. Four verses on, the voice breaks over Jerusalem (v. 37). Nobody weeps over people he wants destroyed. The woes are the hen’s sharp cry when the hawk is overhead; the lament is the same hen with her wings spread. Both are the same care; only one of them is comfortable to hear.

May I speak like this? No, and a guard is needed here. This does not license us to talk this way about religious people we have judged to be hypocrites. Every word here is spoken by the one who can read a heart and who will judge it, and this book has already told us plainly to take the log out of our own eye first (7:1–5). We do not have his sight, and we are not appointed to his bench. What we may do is what these woes were given to us for: read them as a mirror before we ever read them as a weapon, and ask, quietly, which of the seven is describing me.

The seven today. In today’s forms: shutting the door (v. 13) is making entry to Christ harder than he made it, with vocabulary and politics quietly added to repentance and faith. The proselyte (v. 15) is a convert to a tribe rather than to a Saviour. Splitting oaths (vv. 16–22) is technically true speech that misleads.

The seven today, continued. Gnats and camels (vv. 23–24) is being exact about doctrine and careless with people. The outside of the cup (vv. 25–26) is the marriage that works in public, with greed untouched underneath. Whitewashed tombs (vv. 27–28) is the gap between the person others describe and the person you are at eleven at night. And building the prophets’ tombs (vv. 29–30) is admiring dead saints while resisting living correction: reading Spurgeon warmly and unable to take one sentence from your own pastor.

Do not put the chapter down flattened. Every one of the seven is the same disease, an outside kept while an inside is neglected, and the cure was named at the cup (vv. 25–26): clean the inside first, which is the one thing no man can do for himself and exactly what God has promised to do (Ezekiel 36:26). The man pronouncing these woes walked out of this chapter toward a cross on which he died for Pharisees, and within a few years a Pharisee more zealous than most (Galatians 1:14) was preaching the grace he had persecuted. Nobody here is beyond the reach of what he came to do.

Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes. Jesus speaks as God, who sends prophets (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). The messengers are his apostles and followers. He sends them knowing they will be killed, because God’s way of dealing with sin is to send grace into the middle of it, and through their blood the gospel ran from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Some of whom you will kill and crucify. Stephen was killed (Acts 7:58–60); James was killed (Acts 12:2); Peter, by tradition, was crucified.

And some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town. Paul did this before his conversion (Acts 22:19), and later suffered it five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).

Does God still send prophets today? Not in the sense of new revelation. The apostles and prophets of the first generation laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and what they taught is now written in the New Testament, which is complete. This is the cessationist conviction, that the gifts which gave new revelation ceased with the apostles, and it rests on the foundation being laid once and Scripture being sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). Many faithful Christians believe God still gives prophecy today, and most of them agree that any such word must be tested by Scripture and never stands beside it; we differ from them as brothers. But Christ still sends messengers: every faithful preacher, missionary and witness who carries his finished word to the world is sent by him, and is often treated as these were. So the promise and the warning still stand. The world still flogs and persecutes those who speak for Christ, and he still counts what is done to them as done to him (Acts 9:4).

On a Tuesday. Pray for those today who are flogged and persecuted from town to town for Christ. Find out the name of one persecuted believer or church, and carry that name to God every day this week.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna.

verseByVerse.quote: "so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth. This generation will complete the pattern by killing the Son, refusing the greatest light most completely.

From the blood of righteous Abel. The first murder (Genesis 4:8–10). Abel was not a prophet; he was killed over an act of worship God had accepted. That is what this list is made of: people God accepted whom other people could not tolerate.

To the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest was stoned in the temple court at the king’s command, and as he died he said, May the LORD see and avenge (2 Chronicles 24:20–22).

Cover to cover. Chronicles commonly stood last in the Hebrew Bible, so the Zechariah of 2 Chronicles is its last named martyr. Jesus names not the earliest and latest by date (Uriah died later, Jeremiah 26:23) but the first and last in the book.

The Righteous One at the end of the list. Within three days the list had one more name, the one every earlier name pointed toward. Stephen told the same council: your fathers killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, and you have now betrayed and murdered him (Acts 7:52). Every martyr’s blood from Genesis to Chronicles was a shadow of that death. His was the substance, and it was shed not only by the guilty but for them.

Why son of Barachiah? The prophet Zechariah, who wrote the book of Zechariah, was the son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1), and his murder is not recorded. Possible explanations: Jehoiada may have been Zechariah’s grandfather (with Barachiah his father), as son can mean descendant, and Jehoiada lived to a hundred and thirty (2 Chronicles 24:15); or the names have been conflated in transmission (Luke 11:51 omits the father’s name, and one important early manuscript of Matthew omits it too); or Jesus combines the two Zechariahs, both prophets, both martyrs by tradition. The details fit 2 Chronicles exactly, down to the place of the killing and the dying cry for the LORD to see and avenge. None of these explanations is certain, and believers who hold Scripture true can say honestly that this question remains open. This commentary’s view: uncertain; the point is clear: from the first to the last martyr.

Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. Within that generation, judgment fell: the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70 (24:34).

Covenantal, not mechanical. One guard: this has been tragically misused to justify persecution of Jews. All humanity was responsible for the death of Christ, and he died for sinners of every nation, Jew and Gentile (Acts 4:27–28). The judgment Jesus sees is the fall of the city within forty years, on the generation that had the greatest light and refused it. It is not a statement that every individual then alive was lost, and the book of Acts is the proof. Thousands in that city and generation were baptised, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (Acts 6:7). The measure was full for a system about to be swept away, and the door stayed open for every person in it.

In the flow. The woes reach their climax: when the bill falls due, this generation (as again in 24:34). At once the voice breaks into the lament of verse 37. Matthew will not let us separate the Judge from the one who weeps.

How is it fair for one generation to bear the guilt of earlier ones? Because they did not merely inherit it; they joined it. Scripture is clear that each person dies for his own sin, not his father’s (Ezekiel 18:20). But a generation that sees what its fathers did, condemns it in words, and then does the same thing on a greater scale against a greater light, takes the whole history onto itself. They were not punished for Abel’s murder as though they had been there. They were judged for rejecting the One to whom every martyr had pointed, and so they became the climax of the story. Greater light brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:48).

For worship. Abel’s blood cried from the ground for vengeance, and Zechariah died praying that the LORD would see and avenge. But there is blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). The blood of Jesus cries not for vengeance on those who shed it but for pardon: Father, forgive them. It was shed for murderers, so that even those who killed the prophets might be washed.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles. On “son of Barachiah,” see the commentary.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court
blood that speaks a better word than Abel’s

verseByVerse.quote: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you desolate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem. The double name is deep emotion, like David’s O my son Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33). Luke says he wept over the city (Luke 19:41).

Killing the prophets, stoning the sent. Jerusalem, the holy city, had a long record of rejecting God’s messengers; Jesus could even say that a prophet should not perish away from Jerusalem (Luke 13:33).

How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings. A tender, motherly image, used of God in the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:11; Psalm 91:4). How often: Jesus speaks as the God who had sent prophet after prophet, and perhaps of his own visits to Jerusalem (John 2; 5; 7). The heart of Christ is exposed here: longing, repeated, patient, refused.

Your children. He does not say how often would I have gathered you. He says how often would I have gathered your children, and you were not willing. Set beside the first woe (v. 13), the ones addressed include the leaders who stood between the Shepherd and the flock, and the children are the people they kept from him. The lament is not only that Jerusalem refused; it is that her teachers would not let her come. This should be held lightly, since a city is being spoken to as a person, but it explains why the woes and the weeping belong in one chapter.

And you were not willing! The tragedy. God was willing; they were not.

God’s will and human refusal. Scripture holds both: God sincerely calls and grieves when people refuse (2 Peter 3:9), and he works all things according to his purpose (Ephesians 1:11). Those who perish were not willing; those who are saved were made willing (Psalm 110:3). His secret plan is his business; what he tells us to do is ours (Deuteronomy 29:29).

Where Christians differ: was God’s will defeated here? Arminian Christians read you were not willing as proof that God desires all to be saved but that his grace can be finally resisted, so that the human will is decisive. The Reformed answer distinguishes what God desires and commands from what he has decreed (Ezekiel 33:11; Deuteronomy 29:29). God genuinely desires the repentance of sinners and genuinely grieves over their refusal, and yet his saving purposes are never thwarted: all that the Father gives the Son will come to him (John 6:37). This commentary’s view: the Reformed reading is the more likely. Jesus weeps over a city that refused him, and the refusal is wholly theirs; but nothing in the verse says that God failed to save anyone he purposed to save, and the same Gospel teaches that no one knows the Father except the one to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (11:27). Faithful believers on both sides of this question weep with Christ over the lost and plead with them to come.

Not the face of a reluctant Christ. Whatever remains mysterious, he wanted to gather them, and no one may picture a cold or reluctant Christ. As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11) is not a footnote to the Reformed faith; it is its own preaching.

See, your house is left to you desolate. Days before he had called it my house (21:13); now it is your house. As in Ezekiel’s vision the glory left the temple before its destruction (Ezekiel 10:18–19), Jesus now leaves it for the last time (24:1–2). The Lord of the temple walks out of it, and the glory goes with him.

What if I am afraid I have been unwilling too long? Then listen to the hen. The voice that said you were not willing also said how often, and it was spoken to the very people who were about to kill him. Many of them, seven weeks later, were cut to the heart at Pentecost and received him (Acts 2:36–41). The fact that you are troubled about your unwillingness is evidence that God is making you willing. Do not wait to understand the decree before you come. You are not invited to read God’s secret will but to obey his revealed one, and it is this: come. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

For worship. The Son of God stood over the city that would kill him within the week and grieved like a mother bird over a brood that would not come. He was about to be lifted up on a cross outside that city’s wall, and there the fire of judgment fell, and it fell on him. An old farmyard story tells of a hen found dead after a fire with her chicks alive beneath her. Under the wings of Christ the fire burned itself out on him, and all who shelter there live.

parallels.desc: under his wings you will find refuge
this house shall become a desolation

verseByVerse.quote: "For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I tell you, you will not see me again. His public ministry to the city ends here.

Until. He does not say you will never see me again. He says you will not see me again until, and a sentence with until in it is not a door closing. It is a door with a date on it.

Until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Psalm 118:26, the words the crowds sang at his entry (21:9). The psalm frames the whole week: shouted in ignorance on Sunday, quoted against the builders who rejected the stone (21:42), and now promised as this city’s confession.

Where Christians differ: hope or warning? This may be a hope: one day Jerusalem will welcome its Messiah. Paul speaks of a future turning of many Jews to Christ: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:1, 25–27). The same little word, until. Or it may be a warning: when he returns in glory, they will have to acknowledge him, willingly or not (Philippians 2:10–11; Zechariah 12:10). Every eye will see him, including those who pierced him (Revelation 1:7), and the words will be said by all, some in worship and some in terror. This commentary’s view: both. At his return every knee will bow; and there is hope that many in Israel will welcome him with faith, which is the most natural reading of Romans 11, held with humility.

What kind of future for Israel? Christians who share that hope still differ on its shape, and the views deserve stating fairly. Many Reformed teachers, following Romans 11, expect a large turning of ethnic Israel to Christ before his return; others read all Israel as the full number of God’s elect from Jew and Gentile together, gathered through the whole age. Neither view requires an earthly millennial kingdom or a separate plan for Israel apart from the church. Premillennial Christians, who expect Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years after his return, often place this turning then; this commentary takes the amillennial view, that the thousand years of Revelation 20 describe Christ’s present reign from heaven, but it honours brothers who read the timetable differently. Whatever the scale, it is the gathering of Jews into the one people of God, by faith in the same Christ, grafted back into the one olive tree.

Does this mean Jewish people can be saved apart from Jesus? No. The very words Jesus expects them to say are a confession of him: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Any future turning of Israel is a turning to Jesus as Messiah, by repentance and faith, in exactly the way every Gentile is saved (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:9–13). That is why Paul, who loved his people more than his own life, preached Christ to them in every synagogue he could enter. Love for Jewish people does not mean leaving them without the gospel. It means bringing it to them first, with humility and gratitude, because salvation is from the Jews and their Messiah is our Lord (John 4:22).

The last word to Jerusalem. The last word Jesus speaks to Jerusalem before he dies for her is not desolate but until. After seven woes, the last thing he does before going out of the door is to promise that these people will one day greet him with a blessing. Nothing required it. The case was closed, and he opened it again with one word, on his way to die.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

23.theology: The danger of religious hypocrisy. The sins Jesus names here (outward conformity hiding inward corruption, burdens laid on others and never lifted, precision in small matters and blindness to great ones) are not peculiar to the Pharisees. They are the natural drift of religion wherever the heart has not been made new, and the only cure is the new heart God promises in Ezekiel 36, which produces obedience from the inside rather than performance for the outside. So the woes are a mirror before they are anything else.
23.examples:
Then: The Pharisees were the most serious religious people of their day. Jesus pronounced seven woes over them. Religious seriousness is not the same as knowing God.

Now: Every church tradition has its own version of the trap: the believer who is doctrinally precise and personally unkind, the churchgoer who loves the service and not the neighbour, the activist with no life with God. The question is not whether I am religious, but whether my religion comes from a heart that loves God and my neighbour.

24.title: The End of the Age
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Jesus left the temple and was going away, when his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. <sup>2</sup>But he answered them, “You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?” <sup>4</sup>And Jesus answered them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>5</sup>For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>6</sup>And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>7</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places. <sup>8</sup>All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>“Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations for my name’s sake. <sup>10</sup>And then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. <sup>11</sup>And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. <sup>12</sup>And because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold. <sup>13</sup>But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come. <sup>15</sup>“So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), <sup>16</sup>then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>17</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house, <sup>18</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>19</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>20</sup>Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath. <sup>21</sup>For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be. <sup>22</sup>And if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short. <sup>23</sup>Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘There he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>24</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. <sup>25</sup>See, I have told you beforehand. <sup>26</sup>So, if they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out. If they say, ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. <sup>27</sup>For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>28</sup>Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. <sup>29</sup>“Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>30</sup>Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. <sup>31</sup>And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. <sup>32</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>33</sup>So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>34</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>35</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>36</sup>“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only. <sup>37</sup>For as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, <sup>39</sup>and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>40</sup>Then two men will be in the field; one will be taken and one left. <sup>41</sup>Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left. <sup>42</sup>Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. <sup>43</sup>But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what part of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into. <sup>44</sup>Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. <sup>45</sup>“Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his master has set over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? <sup>46</sup>Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>47</sup>Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>48</sup>But if that wicked servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’ <sup>49</sup>and begins to beat his fellow servants and eats and drinks with drunkards, <sup>50</sup>the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know <sup>51</sup>and will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
24.overview:
Chapters 24–25, the Olivet Discourse, are Jesus’ teaching on the end of the age, given on the Mount of Olives across the valley from the temple. Jesus answers both questions the disciples ask: first the years leading to Jerusalem’s fall in AD 70, then his own return at the end of history. The near judgment is a real event and also a foretaste of the far one.

The chapter gives no calendar. No one knows the day or the hour (v. 36), so the fitting posture is not calculation but watchfulness. Meanwhile the gospel of the kingdom goes to all nations (v. 14), and the Son of Man will come like lightning, suddenly and unmistakably. Until then: stay awake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — Signs of the End and the Great Tribulation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus walks out of the temple and foretells its complete destruction. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask what they take to be one question. He warns of false messiahs, of wars and famines that are not the end, of betrayal inside the church and love growing cold, and he promises that the one who endures will be saved and the gospel will reach all nations. Then comes the one concrete sign, the abomination of desolation, with an order to flee, a tribulation cut short for the elect, and a warning that his real coming will be as unmistakable as lightning.
verseByVerse.theology: The discourse answers a double question, and like Old Testament prophecy it sees a near horizon and a far one together. Everything to v. 35 comes with signs and is set inside a generation; from v. 36 there are no signs. Endurance to the end is the mark of genuine salvation, kept by the God who promises to keep, rather than a feat the anxious must manage. And the days are cut short for the sake of the elect, people whose names appear in no chronicle.
verseByVerse.examples: The clause most often ignored is the end is not yet (v. 6). A better question than the timetable is personal: when the headlines are bad, does your confidence in God’s government move? Verse 12, love growing cold, comes closer to home than the tribulation does, and its remedy is the one given to Ephesus: remember, repent, and do the works you did at first. And the response to the sign in v. 15 is plainly practical: not to gather or interpret, but to leave the district. The Christians of Jerusalem did, and lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus left the temple and was going away, when his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. But he answered them, "You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 24 is Jesus’ answer to two questions his disciples thought were one: when will the temple be destroyed, and what will be the sign of his coming and the end of the age? He describes first the years leading to AD 70, then his own public, visible return, whose day no one knows. Many Christians have been taught to expect a secret rapture, a hidden removal of believers before a final tribulation; this commentary reads the chapter differently, because the coming Jesus describes is public and seen by all (vv. 27, 30), while gladly honouring brothers who hold that view. There is no timetable here either, only four commands: do not be led astray, do not be alarmed, endure to the end, stay awake.

The setting. Chapters 24–25, the Olivet Discourse, are the last of Jesus’ five great teaching sections in Matthew. He speaks of both events the disciples ask about, and the reader’s task is to see which he means at each point.

Jesus left the temple and was going away. His last departure from the temple, right after announcing that its house would be left desolate (23:38). He does not go back. Ezekiel had watched the glory of the LORD rise from the threshold, move to the east gate, and go up from the city to stand on the mountain on its east side (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23): the Mount of Olives, which is exactly where Jesus is about to sit down. The last time God left that building, the building came down.

The buildings of the temple. The disciples were not being naive. Herod began rebuilding the temple in 20 BC, and it was finished only around AD 63 (John 2:20). Some stones were over forty feet (12 metres) long, and parts were covered with gold, so that, according to Josephus, it shone like a snowy mountain in the sun.

You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down. Look carefully, he says, and then makes an astonishing prophecy. Some forty years later, in AD 70, the Roman general Titus besieged and destroyed Jerusalem. The temple was burned, and the stones were thrown down; an old tradition says the soldiers levered them apart to get at the gold that had melted and run into the joints. Josephus, who had known the place, describes it in detail, and says the ground was afterwards cleared so thoroughly that a visitor would not believe it had ever been inhabited. Only parts of the retaining walls of the temple platform remain, including the Western Wall.

How exact it was. What survives today, the Western Wall, is a retaining wall of the platform. The temple itself, the building the disciples were pointing at, has not one stone standing on another. He did not say the mountain would be flattened. He said the house would not have two stones left in contact, and that is precisely what happened.

Two men, one wall. The disciples saw permanence. Jesus saw a building whose purpose was about to be fulfilled in himself and which was therefore a single generation from rubble. The temple existed so that a holy God could dwell among sinful people and so that sin could be covered by sacrifice. Jesus is God with us (1:23), and his death would be the one sacrifice all the others pointed to (Hebrews 10:12), so the building’s work was about to be done. It is easy to read the solidity of religious institutions as evidence of God’s pleasure. Stone is not evidence of anything.

Will the temple be rebuilt? Dispensational Christians (those who see God’s plans for Israel and for the church as running on separate tracks) expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, pointing to Daniel 9:27, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11. The more likely reading is that Christ has replaced the temple once for all: his body is the true temple (John 2:19–21), and his people are now God’s dwelling (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22). Hebrews shows that the sacrifices are finished (Hebrews 10:11–14). Nothing in Jesus’ words here looks for the building to rise again, and a Christian need not watch the Temple Mount for signs of the end. The temple God is building now is made of living stones, from every nation. Many godly believers read those passages differently, and this is a question on which Christians can disagree in love.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt and enlarged the temple on a vast scale; work was still going on. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he sat on the Mount of Olives. Facing the temple across the Kidron Valley, on the hill where Ezekiel saw the departing glory rest (and where, says Zechariah 14:4, the LORD’s feet will stand). He sits, as teachers did.

The disciples came to him privately. Peter, James, John and Andrew (Mark 13:3). These things means the destruction of the temple he has just foretold.

And what will be the sign of your coming and of the close of the age? Their two questions really touch three things (the temple, his coming, the close of the age), and the whole chapter turns on the fact that they thought these were one. To them they were three faces of a single event, and it is not hard to see why: if the house of God comes down, what could possibly follow but the end of everything? Close of the age is the end of the present world (13:39–40; 28:20). Jesus gently pulls the events apart, while showing that the fall of the temple is a preview of the end of the age.

A royal visit. The word for coming, parousia, was the word for a royal visit: the formal arrival of a king at a city, with escort and honours. Matthew uses it four times, all of them in this chapter (vv. 3, 27, 37, 39), and nowhere else in his Gospel.

How to read the discourse. Interpreters differ. Futurists see most of the chapter as about the end of history. Preterists see most of it as fulfilled in AD 70. Many evangelical and Reformed interpreters see verses 4–35 as mainly about the destruction of Jerusalem within that generation (v. 34), and verses 36 onward as about the final coming of Christ, whose day no one knows. Others see both events throughout, the near event foreshadowing the far, as Old Testament prophecy sees a near horizon and a far one in a single view. Faithful Christians hold each of these views. This commentary’s view: verses 4–35 speak mainly of the events leading to AD 70, which also foreshadow the end; verses 36–25:46 speak of Christ’s personal return at the end of the age. This reading takes seriously Jesus’ statement that this generation will not pass away until all these things take place (v. 34).

The seam in the text. The discourse has a visible seam. Everything down to verse 35 is hedged about with signs and told to a generation that will see them. Then verse 36 begins: but concerning that day and hour no one knows. From there on Jesus gives no signs to count down by, no timetable, and a coming compared to a thief in the night and a flood nobody expected. Signs and no signs cannot describe the same event. The seam is where the second question begins to be answered.

Why should I care about AD 70, so long ago? For three reasons. First, it proves that Jesus’ words come true. He named a building, a city and a generation, and within about forty years it happened exactly as he said; the Lord who kept that word will keep his word about his return. Second, it marks the end of the old covenant order. With the temple gone, no sacrifice for sin has been offered there since, because the one sacrifice of Christ has made all others obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:18). Third, it is a preview. The judgment on Jerusalem is a small-scale picture of the final judgment, a warning to every generation that God’s patience has an end, and a call to flee to Christ while there is time.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that no one leads you astray. His first word is not catastrophe but deception. The greatest danger in a crisis is not suffering but being misled (vv. 11, 24).

Many will come in my name. False messiahs were not hypothetical. Josephus catalogues them: a Theudas who promised to part the Jordan; an Egyptian who led thousands to the Mount of Olives expecting Jerusalem’s walls to fall (Acts 21:38). In AD 132 Simon bar Kokhba was hailed as messiah and led the nation into a second catastrophe.

In my name. Here is the precise danger. Not denying him: using him. That is harder to detect than open opposition. The wolves in this Gospel do not arrive announcing themselves; they arrive in sheep’s clothing (7:15).

And they will lead many astray. One after another, those first-century movements ended with the followers killed or scattered.

The Messiah who refused the wilderness road. Every false messiah offered what the true one had refused: the kingdoms of the world without the cross (4:8–10), a crown by force (John 6:15). The men who led crowds to the Jordan and the Mount of Olives promised deliverance without a cross. The real Christ went to his throne by way of one, and that is still the surest mark of the difference.

The modern form. It is rarely a man claiming to be Jesus. The dangerous version is a man who functions as though he were, without ever making the claim: whose pronouncements cannot be questioned, whose approval has become the measure of standing in a community, who mediates access to God for people who have stopped going directly. Nobody believes their leader is the Christ; they simply behave as though he were, and the seat that belongs to the one Teacher, the Christ, has been quietly occupied.

Not a habit of suspicion. Jesus is not telling disciples to audit other Christians. The safeguard is positive: know the real thing well enough that the counterfeit does not persuade you. A man who is impressed by confidence, and has nobody with the standing to disagree with him, is exactly the person these movements were built for.

How can I tell a false teacher? Ask three questions. What does he say about Jesus: is Christ the eternal Son, the only Saviour, crucified and risen, or has he been reduced or replaced (1 John 4:1–3)? What does he say about the gospel: is salvation by grace through faith in Christ alone, or has something been added (Galatians 1:6–9)? And where does his authority come from: does he open the Bible and submit to it, or claim a special word that the Bible must make room for? Watch his life too, because Jesus said you will recognise them by their fruits (7:15–20): greed, control and a refusal to be accountable are warning lights. And stay in a church where you are known, where elders and friends can tell you when you are being drawn away.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wars and rumors of wars. Before AD 70 came the Jewish revolt (from AD 66) and civil war after Nero’s death in AD 68.

See that you are not alarmed. Do not read every war as a sign of the end. It is a command, to men who will live through the fall of their own capital: panic is a thing to be resisted, by faith.

For this must take place. These things are part of God’s plan in a fallen world. They do not mean God has lost control.

The same must as the cross. The little word must (dei) is the must of 16:21: he must go to Jerusalem and suffer, be killed and be raised. The necessity that governs the wars of history is the same necessity that took the Son of God to the cross. Not two plans, but one purpose, held in one hand. The God who could bring the world’s redemption out of its worst crime is not at a loss over its wars. That does not make God the author of the evil in them. The men who crucified Jesus were guilty, though he was delivered up according to the definite plan of God (Acts 2:23), and every army that sheds blood answers for it, even while God’s purpose runs through its campaigns.

But the end is not yet. This is not the sign. Such things are the ordinary texture of the age and must not be read as a countdown.

Famines and earthquakes. A famine struck under Claudius (Acts 11:28), and earthquakes came in the decades before AD 70, as they have ever since.

The church has ignored it in every century. The fall of Rome, the Black Death, Napoleon, 1914, Hitler, the atom bomb, and a dozen dates confidently published and quietly forgotten. In every case sincere Christians read the headlines as the timetable, and in every case they were wrong, and in every case this verse had already told them they would be.

Why it keeps happening. Not because of stupidity. Reading the news as a countdown feels like faith. It produces urgency, it makes the world legible, and it flatters the reader with the sense of being one of the few who understand. Jesus offers something less exciting and considerably more useful: expect all of this, refuse to be shaken by it, and get on with what you were given to do.

Is it wrong to be afraid when the news is bad? Feeling fear is human, and Jesus does not scold frightened people. But he commands us not to be governed by it. You can check this without any prophecy chart: when the headlines are bad, does your confidence in God’s government of the world move? If a war, an election or a market can alter your sense of whether he is in control, you are being alarmed in the precise sense he forbids. The remedy is not better information about the end but a firmer grip on the one who told you in advance that all this would happen. Pray about what frightens you, limit how much of the news you swallow, and do the next faithful thing. He has overcome the world (John 16:33).

verseByVerse.quote: "All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beginning of the birth pains. A Jewish image for the sufferings before the messianic age (Isaiah 26:17–18). Birth pains are not the pains of dying. They come in waves; they are purposeful, they cannot be stopped once they have properly begun, and they end not in death but in a new life. And they are only the beginning.

The world is in labour. Paul uses the same image of creation groaning in childbirth (Romans 8:22). The troubles of history are the labour pains of the new creation.

They will deliver you up. Jesus had warned of this in 10:17–22. James was killed (Acts 12:2), and Nero persecuted Christians in Rome in AD 64. The verb, paradōsousin, is the word used of Judas handing Jesus over and of Jesus being handed over to Pilate. His followers will go through what he went through, in the same vocabulary. That is not incidental to the age between his comings; it is the shape of it.

Hated by all nations. Early Christians were accused of atheism and hatred of the human race. The scope is total, and the cause is exact: not for their politics or for being difficult, but for the name. Whatever hostility a Christian meets that has nothing to do with Christ is not this, and should not be dignified with the label.

Am I being persecuted if people mock my faith? Honesty is needed in both directions. If you live somewhere the faith is merely unfashionable, do not manufacture persecution out of social awkwardness or an argument at work; treating an eye-roll as martyrdom trivialises the real thing and makes the church look self-pitying. Bear mockery patiently and graciously, and examine whether the offence is the name of Christ or your own manner (1 Peter 4:14–16). But do not conclude from your own comfort that the verse has expired. Most Christians alive today are not in your position. There are believers this morning in prison for a Bible, families who lost a house for a baptism, and congregations meeting where a knock at the door would end it. This verse is their daily weather, and the comfortable part of the church owes the rest of it to stop reading these words as metaphor.
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

parallels.desc: the whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth

verseByVerse.quote: "And then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many will fall away. To stumble, abandon the faith under pressure (13:21). Three verbs, getting worse: many will fall away, and betray one another, and hate one another. All three describe damage done inside the church. Earlier the world did the hating; now the brothers do it.

And betray one another. Even in families (10:21). The verb is paradōsousin again: the same word used of the world handing Christians over (v. 9), and the same word used of Judas. So the sentence means: they will do to each other what Judas did to me. In Nero’s persecution, says Tacitus, Christians were arrested on information from others who had been arrested.

And hate one another. The most disturbing clause: persecution turns the church on itself. Sustained fear makes people suspicious, and suspicion in a small frightened group looks for somewhere to land. The ones who held out despise the ones who cracked; the ones who cracked cannot bear the sight of the ones who held out; and everybody has a theory about who talked.

The low-grade version. Any congregation under real strain, a scandal, a split, a long illness in a leader, will discover the same instinct at a lower temperature. Positions harden, factions form around men rather than around truth, motives get assigned, and people who prayed together last year cannot be in the same room. Nobody involved thinks of it as falling away. It presents itself as conviction.

Many false prophets. False teachers within the church (7:15; Acts 20:29–30), placed straight after the betrayal and the hatred. A frightened, divided, exhausted church is exactly the market for a confident new voice with a simpler explanation. The damage such men do is not usually measured in the people they take from a strong church. It is measured in the people they take from a wounded one.

What should I do when my church is fighting? First, refuse to join the hating. You may hold convictions firmly and still refuse to assign motives, spread stories or speak of brothers with contempt (Ephesians 4:29–32). Second, go to people, not about them (Matthew 18:15). Third, keep the gospel at the centre: ask whether the dispute is about the truth of Christ or about preferences and personalities, and be willing to yield on the second. Fourth, pray for those you disagree with by name, because it is very hard to keep hating someone you are praying for. And be wary of any new voice that offers to explain everything if only you will follow him out.

For worship. Judas handed him over, Peter denied him, and all the disciples fled, and still he loved his own to the end. On the night he was betrayed he prayed for those who would fail him, that their faith would not finally fail (Luke 22:32). He is faithful when his people are faithless (2 Timothy 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "And because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lawlessness will be increased. Lawlessness (anomia), the word used of the whitewashed tombs (23:28). The logic is not that wicked people force Christians to stop loving; it is that living for years in an environment where God’s order is ignored has an effect on the person living there. You stop being shocked. Then you stop being grieved. Then you stop noticing that you stopped, and the whole adjustment feels like maturity.

The love of many will grow cold. This is the verse most likely to describe the reader, and the quietest. The verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to be cooled. The picture is not a fire put out but a fire no longer fed, like embers left untended, going grey at the edges while nobody notices. The church in Ephesus was warned that it had abandoned the love it had at first (Revelation 2:4). There is no dramatic moment in it, and that is precisely what makes it dangerous: a man can watch for the sins he has been warned about and never once check the temperature.

What cooling looks like. Prayer becomes a duty discharged rather than an appointment kept. Scripture is familiar: you know the passage, you have heard the sermon, there is nothing new here. Other Christians’ troubles become mildly tiresome; you help, but you time it. Worship is assessed rather than entered. The gospel is information you possess rather than news you still cannot quite believe. It is common in a mature congregation, and almost nobody says it out loud. But not every dryness is cooling. Grief, illness, depression and exhaustion can numb the feelings of a believer whose love has not cooled at all; the psalmists prayed from that numbness (Psalm 42; 88), and the one who is troubled by his coldness is showing the very warmth he fears he has lost.

Of many, not all. It is not inevitable, and it is not a description of what age does to everybody. There are people at eighty who are warmer than they were at thirty, and everybody who has been in a church long enough has met one and been slightly unnerved by them.

How do I rekindle a love that has grown cold? Not by trying to feel more, which never works. The apostolic prescription is unexpectedly concrete. To a church whose first love had cooled, the risen Christ said three things in one breath: remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first (Revelation 2:5). Remember: think back to when it was warm, and be specific about what was different. Repent: call the coldness sin rather than a season, which is the step everybody skips. And do the first works: not feel the first feelings, but resume the actions you did when it was easy, before the feeling has returned. Above all, look again at Christ. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19), and love for him is rekindled not by staring at our own hearts but at his cross.

parallels.desc: you have abandoned the love you had at first

verseByVerse.quote: "But the one who endures to the end will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who endures to the end. As in 10:22. Endurance is not earning salvation by persisting; it is the evidence of genuine new birth (1 John 2:19). The perseverance of the saints means that everyone God has truly made his own will go on trusting Christ to the end. They will stumble, sometimes badly, but they will not finally fall away, because God keeps them; a faith that does fall away for good shows that it was never living faith.

Who does the keeping. Many long-time believers fear: will I still believe at the end? The verse does not say the one who is strong enough to hold on. Endurance is described here as the mark of the saved, not prescribed as a feat to be managed by the anxious. Elsewhere the keeping is God’s: no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29); believers are guarded by God’s power through faith (1 Peter 1:5). Perseverance is a promise before it is ever a duty, though it is genuinely a duty, and both halves have to stand.

The ordinary machinery. Will I endure? is not settled by introspection; it is settled by tomorrow, and the tomorrow after that. Endurance is an accumulation of very ordinary actions. Almost nobody falls away in a single dramatic crisis; they drift, over years, out of the means God gave to hold them: Scripture, prayer, the Lord’s Table, the honest confession of sin, and the company of other believers. Those are the ordinary machinery of perseverance, and they are unglamorous on purpose. Stay inside them and the question largely answers itself.

The company of believers. The last is the one most easily lost. Hebrews tells the church to exhort one another every day, that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13). God’s normal method of keeping his people is other Christians. A Christian who has quietly stopped being known by anybody has removed the very instrument God usually uses.

This gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed. Despite persecution, the gospel will spread. The whole world (oikoumenē) often meant the Roman Empire. The testimony is both an offer of salvation and evidence for judgment.

And then the end will come. In the immediate context, the end of the temple and the old order in AD 70. In the wider sense, the gospel will reach all nations before the final end (28:19–20; Revelation 7:9). Together: personal endurance and worldwide mission, the shape of Christian life between the comings.

Has this happened? In one sense, yes: before AD 70 Paul could say that the gospel was bearing fruit in the whole world (Colossians 1:6; Romans 16:26). In its fullest sense the gospel goes on reaching the nations until the end, and Revelation sees people from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, before the throne (Revelation 7:9). But Christ’s return is not triggered by our success. Its day is fixed by the Father (v. 36); our part is to be faithful in the task.

What if I have already had a season away? Then read the fact that it troubles you. The person who finally abandons Christ does not come back uneasy; he leaves and does not miss it. Peter denied his Lord with oaths in a courtyard and was eating breakfast with him on a beach a few weeks later. Falling is not the same as falling away, and the God who intends to finish his work in you has dealt with worse than your worst month. Come back to the means of grace this Sunday, tell a pastor or friend where you have been, and let the Shepherd who went looking for you carry you home.

For worship. The gospel has run where Caesar’s legions never went, and has never once been stopped. The same King who sends his word to the ends of the earth keeps every one of his own to the end of the road, and at the last a great multitude from every nation will sing that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The abomination of desolation. From Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11. Something detestable to God, especially an idol, that leaves the temple desolate. In 167 BC Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up an altar to Zeus in the temple, and Jewish writings called it the abomination of desolation (1 Maccabees 1:54). So everyone listening had a template: a pagan thing standing where it must not stand.

In the flow. After the general picture of the age (vv. 4–14), Jesus gives the one concrete sign that answers the first question, when the temple will fall.

Standing in the holy place. Luke’s parallel explains: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). In AD 66–70, Roman armies with their pagan standards, which bore images of the emperor and were worshipped by the soldiers, surrounded Jerusalem. Before that, Jewish Zealots occupied the temple, committed murders in it and installed an unqualified high priest, which Josephus describes as a profanation. When the temple fell, Roman soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and offered sacrifices to them. Earlier still, in AD 40, the emperor Caligula had ordered a statue of himself erected in the sanctuary, and Judea came within a hair of open revolt before he died and the order lapsed: an episode within the lifetime of these disciples that made the prophecy feel entirely live.

Let the reader understand. A note in brackets to the person holding the scroll, the only one of its kind in Matthew: work it out, and when you see it, act on it.

Daniel’s Anointed One cut off. The prophecy Jesus points to holds a further detail. Daniel was told that an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing, and the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary (Daniel 9:26). Many Reformed interpreters have read that of Christ: first the Anointed One cut off, then the city and the sanctuary destroyed. The sanctuary falls after the Messiah dies, and because its work is finished in him.

Flight to the mountains. The mountains are the old refuge of the hunted in Israel (Genesis 19:17; 1 Samuel 23:14), and early Christian tradition says the Jerusalem church did exactly what it was told.

A practical response. Given the greatest sign, Jesus tells them not to defend the holy place or interpret, but to leave the district. Prophecy produces action, usually ordinary. It guards against fatalism and against the endless identification of the sign in the newspaper, which produces excitement and no action whatever. Jesus gave a sign and a route out. The people who obeyed him packed.

What it does not mean. Many dispensationalist believers (who see God’s plans for Israel and the church as separate tracks) see the abomination of desolation as a future Antichrist setting up an image in a rebuilt temple during a seven-year tribulation. But Jesus tells his own disciples, in Judea, to flee when they see it. The instructions are local and practical: Judea, housetops, fields, winter, Sabbath (vv. 16–20). This fits AD 70. This commentary’s view: the abomination of desolation was fulfilled in the Roman desecration and destruction of the temple in AD 66–70. It may also foreshadow the final rebellion against God before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4).

Is the Antichrist still to come? Scripture teaches both a present spirit and a final figure. John says many antichrists have already come, and the spirit of antichrist is already in the world, denying the Father and the Son (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3). Paul speaks of a final man of lawlessness, a last great rebellion against God before Christ returns, whom the Lord Jesus will destroy by the breath of his mouth and the appearance of his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8). So Christians should neither scan the headlines for a particular world leader nor imagine the danger is past. Every age has its antichrists, opposition to Christ dressed as religion or power, and the church is to resist them by holding fast to the truth. And the final rebel, whoever he proves to be, has a very short future: one word from the returning King.

On a Tuesday. Jesus warned his followers because he meant them to live, and he warns you for the same reason. Is there something you are holding on to, a relationship, a habit, a place, that Scripture has plainly told you to leave? Leave it, in the strength of the Spirit who raised Jesus and now lives in you (Romans 8:11).
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple. It was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
