On the housetop. Flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase, were living space. Speed is everything, and the instructions are domestic and exact.

Not turn back for his cloak. Workers left their outer cloaks at the edge of the field and worked in their tunics. That cloak was a man’s blanket (Exodus 22:26–27). So the command is: leave behind the one possession you will genuinely need tonight. Lot’s wife looked back and was lost (Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32).

They took him at his word. Eusebius records that before the siege the Jerusalem Christians, warned by prophecy, left for Pella across the Jordan. Some question the details, but the tradition is early: they did not stay to trust the walls, and they lived.

The grip of things. The principle underneath is not that possessions are wicked. It is that they have a grip which shows up only under time pressure. Nobody discovers what he is attached to while sitting comfortably; he discovers it in the four seconds when he has to choose between the thing and the door. This is why Jesus attaches the warning to a crisis rather than to a sermon on contentment: the crisis is the only reliable diagnostic.

The one who did not turn back. The command not to look back was first kept by the man who gave it: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). He left his Father’s glory and did not go back for it. In Gethsemane he could have asked for twelve legions of angels (26:53), and he walked out to meet the arresting party instead. Every disciple who leaves a cloak in the field is following someone who left far more and never once turned round.

What would I grieve over? That gives a test that requires no crisis to run, only honesty. If you had two minutes and one bag, you would take the passports and the photographs. Everybody knows that list. The more revealing question is the other one: what would you be quietly grieving over three weeks later? That is the thing with the grip on it, and knowing its name now is a considerable advantage over discovering it on the stairs. And the cure is not to despise it but to hold it as a gift from a Father who can give it again, or something better (19:29).
verseByVerse.note: Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: "And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alas for women who are pregnant. Alas (ouai), the word of the seven woes, here a lament. He has told them to run, and now he thinks about who will not be able to: the people at the back of the column. Josephus records famine so severe in the siege that a mother ate her own child.

Pray that your flight may not be in winter. Winter was the rainy season, when roads turned to mud, stream beds flooded, and a night in the open on the Judean hills could kill a child.

Or on a Sabbath. Travel was restricted, gates might be shut, nothing could be bought, and people trained from infancy in the Sabbath limit would hesitate when hesitation was fatal. This detail shows Jesus was speaking to Jewish believers in first-century Judea, thinking about roads and weather and what people will actually do.

Why pray about what is decreed? The striking thing is that he tells them to pray about it, and that raises the difficulty most people have with prayer generally. He has just declared, with absolute certainty, that this catastrophe is coming. What is the use of praying about the timing of a thing God has decreed? Two answers, and the second is the one that helps. The first is that God’s decree includes the prayers of his people; they are not an attempt to get round his purpose but part of the way it is carried out, which is why Scripture can hold both without embarrassment. The second is simpler: he told them to. The man who knew with complete certainty what was coming instructed frightened people to pray about the weather on the day, and that settles whether such prayers are worth praying rather better than any argument about mechanism.

Praying about fixed things. That is the shape of a great deal of Christian praying. The scan has already been done and the result is already on a screen somewhere. The letter is written. The decision was taken at a meeting last week. The thing is, in every practical sense, fixed, and you are told to pray about it anyway, and about the details, and about the timing, by someone who was never once in any doubt about how it would go. Pray about winter. He did not think it was a foolish request.

Does this mean Christians must keep the Sabbath? This verse does not settle it: it is a word about the practical dangers of AD 70, not a command about keeping the day. (See Luke 23:56 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. Prophesying the fall of a nation, the Lord of history stops to think about pregnant women and the roads in February. He counts the stars and calls them by name, and he gently leads those that are with young (Isaiah 40:11, 26). Nothing is too large for his rule, and no one is too small for his tenderness.
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard; Sabbath rules restricted travel.

verseByVerse.quote: "For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be. And if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great tribulation. Tribulation (thlipsis) means distress, affliction, crushing pressure. A prophetic phrase for an unparalleled disaster (Daniel 12:1; Joel 2:2). Josephus, an eyewitness, put the dead of the siege at over a million; most historians think his total too high, but nobody doubts the slaughter was immense. Never will be shows that history continues after this event: it is not the end of the world. But it was the end of a world. The sacrificial system of a thousand years stopped that summer and has never restarted.

If those days had not been cut short. Saved here means survive physically.

For the sake of the elect. The elect are those God chose in Christ before the foundation of the world to be his own (Ephesians 1:4), not because of anything in them but out of his free grace; here they are his people living through those years in Judea. God’s sovereignty extends even over the length of disasters. The days are shortened for the sake of the elect, and that is the only reason given.

History bends around people nobody was counting. That reorganises the whole picture of who matters in history. Empires keep records of themselves; the annals are full of emperors and legions and the dates of campaigns, and the people God has chosen appear in none of them. And Jesus says the length of the catastrophe was set with reference to them. The calendar of the worst years in that nation’s life was adjusted for the benefit of a group whose names occur in no chronicle and whose existence the men prosecuting the war never once considered. History does not bend around Titus. It bends around the people of God, and the reason is not their importance but their price: they are the people the Son was about to buy with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and the Father will not let a siege outlast the purpose for which he gave him.

What it does not mean. Not necessarily a future Great Tribulation of exactly seven years before Christ’s return, as some dispensationalists sincerely teach, from which Christians will be removed by a secret rapture beforehand. Jesus speaks to his disciples about a tribulation they would go through, and from which they would flee. This commentary’s view: the great tribulation of these verses refers first to the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70, which also pictures the tribulation God’s people suffer through the whole age (John 16:33; Acts 14:22; Revelation 7:14); Scripture expects a final intensification before the end (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4), and no secret rapture removes the church from it.

Shortened, not removed. Not the comfort of being spared: the elect are plainly in the tribulation. What it says is that the thing has a measured end, and that the measuring was done with them in view.

What if my suffering seems to have no end? Then hold on to this verse, because it was written for that feeling. God has not promised that you will not suffer, but he has promised that your suffering is measured: he knows its length to the day, and he has set its limit with you in view. He will not let you be tested beyond what you are able, but with the testing he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it (1 Corinthians 10:13). Paul, who suffered more than most of us ever will, called his afflictions light and momentary compared with the eternal weight of glory they were preparing (2 Corinthians 4:17). Tell God honestly how long it feels. Then ask him for strength for today, which is all he has promised to give at once.

For worship. There was one tribulation that was not shortened. The Son of God entered the full measure of the wrath our sins deserved, and no one cut those hours short for his sake. He drank the cup to the bottom, so that every cup his people drink would have a bottom.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: "Then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'There he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look, here is the Christ. In the crisis, many would claim the Messiah had come to save the city.

Great signs and wonders. The third warning about deception, unsettling to anyone who assumes the supernatural settles arguments. Signs and wonders do not prove that someone is from God (7:22–23; 2 Thessalonians 2:9–10).

Power was never the test. The law was blunt: if a prophet arises and gives you a sign, and the sign comes to pass, and he then says let us go after other gods, you shall not listen to him, for the LORD your God is testing you (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). God does not say the sign will fail. He allows that it may come true, and instructs Israel to disobey the man anyway.

The test is the gospel. So the criterion is doctrinal: what does the man say about Christ? Paul: even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed (Galatians 1:8). The church’s defence against a powerful counterfeit is not discernment about power, which nobody can assess, but familiarity with the gospel. You cannot tell a false miracle from a true one by looking. You can tell a false gospel from a true one by reading.

If possible, even the elect. If possible implies that it is not possible: God protects his chosen people from final deception (John 10:27–29). But they must be on guard. The security is genuine, and not a reason to relax.

How the elect are kept. Not by being lifted above the danger, but by being warned about it in advance, three times in one chapter. The warning is not a caveat on the promise of preservation; it is the machinery of it, though they may be confused for a time. God keeps his people through means, and the chief of them is that he tells them the truth.

Should I be suspicious of every report of a miracle? Not cynical, but careful. God is free to answer prayer in extraordinary ways, and Christians should thank him when he heals or rescues. Many believers, including this commentary, hold that the sign gifts given to authenticate the apostles and the new revelation they brought ceased with the apostolic age, and that God now works through his finished word; other believers sincerely disagree, and we can hold our view without contempt for theirs. But on this every Christian should agree: a miracle never validates a message. If someone’s teaching contradicts Scripture, no healing, prophecy or wonder can make it true. And if a ministry asks you to trust it because of its power rather than because of its faithfulness to the gospel, that is reason enough to walk away.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I have told you beforehand. So, if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out. If they say, 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, I have told you beforehand. Prophecy exists not to satisfy curiosity but to remove surprise. Jesus did the same for the disciples about his own death, three times, in detail, and they still fell apart; but they had it to remember afterwards, and the remembering is what put them back together.

In the wilderness. Would-be messiahs led crowds into the wilderness promising a new exodus (Acts 21:38), and the Romans slaughtered them. The wilderness is out beyond the settlements, austere, radical, away from the compromised institutions, where a hard prophet gathers a following.

In the inner rooms. The inner rooms are the hidden circle, knowledge for those admitted. One movement says the truth is out on the edge; the other says it is in the back room. Both are false, and both are still trading.

The family likeness of every counterfeit. What they have in common is worth naming: each offers access that other people do not have. The wilderness version flatters you with radicalism: the ordinary churches have sold out, and you have seen through them. The inner-room version flatters you with initiation: there is more to this than what is preached on Sundays, and you are among the few who have been let in. Both make the hearer feel distinguished, and both require him to leave the ordinary company of God’s people to get what is on offer.

Do not travel. The instruction is flat: do not go out; do not believe it. No going to hear him once to see. It can be that simple because his real coming will be like lightning, visible from horizon to horizon, and any claim that requires directions refutes itself. You will not need to be told where he is.

What about people who say God has shown them secret truths? Be very cautious. God has given his church everything it needs in the Scriptures, which are complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17; Jude 3), and he gives the same truth to the whole church, not a private version to an inner circle. A teacher who says the real meaning is hidden from ordinary Christians, or who offers revelations the Bible does not contain, is offering the inner room. Stay with the open Book and the ordinary congregation. The deepest truths of the faith are preached on Sunday mornings to whoever walks in.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the lightning. Every feature of the comparison works. Lightning is not local; it is seen across a whole sky at once. It is not gradual; there is no moment when a man is halfway to noticing it. It comes from above, not from any movement on the ground. And nobody has ever had to be told that it happened.

So will be the coming of the Son of Man. His return will be public, sudden and visible to all (Revelation 1:7), unlike the false messiahs who need advertising. Any announcement of it is disproved by the fact that it needed announcing. He will not be reported. He will be seen.

There the vultures will gather. A proverb (Job 39:30): vultures (or eagles) circling show where a body lies. Two possible meanings: just as vultures inevitably find a corpse, so judgment will inevitably fall on Jerusalem, now spiritually dead; the Roman legions, whose standards bore eagles, would gather there. Or: Christ’s coming will be as obvious as vultures over a carcass. This commentary’s view: probably judgment: where there is spiritual death, judgment will come.

The eagles. The judgment reading gains force from the Greek word aetoi, which means eagles as readily as vultures. The Roman legions carried the eagle as their standard, a metal bird on a pole that was the object of near-religious devotion in the army, and those standards would be planted in the ruins of Jerusalem within the lifetime of the men listening. Read so, the sentence is a veiled and terrible piece of specificity: the eagles gather where the body is, and the body is the city. What the sentence establishes either way is that judgment does not need to be arranged. Nobody has to summon vultures; they arrive because the thing is dead. And the interval between the two is never long enough for anybody to make arrangements.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ will come secretly to remove his church, with a later public coming. His coming is like lightning: visible to all.

Will people on the other side of the world see him at the same moment? Scripture does not explain the mechanics, and we should not pretend to. But it is clear on the fact: every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7), and his coming will be as unmistakable to all as lightning across the whole sky. The God who made light and space is not limited by the curve of the earth. The point Jesus presses is not physics but certainty: no one will miss it, no one will need it explained, and no one will be able to hide from it or argue about whether it has happened.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “eagles” for “vultures.”

parallels.desc: where the slain are, there is he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–51 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The discourse turns to the coming itself: the heavens shaken, the Son of Man on the clouds, and angels gathering the elect from one end of heaven to the other. The fig tree teaches the season, not the date, and this generation will see all these things. Then comes the hinge at v. 36: no one knows the day or the hour, only the Father. From there the teaching is all readiness: Noah, the field and the mill, the thief, and two servants.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 36 is the seam of the discourse. Before it come signs and a generation; after it, no signs and a coming likened to a burglary and a flood. That is the text’s own answer to the charge that Jesus wrongly predicted his return within his hearers’ lifetime. Nor the Son is answered from the two natures: as God the Son knows all things, and the human mind he truly took grew and learned. The gathering of the elect from the four winds is the comfort of the section: nobody is mislaid.
verseByVerse.examples: Stay awake does not mean reading the news apocalyptically, since no one knows the day, and it does not mean living in dread, since see that you are not alarmed is a command in this same discourse. What it does mean can be asked tonight: is there anything in your week you would need to stop or start if you knew he were coming on Thursday? Jesus’ picture of readiness is a steward handing out food at the proper time. And the wicked servant’s ruin begins in a sentence never said aloud: my master is delayed. He does not deny the master; he postpones him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sun will be darkened. Quoted from Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4. In the prophets these cosmic images describe the fall of nations: Isaiah’s darkened sun is the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:1, 10), his rolled-up sky the fall of Edom (34:4–5). And Peter at Pentecost said Joel’s sun turned to darkness was being fulfilled, on a morning when nothing happened to the sun at all (Acts 2:16–20).

The language of an order coming down. In the prophets, the collapse of the sky is how you say that a world is ending: a kingdom, an order, a settled arrangement of things that everybody assumed was permanent. Here that order is the old covenant order: the whole system of temple, priesthood and animal sacrifice through which Israel drew near to God under Moses. With the temple gone it could not go on, and God’s people now draw near through Christ alone (Hebrews 8:13; 10:19–22).

Two readings. If verses 4–35 speak of AD 70, this describes the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the old covenant order, in the prophets’ symbolic language. If it speaks of the end of history, it describes literal cosmic upheaval at Christ’s return (2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 6:12–14). Careful believers hold both. This commentary’s view: in context, the fall of Jerusalem described in prophetic imagery, which also foreshadows the final shaking of heaven and earth at Christ’s return (Hebrews 12:26–27).

The point on any reading. When God acts in judgment, creation does not carry on in the background. The sun and moon, the steadiest things there are, are described as failing, not because the universe is fragile, but because it is his.

Darkness at noon. Once the prophets’ language came true literally, over Jesus. From the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour (27:45), and when he died the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (27:51). The sun failed over the cross, and the temple’s world began to end there, in the hour its sacrifices were fulfilled. What Rome did in AD 70 made visible what had been settled at Golgotha: the old order fell because he had finished its work.

So should I expect literal signs in the sky? Do not build your hope on them. Jesus uses the prophets’ language, and in its first sense here it describes the fall of the temple order, which really was the end of a world. Scripture does teach that at the last day the present heavens and earth will be shaken and renewed (2 Peter 3:10–13; Hebrews 12:26–27), and that will be no metaphor. But Jesus has just told us not to look for him in signs and reports, and he is about to say that his final coming will be as unexpected as a flood. The sign to watch is not an eclipse. It is the state of your own heart when he comes.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: the stars will not give their light
the host of heaven rotted away

verseByVerse.quote: "Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sign of the Son of Man. Perhaps the sign is the Son of Man himself, revealed in glory; others since the second century have suggested a cross in the sky or a banner. The text does not say, and it is better to admit that than to decorate it.

All the tribes of the earth will mourn. The Greek can mean the land (of Israel) or the whole earth. The mourning is usually read as terror, and it may include something better. In Zechariah the mourning is repentance: they look on the one they have pierced, and mourn for him as one mourns for an only child, family by family (Zechariah 12:10–12). If the allusion is deliberate, and the wording is very close, the mourning at his appearing is not only the panic of the condemned. It includes the grief of people finally seeing what they did to him.

Coming on the clouds of heaven. From Daniel 7:13–14. In Daniel the Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and is given everlasting dominion: a coming up to God’s throne, not first a coming down to earth. Jesus used the same words at his trial (26:64). The fall of Jerusalem would show that Jesus had been vindicated and enthroned. The vision is also fulfilled finally at his return to earth (Acts 1:11; Revelation 1:7).

Riding the clouds. In the Old Testament, riding the clouds is not something a man does; it is what God does. He makes the clouds his chariot (Psalm 104:3); he rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt (Isaiah 19:1). Jesus takes Daniel’s vision, applies it to himself, and will repeat it under oath at his trial, which is the moment the high priest tears his robe, because everyone in that room knew exactly what had been claimed.

A loud trumpet call. A homecoming instrument rather than a military one (1 Thessalonians 4:16): Isaiah’s great trumpet gathers the lost from Assyria and Egypt to worship the LORD (Isaiah 27:13).

From the four winds. Angels (angeloi) can mean messengers. Some see the gathering of the elect from all nations through the preaching of the gospel after AD 70, as the kingdom passes from the temple to the worldwide church. Others see the final gathering at Christ’s return. Both are true: the gathering has begun through the gospel and will be completed at the end (Isaiah 27:12–13; Deuteronomy 30:4).

Nobody is mislaid. The pastoral weight of the passage. Believers buried at sea, and in unmarked ground, and in war graves with the wrong name on them, or no name. Children whose parents never had a grave to visit. Christians who died alone in places where nobody knew what they were. The sentence has no exceptions in it.

Is Christ reigning now, or only when he returns? Both, in different ways. Daniel’s vision is a coming to the throne, and Jesus says that from now on, from his trial onward, the Son of Man is seated at the right hand of Power (26:64). After his resurrection he says all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (28:18). So Christ reigns now, gathering his elect from every nation through the gospel, and the fall of Jerusalem was a public sign of that enthronement. This is the heart of the amillennial reading: the kingdom is not postponed to a future thousand years on earth; the King is already on his throne. Amillennial simply means that the thousand years of Revelation 20 are not a future golden age on earth but a picture of Christ’s present reign, which runs from his resurrection and ascension to his return. And at his one visible return that reign will be revealed to all, the gathering completed, and every enemy put under his feet. Premillennial believers, who expect a thousand-year reign on earth after his return, and postmillennial believers, who expect the gospel to bring a long golden age before it, read Revelation 20 differently; they are brothers who love the same coming King, and the Lord’s return will settle the question for us all.

For worship. The prisoner before the high priest, beaten and spat on, was telling the plain truth. The hands that were tied in the high priest’s court now hold the trumpet’s summons and the angels’ commission, and the exiles of every century are coming home to him at his word. To him be dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man with the clouds

verseByVerse.quote: "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the fig tree learn its lesson. Olive, pine and cypress hold their leaves through winter; the fig loses its leaves and is among the last to come into leaf, so its new leaves in spring are a clear sign that summer is coming.

The other fig tree. The last fig tree in this Gospel was the one he cursed a day or two earlier, all leaves and no fruit (21:19). The emblem of judgment now serves as the emblem of watchfulness.

When the branch becomes tender. All these things are the signs Jesus has described. The Greek can equally be read it is near, the destruction of Jerusalem: when the disciples saw these signs, they would know the end of the temple was close.

What the parable licenses, and what it forbids. It licenses reading the signs; the disciples are expected to watch and to draw a conclusion. But buds tell you the season, not the date. No gardener has ever looked at a branch and named a Tuesday. A Christian may say with confidence that these are the last days, as every generation since Pentecost has rightly said (Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18). The moment he names the date he has contradicted verse 36 and joined a long procession of sincere men whose dates are now footnotes.

Is the fig tree Israel, so that 1948 is the sign? Many have been taught so, that the founding of the modern state of Israel in 1948 started a countdown to Christ’s return within a generation. But Jesus does not say the fig tree is Israel. He explains his own parable: when you see all these things, the season is near. In context the things are the events leading to AD 70. And every attempt to count from 1948 to a date has run straight into verse 36, and failed. Christians differ about what God has in store for the Jewish people, but this parable is not about a modern nation state. It is about reading God’s warnings and responding in time.

Why the pull toward dates is so strong. It is not really about prophecy. A date would make the waiting finite. Watching indefinitely for something certain but unscheduled is one of the hardest things a person can be asked to do, and a timetable would convert it into something manageable. Jesus withholds it, not to tantalise, but because the readiness he wants cannot be produced by a deadline. A man who prepares because the date is close is not watchful. He is punctual.
verseByVerse.note: Unlike many trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter; its new leaves mark the coming of summer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This generation will not pass away. This generation in Matthew consistently means the people living in Jesus’ time (11:16; 12:39–45; 16:4; 17:17; 23:36). All these things are the events of verses 4–31, and in AD 70 they happened within that generation: strong evidence that verses 4–35 refer mainly to the fall of Jerusalem. Others take generation to mean race (the Jewish people will survive until the end) or the generation that sees the signs, but these readings are less natural.

The sceptic’s prize exhibit. Sceptics say Jesus flatly predicted his second coming within his hearers’ lifetime, and the lifetime passed, and he did not come. But at verse 3 the disciples asked two questions, and most of the discourse to this point has answered the first, about the temple. Every one of all these things did happen within that generation, in AD 70, exactly as he said.

The hinge at verse 36. Then the very next sentence turns a corner (v. 36), and of his final coming Jesus says the very opposite: no countdown of signs, no one knows the day. So the discourse deliberately holds two events apart: the near judgment on Jerusalem, set inside that generation, and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date. Read this way, Jesus was not mistaken. Honest readers still find this verse among the harder ones, and believers have offered more than one answer; but the seam at verse 36 is in the text itself, not invented to rescue it, and it gives a coherent account of every sentence in the chapter.

My words will not pass away. Only God’s word is said to stand for ever: the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isaiah 40:8; Psalm 119:89). Jesus claims the same for his own words: a claim to deity.

What does it mean for me that his words will not pass away? It means you can build on them. Every promise Jesus made, that he will never cast out anyone who comes to him, that he is with you always, that he is preparing a place for you, that he will come again and take you to himself, is more certain than the ground under your feet. Feelings change, circumstances collapse, scholars revise, and his words stand. So when you are anxious, do not argue with your feelings first; open the Gospels and read what he said. The Sermon on the Mount will still be true when the mountains are gone.

parallels.desc: the word of our God will stand forever

verseByVerse.quote: "But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That day and hour no one knows. After those days (vv. 19, 22, 29), with signs to watch for, now that day: the day of his final return and judgment (7:22; 26:29). For this no timetable is given. Scripture does name things that will come first, such as the final rebellion (2 Thessalonians 2:3), but none of them lets anyone set a date, and to those who are not watching it will come without warning (vv. 37–44). God has deliberately kept the day and the hour to himself.

Nor the Son. Jesus, in his human nature, during his earthly ministry, did not know the day.

Real, not a performance. The church’s classic answer is two natures, one Person: remaining what he was, he became what he was not. According to his deity the Son knows all things, for he is God and knows the Father’s mind as his own. According to the true human nature he took, he grew and learned like any of us; the same man got tired at a well, slept in a boat, and asked who touched him. The not-knowing is real, not a performance. He was not pretending ignorance while secretly consulting his divinity. He had genuinely taken a human mind, and lived within it, for us.

Ranked above the angels. He names a rising scale of those who do not know: not men, not the angels of heaven, not even the Son, but the Father only. He has placed himself above the entire angelic host and named himself in the same breath as the Father, absolutely, as the Son. The verse the sceptic reaches for to make Jesus less than God is a verse in which he calmly ranks himself above every created thing in heaven.

But the Father only. The timing belongs to the Father (Acts 1:7).

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit nor the Son, perhaps because scribes found it difficult. This commentary’s view: original; it is in Mark 13:32 without question. A reader of the King James Version will find no such words here, because the translators followed manuscripts that left them out. Nothing whatever is at stake, because the same words stand undisputed in Mark’s account of this moment. And the direction of the change is easy to guess: a copyist troubled by the words might quietly drop them, but a copyist would hardly invent a sentence that made Scripture harder to explain. That is a rule worth carrying: the more difficult reading is usually the original one, because copyists seldom made the Bible harder on purpose.

Does the risen Jesus know the day now? Scripture does not say directly, but it is reasonable to believe so. Jesus’ statement belongs to his earthly ministry, his state of humiliation. Since his resurrection and exaltation, his human nature has been glorified, and he has received all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18), and in Revelation he is the one who opens the scroll of history (Revelation 5:5–7). But even after the resurrection, when the disciples asked about times, he said it is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7). Whatever the Son now knows, the church has not been told, and is not meant to be.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “nor the Son.”

parallels.desc: not for you to know times or seasons

verseByVerse.quote: "For as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As were the days of Noah. Peter uses the flood as a picture of the final judgment (2 Peter 3:5–7).

In the flow. From here Jesus shows what no one knows the day means for how to live: his coming will be sudden, it will divide people who looked alike, and the only preparation is to be ready already.

Eating and drinking, marrying. Not one sin in the list: four ordinary human goods. Genesis says the earth was filled with violence (6:11), and Jesus does not reach for that. His point is not that they were monsters, but that they were busy.

The long warning. Noah built for years, in public, a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). Nobody was ambushed. What they also had was a Tuesday that looked exactly like Monday, and that turned out to be enough.

An ark already built. Peter draws the line from Noah to Christ: eight were brought safely through water, and baptism now saves, not as a washing of the body but as an appeal to God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 3:20–21). And he names the ark’s substance: Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (3:18). For the generation that will see the Son of Man come, the ark is not still being hammered together. It is finished, it is a Person, and its door stands open.

Until the day when Noah entered the ark. Then it was too late. And the LORD shut him in (Genesis 7:16).

The weight of the ordinary. What is the strongest argument in your own mind against taking the return of Christ seriously, not as doctrine, which you would affirm, but as something that could interrupt this week? For most people it is not an argument at all. It is the sheer weight of the ordinary: the school run, the deadline, the appointment on Thursday, the fact that nothing like that has ever happened in living memory and today looks very like yesterday. That is precisely the case Noah’s neighbours made, and it was the best case available right up until it was not.

Normality as anaesthetic. Normality is a more effective anaesthetic than vice. The rebel at least has a position on God. The generation of the flood had none. They were not opposing the ark. They were planning a wedding, and it was a perfectly good wedding, and the rain began during the reception.

So is it wrong to plan weddings, buy houses and enjoy ordinary life? No. Eating, drinking and marriage are God’s good gifts, and Noah himself had a wife and sons and daughters-in-law and presumably ate his dinner. Paul tells Christians to work with their hands and live quietly while they wait for Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). The danger is not ordinary life but ordinary life lived as if God had not spoken. A ready Christian plans the wedding, and prays over it, and holds it before the Lord, and would be glad if the Bridegroom came during the reception. The question is not whether you are busy, but whether there is room in the busyness for the one announcement that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: "and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Then two men will be in the field; one will be taken and one left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were unaware. What made Noah’s flood so terrible for the unprepared was not only its violence but its surprise.

One will be taken and one left. Which is the good outcome? In the flood, those taken were swept away in judgment (v. 39); those left (Noah’s family) were saved. So here, taken may mean taken in judgment, and left means remaining safe. Others see taken as taken to be with Christ (John 14:3). Either way: same place, same work, radically different destinies.

What it does not mean. This verse is often used to teach a secret rapture, in which Christians suddenly disappear before a period of tribulation, leaving unbelievers behind. But the context compares this to the flood, where those taken were taken in judgment, and the event is Christ’s public, visible coming (vv. 27, 30). This commentary’s view: no secret rapture. At Christ’s one public return, believers will be gathered to him (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17), and unbelievers judged; this verse pictures that sudden separation.

The text behind the rapture. Many warm-hearted believers hold that Christ will quietly remove his church before the tribulation, and they long for his appearing. But the verse will not carry it, because of the analogy Jesus has just supplied. In Noah’s day, who was taken? The flood took the wicked. Noah was the one left. If the days of Noah govern this picture, and Jesus says twice that they do, then to be taken is not rescue but judgment, and the popular reading has the verse the wrong way round.

Not quiet, and not secret. This chapter has insisted three times: the coming is like lightning from east to west (v. 27), all the tribes of the earth see him (v. 30), and there is a trumpet loud enough to gather the elect from the four winds (v. 31). A silent disappearance is the one thing Matthew 24 has gone out of its way to rule out.

But what about 1 Thessalonians 4? There Paul says that the living will be caught up together with the dead in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17). That passage is gloriously true, and it is not secret either: it has a cry of command, the voice of an archangel and the sound of the trumpet of God, with the dead in Christ rising first. And the word Paul uses for that meeting was often used for a civic welcome. When a king or governor approached a city, the citizens went out to meet him on the road and escorted him back in; it is the same word used when the believers in Rome came out to meet Paul and walked with him into the city (Acts 28:15). That is the picture: not the church evacuated away from the earth, but the church going out to meet her returning King and coming back with him. Paul and Matthew describe one event, not two, and the church has no need of a secret preliminary coming to make sense of either.

A harder comfort and a better one. A rapture before the trouble promises that Christians will be spared the worst. Jesus promises something sturdier: the one who endures to the end will be saved (v. 13), and for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short (v. 22). The storm has been measured, and he will be there at the end of it. That comfort has held for every generation of martyrs who were not spared and were never once abandoned.

I was taught the rapture all my life. Must I give up my hope? No, only its timetable. Everything you loved in that teaching is true: Jesus is really coming back, bodily and gloriously; he will really gather his people to himself; the dead in Christ will really rise; and we will really be with the Lord for ever. What changes is only the idea of two comings, one secret and one public, and of being lifted out before the trouble. Your hope is not smaller for that; it is safer, because it no longer depends on escaping suffering. And treat brothers and sisters who still hold the other view with warmth. They are longing for the same Lord.

On a Tuesday. You may work beside someone every day who is not ready for Christ’s coming. Hold before God the person at the next desk or on the same shift, and ask him for one natural opportunity this week to speak of him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two women will be grinding at the mill. Daily work in every household, often two women sitting opposite each other at one hand mill, close enough to talk all morning.

One will be taken and one left. Outdoors and indoors, men and women: no occupation is exempt from this reckoning.

Nothing visible separated them. To anybody watching, the two women were the same, and something separated them. The present age produces apparent equality; his coming produces the real division, and the second bears no reliable relation to the first.

The Shepherd who divides. What separated them was whether each woman belonged to the Lord who knows his own. I am the good shepherd, Jesus said; I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). In the next chapter he pictures the same moment as a shepherd separating the sheep from the goats (25:32). The line is drawn by Christ, not by chance or merit.

Two directions. That cuts two ways. It forbids confidence about anybody else: you cannot read the state of the person beside you at the mill, and a great deal of religious conversation consists of pretending otherwise. And it forbids confidence about yourself on the grounds of nearness. Sitting at the same stone as a believing woman, for years, sharing her work and her talk and her table, did not make the second woman what the first one was. Nearness to the faithful is not the same as faith, and it is the most comfortable substitute there is.

What about my children or my husband who are not believers? This verse is hard to read when you love someone who is not in Christ, and it is meant to move you to prayer, not despair. You cannot believe on their behalf, and your faith does not cover them. But God often works through the believer at the same stone: Peter tells believing wives that their husbands may be won without a word by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2), and Paul says the unbelieving spouse is in a sense set apart by the believer’s presence (1 Corinthians 7:14). So pray for them daily and by name, live the gospel before them, speak of Christ when the door opens, and leave them in the hands of the God who saves. The separation has not happened yet. Today is still the day of salvation. And if someone you love has already died with no sign of faith that you could see, you are not asked to pronounce on them. You may grieve, and leave them with the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25).
verseByVerse.note: Grinding grain with a hand mill was daily work, often done by two women together.

parallels.desc: the slave girl behind the handmill

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what part of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, stay awake. Stay awake (grēgoreite), the command the whole discourse builds toward, and the one he would give in Gethsemane two days later (26:38–41). The reason: you do not know on what day your Lord is coming, and the Lord he means is himself.

If the master of the house had known. Thieves literally dug through mud-brick walls (6:19). Jesus compares his coming to a thief’s (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 16:15), not in its character, but in its timing.

What stay awake does not mean. It has been made to mean several things Jesus plainly did not mean. It does not mean reading the news apocalyptically. Generation after generation has believed itself the last, and the ones most certain of it have been most reliably wrong, and Jesus has just said that no one knows the day. A Christian who is confident he has worked out the timetable has not achieved deeper insight than his Lord; he has contradicted him. Nor does it mean living in dread. See that you are not alarmed is a command in this very discourse (v. 6), and Jesus’ own picture of a ready servant is not a man scanning the horizon but one handing out food at the proper time, the most ordinary duty imaginable, done on schedule.

What if the thought of his return frightens me? Some people were raised on end-times films and wall charts and can remember being frightened as children by an empty house, and the fear has never entirely gone. It should be said plainly that this is not what the chapter is for. Wherever the New Testament speaks of the church’s own attitude to that day, the emotion is longing, not terror: Maranatha, our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22); a crown laid up for all who have loved his appearing (2 Timothy 4:8); the Spirit and the Bride say, Come (Revelation 22:17). The One who is coming is the One who died for you. If the thought of his return frightens you more than it gladdens you, the remedy is not more information about the timeline but more time with the Saviour himself. John says that perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

What it does mean. It is simple enough to act on tonight: live so that his arrival would not require a change of plan. Is there anything in your week you would need to stop, or start, if you knew he were coming on Thursday? An account to settle, a habit to end, a person to forgive, a conversation you have been avoiding, a promise to keep. If something came to mind, you have your instruction, and the reason to act is not that the date is near but precisely that it is unknown.

A thief only to the unready. A thief is a disaster only to a house that was not ready. To a household waiting for its own master, the same unannounced hour is the best news of the year. Paul says exactly this: you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief (1 Thessalonians 5:4).

For worship. He watched when we slept. In Gethsemane, while his friends could not stay awake one hour, he kept vigil alone, sorrowful even to death, and prayed three times over the cup (26:38–44). Our watchfulness is weak and fitful, but it rests on his, and he will come not as a thief to those who love him, but as the Bridegroom to his bride.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had walls of mud brick that a thief could dig through.

parallels.desc: like a thief in the night

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore you also must be ready. Readiness is not calculating dates, but living faithfully. Ignorance of the time is not an excuse for delay; it is the entire argument for readiness now.

For the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. Stronger than unknown: the hour you would not have guessed. The natural instinct about when is not simply uninformed; it is actively wrong, and the more confident it is the more wrong it will prove.

The unspoken assumption. Very few Christians deny the return of Christ. What we do instead is assume, without ever putting it into words, that it will not be soon: not this year, not before the children are grown, not before the thing we are in the middle of has resolved. Never stated, it quietly organises the calendar.

Being ready and getting ready. The difference between a fire drill and a fireproof building. A drill assumes an alarm. What Jesus describes has none, only the state of the house beforehand.

Faithfulness, not withdrawal. Calvin’s observation is the right corrective to the obvious misuse of this verse. Christian hope has never produced its best fruit in men who withdrew from the world to wait; it produces servants who get on with their work precisely because the Master may arrive during it. Readiness in this chapter looks remarkably like ordinary faithfulness, done today, in case today is the day.

How do I know if I am ready? Readiness begins with being in Christ: trusting him alone for forgiveness and standing in his righteousness, not your own. No amount of activity makes up for that, and no unfinished task undoes it. If you belong to him, you are ready in the deepest sense, because the Judge is your Saviour. Then readiness grows as the shape of a life: keeping short accounts with God and with others, doing the work he has given you, loving the people in front of you, and holding this world loosely. You will never feel perfectly prepared. The question is not whether everything is finished, but whether you are his, and found at your post.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his master has set over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who then is the faithful and wise servant. The first of four pictures of readiness (24:45–25:46). After all the cosmic language, the landing is deliberately small. Faithful: he can be left. Wise: he knows what is needed and when. Neither word is about brilliance or scale.

Whom his master has set over his household. A steward over the other servants: especially church leaders (Luke 12:41–42), but every disciple given responsibility.

Their food at the proper time. For pastors, feeding God’s people with his word (John 21:15–17). That clause is the entire job description: not to expand the estate or watch the road, but to feed the household on time.

The Servant who fed the household. There has been one steward over God’s house who never failed to feed it on time. Jesus fed five thousand when the disciples wanted to send them away (14:15–21), and on the night he was betrayed he took bread and gave it to them, saying, take, eat; this is my body (26:26). Hebrews says he was faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:6). Every faithful servant in this parable is a small likeness of the Servant who did it first and perfectly, and whose faithfulness is counted to his servants, so that their patchy stewardship is accepted for his sake.

Blessed is that servant. The blessing falls on what he is found doing. Not the one who had stopped, nor the one who intended to start. So the question is never what you have achieved in the abstract but what you would be found at, and that question can be asked about this afternoon.

Your own food at the proper time. Everybody has one, and it is almost never impressive: a class, an aged parent, a struggling friend, three grandchildren. The food is whatever they need from you, when it is needed rather than when it is convenient. The whole weight of this chapter, the signs, the tribulation, the shaking of the heavens, comes down at last on whether a man did the small thing he was given, on the day it was due.

What if my work seems too small to matter? Then this parable is for you. The master does not ask the steward to do something remarkable; he asks him to feed the household on time. Changing nappies, caring for an elderly parent, teaching a Sunday school class of four, doing honest work in an office: these are exactly the kind of service the returning Lord looks for. Paul tells slaves that whatever they do, they serve the Lord Christ, and will receive the inheritance as their reward (Colossians 3:23–24). God does not measure by the size of the task but by faithfulness in it, and he sees what nobody else notices.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. But if that wicked servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over all his possessions. The reward for faithfulness is greater responsibility (25:21). In the kingdom, the faithful will share Christ’s rule (19:28; Revelation 3:21). Nothing in Scripture suggests that heaven is a retirement. The reward for work is work, on a scale the worker could not previously have carried.

Fellow heirs with the Son. The servant’s reward is borrowed from his Master’s. The Son is heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and the faithful are given a share: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if we suffer with him that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). The reward is not a separate prize. It is the Son’s own inheritance, shared.

My master is delayed. The same servant, choosing differently. Everything about the wicked servant begins in one sentence he never says out loud.

A revised timetable. The verb is chronizei: he is taking his time. This is not unbelief. The servant does not conclude that there is no master, or that the master is never coming back, or that the estate is now his. He revises a timetable. Everything that follows, the violence, the drinking, the ruin, is downstream of a small adjustment to an expected date, made privately, and never examined again. That is how respectable people go wrong: nobody decides to become the wicked servant. The doctrine of delay is never professed. It is simply operated.

Its innocent vocabulary. Its everyday words are completely innocent. I will deal with that later. There is time. Not this year. When things settle down. When the children are older. Once this project is finished. Every one of those sentences may be perfectly reasonable about a diary. Applied to a debt owed to God, a sin to be abandoned, a person to be forgiven, a wrong to be confessed, a call to be obeyed, each is the servant’s sentence in modern dress, and it works the same way: it does not deny the master, it postpones him, and the postponement does all the damage the denial would have done.

Has the master not been delayed after all, after two thousand years? From where we stand it looks long, but Scripture answers the scoffers directly: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:8–9). Every year of waiting has been a year of the gospel reaching another people (v. 14), and you are probably reading this because of it. The servant’s mistake was not that he noticed time passing. It was that he let the passing of time make his master less real to him.

Will there be different rewards in heaven? Yes, Scripture teaches that the faithful will be rewarded, and not all identically (25:21–23; Luke 19:17–19; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). But the rewards are all of grace. God crowns his own gifts in us, and no one earns heaven itself, which is given freely to all in Christ. That means every good work he rewards is one he first worked in us (Philippians 2:13), so even the reward is grace. The greatest reward is the Master himself and the joy of hearing his well done. There will be no envy in glory, because every vessel will be full, and every crown will be cast before the throne.

parallels.desc: “Where is the promise of his coming?”

verseByVerse.quote: "and begins to beat his fellow servants and eats and drinks with drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Begins to beat his fellow servants. Abuse of power is the sign of a heart that does not expect to give account (1 Peter 5:3). He turns on the very people he was appointed to feed. Authority given for service, turned against those it was given for, is one of the ugliest things in Scripture, and Jesus has already named it in this Gospel: the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them; it shall not be so among you (20:25–26). And he gave the reason in himself: even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28).

Eats and drinks with drunkards. The detail is the company rather than the drink: a man behaving badly assembles company that will not raise an eyebrow. First the timetable moves, then the company changes, then the behaviour follows the company, and at every stage it feels like a series of small social decisions rather than anything spiritual.

Aimed with precision. It is a warning to people with authority over other people in the Master’s house: pastors, elders, teachers, employers, fathers, anyone who has been set over a household of any kind. The higher the trust, the more the doctrine of delay costs the people underneath it.

A day he does not expect. The unexpectedness he had been banking on is what catches him: the licence turns out to be the trap.

What if a leader in my church, or someone in my home, is abusing their power? Christ’s verdict on this servant is clear, and so should ours be: abuse is never to be tolerated, excused or covered up, and certainly not in the name of submission or church unity. If you are being harmed, or a child or vulnerable person is, get to safety and report it to the civil authorities, who are God’s servants for exactly this purpose (Romans 13:3–4), and tell church leaders you trust. Scripture calls those in authority to give account (Hebrews 13:17; James 3:1), and it rebukes publicly an elder who persists in sin (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Headship in the home and leadership in the church are given for self-giving service, never for domination. The Master will judge the one who beats his fellow servants, and he wants his church to protect them now.

verseByVerse.quote: "and will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cut him in pieces. Literally cut him in two (dichotomēsei), a real ancient punishment (Hebrews 11:37), and shocking on purpose. The parable of meals and keys ends with extreme severity, because the betrayal of a trust of that kind is not a small thing in the master’s eyes.

Put him with the hypocrites. The word of the woes in chapter 23: the actor in the mask. He is not sentenced as a rebel or an unbeliever. He is sentenced as a performer, because that is what he was: a man who held the office, wore the role, and had privately decided the master was not coming.

The weeping and the gnashing of teeth. Matthew’s refrain (8:12; 25:30): grief and rage together; sorrow that has not become repentance.

Is the wicked servant a believer who loses his salvation? The more likely reading is that he is an insider who never truly shared his master’s heart, the same as those in 7:21–23 and the foolish virgins of 25:12; his conduct shows what he was (1 John 2:19). Those who belong to Christ endure to the end (v. 13), because Christ keeps them.

Does cut in pieces mean the wicked simply cease to exist? No. The very next words describe a place where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, and you cannot weep if you no longer exist. Cut in pieces is a picture of the severity of judgment, not a description of annihilation. Jesus teaches consistently that the punishment of the wicked is conscious and unending: they go away into eternal punishment, as the righteous into eternal life (25:46), and the same word eternal describes both. This is a terrible truth, and it is often noted that Jesus spoke of it more than anyone else in Scripture; he did so as the One who wept over the city that refused him (Luke 19:41), so that no one need go there. It is meant to drive us to the One who bore judgment for all who trust in him.

Is such severity fair? It feels excessive only if sin is small. The weight of a wrong is measured partly by the one it is done against, and this servant betrayed a trust from a holy Master and used it to beat the very people he was given to feed. We do not call a judge cruel when he is severe with a man who abused the children in his care; we would call him corrupt if he were not. God’s judgment is not a loss of temper but his holiness meeting what is evil, and it will be exact, never more than is deserved (Romans 2:5–6). And the same God took the full severity of it on himself at the cross, so that no one who comes to Christ need bear it.

Stand back and look. The discourse’s shape is the answer to the question that started it. The disciples pointed at masonry and asked when, and what the sign would be. A chapter of extraordinary material follows: armies, false messiahs, the abomination, the sun darkened, the Son of Man on the clouds, angels and a trumpet from one end of heaven to the other. And it comes to rest on a servant, in a kitchen, handing out food at the proper time. They asked for a date and were given a job.

Sober, not terrified. The chapter ends on sobriety, not terror. The threat is not aimed at the frightened; it is aimed at the comfortable, and specifically at the trusted. A servant who is anxious about his master’s return is not the man in this parable; the man in this parable had stopped thinking about it altogether.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s return is good news for faithful servants and terrible news for hypocrites. If you are unsure which you are, do not try to settle it by looking at your record. Go to Christ today as a sinner, and serve him from there.

For worship. The faithful Servant was cut off from the land of the living for us. He who never wore a mask was numbered with the transgressors, handed over at an hour he knew exactly, and bore the judgment hypocrites deserve, so that sinners who had played at religion might become true servants and sons. Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up (Isaiah 52:13). The Master who is coming is the Servant who died, and those who are his will hear from his own lips: well done, enter into the joy of your master.

24.theology: The already and the not yet. The kingdom has arrived in Christ but is not yet complete. AD 70 belongs to the already: the end of the old covenant order and a public sign that the Son of Man had been enthroned. His final return is the not yet: the resurrection of the dead and the new creation. The church lives and works between the two, certain of the end and ignorant of its date.
24.examples:
Then: For the first Christians the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 could have shaken their faith. Jesus had prepared them: this was foretold, it is not the end, and the gospel must still go to all nations. The church survived because it had been warned.

Now: Every generation has voices announcing the end from the news. Jesus’ commands do not change: do not be alarmed, do not be led astray, stay awake, keep working. The day and hour are known only to the Father, so the church’s calling today is what it was yesterday: proclaim the gospel and be found faithful when he comes.

25.title: Ready, Faithful, and Merciful
25.text: <sup>1</sup>“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. <sup>2</sup>Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. <sup>3</sup>For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, <sup>4</sup>but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps. <sup>5</sup>As the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. <sup>6</sup>But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’ <sup>7</sup>Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. <sup>8</sup>And the foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ <sup>9</sup>But the wise answered, saying, ‘Since there will not be enough for us and for you, go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves.’ <sup>10</sup>And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut. <sup>11</sup>Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, ‘Lord, lord, open to us.’ <sup>12</sup>But he answered, ‘Truly, I say to you, I do not know you.’ <sup>13</sup>Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour. <sup>14</sup>“For it will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. <sup>15</sup>To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability. Then he went away. <sup>16</sup>He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them, and he made five talents more. <sup>17</sup>So also he who had the two talents made two talents more. <sup>18</sup>But he who had received the one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master’s money. <sup>19</sup>Now after a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. <sup>20</sup>And he who had received the five talents came forward, bringing five talents more, saying, ‘Master, you delivered to me five talents; here, I have made five talents more.’ <sup>21</sup>His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.’ <sup>22</sup>And he also who had the two talents came forward, saying, ‘Master, you delivered to me two talents; here, I have made two talents more.’ <sup>23</sup>His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.’ <sup>24</sup>He also who had received the one talent came forward, saying, ‘Master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed, <sup>25</sup>so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours.’ <sup>26</sup>But his master answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant! You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed? <sup>27</sup>Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received what was my own with interest. <sup>28</sup>So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents. <sup>29</sup>For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>30</sup>And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ <sup>31</sup>“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. <sup>32</sup>Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. <sup>33</sup>And he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on the left. <sup>34</sup>Then the King will say to those on his right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. <sup>35</sup>For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, <sup>36</sup>I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.’ <sup>37</sup>Then the righteous will answer him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? <sup>38</sup>And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you? <sup>39</sup>And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?’ <sup>40</sup>And the King will answer them, ‘Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’ <sup>41</sup>“Then he will say to those on his left, ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. <sup>42</sup>For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink, <sup>43</sup>I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.’ <sup>44</sup>Then they also will answer, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?’ <sup>45</sup>Then he will answer them, saying, ‘Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.’ <sup>46</sup>And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
25.overview:
Chapter 25 closes the Olivet Discourse with three pictures of how to live between Christ’s ascension and his return. The ten virgins teach readiness: oil cannot be borrowed at the last moment. The talents teach faithfulness: the servant who buries what he was given is condemned not for wickedness but for fearful inaction. The sheep and the goats show that love for Christ is expressed in love for the hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner.

Together they describe the waiting Christian life: ready, through the Spirit’s inward work; faithful, putting to use what has been given; and merciful, serving Christ in the neighbour who suffers. The final scene, the most solemn in Matthew, does not teach salvation by works; it shows the fruit of faith, for those who love the King will love those he loves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — The Ten Virgins and the Parable of the Talents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two parables press the same point from opposite sides. Ten girls go out to escort a bridegroom; five have brought oil and five have not, and the difference is invisible until a cry at midnight and a door that shuts. Then a man going abroad entrusts three servants with a fortune; two trade and double it, and the third buries his. The first parable asks what you brought. The second asks what you did.
verseByVerse.theology: Neither failure in these parables is an act of wickedness. The foolish girls lacked something inward that could not be borrowed or bought in a hurry. The one-talent servant stole nothing and lost nothing, and his ruin traces to his picture of God: I knew you to be a hard man. Both parables expose nominal religion: enough to look ready, and nothing underneath that lasts a delay.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch, in v. 13, cannot mean stay awake, because all ten slept and five were commended. It means be provisioned, in the ordinary, unhurried hours. In the talents parable the bank, requiring no skill and no nerve, would have been enough. And no servant in the story tries and fails; the failure judged is not the failed attempt but the burial. The cure for the third servant’s fear is to know God better.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 25 completes Jesus’ teaching on his return with three pictures of the last day. Ten bridesmaids wait for a delayed bridegroom, and only those with oil go in: be ready, with a faith that is real, however long the wait. Three servants receive their master’s fortune, and one buries it: be faithful with all God has given. Then the Son of Man sits on his throne and separates the nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. In each scene the dividing line runs through a group that looked the same. And the speaker, two days later, would be judged in our place.

The setting. Jesus is still on the Mount of Olives (24:36–51), and the chapter’s first word, Then, ties what follows to the coming of the Son of Man.

Ten virgins. Virgins means young unmarried women, bridesmaids, friends of the bride. At a Jewish wedding of the time the bridegroom seems usually to have gone with his friends, in the evening, to the bride’s home to fetch her, and then led a procession back to his own home for the feast. The bridesmaids were not guests killing time. They were the escort, and their task was to be at the door with light when he came, and to walk him in.

The Bridegroom is the LORD. Jesus has already called himself the bridegroom (9:15), and no Jew could hear that title without remembering whose it was. Your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name (Isaiah 54:5); I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19). Now a carpenter from Nazareth casts himself, without explanation, in the role that belongs to God alone. John the Baptist understood it: the one who has the bride is the bridegroom, and he was only his friend (John 3:29). The night, the lamps and the shut door all matter because of who is coming down the street.

Lamps or torches. The word lampas can mean a small clay lamp but often means a torch: oil-soaked rags wrapped round a stick, which burn brightly and fast and need fresh oil to keep going. If that is the picture, the flask is not a spare but the whole means of lasting the night.

Foolish and wise. The two adjectives, phronimoi and mōrai, are the pair Matthew used at the close of the Sermon on the Mount, of the man who built on rock and the man who built on sand (7:24–27). Those two houses also looked identical until the weather arrived.

Count what the ten share. All ten were invited, had lamps, waited at the same door, fell asleep and woke at the cry. There is exactly one difference in the whole parable, and it is a flask that nobody could see. The division at the end does not run between the church and the world. It runs down the middle of the group that came out to meet him, and no one could have drawn it, least of all the foolish girls, who had no idea until midnight.

So are the foolish virgins Christians? They are people who looked like Christians, and probably thought they were. They belonged to the wedding party, carried the right equipment and waited in the right place. The parable is not describing true believers who lose their salvation; at the end the bridegroom says I do not know you (v. 12), not I no longer know you. It is describing the visible church, which in every age contains real believers and those who have only the outward form. That is why the parable is addressed to insiders. It does not ask whether you are in the right group. It asks whether you have the one thing that cannot be seen.
verseByVerse.note: At a wedding the bridegroom went at night to fetch his bride, and the party escorted them with lamps — probably torches fuelled with oil.

verseByVerse.quote: "For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is the oil? Jesus does not say, and we should not press the details too far. The main point is preparedness. But many have seen the oil as the reality of saving faith and the inner life of the Spirit (in Scripture, oil often pictures the Holy Spirit, Zechariah 4:1–6), as opposed to the outward appearance of religion (the lamp). The foolish have the form of godliness without its power (2 Timothy 3:5). The lamp without oil is a profession of faith without genuine faith and new life. What does the inner life of the Spirit actually mean? It is God himself living in a believer, giving him a real trust in Christ, a new love for God and a desire to please him, which no amount of church attendance can supply (Romans 8:9; Galatians 5:22–23).

Four clues. The oil is needed for the long haul, cannot be borrowed, cannot be obtained at the last minute, and is invisible from outside. Whatever meets that description is an inward reality, held personally and acquired in advance.

The lamp and the flask. Put this question to yourself in the daylight, the only time it can be answered. The lamp is the part other people see: the attendance, the answers, the role you fill, the way you pray aloud. The flask is whatever is there on a Tuesday when nobody is watching: a heart that actually trusts Christ, turns to him in secret, and is being changed by his Spirit. Everybody has a lamp. It is entirely possible to reach the age of sixty in a church without ever having been asked about the flask.

Anointed with the oil of gladness. Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song, and of the bridegroom king it says: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions (Psalm 45:7). Hebrews 1:9 applies those words to the Son. The name Christ itself means the Anointed One. Risen and exalted, he received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out on his church (Acts 2:33). So the oil the bridegroom looks for in his bridesmaids is oil that first ran down on him. Nobody brings to this wedding anything the Bridegroom did not first possess in fullness and then give.

How do I get oil? Not by anxious effort, which is precisely what the foolish girls attempted at midnight and precisely what failed. Saving faith and the life of the Spirit are gifts of God, received by coming to Christ (Ephesians 2:8; Luke 11:13). Jesus promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him. So ask, now, in the daylight. Turn from relying on your own religion, trust Christ himself for forgiveness, and keep coming to him through his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and his people, which are the means by which he keeps the flask full.
