And if this raises the fear that you are one of the foolish five, hold on to the promise that has no conditions about how much oil you bring: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "As the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. But at midnight there was a cry, 'Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the bridegroom was delayed. The word, chronizontos, is the one the wicked servant used in the previous chapter: my master is delayed (24:48). One man reorganised his life around the delay; these girls simply got sleepy. In neither parable is the delay the problem. It only reveals what was already true.

Delay is built in. Jesus puts it deliberately into a parable told to men who wanted his return soon. Christians who assumed a short wait and grew disillusioned have not been let down by God; they have misread the story.

The Bridegroom who keeps his word. The one who is delayed is the one who said, I will come again and will take you to myself (John 14:3). His lateness is not forgetfulness. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but patient (2 Peter 3:9), and every hour of the long evening is an hour in which the gospel goes out to the nations (24:14) and another guest is brought in for the feast. The Bridegroom waits until the last of those the Father gave him is ready, and then he comes, not a minute early and not a minute late.

They all became drowsy and slept. Sleep is not the problem here (unlike 24:42–43); the wise slept too. The difference is preparation made before they slept. Whatever readiness means here, it is compatible with being asleep at the moment of arrival.

At midnight there was a cry. At the hour of least readiness (24:44): not at dusk, when the street was full, but when the shops were shut and every one of the ten was asleep.

Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him. To meet (apantēsin) is the word Paul uses of believers meeting the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17), a word often used of a welcoming party going out to escort an arriving dignitary home. The cry comes once, without warning, and does not wait for anybody to get organised.

Is it wrong to be tired in my faith? No, and this parable is gentle on exactly that point. Long waiting is tiring, and there are seasons when believers feel drowsy, dry and weary. The wise virgins slept, and were still ready, because their readiness did not depend on how alert they felt but on what they had. If you are in a dull season, do not conclude that you have lost your oil. Keep to the ordinary means of grace, rest in Christ’s keeping, and ask him to revive you. Readiness is not a feeling you sustain; it is a relationship he sustains.

parallels.desc: lest he come suddenly and find you asleep

verseByVerse.quote: "Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. And the foolish said to the wise, 'Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trimmed their lamps. They cut away the charred wick, or re-soaked the rag, the ordinary business of getting a light to burn. In the middle of it five of them discover something has gone wrong.

Our lamps are going out. Note the tense: not our lamps will not light, but they are going out, guttering. They had been burning for hours, and looked exactly like everybody else’s. The appearance of faith can last a while, then fail (13:20–21), and the failure shows only at the end of the supply.

A request that cannot be granted. The request is perfectly reasonable between friends, and it is refused, and the refusal is not unkindness. If the oil stands for an inward reality personally held, then sharing it is not stingy but impossible, in the same way that a man cannot lend another his eyesight, or eat a meal on his behalf.

From his fullness we have all received. The wise girls cannot share their oil, and no believer can hand another his faith. There is one exception, and the whole gospel hangs on it. Of Christ alone it is written that from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16). He is not a bridesmaid with a single flask but the source of every drop (John 3:34). What the wise could not do for the foolish, he does for all who come to him, and the request the foolish made of the wrong people at the wrong hour he grants every day, in daylight, to anyone who asks.

If someone I knew seemed to believe and then fell away, was their faith never real? Scripture speaks soberly here. John says of some who left the church that they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19), and Jesus describes seed that springs up quickly and withers under pressure (13:20–21). So it is possible to have a flame that burns for years and is not saving faith. But be careful in applying this to any particular person. You do not know the end of their story; Peter fell badly and was restored. Pray for them, keep the door open, and leave the final judgment to the Bridegroom, who alone knows his own. And let it make you humble rather than proud: by grace alone you stand.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the wise answered, saying, 'Since there will not be enough for us and for you, go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves.' And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not transferable. Many people are quietly relying on exactly this arrangement. A mother’s faith does not cover her son. A congregation’s soundness does not cover the member sitting in it. A Christian upbringing, a name on a roll, a family with a long history in the church: every one of those is a flask belonging to somebody else. On that night five girls who had known the other five all their lives discovered that nearness carries nothing across.

The one righteousness that does transfer. And yet the gospel announces one great transfer, and it is not between bridesmaids. No sinner can borrow a neighbour’s goodness, but every sinner who trusts Christ is clothed in his. For our sake God made him to be sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). Our guilt was laid on him; his obedience is counted as ours. Justification is Scripture’s name for this: the Judge pronounces a sinner right with him, not because the sinner has turned good, but because Christ’s perfect record has been put to his account (Romans 4:5). The oil cannot pass from friend to friend, because it was never the friends’ to give. It passes from the Bridegroom to his bride, and he gives it gladly, freely, and before midnight.

Go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves. It sounds like practical advice and is an impossible errand, and everyone listening knew it. It is midnight in a village; the dealers are asleep and the procession is already in the street. The parable lets it stand as a measure of how late it now is.

While they were going to buy. They were absent for the one minute that mattered, and absent because they were off trying to fix the problem: the last-minute scramble is the very thing that keeps them from the door. Ready is the key word (24:44), and the feast is the joy of the kingdom (22:2; Revelation 19:9).

And the door was shut. Final and irreversible, like the door of Noah’s ark, which God shut (Genesis 7:16). These are quiet words and frightening ones: no thunder, no scene, only the household door barred once the wedding party was inside. And the bridegroom answers from inside. The door is his door, and by telling the story at all he issues the warning while it stands wide.

Then are my prayers for my family useless? Not at all. God has answered ten thousand such prayers, and a praying mother is one of the great instruments in his hand (Acts 16:31; 2 Timothy 1:5). The point is narrower and harder. Your faith is not a substitute for theirs. But your prayers, your example and your words may be the very means by which they come to have oil of their own. So keep praying, and speak to them of Christ while the door is open. They will have to have it of their own, and God delights to give it.

For worship. The door that will one day be shut stands open now, held by the One who said, I am the door. He opened it at the cost of his own body, and he stands in it calling the weary and the late. Blessed be the Bridegroom who warns before he shuts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, 'Lord, lord, open to us.' But he answered, 'Truly, I say to you, I do not know you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, lord, open to us. The same words as 7:21–22, and the connection with the Sermon on the Mount is deliberate.

I do not know you. The same verdict as 7:23: I never knew you. They had a lamp, an invitation, a place in the group, but no relationship with the bridegroom. Knowledge here is the intimate, covenant knowledge of union with Christ through faith, not information about him (Galatians 4:9). It is the final verdict on merely nominal religion: the outward trappings without the inward reality of new birth and living faith. What does it actually mean to be known by Christ? It means to belong to him, as a shepherd knows his own sheep: he has set his love on you, joined you to himself and calls you his own (John 10:14; 2 Timothy 2:19). The foolish knew a great deal about the bridegroom; he had never made them his.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn entry by having enough oil, as if the oil were good works. The oil pictures genuine readiness: true faith, which God gives.

What if I am afraid I am one of the five? A word must be said to the reader those words have frightened, because this chapter will produce that reader by the hundred. Three scenes in a row, and in every one of them somebody who looked like an insider is shut outside. A tender conscience closes the chapter and asks: is that me? Then look hard at the ones who are actually condemned here, and notice what none of them is doing. The foolish virgins are not anxious; they are untroubled right up to the midnight cry. The one-talent servant is not worried about pleasing his master; he is resentful, and calls him a hard man to his face. The goats are not lying awake wondering whether they have neglected anyone; they are genuinely astonished to hear that they did. Not one of the lost in this entire chapter is troubled about their standing. The very fear you are feeling is the one thing none of them had. The same is true of another terror: the man who dreads having committed the unforgivable sin (12:31–32) has given the surest evidence that he has not, because the sin Jesus warns of there is a hardened refusal of the Spirit, not a troubled conscience.

Where assurance comes from. Assurance is not manufactured by inspecting your own lamp in a panic; that always finds too little. It comes from coming to the Bridegroom now, while the door stands wide. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37) is the promise, and it has no small print about how much oil you brought. And as you rest in him, the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16), and the fruit he produces confirms it.

Let the warning do its own work. It is real, and meant to be felt, but its purpose is to send you to him this evening. A warning that persuades you the door is shut has been misread.

verseByVerse.quote: "Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch therefore. The same command as 24:42.

An oddity in the moral. In the story just told, every one of the ten was asleep when he came, and five were commended anyway. If watching meant staying awake, the parable would have condemned all ten. So watchfulness here means being provisioned. The wise were asleep at the cry and entirely ready, because everything that made them ready had been done in the afternoon.

Freeing and demanding. That is freeing, because no Christian is required to sustain a fever of expectancy, which produces exhaustion and guilt in about equal measure. And it is demanding, because readiness is built in daylight, on ordinary days: a servant handing out food at the proper time (24:45–46), a sentry found at his post whenever the inspection falls.

Five times over. He has now given the reason five times in one discourse (24:36, 42, 44, 50 and here), and every man who has published a date has had to get past it.

The one who watched while we slept. Two nights after telling this parable, Jesus took three of his disciples into Gethsemane and asked them to do exactly this: remain here, and watch with me (26:38). The same verb. And three times he came back and found them sleeping. In the hour that decided everything, the only one awake was the Bridegroom himself, watching and praying alone while his friends slept on the ground beside him. Our readiness was secured by a vigil we did not keep. He watched for us in the garden and was taken for us to the cross, and those who belong to him are kept by his wakefulness, not their own.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability. Then he went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man going on a journey. The second parable of readiness. Everything the servants manage is his.

Five talents, two, one. A talent (talanton) was a unit of weight for silver or gold, worth about 6,000 denarii, about twenty years’ wages for a labourer. Our English word talent, meaning a natural ability, comes from this parable. But in the parable, the talents represent everything God entrusts to us: abilities, opportunities, money, time, relationships, the gospel itself.

A fortune, not pocket money. Most readers now hear a story merely about using your gifts, but the money is staggering. The master puts a fortune into the hands of slaves and leaves the country, and the scale is part of the meaning: what has been entrusted to the servants of Christ between his going and his coming is not small.

To each according to his ability. The phrase carries two comforts and one demand. Nobody is handed more than he can carry; the master assessed each man before he gave anything. And nobody is handed nothing: there is no fourth servant standing empty-handed, and no Christian anywhere who has been given no capital to trade with. The demand is that the measure cuts both ways: being given less is not a reason to expect less to be asked.

The Lord who gave gifts and went. The man on the journey is Christ, and the parable is his own account of the years between his ascension and his return. Before he went, he gave. When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men (Ephesians 4:8): apostles, evangelists, shepherds, teachers, and to each of his people grace according to the measure of his gift (Ephesians 4:7). The property is his twice over: he made all things, and he bought his servants with his blood (1 Corinthians 6:20). Every capacity a Christian has is a deposit from the hand of the ascended King, entrusted by someone who knows him by name.

Then he went away. No supervision, no timetable. The whole test happens in the master’s absence, the only condition under which what a servant is really like can be discovered. The talents answer the question of 24:45, who then is the faithful and wise servant?

Two parables, one point. The ten virgins turn on what you brought: an inward provision nobody could see. The talents turn on what you did: an outward return everybody could count. Between them they close both escape routes. A man cannot say his private faith is sound while nothing whatever comes of it, and he cannot say his record is impressive while there is no flask.

What if I feel I have no talents at all? Then you are mistaken, though humbly so. Every believer has been given something: the gospel itself, the Holy Spirit, a place in the body of Christ, time, a set of relationships, some ability to help, some measure of money, a voice to pray with. Paul says each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7). Your talent may not be visible on a platform. It may be faithfulness at a hospital bedside, patience with a difficult child, a gift for noticing the lonely, or the simple capacity to pray. Ask God, and ask a mature friend: what has he put into my hands? Then begin there.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a talent was worth about twenty years’ wages for a labourer — a huge sum even for the one-talent servant.

parallels.desc: a man going on a journey

verseByVerse.quote: "He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them, and he made five talents more. So also he who had the two talents made two talents more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Went at once and traded. At once: not after due consideration, not when the market looked favourable, but before the size of the sum could frighten him. Traded (ērgasato) means worked, did business.

Faithfulness is not safety. The verb is a merchant’s word: he put his master’s money at risk, and this is the behaviour commended. Whatever faithfulness means here, it does not mean safety.

Two talents more. Different sums, identical proportion, and in a few verses, word for word, an identical commendation. The two-talent man is never once compared to the five-talent man, and the comparison a Christian is most tempted to make is simply not one the master ever performs.

A small allocation is not a light one. Both men doubled. The two-talent servant is expected to do with two exactly what the other did with five, which is everything he could.

Free from comparison. There is a quiet freedom here for anyone who has spent years measuring himself against somebody more gifted: whatever was put into your hands was put there by someone who had already weighed what you could carry.

The faithful Servant behind the faithful servants. The word the master will use for these men, faithful, belongs first to the Lord who tells the story. Jesus was faithful to him who appointed him, as a son over God’s house (Hebrews 3:2, 6). He is the Servant in whom God’s soul delights (12:18), who set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Everything these servants do, they do by the Spirit he gives and on his capital: apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). Every doubled talent in the history of the church is fruit grown on his vine.

What does trading with my talents look like in ordinary life? It means putting what God has given you to work for him, starting now, without waiting for ideal conditions. If you can teach, offer to teach. If you have money, give and invest it for the kingdom, generously and thoughtfully. If you have a home, open it. If you have time in retirement, give some of it to the young mothers, the lonely or the church’s work. If you know the gospel, tell it. It will involve some risk: you may be awkward, misunderstood, or occasionally fail. That is part of trading. Faithfulness looks for opportunities rather than waiting to be pushed.

verseByVerse.quote: "But he who had received the one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master's money."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dug in the ground. Burying money was a common way to protect it from thieves (13:44). Under later Jewish law, someone who buried money entrusted to him was not liable if it was stolen, whereas one who merely wrapped it in a cloth was held responsible. He chose the option with the best legal protection. He covered himself.

What he did not do. He did not steal the talent, gamble it away or lose it. He still has it, all of it, and can produce it on demand. But preservation was not the assignment: the money was given to be used.

A failure no discipline catches. The parable is aimed at a failure that no church discipline has ever caught. Nothing here would show up in a confession, and the man does not think he has done anything wrong. He has simply removed himself from the enterprise, quietly, in a way that looks like prudence. And when he explains himself, his motive is neither greed nor sloth in the ordinary sense but fear, rooted in a false picture of the master.

The grain that went into the ground. Jesus used the same image of the earth for himself, and turned it the other way. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). The servant put the treasure into the ground to keep it. The Son of God went into the ground to give himself away. He was buried in a borrowed tomb, not to be preserved but to be planted. A buried talent stays exactly as it was. A buried Saviour rose, and brought up with him everyone who belongs to him.

Is playing it safe in my Christian life always wrong? Caution is not sin, and wisdom considers risks (Luke 14:28). But there is a difference between wise care and a buried talent. Ask what your caution is protecting. If it protects others from harm, or your family from foolish debt, it may be wisdom. If it protects only your comfort, your reputation or your fear of failure, while a gift God gave you lies unused, it is the third servant’s choice. A useful question: if Christ asked me tomorrow what I did with this, would my answer be I kept it safe?
verseByVerse.note: Burying money was a common way to keep it safe.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now after a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. And he who had received the five talents came forward, bringing five talents more, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me five talents; here, I have made five talents more.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a long time. Another hint that Christ’s return would be delayed (24:48; 25:5): long enough for the master to become an idea rather than a presence, and for a buried talent to stop feeling like a decision and start feeling like a fact.

And settled accounts with them. The day of reckoning: every servant will give account (Romans 14:12; 2 Corinthians 5:10). The phrase, synairei logon, is the one used of the king who settled accounts in the parable of the unforgiving servant (18:23–24). Both reckonings are begun by the master, not requested by anybody, and both bring into the open what had been quietly true for years.

You delivered to me five talents. He begins with what he was given, not with what he achieved or how hard it had been, and the results follow as a plain fact.

Two opening lines. The third servant will begin with his opinion of the master (v. 24): one starts with what he received, the other with what he thought of the giver, and everything in both lives followed from that. For a servant who has traded faithfully, the reckoning is the day he has been working toward, and he comes forward first.

The Judge who settled our account. The master who returns to settle accounts is the Son, for the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). That is fearful news for anyone who has despised him, and the best news there is for those who trust him, because the Judge of their account is the one who has already paid it. He cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, setting it aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The ledger that remains is a ledger of his gifts and what his grace did with them, and he has come home to delight in it.

Should a Christian dread the day of reckoning? No. Believers will give account (2 Corinthians 5:10), but not to decide whether they belong to Christ; that was settled at the cross, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The reckoning for a believer is a Father’s assessment of his children, at which what was done for him is acknowledged and rewarded, and some worthless work is lost while the believer himself is saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). It should make us serious, and not afraid. The first servant came forward first, because he knew his master.

On a Tuesday. Begin your prayer tonight as the faithful servant began: Lord, you gave me.

verseByVerse.quote: "His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' And he also who had the two talents came forward, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me two talents; here, I have made two talents more.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Well done, good and faithful servant. The words every Christian longs to hear. Good is character; faithful is reliability; neither word is about results. What is praised is the sort of man he turned out to be while nobody was checking. Most of us live for somebody’s well done: a parent’s, a boss’s, the room’s. The hunger is not wrong; it is aimed at the wrong face.

You have been faithful over a little. Five talents was a fortune, yet the master calls it a little. From where the master stands, a fortune that took a lifetime to double is a trial run. Whatever you are carrying, and however heavy it has been, the master’s own assessment is that it was the little one.

I will set you over much. The reward for faithfulness is greater responsibility in the kingdom (24:47; Luke 19:17). The faithful are not retired; they are promoted.

Enter into the joy of your master. This reward is not like the others. He is not handed a bonus or an estate of his own. He is invited inside, into the master’s own gladness, which was never about the money.

He also who had the two talents. Matthew does something that costs him space and is entirely deliberate: he writes the whole commendation out a second time, word for word, for the man who brought two. Whatever envy a Christian has felt toward the more gifted, and whatever false modesty he has hidden behind, both are answered by a piece of repetition an editor would have cut.

The joy of the Master is the joy of Christ. Whose gladness is this? It is the joy of the Son, the joy that was set before him, for which he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). It is the delight he takes in the people he has redeemed (Zephaniah 3:17). Hours before his arrest he prayed that his people might have my joy fulfilled in themselves (John 17:13). The parable’s last reward is that prayer answered: the servant is taken into the happiness of the Son, which no one can take from him.

What will we do in heaven, if it is not rest? Scripture promises both. There is rest: a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9), rest from toil, sin, sorrow and frustration. But it is not idleness. His servants will worship him and reign for ever and ever (Revelation 22:3–5), and this parable says the faithful will be set over much. We are not told the details, and should not invent them. But whatever we do, it will be work without weariness, service without sin, and joy without end, in the presence of the Master whose joy we share.

For worship. Only one Servant ever deserved the words well done outright. Over the waters of the Jordan the Father said of his Son, with whom I am well pleased (3:17), and every well done spoken on the last day is an echo of that voice. The Father sees servants who were faithful over a little in the One who was faithful over all.

verseByVerse.quote: "His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' He also who had received the one talent came forward, saying, 'Master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who had received the one talent. The third servant speaks, and what comes out first is not an account of his conduct but a doctrine of God.

I knew you to be a hard man. Hard means harsh, severe. What he did with the money was a consequence; this was the cause.

Reaping where you did not sow. It is the portrait of an owner who profits from others’ work, impossible to satisfy and dangerous to disappoint. A man who believes he works for such a person will make exactly this servant’s calculation: nothing to gain by trying, everything to lose by failing, so protect yourself.

Refuted by his own hand. The accusation is refuted by the thing he is holding while he makes it. He says the master reaps where he did not sow, and he stands there with twenty years of wages in his hands that the master sowed into them, freely and without conditions.

The unexamined picture. Bad thinking about God is not usually held as a formal belief. It sits underneath and shows up in behaviour long before words. What do you assume, in the part of your mind that never gets audited, about the God you serve? Is he slightly disappointed with you? Would he be more interested in you if you were doing better? Nobody says these things aloud. People simply act on them, and the acting looks like caution, and the caution looks like humility.

Gentle and lowly in heart. The man telling this parable has already given his own portrait, and it is the exact opposite of the servant’s. Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (11:28–29). The hard man of the servant’s imagination reaps where he did not sow. The real Master sowed where nothing deserved it, and within a few days would let himself be bound, mocked and crucified for servants who had misjudged him. That is the face of the Master, and it is the face of God.

How can I change a hard view of God? Not by telling yourself to feel differently, but by looking at what God has actually shown of himself. Read the Gospels and watch Jesus with sinners, with children, with the frightened and the failing: he is the exact imprint of the Father’s nature (Hebrews 1:3). Look at the cross, where the God you fear as demanding gave his own Son for you while you were still his enemy (Romans 5:8–10). Notice the master in this very parable, who trusts lavishly and rejoices generously. Then bring your false picture to God in prayer, name it, and ask him to replace it with the truth. A right view of God will not make you careless. It will make you brave.

On a Tuesday. Your view of God shapes your service. Finish this sentence honestly in prayer today: Lord, I suspect you are.

verseByVerse.quote: "'so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours.' But his master answered him, 'You wicked and slothful servant! You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I was afraid. Of the three failures in this chapter, this is the one most readers will recognise in themselves: the third servant is frightened, and frightened people are usually sincere. Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18); his fear showed that he did not know that love. That is not a sentence on every anxious believer. Many of God’s children serve him trembling, and he is gentle with them: a bruised reed he will not break (12:20). This servant’s fear was of another kind. It made him think ill of his master and refuse the work altogether.

What he feared. Not punishment for wrongdoing, but getting it wrong: standing before his master with less than he started with. So he chose the option with no downside, and it turned out to be the only option in the parable with a guaranteed one.

His speech in modern clothes. I am not gifted enough to be much use. If I try and it fails publicly, that will be worse than never having tried. Someone else already does this better than I would. I will start when I am more mature, less busy, further on, more certain. Every one of them sounds like modesty.

Here, you have what is yours. He returns it unchanged and thinks this is enough: he has lost nothing.

You wicked and slothful servant! Slothful (oknēre) means lazy, hesitant. His sin was not theft but doing nothing, and sins of omission are real sins (James 4:17). Fear of failure, when it paralyses, becomes the very failure it was afraid of.

You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed? The master does not agree with his description, but takes him at his word: if you really believed that, you should have acted accordingly. His theology of God’s harshness should have produced urgency, not paralysis.

The missing scene. One servant never appears in this parable: one who traded and lost. Nobody says, I invested and it went badly. The scene most of us are afraid of is missing. The failure judged here is not the failed attempt. It is the burial.

He had the wrong God. Men do not take risks for someone they believe is waiting to catch them out. So the cure is not to try harder but to know God better, as he is seen in Jesus: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). Sons may take risks in their Father’s business, because their place in his house does not depend on the result.

What if I tried to serve God and failed? Then take heart from the missing scene. Nowhere in Scripture does God condemn a servant for trying in faith and seeing little result. Jeremiah preached for decades with almost no visible fruit, and was faithful. Paul planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Success is God’s business; faithfulness is yours. If an attempt went badly, learn what you can, confess any sin in it, and try again, perhaps differently. The Master who gave the talent knew you would make mistakes with it. What he cannot use is a talent in the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received what was my own with interest. So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the bankers. The alternative is almost insultingly modest: a deposit earning interest required no skill, nerve or work whatever.

The fear did not explain it. He said he was afraid of losing the money. The bank was the one option that removed that risk entirely, and he did not take it either. Something else was going on: a heart that did not care about the master’s interests at all, and the master’s words, you ought to have, expose it in a single clause.

What was my own with interest. The standard is far lower than anyone imagines: the least impressive option available would have been accepted. That lifts a weight off anyone waiting until he is capable of something significant, and it removes the excuse.

Give it to him who has the ten talents. It is not a reward for being rich. The master moves a resource that is producing nothing to where it will be used. The talent was never the servant’s property. It was capital on loan, and capital that is not working gets reassigned.

He notices the cup of cold water. That the master would have welcomed the smallest return tells us what kind of Lord Christ is. He sat opposite the temple treasury and saw a widow put in two small coins, and said she had given more than all the rest (Mark 12:41–44). He promised that whoever gives one of his little ones even a cup of cold water will by no means lose his reward (10:42). The Lord of this parable is not hard to please. He is easy to please and impossible to fool, and the one thing he will not accept is a gift handed back untouched.

Isn’t that unfair? It offends many modern readers on first hearing, but notice that no one is robbed. The talent belonged to the master throughout, and the third servant had shown he did not want to use it. What God entrusts is not held on indefinite terms regardless of use. A gift left buried long enough is not merely wasted; it is eventually taken up by somebody else, and the work gets done. The Master’s estate does not suffer for one servant’s caution. The loss in this parable is not the master’s. It is entirely the servant’s. And for us it is a mercy to be warned: the opportunities God gives are real, and they do not last for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To everyone who has will more be given. It is the same principle Jesus gave when he explained why he taught in parables (13:12). Read as economics it sounds monstrous, but he is stating a law about capacity that everyone has observed. A language used is kept, and a language neglected is gone in a decade; a muscle worked grows, and a limb in plaster wastes. Use enlarges, disuse shrinks, and this is true of every good thing God gives, including grace.

The worthless servant. Worthless (achreion) means useless, unprofitable. Not thief, not traitor: the judgment falls on a man whose distinguishing mark is that nothing whatever happened because of him. The outer darkness, with its weeping and gnashing of teeth, is Matthew’s settled language for final exclusion (8:12; 24:51). He is thrown out not for what he did to the master, but for what he declined to do for him.

Three absences. This is the second of the chapter’s three warnings, and the three are carefully different. The first condemns women who lacked something invisible, the second a man who did nothing with something valuable, and the third will condemn people who did not notice somebody in front of them. Not one is condemned for an act of wickedness. All three are condemned for an absence, and between them they cover most of the ways a respectable person is actually lost.

Unworthy servants, all of us. The same word appears once more in the Gospels, and it changes how a Christian hears this verse. When you have done all that you were commanded, Jesus told his disciples, say, We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty (Luke 17:10). Unworthy there is achreioi, the word for this man. In ourselves, the faithful and the slothful alike are unprofitable to God, who needs nothing from anyone. What makes the difference is not native worth but grace: the faithful have been joined to the one Servant whose work was of infinite worth, and his profit is counted as theirs. The talent-traders in heaven will not boast of their returns. They will boast of him.

Does the parable teach salvation by works? No. The one-talent servant’s problem is not that he earned too little but that he did not know or trust his master; he thought him a hard man (v. 24). He represents nominal religion that never knew the Lord. The fruit of the faithful servants is the evidence of a living faith, not the payment for salvation (James 2:26).

May a Christian invest and receive interest? The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25), which is a different thing from investment. The parable uses ordinary business as a picture and does not teach investment ethics, but it does not condemn a fair return. The point is that God expects his gifts to be used, not buried.

For worship. He who was the only truly profitable Servant was counted worthless. He was taken outside the city, numbered with the transgressors, and at noon on a Friday darkness covered the land while he bore the outer darkness that unprofitable servants deserve. There he cried out forsaken, so that servants who had buried their talents and wasted their years might be forgiven and brought into the light of his Father’s house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–46 — The Judgment of the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The discourse closes with the Son of Man on his throne, all the nations gathered, and the flock parted as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Both groups are judged by the same six acts of mercy, and both are surprised: the sheep because they cannot remember doing them, the goats because they never noticed the chance. This is not a parable but a description.
verseByVerse.theology: Who are the least of these my brothers? In Matthew my brothers nearly always means Jesus’ disciples, so the nations are judged by how they received the King through his often despised people; the principle beneath it holds wherever need is found. Before a single deed is named, the sheep inherit a kingdom prepared before there was anything to reward. The works are evidence, never the purchase price. At v. 41 the curse, unlike the blessing, is attributed to nobody, and the fire was prepared for the devil, not for human beings. At v. 46 one adjective governs both destinies, so the punishment cannot run out unless the life does too.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything on the King’s list is a service to somebody who cannot repay it. Today it is the long illness after the cards have stopped, the man whose trouble is his own fault, the visit to someone with dementia who will not remember you came. The goats’ defence admits that their service was available to importance and not to need. So ask whether the trouble you take over a person varies with what that person can do for you.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Son of Man comes in his glory. Christ’s return in glory (16:27; 24:30). The carpenter who is about to be crucified describes himself as the Judge of all the earth. The two preceding passages were parables; this one, despite the comparison of sheep and goats, is not. He has stopped illustrating and started announcing.

His glorious throne. Earlier the Son of Man was coming in the glory of his Father (16:27); here it is his glory and his throne, and the angels are his attendants (19:28). This is the Son of Man of Daniel 7, who came to the Ancient of Days and was given dominion (Daniel 7:9–14), now seated with every nation of every century before him, doing what in the Old Testament only God does: judging the earth. John tells us that the glory Isaiah saw on the throne, high and lifted up, was Christ’s (Isaiah 6:1–5; John 12:41).

All the nations. All the nations (panta ta ethnē) settles the scope: Jew and Gentile, believer and unbeliever, every people and every individual within them (Romans 14:10; Revelation 20:11–15), including everyone who was confident it would not happen. Nobody is outside the summons, and the Judge is the man who was crucified.

As a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. In Palestine, sheep and goats often grazed together during the day in mixed flocks, but were separated at night, probably because goats needed to be kept warmer. They looked similar from a distance, but a shepherd could tell them apart easily. Ezekiel 34:17 pictures God judging between sheep and sheep, rams and goats.

The work of an evening. Here is the comfort buried in a terrifying scene. The separation was a routine daily operation. The sorting of the human race looks to us impossible: billions of people, mixed motives, hypocrites indistinguishable from saints. To the shepherd it is the work of an evening. He does not investigate; he recognises.

Will my confessed sins be exposed at the judgment? For those in Christ, the judgment holds no condemnation. God has removed our transgressions as far as the east is from the west, and he remembers our sins no more (Psalm 103:12; Hebrews 8:12). Notice that when the King speaks to the sheep, he mentions only their good works, many of which they had forgotten, and says nothing of their sins. Their sins were judged already, at the cross, in their Shepherd. Whatever is brought to light on that day about a believer will be brought to light as forgiven, to the praise of the grace that covered it. The Judge on the throne is the Lamb who was slain for you.

On a Tuesday. Every person you meet today will stand before Christ’s throne. Let that shape how you see and treat them. C. S. Lewis said there are no ordinary people. Look at the cashier and the colleague and the child with that in mind.
verseByVerse.note: Sheep and goats often grazed together in mixed flocks and had to be separated.

parallels.desc: the Son of Man given dominion
all the holy ones with him
I judge between sheep and sheep, rams and male goats

verseByVerse.quote: "And he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sheep on his right. The right hand was the place of honour and blessing (Genesis 48:13–20), the left the place of rejection. Goats are not evil animals; the image simply describes the separation.

At the right hand of the one at the right hand. This Gospel has already used the right hand at its highest pitch: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet (Psalm 110:1), the psalm Jesus quoted against the Pharisees three chapters before (22:44). The King who places his sheep on his right is himself enthroned at the Father’s right, so to be set there is to be given a share in his own place: God has seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6). The sheep stand where they stand because they belong to the Shepherd who sits where he sits.

Revealing, not creating. The separation does not create the difference; the shepherd sorts what is already the case. This is the third time the chapter has said it: one flock grazes together until evening, as with the wheat and the weeds (13:29–30).

You are not the shepherd. The present church is a mixed flock, and no amount of vigilance will sort it. That is freeing: the responsibility for identifying goats has never been given to you, and the only animal in the flock whose position you have any business examining is the one you are standing in.

Can a goat become a sheep? Not on the last day, but today, yes, by the grace of God. The image describes what people are at the end, not a fixed nature they are born with and can do nothing about. Every sheep on the right was once a lost sheep, and Paul says of the believers in Corinth: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (1 Corinthians 6:11). The Shepherd came to seek and to save the lost. If you fear you are on the wrong side, do not try to change your nature by effort. Come to the Shepherd, and he will make you his.
verseByVerse.note: The right hand was the place of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, you who are blessed. The Son of Man is the King: Jesus calls himself King only here in Matthew, a few days before he is crowned with thorns. Come is the invitation of 11:28, now completed. Blessed means favoured by the Father; their blessing comes from God’s grace.

Inherit the kingdom. Prepared from the foundation of the world: God planned their salvation before creation (Ephesians 1:4; 2 Timothy 1:9). This is grace, rooted in God’s eternal choice: before anyone had done good or bad, God freely set his love on a people to save in Christ, out of his own mercy (Romans 9:11). Some Christians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe; this commentary follows Paul’s point that the choice was made before anyone had done good or bad, so that it would stand on God’s call and not on works.

Settled before the deeds. This passage is often produced as proof that heaven is earned, yet before a single deed is mentioned, the question has been settled twice over. Nobody has ever earned an inheritance; it depends on whose family you belong to. And the kingdom was ready before the first cup of water was given. The works are named in the courtroom as evidence, never as the purchase price, and the timing makes it impossible that they could be.

I was hungry and you gave me food. The evidence, and it is strikingly ordinary. Not one item requires money, training, a platform or any particular ability. The kingdom’s evidence turns out to be bread, water and an opened door.

I was a stranger. Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in Scripture (Leviticus 19:34; Hebrews 13:2). The stranger is the person with no claim on you, whom nobody would blame you for ignoring. Hospitality to people who already matter to us is mostly a pleasure. This is the other kind, and it costs an evening and some awkwardness, and it is on the list the King reads out at the end of the world.

Does this mean only practical service counts, not belief? No. These works are the fruit of faith, not a substitute for it. The sheep are those blessed by the Father, given a kingdom prepared for them by grace, and in the rest of the Gospel such people are those who come to Christ, trust him and follow him (11:28; 16:24). What the King points to on the last day is the visible evidence that they truly belonged to him, because real faith always shows itself in love (Galatians 5:6; James 2:14–17). Belief and mercy are not rivals. A faith that never fed anyone was never the faith that saves, and good works without Christ cannot earn the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. The King welcomed you when you had no claim on him. Invite someone this month who has no claim on you, and who could not repay you, to share a meal at your table.

parallels.desc: share your bread with the hungry
chosen before the foundation of the world

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You visited me. Visited means cared for, looked after. The word, epeskepsasthe, carries the force of the God who sees and comes, the word Zechariah used when he sang that God had visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68).

I was in prison and you came to me. Prisoners in the ancient world depended on friends and family for food and care. Visiting Christians in prison could be dangerous, as it identified you with them (Hebrews 10:34; 13:3; 2 Timothy 1:16–17).

A word to the one being visited. There is somebody else in the scene. If you are the one who is ill, or out of work, or alone in a hospital bay, or inside a prison of some kind, literal or made of illness or shame or a house nobody calls at, then read what the King says about you. He does not say, I saw what they did for you. He says they did it to me.

Visited and not visited. Where you were visited, Christ counts it as a visit paid to himself. And where you were not, the phone that did not ring, the church that meant to come and did not, he counts that as a neglect of himself, and he says so in front of the nations. He is not a spectator of your situation. He has stepped into it and put his own name on it, and the kindness you received was Christ being served in you, which may matter a great deal to someone who has always hated being helped.

He knows the ground. He fasted forty days in a wilderness and was hungry (4:2), thirsty on a cross, a stranger with nowhere to lay his head, stripped bare before a crowd at his execution, and led away under armed guard. Only sickness is missing from his own story, and even there Matthew says that he took our illnesses and bore our diseases (8:17). He is not describing a class of people he has heard about.

On a Tuesday. If you are the one who is sick or alone, tell a believer you trust. Letting others serve Christ in you is also a kind of faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the righteous will answer him, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the righteous will answer him, Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? They are surprised. They did not serve these people in order to earn a reward, or even consciously as serving Christ. They simply showed love; their left hand did not know what their right hand was doing (6:3). This is not modesty. They are asking a real question, because they genuinely do not have the memory.

Nothing was filed. A man who is keeping account can always produce the account, and these people cannot produce anything. The deeds went out of their minds within the week, as happens when you help somebody because they needed help and you were there. Here is the difference between religion and the gospel. The moralist does good to get something, God’s favour or a good opinion of himself, and so he must keep the receipts. The believer does good because he has already been given everything in Christ, and so he can afford to forget.

Could you produce a list? This question is uncomfortable, and in an unusual direction. Most people, asked what they have done for the poor or the sick or the stranger, can retrieve two or three examples fairly quickly, and the retrieval is the problem, not the deeds. The ones commended here could not have answered that question. What they had done had never been converted into evidence about themselves.

Righteous with a righteousness they never claimed. The King calls them the righteous, and they never once call themselves that. Their standing comes from him: this is the name by which he will be called, The LORD is our righteousness (Jeremiah 23:6), and Christ has become to us righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30). And their unselfconscious love is his family likeness: Jesus went about doing good (Acts 10:38) and told those he healed to tell no one (8:4). The sheep forget their kindnesses because they have learned them from a Lord who never advertised his own.

So should I avoid planning good deeds? No. One guard, because this can be twisted into a reason to stop planning any good at all, on the grounds that self-consciousness spoils it. It does not follow. A man may deliberately set aside a Saturday to visit a prison, put it in his diary, and arrange the transport; the deliberateness is not the trouble. The trouble is keeping the receipt. Do it on purpose, and then let it go. And if in forty years you find you cannot remember much of it, you are in the company of the people standing at the King’s right hand and asking him what he is talking about.

Everyone calls him Lord. Listen to how they address him: Lord, when did we see you hungry? The five shut outside said it (v. 11), and the goats will say it too. Nobody is condemned for failing to, and nobody is saved for managing it (7:21).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you? Their surprise continues. They had not seen Christ in those they served; but Christ was there. The last two on the list are the costliest.

The costliest two. Visiting the sick is unpleasant in ways nobody admits. You cannot fix anything, you will not know what to say, and illness is dull. The third visit is harder than the first, and the twentieth is when almost everybody stops.

A supply line. The prison visit is harder still. A Roman prisoner often ate only what his friends carried in, so a man with no visitors went hungry, and could die of it. You came to me was a supply line. And to be seen carrying food through that door was to announce that you were associated with a criminal.

The modern equivalents. The long illness, where the cards stop after the third week and the person is still ill in the second year. The man whose troubles are his own fault, where visiting looks like approval. And most purely, the visit to someone with advanced dementia, who will not recognise you or remember by teatime that you came. There is no possible return on that visit, and that is exactly why it belongs on this list.

The King whom no one visited. Within two days of speaking these words, Jesus was himself arrested, bound and led away by night, and all the disciples left him and fled (26:56). His closest friend swore he did not know him. The King who names the prisoner on this list was a prisoner deserted by every friend he had, and he went through that abandonment for the very friends who abandoned him. So no believer in a cell or a ward is outside his understanding. He has been the one nobody came to, and he came to us.

How do I begin visiting when I do not know what to say? Go anyway, and say less than you think you should. Most people who are ill, grieving or in prison do not need answers; they need company. Sit, listen, ask how they are and wait for the answer. Bring something small if it helps: a meal, a book, a card from the children. Read a short psalm and pray briefly if they welcome it. Keep visits short, and come back, because the second and tenth visits mean more than the first. Many churches have prison or hospital ministries you can join, so that you are not alone. And remember who you are visiting.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the King will answer them, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You did it to me. The heart of the passage. Christ identifies so closely with the least of these my brothers that what is done to them is done to him. When Saul persecuted the church, Jesus asked, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

Who are my brothers? Two main views.

1. The poor and needy in general. Christ identifies with every suffering person, and the passage calls everyone to care for the poor. This is the most common view today.

2. Christ’s disciples. In Matthew, Jesus calls his disciples his brothers (12:48–50; 28:10), and the least or little ones refers to humble disciples (10:42; 18:6). In 10:40–42, those who receive his messengers, even with a cup of cold water, receive him. So the nations will be judged by how they treated Christ’s people, especially his messengers in need: hungry, homeless, imprisoned for the gospel.

This commentary’s view: in Matthew’s usage, the second is more likely: Christ’s needy disciples. But the rest of Scripture clearly commands care for all who are poor and suffering (5:44–45; Galatians 6:10; Proverbs 19:17; James 1:27). The passage cannot be used to excuse indifference to anyone in need.

Honouring both. The principle beneath the narrower reading, that the King so identifies with the lowly that what is done to them is done to him, holds wherever need is found (Luke 10:25–37). The text is neither a licence to reduce the gospel to social work, nor an excuse to spiritualise away the plain call to feed and clothe and visit.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by doing good works to the poor, or that anyone who does good is secretly a Christian. The kingdom was prepared for them by grace (v. 34). Their works were evidence of their belonging to Christ, not the cause of it. The Reformers put it this way: we are justified by faith alone, declared right with God by trusting Christ, not by doing; but the faith that justifies is never alone; it works through love (Galatians 5:6). They are surprised by their own good works precisely because those works flowed from a renewed heart, not a calculating one.

If the brothers are Christians, should I help only Christians? No. Paul’s rule is to do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). Both halves stand. Jesus told us to love our enemies and be like our Father, who sends rain on the just and the unjust (5:44–45), and the good Samaritan helped a stranger without asking his religion. But the church has a special duty to its own suffering members, at home and around the world. A congregation that funds projects for the needy far away while a widow in its own pews has no one to drive her to the doctor has missed the first application of this verse.

For worship. So closely does the King bind himself to his people that he feels their hunger as his own and counts their prisons as his. He is not ashamed to call them brothers. What love is this, that the King of kings should say of the smallest, weakest and most despised of his people: that was me.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he will say to those on his left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Depart from me, you cursed. The opposite of come (v. 34): separation from Christ, the source of every good (7:23; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Cursed is the opposite of blessed, but it is not cursed by my Father.

Prepared for the devil and his angels. Hell was not prepared for human beings, but for the devil and the fallen angels (Revelation 20:10). Those who go there join him because they refused God, who is not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9).

The asymmetry. Set this sentence beside verse 34. The blessing has an author; the curse is attributed to nobody. And the kingdom was prepared for you, while the fire was prepared for someone else. Heaven is a home prepared for guests; hell, on the King’s own account, was not built with human beings in mind.

The King who heard depart. Within a few days the one who speaks this sentence would have it spoken over him. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). At the ninth hour he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (27:46). That cry is depart from me heard from the inside, by the only man who never deserved it, and borne in full in the place of every one who flees to him.

You gave me no food. Their sins were sins of omission: not cruelty, but neglect. It is the same list with every verb negated. Nobody is accused of beating a prisoner or mocking the sick; the whole case against them is a series of things that did not happen.

A life, not an instance. That needs a guard, because it can crush the wrong reader. Everybody has failed somebody in trouble. What is described here is a life: a settled pattern running to the end, with not one occasion when he did otherwise. And the sheep are not people who never failed anybody either. Something was true in them, and it showed.

Is it fair to condemn people for what they did not do? We already think so in ordinary life. A lifeguard who watches a child drown and does nothing is guilty, though he never pushed her in. A father who never strikes his children but never feeds them is not a good father. The goats are not condemned on a technicality. Their neglect showed what was in their hearts: no love for the King, and so none for the people he loves (1 John 3:17). And the gospel is for exactly such people. Christ died for sins of omission as surely as for any other, and he receives everyone who comes to him confessing them.

Will God condemn people who never heard of Jesus? Scripture says that all people will be judged justly, according to the light they had, and that no one will be condemned for what they could not know (Romans 2:12–16; Luke 12:47–48). But it also says that all have sinned against the light they did have, the witness of creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 3:23), and that there is salvation in no one else but Christ (Acts 4:12). We should not imagine a second way of salvation for those who are sincere, nor imagine God being unjust to anyone. The Judge of all the earth will do right. What this means for us is urgency: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14)? The answer to that question is the church’s mission.

On a Tuesday. Not doing good is a real sin. What good are you leaving undone? Confess one omission to God today by name, knowing Christ died for that sin too, and then do it.

parallels.desc: the devil thrown into the lake of fire

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You did not welcome me. The fourth time the list has been recited in ten verses: repetition used as a hammer.

You did not visit me. Neglect of every kind of need reveals hearts without love, and so without Christ (1 John 3:17). The goats did not hate the stranger; they had no particular feelings about him at all.

How it happens. Nobody walks past need by deciding to. The mechanisms are respectable: busyness, which is real; distance, so that the need is known about rather than seen; the assumption that somebody else is handling it; fatigue; and the quiet postponement, not this week, which is my master is delayed (24:48) in a gentler key. Together they are how a person arrives at the judgment genuinely puzzled about what he did wrong.

Jesus stopped. The Gospel that records this sentence is full of a Lord who did not walk past. On the road out of Jericho, with a crowd pressing him toward Jerusalem and the cross, two blind men shouted, and Jesus stopped and called them (20:32). A woman touched his garment from behind and he turned and saw her (9:22). The goats’ list is the exact negative of his life, and the sheep’s list is simply what his life looks like when it is lived again in his people.

Has anything cost me lately? So the practical question this verse puts is not whether you are a cruel person. Almost nobody reading it is. The question is whether anything at all has been costing you lately: an evening, a Saturday, a sum of money you noticed spending, a friendship with somebody who cannot do a thing for you in return. If the honest answer is nothing, that is worth knowing now, while the list can still be added to.

The need is overwhelming. How can I respond to all of it? You cannot, and Christ does not ask you to. The King does not commend the sheep for solving world hunger; he commends them for the hungry person in front of them. Begin with the need God puts on your doorstep: your church family, your neighbours, the people your life actually touches. Give regularly through your church and trusted agencies for what is further away. Pray for what you cannot reach. And accept that you are one member of a body; others will meet needs you cannot. The danger is not doing too little to fix everything, but letting the size of the need excuse doing nothing for anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they also will answer, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?' Then he will answer them, saying, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you? They also call him Lord, and they are also surprised. It looks like the sheep’s bewilderment, but their question claims something, and they mean it sincerely: had we recognised you, we would have acted. We are not the sort of people who leave the Lord of glory standing in the road.

A confession they do not hear. They are saying that their service was available, but it was available to importance. Show them a King and they would have moved; show them a hungry nobody and they had other things on. The sheep never asked who the person was. The goats would have needed to know. That is the idol of status: giving ourselves to the people who can raise us, and having no time for those who cannot.

You did not do it to me. My brothers does not appear in this second version; it is simply the least of these. The point pressed is the identification itself, and it is total.

The searching test. Does the trouble you take over a person vary with what that person can do for you? Everybody’s does to some extent; the goats’ did entirely. The King has told us in advance that the people who cannot repay you are the ones he is standing behind. It is not a trap but an invitation with the answers printed.

I love Jesus, but I struggle to love some Christians. What then? Be honest about it, and bring it to him, because this verse will not let the two be separated. Whoever does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20). Love here is not first a warm feeling but a practical commitment to someone’s good: you can serve, pray for and speak kindly of a believer you find difficult long before you feel affection. Remember what Christ has borne with in you. And ask him to let you see the difficult brother as he does: as one for whom Christ died, and as one in whom, mysteriously, Christ is waiting to be served.

For worship. The Lord of glory came the first time from Nazareth, without form or majesty that we should look at him, and still he hides himself in the lowly, so that whoever would find him must stoop.

parallels.desc: whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker

verseByVerse.quote: "And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eternal punishment, eternal life. Punishment (kolasin) means penalty. Eternal (aiōnion) means belonging to the age to come, and since that age never ends, it is without end. Eternal life is the life of the age to come, with God, for ever (19:16, 29; John 17:3).

The same word. Eternal describes both the punishment and the life, in the same sentence. This is one of the strongest texts for the traditional view of hell as everlasting, conscious punishment. The word need not by itself mean unending, so the force lies in the balance: whatever weight you give it on one side, you must give it on the other. If the punishment quietly runs out, so does the life.

What it does not mean. Not that God takes pleasure in punishment (Ezekiel 33:11). Hell is the just consequence of rejecting God, and it is real. Nor does it mean that all who go to hell suffer equally. Jesus speaks of degrees of punishment (10:15; 11:22–24; Luke 12:47–48).

Where Christians differ: hell. Universalists hold that all will eventually be saved. Annihilationists (conditional immortality) hold that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist, so that the eternal punishment is eternal in its result, not its experience. The traditional view, held by most of the church throughout its history and by the Reformed confessions, is that hell is eternal, conscious punishment (the Westminster Confession 33.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 32.2). This commentary’s view: the traditional view. The parallel between eternal punishment and eternal life in this verse is decisive. It should make us sober, humble and urgent in sharing the gospel.

Argued with, not sneered at. The annihilationist view is not a fringe position; John Stott held it tentatively and with evident sorrow, and others of real godliness have followed him. Its holders have reasons: Scripture speaks of the wicked as destroyed and perishing (10:28; Philippians 3:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:9), fire consumes, and death is the wages of sin. But the weight of Jesus’ own words lies the other way. He sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence; he speaks of the fire that is not quenched and the worm that does not die (Mark 9:48), and of weeping and gnashing of teeth, which only the living can do; and Revelation says the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever (Revelation 14:11). Destruction in Scripture means ruin, not non-existence. This is among the hardest truths in the Bible, and it is meant to send us to Christ, who bore judgment for all who come to him.

How can a God of love do this? Two things are worth holding. The first is who is speaking. It is often said, and it is close to the truth, that more is said about judgment by Jesus than by anyone else in Scripture. The outer darkness, the closed door and the fire prepared for the devil are all his images, not some later hardening of a gentler message. And this is the same voice that broke over Jerusalem two chapters ago, how often would I have gathered your children (23:37), and that within days would be nailed to a cross precisely so that people would not have to hear depart from me. The doctrine did not reach us from hard men. It came from the tenderest voice in the Bible, and it cost him everything to open a way out of it. The second is that hell is not God losing his temper but God being just: sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious, and a God who shrugged at evil would not be good. What does infinitely serious actually mean? The weight of a wrong depends partly on whom it is done against: to insult a neighbour is wrong, to strike a king is worse. God is not merely greater than kings but holy, of eyes too pure to look on evil (Habakkuk 1:13). To treat him as worth nothing is no small thing.

In the flow. This is the last sentence of Jesus’ last great discourse (24:3), and the very next words announce that after two days the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified (26:1–2). The Judge goes straight on toward the cross, to suffer so that his people need never fear that day.

How a Christian should carry it. Not with relish, ever, and not with speculation: Scripture pictures the same reality as fire and as darkness, which tell us the loss is total, not furnish a map. What we are told is enough, and it is the ground of urgency in mission. No one who believes it can be casual about the person sitting next to them.

How can I be happy in heaven if someone I love is lost? This is perhaps the most painful question a believer can ask, and Scripture does not answer every part of it. But it tells us enough to trust. In glory we will see God as he is, and we will understand his justice and his goodness far more fully than we can now; nothing he does will seem to us unjust or unloving. God himself will wipe away every tear from our eyes (Revelation 21:4), not by making us forget, but by making all things right. And until then, we do not know the end of anyone’s story. Many who seemed far off have been brought near at the last. So pray for those you love while there is time, speak to them of Christ, and leave in the hands of the Judge of all the earth what only he can know.

On a Tuesday. Every person you know will spend eternity in one of two places. Write down three names, pray for them daily this month, and ask God for one conversation.

For worship. The same word that measures the loss measures the gift, and the gift belongs to Christ. The King who spoke of eternal punishment went within days to bear the judgment of all who trust him, and rose to give them the life of the age to come, without end.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to everlasting contempt

25.theology: Faith and works in the final judgment. The sheep and the goats is sometimes read as teaching salvation by charity. It teaches the reverse: those blessed by the Father, for whom the kingdom was prepared from the foundation of the world (v. 34), show what they are by the fruit of mercy. Works do not earn salvation; they reveal it. Paul (Romans 3:28) and James (James 2:26) do not contradict each other. A settled absence of mercy is evidence of a heart that has never truly met the merciful King.
25.examples:
Then: The early church became known for its care of the poor, the sick, the orphan and the widow, at a time when the vulnerable were often left without help. The Roman emperor Julian complained: “The godless Galileans feed not only their own poor but ours also.”

Now: The parable of the talents speaks to every Christian who sits on his gifts out of fear of failure, criticism or cost. Everyone has been entrusted with something, and the question at the end will not be how much you had but what you did with it.

26.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
26.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, <sup>2</sup>“You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” <sup>3</sup>Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, <sup>4</sup>and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him. <sup>5</sup>But they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.” <sup>6</sup>Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, <sup>7</sup>a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table. <sup>8</sup>And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste? <sup>9</sup>For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor.” <sup>10</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>11</sup>For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me. <sup>12</sup>In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it to prepare me for burial. <sup>13</sup>Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” <sup>14</sup>Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests <sup>15</sup>and said, “What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?” And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. <sup>16</sup>And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>17</sup>Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>18</sup>He said, “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, ‘The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.’” <sup>19</sup>And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>20</sup>When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve. <sup>21</sup>And as they were eating, he said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” <sup>22</sup>And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, “Is it I, Lord?” <sup>23</sup>He answered, “He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. <sup>24</sup>The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>25</sup>Judas, who would betray him, answered, “Is it I, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You have said so.” <sup>26</sup>Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” <sup>27</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, “Drink of it, all of you, <sup>28</sup>for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>29</sup>I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.” <sup>30</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>31</sup>Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away because of me this night.
