For it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ <sup>32</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>33</sup>Peter answered him, “Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.” <sup>34</sup>Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” <sup>35</sup>Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!” And all the disciples said the same. <sup>36</sup>Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go over there and pray.” <sup>37</sup>And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled. <sup>38</sup>Then he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me.” <sup>39</sup>And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” <sup>40</sup>And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter, “So, could you not watch with me one hour? <sup>41</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>42</sup>Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” <sup>43</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. <sup>44</sup>So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. <sup>45</sup>Then he came to the disciples and said to them, “Sleep and take your rest later on. See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>46</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>47</sup>While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. <sup>48</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man; seize him.” <sup>49</sup>And he came up to Jesus at once and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you came to do.” Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him. <sup>51</sup>And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>52</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword. <sup>53</sup>Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? <sup>54</sup>But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?” <sup>55</sup>At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. <sup>56</sup>But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled. <sup>57</sup>Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. <sup>58</sup>And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the end. <sup>59</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, <sup>60</sup>but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward <sup>61</sup>and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.’” <sup>62</sup>And the high priest stood up and said, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>63</sup>But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.” <sup>64</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” <sup>65</sup>Then the high priest tore his robes and said, “He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy. <sup>66</sup>What is your judgment?” They answered, “He deserves death.” <sup>67</sup>Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, <sup>68</sup>saying, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>69</sup>Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” <sup>70</sup>But he denied it before them all, saying, “I do not know what you mean.” <sup>71</sup>And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” <sup>72</sup>And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.” <sup>73</sup>After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, “Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you.” <sup>74</sup>Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know the man.” And immediately the rooster crowed. <sup>75</sup>And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went out and wept bitterly.
26.overview:
In a single evening Jesus gives his disciples the Lord’s Supper, names his betrayer, foretells Peter’s denial, prays in anguish in Gethsemane, is arrested by an armed crowd, and is condemned by the council. Again and again Matthew shows Scripture being fulfilled, from the thirty pieces of silver (Zechariah 11:12–13) to the enthroned Son of Man (Daniel 7:13).

Gethsemane stands at the centre. Jesus does not walk to the cross untouched; he falls on his face and asks that the cup might pass, because it is the cup of God’s wrath against sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Then he prays, not as I will, but as you will. The cross is not the Son’s defeat but his obedience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–46 — The Plot, the Anointing, the Last Supper, and Gethsemane
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus finishes his teaching and names the day of his death. The council plots to avoid the feast; a woman breaks a costly jar over his head and is scolded for waste; Judas lets the priests set his price. In a borrowed upper room Jesus keeps the Passover, names his betrayer, and gives bread and a cup as his body and his blood of the covenant. Then the walk to Gethsemane, the warning that all will fall away, and his prayer on the ground that the cup might pass.
verseByVerse.theology: Again and again what seems to be happening is not what is happening. The council rules out the feast, and he dies during it; Judas lets them value the Son of God at the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32; Zechariah 11:12–13); the disciples see waste where Jesus sees a burial anointing. At the table the words of Sinai return with one word added, my blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8), and Jeremiah’s promise of forgiveness is attached to a cup. In Gethsemane he faced the cup of wrath with no shield from its horror. He asked three times for it to pass, was refused, and got up to meet the betrayer.
verseByVerse.examples: You always have the poor with you is often quoted as an excuse for doing nothing, but it echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, where the lasting presence of the poor is the reason for a lasting open hand. And Gethsemane is the passage for anyone in deep anguish: Jesus said how bad it was, asked his friends to stay near, asked three times for relief, and was given not the removal of the cup but strength to drink it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 26 is the night on which everything turns. Jesus names the day of his death, a woman anoints him for burial, and one of the twelve sells him for the price of a slave. At the Passover table he gives bread and wine as his body and his blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins. In Gethsemane he falls on his face before the cup and says, your will be done. Then he is betrayed with a kiss, deserted by all, condemned for telling the truth about who he is, and denied three times by his boldest friend. Through it all the one who seems helpless is the only one in control.

The passion narrative. Chapters 26 to 28 tell of Jesus’ suffering (his “passion”), death and resurrection: the climax toward which everything has moved since 16:21.

When Jesus had finished all these sayings. Matthew has used this formula four times already, at the close of each great block of teaching (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). Here, for the fifth and last time, he adds one word: all. The teaching is over. From this sentence to the end of the book he does almost nothing but suffer, and the Teacher becomes the Lamb.

You know that after two days the Passover is coming. Passover was the great annual festival commemorating Israel’s rescue from Egypt (Exodus 12). On the night of the exodus each household killed a lamb and put its blood on the doorposts; when the LORD struck Egypt’s firstborn, he passed over the houses marked by blood. It was probably Tuesday or Wednesday when Jesus said this. Israel had kept that meal for some fourteen centuries, and he arranges to die during it.

Delivered up to be crucified. Nobody speaks like that. Men who expect to be killed may say so in general terms; they do not hand their friends a timetable with the method on it. He has told them three times already (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:18–19), and now he gives them the day. He links his death to the Passover because he is the true Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7): as in Egypt judgment passed over the house where a lamb had died, so the judgment his people’s sins deserve falls on him, and passes over them (1 Peter 3:18).

Handed over. The verb is paradidotai, is handed over. The passive leaves unsaid who is doing the handing. Judas hands him over to the priests; the priests hand him over to Pilate; Pilate hands him over to be crucified. But Paul reaches behind all three: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). The chain of betrayals runs all the way back, and at the top of it the Father is handing over the Son, and the Son is walking toward the date he has just announced. The next seventy verses will show him bound, struck and led about by men who appear to be running the operation. Not one of them surprises him. He named the week.

If Jesus knew what was coming, was his suffering any less? No. Knowing the day did not make the day lighter; it meant he carried it for longer. Most of us are spared the foreknowledge of our worst hours, and it is a mercy. He was not spared it, and he chose to walk toward it with his eyes open, teaching in the temple, eating with his friends, and sleeping on the Mount of Olives while the date came nearer. Foreknowledge in a coward produces flight. In him it produced a steady approach, and Gethsemane will show that it cost him everything.

On a Tuesday. Your salvation was not a rescue God improvised once things had gone wrong: it was planned, named and kept. And when you face a day you dread, a hospital appointment, a hard conversation, a court date, you are not facing it before a Saviour who does not understand what it is to see the calendar and know.
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt, when the blood of a lamb protected each household. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the chief priests gathered. Matthew sets two meetings side by side: a man speaks openly to his friends about his own death, and powerful men meet behind a closed door to arrange it. Two plans meet: God’s and theirs (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28).

Caiaphas. Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, an extraordinary run when the three men before him had each lasted about a year before Rome removed them. In 1990 an ornate ossuary (bone box) inscribed “Joseph son of Caiaphas” was found in Jerusalem, probably his. The man chairing this meeting is not a fanatic but a manager, protecting an arrangement that worked.

The arrangement being defended. John records Caiaphas making the case not long before, after the raising of Lazarus: if we let him go on, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation, and it is better that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation should perish (John 11:48–50). John adds that, being high priest, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation (John 11:51–52). Read as politics it is not even unreasonable. He is managing risk, and in managing it he speaks the gospel without knowing it.

By stealth. That is, by trickery, because the crowds made a public arrest impossible. The men who killed Jesus did not think of themselves as opposing God; some may well have called it a painful duty. Underneath the duty lay something every heart knows: the need to stay in control. Jesus could not be managed, and in that room a man who cannot be managed has to be removed. It is the same instinct that makes us keep him at arm’s length when he asks for more than we planned to give.

He who sits in the heavens laughs. David had already described this scene: the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed (Psalm 2:2). The psalm’s next lines are what the conspirators never suspect. He who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:4). Not because their power is imaginary, but because the meeting they have convened to end this man’s work is the meeting at which his work begins.

Does this mean the Jewish people are to blame for the death of Jesus? No. These verses name a particular group of leaders, and the New Testament spreads the guilt far wider: Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against him (Acts 4:27). The church has sometimes used this chapter to justify contempt for Jews, and that is a grievous sin against the text and against the Jewish Messiah who wept over Jerusalem. The first believers were Jews, and Peter could say to a Jewish crowd both that they had killed the Author of life and that the promise of forgiveness was for them (Acts 3:15, 19). In the end the honest answer is the one a modern hymn gives: it was my sin that held him there.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; his father-in-law Annas had held the office before him.

verseByVerse.quote: But they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not during the feast. The concern is crowd control. At Passover the city swelled several times over with pilgrims celebrating a national deliverance while a foreign power watched from its fortress. A popular teacher arrested in front of that crowd could have set the city alight and brought Roman retaliation (John 11:48).

God’s timing. Within two or three days Jesus is dead, at Passover, the one occasion the council had ruled out, because while they were still saying not during the feast, Judas was on his way to them (v. 14). Their timetable bent to God’s.

Providence. Providence means God’s constant care and rule over everything he has made, so that nothing, not even a council’s scheming, happens outside his purpose (Ephesians 1:11). It works not by suspending anybody’s freedom but by employing it. Caiaphas made a calculation and meant it; Judas made a choice and meant it; and the Lamb of God was killed during the feast of the lamb, at the hour appointed before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:19–20).

If God uses people’s free choices, are they still responsible? Yes, entirely. Scripture holds both truths in a single sentence: this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). The plan does not reduce the guilt, and the guilt does not threaten the plan. You do not need to solve how these fit to believe both. What you need is to see that they protect you: because God is sovereign, evil never has the last word; because people are responsible, evil is never excused.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the house of Simon the leper. Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem (John 11:18), where Jesus had been lodging that week (21:17). Simon had probably been healed, perhaps by the man now reclining at his table. One of the last meals of hospitality Jesus receives before his death is taken in a house religious Jerusalem would once have crossed the road to avoid. John names the woman, Mary, sister of Lazarus (John 12:1–8); Matthew does not.

Is this the same anointing as Luke 7? No. Luke’s story is set earlier, in Galilee, in the house of Simon the Pharisee, with a sinful woman (Luke 7:36–50). This is the anointing at Bethany that John also records (John 12:1–8), where the woman is Mary, Lazarus’ sister. John dates the meal six days before Passover; Matthew and Mark place the story here, not necessarily in strict time order, to set it beside the plot against Jesus and to contrast the woman’s love with Judas’ betrayal. John mentions his feet, Matthew his head; she probably anointed both.

An alabaster flask. Alabaster was a soft, translucent stone used for perfume flasks sealed at the neck. Mark and John say it was pure nard, imported from the mountains of northern India, worth over three hundred denarii, nearly a labourer’s wages for a year (Mark 14:3–5; John 12:3, 5). This was not a gift she could repeat. It may have been everything she had, or the security a woman kept against disaster.

She broke it. Mark adds that she broke the flask, snapping its sealed neck to use it (Mark 14:3). A sealed jar cannot be opened by halves. Before a drop touched him she had already decided that none of it was coming back, and the extravagance was in that decision.

She poured it on his head. Anointing the head was done for honoured guests (Psalm 23:5), but pouring out a flask over the head is what Samuel did to Saul and to David, and what was done to Israel’s kings and priests at their installation (1 Samuel 10:1; 16:13; 2 Kings 9:6). In a leper’s house, at a private supper, an unnamed woman performs a coronation. Jesus is the Messiah, the Anointed One, and he is anointed by a woman’s love.

She understood. She acted as if she knew what the men at that table had not grasped: he was the anointed King, he was going to die, and the moment for arithmetic had passed.

On a Tuesday. What is your alabaster flask: your savings, your evenings, your ambitions, your reputation? It is easy to give to Christ in measured portions and keep the seal intact. He held nothing back for you, so ask whether there is anything in your life that you have decided in advance is not coming back because it has been given to him.
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks; Mark and John say the ointment was pure nard, worth about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: a different anointing, by a sinful woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, "Why this waste? For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were indignant. The objection is unanswerable, which is what makes it dangerous. Nobody at that table was wrong about the arithmetic, and put in a church meeting today the objection would carry the room. John says Judas led the complaint, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief who kept the money bag and helped himself from it (John 12:4–6). The others joined in, and there is no sign they were pretending. They meant it.

Why this waste? The word is apōleia: loss, destruction, ruin. It is the language of an asset written off. The same word is used of Judas himself, the son of destruction (John 17:12). They are looking at an act of worship and seeing a balance sheet with a hole in it, and their indignation has a moral shape to it. That is precisely the trouble. Bad motives are easy to identify; this is a good motive standing in the wrong place, which is much harder to see and nearly impossible to argue with.

Given to the poor. It sounded pious, and giving to the poor was especially expected at Passover (John 13:29). But it missed the moment: Jesus was about to die. What kind of religion cannot recognise worship when it is standing in front of it? The kind that justifies everything by usefulness, where a thing done simply because Christ is worth it has no category to sit in.

The greatest waste. Within a week the disciples would watch a far larger loss. The most perfect life ever lived would be poured out while he was still in his thirties, in public disgrace, on a Roman cross, and anyone keeping accounts would have written it off as the saddest waste in history. It was the ransom for many (20:28). The broken jar is a small picture of what was about to happen to the one it was poured on: nothing held back, and the apparent loss the richest gift God ever gave.

So is it wrong to spend money on church buildings, music or beauty when people are hungry? The verse does not give a blank cheque for lavish spending, and it does not condemn it either. The test is the woman’s: was this done for Christ, out of love, at the right time? Some spending on worship is really spending on ourselves, our comfort or our status, and the disciples’ question rightly exposes it. But some giving has no measurable output and is still right, because God is worth it. The healthy church does both: it gives generously to the poor and it is not ashamed to give beautifully to God. If you notice that you only ever criticise the second, ask where Judas’ voice is coming from.

On a Tuesday. Be slow to criticise other people’s devotion. There were twelve men in that room who could have written the report, and one woman who broke a jar, and only one of them was commended. Nothing given to Christ is wasted, because he is not a means to some other end. He is the end.
verseByVerse.note: John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you trouble the woman? He defends her, and he defends her against his own men. That is worth registering before anything else. The disciples are ranged on one side of the room with an argument that sounds like conscience; one woman is on the other with an empty jar; and he takes her side. He is still that kind of Lord: the advocate of his people, now at the right hand of the Father (1 John 2:1).

A beautiful thing. The word is kalon, which in Greek means noble and fine as much as lovely: not merely a pleasing gesture but an act of moral excellence, love expressed lavishly and at the right moment. He is not being gallant about a well-meant mistake. He is saying she got it right and they got it wrong.

You always have the poor. This sentence has been quoted for centuries as though Jesus were shrugging at poverty. That reverses the sentence he is quoting. Deuteronomy 15 says there will be no poor among you if you keep the commandment, and then, realistically, there will never cease to be poor in the land, therefore you shall open wide your hand to your brother (Deuteronomy 15:4, 11). Every Jew at that table knew how the verse ended. He quotes the middle and lets them supply the rest.

But you will not always have me. There was a window, a few days wide, that would not come again, and this woman had understood it. He is saying: you will have the poor to serve for the rest of your lives, and that obligation never lapses; but this opportunity to honour me in person is closing.

A lesson about timing. There are things that can be done at any point and things that can only be done now, and the second kind usually look least urgent. The visit to a dying man can be made this week or not at all. The word of thanks to someone old can be said now or said at a funeral to people who cannot hear it. Care for the poor is a lifelong duty precisely because the poor will still be there. Some things will not be.

Christ is no longer with us bodily, so how do we do what she did? In two ways. First, in worship: the risen Christ is present by his Spirit among his people, and praise, prayer and giving offered to him are offered to him truly. Second, through his people: he said that what is done for the least of his brothers is done for him (25:40). The woman’s act was unique in its timing, but its heart is not. Every time you give him something costly because he is worth it, in time, money or obedience, you are standing where she stood.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: "In pouring this ointment on my body she has done it to prepare me for burial. Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To prepare me for burial. He tells them what she has done, and it is not necessarily what she thought she was doing. In Jewish custom, bodies were anointed with spices and perfume before burial. She came to honour him, and he receives it as embalming.

Too late on Sunday. Jesus would be buried in haste, before the Sabbath (27:57–61). When the women came on the Sunday morning with their spices, intending to anoint him themselves, they were too late: he was not there (Mark 16:1–6). The only anointing poured out on him for burial while he still lived was this one, given in love, days early, by a woman who was being told off for it at the time.

Wherever this gospel is proclaimed. Think where he is standing as he says it: in a leper’s house in a village outside Jerusalem, two days from execution, with a movement of eleven frightened men and one traitor. And he says the whole world will hear of it (24:14; 28:19).

In memory of her. It has been, in every Bible, in every language, and it is being fulfilled now, on this page. Judas’ name is remembered with shame; her act with honour.

And no name. The one human act Jesus promises the whole world will hear of is performed by a woman with no name in Matthew’s text. That is its own kind of comfort for anybody whose best work has gone unrecorded and unattributed. He remembers what she did. He was not depending on Matthew to keep the record.

Does Jesus remember small things done for him? Yes, and with a precision that should both comfort and steady us. He said that not even a cup of cold water given to one of his little ones will lose its reward (10:42), and that the Father who sees in secret will reward (6:4). The hidden prayer, the meal taken to a neighbour, the patience shown to an aged parent: none of it disappears. You do not need anyone else to notice. Your service is not wasted if no one writes it down, because the one who matters already has.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial; Jesus would be buried in haste.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, "What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?" And they paid him thirty pieces of silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the twelve. Matthew’s placing is deliberate and merciless. A woman has just poured out a year’s wages on him; the very next sentence has a man walking out to find a price for him, and he is an insider, chosen by Jesus, who had seen everything (10:4).

Judas Iscariot. He went on his own initiative. Luke and John say that Satan entered him (Luke 22:3; John 13:27). Both are true: Judas chose freely, and Satan used him.

What will you give me if I deliver him over to you? Look at how he opens the negotiation. He does not name a figure; he asks them to. A man selling something valuable states his price; a man who has decided to sell and does not much care what he gets asks what is on offer. Judas let the buyers set the value, and they did. His motive was at least partly money (John 12:6). Some suggest disappointment that Jesus was not a political Messiah, or anger at the rebuke at Bethany. Scripture does not fully explain; sin is never fully rational.

Thirty pieces of silver. Only Matthew names the sum, and it is not random. In Exodus, if an ox gores a slave to death, the owner pays the slave’s master thirty shekels of silver (Exodus 21:32): the damages for a dead slave. Zechariah uses the same figure with heavy irony: the LORD’s shepherd is weighed out thirty pieces of silver as his wages, and the LORD himself calls it the lordly price at which I was priced by them, and has it thrown to the potter (Zechariah 11:12–13). Judas will do exactly that (27:3–10). The insult once offered to God is offered again, to God in the flesh.

Nobody could see it. What is unnerving about Judas is not that he was a monster but that nobody could see it. For about three years he had heard every sermon in this book, watched the blind receive sight, been sent out to preach (10:1–4), and held the common purse. When Jesus said at the table that one of them would betray him, each of the eleven asked, Is it I? (26:22). None of them asked whether it was Judas.

Was Judas ever a true believer? Scripture suggests not. Jesus said that he knew from the beginning who would betray him, and called him a devil while he was still among the twelve (John 6:64, 70). John says he was a thief (John 12:6), and Jesus in his prayer calls him the son of destruction, lost so that Scripture might be fulfilled, while every one the Father gave him was kept (John 17:12). So Judas is not a true believer who lost his salvation; he is a professing disciple who never truly belonged. That is sobering, because it shows how far outward closeness can go. It is also comforting, because those whom the Father has given to Christ are kept (John 10:28–29).

On a Tuesday. Betrayals of Christ are usually done for small change: a little silence to keep a promotion, a little compromise to keep a friend.

For worship. The Son of God let himself be priced at the cost of a slave, so that slaves could be bought at the cost of his blood. You were not ransomed with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). Judas sold him cheaply. The Father valued him above all worlds and gave him anyway.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty shekels of silver was the price the law set for a slave gored by an ox.

parallels.desc: thirty pieces of silver, the shepherd’s wages

verseByVerse.quote: And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sought an opportunity. The word is eukairia: a good moment, the right time. It is the language of a man waiting for a gap in a diary. He knew where Jesus went at night to pray (John 18:2).

Patient sin. This was not a flash of rage, regretted by morning. He made a decision and went back to work, eating with them and keeping the money bag, while watching for a convenient evening. A decision lived with for days stops feeling like a decision. It becomes a fact about the man.

How serious wrong is done. Most serious wrong gets done not in the moment of temptation but in the long quiet stretch afterwards, when the thing has been decided and is merely awaiting a convenient hour. The affair that has not happened yet but has been agreed to in the mind. The resignation letter written and saved. The lie that will be told when the question finally comes. Judas had days in which nothing had happened yet and everything had already happened.

Still loved. Yet during those days Jesus went on loving him. He washed his feet with the others (John 13:5), gave him the morsel at the table (John 13:26), called him friend in the garden, and asked him a direct question that would have let him stop. That is the measure of Christ’s patience: he served the man who was selling him, and did not stop until Judas himself walked out into the night.

What if I have already decided on something wrong in my heart, but not yet done it? Then this verse is God’s mercy to you, because the opportunity has not yet come. A decision made in the heart can be unmade, and the time to unmake it is now, before the convenient hour arrives. Tell God plainly what you have agreed to, and renounce it. Then cut off the opportunity: delete the message, end the contact, tell a trusted friend, remove what makes it easy. Do not reason that because you have already sinned in your heart you may as well finish it. Judas’ tragedy was not that he had a dark thought, but that he kept it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, "Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?" He said, "Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, 'The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first day of Unleavened Bread. The Feast of Unleavened Bread lasted seven days, beginning with the Passover meal (Exodus 12:15–20; Leviticus 23:5–6). All leaven was removed from homes. The Passover lambs were sacrificed in the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, and the meal eaten after sunset, which began 15 Nisan. This was Thursday.

Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover? Preparation involved buying a lamb, having it sacrificed at the temple, roasting it, and preparing unleavened bread, wine, bitter herbs and a sauce. The meal had to be eaten within Jerusalem. They are about to eat the meal that commemorates Egypt’s slavery and the redemption by blood, and Jesus will transform it into the memorial of the ultimate redemption. Every detail of the Last Supper is dense with the meaning of the exodus.

To a certain man. Jesus keeps the place secret, perhaps so that Judas could not tell the authorities in advance. Mark and Luke say they would meet a man carrying a water jar (Mark 14:13; Luke 22:10), which would have stood out, since women usually carried water.

My time is at hand. My time (kairos) is the appointed moment of his death (John 13:1), the hour fixed in salvation history, not a tragic accident. The house had a large upper room, already furnished (Mark 14:15); some think it belonged to Mark’s mother, where the church later met (Acts 12:12).

Was it a Passover meal? Matthew, Mark and Luke present it as the Passover meal. John seems to place Jesus’ death on the day of preparation, when the lambs were being killed (John 18:28; 19:14). Explanations include different calendars used by different groups, or John’s phrases referring to the whole Passover week. This commentary’s view: the Last Supper was a Passover meal, as the first three Gospels say; John’s language fits this when read carefully, and his emphasis is that Jesus died as the Passover Lamb.

How John’s language fits. This is a real difficulty, and two answers carry weight. First, Preparation (paraskeuē) is the ordinary Greek word for Friday, so the day of Preparation of the Passover can mean the Friday of Passover week, and the Passover the priests wished to eat (John 18:28) can mean the festival meals that ran through the seven-day feast. Second, different groups of Jews may have reckoned the day differently, so that Passover was kept on two consecutive evenings, Jesus and his disciples on the earlier one.

What should be resisted. What should be resisted is the suggestion that John simply moved the date to make a theological point. He is the most precise of the four about hours and feasts. Believers can hold both accounts true while admitting that the exact reckoning is not certain, and both land in the same place: Behold, the Lamb of God (John 1:29); Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). The meal in the upper room and the death outside the wall are the same feast seen from its two ends: the supper he gave them, and the sacrifice he became.

Why does it matter whether it was a Passover meal? Because it tells us what the Lord’s Supper means. Jesus did not invent a new ritual out of nothing. He took the meal in which Israel remembered that a lamb had died and its blood had turned away judgment, and said, in effect: this was always about me. So when you come to the Lord’s Table you are not doing something strange; you are standing at the end of a story God has been telling since Egypt, in which he rescues slaves by the blood of a substitute.

In the flow. Verses 1–16 have shown other people making plans. From verse 17 the one making the arrangements is Jesus: he names the house and claims the hour. The plotters act, but Jesus leads.
verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; lambs were sacrificed at the temple that afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They prepared the Passover. The lamb, the swept room, the bitter herbs, the bread and the wine: the work done in tens of thousands of houses that week, by men with no idea they were preparing the most consequential meal in history.

He reclined at table. At the first Passover, Israelites ate standing, ready to leave (Exodus 12:11). By Jesus’ time Jews reclined at the Passover, leaning on the left elbow around a low table, precisely because slaves ate standing and this was the meal of a liberated people. He takes the posture of a free man on the last night of his life, beside the man arranging his arrest.

The Passover meal. The meal had a set order. The head of the household explained its meaning: the lamb (God passed over the houses marked with blood), the unleavened bread (the haste of the exodus), the bitter herbs (the bitterness of slavery). By the custom later written down in the Mishnah (the early collection of Jewish law), four cups of wine were drunk at different points, and the Hallel psalms (113–118) were sung. Jesus would give new meaning to the bread and one of the cups.

A borrowed room. The new covenant is going to be inaugurated not in the temple but in a borrowed room up a flight of stairs, thirteen men round a table, one of them a traitor. God has a settled habit of doing the largest things in the least impressive rooms. In a borrowed room, with borrowed bread, he was about to give the one thing that was entirely his: himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, "Is it I, Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of you will betray me. He waits until they are eating: not before the meal, when it would have ended it, nor after, but in the middle, with food in front of them and the man in question within arm’s reach.

The setting is the whole weight of it. To eat at a man’s table was to be bound to him in friendship and loyalty. David had felt the same wound and written it down: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Psalm 41:9), and Jesus applies that psalm to this night (John 13:18). Betrayal from a stranger is a misfortune. Betrayal from a man with your bread in his mouth is something else.

And began to say to him one after another, Is it I, Lord? The Greek is sharper than the English. The question begins with mēti, which expects the answer no: surely it is not I, Lord? It is exactly how a man asks a question he badly wants a particular answer to. What Matthew does not record is just as telling: eleven men, told there is a traitor at the table, and no accusation, no comparing of notes. Each asks about himself, one after another. None was certain of himself; they knew their own hearts were capable of betrayal. This is healthy self-suspicion (1 Corinthians 10:12).

Should a Christian live in constant fear that he might be a Judas? No. The disciples’ question is a healthy response to a warning, not a permanent state of terror. Scripture calls us to examine ourselves (2 Corinthians 13:5) and also to have full assurance (Hebrews 10:22). The way to hold both is to look away from yourself to Christ. Judas never asked out of sorrow; he asked as cover. If you ask this question because you are afraid of offending the Lord you love, that very fear is a mark of grace. Ask it, bring your answer to Christ, and then rest in his promise that none of his sheep will be lost (John 10:28).

On a Tuesday. When you hear of sin in the church, a fall, a scandal, a broken marriage, ask first, Lord, is it I?, and pray for the one who fell before you discuss him.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dipped his hand in the dish. At the Passover meal a common bowl of sauce stood on the table and everyone dipped bread or herbs into it, so the answer does not single out Judas to the others; all twelve had dipped. The betrayal comes from the closest fellowship.

The Son of Man goes as it is written of him. Jesus’ death fulfils Scripture (Psalm 22; Isaiah 53; Zechariah 13:7). The cross is not a breakdown of the plan but the plan.

Woe to the betrayer. Two sentences stand side by side, and none may pull them apart: the Son of Man goes as it is written, and woe to the man who betrays him. God planned it and wove it into his saving purpose, but he did not put evil into Judas’ heart (James 1:13), and Judas is fully responsible (see v. 5; Acts 2:23).

What must not be done with it. Judas cannot be excused on the ground that prophecy required somebody. Nor was he a pawn past repentance: he will shortly say I have sinned (27:4), but his remorse led to despair, not to Christ.

Better never to have been born. It cannot be read as anything but a fate worse than never existing. And it implies that Judas’ punishment would be eternal: if he were finally saved, his existence would not have been worse than non-existence.

Who is speaking. Not a preacher working up a congregation, but the man about to die for the sins of the world, saying quietly at a supper table that non-existence would have been the kinder outcome. The most loving man who ever lived is the one who said it.

How can a loving God allow someone to end up so badly? Jesus does not answer by softening the outcome; he answers by placing the responsibility where it belongs and by showing his own heart. Judas was warned, loved, served, and given every opportunity, right up to the kiss. God is not unjust in judging those who reject such love; the wonder is that he saves anyone at all. If the question troubles you, do not settle it by doubting the warning. Settle it by running to the Saviour who gave it, because he has never turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: Judas, who would betray him, answered, "Is it I, Rabbi?" He said to him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas, who would betray him, answered, Is it I, Rabbi? Every other man at that table has just said Lord (v. 22). Judas says Rabbi. Rabbi is a respectful word, teacher, and that is what makes it revealing: Judas has an honourable category for Jesus, but not the one the others have. In Matthew no disciple except Judas ever calls Jesus Rabbi. He will use the same word in the garden, an hour or two later, as the signal for the arrest (v. 49). He has already sold him (v. 15).

A warning for admirers. The ground Judas stood on is more populated than anybody expects. A very high regard for Jesus’ teaching and ethics is not the same thing as calling him Lord, and Judas is the proof that it can be held to the end, in the inner circle.

You have said so. A guarded yes: your words, not mine, or you said it. Jesus will use the same phrase to the high priest (v. 64) and to Pilate (27:11). It is a quiet, unmistakable answer, probably not heard by the others (John 13:28–29). He does not denounce him to the room. He simply lets Judas know that he knows.

The last door held open. Judas now knows that the man he is selling has seen the whole transaction, and that nothing has yet been said in front of the others. He could have stood up at that moment and gone the way Peter would go before the week was out, from betrayal to tears to restoration. John records that he went out, and it was night (John 13:30).

Seen and unchanged. The most sobering fact is that he was seen, addressed and given a direct answer, and none of it reached him: not because Christ was distant, but because a man can sit that close and keep the door shut.

How do I know whether Jesus is my Lord or only my respected teacher? Ask what happens when his word crosses your will. A teacher is someone whose advice you weigh; a Lord is someone you obey when you would rather not. Ask, too, whether you need him or only admire him: whether you trust his death for your forgiveness or only value his example. Those who call him Lord in truth do so by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3), and they show it not by perfection but by bowing, returning, and wanting him more than the things he forbids.
verseByVerse.note: “You have said so” is a guarded yes.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, "Take, eat; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, "Drink of it, all of you,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus took bread. The unleavened bread of the Passover. At the meal the head of the household broke the bread and explained it as the bread of affliction that Israel ate in Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:3). Now Jesus gives the bread a meaning it had never carried before: the memorial and present enjoyment of a greater rescue.

Blessing, broke, gave. The same actions as at the feedings of the crowds (14:19; 15:36): took, blessed, broke, gave. The one who fed thousands in the wilderness is about to give them bread that is himself.

Take, eat. The bread represents his body, which will be broken in death for them. Luke and Paul add: which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). Eating it pictures receiving him and his benefits by faith. He does not ask them to look, or to admire, or to offer, but to receive. Salvation is not something we make and bring to God; it is something he gives and we take.

When he had given thanks. Probably the third cup of the Passover meal, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), after the meal. “Given thanks” is eucharistēsas, from which comes Eucharist. The night he was betrayed, over the cup that stood for his own blood, the Son of God thanked his Father.

Drink of it, all of you. (The medieval church withheld the cup from lay people; the Reformers restored it, on the basis of this verse.) The cup is given to all the disciples: at this table there is no inner ring, for every Christian comes to God directly through Christ, the one great High Priest (1 Peter 2:9; Hebrews 4:14–16).

The Lord’s Supper. Jesus here institutes what the church calls the Lord’s Supper, Communion or the Eucharist, to be repeated until he returns (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). The Passover’s backward-looking memorial becomes a proclamation that looks back to the cross, feeds on Christ now, and looks forward to the feast.

In the flow. Before a nail is driven, Jesus tells his friends what his death will mean and puts it into their hands. Everything that follows is to be read in the light of this table: the men who seize him think they are disposing of a troublemaker; he has already said that he is giving himself away.

Where Christians differ: “This is my body.” What does “is” mean? Four main views:

1. Transubstantiation (Roman Catholic). The bread and wine are changed in substance into Christ’s actual body and blood, while keeping their appearance.

2. Real presence (Lutheran). Christ’s body and blood are truly present “in, with and under” the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine.

3. Memorial (Zwinglian). The bread and wine are symbols that remind us of Christ’s death.

4. Spiritual presence (Calvin and the Reformed). The bread and wine remain bread and wine, and Christ’s body is in heaven, but by the Holy Spirit believers truly feed on Christ, spiritually and by faith, receiving his life and benefits. The sign and the thing signified are united in the Spirit’s work.

This commentary’s view: the spiritual presence of Christ, as Calvin taught (Westminster Confession 29.7). Jesus was physically present, holding the bread, when he said “This is my body”; the disciples would not have thought they were eating his literal flesh. He often spoke in pictures (“I am the door”, John 10:9). But the Supper is not a bare symbol. Christ truly meets his people there, and feeds them by faith (1 Corinthians 10:16).

The history behind the views. The debate over these four words divided the Reformation. Rome defined transubstantiation in 1215: the whole substance of the bread becomes Christ’s body, so the host is adored and the Mass re-presents his sacrifice. On Luther’s view all who eat receive Christ’s body and blood, believing or not. Calvin steered between: against Zwingli, the Supper is a genuine feeding on the living Christ; against Luther, the feeding is spiritual and received by faith.

Really, but spiritually. The Westminster Confession (29.7) puts it precisely: worthy receivers, outwardly partaking of the visible elements, “do then also inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified, and all benefits of his death.” Really and indeed: Christ is not absent, and the Supper is not a mental exercise in remembering. Yet spiritually: the bond is in the Holy Spirit, who unites us to Christ where he is. Calvin loved to say that the Spirit lifts our hearts up to heaven, so that the Christ who sits at the Father’s right hand truly nourishes his people at a plain table on earth. That is why the old liturgies began with the words, lift up your hearts.

Where Protestants press back on Rome. On two things. First, this is my body was spoken while his body sat whole at the table, the same manner of speech as I am the vine, or the Rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4): the bread signifies and conveys; it does not become. Second, and weightier, a re-presented sacrifice sits uneasily with Hebrews: Christ offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12–14). Yet Rome, Luther and Calvin all confess that Christ truly gives himself to his people at this table.

Who may come to the Lord’s Supper? It is for those who belong to Christ: baptised believers who trust him and are willing to turn from their sin. Paul tells each person to examine himself and then eat (1 Corinthians 11:28). No one comes because he is worthy; we come because we need Christ. The person who should hold back is the one who is unwilling to repent, not the one who is struggling and grieving over his sin.

So what actually happens when I take the bread and the cup? Three things, all at once. You remember: you look back to the cross and the body given for you. You receive: by faith, Christ himself feeds your soul through the Spirit, strengthening your union with him, your assurance and your love, as truly as the bread feeds your body. And you proclaim: you announce his death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), and declare that you belong to him and to his people (1 Corinthians 10:17). You do not need to feel something dramatic for this to be real. Come with faith, however weak, and he keeps his promise.

What should I do with my mind while the bread is passed? Do not spend the moment searching your heart for one last unconfessed sin, as though your welcome depended on your thoroughness. Examine yourself before you come; at the table, look to Christ. Think of his body given and his blood shed for you by name. Thank him. Trust him for one specific thing you need: forgiveness for a sin that haunts you, strength for a hard week, love for a difficult person. Remember the believers eating beside you, who are one body with you. And look ahead to the day when you will eat with him in the kingdom.

For worship. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord of glory gave thanks and gave himself. He did not wait until his friends were faithful; he fed them on the night they failed, and he still does.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: "for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is my blood of the covenant. Every phrase is quarried out of the Old Testament. At Sinai Moses threw the blood of the sacrifices over the people and said, Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Exodus 24:8). Jesus takes the sentence, puts my in front of it, and hands round a cup. A covenant is a binding bond that God makes with a people: he pledges to be their God and claims them as his own (Jeremiah 31:33). Blood marked it as a matter of life and death.

The new covenant Jeremiah promised. Jeremiah had promised there would be another covenant: not like the covenant made when God took them by the hand to bring them out of Egypt, which they broke, but one written on hearts, with the promise attached, I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The blood is his, and the covenant that it seals is the one in which God himself guarantees the forgiveness, the new heart and the knowledge of God.

Which is poured out for many. As the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the altar (Leviticus 4:7, 18), Jesus’ death is a sacrifice: a life given in place of other lives. For many echoes Isaiah 53:12: he poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (20:28). The many are Isaiah’s: the servant who will make many to be accounted righteous (Isaiah 53:11).

Does for many mean that Christ did not die for all? Some read many as a Hebrew way of saying “all,” contrasting the one with the multitude (compare Romans 5:15, 19). Others read it as the definite people for whom Christ’s blood is shed, his sheep and his church (John 10:11; Ephesians 5:25). The second is the more likely in the Reformed reading, since Jesus speaks of a covenant made with his people; it is often called definite or particular atonement, the belief that Christ died with the settled purpose of saving those the Father gave him. Many faithful Christians read these verses the first way, and both sides love the same cross. Both agree that his death is sufficient for all and offered to all, and that no one who comes to him is turned away.

For the forgiveness of sins. Only Matthew includes these words. This is why Jesus came: to save his people from their sins (1:21). It is one of the plainest statements Jesus ever gives of what the cross achieves: not an example or a tragedy turned to good, but blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins. He dies in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty their sins deserved, so that God may justly forgive them (Romans 3:25–26).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “new” before “covenant”, probably from Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. This commentary’s view: not original in Matthew, but the meaning is the same: this is the new covenant Jeremiah promised.

Until that day. “Fruit of the vine” was the phrase used in the Jewish blessing over wine. Jesus looks beyond his death to the messianic banquet, when he will eat and drink with his people again in the fully come kingdom (8:11; Revelation 19:9). The Lord’s Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the feast (1 Corinthians 11:26).

A vow kept. He is fasting from wine until the wedding feast. The next day he is offered wine mixed with gall and will not drink it (27:34); the sour wine he received at the very end (John 19:30) was the soldiers’ cheap drink, not the cup of the kingdom.

With you. Do not hurry past the two words in the middle of the promise. He is sitting with men who will all abandon him within hours, and he is making an appointment to drink wine with them at his Father’s table. The invitation was issued before the failure, not after it, and every hard day since is a day nearer to that table.

Why blood? Is that not a primitive idea? In Scripture blood stands for a life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11), and real forgiveness always costs the one who forgives: either the sinner dies, or a substitute dies in his place, and God provides the life himself. (See Ephesians 1:7 for the fuller answer.)

If my sins are forgiven, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings lag behind facts, and because the accuser loves to repeat old charges. Forgiveness in the new covenant is not a feeling God gives you but a verdict God pronounces on the basis of Christ’s blood: I will remember their sin no more. When guilt returns over a sin you have confessed, answer it with the blood, not with your own efforts: Christ died for that sin, and God is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). Where there is something still to put right with another person, put it right. Then let the verdict stand, and let the Lord’s Supper itself remind you, every time, that the cup was poured out for this.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away because of me this night, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had sung a hymn. The Passover ended with the second half of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 115–118), and this was almost certainly the hymn, so it is worth knowing what the words were: he sang them on his way out to be arrested. He sang the snares of death encompassed me (Psalm 116:3). He sang the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (118:22), the verse he had quoted against the chief priests two days before. And he sang the last line: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever (118:29). He went to Gethsemane singing about the goodness of God.

You will all fall away. They went out across the Kidron Valley to the Mount of Olives (21:1), and on the walk he said it to their faces, with not one exception. The word means to be tripped, made to stumble. He is not predicting treachery like Judas’ but collapse: the sudden giving way of men whose legs will not hold them.

I will strike the shepherd. Zechariah 13:7. Not the soldiers and not the council: in Zechariah God summons his own sword, Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and Jesus quotes it as God’s own act. Jesus is the shepherd struck by God, bearing God’s judgment, and when the disciples run they will be running inside a sentence he has already quoted to them.

Did Peter lose his salvation? Jesus had warned that whoever denies him before men he will deny before his Father (10:33). That warning describes a final, settled disowning, not a fall ended by repentance. Jesus had prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and it did not; he wept bitterly and was restored (John 21:15–19). Judas was sorry and went out to die; Peter was sorry and came back. The difference was not that Peter’s sin was smaller, but that Christ kept him.

How could Jesus sing at a time like that? Because his joy did not depend on his circumstances but on his Father. The psalms he sang were not cheerful songs that ignored suffering; they were songs that looked death in the face and still said the LORD is good. That is what Christian singing is meant to be. When you sing in church in a season of grief or fear, you are not pretending. You are doing what Jesus did on the way to Gethsemane: telling the truth about God over the truth about your situation, until your heart begins to follow your mouth.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

parallels.desc: you will be scattered, each to his own home
strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee." Peter answered him, "Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will go before you to Galilee. He has just told eleven men that every one of them will desert him tonight, and the next thing out of his mouth is not a reproach or a condition but an arrangement: a shepherd telling scattered sheep, in advance, where the flock will re-form (28:7, 10, 16). Galilee is where he found most of them. He will take them back to the beginning.

Restoration booked in advance. We assume restoration is arranged after the failure, in response to sufficient contrition. Here the reunion is booked before the betrayal, by the one who is going to be betrayed, and the men it is booked for are at that moment insisting it will not be needed.

Though they all fall away. Peter answers only the prophecy of collapse, to contradict it. And there is a comparison in the sentence: though they all. His confidence is stated at the expense of the others, and he is correcting his Lord’s assessment of his own heart. Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18).

He meant every word. Peter was not boasting emptily: within the hour he will draw a sword against an armed detachment (John 18:10), which is more than the others manage. His courage was real. It simply was not as deep as his estimate of it, and there was no way for him to discover the difference except the way he discovered it.

Is it wrong to make promises of loyalty to Christ? No. Christians rightly make vows: at baptism, in marriage, in church membership. The fault in Peter was not the promise but the ground of it. He rested it on his own strength and compared himself favourably with others. The right way to promise is with the psalmist’s dependence: I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart (Psalm 119:32). Promise, and then pray that God will keep you in the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." Peter said to him, "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!" And all the disciples said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the rooster crows. The specificity, tonight, before dawn, three times, is a mark of his divine foreknowledge. The crowing may be an actual rooster, or the Roman trumpet signal that ended the watch called cockcrow (about 3 a.m.).

Mark’s two crowings. Mark has before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times (Mark 14:30), and alone records the second crowing (Mark 14:72); Luke and John agree with Matthew. From the earliest days the church held that Mark wrote down the preaching of Peter, so the one Gospel that counts the crowings comes from the one man who had reason never to forget them.

All the disciples said the same. Peter raises the stakes, and he meant it; but he did not know his own heart, and all of them fled (v. 56) within hours. Confidence that rests on what we think we know about ourselves, rather than on the grace of God, is always shown up in the end as presumption.

If Jesus knew Peter would fall, why did he not stop him? He did something better than prevent the fall: he prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail in it, and told him beforehand so that afterwards the memory of his words would bring him back (Luke 22:31–32; Matthew 26:75). God sometimes lets his children discover their weakness the hard way, because nothing else will cure their self-confidence. Peter came out of that night humbler, gentler, and far more useful (1 Peter 5:5–6). The fall was real and grievous; the grace was greater.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, "Sit here, while I go over there and pray." And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A place called Gethsemane. Gethsemane means oil press. It was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, probably with a press in it: a great stone wheel, or a beam weighted with stones, that crushed the fruit until the oil ran. He spends the last free hours of his life in a place named after the machine that crushes something until it yields.

Peter and the two sons of Zebedee. These are the same three who were taken up the mountain and saw his face shine like the sun (17:1–2). He is showing the same three the two ends of who he is.

He began to be sorrowful and troubled. Troubled (adēmonein) means anguish bordering on horror, the state of a man in the grip of something he can hardly bear. He was not a calm philosopher facing death, like Socrates. He faced something far worse than death.

He began. A few days earlier he had named the date without a tremor. In this garden the composure gives way. There is a version of Christianity in which the Son of God walked to the cross serene, insulated by his divinity. Matthew will not allow it. He was not protected from feeling the whole weight of it in advance, and he went anyway.

How can the Son of God be troubled? Because he is truly man as well as truly God. The eternal Son took to himself a real human body and a real human soul, with human emotions (Hebrews 2:14–17). His divine nature did not swallow up his human nature or numb it. So he could weep at a grave, be exhausted at a well, and be appalled in a garden. This is not weakness in him but the depth of his identification with us. We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me." And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, "My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even to death. Echoing Psalms 42:5 and 43:5: why are you cast down, O my soul? Grief so heavy it could kill. Luke says his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44); those two verses (Luke 22:43–44) are missing from some early manuscripts, though many others include them. Watch means stay awake (24:42). He was truly human, and he wanted his friends near.

My Father. Prostrate on the ground, in extreme anguish and humility, he still addresses God as Father (Mark has Abba, Mark 14:36).

If it be possible, let this cup pass from me. The cup in the Old Testament is the cup of God’s wrath against sin (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). This wrath is not a mood but the holy opposition of perfect goodness to evil. What Jesus dreaded was not merely physical pain or death, terrible as crucifixion was. It was bearing the full weight of God’s judgment on the sins of his people: being made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21), becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and being forsaken by his Father (27:46). Being made sin does not mean that Jesus became sinful. It means that God counted his people’s sins as his and dealt with him as those sins deserve, so that he could count Christ’s righteousness as theirs. The holy Son, who had known only the Father’s love, was about to experience God’s wrath. That is why he trembled.

Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will. Perfect submission. Jesus had a true human will, which naturally shrank from such suffering. He submitted it entirely to his Father’s will. Where Adam, in a garden, said my will, Jesus, in a garden, said your will. This is the obedience that saves us (Hebrews 5:7–9).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was reluctant to save us, or that he and the Father were in conflict. He came to do the Father’s will (John 6:38), and willingly laid down his life (John 10:18). His prayer shows the real cost of our salvation, and his real humanity.

For anyone in anguish. Watch what he actually does here, because this is the passage for anyone in real mental anguish: the kind that arrives at three in the morning and makes the next day look unsurvivable. Christians in that condition are often quietly ashamed of it. This garden is for them.

He said out loud how bad it was. My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. There is no managing of appearances. He named the extremity of it in plain words to the people nearest him.

He wanted company in it. Remain here, and watch with me. He asked three men to stay close, not to fix anything or say anything, simply to be awake nearby. He was disappointed three times and went back and asked again. Wanting people near you in the worst hour is not weakness, and it does not stop being right when they let you down.

He asked for it to be taken away. Not once but three times, the last two in the same words. Submission did not mean declining to ask; the nevertheless came after the asking and not instead of it. Anyone who has been told that a truly surrendered Christian would stop pleading for relief should notice who is on his face in this garden, asking again.

He fell on his face. The posture of collapse, not of composure. Luke adds that an angel came and strengthened him (Luke 22:43). What heaven sent was not removal of the cup, which he had asked for, but strength to drink it. That is very often the shape of the answer, and it is not a lesser one: it is what was given to the only perfectly faithful man who ever prayed.

So if you are in that country. Say how bad it is, to God and to somebody. Ask for it to be lifted, and ask again tomorrow. Let people sit near you even though they will sleep. And do not read the absence of rescue as the absence of God. The Son of God went through this before you, and he was not delivered from it. He was strengthened in it, and came out the other side, and went on to do the thing he had been dreading.

Was there really no other way? Jesus’ own prayer answers it: he asked, if it be possible, and the Father did not remove the cup. If sinners could have been saved without the death of the Son, the Father would not have handed him over (Acts 4:12). (See Mark 14:35–36 for the fuller answer.)

Why did Jesus dread it if he knew he would rise? Because the resurrection did not make the cup less bitter; it only meant the cup would not have the last word. A believer facing surgery may know he will recover and still be afraid of the knife. Jesus was not facing a knife but the wrath of God against the sins of his people, a horror no one else has ever known. His dread measures what he bore. And the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2) was what carried him through it, not what took away its weight.

Is it not cruel for a Father to punish his own Son? It would be, if the Son were an unwilling victim and the Father a separate party venting his anger on him. Neither is true. The Son is God himself, one with the Father (John 10:30), and he lays down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). The cross is not one person punishing another against his will. It is the triune God, Father, Son and Spirit, bearing in himself the cost of forgiving us. Gethsemane shows that the Son was not dragged to it. With his human will trembling, he chose it: not as I will, but as you will. The Judge stepped into the dock himself.

For worship. He drank the cup of wrath so that his people never will. The cup that should have been put into our hands he drained, and now he holds out to us the cup of blessing. There is no love deeper than the love that trembled in that garden and did not turn back.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter, "So, could you not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Found them sleeping. It was late, after a large meal and wine, and Luke adds that they were sleeping for sorrow (Luke 22:45). Grief of that order does not keep a man awake; it flattens him. Their failure was, in part, exhaustion from caring.

And he said to Peter, So, could you not watch with me one hour? The question is put to Peter, by name, and Peter is the one who said an hour ago that he would die first (v. 35). It is not sarcasm. It is grief. The you is plural: all three.

Watch and pray. The temptation that was coming: to desert him, to deny him. The word is peirasmos, and it is the same word these men had been taught to use every day in the prayer he gave them: lead us not into temptation (6:13). In the last hour before the test they sleep through the prayer he had put in their mouths, and within hours every one of them enters exactly that trial. Jesus prayed and stood firm; the disciples slept and fell.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. Jesus understands. They sincerely wanted to be faithful; that is the willing spirit. But their human weakness could not carry it out, and good intentions are not enough without God’s strength, sought in prayer: the strength of his Spirit, who now lives in all who are Christ’s (Romans 8:11). He is more generous about them than most Christians are about their own failures. And where his people still fail, as these three did twice more that night, the one man who stayed awake obeyed for them, and his perfect obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19).

What it does not mean. Not that the body is evil and the spirit good. Flesh here means human weakness in general: frail, tired, frightened human nature, which Jesus himself shared that night (v. 38) and does not despise.

When prayer has to happen. The disciples did not fail in the courtyard; they failed in the garden, an hour earlier, while nothing was happening. Peter’s denial was decided before the servant girl opened her mouth.

Is falling asleep when I try to pray the sin Jesus rebuked here? Not exactly. The disciples’ fault was sleeping through a specific call to watch at a moment of crisis, not having a tired body. Jesus himself says the flesh is weak, and he is gentle about it. But take the lesson practically: pray at times when you are able to be awake, not only at the end of an exhausted day; pray aloud or walking if that helps; keep it short and honest rather than long and drowsy. And when a hard day is coming, pray before it, not only during it.

For worship. He who could not find one friend to watch with him one hour now watches over his church day and night, and ever lives to make intercession for them. The vigil they could not keep, he keeps for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done." And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless I drink it. The second prayer is not a mere repetition: if possible has become if this cannot pass. The request has been answered in the only way it could be, and he has heard the answer. He accepts that there is no other way to save his people, and he agrees to drink it.

Your will be done. The words are a line from the prayer he taught these men in Galilee (6:10). On the worst night of his life the Son of God prays his own prayer, as a man asking for something and being told no. Your will be done is not a formula for tidying up the end of a prayer. It is what Jesus said in a garden with his face on the ground, having asked for another outcome and not received it.

Their eyes were heavy. Matthew does not moralise. The loneliest man in Jerusalem went back for company a second time and found the three asleep again. He does not demand support, and he does not abandon the prayer. He goes back to the Father. When human company fails in the hour you most need it, this is the pattern: not resentment, not despair, but a third time on the ground alone.

Does praying your will be done mean I should stop asking for what I want? No. Jesus asked first and submitted second; the submission did not replace the request. God invites you to ask plainly (Philippians 4:6). Praying your will be done means you trust him enough to let him say no, and that you want his will more than your own way. Often the change prayer makes is in us before it is in our circumstances: we come to the place where we can drink what he gives, because we know whose hand is giving it.

verseByVerse.quote: So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. Then he came to the disciples and said to them, "Sleep and take your rest later on. See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third time. Three times, like Paul praying three times about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8). He had nothing new to say and he said the old thing again, which is what people do in real distress, and it is not the vain repetition he warned against (6:7).

Settled in the dark. And then it is over. From this point to his death he does not waver once. The composure the world will see was won on this ground, in the dark, in front of nobody. What is done in public was done first in private, and usually on the floor.

Why does Jesus say Sleep and take your rest later on, and then Rise, let us be going? The words can be read as a question, “Are you still sleeping?”, or as a sorrowful concession that the hour for watching has passed. The second is the more likely: the time when their watching could have helped is over, and now the betrayer is here.
