The hour is at hand. The hour of his betrayal and death (John 12:23, 27; 17:1). Always before it was not yet. It has arrived.

Into the hands of sinners. Is betrayed, handed over: the passive verb that has been running under this whole chapter. The holy one is delivered to the unholy, the sinless one handed over to sinful men, who will do what sinful men do.

Why did Jesus need to pray at all if he was God? Because he was also truly man, living by faith and dependence on his Father as a man must. He did not use his divine nature to bypass the life of prayer. He prayed before choosing the apostles, before the cross, on the cross. If the Son of God needed to pray in order to face his hour, it is not a mark of weakness that you need to. It is the way God has appointed for every human being to receive strength.

verseByVerse.quote: "Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rise, let us be going. Every instinct expects a man with an armed party coming for him and the Judean wilderness behind him to mean away. The verb can mean either. What settles it is the next clause.

My betrayer is at hand. Judas and the crowd are approaching, with torches and lanterns visible in the dark (John 18:3). He is not moving away from the torches. He is walking toward them, and toward the cross.

Nothing compelled it. He is about to say out loud that twelve legions of angels are available for the asking. He could have left the garden ten minutes earlier and the arresting party would have found an empty grove. The only thing keeping Jesus in Gethsemane was that he had decided to be there, and the prayer that ended your will be done goes straight into let us be going. So the arrest that follows is not something that happens to him. It is something he goes out to meet.

Let us. The pronoun matters. Not I am going but let us be going. He takes the three with him, the same three who could not stay awake, who are about to run, one of whom will curse himself in a courtyard before morning. He does not go on without them.

How do I know when to walk toward a hard thing and when to avoid it? Jesus walked toward suffering because it was his Father’s revealed will and the way of obedience. He did not seek suffering for its own sake; elsewhere he withdrew from danger when his hour had not yet come (12:15; John 7:1). So the question is not whether a path is hard, but whether it is the path of obedience. If God’s word and a good conscience point you toward the hard conversation, the confession, the costly stand, then pray, rise, and go. If the hardship is only the result of foolishness, there is no virtue in walking into it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 47–75 — The Arrest, the Trial before the High Priest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies Jesus with a kiss; a disciple draws a sword and is told to put it away; all the disciples flee. At the high priest’s house a court that cannot find two agreeing witnesses condemns Jesus from his own mouth once Caiaphas puts him on oath. He is spat on, blindfolded and struck. Outside, by the fire, Peter three times denies knowing him, and hears a rooster.
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew cuts between two men. Inside, under oath and with his life at stake, Jesus tells the truth about who he is; outside, with nothing at stake but embarrassment, Peter lies about knowing him. Jesus answers with Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 together: the prisoner tells the court that from now on the seating will be reversed. Caiaphas understood the claim at once and called it blasphemy, which makes it hard to say the claim to deity was invented later by the church.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter followed at a distance (v. 58). It was the distance that undid him: close enough to be recognised, far enough back to want not to be. He had prepared to die; he had not prepared for a servant girl by a fire. Denials of Christ often happen in such ordinary places, at work or at the family table. And one lie leads to another: evasion, then an oath, then a curse, each answer covering the one before.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man; seize him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas came, one of the twelve. The words are barely out of Jesus’ mouth before the thing he has just described walks into the garden. And Matthew names Judas as he has all chapter: one of the twelve (v. 14). It is not information; it is the wound.

Swords and clubs. The highest religious authority in the land has sent temple police with clubs and, according to John, a detachment of Roman soldiers (John 18:3, 12). They have come by night, in force, to arrest one unarmed teacher and eleven frightened men: an absurd deployment, and a confession of fear.

The one I will kiss. In the dark, the soldiers might not recognise Jesus or might seize the wrong man. A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher, the thing Judas had presumably done a hundred times on ordinary mornings.

He did not have to. In a garden lit by torches, a pointed finger would have done, or a name spoken aloud. Judas chose the one sign that required him to put his face against his Master’s face. That is the particular horror of this verse: sin habitually takes the forms of love and uses them backwards, because those are the forms that get close enough to do damage. And it was planned.

How can I tell genuine love from flattery that hides an agenda? Look at what the affection asks of you and where it leads. Genuine love in Scripture is patient, truthful and self-giving; it rejoices with the truth (1 Corinthians 13:6), and it is willing to wound you honestly for your good (Proverbs 27:6). Flattery is warm on the surface but serves the flatterer. Be slow to be swept along by sudden warmth from someone who wants something from you, and more importantly, examine your own affection for others: make sure your love is without hypocrisy (Romans 12:9).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came up to Jesus at once and said, "Greetings, Rabbi!" And he kissed him. Jesus said to him, "Friend, do what you came to do." Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greetings, Rabbi. Greetings (chaire) is literally rejoice, an ordinary greeting; Rabbi, as in verse 25, not Lord. And the verb for the kiss is kataphileō, to kiss warmly, the word used of the father kissing the prodigal (Luke 15:20). Profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Proverbs 27:6). Luke records Jesus’ question: Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48).

Friend, do what you came to do. Friend here is hetaire, and Matthew has used it twice before: to the labourer grumbling about his wages (20:13) and to the man at the wedding without a garment (22:12). It is a cool address to someone abusing a bond, and it carries reproach. But it is still a relationship named out loud, and it is the last mercy Judas ever receives from his lips.

What is not said. No curse. No traitor. No withdrawal of the face that is being kissed. And do what you came to do is not permission and it is not resignation. The Greek is compressed (the KJV reads it as a question), but most modern Bibles take it almost as an instruction. He is running his own arrest.

They laid hands on Jesus. Jesus allowed it. Until now the hands reaching out have nearly always been his: touching a leper, raising a dead girl by the hand (8:3; 9:25). The direction of touch has reversed, and it will not turn round again until Sunday, when the women take hold of his feet and worship him (28:9).

How should I treat someone who has betrayed me? Jesus shows the way without minimising the wrong. He named it (Luke 22:48), he did not retaliate, and he did not curse. He left judgment to God (1 Peter 2:23). You may name what was done, protect yourself and others from further harm, and even report a crime. What you may not do is take revenge or nurse hatred (Romans 12:19). Forgiveness begins by handing the debt to God, even when trust cannot yet be restored. And bring your hurt to Jesus, who has been where you are.

For worship. He who could have spoken one word and laid them all on the ground (John 18:6) said friend and gave himself up. Such meekness is not weakness. It is omnipotence on its way to the cross for us.

parallels.desc: profuse are the kisses of an enemy

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drew his sword. John names him: Simon Peter (John 18:10), and nobody is surprised. The man who could not stay awake wakes up fighting. One of two armed men facing a detachment in the dark (Luke 22:38), he draws anyway: the bravest act of the night by anyone except Jesus. It was simply the wrong kind of loyalty: the wrong weapon, at the wrong moment, for the wrong kingdom.

Cut off his ear. John names the servant: Malchus (John 18:10). Luke adds that Jesus touched his ear and healed him (Luke 22:51). It is the last recorded healing before the resurrection, done for one of the men who came to arrest him, repairing damage done by his own disciple.

Put your sword back. Not throw it away, but back into its sheath, where it belongs. Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36). Those who later took up arms against Rome in the hope of a messianic kingdom perished in AD 70.

Does this forbid self-defence? Jesus was not ruling on every use of force. He was refusing to be defended against the cross he had come to bear (v. 54), and rebuking Peter for using the sword to resist God’s plan. Earlier he had told the disciples to take swords (Luke 22:36–38), probably to show that they would now be treated as outlaws, and said It is enough when they took him literally. Scripture allows the defence of life (Exodus 22:2), but forbids violence to advance the kingdom of Christ.

The best motive available. Peter had the best motive available to a human being: defending the Son of God from unjust arrest. If that motive does not license the sword, none ever will. That is the standing judgment on every crusade and every burning in the church’s history: it was tried first in a garden, and Christ stopped it, healed the casualty, and went with them quietly.

What are the swords Christians are tempted to use today? Rarely steel. More often it is the sharp tongue in an online argument, the contemptuous dismissal of opponents, the attempt to win a culture by power, pressure or political force rather than by persuasion, prayer and holy lives. The weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:4). You may argue for truth vigorously, vote, and seek just laws; but the moment you begin to treat the people you disagree with as enemies to be cut down rather than neighbours to be won, you have drawn Peter’s sword.

On a Tuesday. Aggression is not the way he won you. If you have wounded someone in defending the faith, go and help heal what you cut, as he healed Malchus.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? He is standing with his hands being tied, and he tells them what he could do instead. A Roman legion at full strength had about six thousand soldiers, so twelve legions is some seventy-two thousand, and he says more than. Twelve, perhaps one for each disciple and one for himself, or one for each tribe of Israel. Measure it against what one angel has been known to do in Scripture: a single angel of the LORD once struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the Assyrian camp in a night (2 Kings 19:35). Against that arithmetic, the detachment holding him is nothing. And they are available at once, for the asking. He does not say his Father could be persuaded, or that a case could be made. One request, immediately answered. The rescue was one sentence away for the whole of that night, and it stayed one sentence away through the trial, the flogging and the hours on the cross. He refused it, as he refused the devil’s suggestion that angels would catch him (4:6–7).

But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so? Must: God’s plan, revealed in Scripture, required Jesus’ suffering and death (16:21; Luke 24:25–27, 44–46). He submits to God’s word. So the question the passage forces is the right one to ask about every part of the passion: what is holding him? Not the ropes. His answer is a single clause: that it must be so. That is the only thing holding him anywhere in this chapter. Not the soldiers, not Caiaphas, not Rome, not Judas. The Son of God is held in place by the Father’s stated purpose and by nothing else whatsoever, which means every picture of Jesus as a good man overwhelmed by forces too strong for him is exactly wrong. He was never overwhelmed. He was committed.

Keeping faith with what was written. Between seventy thousand angels and the salvation of the people who were arresting him, he chose, while they were putting the ropes on.

If God could rescue me, why does he sometimes not? Because, as here, there may be a greater purpose in the suffering than in the rescue. The Father could have sent angels for his Son, and did not, because a world was being saved. God does not owe us an explanation each time, but he has shown us at the cross that his refusals are never indifference. If he did not spare his own Son, he will not withhold any good thing from those who are his (Romans 8:32). Ask for rescue; and if it does not come, ask for the strength he gave his Son, and trust that the story is not finished.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers.

parallels.desc: my servants would have been fighting

verseByVerse.quote: At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled." Then all the disciples left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? The word is lēstēs. It does not mean a pickpocket. A lēstēs was a bandit or an armed revolutionary, the kind of man who took to the hills and raided; the Romans crucified them. It is precisely the word Matthew will use of the two men crucified on either side of him (27:38). They have turned out in force as though arresting a guerrilla, and in a few hours they will hang him between two of the real thing.

Day after day I sat in the temple. He had been in their own building, in daylight, every day that week, entirely available. They came at night with clubs instead, and the manner of the arrest is a confession about the strength of the case. Truth does not need darkness (John 3:20).

All the disciples left him and fled. He was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12), and the shepherd was struck (Zechariah 13:7). All of them fled, exactly as he had said, the three from the mountain and the man who drew the sword with them. Mark adds a young man who ran so hard he left his clothes behind (Mark 14:51–52). Jesus was utterly alone.

A failure and a prophecy. Their desertion is a failure and also a prophecy: at the moment he was most alone, what was happening was not the collapse of his mission but a line of Zechariah coming true on schedule. It is also a mark of honesty. A movement inventing a heroic past would hardly write its first leaders as men who ran in the dark, yet these leaders let the story be told against themselves. Something turned these runaways into the men who later stood before this same council and would not be silenced (Acts 4:13, 19–20), and the explanation they gave was that they had seen him risen.

What should I do when I feel completely alone? Remember that Jesus has been there, and that he went there so that you would never be alone in the deepest sense. Because he was forsaken, he can promise, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5). Tell him plainly how alone you feel; he knows. Then take one small step toward his people: a call, a visit, a church meeting, even if you go reluctantly. Loneliness is not always a sign of sin, but isolation can become a trap. And if others have deserted you, remember that the disciples who fled were brought back.

parallels.desc: the young man who fled naked

verseByVerse.quote: Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Led to Caiaphas. John records a preliminary hearing before Annas, Caiaphas’ father-in-law (John 18:13, 19–24). Members of the Sanhedrin were called together in the middle of the night, in unjust haste.

Two men followed. The rest of the chapter cuts between Jesus inside with the high priest and Peter in the courtyard outside. Inside, a man tells the truth and it kills him. Outside, a man tells lies to stay alive, in the same building, at the same hour.

Following at a distance. Give him his due. The others are gone; he is here. He has walked into the residence of the man who is trying to kill his Master, which took real courage. His love brought him; his fear kept him at a distance. He has not abandoned Jesus. He is simply not standing next to him.

The distance, not the flight. And it is the distance, not the flight, that undoes him. Peter has put himself exactly where he will be questioned, with exactly the amount of commitment that cannot answer the question: far enough in to be recognised, far enough back to want not to be. A great many believers live in that middle distance.

To see the end. He sat among Jesus’ enemies, wanting to see what would happen but not to be identified with Jesus. He has become a spectator of his own Lord’s trial, warming himself at the enemy’s fire (John 18:18).

What does following at a distance look like today? Attending church but keeping faith out of your conversations at work. Reading about Christ but avoiding the church that would know you. Being a Christian among Christians and a neutral among everyone else. Staying near enough to watch and far enough to be uncommitted. It rarely begins with a decision; it begins with small adjustments for comfort. The remedy is not a heroic leap but to close the gap: join the people of God openly, be known as his in one place where you are not yet known, and pray for courage before the questions come.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole Council. The Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council of seventy-one members: chief priests, elders and scribes, presided over by the high priest. Under Roman rule it had authority over Jewish religious matters, but not to carry out executions (John 18:31).

Seeking false testimony. They had already decided the verdict and were looking for evidence to justify it. The object of the search was false testimony.

They found none. Mark says their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:56). The law required two or three witnesses to agree, and false witnesses were to suffer the penalty they tried to bring on another (Deuteronomy 19:15–19). They had motive, authority and no scruples, and the supply of usable perjury ran out. The impossibility of assembling a charge is Matthew’s quiet argument for Jesus’ sinlessness. At last two came, the minimum the law required.

How far outside their own rules. Later Jewish law (the Mishnah) preserves the safeguards meant to govern a capital trial, and if those rules were in force then, this proceeding breaks them one after another: capital cases were to be heard in daylight, in the court’s own chamber, not on the eve of a festival, and a night had to pass before a death sentence, so that mercy had time to work.

Why does it matter that Jesus was innocent? Because only an innocent substitute could die for the guilty. If Jesus had been guilty of anything, his death would have been for his own sin. Scripture insists that he was the lamb without blemish, who knew no sin, so that he could be made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 1:19). This trial, where the most determined enemies in the land could find nothing, is God’s public certificate of the spotlessness of the sacrifice.

For worship. The verdict that should have been ours was read over him in a crooked court; the verdict that was his, not guilty, is read over all who trust him.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin, the ruling body of about seventy elders, chief priests and scribes. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "This man said, 'I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am able to destroy the temple. Here at last is the charge that sticks, and it is a half-truth. Early in his ministry, in the temple courts, he said: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). John explains that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:21).

Two alterations. Destroy this temple was an imperative addressed to them, and it has become I am able to destroy, a boast. And the reference to his body has been dropped, so that a saying about resurrection becomes a threat. That is how the most effective false witness has always worked, in courts and in churches and in families: not fabrication, which can be disproved, but accurate quotation with the context stripped off.

A well-chosen charge. The temple was the centre of the nation’s identity, economy and worship, and the accusation would carry political weight with Rome as well as religious weight with the council.

Truer than they knew. What none of them can see is that the distorted version is truer than they think. The temple building was destroyed within forty years, as he had said (24:2). And the true temple, the one he meant, was standing in front of them bound: in killing him they would destroy it, and in three days he would rise. They condemned him for a prophecy they thought was a boast, and it came true on both counts.

Why is Jesus called the true temple? Because the temple was the place where God dwelt among his people and where sins were atoned for by sacrifice. Jesus is both: God with us in the flesh (John 1:14), and the sacrifice that ends all sacrifices. Since his death and resurrection we no longer need a building in Jerusalem to meet God. We come to God through Christ, wherever we are (John 4:21–24), and those who are united to him become a temple of the Holy Spirit together (Ephesians 2:21–22).

parallels.desc: “Destroy this temple” — the temple of his body

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up and said, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, "I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest stood up and said, Have you no answer to make? The high priest has stood up, perhaps the gesture of a man losing control of his own courtroom.

But Jesus remained silent. Isaiah 53:7: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. Jesus has spent the week answering every question the authorities could devise; he could have dismantled this testimony in a sentence. He declines.

I adjure you by the living God. Adjure means put under oath. It placed a witness under obligation before God to answer truthfully (Leviticus 5:1). Having failed to convict him on evidence, the high priest puts the accused on oath and asks him to convict himself.

Tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. The real question. If Jesus claimed to be the Messiah and the Son of God, they could charge him with blasphemy. The words are almost exactly Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi (16:16–17). One man said it and was called blessed; the other says it looking for a capital conviction.

Is it right to take an oath, since Jesus said do not swear at all? Here Jesus is put under oath by the high priest, and he answers. That shows that his words in 5:34 forbid casual and evasive swearing, not a lawful oath before a judge (compare Hebrews 6:16–17).

The right question. The question Caiaphas asks is the only question that matters, and he is entirely correct that everything depends on the answer. He gets the answer. It is the truth. And he tears his clothes.

When should a Christian stay silent and when should he speak? Jesus was silent when answering would only have meant arguing with lies, and he spoke the moment he was asked directly who he was. That is a good guide. You need not defend yourself against every false accusation; often it is wiser to entrust yourself to God (1 Peter 2:23). But when you are asked plainly whether you belong to Christ, silence becomes denial. Defend his name before your own.
verseByVerse.note: An oath “by the living God” obliged the one questioned to answer.

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven." Then the high priest tore his robes and said, "He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have said so. Yes (see v. 25); Mark records: I am (Mark 14:62). It is a formal affirmative, not an evasion. Silent through the whole proceeding, put on oath he speaks, and what he says is the most extravagant claim ever made in a courtroom.

At the right hand of Power. Jesus adds a sentence nobody asked for, built out of two of the highest texts in the Hebrew Bible. Seated at the right hand is Psalm 110:1, which he had used against these same men days before (22:44). Power was a reverent Jewish way of saying God without saying his name. Jesus claims that he will sit at God’s right hand: not merely be honoured, but share God’s throne.

On the clouds of heaven. Daniel 7:13–14 (24:30): the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion, a kingdom that shall not pass away. From now on they would see the evidence of his enthronement: the resurrection, the outpouring of the Spirit, the spread of the church, and at the last his coming in glory as Judge, when all authority given him (28:18) is seen by all.

The seating reversed. Put together, the two texts say: you are trying me tonight, and you will stand before me. The next hearing will have the seating reversed, and the enthronement begins here, with the condemnation.

Caiaphas understood him. That should be said plainly, because it bears on the suggestion that Jesus never claimed to be divine and that his followers invented it later. The one man in the room with every professional reason to find a lesser meaning heard the claim, recognised it instantly, and called it blasphemy, which it would be from anyone else. A sceptic may answer that the church wrote the scene; but a blasphemy verdict and a Roman cross are hard to explain if Jesus claimed nothing of the kind.

He tore his robes. Tearing one’s clothes was a sign of grief or horror (2 Kings 18:37). Later tradition required judges to tear their clothes on hearing blasphemy, though the law forbade the high priest to tear his clothes in mourning (Leviticus 21:10). The picture is hard to miss. In the act of condemning the Son of God for blasphemy, the high priest of the old order tears his own robes, in front of the council, at the very moment the true High Priest is condemned to die. Within a day the curtain of the temple will be torn too (27:51).

He has uttered blasphemy. Blasphemy means speaking of God with contempt, and that includes claiming for yourself honour that belongs to God alone. If false, this was the worst blasphemy. And it was true: the council was in the presence of the holy God in human flesh, and it did not tremble.

Why did Jesus not soften his claim to save his life? Because the claim was the truth, and the truth was the reason he had come. He could have stayed silent, or given a vague answer, and walked out alive. He chose to be condemned for who he is rather than acquitted for being less. That bears directly on a question many people still ask: was Jesus only a good teacher? No good teacher would die rather than retract a false claim to share God’s throne. Either he is the Son of God seated at the right hand of Power, or he is not good. He has left us no middle option.

For worship. The robes Caiaphas tore belonged to a priesthood whose work was finished that night. Our High Priest wears no torn garment. He lives for ever, enthroned, interceding, coming.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s robes was a sign of horror or grief; the high priest does it at what he hears as blasphemy.

verseByVerse.quote: "What is your judgment?" They answered, "He deserves death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is your judgment? The high priest asks the council for its verdict. He asks for it immediately, having supplied the only evidence himself.

He deserves death. The Greek is two words, enochos thanatou, liable to death. The penalty for blasphemy under the law was death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Mark says they all condemned him (Mark 14:64). But they could not carry out the sentence themselves; they needed Rome (27:1–2). The most consequential judicial decision in human history is taken in the middle of the night, in a private house.

The parable comes true. This is the destination the Gospel has been travelling toward since chapter 21. He told the leaders about a vineyard whose tenants killed the owner’s son, and they knew he was speaking about them (21:38, 45–46). Now the tenants have the son, and they say what the parable said they would say.

Who these men were. This was not a mob, and it was not Rome. This was the supreme court of the people of God, men who had given their lives to the Law and the Prophets. They had every advantage, and it was the worst verdict ever returned. That is a warning aimed squarely at the religious: it is possible to know the Scriptures thoroughly, to hold the highest office, and to be so certain of your own reading that when the truth walks into your courtroom you condemn it for blasphemy, and go home believing you have defended God.

The one true sentence of the night. “He deserves death.” They were wrong about Jesus: he was innocent. But they spoke a truth about us. We deserve death for our sins (Romans 6:23). Jesus, who did not deserve it, took the death we deserved (1 Peter 3:18). It was true of everyone in the room except the man they were sentencing, and he was on his way to bear it for them.

How can I make sure I do not become like these religious leaders? Hold your knowledge of Scripture with humility, and let it judge you before you use it to judge others. Pray as you read that God would open your eyes (Psalm 119:18). Be willing to be corrected, especially by the plain words of Christ. And watch for the moment when protecting your position, your reputation or your church’s comfort becomes more important to you than the truth. The council’s problem was not too much Bible but too little submission to the one the Bible was about (John 5:39–40).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, saying, "Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They spit in his face. The verdict is delivered and the court dissolves into a beating, not yet by soldiers but by the council and its attendants. Spitting in the face was the deepest insult, reserved for someone placed outside the community altogether (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9). Matthew’s wording suggests that the judges themselves joined in the abuse.

Isaiah had written the scene. Isaiah 50:6: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting. They are mocking him for claiming to be the one the prophets spoke of, while acting out a paragraph of the prophets.

Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you? Some slapped him; Mark says they blindfolded him first (Mark 14:65), which is what makes it a game: blindfold the prophet, hit him, and ask him to name the hand. They are not merely hurting him; they are ridiculing the claim he made under oath. And at that very moment his prophecy about Peter was being fulfilled in the courtyard below.

He knew. Their question has an answer. The men taking turns at a blindfolded prisoner were asking the coming Judge to identify them, and he could have named every one of them. He said nothing. And within weeks Peter would stand up in Jerusalem and preach to a crowd that may well have contained some of them, and offer them forgiveness in the name of the man they had blindfolded (Acts 2:36–38). That is the only reason any of us should be glad he did not answer the question.

How should I respond when I am mocked for my faith? As he did: without retaliating and without abandoning the truth, entrusting yourself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). (See Luke 22:63–65 for the fuller answer.)

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, "You also were with Jesus the Galilean." But he denied it before them all, saying, "I do not know what you mean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Outside in the courtyard. At the same time as Jesus was confessing the truth under oath inside, with his life at stake, Peter was denying it outside, at a fire, with nothing at stake but embarrassment and fear.

A servant girl. Not a soldier or a priest, but a servant girl, probably young, the lowest-ranking person in that courtyard. She has recognised a face, perhaps from the temple or in the light of the fire (Luke 22:56), and said so out loud.

I do not know what you mean. The first denial is evasion. The man who drew a sword against armed soldiers was afraid of a servant girl. He had prepared himself, sincerely, for death, not for a girl by a fire on a cold night. His answer is just enough fog to make the conversation move on: the smallest possible step in the wrong direction, and it makes the next two possible.

Where denial happens. Very few denials of Christ happen under interrogation. They happen at work or at the family table, when the subject comes up and a laugh is available. Nobody plans it; the mouth is faster than the conviction. What rules the heart in that moment is rarely hatred of Christ. It is the hunger to be accepted by the people round the fire, what Scripture calls the fear of man, which lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not more willpower but a greater fear: to be so taken up with the approval of Christ that the approval of the room shrinks to its true size.

What can I say when someone asks me about my faith and I feel unprepared? Something simple and true. You do not need an argument; you need a confession. Yes, I am a Christian; Jesus means everything to me; I would be glad to tell you why. Peter later wrote that we should always be prepared to make a defence for the hope that is in us, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Prepare a short honest answer in advance, and ask God each morning for courage in the small moments. One plain sentence spoken kindly is better than a clever silence.

For worship. The Son’s confession inside covers the disciple’s denial outside. Christ, who made the good confession (1 Timothy 6:13), confessed for us when we could not confess for ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." And again he denied it with an oath: "I do not know the man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the entrance. He moves away from the fire toward the gate, and stays there, the worst place in the courtyard: still inside, already looking out.

Another servant girl. Mark seems to mean the same girl and Luke speaks of a man, which suggests that in a crowded gateway more than one voice took up the charge. This time it is said to the bystanders, so the denial has to be made in front of an audience. The pressure rises, and so does the denial.

With an oath. The second denial calls God to witness, and it is more definite: I do not know the man, not even using his name. He has stopped fogging the question and started answering it, falsely.

A bitter detail. This same Lord had told them not to swear at all (5:33–37). Peter is using God’s name to make the lie more convincing, in the act of denying the one who forbade it.

Lord, you know. His words are I do not know the man. Weeks later, on a beach, the risen Christ will ask him three times whether he loves him, once for each denial, and Peter will answer, Lord, you know (John 21:15–17). The man who claimed not to know will end up resting everything on being known.

Escalation. Escalation is the signature of a lie under pressure: a single untruth has to be defended, and each defence costs more than the last. Evasion, then an oath, then a self-curse, in perhaps an hour: Peter is a man further down a slope he stepped onto with one small evasion.

Is it too late to stop once I have already compromised? No. Every moment is a moment to stop, and the sooner the better. The slope gets steeper the further you go, but you can always turn back while you are still on it. Do not defend the first lie with a second. Go back, tell the truth, apologise where you need to, and accept the embarrassment as a small price. Peter could have stopped at the gateway. It is always better to be humbled now than hardened later.

verseByVerse.quote: After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, "Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you." Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know the man." And immediately the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your accent betrays you. After a little while, about an hour by Luke’s reckoning (Luke 22:59), it is not one accuser but a group, and the evidence is his own mouth. Galileans had a distinctive accent, and the more Peter talked, the more obvious he became. John adds that one of them was a relative of Malchus, who had seen Peter in the garden (John 18:26).

A curse on himself. The third denial, the strongest, which goes as far as language allows. He called down a curse on himself if he was lying (may God strike me if I know him), or perhaps cursed Jesus. He is asking God to destroy him if he knows Jesus, and Jesus is a short distance away being spat on.

Immediately the rooster crowed. At the very moment, as Jesus had said (v. 34). Luke adds that the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61). Matthew puts the crow directly against the curse with nothing in between: an ordinary bird at the ordinary hour, and the most precisely timed sound in the New Testament.

A hard mercy. The sound is evidence that his Lord had been exactly right about him and had not been surprised. It is a hard mercy, and unmistakably a mercy: God arranged in advance for Peter to be stopped before he could go a step further.

Does God still use ordinary things to stop us? Yes. He rarely sends a voice from heaven, but he often sends a rooster: a verse that comes to mind at the very moment of temptation, a friend’s question, an interrupted plan, a sermon that seems written for you, a sudden memory of something Jesus said. When an ordinary thing pulls you up short just as you are going wrong, do not dismiss it as coincidence. Stop, remember his words, and turn back. It may be the Lord looking at you across the courtyard.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter remembered. This is the turning point. Memory of Christ’s word, confronting his own failure, produces not despair but grief.

He wept bitterly. Deep, broken grief: true repentance. Paul describes the difference between Peter’s tears and Judas’ remorse (27:3–5): godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation, but worldly grief produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Peter went on to preach at Pentecost and to die for Christ.

Two kinds of tears. The chapter that began with a woman’s extravagant love ends with an apostle’s extravagant tears. Bitter weeping before God is one of the most hopeful sounds in Scripture: the heart is awake to its own failure, and hearts that are awake can be healed.

Which of the two am I? Matthew has deliberately braided the two men together: Judas betrays and Peter denies, both on the same night, both wretched about it afterwards, and one is restored and one is destroyed. Anyone who has failed badly reads that and wants to know which of the two he is. Start by refusing the answer that suggests itself first, which is that Peter’s sin was smaller. It was not obviously smaller. Peter denied with oaths and curses, three times, having been warned by name a few hours earlier, and he did it while his Lord was on trial for his life.

The direction the sorrow travels. The difference is the direction. Both men felt terrible. But remorse is what a man feels about consequences and about himself: Judas went to the priests, tried to undo the transaction, and when that failed he went out alone. He never went to Jesus. Peter’s grief drove him in exactly the opposite direction, back to the only person who could do anything about it, and within weeks he is eating breakfast on a beach with him. One kind of sorrow ends in a rope; the other ends in a charcoal fire and a threefold restoration (John 21:9, 15–17). If you have lost someone to suicide, hear this gently: Matthew is showing a refusal to come to Christ, and he is not handing you a verdict on the one you grieve.

The practical test. So the test is not how badly you feel but which way you are facing while you feel it. Do you find, underneath the shame, that you still want him, or only that you want the mess undone? A man may be in pieces and still be crawling in the right direction, and that is Peter. So take it to him tonight, and stop conducting the trial yourself. He restored a man who cursed himself in a courtyard, without a single reproach on the beach.

How long should I keep grieving over a sin I have repented of? Grieve until it drives you to Christ, and then let him lift your head. Peter wept bitterly, but he did not weep for ever; on the beach Jesus gave him a task, feed my sheep, and Peter spent the rest of his life doing it. Continued self-punishment after repentance is not deeper humility; it is a refusal to believe the gospel. Remember the sin enough to stay humble and grateful, and to be gentle with others who fall. But do not keep reopening the account that Christ has closed.

On a Tuesday. If someone you know has fallen, be the friend on the beach, not the voice in the courtyard.

For worship. The Lord who was spat on inside the hall was praying for the man who cursed himself outside it, and that prayer could not fail. He went to the cross for the man who would not own him, and came back from the dead to light a charcoal fire on a beach and cook him breakfast. There is no failure of his people that his love cannot outlast.

26.theology: The cup of wrath and the death in our place. The cup Jesus asks to be spared in Gethsemane, and then drinks on the cross, is the Old Testament cup of God’s judgment on sin. His blood is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (26:28), which is Matthew’s plainest statement of penal substitution: Christ bearing in our place the penalty our sins deserved, so that God can justly forgive us. In his Son the holy God took the penalty himself, so that justice and mercy meet at the cross.
26.examples:
Then: The disciples slept while Jesus prayed, and could not watch one hour. Matthew records it not to shame them but to show that the cross was won by the Son’s obedience, alone in the dark, and not by the resolve of his friends.

Now: Every Lord’s Supper carries the weight of that night. To eat and drink in a worthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27–29) is to remember the present ground of our standing before God: his blood, poured out for the sins we bring to the table today.

27.title: The Crucifixion of the King
27.text: <sup>1</sup>When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. <sup>2</sup>And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor. <sup>3</sup>Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, <sup>4</sup>saying, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” They said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.” <sup>5</sup>And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. <sup>6</sup>But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money.” <sup>7</sup>So they took counsel and bought with them the potter’s field as a burial place for strangers. <sup>8</sup>Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day. <sup>9</sup>Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, <sup>10</sup>and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.” <sup>11</sup>Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus said, “You have said so.” <sup>12</sup>But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer. <sup>13</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?” <sup>14</sup>But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed. <sup>15</sup>Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. <sup>16</sup>And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. <sup>17</sup>So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, “Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” <sup>18</sup>For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up. <sup>19</sup>Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream.” <sup>20</sup>Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. <sup>21</sup>The governor again said to them, “Which of the two do you want me to release for you?” And they said, “Barabbas.” <sup>22</sup>Pilate said to them, “Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said, “Let him be crucified!” <sup>23</sup>And he said, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Let him be crucified!” <sup>24</sup>So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, “I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves.” <sup>25</sup>And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!” <sup>26</sup>Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified. <sup>27</sup>Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor’s headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. <sup>28</sup>And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him, <sup>29</sup>and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>30</sup>And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head. <sup>31</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him. <sup>32</sup>As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross. <sup>33</sup>And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), <sup>34</sup>they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it. <sup>35</sup>And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. <sup>36</sup>Then they sat down and kept watch over him there. <sup>37</sup>And over his head they put the charge against him, which read, “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.” <sup>38</sup>Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left. <sup>39</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads <sup>40</sup>and saying, “You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” <sup>41</sup>So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, <sup>42</sup>“He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. <sup>43</sup>He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” <sup>44</sup>And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way. <sup>45</sup>Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. <sup>46</sup>And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>47</sup>And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, “This man is calling Elijah.” <sup>48</sup>And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink. <sup>49</sup>But the others said, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.” <sup>50</sup>And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit. <sup>51</sup>And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. <sup>52</sup>The tombs also were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised, <sup>53</sup>and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many. <sup>54</sup>When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said, “Truly this was the Son of God!” <sup>55</sup>There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him, <sup>56</sup>among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. <sup>57</sup>When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus. <sup>58</sup>He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him. <sup>59</sup>And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud <sup>60</sup>and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away. <sup>61</sup>Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. <sup>62</sup>The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate <sup>63</sup>and said, “Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’ <sup>64</sup>Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, ‘He has risen from the dead,’ and the last fraud will be worse than the first.” <sup>65</sup>Pilate said to them, “You have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can.” <sup>66</sup>So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.
27.overview:
This is the chapter of the cross, the event the Old Testament moves toward and the New Testament flows from, by which God reconciles a broken world to himself. Matthew tells it with restraint, saying little of the physical agony, but fills every scene with the Old Testament: Psalm 22, Zechariah 11 and Isaiah 53.

At the moment of his death three signs come together: the temple curtain is torn from top to bottom, the earth shakes, and tombs open. The torn curtain is God’s own act: the way into his presence is open to all who come through the crucified King. And a Roman centurion, at the foot of the cross, confesses what Peter confessed in chapter 16: truly this was the Son of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — The Trial before Pilate and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At dawn the council confirms its verdict and takes Jesus to Pilate, because it may condemn but not execute. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself; the money buys a burial field for foreigners. Before Pilate the charge becomes kingship. Pilate tries the Passover custom, is warned by his wife, finds no fault, washes his hands, and condemns him anyway. Barabbas goes free. Jesus is scourged, mocked and crowned with thorns, then crucified at Golgotha between two rebels and jeered at by passers-by, priests and the dying.
verseByVerse.theology: Substitution is the shape of the story itself. There is one cross and two candidates: a guilty rebel walks free because the innocent man takes his place (v. 26). The mockery says the same in reverse: he saved others; he cannot save himself is true in every word and false in every intention.
verseByVerse.examples: Pilate is the warning in this section. No one sees more clearly: he is amazed at the prisoner, warned by his wife, aware that the charge comes from envy. And no one does less with what he sees. He looks for a way to be just at no cost to himself, and when there is none he lets the innocent man pay.

verseByVerse.quote: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 27 is the day the Son of God died. Judas hangs himself, Pilate frees a murderer and condemns the innocent, the soldiers mock, the sky goes dark, and the Son is buried and guarded. Every hand in the chapter is set against him, and every hand serves the purpose for which he came: to be numbered with the transgressors, so that transgressors might go free.

When morning came. Friday morning, at dawn. Much that was done in Caiaphas’ house during the night was irregular, at least by the rules later written down for the council, so a formal session confirms the verdict in daylight (Luke 22:66–71) to give it a form that will stand. It changes nothing; this is paperwork.

They took counsel. They had condemned him for blasphemy (26:65–66). But under Roman rule they could not carry out a death sentence: it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death, as they tell Pilate in John’s account (John 18:31). They can condemn; they cannot execute. So to kill him they must persuade a Gentile governor, and for that the charge must change.

They bound him. Bound like a criminal. He had spent three years loosing people: a bent-over woman loosed from her disability, a dead man loosed from his grave clothes, sinners loosed from their debts. The last thing done to him before the Gentiles take him is that his hands are tied.

Pilate the governor. Pilate governed Judea for Rome as prefect for ten years, from AD 26 to 36. His usual residence was at Caesarea on the coast, but he came to Jerusalem at festivals with troops to keep order. Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh and insensitive to Jewish feelings, and he slaughtered Galileans at the temple (Luke 13:1). An inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea in 1961. His name is in the Apostles’ Creed: suffered under Pontius Pilate, anchoring Jesus’ death in real history.

Handed on. The verb is paradidōmi, delivered over, the word that runs under the whole Passion story. Judas delivered him to the priests; the priests deliver him to Pilate; Pilate will deliver him to be crucified. Each hand-off is a small act of evasion: nobody wants to be the one holding him at the end. But Paul uses the same verb of the Father: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Behind men avoiding responsibility is the Father handing over the Son, on purpose, for us.

Why does it matter that the Creed names Pilate? Because it fixes the gospel to a date and a place. Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas about God, which could be true even if Jesus never lived. It is news about something that happened in Judea when a particular Roman official was in office, and could be checked. Pilate’s name in the Creed is a standing claim that the death of Christ is history. That is why the apostles preached it as witnesses (Acts 2:32), and why you can trust it as fact, not as myth.
verseByVerse.note: The Jewish leaders could not carry out a death sentence under Roman rule. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

parallels.desc: not lawful for us to put anyone to death

verseByVerse.quote: Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." They said, "What is that to us? See to it yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Judas saw. Something he had not expected has happened. Perhaps he assumed the council would release Jesus, or that Jesus would escape or finally act with power. The verdict lands, and the thing becomes real.

He changed his mind. “Changed his mind” (metamelētheis) means regretted, felt remorse. It is not the word usually used for repentance (metanoeō), a change of mind that turns and goes the other way, though the two overlap (21:29, 32). Judas felt the full weight of what he had done, and he brought back the thirty pieces of silver as if returning the money could undo it. What he did not do was turn round.

I have sinned by betraying innocent blood. A true confession: Jesus was innocent, and even his betrayer testified to it. He names the act, calls it sin, uses the first person, and declares the victim innocent, which is more than Caiaphas, Pilate or the crowd would say. If words could save a man, these would have done it. But he confessed to the wrong people. The priests could not forgive him. The only man in Jerusalem who could have done anything with that sentence was a short distance away, bound, and Judas took it to a committee instead.

What is that to us? See to it yourself. Total callousness. The religious leaders, whose job was to care for souls, had no interest in a sinner’s guilt. They had used him, paid him, and were finished with him, and they tell him his conscience is his own business.

Was Judas truly sorry? He felt remorse, and he confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood. But he did not turn to Christ. Paul distinguishes godly grief, which produces repentance, from worldly grief, which produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Peter’s tears led him back; Judas’ led him away. Jesus called him the son of destruction (John 17:12) and said it would have been better for him not to have been born (26:24). Judas was lost not because his sin was too great to forgive, but because he would not come to the one who forgives.

See to it. In twenty verses Pilate will wash his hands and say see to it yourselves: the same formula, handed on from the priests to the governor and back to the people. Everybody in this chapter is trying to put the blood somewhere else. Judas tries to give the money back; the priests will not take it into the treasury; Pilate calls for a basin; the crowd shouts that they will have it on their own heads. Not one of them can get rid of it, because there is only one place that blood can actually go, and none of them will take it there.

The blood that answers blood. The irony is the gospel itself. The innocent blood Judas cannot get off his hands is the very blood that was about to be poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28). The guilt he carried to the temple could have been carried to the cross, where the one he betrayed was taking the guilt of betrayers on himself. The blood of Abel cried out for vengeance; the blood of Jesus speaks a better word (Hebrews 12:24), and it speaks it over every sinner who comes, including the one who sold it.

If I confess my sin to God but still feel terrible, is my sorrow the wrong kind? Not necessarily. Feeling terrible is not the test; Peter felt terrible too. The question is where the sorrow takes you. Judas’ sorrow took him away from Christ to people who could not help him, and then to himself alone. Godly sorrow takes you to Christ, trusting that his blood covers the very sin you grieve over. If you have brought your sin to him and are clinging to him, your sorrow is doing its proper work, even if the feelings take time to settle. Keep looking to him, not to the size of your feelings.

On a Tuesday. If you are a leader in the church, never answer a troubled conscience with what is that to us; take it, and the person carrying it, to the one who forgives.

verseByVerse.quote: And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Throwing down the silver. Into the sanctuary itself, perhaps. Zechariah 11:13 foretold the thirty pieces thrown into the house of the LORD. A futile act of rejection: he cannot unspend the price.

He hanged himself. Despair, recorded without embellishment.

Two men on a tree. On the same day, it seems, two men hung on wood near Jerusalem. One hanged himself under the weight of his own guilt. The other was hanged by others under the weight of everyone else’s. The law said a man hanged on a tree is under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23); Judas, refusing the one who would bear that curse, carried his guilt alone, as his own judge and executioner. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Judas’ rope is what despair does with guilt; the cross is what God does with it. The betrayer would not come to the tree on which his sin could have been borne, and so he bore it himself on another.

Two accounts of one death. Luke, reporting Peter, says that falling headlong Judas burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out (Acts 1:18), and that Judas acquired the field, where Matthew says the priests bought it. The likeliest explanation is that the two are the beginning and the end of one event: a man hangs himself, then the rope or branch gives, and the body does what Luke describes when it strikes rock. Matthew tells what Judas did; Luke tells what was found. As for the field, the money was legally Judas’, which was exactly the priests’ problem, so a purchase made with it is naturally credited to him. And both accounts point to a field everybody in Jerusalem could name. Invented stories do not usually come with an address.

Blood money. Astonishing hypocrisy. They had paid the money to have an innocent man killed, and now they scrupled over the ceremonial law about where to put it (Deuteronomy 23:18). They strained out a gnat and swallowed a camel (23:24). It is religion without conscience: the rulebook consulted over the money, and never once over the killing it paid for.

Is suicide the unforgivable sin? No. Judas’ death is recorded, not approved, and he was lost because he rejected Christ, not because of how he died. Scripture never makes suicide the one sin Christ cannot forgive, and the believer’s security rests on Christ’s grip, not on the state of his mind in his last moments (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:38–39). Anyone tempted to take his own life should speak to someone today, a friend, a pastor or a doctor, and look to the one who restored Peter.

I have lost someone I love to suicide. What should I believe? Grieve, and do not let this passage be used to torment you. Judas is not a picture of every person who has died this way; he is a man who rejected Christ. If the one you lost trusted Christ, his salvation rested on Christ’s finished work, not on the darkness of his final hours, and nothing in all creation can separate Christ’s people from his love (Romans 8:38–39). If you do not know, leave him with the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25). Do not carry the guilt of his choice as if it were yours. Find people to grieve with, and take your questions to God honestly. He is near to the broken-hearted (Psalm 34:18).

parallels.desc: the wages of a dog into the house of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: So they took counsel and bought with them the potter's field as a burial place for strangers. Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The potter’s field. They will not put the money in the treasury and cannot give it back, so they spend it. A potter’s field was probably worked-out clay ground, useless for farming and littered with broken pots: cheap because it was finished. Tradition places it in the Hinnom Valley, south of Jerusalem: the same valley that gave Gehenna its name (5:22).

As a burial place for strangers. For pilgrims and foreigners who died in Jerusalem without a family tomb. They have found a way to be charitable with the price of a man’s life. And there is a quiet picture in it: the money paid for Jesus’ death bought a burial ground for outsiders, and within a few years the message the priests tried to suppress would reach exactly such foreigners, the very people the Son of God had just died for.

The Field of Blood. In Aramaic, Akeldama (Acts 1:19). To this day: the place was still known when Matthew wrote, in a city where anybody reading his account could walk out and look at it. The priests bought a plot to keep their books clean, and instead put up a permanent public monument to what they had done. They protected the treasury and named a graveyard after their own crime.

The same trick as before. Jesus had exposed the same reasoning in the gift dedicated to God to avoid supporting parents (15:5–6). The silver is treated as defiled, and the men who paid it out as untouched. It is possible to build a whole moral system that asks scrupulous questions about objects and none at all about the man holding them.

Can God really bring good out of something so evil? Yes, and the cross is the supreme proof. The worst act ever committed, the murder of the Son of God, became the salvation of the world, and even its blood money ended up burying strangers. That does not make the evil good, or excuse those who did it. It means evil never has the last word in God’s world. What others meant for evil against you, God can mean for good (Genesis 50:20). You may not see the good this side of glory, but you can trust the God who did it at Golgotha.
verseByVerse.note: A potter’s field was probably land used for digging clay. Acts calls it Akeldama, “Field of Blood.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spoken by the prophet Jeremiah. An honest reader with a reference Bible will stop here, and should. The words are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, where the good shepherd of God’s people is paid off with thirty pieces of silver, a contemptuous wage, which he throws to the potter in the house of the LORD. Turn to Jeremiah for those words and you will not find them. Why does Matthew name Jeremiah? Jeremiah also visited a potter (Jeremiah 18–19), smashed a potter’s jar in the Hinnom Valley as a sign of judgment on Jerusalem, renaming it the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 19:1–13), and bought a field as a sign (Jeremiah 32:6–15). Matthew combines Zechariah’s words with Jeremiah’s themes, and names the more prominent prophet, as Jewish teachers sometimes did (compare Mark 1:2, which combines Malachi and Isaiah under Isaiah’s name). This commentary’s view: not an error, but a combined reference, naming Jeremiah because the themes of the potter, the field, the Hinnom Valley and judgment on Jerusalem come from him.

In the flow. The only other time Matthew names Jeremiah this way is at the slaughter of the children of Bethlehem (2:17). Both times the deed is evil, and both times Matthew writes then was fulfilled, not in order that: God did not make Herod kill or the priests bribe, yet neither crime slipped outside his word.

What Jeremiah 19 actually says. Before elders and priests in the Valley of Hinnom, Jeremiah breaks a potter’s flask and announces that because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents it shall be called the Valley of Slaughter, and they will bury in it (Jeremiah 19:1–6, 11). Broken pottery, priests and elders, innocent blood, a burial ground, a new name: six centuries later the same kind of officials buy the same kind of ground with blood money, and the city renames it. In some Jewish orderings Jeremiah also stood first among the prophets, a natural label for the whole collection.

The price of him. Israel’s leaders valued Jesus at the price of a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32).

The LORD who was priced. Read Zechariah 11 again: it is God who is insulted. The shepherd holds out his hand for wages, but it is the LORD himself who speaks of the lordly price at which I was priced by them (Zechariah 11:13). Matthew sets that sentence over thirty coins counted out for Jesus: the one weighed out at a slave’s price is the LORD of Israel come as their shepherd. He let them do it, because the shepherd had come to lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

As the Lord directed me. The men handling that silver thought they were tidying up an administrative problem. They were walking, step by step, through a prophecy about themselves.

Does this mean the Bible has mistakes in it? No. A difficulty is not the same thing as an error. Here the apparent problem is best explained by how Jewish writers cited the prophets, and the solution actually deepens the meaning. Not every scholar is satisfied with it, and it is honest to say so; but it fits how Matthew handles Scripture elsewhere. Christians hold that Scripture, as God breathed it out, is true in all it affirms (2 Timothy 3:16; John 10:35). When you meet a difficulty, do not panic and do not pretend it is not there. Look it up, read carefully, ask a trusted teacher, and expect, as here, to find that the text is wiser than the objection.
verseByVerse.note: The words are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, but Matthew names Jeremiah, who bought a field and visited the potter.

parallels.desc: thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" Jesus said, "You have said so." But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the governor. The Judge of all the earth stands before a Roman official, probably at Herod’s palace on the west side of Jerusalem, or at the Antonia fortress next to the temple.

And the governor asked him, Are you the King of the Jews? The charge has changed. Before Caiaphas the demand was tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God; before Pilate it is are you the King of the Jews? Blasphemy meant nothing to Rome. But claiming to be king, without Caesar’s appointment, was treason. Luke records their accusations: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and calling himself Christ, a king (Luke 23:2). The same man is accused of a different crime in a different building an hour later, and everyone knows why. Pilate’s question has an emphatic pronoun in it, you are the King of the Jews?, and the emphasis is probably contempt. He is looking at a man who has been up all night, beaten, bound, deserted by his followers and handed over by his own nation’s leaders. Rome had seen pretenders before; they generally arrived with an army. This one has arrived with rope marks on his wrists. The magi had asked for the King of the Jews at his birth (2:2).

You have said so. Yes, but not in the sense you mean. It is the same form of words he gave Judas and Caiaphas: an affirmative that hands the sentence back to the speaker. Pilate means a rival to Caesar; the answer is yes to something immeasurably larger, and Pilate will soon have it written over his head without believing a word of it. John records Jesus’ explanation: my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:33–37).

He gave no answer. Silence before false accusations (26:63; Isaiah 53:7). This is the man who silenced the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the lawyers so completely that no one dared to ask him any more questions (22:46). He could have taken this court apart. The silence is not helplessness: a man who could clear himself and will not has decided something in advance.

If Jesus is King, why does the world look as though he is not? Because his kingdom comes in two stages. Now he reigns from heaven, gathering his people by the gospel and ruling the nations for the sake of his church (28:18; Ephesians 1:20–22), while evil is still permitted for a time. At his return his reign will be visible to all, and every enemy will be put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). His kingdom is not of this world in its source and methods; it does not advance by armies or elections. But it is very much in this world, in every heart he rules and every church that bows to him.

For worship. Pilate asked his question with a sneer, and the answer was yes. The crown he received that day was thorns; the crown he wears now is many diadems (Revelation 19:12), and the hands that were tied before Pilate hold the sceptre over every province and every governor that has ever been.
verseByVerse.note: “King of the Jews” was the political charge that mattered to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate said to him, "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not hear how many things they testify against you? Pilate cannot understand it. He expected the prisoner to defend himself; under Roman law a defendant who did not respond could be convicted. And the astonishment in the question is genuine. He is offering the prisoner an opening. Say something. Give me one thing I can work with.

Not even to a single charge. The Greek is emphatic and total. What Pilate took for an inexplicable failure of self-preservation was a prophecy being kept in front of him, by a man who had decided in a garden the night before that he was not going to be talked out of this.

Greatly amazed. The word this Gospel has used of crowds watching a mute man speak and disciples watching a storm go quiet (9:33; 8:27). The power of Rome in Judea is the one left staring. He had seen men beg, bribe and bluster; he had never seen a defendant not interested in getting out. Isaiah 52:15: kings shall shut their mouths because of him.

Impressed is not enough. A great many people today are impressed by Jesus and say so warmly. Pilate was amazed at him in the morning and signed his death warrant before noon. Admiration is not allegiance.

How do I move from admiring Jesus to trusting him? By seeing that he is not only remarkable but necessary: that you need him, not just his example. Admiration keeps Jesus at a safe distance, as an object of interest. Faith comes close and says, you are my Saviour and my Lord. Ask God to open your eyes to your own sin and to Christ’s death for it (Acts 16:14). Read one of the Gospels through, asking at each page, what does this demand of me? And then do what Pilate never did: act on what you see. Confess him, obey him, join his people.

parallels.desc: when he suffered, he did not threaten

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover release. No document outside the Gospels mentions it, but similar amnesties are known in the Roman world, and a goodwill release is plausible for a governor managing a restless province at its most crowded moment. At Passover, which celebrated Israel’s release from slavery, it was fitting.

A notorious prisoner. Matthew calls him notorious, episēmos, literally marked: he had a reputation. Mark and Luke say he had been arrested for insurrection and murder (Mark 15:7; Luke 23:19); John’s word, robber (John 18:40), was used for violent revolutionaries. Barabbas is not a burglar but a fighter who has killed to get Rome out of Israel, exactly the kind of messiah many in that city were hoping for.

Textual note. Some manuscripts call him “Jesus Barabbas” (ESV footnote), in verses 16 and 17. Jesus was a common name. Scribes may have removed it out of reverence. If original, Pilate’s choice was stark: “Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus called Christ?” “Barabbas” means “son of the father”: another irony, set beside the true Son of the Father. Origen in the third century knew the reading and disliked it, thinking it improper that a criminal should share the Lord’s name, and that kind of reverent squeamishness is exactly how a name gets quietly dropped from a text.

A picture of substitution. Whatever the manuscripts say, this is as clear a picture of substitution as the New Testament gives. There is one cross and two candidates.
