Barabbas is guilty and everyone knows it; he has no defence and expects none. He is released, and he is released for exactly one reason: the other man took his place. Every person who has ever been forgiven is standing where Barabbas stood that morning, listening through a cell door to a crowd deciding, and walking out into the sunshine while somebody else is led away to the cross that had been meant for him.

Am I really like Barabbas, when I have never killed anyone? In the way that matters, yes. Barabbas is not chosen because he was the worst sinner in Jerusalem, but because he was guilty and Jesus was not. Before God every one of us is guilty, by nature and by choice, and has no defence to offer (Romans 3:19, 23). Jesus said that hatred is murder of the heart (5:21–22). The point is not that you are as violent as Barabbas, but that you are as helpless: your release depends entirely on another taking your place. That is humbling, and it is the best news there is.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “Jesus Barabbas.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?" For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? Pilate hoped the crowd would choose Jesus, and that he could release him without offending the leaders. A murderer and rebel, or a healer and teacher: let the crowd’s affection override the leaders’ spite. It has the great advantage of costing Pilate nothing; he does not have to acquit or defy anybody.

Out of envy. Pilate is not confused. Envy is the right diagnosis: not zeal for the law or public order, but resentment of Jesus’ standing that curdles into a wish to see it destroyed. Whatever the charges said, the council’s motive was that this Galilean had taken the crowds they thought belonged to them, and a professional reader of provincial politics saw it quickly. A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot (Proverbs 14:30).

Pilate’s method. He never once considers simply doing what a judge is for. He has an innocent man and absolute authority, and he looks instead for a procedure no one can blame him for: the crowd, the custom, then a basin of water. There is no such route. Doing right when it is unpopular has a price, and anything that removes the price also removes the rightness. When he could not find a cheap way, he chose the cost he could bear and let the innocent man pay the other.

Justice that paid for itself. Pilate could not find a way to be just without paying, and the innocent man in front of him was the only one in history who did pay. God would not acquit the guilty by a procedure that ignored their guilt; that would have been Pilate’s kind of justice. Instead he put forward his Son as a propitiation, a sacrifice that absorbs God’s just anger, to be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26). At the cross justice was not dodged but satisfied, and mercy was not cheapened but bought at the highest price there is. Pilate looked for a route around the cost. Christ walked straight through it.

The envy Pilate spotted. It is a sin few of us escape, and it never arrives announcing itself. Not one of those priests thought he wanted the Galilean dead because the crowds preferred him; each had a reason, and the reasons were theological. Envy borrows the language of principle, because it cannot survive being named. The test is simple and unpleasant: when someone doing your kind of work is praised, do the objections you raise to his methods occur to you before or after the praise? Christ died for the envious too, and the cure begins there.

How do I fight envy once I see it in myself? Name it to God as envy, not as concern or principle. Then do the opposite of what envy wants: pray for the person’s good, speak well of him to others, and thank God for the gifts he has given him. Envy forgets that God is the giver of every gift and that he is not stingy with you. Remember what you have in Christ, an inheritance that cannot be taken (1 Peter 1:4), and that in his body every member’s honour is shared (1 Corinthians 12:26). Rejoicing with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15) is hard, and it is the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment seat. The bēma, the raised platform from which Roman officials gave judgment. In the middle of the trial a note arrives: his wife thought this urgent enough to interrupt a capital case in public. Only Matthew records it; later tradition named her Procula.

Have nothing to do with that righteous man. A Gentile woman declares Jesus righteous, dikaios: not merely innocent of this charge, but righteous. The council would not say it, and Pilate never quite says it. A Gentile woman who has never met him says it on the strength of a dream.

The righteous one for the unrighteous. Her word holds the meaning of the whole day. If Jesus were not righteous, his death would be one more sinner paying for his own sins. Because he is righteous, his death can be for others. Isaiah had promised exactly this: by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities (Isaiah 53:11). Pilate’s wife pleaded that the righteous man be spared. God’s purpose was deeper and kinder: that the righteous man be condemned, so that the unrighteous might be counted righteous in him (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is justification: the guilty walk out declared righteous, not because they have become good enough, but because their sin was laid on the condemned Christ and his righteousness is credited to them.

In a dream. Romans took dreams seriously as omens, and this one was a warning from God to Pilate, which he ignored.

The last dream. Matthew’s account of the birth is full of God protecting his Son by warning people in their sleep, foreigners included (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19). Now, at the end, one last dream and one last foreigner. Every warning at the beginning was heeded and the child lived. This one is set aside, and the man dies.

The mercy still knocking. God is under no obligation to warn Pilate, and the outcome is fixed, yet heaven still sends word into the governor’s house at the last hour, through the one person who might reach him. Even in the hour of the greatest crime ever committed, mercy is still knocking, for a man who will wash his hands and do it anyway.

Does God still speak through dreams today? God is free to use any means to stir a conscience, and some people testify that a dream first made them seek Christ. But dreams are not a source of new revelation for the church. God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and his word in Scripture is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). Christians differ on how God guides today, and many who expect him to speak in dreams are careful to test them by Scripture; on that test all agree. Test any dream, impression or feeling by the Bible, and never let one override it. The warning Pilate needed was the same as yours: have nothing to do with condemning the righteous one. God has already said that plainly in his word.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. Only Matthew records the message from Pilate’s wife.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor again said to them, "Which of the two do you want me to release for you?" And they said, "Barabbas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persuaded the crowd. The crowd does not arrive with a demand; it is worked, by argument and pressure. This was probably not the same crowd that welcomed Jesus on Palm Sunday, mostly pilgrims from Galilee, but people gathered early at the governor’s palace, perhaps including supporters of Barabbas.

Which of the two do you want me to release for you? Pilate asks again, and the answer comes at once: Barabbas. They chose the guilty man and rejected the innocent one. The murderer goes free; the giver of life goes to death. Peter would say it to their faces: you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life (Acts 3:14–15). Barabbas is a picture of every sinner: guilty, condemned, and released because Jesus took his place.

Who was in that courtyard. Not the nation of Israel, most of whom were at home or scattered across the empire, but people assembled at dawn by men with a specific outcome in mind (see on v. 25).

What the crowd teaches. These were not monsters. What moves a crowd is rarely the evidence and usually the direction of the pressure. The instinct to go with the room does not feel like cowardice while it is happening; it feels like consensus, and it can move ordinary people from Hosanna to crucify inside a week. Jesus was never deceived by it. He did not entrust himself to the crowds, because he knew what was in man (John 2:24–25), and he rode in on Sunday knowing what the same streets would shout on Friday. He went on anyway, and died for the fickle as well as the faithful.

How do I keep from being carried along by the crowd? Decide what you believe about Christ from his word, not from the mood of the room, whether that room is a workplace, a university, a newsfeed, or even a church. Notice who is doing the persuading and what they stand to gain. Be slow to repeat what everyone is saying. And keep company with believers who will tell you the truth. The crowd’s voice is loud and immediate; Christ’s voice is steady and written down. Read it daily, and it will become louder in you than the shouting.

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to them, "Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" They all said, "Let him be crucified!" And he said, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Let him be crucified!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ? The question every person must answer. Pilate asks it as a man who has run out of manoeuvres, and it is the question the whole Gospel has been driving toward. He is not asking what is true about Jesus but what he will do about him, which is the harder question. And the one option most people assume they have is not available to him: he cannot leave the prisoner in the cell and think about it. The man must be released or executed before the feast, and doing nothing is a decision with a body attached.

Let him be crucified. Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals (see 20:19). They wanted the most shameful death Rome had.

And he said, Why? What evil has he done? Pilate declares Jesus innocent. He could find no crime (Luke 23:4, 14, 22; John 18:38). The judge knew the prisoner was innocent. It is the right question, asked by the right official, and it is almost the only genuinely judicial sentence spoken in the entire proceeding. Nobody answers it.

They shouted all the more. Matthew records not a single charge in reply: not a better argument but a louder one, the noise doing the work that reasons cannot.

What if I am honestly not sure yet what I think of Jesus? Then keep looking, and look honestly, because the question will not wait for ever. It is not wrong to have questions; it is wrong to use them as a way of never deciding. Read a Gospel through, slowly, asking who this man is. Talk to a Christian you trust. Ask God, if he is there, to show you the truth about Jesus, and be willing to follow where it leads (John 7:17). Many have come to faith that way. But do not treat uncertainty as a safe resting place. Pilate thought he could avoid choosing, and he chose.

On a Tuesday. If you have already received him, ask Pilate’s question in a narrower form for this week: what will I do with him at work, at home, with my money, with my time?

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, "I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves." And all the people answered, "His blood be on us and on our children!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A riot was beginning. Pilate feared a riot at Passover, which could cost him his position. John adds that the leaders threatened him: if you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend (John 19:12).

He washed his hands. The basin is borrowed theatre. Washing the hands to disclaim blood is above all a Jewish rite (Deuteronomy 21:6–9; Psalm 26:6): when a body was found in open country and the killer was unknown, the elders of the nearest town washed their hands and declared that their hands did not shed this blood. Pilate uses the gesture the crowd would understand. Only Matthew records it.

See to it yourselves. The same words the priests used to Judas that morning (v. 4). But Pilate could not wash away his responsibility with water. The rite in Deuteronomy is for men who genuinely do not know who did it. Pilate knows exactly who is doing this, because he is. A judge cannot become a bystander by getting his hands wet. Underneath the cowardice was a god he served more than justice: his own position. He would sooner lose an innocent man than lose Caesar’s favour (John 19:12), and anything we cannot bear to lose will sooner or later make us betray what we know is right. The creed remembers him for it.

His blood be on us. A formula accepting responsibility for a death (2 Samuel 1:16; Jeremiah 26:15). The crowd accepted the guilt.

What it does not mean. This verse has been terribly misused through history to justify hatred and persecution of Jewish people as “Christ-killers”. That is a grave sin and a grave misreading. First, this was a particular crowd, not the Jewish people then or since. Second, Jesus prayed for his executioners’ forgiveness (Luke 23:34), and Peter offered forgiveness to the very people of Jerusalem who had demanded his death (Acts 2:36–39; 3:14–19). Third, Jews and Gentiles together were responsible (Acts 4:27), and in the deepest sense, all humanity, including us, put Jesus on the cross by our sins. The man on trial is a Jew, as are his mother, every apostle, the women at the cross and the author of this Gospel.

No crowd can bind its children. A shout from a managed crowd at dawn is not a legal instrument, and no crowd on earth can bind the unborn generations of a whole people. Scripture rules the principle out: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20). Paul, a Jew, writes that the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), and that his heart’s desire and prayer for his own people is their salvation (Romans 10:1).

The prayer turned inside out. This is why a Christian should be the last person on earth to use the verse as a weapon. His blood coming upon a person is the best thing that can happen to anyone alive. Seven weeks later Peter preached in that city to people who may well have been in that crowd, and three thousand were baptised (Acts 2:41); the blood they had called down on their own heads did not condemn them. It washed them.

Can I wash my hands of decisions I go along with? No. If you have the power to stop a wrong and you let it happen to protect yourself, you share in it, whatever you say aloud. That does not mean you are responsible for everything you cannot control. But in the decisions that are yours, at work, in your family, in your church, refusing to choose is a choice. Ask God for courage to do what is right when it is costly, and when you have failed, do not reach for Pilate’s basin. Reach for the blood of Christ, which cleanses what water cannot.
verseByVerse.note: Washing the hands was a public declaration of innocence in a death.

parallels.desc: the elders wash their hands over the heifer
I wash my hands in innocence
to bring this man’s blood upon us

verseByVerse.quote: Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He released Barabbas. The guilty man walks; the innocent man is flogged and handed over. Substitution is not imposed on this verse by later theologians. It is the shape of the sentence.

Having scourged Jesus. Roman scourging (flagellatio) was brutal. The victim was stripped and tied to a post, and beaten with a whip made of leather thongs with pieces of bone or metal tied in. Roman scourging had no fixed limit of strokes as Jewish law did (Deuteronomy 25:3). It tore the skin and flesh, sometimes exposing bones and organs. Many died from it. It was administered before crucifixion partly to weaken the condemned.

Restraint. Matthew gives the scourging a participle, on the way to something else. All four Gospels refuse the kind of devotion that dwells on physical horror until the emotion becomes the point. What they want understood is not chiefly how much it hurt but what it accomplished, and Isaiah had said it: he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). Isaiah saw whose the lash was, and wrote the pronoun: our.

Delivered him to be crucified. The gospel lives in the gap between the two clauses: a convicted murderer went home free, and the man who had taken his place was tied to a post. That is why the word gospel means news rather than advice.

Does with his wounds we are healed mean every believer will be healed of illness now? Isaiah’s healing is first of all healing from sin and its guilt: Peter quotes the verse about our sins and returning to the Shepherd (1 Peter 2:24–25). Christ’s death does also secure the final healing of our bodies, at the resurrection, when there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Meanwhile God often heals in answer to prayer, and we should ask. But believers still get ill and die, as Paul’s friends did (2 Timothy 4:20). Illness is not proof of weak faith. The full harvest of these wounds is still to come.
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor's headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The governor’s headquarters. The praetorium, the governor’s official residence in Jerusalem. A battalion (speira, cohort) was nominally six hundred soldiers, though the detachment on duty would have been smaller. These were probably auxiliary troops recruited from non-Jewish areas like Samaria and Syria, often hostile to Jews, and a Jewish king was an object of mockery to them.

Gratuitous cruelty. This part of the passion serves no judicial purpose. It is done because it was funny. Boredom in an occupying garrison, a prisoner who will be dead by evening, and a man who will not retaliate: out of those ordinary ingredients comes an entirely gratuitous cruelty. Nobody in that courtyard was a monster. They were soldiers with an hour free.

A scarlet robe. It was probably a soldier’s own faded red military cape, near enough to imperial purple to make the joke. Mark and John say purple (Mark 15:17; John 19:2): scarlet and purple were often confused. Stripping a man was a deep humiliation, and it is the second stripping of the day.

Every element true. Every element of the mockery is true: a real coronation robe on a real King. In a few hours a sign will be put over his head naming his title, in three languages (John 19:20), by order of the governor. They are dressing him for a throne while thinking they are dressing him for a laugh, and the only person in the courtyard who knows what is actually being enacted is the man in the cloak.

Why would God let his Son be humiliated like this? Because humiliation is part of what sin deserves and part of what sin does. We were made to be crowned with glory and honour (Psalm 8:5), and our rebellion has made us objects of shame. Christ took the shame as well as the pain, so that he could take away our shame before God (Hebrews 12:2). He is therefore a Saviour for those who have been mocked, stripped, used or despised. Whatever shame has been put on you, by others or by your own sin, he has worn worse, and he can clothe you with honour.

On a Tuesday. Watch the cruelty that comes from boredom and crowds: the joke at someone’s expense, the online pile-on. Do not join the courtyard.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. A soldier’s red cloak served as a mock royal robe.

verseByVerse.quote: and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A crown of thorns. A mock crown, perhaps from thorny branches used for kindling, imitating the radiant crown of a ruler on coins. It was not a costume piece: the spines on some thorn scrub there are long and hard, and it caused real pain. Into his right hand they put a reed for a sceptre: the hand of authority given a stalk.

The curse as a crown. Of all the things a soldier could have grabbed for a joke, this one reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible. When the ground was cursed because of man the sentence was: thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you (Genesis 3:17–18). Thorns are the visible signature of a world under judgment. The curse of the ground was gathered into a circle and pushed onto the head of the man who came to carry the curse away, by soldiers who thought they were being witty.

Hail, King of the Jews. A parody of the greeting to Caesar, Hail, Caesar! They performed the kneeling correctly in order to make it ridiculous, not knowing they were speaking the truth. They were rehearsing. One day every knee in heaven and on earth and under the earth will bow at this name, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11). The first knees bent to the crowned Christ belonged to a Roman execution detail, and they were not wrong about the posture, only about the reason.

Struck him on the head. Driving the thorns deeper. Spitting, as at the Jewish trial (26:67): Jews and Gentiles alike mocked him. The man spat at by a bored garrison holds their beating hearts in his hand. He could have asked his Father for twelve legions of angels; the cohort in that yard was playing games with the one person present who could have ended it, and who had already decided not to.

Is it wrong to wear a cross or display a crown of thorns? Not in itself; many believers use such signs to remember what Christ has done, and they can be a quiet confession of faith. The danger is that the sign becomes decoration, or a charm, or a substitute for the faith it represents. The crown of thorns is not a pretty thing; it is the curse of our sin worn by our King. If you display it, let it humble you, not merely adorn you. And remember that the real mark of a Christian is not a symbol on the wall but a life that bows to the King.

For worship. Now he is crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). He bore the curse of the ground so that creation itself will be set free (Romans 8:21), and instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress (Isaiah 55:13). Hail, King of the Jews, King of the nations, King of our hearts.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His own clothes. The robe would probably have stuck to his wounds, and removing it reopened them. A condemned man was walked to execution in his own clothing, so the crowd could see who was being crucified. He is stripped again and again in a single morning: for the scourging, for the joke, and at Golgotha.

Led away to crucify him. Crucifixions took place outside the city walls, on main roads, so that passers-by would see and be warned (Hebrews 13:12). Matthew has been building to these words since Jesus first told them plainly that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things and be killed (16:21).

Every step chosen. Not one step of this walk is forced on him. He chose it in the garden, aloud, with his face on the ground: not as I will, but as you will. He could have stayed in Galilee, accepted the crowd’s crown after the loaves (John 6:15), or answered Pilate and walked out. At every junction a door stood open, and he did not take it. This is not a man swept along by events but the most deliberate walk in history, and he kept walking because the people he was doing it for could not have walked it themselves.

What does it mean to go to him outside the camp? Hebrews uses this detail to call believers to share Christ’s rejection: let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:13). It means being willing to be counted with Jesus where he is not honoured: to be thought old-fashioned, narrow or foolish for his sake, to lose standing in a group because you belong to him. It does not mean seeking persecution or being needlessly offensive. It means that when the choice is between the comfort of the camp and the company of Christ, you go to him, because here we have no lasting city (Hebrews 13:14).

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon of Cyrene. Cyrene was a city in North Africa (modern Libya), with a large and long-established Jewish community. Simon was probably a Jewish pilgrim come for the Passover, or he may have lived in Jerusalem among the Cyrenian Jews (Acts 6:9). He was coming in from the country (Mark 15:21) when a soldier picked him out of the crowd.

They compelled him. The word is a technical term for requisition: a Roman soldier could compel any provincial to carry his gear for a distance. Matthew’s readers had met it in the Sermon on the Mount, from the man now being led up the road: if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles (5:41). A condemned man normally carried the crossbeam (patibulum), weighing perhaps 30–50 kilos, to the place of execution. Jesus, weakened by the scourging, probably could not go on. Simon literally took up a cross, and Luke adds that he carried it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), a living picture of the call to take up the cross and follow him (16:24).

The wood and the weight. Simon could carry the timber. He could not carry what the timber was for. The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6), and that load was never shared with anyone. So Jesus accepted help on the road and refused it on the hill: he would be helped to the cross, but not on it. Simon’s shoulders took the beam for a few hundred yards; Christ’s soul took the curse that beam would hold.

The father of Alexander and Rufus. Mark adds that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), naming two men as though his readers already knew them. And when Paul sends greetings to Rome he includes Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Romans 16:13). It cannot be proved that this is the same family, but if it is, the woman who mothered the apostle Paul was married to the man who carried the cross.

A ruined morning. Simon did not volunteer. By any ordinary reckoning it was a disaster of a day. It is also the only reason anybody has heard of him, and it appears to have put his sons in the church.

What should I make of the interruptions that ruin my plans? Hold them more loosely than they feel. Simon’s worst morning became the day he walked closest to Christ. Not every interruption is a hidden blessing you will see in this life, but every one is under the hand of the God who directs our steps (Proverbs 16:9). When you are pressed into a burden you did not choose, caring for a sick relative, covering someone’s work, a crisis that lands on you, carry it as Simon did, behind Jesus. It may be the very road on which you learn what it means to follow him.

On a Tuesday. Because he bore the one load no helper could share, you are free to carry other people’s loads (Galatians 6:2): go the second mile this week for someone who has pressed you into the first.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Mark adds that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Golgotha. Golgotha is Aramaic for skull; the Latin is Calvaria, from which comes Calvary. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a known place of execution. It was outside the walls but near the city (John 19:20), beside a road, because the point of crucifixion was that people should see it. The traditional site, inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, appears to have been outside the walls in Jesus’ day.

Wine mixed with gall. Mark says wine mixed with myrrh (Mark 15:23), a narcotic to dull the pain. Jewish women of Jerusalem reportedly provided such a drink to the condemned out of mercy, on the strength of the proverb about giving strong drink to one who is perishing (Proverbs 31:6). Gall means something bitter; Matthew echoes Psalm 69:21.

He would not drink it. He tasted it, so the refusal is informed, and no one would have thought less of him for taking it. Twice that night he had prayed about a cup, and twice he had said that if it could not pass, he would drink it (26:39, 42). He was not going to numb the cup he had agreed to drink, and he kept the vow of the upper room (26:29).

Borne awake. Everything that follows, the mockery, the darkness, the cry, was undergone by a man in full possession of his senses. Some love will not take the edge off the thing it has agreed to carry.

Is it wrong for a Christian to take pain relief? No. Jesus’ refusal was about his unique work: he had to bear the cup of wrath fully and consciously as our substitute. That is not a pattern for us to copy in illness. Medicine is a good gift of God, and Scripture itself commends relief for those in distress (Proverbs 31:6; 1 Timothy 5:23). Take the painkiller with thanks. What we can learn from Jesus here is the willingness to face reality rather than escape it, especially the reality of our sin and our need, which many try to drown in other ways.
verseByVerse.note: Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” The drink was probably a drugged wine to dull pain; Jesus refused it.

parallels.desc: they gave me poison for food

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. Then they sat down and kept watch over him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crucified him. Matthew describes it in three Greek words; his first readers needed no explanation. Crucifixion was reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst class of criminals; Roman law exempted citizens from it. The victim was stripped, fixed to a wooden cross with nails through the hands or wrists and the feet (or sometimes with ropes), raised upright, and left to die slowly, often over hours or days, from exhaustion, blood loss and suffocation.

Every breath bought. Hanging from outstretched arms, many physicians think, made breathing desperately hard; to take a full breath the victim probably had to push up against the nail through his feet. When the Romans wanted to end it quickly, as they would that evening before the Sabbath (John 19:31–32), they broke the legs, and it was soon over. Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting punishment, and said the very word should be kept far from Roman ears. To preach a crucified Messiah was therefore a social obscenity, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23). No one setting out to win followers would readily invent a founder who died this way.

Casting lots. The clothes of the condemned belonged to the execution squad. Psalm 22:18: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (John 19:23–24 quotes it). Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add that quotation to Matthew’s verse here; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it. Roman victims were usually crucified naked. Soldiers playing a game to pass a slow afternoon are, without the faintest idea of it, performing a line of the psalm he will quote from the cross in a few hours.

They kept watch over him. To prevent rescue, and to make sure he died. It is the flattest sentence in the chapter and one of the most terrible. This was a shift. The most significant hours in the history of the universe were, to the men closest to them, a slow day at work. Some of the greatest things God has ever done have looked, to everyone standing nearby, like nothing much happening.

Why did Jesus have to die by crucifixion, rather than some other way? Because crucifixion meant hanging on a tree, and the law said that a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23). Paul draws the line: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). The manner of his death displayed its meaning. He did not merely die; he died as one under the curse, in the place of those who deserved it. The shame was part of the payment, and the public display was part of the proclamation.
verseByVerse.note: The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And over his head they put the charge against him, which read: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews." Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge against him. A board (titulus) stating the crime, carried before the condemned and then nailed to the cross, so that all would know why he died and take the lesson. John says it was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek (John 19:20).

This is Jesus, the King of the Jews. The charge was treason. Pilate meant it to mock the Jews, and it was the truth. The only crime the authorities could state in writing was that he was the King. The chief priests asked Pilate to change it to say he claimed to be, and Pilate, who had given way on everything that morning, chose this of all things to be immovable about: what I have written I have written (John 19:21–22). A weak man’s one act of stubbornness fixed the truth over the cross where nobody could take it down.

Rome said it first. Aramaic for the people of the land, Latin for the government, Greek for everybody else: the first public written proclamation that Jesus of Nazareth is King went up in the languages of the known world, at the expense of the Roman state. The church would spend three centuries saying the same sentence and being killed for it. Rome wrote it first, by accident, in triplicate.

Two robbers. Robbers (lēstai), probably insurgents like Barabbas, perhaps even his associates, in which case the middle cross had been built for him. Isaiah 53:12: he was numbered with the transgressors. Not near them: counted in, given the central place the crowd would read as the worst of the three, because he had agreed to be counted as one of them, the only way any of them could be counted righteous. James and John had asked for the places at his right and left in his kingdom (20:21). Here are the ones at his right and left as he is enthroned.

Was Jesus really a king, if he died like that? Yes, and the cross is where his kingship was most fully shown. Earthly kings rule by taking lives; this King rules by giving his. He conquered sin, death and the devil not by escaping the cross but by enduring it (Colossians 2:15). The resurrection then declared him Son of God in power (Romans 1:4), and he now reigns at the Father’s right hand. When you look at the cross, you are not looking at a king who failed, but at a King winning his greatest battle.

On a Tuesday. Do not despise those whom the world counts as transgressors. Your King died among them.
verseByVerse.note: The charge was written on a board for all to read. The “robbers” may have been insurgents.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wagging their heads. Psalm 22:7: all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads. The mockery comes in three waves: the passers-by, then the clergy, then the men dying beside him. The soldiers played out verse 18 of the psalm with their dice; the crowd now plays out verse 7 with their heads.

Rebuild it in three days. The false charge from the trial (26:61). A charge does not have to survive cross-examination to survive in the mouths of a crowd. The irony: he was at that moment fulfilling it. His body, the true temple, was being destroyed, and in three days he would rise (John 2:19–21).

If you are the Son of God. The words of the devil in the wilderness: if you are the Son of God (4:3, 6). Same offer: prove the title, take the shortcut, avoid the cross. The last temptation is the first, arriving through human voices: a Son of God who will not suffer. Jesus could have come down. He stayed because he is the Son, obedient to the Father; it was not nails that held him there, but love. He was never more evidently the Son of God than in the hours he refused to act like it.

Why do people still say, if God is real, let him prove it? Because the human heart still wants a God on its own terms: a God who removes suffering on demand, who performs when challenged, who never asks us to trust. Jesus refused that demand on the cross because meeting it would have meant abandoning us. God has given proof enough: the cross itself, the empty tomb, the witnesses, the changed lives (Acts 17:31). Honest questions are welcome, and the gospel offers reasons, not only demands (1 Peter 3:15). What he will not do is bow to our terms. If you find yourself saying, God, show me and I will believe, ask whether you are asking for evidence or for control.

parallels.desc: “If you are the Son of God”

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests mocked him. The second wave is the clergy: the highest religious leaders of Israel came to gloat. These men would not enter the governor’s headquarters for fear of defilement (John 18:28) and had no scruple at all about this. They talk about him in the third person, over his head, which is its own kind of contempt.

He saved others; he cannot save himself. It may be the most accidentally accurate thing ever said about Jesus. He saved others is an admission from hostile witnesses that the works were real; his enemies never deny the miracles (12:24). And he cannot save himself is true as well, not for lack of power: because he was saving others, he could not save himself.

And we will believe in him. A false promise: they had already seen many signs and did not believe. In three days he did something harder than climbing down from a cross, and these same men paid the guards to say the body was stolen (28:11–15). The problem was never the quantity of evidence.

If Jesus saved others, why does my unbelieving friend not see it? Because unbelief is not mainly a problem of evidence but of the heart. These leaders saw miracles and still mocked. No one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4). That is not a reason for despair but for prayer. Keep telling your friend the truth, live it before him, and pray that the God who said, let light shine out of darkness, will shine in his heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). Some of the priests became believers later (Acts 6:7).

How could such religious men stand at a cross and jeer? Because religion can be used to save yourself instead of to seek God. These men had built their whole sense of worth on being right, clean and respected. A religion like that always needs someone to look down on, and it cannot bear a Saviour who says the respectable need rescue as much as the immoral (9:12–13). The same danger lives in every churchgoer. One test is how you feel when grace is given to someone you think less deserving than you (20:15). The cure is to see that you are among the others he saved, not one of the few who never needed it.

verseByVerse.quote: "He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'" And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He trusts in God. Almost word for word Psalm 22:8: he trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him. Reaching for the cruellest thing they can think of to say, the leaders of Israel produce a near-verbatim line of Scripture written about this very scene. They had sung that psalm, and they could not hear themselves saying it. There are few sharper illustrations of the difference between knowing the Bible and understanding it.

I am the Son of God. Their reasoning is the argument of Job’s friends, and of a great many people since: if God delighted in him, God would rescue him; God has not rescued him; therefore God does not delight in him. The logic is clean and the conclusion false: at that moment the Father’s delight in the Son’s obedience was complete, and the Son was exactly where the Father’s purpose had sent him.

The same arithmetic about your life. Hold onto that if you have done the same arithmetic: if God loved me, this would not be happening. The most loved man who ever lived was hanging on a cross while the clergy explained that his situation proved otherwise.

The robbers also reviled him. This is the bottom of the descent: two men in the same agony spent some of their little life mocking the man beside them. Matthew wants the darkness total before anything else is said. Luke records that one later repented and asked Jesus to remember him, and Jesus promised him paradise that day (Luke 23:39–43). But Matthew leaves it here. Every human voice at Golgotha is against him, and he is dying for the owners of every one of them.

What does the dying thief teach about how a person is saved? That salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, not by works. The thief had no time for baptism, church membership, or a changed life to show; he simply turned to Jesus, owned his guilt, and trusted him as the King (Luke 23:40–42). And Jesus promised him paradise that very day. That does not make baptism or obedience unimportant for those who have time; Jesus commands them (28:19–20). But it shows what they rest on. No one is ever saved by anything except Christ, received by faith. It also shows that a man can be saved at the very end, though no one should presume on having that time.

For worship. He trusted in God, and God did deliver him, not from death, but out of it, on the third day. The beloved Son was mocked by every voice on earth, and heaven was silent, so that heaven’s voice might one day say of us, these are my beloved children.
verseByVerse.note: Luke records that one of the two later repented.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–66 — The Death, the Burial, and the Guard at the Tomb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Darkness covers the land from noon until three. Jesus cries out the opening line of Psalm 22, is offered sour wine, cries out again and yields up his spirit. The temple curtain is torn, the earth shakes, tombs open, and the centurion confesses him the Son of God. The women from Galilee look on; Joseph of Arimathea buries him in his own new tomb; two Marys sit opposite it. On the Sabbath the council has the stone sealed and a guard posted.
verseByVerse.theology: The cry of forsakenness needs two truths held together. Jesus is quoting the first line of Psalm 22, which names the whole psalm, and that psalm ends not in darkness but in vindication and the words he has done it. Yet the forsakenness is real: the Trinity was not torn apart, but the Son bore the full judgment due to the guilty. He lost the sense of his Father’s face without losing his hold on his Father’s faithfulness, and he still said my God.
verseByVerse.examples: The curtain is the comfort of this section: anyone waiting until he is clean enough to pray can stop waiting. And the rest of the section is filled with unlikely faithfulness: women who stayed when the apostles ran, and a council member who found his courage when there was nothing left to gain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?" that is, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Darkness over all the land. From noon to 3 p.m. In Scripture, darkness pictures God’s judgment, as in the plague of darkness in Egypt before the first Passover (Exodus 10:21–23). God’s judgment on sin was falling on his Son.

Was the darkness an eclipse? It cannot have been: Passover fell at full moon, when a solar eclipse is impossible, and an eclipse lasts minutes, not three hours. It was a sign from God, like the judgment Amos foretold: I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9).

With a loud voice. About 3 p.m., the hour of the afternoon sacrifice in the temple. Not a whisper of despair but a full-voiced cry of anguished prayer to God.

Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani, that is, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The first line of Psalm 22, in Aramaic and Hebrew. The only words from the cross that Matthew records. Not “Father”, as in every other prayer of his that the Gospels record, but “My God”. In his agony, Jesus experiences being forsaken by God. This is the cry of dereliction (that is, of being forsaken), among the weightiest sentences in the Gospels.

What does it mean? On the cross, Jesus bore the sins of his people and the judgment they deserved (1 Peter 2:24; 2 Corinthians 5:21). The heart of that judgment is separation from God, his face turned away in holy wrath (Isaiah 59:2). Jesus experienced, in his human soul, the God-forsakenness that sinners deserve, so that we would never be forsaken. This is the darkest moment in all of history, and the heart of penal substitution: Christ took the penalty of our sin in our place. That wrath is no flare of irritation. It is the steady recoil of a perfectly holy God from evil, the just sentence on all that spoils what he made, and on the cross it fell on the one man who had no sin of his own.

The whole psalm. In his world a text was named by its opening words, so to cry out the first line of Psalm 22 was to put the entire psalm on the table: bones out of joint, a tongue stuck to the jaws, hands and feet pierced (the Hebrew of that line is difficult, but the ancient Greek translation reads it so), garments divided and lots cast, written a thousand years before anyone had seen a Roman cross. And it ends in vindication. God has not hidden his face from the afflicted one, but has heard when he cried (Psalm 22:24); all the ends of the earth shall turn to the LORD (22:27); and the last words are of a work done for a people not yet born: he has done it (22:31), remarkably close to what John records moments later: it is finished.

But the forsakenness was real. Some take the whole-psalm point to mean that Jesus was only reciting a hopeful poem to steady himself. That will not stand. The darkness was real, the cry was a real cry, and the New Testament means what it says when it tells us he was made sin for us and became a curse for us (2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). Both are true at once: he entered a real forsakenness, holding the psalm that ends in vindication.

What it does not mean. Not that the Trinity was broken, or that the Father stopped loving the Son, or that Jesus stopped being God. The eternal union of the Father and the Son cannot be destroyed. The Father was well pleased with his Son’s obedience even then (Ephesians 5:2; John 10:17). What Jesus lost was the experience of the Father’s comforting presence; what he bore was the Father’s wrath against sin, which he had taken as his own. It is a mystery we can only worship.

My God. One small word has carried more comfort than most sermons. Twice he says my, to the very one he cannot feel. If you have ever prayed in the dark and got nothing back, and wondered whether the silence proved your faith had failed, it does not. That prayer is not the sound of faith collapsing. It is the sound of faith with everything else stripped off it, still addressing God as its own. He prayed it first, in a worse darkness than yours, and he prayed it so that you would never have to pray it alone.

Why did he have to be forsaken? Could God not simply forgive? God is love, and God is holy, and he cannot pretend sin does not matter. To forgive by simply overlooking evil would make him unjust, as a judge who lets a murderer walk free is unjust (Proverbs 17:15). At the cross God did not lower his justice; he satisfied it, by bearing the penalty himself in the person of his Son. That is how he can be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The forsaking was the price, and the Father and the Son paid it together, out of love for us.

Is it not cruel for a father to forsake his son for others? Only if the Son were an unwilling victim or a third party dragged in. He was neither. The Son came of his own will: no one takes his life from him, he said, but he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). And the Son is not someone other than God; he is God the Son, one with the Father in a single purpose of love. In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself (2 Corinthians 5:19). The cross is not a harsh father punishing a reluctant child. It is the Judge himself, in the person of his Son, stepping down to bear the sentence he pronounced. Even the cry of verse 46 is taken from Psalm 22, a psalm that moves from forsakenness to praise: the Son spoke it in the dark as one who still called the Father my God.

Will I ever be forsaken by God? If you are in Christ, no. You may feel forsaken: in grief, in depression, in long seasons of unanswered prayer. The psalmists did, and so do many faithful believers. But feeling forsaken and being forsaken are not the same. Christ was truly forsaken so that the promise could be made to you without condition: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5). On your darkest day, pray his prayer, my God, and hold on to the my. It is yours because it was his.

For worship. At the hour of the afternoon sacrifice the true Lamb cried out under the judgment the altar had only pictured, and bore in three hours what we could not have borne in eternity. My God, my God: he said it so that we might say for ever, my Father.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, "This man is calling Elijah." And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man is calling Elijah. They misheard Eli (my God) as Elijah; Eli sounds like the beginning of Eliyahu. It may have been genuine confusion or one more piece of mockery. Elijah was expected to come before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), and later Jewish writings show a popular belief that Elijah would come to help the righteous in distress.

The wrong rescuer. Jesus had said that Elijah had already come, unrecognised, in John the Baptist (17:12–13): the help these bystanders are waiting for came, preached, and was beheaded. And Elijah was sent to prepare for the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), and that day had arrived, in darkness at noon, falling on the man in front of them. The one they thought was calling for help was himself the help. The LORD whose coming Elijah announced was on the cross, taking the judgment of his own day so that it would not fall on his people.

A sponge of sour wine. Sour wine (oxos) was the cheap, vinegary wine of soldiers and labourers, and there would have been a jar of it on site. Perhaps mercy, or a way to prolong his life and see if Elijah came; possibly both. John records that Jesus said I thirst (John 19:28–30). It is the last thing any human being does for Jesus before he dies, and more than anyone else in the crowd thought of doing.

Does a small kindness matter if it comes with mixed motives? It still matters, though God sees the heart. Most of our good deeds are mixed; that is no reason not to do them. Jesus said that even a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (10:42), and he will one day say that what was done for the least of his brothers was done for him (25:40). Do the small kindness. Ask God to purify the motive as you go. And remember that the greatest good deed on that hill was not this soldier’s, but Christ’s, who thirsted so that we might drink.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: But the others said, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wait, let us see. Mockery or curiosity: they would rather find out how it ends, and the small mercy of a drink is set aside so as not to interfere with the experiment.

Spectators. That is colder than the jeering of the priests, and more recognisable. Contempt at least engages; this is spectatorship. It is possible to be in that position for years: to attend church, follow the argument, enjoy the music, and wait the entire time for something that settles it, while the thing that settles it is going on in front of you. Proximity is not faith. The men closest to the cross were watching to see whether God would do something, and God was doing it.

No one came. They were watching for someone to take him down, and what was being accomplished was a far greater rescue. No one came to save him. That was the point. He was saving them. No one would save Jesus from death; but the Father who heard his loud cries would save him out of it (Hebrews 5:7).

Not a final verdict. One man on that hill was in their position at noon and in a completely different one by three o’clock: the centurion, with the same view and more blood on his hands. Standing where the spectators stood is not a final verdict on anybody.

What should I do if I have been in church for years and still feel like a spectator? Stop waiting for something to happen to you, and respond to what has already happened. The cross is not a show to evaluate but an offer to receive. Tell God honestly where you are: I have been watching, and I want to believe. Then act on what you know: confess your sin, trust Christ by name, ask to be baptised if you have not been, step into the life of the church rather than sitting at its edge. Faith often grows by obeying, not by waiting for feelings. The centurion did not stay a spectator, and neither must you.

parallels.desc: Elijah before the day of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cried out again. A crucified man in his last minutes would scarcely have breath to speak, let alone shout. Jesus died with a loud cry, in full control. John records the words: It is finished (John 19:30), one word in Greek, tetelestai, meaning completed, brought to its goal. It is often said that the word was written on receipts for a settled debt; that is uncertain, but the debt was settled all the same. Luke gives his last words as a prayer from Psalm 31:5, a psalm of trust, with the word Father set at its head: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46).

Two cries. Two shouts bracket the end of the darkness: one names the forsakenness, and one announces the work finished. He went into it crying out a question and came out of it declaring a completed thing, and what happened between belongs to the Father and the Son alone.

Yielded up his spirit. Literally released his spirit, an active verb with Jesus as its subject; John says he handed it over (John 19:30). This is the language of a deliberate act rather than a body giving out. He gave up his life at the moment he chose, as he had said of himself as the good shepherd: he had authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again (John 10:17–18). The Romans provided the occasion; he chose the moment.

The last act is his. He has been handed over, bound, condemned, flogged, mocked, stripped and nailed, at every point appearing to be the object of everybody else’s decisions. And the last act of the day is his. The centurion, who had probably watched many men die and never seen one do it like that, drew the only conclusion available to him (v. 54).

What exactly was finished? The work the Father gave him to do (John 17:4): the full obedience of his life, and the full payment for the sins of his people. His life matters as much as his death: he kept God’s law perfectly where we failed, and that obedience is counted to everyone who trusts him (Romans 5:19). Nothing remains to be added by us, by the church, or by any priest. That is why Christians do not try to earn God’s favour, and why no further sacrifice for sin is needed (Hebrews 10:12–14, 18). The resurrection would declare it accepted; his intercession in heaven applies it. But the price was paid in full on the cross. When your conscience accuses you, answer with his word: it is finished.

For worship. The record of debt that stood against us was nailed to the same wood (Colossians 2:14). He who chose the moment of his dying holds the moment of ours, and into the Father’s hands, made safe for us by his death, we commit our spirits.

parallels.desc: I lay it down of my own accord

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. The tombs also were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curtain was torn in two. The great curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where God’s presence dwelt (Exodus 26:31–33). Only the high priest could pass through it, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). Later Jewish tradition made it about sixty feet high and as thick as a man’s hand. From top to bottom: torn by God, not by man. The way into God’s presence was now open to all, through the death of Christ (Hebrews 10:19–22), and the temple sacrifices were finished.

What the curtain was for. It was put there to keep people like you out. The whole point of it was distance, the visible form of a message every worshipper understood: not yet, not you, not here. And at three on a Friday afternoon, by no human hand, it was ripped from the top to the bottom. Its tearing does not mean God has become less holy or sin less serious. The way is open because his holiness was satisfied, not set aside, which is why we still come in only by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19).

Come in. Hear that, if you have stood at a distance from God, sure you are too unclean, too late or too far gone. The barrier was not removed by your improving until you were fit to pass it; it was opened from God’s side, downward, by a death. The invitation to draw near with confidence (Hebrews 4:16) is for those who know they could never make themselves presentable. The room that was sealed your whole life is open, and the blood that opened it was not yours.

In the flow. The temple has been at the centre of the conflict for days: cleansed (21:12–13), left desolate (23:38), its stones foretold to fall (24:1–2), and Jesus mocked as the man who would destroy it (26:61; 27:40). Now God himself tears the curtain at its heart. The old sanctuary’s work is done, and on the third day the true temple, the body of the one greater than the temple, will rise out of the grave (12:6; John 2:19–21).

The earth shook. An earthquake, as at Sinai when God gave the law (Exodus 19:18). Creation itself responded to its Creator’s death (compare Joel 2:10).

The saints who had fallen asleep. “Saints” here means holy people of the Old Testament, believers who had died. Only Matthew records this, a sign that Jesus’ death defeats death (Hebrews 2:14–15; Ezekiel 37:12–13). Why should his death open graves? The sting of death is sin (1 Corinthians 15:56). When Christ bore the penalty for sin, death lost its claim on his people. It may hold their bodies for a while, but it cannot keep them.

Who were the saints who were raised? Matthew says only that they were holy people who had died, that the tombs opened at Jesus’ death, and that they came out after his resurrection and appeared to many in Jerusalem (v. 53). Most likely they were real, bodily raisings, a sign that Christ’s death had broken the power of death. What became of them afterwards Scripture does not say.

Does fallen asleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes how death looks from our side for a believer: peaceful, temporary, with a waking to come. It describes the body, which rests in the grave. It does not mean the soul is unconscious. Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and Paul says that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). Believers who die go at once into the presence of Christ, conscious and blessed, and wait there for the resurrection of the body (Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many. When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said, "Truly this was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After his resurrection. Jesus is the firstfruits of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20); they followed. Matthew mentions their raising at his death, because his death caused it, but places their appearance after Easter.

Appeared to many. Their appearance was a sign. Were they raised to resurrection bodies, or restored to earthly life like Lazarus, to die again? Scripture does not say. Some interpreters take the account as symbolic. This commentary’s view: Matthew presents it as a real event, a sign and foretaste of the resurrection Christ’s death secured. We should not speculate beyond what is written.

Why does no other Gospel mention it? Much in each Gospel is unique to it, and this sign fits Matthew’s purpose exactly: to show Jewish readers that the hopes of the prophets were being fulfilled. Some careful scholars have wondered whether Matthew intends vivid prophetic imagery, the language of Ezekiel’s opened graves pressed into service to declare what the cross achieved; but the plain reading is the safer, and it is the one the verdict above takes. The meaning is unmistakable even where the details are veiled: at the instant the Author of life dies, the graves of his people burst open, because his dying has already begun to kill death, and the resurrection of the last day has pushed its first green shoots up through the crust of the old world.

The centurion. The Roman officer in charge of the execution and his soldiers. A professional, he has watched the man refuse the drugged wine, cry out a psalm, and die with a shout. Then the ground moves, and he and his men are terrified.

Truly this was the Son of God. A pagan soldier who had just supervised the killing confessed what the religious leaders had mocked (v. 43), and in Matthew’s narrative he is the first human being to say it of the crucified Christ. Gentiles worshipped him at his birth (2:11) and confess him at his death. Whether the centurion understood it fully or not, it is a sign that this gospel will cross every boundary of religion, race and background.

In the flow. The title Son of God has run through the whole Gospel: spoken from heaven (3:17; 17:5), confessed in the boat, truly you are the Son of God (14:33), put on oath (26:63) and thrown at him on the cross (27:40, 43). Now a Gentile soldier uses the disciples’ own word, truly. The claim that sent Jesus to the cross is confirmed at the cross.

Can someone with blood on his hands really be saved? Yes. The centurion had just nailed the Son of God to a cross, and he is the one who confesses him. Paul, who had persecuted the church, called himself the foremost of sinners and said that he received mercy as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15–16). The blood of Christ cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). No past puts you beyond his reach if you come to him. What keeps people from Christ is not the size of their sin but their refusal to bring it to him.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records the raised saints. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him, among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many women. It is the first mention of them in the passion narrative, and it comes after everything: they had been there the whole time. Judas sold him; Peter denied him; the others fled (26:56). The women stayed. They could not stop it or touch him, and had nothing to offer but this: when he looked out from the cross there were faces that loved him.

Ministering to him. “Ministering” (diakonousai) means serving, supporting. Luke says they supported him from their own means (Luke 8:1–3), and they are mentioned almost nowhere until the moment everyone else has gone.

Mary Magdalene. From Magdala, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had cast seven demons out of her (Luke 8:2). She is not identified in Scripture as a prostitute; that idea comes from later tradition, which confused her with the sinful woman of Luke 7. She became the first witness of the resurrection (28:1–10; John 20:11–18).

The other women. The first was perhaps the wife of Clopas (John 19:25). The second is the mother of James and John, who had asked for her sons to sit at Jesus’ right and left (20:20–21). Now she saw who was at his right and left.

The service they were watching. Matthew’s word for these women is the word Jesus used of himself on the very day that mother made her request: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). They had served him with food and money along the roads of Galilee. Now they watch him serve them in the fullest sense, paying the ransom with his own life, and the mother who had asked for thrones for her sons learned there what greatness in his kingdom looks like.

Women as witnesses. In that culture, women’s testimony was considered less reliable and was often not accepted in court. If the Gospel writers had invented the story, they would hardly have made women the chief witnesses of the death, burial and resurrection. Their presence is a mark of truthfulness. They watch him die, see where he is buried, and come back on the third morning: a continuous chain of witnesses, which is why the resurrection cannot be waved away as a mistake about the address. God rested the central facts of the faith on the eyesight of people nobody would have chosen.

What can I do when I can do nothing to help someone who is suffering? Stay. The women could not stop the cross, but their presence mattered to him and to God. In grief, illness or dying, people rarely need answers; they need faces that love them. Sit with them, pray with them, bring a meal, hold a hand, say little. Job’s friends did best in the first seven days, when they said nothing (Job 2:13). Faithful presence is not nothing. It is often the most Christlike thing you have.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake.

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.quote: When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was evening. Friday evening, before sunset, when the Sabbath began. Under the law, a body hanged on a tree must not remain there overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Romans often left bodies to rot as a warning; governors released one as a favour, not as a right.

A rich man from Arimathea. Arimathea was a town in Judea, probably northwest of Jerusalem. Mark and Luke say he was a respected member of the council, who had not consented to their decision, and was looking for the kingdom of God (Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50–51). Matthew alone says rich, and the reader who knows Isaiah will recall: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9). The first half of that sentence had come true hours earlier, with a criminal on either side of him. Now the second half comes true.

Also a disciple. John says he was a secret disciple, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). Now he came out into the open, at the moment when it was most dangerous, when the other disciples had fled. Nicodemus joined him (John 19:39).

He asked for the body. A bold act. No version of that request leaves him anonymous: his seat on the council, his standing and his safety all go in the same conversation.

Pilate ordered it given. Pilate first confirmed with the centurion that Jesus was dead (Mark 15:44–45). The death was certain: Roman soldiers knew death.

Late courage. Joseph’s courage arrived not when being associated with Jesus looked promising, but on the one evening when the cause was visibly finished and there was no possible advantage in it. There are people who cannot be brave while there is still something to win, and become unanswerable the moment everything is lost.

Can a secret believer be a real Christian? Joseph shows that a person can truly trust Christ while being too afraid to confess him openly, and also that such a state is not meant to last. Jesus calls his followers to confess him before others (10:32), and baptism is the appointed public confession. If you believe but have been hiding it, take courage from Joseph and Nicodemus: your fear is not the end of the story. Tell a Christian friend, speak to your pastor, ask about baptism. The longer faith stays secret, the weaker it tends to grow. Christ was not ashamed of you on the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council (Mark, Luke); John adds Nicodemus. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death
not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A clean linen shroud. Everything is done at speed, because the Sabbath begins at sunset, and with care. John adds that Nicodemus brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39–40), a royal quantity: two members of the council handling a body that was ritually defiling to touch on the eve of a feast.

His own new tomb. A rock-cut tomb was expensive, meant to hold generations of a wealthy family. New: no one had been laid in it before (Luke 23:53; John 19:41), so there could be no confusion with another body. Joseph gave away his own grave at a few hours’ notice.

A great stone. Tombs were closed with a large stone, sometimes a disc rolled in a groove, to keep out animals and grave-robbers. Such a stone would take several men to move back. Jesus was truly dead and truly buried, as the Apostles’ Creed confesses: crucified, dead and buried.

A grain of wheat in a garden. John notes that the tomb was in a garden (John 19:41), and Jesus had already told what a burial like this would mean: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Joseph thought he was laying a body to rest. He was sowing a seed. The first Adam lost a garden and earned the grave; the last Adam was laid in a grave cut in a garden, the firstfruits of a harvest that will empty every grave of his people.

Sealing the case. Every element of this hurried burial turns out to be evidence: a rock tomb with one entrance, new, with a named owner anyone could check, two named women watching, and a stone too heavy for frightened disciples to move quietly. Joseph was sealing the case for the resurrection.

Why does it matter that Jesus was buried? Because burial proves death. If Jesus only fainted, there was no resurrection, and no atonement either. The gospel Paul received was that Christ died, was buried, and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), and the burial stands between the death and the resurrection as the proof of both. It also means that Jesus has been where every believer’s body will go. He has lain in the grave and come out, so the grave is now a resting place for those who belong to him, not a prison (Isaiah 57:2).
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, in wealthier tombs sometimes a disc-shaped stone rolled in a groove.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sitting opposite the tomb. They saw where he was buried (Mark 15:47; Luke 23:55), so on Sunday morning they did not go to the wrong tomb.

Nothing to do. Everyone else has gone. Two women sit facing a closed grave as the light fails on the worst day of their lives. They could not anoint the body or move the stone, and they are not waiting for a resurrection. They are sitting with a grave because they cannot bring themselves to leave it.

What love does. Anyone who has sat in a hospital corridor after the machines were switched off, or stayed at a graveside after the others had gone back to the cars, knows exactly what they were doing. It accomplishes nothing. It is what love does when there is nothing left that love can do, and it is the last thing to go.

Who lay behind the stone. On the other side of that stone lay the one who had stood at a friend’s tomb in Bethany and wept, and then called the dead man out by name. Their love that evening was a small reflection of his: he had stayed with his people to the end, and had gone down into the grave so that every grave his people ever sit beside will one day have to open.

God took note of it. Their sitting there is why they knew the address, and why the first to hear that Jesus had risen were two women who had stayed at a tomb when there was no hope of anything at all. Faithfulness in the hours when it achieves nothing is not wasted. It is very often the thing God builds the next mercy on.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve deeply? No. Christians grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and the hope gives the tears a horizon. (See John 16:6 for the fuller answer.)

On a Tuesday. Is there someone who lost a loved one this year whom everyone else has stopped visiting? Go and sit with them.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate and said, "Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day. Saturday, the Sabbath. The leaders went to Pilate on the Sabbath itself, stretching their own strict rules for the holy day. They cannot rest. And the Pharisees appear beside the chief priests for the first time in the passion story.

That impostor. “Impostor” (planos) means deceiver. They remembered his predictions better than his disciples did. On this Saturday the disciples are in hiding and the women have spices ready for a body they expect to stay where it is. Only his enemies take the prediction seriously enough to act on it, calling him that impostor in the same breath as they take precautions against his word coming true.

After three days I will rise. Jesus had predicted it publicly (12:40) and privately (16:21; 17:23; 20:19).

How does after three days fit a Friday death and a Sunday resurrection? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day, so after three days and on the third day mean the same span: part of Friday, all of Saturday and part of Sunday made three days. Esther fasts three days, night or day, and goes to the king on the third day (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1). The leaders themselves treat them as the same: they ask for the tomb to be guarded until the third day (v. 64). The phrase three days and three nights (12:40) is the same kind of idiom, as Esther’s three days, night or day, shows.

For a discouraged believer. If your grasp on the promises is poor this week, you are in the company of the eleven, not the council. The resurrection happened while his own people had given up on it; it did not wait for anybody’s faith to be in good order.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last fraud will be worse than the first." Pilate said to them, "You have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make the tomb secure. They feared a hoax, and they are right that a stolen body would be hard to answer.

Lest his disciples steal him. Their fear, and later their explanation (28:13). But the disciples were frightened, scattered, and not expecting a resurrection.
