The last fraud. The first fraud was his claim to be the Messiah; the last would be a fake resurrection.

You have a guard. Or Take a guard (ESV footnote). Either their own temple guard, or Roman soldiers. The guards later reported to the chief priests (28:11), but feared the governor (28:14), which suggests Roman soldiers placed under the priests’ authority. Pilate’s reply is short; he has had enough of them.

As secure as you can. Perhaps sarcastic: do your best. No security could stop what God would do.

The pattern of the chapter. Every measure taken to prevent a fraudulent resurrection became part of the evidence for a real one: the guard could not have slept through it and also known what happened. So through the whole chapter: Pilate wrote a mocking title and published the truth; the priests bought a field and named their own crime; the crowd called down on themselves the only blood that could save them; and now the council builds the strongest case for the resurrection while trying to prevent one.

Is there good evidence that Jesus really rose? Yes, and this passage is part of it. The tomb was known, sealed and guarded. The body was never produced, though the authorities had every reason to produce it. The earliest explanation from Jesus’ enemies admitted the tomb was empty (28:13). The women and then the apostles testified that they saw him alive, and suffered for saying so (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Nothing else so well explains the sudden courage of men who had fled. Some sceptics suggest the guard story was added later, since only Matthew tells it; but Matthew says the theft rumour was still going round when he wrote (28:15), so he was answering a story his readers could check. Evidence alone does not make anyone a believer, but you are not asked to believe against the evidence. You are asked to believe because of it.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sealing the stone. A cord across the stone, fastened with wax or clay and stamped: breaking it would be a crime against Roman authority. Compare Daniel 6:17, where the king sealed the stone over the lions’ den, and the stone did not keep God’s servant from coming out alive.

Saturday. The chapter closes with a sealed stone and armed men in front of it, and by every measure available that Saturday evening, the story is over. The teacher is dead; the disciples are scattered; the betrayer is dead by his own hand. Apart from this request for a guard, the whole of Saturday passes in silence in all four Gospels. The Son of God rests in a grave, having cried that it is finished (John 19:30), as the Creator rested on the seventh day when the work was done.

A great deal of Christian life is lived on Saturday. The disaster has happened, the prayers were not answered as hoped, the stone is in place, and the promise about the third day is remembered by nobody except the opposition. Everybody who loved him spent that day certain it was finished in the other sense. On Sunday morning the stone, the seal and the guard were all still in place, and the tomb was empty anyway.

The first witnesses. One last irony. The soldiers posted here to make sure nothing happened will be present when it does. They are at the stone when the angel comes down, and they report to the chief priests what they saw (28:4, 11): the men placed to prevent a resurrection story become the first witnesses of the opened tomb. Nothing in this chapter that was set against him failed to end up serving him.

What do I do while I am waiting for God to act? Do what the women did: keep faith with Christ even when you cannot see what he is doing. Rest, as the Sabbath required, and do not try to roll away stones that only God can move. Keep the promises in front of you, read them aloud, and pray them back to him. Stay with his people. Saturday is not the end of the story, and the silence of God is not the absence of God. He was never more active than on the day he seemed most silent.

For worship. The king’s seal could not keep Daniel in the den, and Rome’s seal could not keep the Son of Man in the grave. The Holy One would not see corruption (Psalm 16:10). Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:57). The stone is sealed, but the morning is coming.
verseByVerse.note: A seal (a cord fixed with wax or clay) would show if the stone had been tampered with.

parallels.desc: the stone sealed over the lions’ den

27.theology: The atonement: what happened at the cross. Reformed theology has always insisted that something real was accomplished at the cross: God’s wrath against sin was borne by the Son, the debt was paid, and the judgment that was ours fell on him. This is not a later theory but the heart of the apostles’ preaching: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3).
27.examples:
Then: The women who had followed him from Galilee and served him watched from a distance (v. 55) and would be first at the tomb on Sunday. Love kept them at the cross when fear drove others away.

Now: The cross is the Christian’s only boast (Galatians 6:14): not our moral achievement, our spiritual progress or our theology, but Christ crucified is the one thing on which salvation rests. Charles Spurgeon preached: “I have a great need for Christ; I have a great Christ for my need.” Matthew 27 is the ground of that confidence.

28.title: He Is Risen — Go and Make Disciples
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. <sup>2</sup>And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it. <sup>3</sup>His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. <sup>4</sup>And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men. <sup>5</sup>But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. <sup>6</sup>He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay. <sup>7</sup>Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you.” <sup>8</sup>So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples. <sup>9</sup>And behold, Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.” <sup>11</sup>While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. <sup>12</sup>And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers <sup>13</sup>and said, “Tell people, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.’ <sup>14</sup>And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.” <sup>15</sup>So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day. <sup>16</sup>Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. <sup>17</sup>And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted. <sup>18</sup>And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. <sup>19</sup>Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup>teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
28.overview:
Matthew’s Gospel ends not with a conclusion but with a commission. An angel announces the resurrection, the empty tomb confirms it, and the women meet the risen Jesus, take hold of his feet and worship him. Then, on a mountain in Galilee, he tells the eleven, worshipping and wavering, that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him.

The chapter closes the bracket the Gospel opened. In chapter 1 the angel said his name would be Immanuel, God with us; in chapter 28 the risen Lord says it himself: I am with you always, to the end of the age. The Gospel does not end so much as send its readers out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Resurrection and the Great Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At dawn on the first day the two Marys come to the tomb. An angel rolls back the stone, the guards collapse, and the women are sent to the disciples; on the way the risen Jesus meets them. The guards report to the chief priests, who pay them to say the body was stolen. In Galilee the eleven meet him on a mountain, and he sends them to all nations.
verseByVerse.theology: Without the resurrection the cross would be a tragedy; with it, the cross is God’s decisive act of redemption, declared accepted. The commission rests on a royal decree, the fulfilment of Daniel 7:14, not on human enthusiasm, and baptism is into one name, singular, held by three persons.
verseByVerse.examples: Three things here are worth carrying away. First, the section only Matthew records (vv. 11–15): the priests hear a full eyewitness account and, instead of going to look, buy a story that defeats itself, since sleeping men cannot say what happened while they slept. They had been promised the sign of Jonah (12:39) and paid to have it denied. Second, my brothers (v. 10), spoken over deserters before one of them had apologised. Third, the clause Matthew did not tidy away: some doubted (v. 17). He sent waverers too, and went with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Matthew 28 is the morning everything was reversed. The women who watched Jesus die find his tomb opened by an angel; the risen Lord calls the men who deserted him my brothers; the priests pay for a lie; and on a mountain in Galilee the King sends worshippers and waverers alike to all nations.

Toward the dawn. Jesus had been in the tomb from Friday afternoon, through Saturday, to early Sunday: three days by Jewish counting, in which part of a day was counted as a day (12:40). From then on, Christians gathered for worship on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

To see the tomb. These are the women who watched him die and saw where he was buried (27:56, 61). Mark and Luke say they brought spices to anoint the body (Mark 16:1; Luke 24:1): they came to honour a dead body, not expecting a resurrection. The same love that would not leave the cross arrives earliest at the tomb.

A great earthquake. The earth shook at his rising as it shook at his death (27:51). The angel did not roll away the stone to let Jesus out; the risen Jesus could pass through closed doors (John 20:19, 26). He rolled it away to let the witnesses in, so they could see the tomb was empty. Then he sat on it: a sign of victory. The seal of Rome is broken, the guard is useless, and heaven’s messenger is sitting on the stone the authorities had made as secure as they could.

Do the four Gospels contradict each other about Easter morning? No episode in Scripture is more often produced as proof that they do, and the differences should be stated plainly. When did the women come? John says while it was still dark (John 20:1); Mark says when the sun had risen (Mark 16:2). How many came? Matthew names two Marys; Mark names three women; Luke names three and adds the other women with them (Luke 24:10); John mentions only Mary Magdalene. How many angels? Matthew has one, sitting on the stone; Mark a young man inside the tomb; Luke two men; John two angels. Take them in order. Dawn is not a moment but a process, and a party that sets out in the dark arrives as the sun is coming up. John himself points to the answer on the number of women: his Mary, apparently alone, runs to Peter and says, we do not know where they have laid him (John 20:2). We. She seems to have had company; John simply followed the one he meant to write about. None of the lists claims to be complete, and a writer who names two has not denied a third. The angels work the same way: where there are two, there is certainly one, and an account that reports the one who spoke has not contradicted an account that counts the company. These are likely harmonisations, not proofs, and some details of the order of that morning are still debated; but nothing in them forces a contradiction, and believers can hold the accounts true while some questions stay open.

The fingerprint of honest witnesses. Four statements agreeing word for word would suggest the witnesses had conferred; four that vary in detail and converge on substance are what honest testimony looks like. And they converge on every point that matters: the stone was moved, the tomb was empty, heaven announced it, the Lord was alive, and the women were there first. In that world a woman’s testimony carried little weight in law, and a movement fabricating a resurrection would have put its most credible men at the tomb. God thought it fitting that the first to know should be the ones who had refused to leave the cross.

Should Christians keep Sunday as a Sabbath? Christians agree that the first day became the day of Christian worship because of the resurrection, and that gathering with God’s people on the Lord’s Day matters (Hebrews 10:25). They differ on how far the fourth commandment carries over. Many Reformed believers, following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that the Sabbath was moved to the first day and is to be kept holy as a day of rest and worship. Others hold that Christ fulfilled the Sabbath, so that the Lord’s Day is a day of worship and gladness without the full Sabbath rules (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5). This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest rather than kept as a law of rules, while honouring those who hold the Westminster and 1689 view; and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). Both honour the risen Christ. Whatever your conviction, do not let the first day of the week become just another day.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like lightning. The brightness of heaven, as in Daniel 10:6 and at the transfiguration (17:2). Lightning was this Gospel’s image for the coming of the Son of Man (24:27), and white as snow the clothing of the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9): the messenger is dressed in the livery of the court he came from.

Like dead men. The irony: the guards set to watch the dead man became like dead men themselves, while the dead man was alive. The guards shook as the earth shook (the same root in Greek). These were probably Roman soldiers, not easily frightened. They were witnesses to the angel and the empty tomb, which is why the leaders later had to bribe them (vv. 11–15).

Only a servant. Whatever knocked those men down was not the glory of Christ but the reflected brightness of a creature sent to open a door. If a servant could do that, think what it will be to stand before the Lord himself (compare 17:2, 6–7). John, who had once leaned against him at supper, saw him in his glory and fell at his feet as though dead (Revelation 1:17).

Nobody saw it. Scripture gives no account of the moment itself: the stone is rolled back and the tomb is already empty. The one event on which everything depends took place in the dark, unobserved, between the Father, the Son and the Spirit.

If no one saw the resurrection, how can we be sure it happened? In the same way we know many events no one saw happen in the moment: by what was left behind and by who saw the result. The tomb was empty, the grave clothes were lying there (John 20:5–7), the body was never produced, and many people saw Jesus alive afterwards, at different times and places, in groups and alone, sceptics among them (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). No other explanation accounts so well for the transformation of the disciples or the birth of the church in the very city where he was buried. The Spirit then persuades the heart (1 Corinthians 2:4–5), but he persuades it of something that really happened.

parallels.desc: his face like the appearance of lightning

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to the women, "Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid. This is God’s word to his people at his great acts of salvation (1:20; Luke 2:10). The same glory that flattened the guards comes to these two with a word telling them they need not be frightened of it.

Who was crucified. The perfect tense in Greek suggests “who has been crucified and remains the crucified one”. It has become a name. The risen Lord bears the marks of the nails (John 20:27), and heaven’s own way of identifying him on resurrection morning is still by the worst thing that ever happened to him. In the throne room John sees a Lamb standing as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6). The marks stay.

He has risen. The central announcement of the Christian faith. The verb is probably best read as passive: he has been raised, by God (Acts 2:24; Romans 6:4). Not a spirit, not a vision, not a memory: raised bodily from the dead.

As he said. He had said it plainly three times (16:21; 17:23; 20:19), and each time it had gone past them. So the angel’s small clause is a verdict on everything else he ever said: if this prediction held, they all hold, from the meek inheriting the earth to his words never passing away.

Come, see. The empty tomb is evidence, and the women are invited to inspect it: not to feel something, not to accept a report, but to walk in and look and satisfy themselves. Christianity has never asked to be believed on the strength of an atmosphere (1 John 1:1–3). It rests on a claim about an event, at an address, on a datable morning, that could have been destroyed at any time by the production of a body. Nor is this a late legend: Paul says he passed on what he had himself received (1 Corinthians 15:3), and most historians, believing or not, date that summary within a few years of the cross.

What it does not mean. Not that the resurrection was spiritual only, or that Jesus “lived on” in his disciples’ hearts. The tomb was empty. His body was raised, transformed and glorified (Luke 24:39; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17).

What difference does the resurrection make to me today? It means your sins are truly dealt with, because God has accepted Christ’s sacrifice: he was raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). Justification is God’s verdict that a sinner is right with him, and the empty tomb is the Father’s public sign that the payment Christ made was enough. It means Jesus is alive now, able to hear you, help you and keep you (Hebrews 7:25). It means death is not the end for you or for those you love who die in him, for your body too will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). And it means that nothing done in the Lord is in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58): your obedience, your prayers, your faithfulness in small things all count, because the future belongs to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you." So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell his disciples. His disciples: the same men who had fled and denied him, still called his. Before there was a church, before Pentecost, before a word of the New Testament existed, the resurrection was preached, by a few women, to eleven men who at first did not believe them (Luke 24:11).

Going before you. As he had promised (26:32), like a shepherd going ahead of his flock, he will regather his scattered sheep (26:31). He announced the reunion in the same breath as the desertion, and it was not cancelled when the failure came.

Galilee. Not the temple or the upper room but the working country, where most of them had first been called away from their boats. The risen Lord’s first appointment with his church is at the place they started from, and he gets there ahead of them.

Fear and great joy. Fear on its own would have sent them home; joy on its own would not have been honest. And they ran to tell his disciples: news this great cannot be told slowly.

Is it right to feel fear and joy at the same time about God? Yes. Scripture calls us to serve the LORD with fear and rejoice with trembling (Psalm 2:11). Holy fear is not terror that drives you away from God, but awe at his greatness that makes his kindness all the more astonishing. When the gospel seems ordinary to you, it is often because the fear has gone out of it, and the joy goes with it. Ask God to show you again how great he is and how great is what he has done, and both will return together.

On a Tuesday. You carry the same news the women carried, and you need not be a preacher; they were not. Tell one person today, simply and gladly, what Jesus has done.

parallels.desc: I will go before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Jesus met them and said, "Greetings!" And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. Then Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus met them. A gracious appearing to those who were faithful first. John records that he appeared first to Mary Magdalene (John 20:11–18).

Greetings. Chairete was the everyday greeting, formed from the verb to rejoice: an ordinary word in an extraordinary moment, and the first word of the risen Christ in this Gospel carries joy in it. The women took hold of his feet: he was physically real, not a ghost or a vision (Luke 24:39).

Did Jesus not tell Mary Magdalene not to cling to him? He did say to her, Do not cling to me (John 20:17). But he was not forbidding all touch; he let these women hold his feet and invited Thomas to touch his wounds (John 20:27). He was telling Mary not to hold on to him as if the old way of being with him had simply returned, because he was going to the Father. Both accounts make the same point: the risen body was real.

And worshiped him. The word is for prostrate homage, and here it is plainly worship. Jesus accepts their worship, as only God may (4:10).

My brothers. My brothers: not those cowards, or those failures. Forgiveness and restoration are already in the word (Hebrews 2:11–12). The last time we saw these men they were running (26:56, 74). The risen Christ had grounds to send a rebuke or a probation. He sends none of that. Before they have apologised, the first thing the risen Lord calls the men who abandoned him is my brothers.

If you have failed him badly. If you went quiet when you should have spoken, or ran when it cost something to stay, this is the sentence to take home. The resurrection reached back and named the men who had let him down family before they had done anything to deserve the name. Your failure, real as it is, does not define what he calls you. He calls you brother, sister. That is where restoration starts: not with your climb back to him, but with his word over you while you are still ashamed to lift your head.

Does this mean sin does not matter once you are forgiven? No. The same risen Lord who called them brothers also took Peter aside and dealt with his denial three times over (John 21:15–19), and then sent them out to teach obedience to all he commanded (v. 20). Grace does not ignore sin; it removes its guilt and then heals its damage. The order matters: he restores the relationship first, and then works on the failure from inside it. You are not forgiven because you have changed. You change because you are forgiven and loved.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.quote: While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two reports. Two reports go into the city at the same time: the women with the good news, the guards with the same facts. They go to the chief priests, who had asked for the guard (27:62–66). For a few hours that morning, apart from the women, the best-informed men in Jerusalem about the resurrection were the men who had condemned him.

Taken counsel. Another council meeting (26:3–4; 27:1). Faced with the evidence, they do not investigate or go and look, though the tomb is a short walk away and they know exactly where it is.

A sufficient sum. Not repentance, but a bribe. They paid Judas to betray Jesus (26:15), and now they pay soldiers to deny his resurrection. Those who reject the truth must keep paying to hide it. And men rarely spend a large sum suppressing a report they believe to be nonsense: the bribe admits that the testimony was credible.

The sign of Jonah. This closes a thread the Gospel opened long before. Twice they had demanded a sign, and twice he had refused them everything except the sign of Jonah (12:39–40; 16:4). It came on the day he specified, attested by their own guards, and they paid to have it denied. And something greater than Jonah is here (12:41). Jonah came up from the deep and a pagan city believed; the greater Jonah came up from the grave, and while the rulers of his own city paid for silence, his news was about to go out to every nation on earth.

Why would anyone reject the truth when the evidence is so clear? Because accepting it would cost them everything: their position, their pride, their whole account of themselves. Jesus said that people love the darkness rather than the light because their works are evil (John 3:19). The heart is not a neutral judge of evidence; it has interests. That should make us humble about our own resistance to God’s word, which is usually not intellectual but moral. When a truth of Scripture troubles you, ask honestly whether your difficulty is with the evidence or with what it would require of you.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Tell people, 'His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.' And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stole him away. The story they had feared (27:64), now used as their explanation. It fails on its own first clause: if the soldiers were asleep, how could they know who took the body? Could frightened, scattered disciples have overcome armed soldiers, broken the Roman seal, and rolled away a great stone without waking anyone? And why would the disciples then suffer and die for a lie they knew to be false?

The folded cloth. John supplies a detail the theory never accounts for: the linen cloths were lying there, and the face cloth that had been on his head was folded up in a place by itself (John 20:6–7). Body-snatchers working against the clock would hardly stop to unwrap a body bound in linen and spices, and fold the face cloth.

It was not possible. Seven weeks later Peter gave the reason the attempt could never have worked: God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it (Acts 2:24). The council was trying to hold down with a story what death itself had been unable to hold.

The governor’s ears. A Roman soldier who slept on watch or lost what he guarded could face death (compare Acts 12:19; 16:27).

The last irony. The day before, the council had gone to Pilate and called Jesus that impostor, asking for a guard in case his followers should deceive the people (27:63–64). The deception they came to prevent is the one they end up committing, knowingly, having heard the truth first.

Other explanations. Other theories of the empty tomb include: the women went to the wrong tomb (but they had seen it, 27:61); Jesus did not really die but revived (but Roman soldiers knew death, 27:50; John 19:33–34); the disciples hallucinated (but hallucinations do not empty tombs, and they are not shared by hundreds at once). None explains the evidence as well as the resurrection itself.

How should I answer a friend who says the resurrection is impossible? Agree that it is impossible by natural means; that is the point. No one is claiming that dead men usually rise. The claim is that God raised this man, and if God exists, that is not impossible for him (Acts 26:8). Then ask your friend to look at the evidence on its own terms: the empty tomb, the appearances, the change in the disciples, the existence of the church. Do it gently and respectfully (1 Peter 3:15). Arguments do not make anyone a believer, but they can clear away false objections, and the Spirit uses the truth.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman soldier who slept on watch could be punished with death.

parallels.desc: the guards executed after Peter’s escape

verseByVerse.quote: So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two prices. The soldiers sold the truth for money, as Judas sold Jesus. Money bought the betrayal, and money bought the lie. Against both stands the price he paid himself: he came to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28), and on the third day the Father declared the ransom accepted. The council’s silver bought a rumour; Christ’s blood bought a people who have been telling the news ever since.

To this day. When Matthew wrote, the story was still being told: he is answering a rumour his readers had heard. In the second century Justin Martyr records that it was still in circulation in his day.

Two monuments. Matthew has used the words to this day once before: of the Field of Blood (27:8). Both monuments were built with the leaders’ silver. But the Gospel’s closing promise runs further than either. The field and the rumour last to this day; the risen Christ is with his people to the end of the age (v. 20).

The earliest concession. The very existence of the story confirms that the tomb was empty. The first anti-Christian explanation on record does not say the women went to the wrong tomb or that he had not really died; it grants the empty tomb and argues about how it got that way. Friend and enemy agreed on the fact and differed only on the cause.

The cheapest refutation never used. The one action that would have ended the Christian movement in a week was to produce the body. They had the motive and the address; and when the apostles preached the resurrection in that city seven weeks later, the leaders arrested, flogged and threatened them (Acts 4–7), and nothing suggests they ever produced the body.

Weigh the two accounts. One asks you to believe that God raised his Son. The other asks you to believe that frightened men pulled off a theft, kept the secret for life, and faced prison, beatings and execution, each able to end his suffering by producing the body, and not one ever doing it. People will die for a lie they believe. It is very hard to believe that a whole group would die for a lie they had invented themselves.

Does this verse mean Jewish people are especially guilty of unbelief? No. Matthew describes a story spread among the Jews because the dispute was then in Jewish communities, where the church was born. Unbelief is the condition of every human heart apart from grace, Gentile as much as Jew (Romans 3:9). The first believers in the risen Christ were Jews, and Paul longed for his own people’s salvation (Romans 10:1). Christians should speak of Jewish people with love and honour, and pray and witness for them as for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eleven, to the mountain. Eleven, not twelve: Judas was gone. Mountains are places of revelation in Matthew: the temptation (4:8), the Sermon on the Mount (5:1), the transfiguration (17:1). Now the final mountain.

But some doubted. They worshipped, as the women had (v. 9) and as they had in the boat (14:33), and yet some wavered (edistasan, the word used of Peter sinking, 14:31). It may mean some of the eleven, or others with them. Perhaps they could hardly believe what they saw; perhaps they were unsure how to respond.

He commissioned doubters. The clause but some doubted is a gift to an honest believer: even with the risen Christ near enough to touch, some wavered, and Matthew left it in. Jesus does not set the doubters aside until they are sure. He gives worshippers and waverers together the same orders and the same promise. Faith that worships with a tremor in it is faith he can use.

Galilee or Jerusalem? A reader who lines up the four Gospels will ask a fair question here: did the risen Jesus appear in Galilee, as Matthew says, or in and around Jerusalem, as Luke and John describe? The accounts do not compete; they select. The appearances stretched across forty days (Acts 1:3), and they moved with the disciples. On the first day the Lord showed himself in and near Jerusalem: to the women, to Mary at the tomb, to the two walking to Emmaus, to the disciples behind locked doors. Then, as both the angel and Jesus had commanded, the disciples travelled north to Galilee, where this mountain meeting took place, along with the lakeside breakfast of John 21 and, perhaps, the appearance to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:6). Afterwards they returned to Jerusalem, and from near Bethany on the Mount of Olives he ascended (Luke 24:50–51; Acts 1:9–12). Each evangelist tells the part that serves his purpose. Luke, whose whole Gospel drives toward Jerusalem, keeps his lens there, and tells his story so compactly that it can read like one day, though in Acts the same author says plainly that the appearances spanned forty days; Matthew, who began with Galilee of the Gentiles (4:15) and whose last word is a mission to all nations, climbs one more Galilean mountain to send the church out from it. None of them claims to tell everything (John 21:25). Different windows onto the same forty days, not different stories.

How do I deal with doubts that will not go away? Bring them to Christ rather than hiding them or nursing them. Tell him honestly what you find hard to believe. Keep worshipping and obeying while you wait; the disciples doubted in the act of worship, not instead of it. Feed your faith on the evidence and on God’s promises, especially the accounts of the resurrection. Talk to a mature believer; doubts kept secret tend to grow. And remember that your salvation rests on Christ’s grip on you, not on the strength of your grip on him (John 10:28). Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves.

parallels.desc: more than five hundred at one time

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus came and said to them, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
All authority. He came near to them, doubters included, and spoke the fulfilment of Daniel 7:13–14, where the Son of Man is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples should serve him. The devil offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world if he would worship him (4:8–9); Jesus refused, went the way of the cross, and now receives all authority from the Father. There is no area of life, no nation, no power, outside his rule.

Go therefore. Because Jesus has all authority, the disciples can go everywhere; the mission rests on his authority, not theirs. Make disciples is the one main verb, and going, baptising and teaching serve it, though go carries the force of a command too. Not just converts, but learners and followers of Jesus who trust and obey him for life.

Of all nations. The mission that began with the lost sheep of Israel (10:5–6; 15:24) now goes to the whole world. The promise to Abraham, that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), is fulfilled. The Gospel that began with the son of Abraham (1:1), with magi at his cradle and a centurion at his cross, ends with the nations given to him.

Baptising them. Baptism is the sign of entry into Christ’s people, union with him, and the washing away of sin (Acts 2:38; Romans 6:3–4). The word means to dip or immerse, and Baptists have generally practised immersion as the fullest picture of being buried and raised with Christ (Romans 6:4). Union with Christ means that believers are joined to him by the Spirit through faith, so that his death and risen life are counted as theirs and begin to work in them (Romans 6:5–11). Baptism does not create that union; it is its sign, given to those who already believe.

In the name. “Name” is singular: one name, one God, in three persons. This is one of the clearest statements of the Trinity in the New Testament. A mere man could not put his own name between the name of God the Father and the name of God the Spirit. The risen Jesus does, and in one sentence gives the church the doctrine it would spend centuries learning to confess: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the same in substance, equal in power and glory.

One name, three persons. In the name of is found in ordinary commercial language of the time for transfer into someone’s ownership: a sum paid into a man’s name became his. To be baptised into this name is to be handed over to the triune God and marked as his: the Father’s adopted child, the Son’s redeemed sheep, the Spirit’s temple.

Why does Acts baptise in the name of Jesus? Every baptism in Acts that names a name is done in the name of Jesus Christ or of the Lord Jesus (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5). Some have concluded that Jesus’ words here were composed later by the church; others, in the opposite direction, hold that only the words in the name of Jesus may lawfully be spoken over the water. Both miss what Luke is doing. He is not recording a liturgy; he is telling you whose baptism it was. That was a live question in a world full of washings: proselyte baths for Gentile converts, the ritual washings of the devout, and John’s baptism of repentance. When Paul meets men at Ephesus who had received John’s baptism, the issue he settles is exactly that one, and Luke reports the outcome in the same shorthand: they were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:1–5). The phrase distinguishes Christian baptism from every rival. To be baptised into Christ is to be baptised into the triune God, which is why Luke’s shorthand and Matthew’s fuller wording sit side by side without strain. As for the suggestion that these words were added later: every Greek manuscript of Matthew contains the triune name; not one lacks it. The early historian Eusebius sometimes quoted the verse in a shorter form, in my name, but he also quoted the full wording, and no copy of Matthew has the shorter one. So if you were baptised with these words, or with the name of Jesus, let no one unsettle you. What matters is not which formula was pronounced over you but the God into whose name you were given.

Where Christians differ: baptism. Paedobaptists baptise the children of believers, seeing them as part of the covenant community to be discipled. Credobaptists baptise those who are made disciples, by profession of faith (Acts 2:41; 8:12, 36–38). This commentary’s view: credobaptist, held charitably: those who are discipled and profess faith are baptised. Christians who differ on this are still brothers and sisters, under the same commission.

Who should be baptised? Christians who baptise infants appeal to the household baptisms in Acts (16:15, 33), to the link Paul draws between baptism and circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12), and to the covenant sign given to Abraham’s children (Genesis 17). The more likely reading is that baptism is for disciples. The command runs in order: make disciples, baptise them, teach them. In Acts, those baptised are those who received the word (Acts 2:41), and no baptism in the New Testament is said to be of an infant.

Honouring our paedobaptist brothers. This is a disagreement within the family, and it should be held that way. Those who baptise infants do it out of a serious conviction that God’s promise is to believers and their children (Acts 2:39), and they pray and teach for those children to own the faith. Many of the church’s finest teachers, Calvin among them, have held this view, and Baptists owe them a great debt. Both sides agree that baptism does not save by itself, that faith in Christ is necessary, and that children of believers should be brought up in the Lord. Argue the point from Scripture with conviction, and then work side by side in the same commission.

Is this commission for every Christian? Yes. The promise that follows reaches to the end of the age, so the command does too. The apostles’ foundational role has ended, but the whole church is sent, and every believer has a share, by going, sending, praying and teaching.

Is it not arrogant to tell every nation to follow Jesus? Arrogance would be a message that says, be like us. But the commission does not send the church to spread a culture or to win by force. It sends servants with news of a King who died for his enemies, to people of every language, and the church has been at its healthiest where it has taken root in many cultures at once (Revelation 7:9). The disciples were sent to teach, not to coerce. And humility does not mean keeping good news to yourself. If Christ really holds all authority and really gives life, the unloving thing would be to say nothing.

So what does making disciples look like for an ordinary believer? Mostly it is ordinary. Pray by name for people who do not know Christ. Speak of him naturally and honestly with family, friends, neighbours and colleagues, and invite them to read the Bible or come to church with you. Support missionaries and gospel work with money and prayer, and consider whether God may be sending you further. Within the church, help a younger believer grow: read Scripture together, pray together, show him how to follow Jesus in daily life. And bring up your children in the faith. Disciples are made one person at a time, over years, by people who are themselves still learning.

Is it fair that people who have never heard of Jesus cannot be saved? Scripture is clear that salvation is through Christ alone, received by faith (John 14:6; Acts 4:12), and that all people are without excuse before God (Romans 1:20). That is exactly why the commission is urgent: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? (Romans 10:14). God is just, and no one will be condemned for what they did not know but for the sin they did commit. Infants dying in infancy who are elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest that child in the hands of a Father far kinder than we are; David, bereaved, expected to go to his son (2 Samuel 12:23). The right response to this truth is not to argue with God but to go, send and pray.

For worship. The kingdoms Satan offered him for a bow, the Father gave him for a cross, and the nations are being gathered, one disciple at a time, to sing to the Lamb who by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: Disciples of every nation are to be baptized into the one name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

parallels.desc: to the end of the earth
all peoples, nations and languages should serve him

verseByVerse.quote: "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To observe all. Not only to know, but to keep, to guard, to put into practice. All: the whole of Jesus’ teaching, including the hard parts. Disciple-making is not the transfer of information but a lifelong learning to live differently. That learning goes on in the power of the Spirit into whose name they were baptised, by disciples who never keep it all, resting on the One who did and whose obedience is counted theirs (Romans 5:19).

The curriculum. Matthew’s Gospel is organised around five great blocks of Jesus’ teaching (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18, 24–25), each closed with the same formula. Now the disciples are to pass it on. The last command is to teach everything he commanded, and the reader has been holding the manual the entire time.

I am with you always. The promise that makes the mission possible. The Gospel began with the promise of Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23); it closes with the man himself saying it in the first person: I am with you. Everything in between is the demonstration.

Every word chosen. I am: a statement about now. With you: not watching from a distance. Always, literally all the days: every single day, including the dull ones, the humiliating ones, and the day nobody wants to think about.

To the end of the age. Until he returns (13:39–40; 24:3). The promise runs exactly as long as the mission does. There is no point at which the church is sent and he is not there, and no missionary, persecuted believer or lonely Christian is ever alone.

How can Jesus be with us if he has ascended to heaven? In his human body he is in heaven, at the Father’s right hand, until he returns (Acts 1:11; 3:21). But as the eternal Son of God he is everywhere present, and he dwells with his people by his Holy Spirit, whom he sent for this very purpose (John 14:16–18, 23). That is why he could say it was better for them that he go away (John 16:7). His presence is not a feeling that comes and goes. It is a fact, promised by him, whether you sense it or not. He meets his people especially in his word, in prayer, in the gathered church and at his table.

The end of Matthew. The Gospel ends not with an ascension scene or a farewell, but with a promise of presence and a mission still going on. There is no departure scene, because the last thing this Gospel wants in the reader’s eye is Christ leaving. He is left standing there, mid-promise, with his people, which is exactly the situation the church has been in ever since. The commission is now ours.

On a Tuesday. Say it to yourself on the hardest day this week: he is with me, all the days, and this is one of them.

For worship. The child of Bethlehem, the crucified King, the risen Lord has not left his people. Immanuel. God with us. Still. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, for ever and ever. Amen (Ephesians 3:21).

parallels.desc: I will not leave you as orphans

28.theology: The resurrection as the foundation. Matthew 28 makes the resurrection the ground of mission, authority and presence. The resurrection is not an extra added to the cross but its vindication: he was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25).
28.examples:
Then: Eleven ordinary men, fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot, were sent to make disciples of all nations. They had no army, money or standing; they had a risen Lord and his promise. Within a generation the gospel had reached Rome. The mustard seed was becoming a tree.

Now: The commission has not been withdrawn. Every church and every believer stands in that Galilean company, some worshipping, some wavering, all sent, under the same authority and with the same promise.
